articles.text: Residents are invited to participate in a special joint study session of the Planning Commission and Housing Advisory Committee tonight, September 29, at 5:30 p.m. Commissioners and Committee members will receive information about the upcoming housing element update. The study session will be virtual and available to viewers on Zoom. The housing element is a required section of the city’s general plan and must assess the city’s housing needs and conditions of housing stock. The current 2015-2023 housing element of the Piedmont General Plan was adopted by City Council in 2014. Planning Director Kevin Jackson is leading the next cycle update of the housing plan for 2023-2031, assisted by Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell, the project manager for the Housing Element Update program. The city is tasked by the state with establishing a roadmap for accommodating projected housing unit demand to reach its Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) over the next eight years. Citywide housing-related goals, objectives, policies, and programs will be discussed. Residents are invited to ask questions and learn more about the process and policies in place. For information on how to watch and participate in the meeting, visit https://piedmont.ca.gov/ government/city_news___notif ications/housing _element_ update_study_session. A detailed agenda for tonight’s meeting can be found on the city’s website by following that link. For more information, email Piedmontishome@piedmont. ca.gov. articles.text: Before entering the ministry, I spent nearly 20 years owning and operating a construction business in Boston, Massachusetts. Some of my contracts were for new construction but a fair amount of my business involved renovation. As a result, I have always seen demolition as part of the process of creating something better. For me, the dust, the piles of debris and the disruption of life don’t bother me because I know it can lead to a better future. As the pandemic rages on with yet another wave of destruction, there are also dangerous riptides of division tearing at the fabric of our country. Being so divided as we are, it seems almost impossible to imagine a future where we, as a society, actually live up to our name, The United States of America. But there is also the very real question of whether we have ever lived up to that name. The threat many feel of becoming a disenfranchised voter is nothing new. For instance, how could our ancestors ever describe our country as The United States of America while black and female citizens were denied a vote? As our narratives are all being brought into question it can feel profoundly chaotic, deeply disturbing and utterly depressing at times. Maybe

articles.text: The Alameda County Fair is the 7th largest in California. The beloved Alameda County Fair is welcoming guests back this fall for a week of family fun. The County Fair will take place October 22 through 31 in Pleasanton at the Alameda County Fairgrounds, located at 4501 Pleasanton Avenue. A plethora of events will transpire over the course of the fair, including the All-Alaskan Racing Pigs, musical events, carnival games, festival food, and a Live concerts will be performed at 8 p.m. nightly, showcasing a range of superstar and “We are so excited that the Fair is back to offer our community the safe, family fun that they’ve always enjoyed here,” said Jerome Hoban, CEO of the Alameda County Fairgrounds. The All-Alaskan Pig Race, a favorite feature of the fair, is returning this year. “We invite everyone to come out, come together, and have fun.” The Alameda County Fair is a local, self-sustaining, non-profit organization. The 2021 theme “Come Together” celebrates the revival of the fair and the community reuniting after nearly two years of COVID-19 related closures. The event will comply with all state and local health requirements. Guests are required to pre-purchase tickets online for specific dates, and due to capacity limitations, tickets are expected to sell quickly. Touch-less and cash-less systems for ticketing, parking, carnival, food and beverage purchases will be employed wherever feasible. Guests will be required to wear face masks while on the fairgrounds and have their temperature checked prior to entering. To purchase tickets, visit https:// annual.alamedacountyfair.com/. articles.text: The City of Piedmont was selected as a winner of one of the Institute for Local Government’s 2021 Beacon Spotlight Awards. Municipalities receive the award and recognition for sustainability efforts and community greenhouse gas reductions. The Institute for local Government’s (ILG) Beacon Program provides recognition and support for local agencies throughout California that are actively working to build more vibrant and sustainable communities. This is the first year the city has participated in the program. As a participant, the City of Piedmont receives technical assistance in collecting, reporting and tracking sustainability best practices, energy savings and greenhouse gas reductions; access to peer-topeer networking and educational events; and invitations to showcase sustainability leadership and agency achievements to a stateOf the four cities recognized for their collective greenhouse gas emissions reductions, Piedmont led the way with a 30% reduction, followed by Thousand Oaks at 28%, San Rafael at 27%, and Fremont at 26%. Piedmont also received a Gold level award for Agency Greenhouse Gas Reductions of 12%. The city made a commitment to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions five years ago. In 2016, Councilmembers joined the Compact of Mayors, a global coalition of city officials with the common goal of reducing their local greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The initial three-year commitment has led to the adoption of the Climate Action Plan (CAP), which sets a goal of reducing GHG emissions 40% below 2005 levels by 2030, and 80% below those levels by 2050. Programs that have contributed to progress toward CAP include reach codes, which require that new residential buildings and accessory dwelling units (ADUs) be outfitted with all-electric appliances, and a Home Energy Assessment Policy, now required when listing a property for sale, which helps buyers decide how to best improve a home’s energy use. The Induction Cooktop Lending program will loan residents an electric cooktop for free. It provides education to residents about the benefits of electrifying a kitchen.
articles.title: City earns award for sustainability efforts

articles.text: The City and Piedmont Connect’s Healthy Landscapes Committee are co-hosting a seminar via Zoom this Thursday, September 30, entitled “Living with Drought, By and For Piedmonters.” Piedmont Connect is a community environmental organization that supports resident initiatives and city efforts and policies for a sustainable future. The virtual event tomorrow will explore drought-related information and education and includes a panel of experts and city staff. Piedmont Parks Manager Nancy Kent will open the event, moderated by Piedmont resident and water expert Eileen White. An overview will be provided by Suzanne Bontempo, a professional horticulturist and environmental educator. Through the Marin County stormwater pollution prevention program, Our Water Our World, Bontempo brings awareness between pesticides and water quality while guiding people to reduce pesticide usage. The panel will discuss how they have transformed their home’s landscaping to chemical-free, water-efficient landscapes that support a range of plants and pollinators. The seminar will provide Piedmont residents an opportunity to offer comments and ask questions about the changes they have made to reduce their water usage and create healthy landscapes. The Zoom seminar will be held from 7 p.m. to 8:15 p.m. The link for the seminar is on Piedmont Connect’s website: https://www.piedmontconnect.org/.
articles.title: Piedmont Connect, City to host draught seminar tomorrow

articles.text: A research report on homelessness was presented at the recent Fall Reception of East Bay Republican Women. The featured speaker was Mary Theroux, SVP of the Independent Institute, Oakland’s non-profit, non-partisan public policy research and educational organization. She presented her extensive research on the causes and solutions to the homelessness problem. She suggested that childhood trauma is at the root of these dysfunctions, and they will not be solved by housing alone. She questioned the wisdom of the current policy, which focuses exclusively on giving brand-new units to the homeless. She described multi-tiered solutions that have worked in other states, offering levels of treatment and accommodation, while eliminating the option of sleeping on the street.
articles.title: Republican Women host talk on homelessness

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department has a brand new addition to its lobby: a three-shelf free book exchange – “Little Free Library” – specifically for young readers age 3 through 11. In the same vein as other traditional free libraries, interested residents may take a book to read or leave one for someone else to find. The “Little Free Library” book exchange relies on volunteer “stewards” to construct, install, and maintain book exchange boxes - they are traditionally placed in front of houses and are supplied through donations from neighborhoods. Officers April Fitzgerald and Nicole Casalnuovo came up with the idea to create a PPD lobby library; and Fitzgerald, a former English teacher, chose to provide the reading exchange specifically for young readers. Officer Tyler Petit and Mo Alrahimi, the Public Works Department’s talented Can-Do man, designed and built the attractive bookcase. “We love it when kids stop by and thought it would be a great way to encourage reading and bring kids to the department so we can connect,” Fitzgerald said. “Even though I’m not in the classroom anymore, that love for teaching and reading doesn’t leave you.” The Police Department’s central location provides for a nice respite to stop and read a book on the way to or back from the park, she added. Passersby can come at any time to drop off a donation - series books, picture books, cardboard books and pop-up books for toddlers are especially welcome. “We’re excited to see what people may bring. My kids have tons and tons of books. So many people have books that they’d like to share, and it’s really a blessing to re-use them,” Fitzgerald said. Kids are encouraged to pick up a reading log when they visit. Fill your child’s reading log with their favorite books and they may even win a prize on their next visit to the department. “It definitely provides a great incentive,” Fitzgerald said with a smile. Stop by the Piedmont Police Department lobby to read or donate a book.
articles.title: Donations sought for young readers age 3 - 11

articles.text: Substitute teachers in Piedmont School District received an early Christmas present. At the September 22 school board meeting, they were given a raise from $140 daily to $200, a 43-percent bump in their base pay. The raise aims to make Piedmont more competitive in attracting substitutes, which have been harder to come by in the last two years. The per diem for substitute teachers in 18 public school districts in Alameda County ranges from $130 to $300. Only Dublin was below Piedmont at $130 per day. In comparison, Albany, with roughly 3600 students, compared with Piedmont’s 2600, pays substitute teachers $300 per day, Berkeley pays $225, and Oakland pays $190. The number of new substitute teachers in California has decreased significantly in recent years. The California Commission on Teacher Credentialing issued 64,000 substitute teaching permits statewide for the 2018- 2019 school year. Only 47,000 were issued for the current school year. school year, 13,558 California teachers retired statewide, an increase of 1,000 retirees from the previous year. Fewer teachers and fewer substitutes available has increased the demand for all teachers. In a memorandum to the school board, Booker stated, “Piedmont Unified, like many districts across the state, [is] struggling to secure qualified substitutes. This results in teachers substituting for their colleagues during their prep periods... In the long-term, this has a negative effect on teacher morale and is more expensive to the District.” The school board vote on September 22 was 4-0, with board member Hilary Copper abstaining because she is a substitute teacher. Booker made a plea to the public: “Community members out there, please, please, please connect with us to learn how to become substitutes. We can use you, for sure.” PHS computer teacher Flint Christensen has volunteered to help advise prospective substitute teachers on the process. He can be reached at fchristensen@ piedmont.k12.ca.us. Havens, Beach, and Wildwood. Identity and affinity groups of small cohorts led by 1 to 2 high school mentors. Groups are cohorted by age and cultural & ethnic affinity. Age appropriate fun for young students with an emphasis on community building. Students get to know their high school mentors as well as each other. - Mentors are creative & committed volunteers trained to use a circle conversation format. - Sessions are monitored by our two adult coordinators. - Mentors are given feedback at the conclusion of each session and attend training sessions to share resources and build their skills. - Community service credit is available to reward mentors for their commitment to this program. 30-40 minute bi-weekly in-person or virtual meetings (depending on comfort level) either after school or on weekends. articles.text: If you have a middle schooler interested in helping their community, I highly recommend Piedmont Service Club (PSC). Often, community service is limited to high school-aged kids, but PSC is for middle schoolers and their parents who are interested in community service. PSC allows its members to lead the club with oversight and support from club advisor Ken Li and parents. Its members get a head start with community service and help the larger community. Since PSC is the middle school arm of the well-established Piedmont Community Service Crew (for high school aged youth), PSC is a great way to gain leadership experience, meet new people, mingle with older role models, and try out different service events. Events that have taken place in the past include cooking for the homeless, building tiny houses, doing local environmental cleanups, trail maintenance, craft projects, and plant nursery work. The recent “Make it Home” event took place for the first time. We refinished used furniture, organized a furniture warehouse and assembled a “kit” of home furnishings for a refugee family. Other beneficiaries include young adults aging out of foster care and Amy Aubrecht learns some refinishing skills while volunteering at Make it Home, an organization that helps formerly homeless people find a place to live. being placed into their first permanent home but empty of furnishings. An amazing aspect of PSC is how the members create and help run service projects. As someone who was in PSC for two years and now helps run it, one of my favorite things was the flexibility available. There is no minimum participation requirement and one can choose to attend an event whenever they have time. Piedmont Service Crew was such a great experience and taught me so much about leadership and what it takes to manage events. If you and your child are interested in learning more about PSC, visit the web page at https:// www.pcservicecrew.org/psc. For more information, contact Ken Li at 510-410-4283 (Ken.I.Li@sbcglobal.net). Bruno Banuelos is the former co-president of the Piedmont Community Service Crew.

articles.text: There are a variety of parent language styles that come into play when toddlers are learning how to talk. The way we speak to our children may impact their language learning. Over the years researchers have studied various parent language styles, and some of the conclusions and recommendations are changing. One style which has shown to be beneficial, and has stood the test of time, is repetition of language input to the child. That is, repeated exposure to new words and sentences is key for language learning. Children need to hear new words and sentences repeatedly, and in multiple situations, before they understand, remember and eventually try to use them. One style which was historically thought to be beneficial is telegraphic speech, where the parent uses speech that includes key words that carry most of the meaning in a sentence but removes the grammatical words and endings. For example, “Daddy go out”, “in box”). Early research suggested that parental use of telegraphic speech may benefit children who are learning to talk as it may be easier for children to imitate and learn language when they hear only the key words. But this prevailing wisdom is being challenged. Newer studies are suggesting a different scenario with regard to parent language modeling. When looking at grammatical (grammatical language models include the small grammatical words and word endings) vs. telegraphic parent language styles, recent research concludes that children can imitate short, grammatical sentences as easily as they can imitate telegraphic speech. Furthermore, grammatical sentences are not more difficult for children to understand than telegraphic speech and likely offers an advantage for language learning. Parents who provide short, grammatically correct sentences to their children may be providing valuable clues as to what words mean and how they can be used (for example, “Daddy is going out.”, “in the box”). By including grammatical markers such as “the” the child is learning to pair articles with nouns, and by including grammatical markers such as “-ing” the child is learning to pair word endings with verbs. So how do parents optimally approach talking to children who are learning to talk? First, we say a bit less, keeping our sentences short but grammatical. Next, we use vocal stress (think: a little louder and more animated) to make key words stand out to highlight the salient message. We slow our speech a bit. Speaking slightly (only slightly) slower than you would when speaking to an adult allows the child time to process what you are saying. Make sure to maintain your natural speaking rhythm. Fourth, it is always a good strategy to incorporate visuals when talking to children who are learning to talk. Showing the child that a word means via pointing, using a gesture or an action, or holding up an object or picture enhances language learning. And finally, we provide repetition of our language models over time and across contexts/situations to build children’s conceptualization of language and efficacy of communication. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C . of heart and spirit.

articles.text: Six students from Piedmont High School recently were named National Merit Scholarship semifinalists for 2022, joining a group of students throughout the U.S. with the highest PSAT scores. The students are Aaron Drumm, Charlotte Levy, Anabel Loucks, Chiara Lundin, Charlie Olcott and Robert Sylvia. They are among 16,000 semifinalists and were chosen from a pool of over 1,500,000 high school seniors taking the PSAT. The students will be considered for 7,500 National Merit Scholarships worth a combined $30 million. “It’s very cool to be named a semifinalist along with people that I know and have grown up with. Through PHS courses I have learned how intriguing the functions of the body at the microscopic level are. I hope someday to do research in a field such as genetics or microbiology,” said Lundin. To become a finalist, the student and high school must submit a detailed scholarship application information, academic record, extracurricular activities and awards. They also must submit an essay and earn scores on the SAT comparable to the PSAT. National Merit Scholarship winners will be announced in April 2022.
articles.title: PHS has 6 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists

One style which was historically thought to be beneficial is telegraphic speech, where the parent uses speech that includes key words that carry most of the meaning in a sentence but removes the grammatical words and endings. For example, “Daddy go out”, “in box”). Early research suggested that parental use of telegraphic speech may benefit children who are learning to talk as it may be easier for children to imitate and learn language when they hear only the key words. But this prevailing wisdom is being challenged. Newer studies are suggesting a different scenario with regard to parent language modeling. When looking at grammatical (grammatical language models include the small grammatical words and word endings) vs. telegraphic parent language styles, recent research concludes that children can imitate short, grammatical sentences as easily as they can imitate telegraphic speech. Furthermore, grammatical sentences are not more difficult for children to understand than telegraphic speech and likely offers an advantage for language learning. Parents who provide short, grammatically correct sentences to their children may be providing valuable clues as to what words mean and how they can be used (for example, “Daddy is going out.”, “in the box”). By including grammatical markers such as “the” the child is learning to pair articles with nouns, and by including grammatical markers such as “-ing” the child is learning to pair word endings with verbs. So how do parents optimally approach talking to children who are learning to talk? First, we say a bit less, keeping our sentences short but grammatical. Next, we use vocal stress (think: a little louder and more animated) to make key words stand out to highlight the salient message. We slow our speech a bit. Speaking slightly (only slightly) slower than you would when speaking to an adult allows the child time to process what you are saying. Make sure to maintain your natural speaking rhythm. Fourth, it is always a good strategy to incorporate visuals when talking to children who are learning to talk. Showing the child that a word means via pointing, using a gesture or an action, or holding up an object or picture enhances language learning. And finally, we provide repetition of our language models over time and across contexts/situations to build children’s conceptualization of language and efficacy of communication. articles.text: In spite of dry weather and parched vegetation, a full reservoir at Del Valle Regional greeted 37 Scouts and Scout leaders from Piedmont Troop 15 the weekend of September 18-19. Located 10 miles south of Livermore, the park provided excellent swimming and kayaking with the daytime temperature in the low 70’s. Julian Procos said kayaking was his favorite activity, while Davey Ackerman chose fishing and working on advancement requirements. After putting on their backpacks and hiking to the campsite, they set up tents. “It was an amazing camping trip where I learned to set up a tent,” raved Connor Fredericks. “My favorite part was hanging out with my troop. I loved getting to know all of their awesome and unique personalities,” said Christiane Zuber. There was time for play and learning some basic Scout skills. Dinner was prepared from ingredients requiring no refrigeration as a way for Scouts to get used to the type of meals they will prepare on an extended backpacking trip next summer. “My favorite part was cooking food at the end of the day”, said Thalay Visessonchoke. “This was my first time making a meal outdoors with boys and girls about my age”, stated Joaquin Fierro, who has been in Scouting for one month. “I learned how to make a campf ire”, exclaimed Gianluca Richmond. “Making a fire in the evening was my favorite part,” echoed Thomas Ero. During a campfire with songs and toasted marshmallows, a waning gibbous moon emerged from feathery clouds. In the night, a lone coyote barked loudly but briefly. Three turkey vultures glided overhead at dawn to a hillside for leftovers. Del Valle Reservoir provides a refreshingly cool place to swim. Scouts examine a deer skeleton found near the reservoir.

articles.text: Nº 41, in a biweekly series L’Arc de Triomphe, Wrapped is fully on display, a draped bonanza from the artist Christo. Traffic is blocked off at Place Charles de Gaulle, allowing Parisians to stroll the magnificent Boulevard Champs-Elysée during two weekends. The revered Arc de Triomphe is impossible not to gawk at, and now draped in shimmering silvery blue and belted by red rope, it’s an awesome sight. Everyone is puzzling about the near-impossible feat of draping the monument, and, moreover, the question of why. Smart phone-holders are hoisting themselves, precariously, onto street-barriers for a view above people’s heads and “selfies.” Under the changing light of etched puffy clouds moving against a brilliant blue sky, the crowd draws closer to the disorienting view of the monument they’ve known their entire lives. The Arc, the photogenic icon every tourist snaps a picture of, is dolled up in Christo’s favorite Rope workers hanging the silvery blue fabric. go-to fabric, a lightweight polypropylene moving sensuously in the breeze, and reflecting between light and dark under the clouds playfully changing the fabric’s color and folds. This installation, completed posthumously, is his last wrap. The artist known as Christo passed away last year at age 84, prior to the Arc installation. Born in communist Bulgaria in 1935 he left to become an artist in the 50s and 60s, and met his wife and fellow artist Jeanne-Claude. Together they joined the hippest artists abandoning easel painting, pushing boundaries from paint and canvas to radically different forms and materials; elevating light and movement, and techno-crafting, to burst through art’s third dimension. Christo, whose full name was Christo Vladimirov Javacheff, fit into the new Contemporary movement with his novel devotion to being a wrappist or wrapman. He celebrated community and freedom, where he imagined gigantism seemingly impossible to build, but achieved it, however fleeting and temporary. Christo L’Arc de Triomphe, a gift from Christo to Paris. who frequently cited Paris as his favorite city, next to New York, was well accepted before L’Arc de Triomphe, Wrapped. His Pont Neuf Bridge and 44 Street Lamps proved wildly successful in 1985, but he’d spent a decade trying to persuade Paris officials about Pont Neuf, literally the “new” bridge built in 1607, and in daily use by cars and pedestrians. President François Mitterrand cut through the French bureaucracy, and several hundred French laborers signed on, including frogmen, alpinists, and craftsmen of ancient guilds. Fabric has fascinated artists through the ages, and in sculpture, paintings, frescoes or reliefs, artists fashioned fabrics’ folds and pleats using wood, marble, bronze, or plaster. Christo experimented with lacquer to get the desired pleated folds, and with Pont Neuf, he and JeanneClaude draped it with polypropylene fabric, finding the ideal traits for meticulous dressmaker finery that became his standard. The couple’s vision for wrapping Berlin’s Parliament began in 1971, when they and fellow artisans battled for permission through the 70s, 80s, and 90s. Finally, in 1995, they wrapped the Reichstag, the couple’s most important joint project. She died in 2009. French President Emmanuel Macron attended the dedication of L’Arc de Triomphe, Wrapped and remarked, “I think what we believe in is that the wildest of dreams must be possible.” The wrapping of a monument of such historical, military, and national symbolism as an “artistic adventure makes the French people extraordinarily proud.” Wrapping is a complex endeavor, both technical and logistical, where the premise is to do the impossible with precision and the highest degree of perfection, and to amaze the public. The chosen monument (or locality) is contained, its feat celebrated, and then it’s released from the wrappings so painstakingly that it appears untouched. Understandably, this performance art is not meaningful to everyone. A few critics are dismissive as a modern-day folly. Materials used in vast quantities are wasteful environmentally; but Christo recycles most of the materials and declines to fundraise or take public money: the costs are parlayed from his own private fortune; and the Arc is believed to cost €14 million. Inspiration sparked 60 years ago when Christo dwelled in a small room on Avenue Foch with a faraway view to the Arc de Triomphe. The stately arch commissioned by Napoléon in 1806 as a tribute to his military conquests and the French la gloire blended with the agony of war inspired Christo to sketch the wrapping. Logistics for L’Arc de Triomphe, Wrapped began in 2017; and last year, by way of introducChristo’s drawing dating to 1961. Christo and his Parisian wife Jeanne-Claude in Central Park, 2005.

articles.text: Photos by Nancy Brahm Antonio Rivera scored had a hat trick against Lick-Wilmerding. Piedmont‘s boys’ water polo team thrashed Lick-Wilmerding in San Francisco, 17-7, on Thursday, September 23, to improve their record to 11-3 entering the final month of the season. Sophomore Peter Krumins opened the game with three goals (hat trick) in the first quarter, followed by senior Antonio Rivera with a hat trick in the second quarter. Rivera, the team’s scoring leader, is a three-year varsity starter. He’s a mobile player in coach John Savage’s system, often swimming on the perimeter or making cuts to the interior for open shots or passes. “For me, it’s doing whatever I can to get open, whether it’s swimming in front of my guy, cutting him off, or pushing off – just trying to get open any way I can, either facilitating the ball or shooting,” said Rivera. Krumins, in his second year on varsity, is a two-sport athlete with baseball as the spring sport. His dad, Rik Krumins, was an All-American with Cal in the 90s, and is on the U.S. Water Polo Masters 45+ Team. He has been an assistant coach on Savage’s staff for several years, and runs the JV program. Asked about the younger Krumins, River said, “He’s a gamer. He goes 100 percent in the pool. He’s filled in the Hole Set spot, and when we need someone in the middle to score goals, he’s the guy. He has a lot of experience with water polo and has learned about the sport at a young age. “Peter has a lot of tricks that his dad taught him,” noted Rivera. Sophomore Peter Krumins scored 3 goals in the first quarter hat trick against Lick. Game Recap The Highlanders dismantled Lick early, taking a 5-1 after one quarter, and expanding it to 11-2 by halftime and 14-5 heading into the final quarter. Lick scored two goals in the waning minutes of the game. PHS opened the game at 3-0 Murray Davis scored two goals in Piedmont’s big win. on goals by Murray Davis, Shane Miller, and Krumins, who added two more with 1:26 left in the quarter. Rivera got on the scoreboard one minute into the second quarter, and George Stein followed with Piedmont’s seventh goal 30 seconds later. Rivera netted his second goal with 4:42 left in the half, then made it 9-2 with 4:17 to go. PHS closed the half with goals from Griffin Stein with 3:27 remaining and Daniel Banin with 30 seconds left. In the third quarter, the Highlander gave up two goals before Miller got on the board at 3:13, and then Davis added the team’s 13th goal at 2:36. Declan Linnane made it 14-5 with 10 seconds remaining. Senior Julian Scherman scored 30 seconds into the fourth quarter, then Farris Saffouri made it 16-6 with 4:30 remaining. Stein scored Piedmont’s last goal with 3:02 left. articles.text: Photo by Brian Mahany Emma Eisemon won 6-0, 6-2 at No. 3 doubles with Cecilia Defazio in a match with Berkeley. She also double-bageled Tennyson’s No. 3 singles starter, 6-0, 6-0. Piedmont’s tennis team soled past league opponent Tennyson 7-0 last Tuesday, September 21, but lost a close 4-3 match with Berkeley two days later back home at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on September 23. The math with the Yellowjackets featured the No. 3 doubles duo of freshman Emma Eisemon and sophomore Cecilia Defazio, who won 6-0, 6-2. Both players have taken on important roles for the team in both doubles and singles. It was their third win as a doubles team. Eisemon, meanwhile, also won 6-0, 6-0 at No. 3 singles against Tennyson. “It’s so nice to feel like you’re improving quickly and helping out the team,” said Eisemon. “We can rely on each other, that’s a big reason why we’re such great partners. We go out there and trust each other’s judgments and communicate really well on the court,” “It feels like we’re getting better,” confirmed Defazio, who was on the JV team last spring. “Emma and I have really good teamwork and call out the ball to make sure we’re in the right spot.” Their pairing is characterized by Defazio’s length and consistent hitting out of the back court, while Eisemon provides a shift and quick presence in front of the net, a key combination found in many of Jim Landes’ teams throughout the years. “I’ve definitely improved on my serving, I feel like I can hit it a lot harder,” added Defazio. “I think I’ve gotten better at volleying, but they things I want to keep working on. “Being aggressive at the net is really key as well. I’d like to work on my serving consistency – it’s a little off and on sometimes,” mentioned Eisemon. 4-3 loss to Berkeley Eisemon and Defazio at No. 3 doubles were the first to win a match against Berkeley. The Yellowjackets took the lead after a 6-4, 6-4 win at No. 2 doubles against Mara LaForte and Rose Siemers, and a barnburner of a match in which Michael Bini lost 7-6 (7-5), 7-6 (7-1) at No. 3 singles. Anne Jumper lost 6-3, 6-0 at No. 2 singles to make it 3-1 Berkeley, but Annika Gilliland brought home a 6-2, 6-2 win at No. 4 single. The No. 1 doubles pair of Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany rolled to a 6-3, 6-4 win to tie the match at 3-3. The final match of the day was No. 1 singles. Not surprisingly it went to three sets before Berkeley’s Maya Curry edged out Bridgette McEfee 6-3, 3-6, 6-2. Her win alongside Eisemon was their third as a doubles team.

articles.text: The girls’ golf team played credibly in a tri-school match on September 21, but finished third in a match with Bishop O’Dowd and reigning league champ Alameda. In a match played at the Metro Links Golf Course near the Oakland Airport, Almeda won with a nine-hole score of 208 – averaging 41 strokes per player – and Piedmont had a team score of 252. O’Dowd was second with a 224. Castro Valley, whose athletic program is suffering, could not field the required five players, and forfeited to the other three schools. “The top three teams in the league mixed it up and we held our own despite the losses,” said PHS coach Howard Oliver. “The measuring stick for high school golf is a team score of 200. All of us are working to get a little better each time out; that’s our motivation,” Metro Links is a par 36 for the front and back nine holes and is noted for its water hazards on the second, fifth, and sixth holes. Wind off the Bay can be disruptive, but the course itself is wide open with only a few trees lining the fairways. Junior Dabney Warner finished with a team-low 44, while freshman Mei Assalian was nextbest with a 47. “Warner was our low medalist, and our freshman, Mei Assalian, had a great round,” said Oliver. Dabney Warner shot a 44 at the Metro Links Golf Course against Bishop O’Dowd and Alameda. Piedmont’s other scoring golfers were Aryana Fisher (51), Mackenzie Seto-Nguyen (54), and Rahimeen Shah (56). NEXT UP Piedmont (3-3) will compete in a 4-school tournament on September 30 with Alameda, Arroyo (San Lorenzo), and San Leandro. The match will be played at the Chuck Corica Course at Alameda Gold Course on Monday, October 4 at 3:30 p.m. Freshman Mei Assalian shot a 47 for the Highlanders. Mackenzie Seto-Nguyen came away with a 54 at Metro Links.

articles.text: Odessa Dando defends for Piedmont. Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team came away with a mighty 19-7 win over Lick-Wilmerding in San Francisco last Wednesday, September 22. It helped take the sting out of a 13-4 loss to Castro Valley the previous day. Of f icial st at s agai n st Lick-Wilmerding were not provided and attendance was not permitted. The Tuesday match with Castro Valley was played at Cal State East Bay in Hayward. It was a test of two programs competing fiercely for the top spot in the Western Alameda County Conference. PHS defeated the Trojans 7-6 on September 11. Last spring in the league tournament, they beat Castro Valley 9-3 for third-place in final league standings. On September 21, the Highlanders opened with a 2-0 lead before the first quarter ended in a 3-3 tie. At halftime, CV held a 6-4 lead. They went on to score d three more goals in the third quarter and added four more in the final period. Junior leader Rosie Feldman opened with a hat trick in the first quarter, starting with a l goal from mid-pool two minutes into the game. She hit a shot from the perimeter with 2:45 left in the quarter and scored her third goal in the period on an angled shot with 20 seconds left. But Castro Valley then pounced, with goals at 5:43, 4:42, and 2:27 to go ahead 6-3. Frankie Broening scored Piedmont’s fourth goal with 44 seconds on the clock, taking a high arcing pass from Odessa Dando. Macie Gard had one last shot for the Goalie Elizabeth Ethington looks for and outlet pass. Frankie Broening (left) swims down a ball. Highlanders with four seconds left before halftime, but her shot clanged off of the crossbar. In the second half, the Trojans added a breakaway goal with 5:45 to go in the third quarter, then increased it to 8-4 with a minute later. They added a ninth goal with 1:20 on the clock. articles.text: The leaves are changing colors, and school is back in session, each a confirmation that it is now Fall. From June until late August, Hiking with Jon spanned nearly 40 miles through seven locations. For the condensed version we start with Oakland’s small treasures of the Bridgeview Trolls and Huckleberry Botanic, make our way to Alamere Falls and Muir Beach in Marin, and finish with three destinations near Lake Tahoe – Horsetail Falls, Emerald Bay, and Squaw Peak. The trolls of Bridgeview Trail (June 23 issue) A 0.7 mile out-and-back, 1.4 mile round trip hike in the Oakland Hills provide whimsical thrills for kids, dog walkers. Those who are young at heart will appreciate its collection of handcrafted rustic trolls hiding along the trail and on trees. It provides slightly less than 200 feet of elevation gain, making it a perfect spot for seniors and families with children. Located with trailheads on Bridgeview Drive or Monterey Boulevard near the Montclair Golf Course, the walk is great for all ages, with well over 20 trolls waiting to be spotted by alert hikers. Several rope swings are there for kids to enjoy. Its uniqueness makes it a popular destination, especially on weekends. Even on a Monday morning, we saw 34 hikers on the narrow trail. Huckleberry Botanic (July 7 issue) This Oakland-hills treasure is noted for its year-round display of blossoming flowers along its easy 2.4 mile loop. Its narrow path with informative panels gives visitors an in depth look at an assortment of ferns, California Staff Photos More than 20 handcrafted trolls on Bridgeview Trail in the Oakland Hills make it a popular hiking destination. Even in July, in the middle of summer, water was flowing at the popular Alamere Falls tidefall. Bay Laurels, Manzanita, monkey flowers, and other foliage. On a sunny Saturday in July, we passed by 54 people. Alamere Falls – the long way (July 14 issue) This hiker tested his legs with the 5.5 mile hike from the Olema Valley Trailhead to the Wildcat Camp of the Pt. Reyes National Seashore, and then took the 1-mile trek to Alamere Falls. It involved 1,200 feet in elevation Hiking from Tennessee Valley Beach in Marin County to Muir Beach you can have a pint and a bite to eat at the historic Pelican Inn for a bite. Horsetail Falls is a four-mile round trip hike in Desolation Wilderness accessible from Highway 50 before entering South Lake Tahoe. It’s a popular swimming hole for families and locals. gain. The normal route to Alamere Falls – the popular tidefall near Bolinas – is 4.5 mile hike from the Palomarin Trailhead, leading to a nine-mile round trip. Tennessee Valley, Muir Beach, & Pelican Inn (July 21) The Post took the trail from Tennessee Valley Beach in Marin County to Muir Beach and the Pelican Inn in July – a strenuous, delicious eight-mile day. Oysters and a classic British pint at the Pelican Inn – not far from Mill Valley – proved to be bracing in the middle of a long day of hiking. The hike along the coast of the ocean requires some sharp ascending and descending portions on the Coastal Trail, with over 1,000 feet in elevation. The Fox Trail is more like a 500-foot gain. For an easier hike (and miss views of the ocean). Fox Trail is the choice. The Post passed 66 people on the mile from the Tennessee Valley Trailhead to the Coastal Fire Road, another 75 people before reaching Muir Beach, but only 27 on the trek back using the less popular Fox Trail. Horsetail Falls (August 11 issue) Horsetail Falls in Desolation Wilderness near Echo Summit, is 30 minutes from South Lake Tahoe. It’s a popular swimming hole that requires just two miles of hiking (four miles round trip) with around 750 feet of elevation gain at 6,100 feet in elevation. The trail is largely unmaintained, but keeping your eyes on the beaten path is simple. There are also small blue spray-painted markings to keep hikers from wandering off the trail. Punch in “Pyramid Creek Trailhead” to your GPS device to access this hike’s parking lot.

articles.text: A group exhibition showcasing a selection of artworks by eight female artists from the East Bay will open at Piedmont Center for the Arts on October 2. The exhibit, titled 8WA, will be on view Saturdays and Sundays through October 24 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., or by appointment. An artists’ reception will take place Sunday, October 3, from noon to 2 p.m. The exhibition features the work of Laura Abrams, Deborah Green, Michelle Lewis, Laura McNall, Juliet Mevi, Jacqui Rubenstein, Ariella Seidenberg, and Caskey Weston. Over 50 works will be on display. “We appreciate this opportunity to present a self-curated show from our personal collections,“ said Deborah Green, the artist who initiated the project. “I am proud to be part of this group of so many talented and accomplished women, and we are looking forward to exhibiting a strong body of artwork in this beautiful space. It’s especially meaningful to be emerging with a collective show after months of pandemic isolation. Works on display showcase a wide variety of styles and media. Growing out of an association through the Northern California Women’s Caucus for Art, many of the artists here embrace its activist mission with works that put forward dynamic feminist, environmental, and social justice messages.” Gallery hours are free and open to the public, and no reservation is required. For more information, email paintpeace@ yahoo.com, or visit www.piedmontcenterforthearts.org. Artwork by Juliet Mevi Artwork by Caskey Weston
articles.title: Eight Women Artists exhibit opens October 2 at PCA

articles.text: Filoli House and Garden in Woodside. Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside is celebrating “Orchard Days” every weekend through October 31. Visit the gardens this fall and stroll through the seven-acre Gentleman’s Orchard, a vital component of self-sustaining estates and a feature of many American country houses at the turn of the century. The acres hold a collection of fruits grown for leisure rather than commercial production. The Bourns, the original owners of the estate, planted their orchard with 1,000 trees - to include apples, pears, plums, apricots, walnuts, figs, and quinces. Only 115 trees remained when the orchard was restored, but there are now over 500 fruit and nut trees of various species. Filoli staff preserve the historic collection of rare and historically significant varieties. Fruit picking is not permitted. Access to “Orchard Days” is included with weekend admission tickets. The gardens are open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https://filoli.org/orchard-days.
articles.title: “Orchard Days” at Filoli every weekend in October

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre is returning to the stage this fall with Charles Mee’s acclaimed play, Wintertime, r unning November 12 through December 19. Tickets are on sale now. The production will be co-directed by Mee and Les Waters, who have teamed up in the past to bring Fetes de la Nuit and Big Love to the stage. Wintertime is the story of a “gloriously eccentric family [who] arrives at their summer house in the winter woods for a supposedly secret rendezvous—and soon bodies collide, doors slam, dishes fly, and everyone’s perfect plans go fantastically awry.” Berkeley Rep requires all patrons to present a vaccination card with matching photo identification and to be fully masked. All productions take place at Roda Theatre at 2015 Addison Street in Berkeley. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/wintertime/ Berkeley Repertory Theatre

articles.text: Arturo Chacón-Cruz The newest release from San Francisco Opera’s video portrait series, “In Song,” features opera singer Arturo Chacon-Cruz and is now available on YouTube, Facebook, and the opera’s website. From his home in Miami, tenor Chacon-Cruz visits with students at Homestead Mariachi Conservatory in Miami to reveal how culture, determination, and passion shape the music they make together. He performs Agustin Lara’s “Granada” with the students. He also sings Vincenzo De Crescenzo’s “Rondine al Nido” and María Grever’s “Júrame.” Chacon-Cruz is a native of Sonora, Mexico and has established himself in recent years as a leading operatic tenor. He Photo by Karli Evans has performed leading roles at Los Angeles Opera, Washington National Opera, and Carnegie Hall. Earlier this month, he released his newest recording, “De Mi Casa a Tu Casa,” featuring traditional mariachi music. San Francisco Opera’s “In Song” series features intimate video portraits of artists from around the world showcasing a wide variety of genres - from classic to bluegrass, spirituals, Samoan and mariachi. “In Song: J’Nai Bridges,” “In Song: Pene Pati,” and “In Song: Jamie Barton” featuring Béla Fleck, are available on demand on Youtube and the San Francisco Opera website. Upcoming episodes include soprano Amina Edris filmed on location in Egypt. Visit sfopera.com/insong to watch the series.
articles.title: SF Opera: “In Song: Arturo Chacon-Cruz” available now online

articles.text: Blues slide guitarist and 2008 Piedmont graduate Jules Leyhe released a new eclectic album, “Your First Rodeo”, on September 17. The album hits a wide range of genres, including blues, funk, big band jazz, and rock, with elements of hip hop and electronica, but each song has his slide guitar leading the way. The Post caught up with Jules for an interview last week. Q: Tell me about the ensemble of musicians on the CD and the instruments we are listening to. A: I mainly play slide guitar on my Gibson SG. We are a traditional blues or funk band, with keyboards, drums, base and a fabulous horn section. Shane Cox, is really the co-captain that is leading the way on trumpet, sousaphone, saxophone and trombone; he does all the horn parts. Q: What went into the decision to make this album totally instrumental without vocals? A: It is like a sonic journey. As much as I love singers, we wanted to tell all the stories with our instruments. I like the less literal meanings of the songs without lyrics; you can derive any kind of meaning you want from these instrumental tunes. We really want to bring attention to the musicians in the band and the creativity of how they are assembled. It is not pop music – it is kind of a wild adventure and an experiment. Q: What is your favorite song on the CD? Piedmont guitarist Jules Leyhe, a graduate of Berklee College of Music, has released his third album, “Your First Rodeo.” Blues slide guitarist and 2008 Piedmont graduate Jules Leyhe A: “The Planetarium” is definitely near and dear to me. There are all these tips of the hat to heroes of mine. The composer Holst produced pieces about all the planets, and our horn themes are a tribute to those. The horns are kind of the call, and the response is the Thin Lizzie or Allman Brothers guitar midis coming back to you. Then it concludes with something like a Jimi Hendrix solo over the rhythm guitar part inspired by “You Never Give Me Your Money,” by the Beatles which is full-on psychedelia. We tried to do it in our style the whole time and not be accused of just copying these great musicians. In four minutes we are throwing all of these things at you in an outer space psychedelic jam. is none of the musicians ever recorded together at the same time. It doesn’t sound like that, though. It sounds pretty natural, like everything goes together. It is amazing that there was never a live take where we all looked at each other, smiled and said, “That’s the one, guys.” And as much as I love Planetarium, it was certainly a challenge to make that not a chaotic storm but a pleasant listening experience. It was definitely tricky to put together. Knowing when to finally say, “Okay it is done,” was like hitting a moving target. Q: What challenges did you face making this CD? A: It was done 100% during the thick of COVID, before anyone was vaccinated. A fun fact Q: The album art is by Cole Crossen, also a PHS graduate. How did you come together? A: Cole Crossen is a buddy of mine from PHS, an important connection for me in keeping it really local and close to home. Cole did the album cover for the Jules Leyhe album cover from 2020 and I loved what he did. He’s a really talented artist and I wanted to get him in the mix. Q: What is next for you? pages.text: Wednesday, September 29, 2021 17 Piedmont guitarist Jules Leyhe releases new album By Jay Russell Blues slide guitarist and 2008 Piedmont graduate Jules Leyhe released a new eclectic album, “Your First Rodeo”, on September 17. The album hits a wide range of genres, including blues, funk, big band jazz, and rock, with elements of hip hop and electronica, but each song has his slide guitar leading the way. The Post caught up with Jules for an interview last week. Q: Tell me about the ensemble of musicians on the CD and the instruments we are listening to. A: I mainly play slide guitar on my Gibson SG. We are a traditional blues or funk band, with keyboards, drums, base and a fabulous horn section. Shane Cox, is really the co-captain that is leading the way on trumpet, sousaphone, saxophone and trombone; he does all the horn parts. Q: What went into the decision to make this album totally instrumental without vocals? A: It is like a sonic journey. As much as I love singers, we wanted to tell all the stories with our instruments. I like the less literal meanings of the songs without lyrics; you can derive any kind of meaning you want from these instrumental tunes. We really want to bring attention to the musicians in the band and the creativity of how they are assembled. It is not pop music – it is kind of a wild adventure and an experiment. Q: What is your favorite song on the CD? Piedmont guitarist Jules Leyhe, a graduate of Berklee College of Music, has released his third album, “Your First Rodeo.” Blues slide guitarist and 2008 Piedmont graduate Jules Leyhe A: “The Planetarium” is definitely near and dear to me. There are all these tips of the hat to heroes of mine. The composer Holst produced pieces about all the planets, and our horn themes are a tribute to those. The horns are kind of the call, and the response is the Thin Lizzie or Allman Brothers guitar midis coming back to you. Then it concludes with something like a Jimi Hendrix solo over the rhythm guitar part inspired by “You Never Give Me Your Money,” by the Beatles which is full-on psychedelia. We tried to do it in our style the whole time and not be accused of just copying these great musicians. In four minutes we are throwing all of these things at you in an outer space psychedelic jam. is none of the musicians ever recorded together at the same time. It doesn’t sound like that, though. It sounds pretty natural, like everything goes together. It is amazing that there was never a live take where we all looked at each other, smiled and said, “That’s the one, guys.” And as much as I love Planetarium, it was certainly a challenge to make that not a chaotic storm but a pleasant listening experience. It was definitely tricky to put together. Knowing when to finally say, “Okay it is done,” was like hitting a moving target. Q: What challenges did you face making this CD? A: It was done 100% during the thick of COVID, before anyone was vaccinated. A fun fact Q: The album art is by Cole Crossen, also a PHS graduate. How did you come together? Upcoming episodes include soprano Amina Edris filmed on location in Egypt. Visit sfopera.com/insong to watch the series. articles.text: Jazz artists have done interpretations of classical music for years. For reference, Google “jazz interpretations of classical music”. Spain by Chick Corea, for example, begins with his rendition of the introduction to Bolero, written in 1928 by Maurice Ravel. I imagined Peter Ilyich Tchaikovsky’s Romance in Fm, Op. 5 as a bossa nova (a soft, romantic Brazilian jazz style). The accompaniment was a typical nylon-string guitar part alternating thumb bass and three-note plucked chords. The melody and improv was electric jazz guitar. The tempo I imagined was “double-time” from the original 70 beats per minute to 135. The melodic rhythm “pushed” most of the notes in the typical floating bossa nova style, playing them before the beat and sustaining them onto the beat. It sounded like Jobim channeling Tchaikovsky. Look up and listen to a version of Tchaikovsky’s Romance in Fm, Op. 5 on Youtube or any streaming service. Then view and listen to my version at: guitarimprov. com/Tchaikovsky.pdf. Tchaikovsky’s father was one of the foremost metallurgists in Russia, wealthy enough to provide his seven children a comfortable living and a good education. Tchaikovsky’s mother played piano only well enough to provide music for her children to dance to. No one in his family was a professional musician. Like Art Tatum with his player piano, Tchaikovsky copied musical pieces by ear from the orchestrion on a player piano his Russian composer Peter Ilyich Tchaikovsky created the foundation for a range of musical adaptation. father bought him. According to Tchaikovsky’s brother Modeste, he replicated everything he heard on the orchestrion. Tchaikovsky graduated from the Saint Petersburg Conservatory in 1865. Nikolai Rubinstein, a renowned pianist and composer, appointed him as Professor of Music Theory at the Moscow Conservatory in 1866. Tchaikovsky’s text, Guide to the Practical Study of Harmony (1872), provides a good basis for understanding music theory, chord progression and voice leading. In 1868, Tchaikovsky wrote Romance in Fm, Op. 5 and dedicated it to Belgian soprano Désirée Artôt. They were engaged to be married, but Artôt broke it off and married baritone Francisco de Asís Mariano del Carmen Marco Padilla y Ramos, surely for his name! Tchaikovsky had probably pursued the marriage to hide his homosexuality, which was illegal in Russia, with punishment of imprisonment. He wrestled with his self-criticism and criticism by others, including Anton Rubenstein, his professor at the Conservatory. His Piano Concerto No. 1, Op. 23 was said to be “unplayable” by Nikolai Rubinstein, Anton’s younger brother, but it has been performed by pianists all over the world, including Nikolai. As Tchaikovsky’s composition matured, he became the foremost Russian composer of the nineteenth century, excelling with his ballets Swan Lake, Sleeping Beauty and Nutcracker. Tchaikovsky provided the bridge for his countryman Igor Stravinsky to take Russian music into the twentieth century. Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. articles.text: First the good news. Holy Names University used to have a respected music school. Sadly, they suffered a severe decline, partly due to the pandemic. The good news is that they have begun to rebuild, beginning with the orchestra. First, they will select a conductor. There are four fine prospects being considered. I attended the first rehearsal and I am happy to report that all is progressing well. On Saturday evening the Quantum Quintet performed a chamber music concert presented by Sunset Music and Arts. The main piece on the program was Dvorak‘s glorious piano quintet. As soon as they began to play, I was transported back in time. It was March 1974 in a small concert hall at USC. The concert was announced as a student recital from the master class of the immortal violinist Jascha Heifetz. The thing to remember here is that it was announced as a student recital. I had an idea that Jascha Heifetz would be one of the performers. The students played one after another in the first half of the program. After intermission, the stage door opened, and out walked Jascha Heifetz and the great cellist Gregory Piatigorsky. Both of these great artists played in the most circumspect manner. They did not want to overshadow their students. This concert was the last they ever played together. What a beautiful memory it was. Time for a recipe from the Gourmet It has been a long time since I offered my readers a recipe. So here goes. CALABRIAN SPAGHETTI Ingredients: spaghetti, a jar of roasted red peppers, smoked salmon, olive oil, anchovy fillets and crushed red pepper flakes. Cook the spaghetti. Combine about 2 ounces per person of the roasted red peppers, and about 2 ounces per person of smoked salmon. Add a little bit of olive oil to moisten and one anchovy per person (use anchovy instead of salt). Add the spaghetti to the other ingredients and heat them together. Stir gently. You can finish the spaghetti with some crushed red pepper flakes for a true Calabrian touch. Do not top with grated Parmesan cheese. Ambrose Bierce And now for something different: Ambrose Bierce was one of the most original writers in American history. His magnum opus, The Devil’s Dictionary, reveals his pugnacious sarcasm to best effect. While there is no information about Bierce’s interest in music, I obtained a document purportedly by Bierce. This “lexicon of musical terms“ has all the earmarks of Bierce’s sharply-pointed humor. Here are a few examples: Piccolo: noun, A small instrument which causes considerable bodily injury. The bane of audiologists. Trombone: noun, the comedian of the orchestra. Given to scatological humor and flatulence. Usually played by mischievous boys who want to annoy girls. Percussion instruments: plural, tone-deaf musicians released on early parole. Some of them become conductors. Violin: noun, when played well, you think you are in heaven. When played badly you think you are in hell. Violin bow: a club made of wood resembling a slender baseball bat and strung with horse hair from the rear end of a horse. Generally used to beat a Violin black and blue. Practice: noun or a verb, an unpleasant hour devoted to repeating your mistakes ad nauseam. Concert: noun, practicing in public. See above. And saving the best for last: Conductor: noun of questionable progeny. Literally the prince of fools. Usually an egotist from highest Valhalla who thinks he knows everything. Despised by members of the orchestra even though they aspire to the position.
articles.title: Good news, beautiful memories, and something different

articles.text: The 64th Monterey Jazz Festival presented Herbie Hancock, Pat Metheny, Lidesi, George Benson and others in an outdoor event Friday through Sunday last weekend, September 24-26, demonstrating the skill of the masters and the talent of rising stars. DAY ONE Pat Metheny, guitarist extraordinaire, and Side Eye, his new project, opened the Festival. Metheny’s fluid command rang from guitars that ranged from a vintage jazz box to his 42-string Pikasso as he reworked pieces like “Timeline “ and presented new compositions. He was backed by James Francies on piano whose style blends lighting runs with a strong left hand movement that grounded Metheny’s lyricism. Herbie Hancock, the legendary pianist, played a set that spanned his body of work from grand piano through the “keytar”. He is at his best at the piano, deftly moving through voice led chords with lyric right-hand flights. Elena Pinderhughes, a Berkeley raised flutist and vocalist, was the surprise of the set. Her flute work was virtuosic and her voice shared joy and strength in her compositions such as “Breath in Breath Out”. The melodic tone of her flute was a perfect complement to Hancock’s piano. DAY TWO Japanese born composer Miho Hazama and her orchestra opened the day with a program of lush orchestral jazz suites including the three-movement “It’s A Planet” commissioned by the Festival. Hazama’s style is lyric and often involves reeds-based jazz riffs emerging from a sweeping wave of strings. Legendary drummer Terri Herbie Hancock Lynn Carrington and Social Science presented a program of rhythm-driven jazz tuned to a theme of social justice in songs such as “Bells”. The jewel of the combo was vocalist Debo Reyes whose soaring and soulful style brought a lyric and haunting tone to the set. Ledisi closed the evening in an electrifying vocal performance. Fresh from her 2021 Grammy Award, Ledisi (LEDes-see) showed herself to be a musical Diva in the best sense of the word: commanding, vulnerable and effortlessly virtuosic. She worked through songs from her CDs including “Anything for You”. However, the most moving piece was her balladic mixture of Nina Simone’s “Baltimore” with her own composition “Shot Down” that created a haunting anthem of social justice. She was the apex of the Festival. DAY THREE Pianist Christian Sands, the Festival’s artist in residence, opened on Sunday with a quartet that focused on his new CD “Be Water”. Sands’ seamless voice leading and fluid lyric style led the audience through the spiritual journey that was the source of this project. Kandace Springs (vocal/ piano) then returned us to the American songbook as she played a set that moved from “Angel Eyes” to “I Put a Spell On You”. A gifted stylist, she made each song her own as her voice and piano often seemed to act as one instrument. George Benson closed the festival as people rose, cheered and danced. As Benson played his many hits, the audience was reminded of the quality of his vocal style that ranges from soft crooning to happy scatting. His bright staccato guitar style is still evident; however closing the Festival before a familiar audience one felt they were listening to Nat Cole or Johnny Hartman – a mature stylistic voice that will live in the history of jazz. The Monterey Festival, like the Piedmont Jazz Festival one week earlier, was not only a celebration of jazz, but the indomitable spirit of musical creation after a long uncertainty. George Benson
articles.title: 64th Monterey Jazz Festival – 3 fabulous days of music

Hazama’s style is lyric and often involves reeds-based jazz riffs emerging from a sweeping wave of strings. Legendary drummer Terri Herbie Hancock Lynn Carrington and Social Science presented a program of rhythm-driven jazz tuned to a theme of social justice in songs such as “Bells”. The jewel of the combo was vocalist Debo Reyes whose soaring and soulful style brought a lyric and haunting tone to the set. Ledisi closed the evening in an electrifying vocal performance. Fresh from her 2021 Grammy Award, Ledisi (LEDes-see) showed herself to be a musical Diva in the best sense of the word: commanding, vulnerable and effortlessly virtuosic. She worked through songs from her CDs including “Anything for You”. However, the most moving piece was her balladic mixture of Nina Simone’s “Baltimore” with her own composition “Shot Down” that created a haunting anthem of social justice. She was the apex of the Festival. DAY THREE Pianist Christian Sands, the Festival’s artist in residence, opened on Sunday with a quartet that focused on his new CD “Be Water”. Sands’ seamless voice leading and fluid lyric style led the audience through the spiritual journey that was the source of this project. Kandace Springs (vocal/ piano) then returned us to the American songbook as she played a set that moved from “Angel Eyes” to “I Put a Spell On You”. A gifted stylist, she made each song her own as her voice and piano often seemed to act as one instrument. George Benson closed the festival as people rose, cheered and danced. As Benson played his many hits, the audience was reminded of the quality of his vocal style that ranges from soft crooning to happy scatting. His bright staccato guitar style is still evident; however closing the Festival before a familiar audience one felt they were listening to Nat Cole or Johnny Hartman – a mature stylistic voice that will live in the history of jazz. The Monterey Festival, like the Piedmont Jazz Festival one week earlier, was not only a celebration of jazz, but the indomitable spirit of musical creation after a long uncertainty. 801 Magnolia Avenue • Piedmont, Calif. 801 Magnolia Avenue • Piedmont, Calif. info@piedmontcenterforthearts.org info@piedmontcenterforthearts.org READ IT IN THE POST George Benson

articles.text: Thomasin McKenzie and Alex Wolff in Old. First things first: I have yet to watch Old, written and directed by M. Night Shyamalan (Sixth Sense, Signs, Split), and now debuting in walk-in theaters; but then I haven’t been inside a local movie house for well over a year. When I heard about the premise of Old, adapted from Sandcastle, a French graphic novel, I immediately Googled it and screened the trailer more than a few times. Not infrequently, a trailer will reveal more than is necessary. This one doesn’t. It just manages to intrigue, even captivate, offering just enough of the plot to create that familiar Shyamalan sense of dread, an emotion that threads through all of his films, with greater effect in some than others. In Old we are introduced to tropical vacationers (a family of four, plus others), who are encouraged by their hotel concierge to visit a remote, secluded beach: white sand, blue water, it seems idyllic. At first the kids discover strange artifacts in the sand (cracked sunglasses). The body of a woman floats toward a swimmer. And then they begin to age. Suddenly the film becomes a meditation on the passage of time. Something is happening. What that thing is, is desperately inexplicable, an impenetrable mystery. And so, the audience is asked to walk through a creepy portal without any exposition that explains what is happening. Or so I assume. Embedded in the plot is the awareness by Shyamalan that our culture (western, European) is obsessed with longevity (diet, prophylactic drugs, exercise), anything that will slow, resist, push back the aging process. We are all dimly aware that there was a time when life expectancy was a mere fraction of what it is today. In the middle 18th century, one’s life span was some 35 years. By 1918 it was 54. Today it is 80, thanks to the miracle of a host of vaccines (smallpox shots, for example), and a bunch of metaphorical, modern medicine seat belts. So to watch Old is to contemplate how time can seem strangely distorted (the pandemic has twisted time in some weird ways), and begs the question whether what Shyamalan has created is a fable for this peculiar moment. Old. Written and directed by M. Night Shyamalan. Starring Gael Garcia Bernal, Alex Wolff, Victoria Kriepa. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: News of the World is an extraordinary, elegiac neo-western adapted from the Paulette Jules 2016 novel. It is set in Texas in 1870, three years after the end of the Civil War. Confederate veteran Captain Jefferson Kyle Kidd (Tom Hanks), once a printer, now makes his improbable living by travelling from to town om Texas reading the news – stories gleaned from newspapers from both near and far, standing stage center in candle-lit rooms, saying, “I read the news to anyone with ten cents and the time to hear it.” His audience is comprised of rough-hewn settlers, many still coming to terms with the defeat of the South. Many of those standing before him either can’t read, or spend every waking hour in physical labor; yet, all remain eager to hear the news of the world. As we soon come to realize, Captain Kidd is not only a respected man of letters, but also a storyteller and entertainer, and an enthusiastic, at times jocular reader of what could simply be the dry words on a page of newsprint. His mission is not only to inform but to capture the imaginations of his audience. On a trip to another town he discovers an overturned wagon on the side of the road. Investigating, he sees the body of a black freedman, hanging from a tree. Hiding nearby, among the brush, he spots a terrified young white girl (Helena Zengel), 12, dressed in Native American clothes, her blond hair bluntly cut. She is able to speak only Kiowa. He discovers some identifying papers in the wagon that say that she is German, her name is Johanna (she later explains that she is called Cicada), and she was abducted as a youngster and her parents were killed. A passing Union patrol captain, after examining the documents, instructs Kidd to take her to the next town where the Bureau of Indian Affairs will arrange to return her to her surviving family, now living in a settlement called Castroville. Reluctantly, he agrees. And so begins an episodic journey where he and Johanna develop a halting bond, despite their inability to fully communicate. Theirs is a road trip through an unstable Texas, across dry plains, stopping in raw, muddy towns filled with gritty, bitter men who resent the presence of Union soldiers, constant reminders of the fact that they lost the war. When Captain Kidd learns that the head of Indian Affairs will not be back for some three months, he is at a loss as what to do with Johanna. But he finally realizes that if she is ever to be reunited with her relatives, it is up to him to help find them. News of the World is a remarkable narrative featuring two people who struggle to move beyond trauma. It is also a wonderful, deeply human character study that is aesthetically striking, stunningly authentic, and photographed beautifully by cinematographer Darius Wolski. The performances by Hanks and Zengel are impressively nuanced and touchingly moving. While spare, the story also makes subtle connections to today’s moment in history in which acrimonious divisions continue to haunt us. News of the World. Now streaming. Directed by Paul Greengrass. Starring Tom Hanks, Helena Zengel, Elizabeth Marvel. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: News of the World another triumph by Hanks

articles.text: Antz feature the voice acting of Woody Allen and Sharon Stone. Antz was the first animated feature created by Dreamworks studio. By design it is a hybrid of sorts, intended to appeal to children age 8 and up, as well as older audiences. The story opens with Ant Z4195 (Woody Allen), a sixlegged neurotic, stretched out on his shrink’s couch, kvetching about the injustice of his life on the anthill. To begin with, he hates dirt, is dissatisfied with being a member of a huge colony, was abandoned by his father when he was just a larva, can’t lift 10 times his weight, and is the middle child in a family of five million. You can hear Woody bringing his signature shtick from the streets of Manhattan to Antz. So here we go: Z is at an ant bar when princess Bala (Sharon Stone), aristocratic daughter of the Queen (Ann Bancroft), decides to go slumming and spend an evening with the worker ants. Z is smitten with the princess, asks her to dance, and the two shock the bar denizens with their own outrageous, freewheeling version of a line dance to the song Guantanamera. Z can’t get Bala out of his mind, and hearing that there will be a military parade passing in front of the royal stands, and hoping to get a glimpse of the princess, he convinces his good friend soldier ant Weaver (Sylvester Stallone) to loan him his helmet so he can join the parade and march with the other soldiers. Meanwhile, the deranged General Mandible (Gene Hackman) is devising a plan to preemptively attack the termites (five times the size of the ants). He manages to convince the queen to support his declaration of war. His hidden objective is to take over the entire anthill. To his consternation, Z is swept into battle with the other soldier ants. The question is, will Z survive, and ultimately win the heart of the fair maiden Bala, who has shared with Z that she also is not happy with her life either. They have even dreamed of escaping to Insectopia (a nearby New York trashcan) where they can live happily ever after. Well, almost. There is a funny scene where the two are stuck to a wad of bubblegum, which is stuck to the bottom of an enormous tennis shoe. Antz is an amusing, witty adventure with some wicked dialogue that touches on the tension that exists between being a conformist or free thinker, all while encouraging the audience to root for the underdog. Actually, it’s hard not to care about these speck-sized creatures, especially Woody as Z. Antz. Animation-adventure. Directed by Eric Darnell. With the voices of Woody Allen, Sharon Stone, and Gene Hackman. 1 hr., 27 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: Antz – Woody Allen in animation

articles.text: To begin with, kids are going to enjoy a Bug’s Life. It’s a superb, animated feature filled with a creepy-crawly menagerie of bugs, inspired by a well-known Aesop’s Fable, The Ant and the Grasshopper. The story opens with a wonderfully natural-looking colony of ants that makes its home on a mound of dirt, near a creek bed. It’s known as Ant Island and is ruled by the Queen ant and her daughter, Princess Atta (Julia Louis-Dreyfus). As we soon learn, every summer a gang of thuggish grasshoppers arrive, led by the swaggering Hopper (Kevin Spacey). They demand to be given food collected by the hard-working colony. A nerdy ant named Flik (Dave Foley), a young tinkerer, has an accident while trying to invent a conveyor belt to move seeds intended for the grasshoppers. When the gadget malfunctions, he knocks the gathered food into the water. Whoops. Hopper is furious, and he demands that the ants give him twice as much food as promised, to make up for the loss. Flik, rebelling and feeling bullied, insists that the demand for double the rations is wrong, and suggests to the Queen that he leave and find warrior type bugs, to help the colony in a fight against the grasshoppers. Enough is enough. Princess Atta, apparently not a fan of Flik, encourages him, assuming it’s unlikely that he will return alive from his mission. Flik journeys to Bug City (a heap of trash piled under a trailer), and it is there that he recruits a cohort of “warriors”. In reality they are actually a troupe of Circus Bugs recently fired by ringmaster P.T. Flea (John Ratzenberger). Having no idea what they are getting into, they agree to return to Ant Hill with Flik, who they assume is a talent scout. When they arrive at the colony, they discover what is afoot, and they are not there to perform. Flik pleads with them to stay and pretend to be what they’re not: fighters, not entertainers. Meanwhile, having discovered that the grasshoppers are afraid of birds, Flik sets about building a giant bird, hoping it will be a kind of scarecrow, and scare off Hopper and his gang. And so this engaging story continues, with one confrontation after another, all while introducing an imaginative coterie of bugs. There’s pill bug, a black widow spider, a praying mantis, a walking stick, a large caterpillar, and a male ladybug. Even P.T. Flea makes an appearance, just to keep things interesting. Flik convinces his assembled crew, which includes his fellow ants, that they outnumber the grasshoppers and have the ability to drive the invaders away – which they do, with the exception of Hopper. And so, Flik, the geeky ant and gadgeteer, saves the Hill and the day, and can now invent whatever he wants. A Bug’s Life. Pixar animation. Directed by John Lasseter. With voices of Dave Foley, Kevin Spacey, and Julia Louis-Dreyfus. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated G. EPISCOPAL CHURCH
