articles.text: Part 29 of a biweekly series In my experience, the most difficult part of painting buildings is not finding the painting contractor, not the scraping, sanding or surface preparation, not dealing with the mess. The most difficult part is the selection of colors. Maybe this is because like most aspects of the architectural field, color selection is a curious mix of art and science, and…we all experience colors differently. Balancing the main color attributes of hue (color: red, blue, etc.), intensity (saturation or purity), and value (lightness/ Photos by Will Adams A variation on the classical color wheel fashioned by Sir Isaac Newton in 1666 that we all learned in grammar school. Although modern physics reveals variants on the principles involved, they still hold true when mixing paint. Colorists continue to use the color wheel to determine harmonious color combinations. darkness i.e., tints/shades) with other associated variables is simply a difficult job. In the end, from the bold, emotion-evoking colors of Mexican architects such as the famous Luis Barragan, to the restrained, subtle colors we are most familiar with in the Bay Area, exterior colors on a building reveal, perhaps more than anything else, the attitudes, ideas and personality of the owners. Building colors should first respond to the character, style, and detailing of the architecture. Schemes with multiple colors require a natural stopping/starting point for color changes such as a different material or corners and offsets in wall planes. Certain interior colors need also be coordinated, most notably curtains and shades which are seen through the windows and have to work with the exterior colors. Because all urban buildings are surrounded by neighboring buildings, as well as landscape planting, paving, and other elements, exterior color selection necessarily also involves urban design considerations; each building is part of a larger neighborhood palate. Evaluation of color requires certain steps to be successful. Most importantly, although not nearly done often enough, is to allow enough time for color selection and approval before painting starts. Once an attitude and concept is settled upon, selection begins with little paint chips – only the first step. Many architectural offices specify that large (100 sf) samples then be painted on at least two different walls of the building with different natural light conditions. These must be allowed to dry for at least a few days before being evaluated. It is good for owners to then reflect on the samples at different times of the day for a good week before modifications are made or final approval given. This is all pretty complex, at least to me. If it’s one thing I’ve learned is that professional help (and patience) is essential in color selection. Color is mysterious, and what it does to the psyche is diverse. But the measure of success is simple in the end. It is the answer to the question: do you like it? Does it make you glad to be at that place? Does it, as Marie Kondo would ask, bring you joy? Thanks to my creative colorist and design consultant Leela Willow for help with this article. Leela can be reached at 510-910- 4244 or www.leelawillow.com Ne x t: C o m m e m o r a t i ve Plaques in Piedmont Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com Retaining Wall Construction in Piedmont Hillside Garage Rebuild in Piedmont To request a free estimate, please visit our website, www.jimgardnerconstruction.com 510.655.3409

But the measure of success is simple in the end. It is the answer to the question: do you like it? Does it make you glad to be at that place? Does it, as Marie Kondo would ask, bring you joy? The traditional detailing on this Piedmont Victorian home provides numerous logical and natural color transitions. I think it enlivens the whole neighborhood. A fine example of a more “calm” color scheme that prioritizes, works with, and enhances the surrounding landscaping. articles.text: Piedmont Connect Piedmonters have four more days – through Sunday, October 3 – to view Piedmont Connect’s Healthy Landscapes Fall Front Garden Tour. Piedmonters can get sidewalk views of 14 front gardens featuring an array of drought-tolerant and native plant landscapes in neighborhoods from Baja to St. James, and Moraga Ave. to Boulevard Way. Check out www.piedmontconnect.org for a map of the street addresses, plus photos and complete descriptions of the front gardens explaining what, when, why and how the gardens were transformed from lawns or ivy patches into healthier landscapes. Additionally, join Piedmont Connect for two related events today and tomorrow. September 29 and 30. Today at 10:30 a.m., join Dick Carter’s Wednesday Walkers group for a guided mini-tour of five of the gardens. A guest from Piedmont Connect will discuss the significant features of the gardens. Meet at the Piedmont Exedra to participate in this free Wednesday walking tour after registering with the Recreation Department. Tomorrow, Thursday, Piedmont Connect will host a Zoom event “Living With Drought” from 7:00 to 8:15 p.m. Join the live webinar via the link at www. piedmontconnect.org. “Living With Drought” will be moderated by dynamic Piedmont resident and water expert Eileen White, following an introduction by Piedmont Parks Manager Nancy Kent. Suzanne Bontempo of Our Water Our World will give helpful outdoor water-saving techniques. For the finale, three Piedmont residents whose gardens are featured on the Fall Front Garden Tour will inspire viewers with their garden transformations, explaining how they use the latest research to sustain healthy ecosystems and maintain chemical-free, water-efficient oases that support a diversity of wildlife. There will be time for viewer questions and answers following the presentations. For residents wanting to reduce water use, limit garden maintenance work, adapt to climate changes, build drought resiliency, and attract beneficial life to the garden, fall is the time of year when planting is recommended. Hoped-for winter rains help young or relocated plants to establish new root systems naturally, without supplemental water. Cooler temperatures also impede a few common plant pathogens to which some young plants are susceptible. Make the change to a healthier landscape now. An example of how even a narrow parking strip provides an ample visual feast for humans and nourishment for pollinators.

pages.text: Wednesday, September 29, 2021 23 The Wine Corner The wines of Grocery Outlet The nearest Grocery Outlet to Piedmont is at Broadway and 29th Street in Oakland. By Pierre DuMont Twenty years ago when I moved to Piedmont, a new friend named Bruce told me about Grocery Outlet. He said it was an amazing place to buy wine at rock bottom prices. He would take a wine glass and a corkscrew, go to Grocery Outlet and buy a few wines for $3.99 or $4.99. He would take them back to his car in the parking lot and try the wines. If he liked them, he would go back in and buy a case. This bit of subterfuge was somewhat unnecessary as G.O. has always had the most generous return policy. Keep the receipt and they will take anything back, no questions asked. The reason Bruce did this, though, was for a reason I have personally experienced. So many times, I have found a great wine at G.O. and returned the next day to buy more only to find the wine totally gone. This leads us to the most important tip about buying wine at Grocery Outlet: Move Fast. Yes, this column comes with a disclaimer: some of these wines will be gone by the time you are reading this review. So treat this as a kind of educational seminar to show you some of the types of values that are available at G.O. Use your imagination and discover your own terrific deals. The Background Seventy-five years ago Jim Read started a store in San Francisco that sold surplus food and discounted goods – he called it Cannery Sales. The name was later changed to Grocery Outlet but the business model was pretty much the same – buy food, wine and other goods that other people are having trouble selling at deep discounts and pass those savings along to the consumer. Every receipt has a number showing how much money has been saved vs. buying these products at regular retail prices. About 10 years ago G.O. decided to expand their product line, adding meat and fish and lots of fresh produce, basically becoming a full-service grocery store. You no longer have to go to G.O. and Safeway to do your weekly shopping. Over the years, the company, still owned by the Read family, grew from that single store to over 300 stores nationwide. In 2019 the company went public. Steven Beckner About a month ago I was at the Family Winemakers of California tasting and I saw a guy with a nametag that said Steven Beckner and underneath it, Grocery Outlet. I approached him and said, somewhat maniacally, “You work for Grocery Outlet? I love Grocery Outlet!” We exchanged cards and a couple of weeks later we met at the flagship store in Oakland on Broadway and 30th. We walked through the wine department and he answered questions about how these wines came to be there and why they were so cheap. Steve is one of three wine buyers at G.O. and has been in the wine business for over 20 years. He said a lot of the wines he buys are submitted by wineries that just have a new vintage coming and have too much old stock and not enough space. If he likes a wine, he buys as much as he thinks he can sell. In the past Grocery Outlet bought some wines without tasting them resulting in the shelves having a certain percentage of too old or just plain awful wines. Steven Beckner, one of Grocery Outlet’s wine buyers, has 20 years’ experience in the wine industry. Nowadays no wines are bought without being tasted first. Steve also attends meetings and conventions where wine producers from Europe show off wines they would like to have someone distribute. Grocery Outlet directly imports some of the wines themselves, helping keep the prices rock bottom. The Rules I truly love Grocery Outlet and have shopped there for 20 years, snagging many, many incredible bargains. Being quite Scottish under my French exterior, I love bargains and hate to see people spend too much money on wine. Frankly, there is little correlation to how much you spend on a wine and the quality of the wine. I feel bad when I see people spending $50 to $100 for a trendy Napa wine because they don’t realize you don’t have to spend that much to get a good wine. However, all that being true, not all the wines at G.O. are great. There are plenty of mediocre wines on the shelf, so it helps to know a few rules. 1. Don’t buy any white wine over 3 years of age. The younger the better. 2. When looking for rose, if you like it dry, stick to rose from Provence and pick the latest vintage you can get. 3. It’s hard to buy a good Pinot Noir because it is a hot grape in high demand and good ones rarely land at G.O. Likewise with Bordeaux. The best bets are Syrah, Zinfandel, Sauvignon Blanc and Spanish and Portuguese wines. The Wines In addition to the earlier admonition to remember that good wines sell out quickly, you need to know that each G.O. store decides which wines it wants to carry. So there is a variety to the selection. If one store does not have the wine you want, you could check nearby stores as their inventory may be different. The following wines were selected from the Oakland Grocery Outlet store and were outstanding examples of their varietals. Every year G.O. has one or two big sales where they take an additional 20% off the already discounted prices making a great deal even better. The next big sale is November 10-14. • 2019 Emma Pearl Sauvignon Blanc, $5.99 Napa Valley Sauvignon Blanc from the most recent vintage for 6 bucks. Go figure! This wine is perfectly made, attractively packaged and packed with delicious nectarine and apricot fruit. • 2018 Pra Vigna Chardonnay, $5.99 If you like big, rich, buttery Chardonnays that are lashed with oak (think Rombauer), this wine is for you. If not, stay away. • 2017 Botte Petite Verdot, $5.99 This wine comes from the non-prestigious wine area of Yuba County. Who cares… it is outright delicious. Tons of dark blackberry fruit. This hedonistic monster is worth buying by the case. • 2017 Cosendido Monastrell Barrica, $5.99 Monastrell is the Spanish name for the Mourvedre grape which is quite popular in southeastern Spain. articles.text: The Oakland Zoo returned to one of its most popular traditions last Saturday, September 25, allowing visitors to help feed the animals. Last year’s Feast for the Beasts was cancelled, so the zoo created an event called Brunch For The Wild Bunch this year, with giraffes, baboons, elephants, and grizzly bears the lucky winners of a free meal. The animal feeding consisted of four areas where guests were able to go into the enclosures and spread out food for the animals. The event was sold out, so I went as an onlooker and writer. I walked around the zoo watching what the animals who didn’t get a feeding were eating at that time. To my surprise, the most discarded food was lettuce. Curious about why lettuce leaves were being tossed back on the ground or left uneaten, I turned to Isabella Linares, a Marketing Associate for the answer. She explained that some animals are quite picky. With lemurs, as example, the females eat first in their hierarchy. They will eat all the fruits first and leave the rest for the males. But whatever they don’t eat they will save for later. On Saturday all the animals were eating at a specific time of the day, but on a normal day or week it will depend on the animal. Grizzly bears will eat 16 times a day when getting ready to hibernate, a process known as hyperphagia. Saturday’s meals A Grant’s Zebra was a show-stopper for avid photographers. A sign inviting visitors with advance reservation to set out food for the elephants at Oakland Zoo.

pages.text: 24 Wednesday, September 29, 2021 your Annual animal feeding event returns By Larissa Edel The Oakland Zoo returned to one of its most popular traditions last Saturday, September 25, allowing visitors to help feed the animals. Last year’s Feast for the Beasts was cancelled, so the zoo created an event called Brunch For The Wild Bunch this year, with giraffes, baboons, elephants, and grizzly bears the lucky winners of a free meal. The animal feeding consisted of four areas where guests were able to go into the enclosures and spread out food for the animals. The event was sold out, so I went as an onlooker and writer. I walked around the zoo watching what the animals who didn’t get a feeding were eating at that time. To my surprise, the most discarded food was lettuce. Curious about why lettuce leaves were being tossed back on the ground or left uneaten, I turned to Isabella Linares, a Marketing Associate for the answer. She explained that some animals are quite picky. With lemurs, as example, the females eat first in their hierarchy. They will eat all the fruits first and leave the rest for the males. But whatever they don’t eat they will save for later. On Saturday all the animals were eating at a specific time of the day, but on a normal day or week it will depend on the animal. Grizzly bears will eat 16 times a day when getting ready to hibernate, a process known as hyperphagia. Saturday’s meals Staff photos A pride of three African lions roams a hilly, forested habitat at the Oakland Zoo. When thy roar, all visitors and animals at the zoo, pay attention. A large number of visitors were allowed to spread food in the elephant and giraffe habitat at Oakland Zoo on Saturday for the zoo’s Feast Day for animals. A Grant’s Zebra was a show-stopper for avid photographers. A sign inviting visitors with advance reservation to set out food for the elephants at Oakland Zoo. A curious sight was seeing hundreds of people watching other people inside the elephant enclosure placing for the animals to eat – at a later time. were all a smaller size – more like a snack. Birds will eat two times a day and will be satisfied. Getting down to what the animals enjoy eating, it all depends on the type of animal and its habitat. In the feeding last Saturday, I saw all sorts of fruits and vegetables, such as carrots, lettuce, peppers, and watermelons being spread around the elephant compound, including carrots and cabbage placed on top of the fence railing so the elephants could reach for them with their trunks. In talking with Linares the next day, she explained that the goal of the Brunch For The Wild Bunch was a way to inspire young children to one day consider becoming an animal keeper, and to provide a way for the community to enjoy the zoo they love. That’s extremely important because in this trying age we need something to hold onto and be a constant in our lives. I think that the Oakland Zoo is a perfect example of that, because it is always finding new ways to bring the community together.

articles.text: Beautiful World, Where Are You, by Sally Rooney Here’s a third smart, sexy novel from Rooney, who received widespread acclaim for her first two, Conversations With Friends and Normal People. This book has a clear autobiographical bent: Alice is a young novelist who has rocketed to worldwide fame. Her close friendship with Eileen anchors the book, with their email exchanges alighting on everything from political and social upheaval to their romantic lives. Farrar, Straus & Giroux. The Wrong End of the Telescope, by Rabih Alameddine Mina, a trans Lebanese American doctor, arrives in Lesbos to volunteer at a refugee camp, and the experience takes on an unexpectedly personal dimension after she meets Sumaiya, a Syrian woman trying to hide the extent of her illness from her family. Grove Press. Chronicles From the Land of the Happiest People on Earth, by Wole Soyinka The Nobel laureate’s first novel in nearly 50 years reads like a sendup of an imaginary Nigeria, equally a mystery and political satire, centered on a black market for human flesh and the doctor trying to get to the bottom of what’s going on. Pantheon Books. won a Pulitzer Prizes for The Underground Railroad and The Nickel Boys, a rich, wild book. Doubleday. Palmares, by Gayl Jones It’s been two decades since Jones released a new novel, and she returns with a multipart series centered on Almeyda, a young enslaved girl in colonial Brazil, who makes her way to a utopia where Black people are free. After the settlement is destroyed, Almeyda crosses the country in search of her lost husband. Beacon Press. Bewilderment, by Richard Powers As with his Pulitzer Prize-winning novel The Overstory, Powers’s new book encourages readers to look beyond ourselves. A widowed father, Theo, is an astrobiologist researching the possibility of life throughout the galaxy. His son, Robin, is struggling with outbursts at school and difficult emotions, but finds relief in an experimental neurofeedback therapy, which allows him to access his dead mother’s feelings. W. W. Norton & Company Inseparable, by Simone de Beauvoir. Translated by Sandra Smith. De Beauvoir may be most closely associated with Jean-Paul Sartre, but this loosely autobiographical novel, written in 1954 and put aside for decades, suggests that her more significant relationship was with her childhood friend Zaza. Ecco. Apples Never Fall, by Liane Moriarty Family tensions bubbling over in Australia, jump cuts between past and present – it’s another novel from Moriarty, known for books like Big Little Lies and Nine Perfect Strangers. This time, she focuses on the Delaney family, headed by two retired tennis stars, and the fallout after their mother goes missing. Henry Holt & Co. Harlem Shuffle, by Colson Whitehead In 1960s Harlem, Ray Carney, a furniture salesman, is trying to lead a mostly upright life — until he’s drawn into a heist that goes awry. Our reviewer called this, Whitehead’s first novel since he Cloud Cuckoo Land, by Anthony Doerr In his first novel since he won a Pulitzer Prize for All the Light We Cannot See, Doerr follows five characters across a millennium, from 15th-century Constantinople to a futuristic spaceship, all linked by a love of books, myth and storytelling. Scribner Publishing. Crossroads, by Jonathan Franzen Set in the 1970s in a Chicago suburb, this novel, the first in a planned trilogy, follows the Hildebrandt family. Russell, an associate pastor whose ethical code is wavering, and Marion, who deals with long-buried traumas, head up the family, which goes on to confront moral and spiritual questions. Joumana Khatib is with the New York Times. WE PROVIDE: • Excellent in-home care • Quality caregiver training • Errands and transportation Start home care today. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I don’t really need a new phone, as I have an iPhone 11. I am a hobbyist photographer, and I do like to take pictures and especially videos with my phone. I am hearing some good things about the new iPhone that just came out. Are you recommending the newest iPhone? My phone works fine, but the battery gives out by late afternoon, especially when I use the camera a lot. So, I am really tempted just to get a new iPhone. Lowell F., Piedmont Dear Lowell: Since you like to take pictures and videos, I would say this is a fine time to get the iPhone 13. If you are shooting a lot of videos on your current phone, this could be the cause of your battery draining. It seems that the camera capabilities on the last couple of phones have increased so much, that I hardly ever use my DSLR for landscape scenes. When I travel for wildlife photo trips, I use my long lens for animals and birds, and my iPhone for beautiful sunsets and scenery. There are many times I have used my phone just to frame a shot, and then realized the results are so spectacular that there is no need to pull out my DSLR. I must say that I see many photographers, both hobbyists and pros, enjoying the photo capabilities of the newer iPhones. As far as the iPhone 13 which just became available on September 24, there are 4 models: the iPhone 13, 13 Mini, 13 Pro, and 13 Pro Max. Personally, I upgraded to the 13 Pro Max from a 12 Pro Max, because the 13 is reported to have better battery life, 2.5 hours longer than its predecessor. And I can attest that this is true, as by the end of today, after using the map, email, messages, taking several photos and a few videos, the battery is at 69% this evening. And of course, the new camera features also drew me in. Since you mentioned that you enjoy taking pictures and videos with your phone, there are some features with this new model that I think you will like. Here is a list of a few of the ones I am excited about: 1. Cinematic Mode: This is a video mode which automatically switches the focus between subjects to give footage a more filmlike aesthetic. You can tap on a subject to switch focus and tap twice to hold focus on that subject. 2. Wide Angle and Night Mode: Like the previous iPhone Apples’ new iPhone 13 and 13 mini. 12 Pro Max, the iPhone 13 uses sensor shift technology for stabilization and also has a much wider aperture and improved (over the iPhone 12) night mode for better shots in the dark. 3. Macro Function: The super wide lens also has a new macro function which allows you to shoot objects less than an inch away from the lens. 4. Telephoto Zoom: This has been increased to 3x, up from 2.5x of the 12 Pro. 5. Apple ProRes: This is an Apple developed video codec that allows you to shoot at 4K resolution at 30 frames per second, a feature available on the 13 Pro and Pro Max. As far as the question about when to upgrade to a new device, I always ask, “What kinds of things do you do on your phone?” If you use the camera a lot, these improvements are worth it, in my mind. The main camera on this new phone has a larger image sensor with a f/1.5 aperture which is why it can let in more light to facilitate better lo light and night mode shooting. But if you just use your phone as a phone, there is no need to upgrade if your model is only a couple of models behind the current one. When you are ready to purchase, make sure to check with your carrier, as they often have better deals than Apple. Apple, as well as many of the carriers have an “upgrade every year” program, where the cost of the phone is split into 24 monthly interest free payments. After you have paid for 12 months, you can turn the phone in for the newer model. Even if your model is a few years old, most carriers and Apple will give you some trade in credit towards the cost of a new phone. Since the phones just came out you should be prepared to wait a few weeks for delivery. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com.

articles.text: Several years ago I read about a community for older adults in the Netherlands that allows university students to live there rentfree. What a deal. In exchange for a small apartment, the students do a variety of activities with the older residents, including watching sports together, celebrating birthdays and, perhaps most importantly, offering personal interaction and companionship to seniors. Here in the United States, intergenerational programs have become a growing trend within senior living. As we emerge from the confines of Covid-19, we can attest to the value of both intergenerational programming as well as intergenerational living communities. The pandemic forced multiple generations of families to live together, to rely on each other as jobs were lost, school was canceled. Younger family members were able to assist their older relatives. The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living is on the leading edge of intergenerational programming. Just last week we hosted a reading by the award-winning young writers from the Oakland Youth Poet Laureate Program. It’s an unprecedented citywide effort to celebrate literacy through poetry and connect young writers to far-reaching opportunities. Two of the program’s finalists, Dara Kashayar and Siara Edmond, were participants with us. They read some of their poetry and then were asked questions by our residents and those watching online. Siara Edmond is a finalist in the Oakland Youth Poet Laureate Program. The first question asked was, “How has interacting with older adults impacted you and your writing?” We got a quick response from Dara who said, “My grandmother and parents emigrated from Iran. Persian culture teaches children to revere the wisdom their elders can impart. This is part of my identity; it definitely impacts my writing.” Another young Oakland poet, Siara, writes poems about her grandparents. “I appreciate the hard work they did in order to better the lives of their children and grandchildren,” she said. For the past five years, The Lake Merritt has initiated an intergenerational program called “Conversation Exchange.” We partner with Laney College students who are learning English as a second language. Students come to The Lake Merritt after classes to meet with our residents and build their English language fluency by conversing on a wide range of topics. This program has been wildly successful and a win-win for both students and our Dara Kashayar, a finalist in the Oakland Youth Poet Laureate Program, read his poetry to Lake Merritt Senior Living residents. residents. Our resident Mary met Etta, a Chinese student through the program. Mary said, “I love working with Etta. Our meetings together are valuable to both of us. She is so bright and her English gets better all the time. It’s a good feeling knowing I have had a hand in helping her,” Mary added. In a world seemingly more divided each day, intergenerational programs offer connective solutions that benefit everyone. According to the California Health Report, intergenerational programming is a solution for two problems at once: kids get the attention they crave – sparking better performance at school – while their elder counterparts enjoy improved emotional and physical health. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, at 1800 Madison Street in Oakland. For more information call 510- 903-3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt.com.
articles.title: Oakland’s Poets, Laney students and our residents – a Win-Win

When you are ready to purchase, make sure to check with your carrier, as they often have better deals than Apple. Apple, as well as many of the carriers have an “upgrade every year” program, where the cost of the phone is split into 24 monthly interest free payments. After you have paid for 12 months, you can turn the phone in for the newer model. Even if your model is a few years old, most carriers and Apple will give you some trade in credit towards the cost of a new phone. Since the phones just came out you should be prepared to wait a few weeks for delivery. For more information, call 520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com.

articles.text: In the Christian Scriptures the Apostle Paul refers to believers as “co-creators with God.” The troubles we face should not be signs of failure alone, but also as opportunities for growth. If a structure excludes others from the advantages we have enjoyed, perhaps it’s time to rip out a wall or two and expand our vision to include all. Perhaps it’s another time in our history to see opportunity in the chaos and blessing in the struggle. As we approach Thanksgiving, let us be cautious about what we are thankful for. I suppose it’s only human practice what I call “comparative gratitude”, that is, being thankful for things we have that others do not. But Jesus actually defined blessings as challenges. In his most famous sermon on the mount, he said, “Blessed are the hungry, blessed are those who mourn, and blessed are those who are persecuted...” One could argue that it is a very un-Christian thing to define a blessing as something we have that others do not. Jesus understood blessings as challenges that open us up to more profoundly rely on each other and inspire us to rebuild together. Perhaps we should allow our “comparative gratitude” to disturb us in a way that leads to action, rather than lull us into complacency. So if a blessing is something that draws us toward a new and larger vision, maybe we should be thankful, not only for what we have now, but also for the opportunity to create and build something more inclusive, more peaceful, more beautiful, that might be described as one nation under God. Perhaps this understanding of what a real blessing is will help us not be discouraged by chaos, but rather, inspire us to pick up our shovels, hammers and levels and begin to build a better future for all. The funds raised by the Giving Campaign help keep Piedmont class sizes small and fund a broad array of student needs, from classroom support and wellness to libraries and arts. These resources help set Piedmont schools apart and motivate families to choose to make this community their home. Piedmont schools rank among the top public schools in California, but this level of excellence comes at a financial cost. As the costs have increased, government funding has remained nearly flat, resulting in a funding gap of $2,140 per Piedmont student, the difference between what it costs to give students a top-notch education and the amount that Piedmont public schools receive from the state and local parcel taxes. “Piedmont schools would look very different without Giving Campaign contributions. With PEF’s help, we can provide our students with the personal support and resources that help them thrive,” said Booker. To help close that funding gap, this year’s Giving Campaign goal is $3 million. articles.text: On September 14, Piedmont’s School Board conducted the first reading to potentially mandate students to receive a COVID- 19 vaccination as a requirement for attending school. All five board members and Superintendent Randy Booker showed every indication that they were in favor of approving the mandate at tonight’s board meeting, September 22, and that it would encompass all students eligible for the vaccine (currently ages 12 and up.) If approved, the only avenue for an age-eligible student to avoid vaccination and attend Piedmont schools would be by medical exemption, in which case a student would take weekly Covid tests. Unvaccinated students without a note from their doctor would be assigned to Independent Study and “excluded from in-person learning,” according to the first draft of the board policy. “I fully support having vaccines,” said Board Member Amal Smith. “I think...we have collective responsibility in that we protect each other. I get a vaccine not just for myself, because that is entirely my choice, but I do it also for those that can’t have one, for those that are medically fragile and have reasons for not being vaccinated,” she added. In 2015 California state law removed the option of filing a religious exemption from vaccinations for students. COVID-19 would be added to Board Policy 5141.31 on Immunizations which also require inoculations for attendance for: • Measles, mumps, and rubella • Diphtheria, tetanus, and whooping cough • Polio • Hepatitis B • Chickenpox • Hib meningitis On September 14 the school board favored the policy to go into effect eight weeks from potential policy adoption. The board also indicated that as a student becomes age eligible during the year, the student would also have eight weeks to be fully vaccinated (and two weeks post). “I would do it as soon as we can,” added board member Hilary
articles.title: School Board to vote on student COVID-19 vaccination mandate tonight

articles.text: Piedmont’s 23rd annual Harvest Festival, held on Sunday, September 19, drew a large crowd for hours of fun in celebration of the changing seasons. Piedmont Park was bustling with imaginative scarecrows, the sounds of jazz music and families happy to be outside at one of the city’s most popular events. The original core of the Festival, the edible food contest, was created by Festival co-founder Susan Hill, a former mayor. The contest features the best homegrown and homemade foods from Piedmont residents. This year’s contest had 121 entries in nearly two dozen categories, including best sauce, biggest tomato, and best pickled cucumber. Contest organizer Alexandra Slatoff noted that the hardest categories for the judges were determining the Best Pesto and Best Strawberry Jam. “There were so many great ones to choose from this year,” Slatoff said with a smile. The talented Piedmont High School Jazz Orchestra, led by Andria Mullan, opened the Jazz Festival component, now in its 21st year. The band ended its performance with Duke Ellington’s C Jam Blues to a large crowd of proud parents and onlookers. They were followed by the Albany Big Band, the Bob Roden Quintet, and the Jim Fleser Band. A boy plays with scarecrow Kevin, from the Pixar animated movie Up. A new addition this year was a free compost and mulch giveaway, organized by the city’s Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman. She confirmed

articles.text: The Piedmont Planning Commission has made a recommendation to City Council to develop a plan for affordable housing using the city’s share of Alameda County Measure A-1 funds. The City of Piedmont was notified four years ago, in 2017, that its share of the county funds would be in excess of $2,000,000. The city’s Planning Commission and its Ad-Hoc Subcommittee on Measure A-1 has recommended that the city launch a low-interest loan program for the construction of rent-restricted Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), commonly known as granny flats. The low-interest loan program could be used towards a traditional multi-family development as the loans are repaid, according to the Committee’s recommendation. Traditional multi-family developments were not recommended at this time due to zoning revisions, which would not be possible within the constraints of the County’s timeline for receipt of Measure A-1 funds. “Unlike the other jurisdictions in Alameda County, Piedmont does not have properties that are readily available for multi-family development,” said Piedmont Planning Director Kevin Jackson. “They are generally too small in size or are occupied by an ongoing use that is not for multi-family. To transition city-owned land for multi-family development would require general plan amendments and revisions to zoning regulations. These are processes that take a good deal of community engagement and time, time that the county’s timeline does not provide.” Voters adopted Measure A-1 in 2016, the Alameda County Affordable Housing Bond, a $580 million property tax revenue bond. The County Board of Supervisors established guidelines for the use of that funding in 2017, and directed that funds be used to create new and affordable housing. Piedmont received a base allocation of $2.2 million in the form of a low interest loan at 3%. All five board members and Superintendent Randy Booker showed every indication that they were in favor of approving the mandate at tonight’s board meeting, September 22, and that it would encompass all students eligible for the vaccine (currently ages 12 and up.) If approved, the only avenue for an age-eligible student to avoid vaccination and attend Piedmont schools would be by medical exemption, in which case a student would take weekly Covid tests. Unvaccinated students without a note from their doctor would be assigned to Independent Study and “excluded from in-person learning,” according to the first draft of the board policy. “I fully support having vaccines,” said Board Member Amal Smith. “I think...we have collective responsibility in that we protect each other. I get a vaccine not just for myself, because that is entirely my choice, but I do it also for those that can’t have one, for those that are medically fragile and have reasons for not being vaccinated,” she added. In 2015 California state law removed the option of filing a religious exemption from vaccinations for students. COVID-19 would be added to Board Policy 5141.31 on Immunizations which also require inoculations for attendance for: • Measles, mumps, and rubella • Diphtheria, tetanus, and whooping cough • Polio • Hepatitis B • Chickenpox • Hib meningitis On September 14 the school board favored the policy to go into effect eight weeks from potential policy adoption. Piedmont Park was bustling with imaginative scarecrows, the sounds of jazz music and families happy to be outside at one of the city’s most popular events. The original core of the Festival, the edible food contest, was created by Festival co-founder Susan Hill, a former mayor. The contest features the best homegrown and homemade foods from Piedmont residents. This year’s contest had 121 entries in nearly two dozen categories, including best sauce, biggest tomato, and best pickled cucumber. Contest organizer Alexandra Slatoff noted that the hardest categories for the judges were determining the Best Pesto and Best Strawberry Jam. “There were so many great ones to choose from this year,” Slatoff said with a smile. articles.text: Editor: Thank you to the Piedmont Recreation Department and community volunteers for organizing a successful Harvest Festival. Recreation Director Chelle Putzer organized the effort with the substantial help from Jackson Stearns, Eva Phalen, Jessica Pomey, Katrina Morris and Cora Wood. The City staff made the park ready for the event and did the setup and removal. The Piedmont Educational Foundation was the lead on the carnival and scarecrows. Heather Frank and Andrea Horvath got things organized and Amber Brumfiel made the carnival and scarecrow exhibition a success. Long time volunteers Jane Reed led with the art show, Greg Slatoff with the music program, and Carolyn George with the edible contest. It is rewarding to see their dedication over the years enhance the Harvest Festival. The presence of community groups was appreciated. Participants left informed about a variety of non-profit organizations that serve our town. Ace Garden Center donated a $60 gift certificate as the Sweepstakes winner prize, the entrant with entries in the most categories. Village Market, in addition to being on site to offer low-cost produce, donated $30 for the Bill Drum award, the entrant with the most blue ribbons. The Harvest Festival is a joyous event with the participation of the entire Piedmont community. – Susan Hill Susan Hill is a co-founder of the Piedmont Harvest Festival.
articles.title: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR Thanks for a successful Harvest Festival

articles.text: Editor: The Piedmont Firefighters Association (PFFA) expressed its stance of opposition to a vaccine mandate in the lead up to the city council meeting on September 7. I would like to offer further explanation on the PFFA stance. Along with the California Professional Firefighters (CPF) and International Association of Firefighters (IAFF), the PFFA’s opposition is not a rebuking of science, an advocate of conspiracy theory or dismissal of the importance of vaccines, but rather a demonstration of the relationship between labor and management. The PFFA is clear that the legal authority rests with the city to enact and enforce a mandate, but also implores the city administration to negotiate the details and impacts of such a mandate. Any workplace mandate has the potential to greatly affect workers. It is the union’s responsibility to be sure that those effects are not detrimental or unfair. As of the September 7 meeting and given the information available, union leadership was not prepared to offer support of a directive that was not fully developed into policy. The goals of the City and the PFFA with regard to addressing Covid are not at odds. articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) has raised working capital to upgrade and rebuild K-12 school buildings with 30-year bond issuances. To repay bond investors the working capital (principal) plus interest, property owners in Piedmont are being charged a debt service line item on their property taxes. Lately, the school district has been exclusively issuing competitively priced current interest bonds to ensure the lowest total repayment cost to the taxpayer and funding new construction with a guaranteed maximum price (GMP). Last year voters passed Measure UU which authorizes the City of Piedmont to issue bonds for a brand new aquatic facility. I endorsed Measure UU and asked to be on its bond oversight committee. Per conversations with the city finance director, I was told this committee will not be formed in time for public oversight of the structure of the new city bond. This structure will be somewhat different than that used by the school district. Financial advisors to the city, including Hilltop Securities and the city’s own Budget Advisory & Financial Planning Committee recommend utilizing a modified current interest bond, called a Premium Bond. In premium bonds, the “true principal” lent to a municipality is divided into two pieces: 1) a par value of the bond that is charged an interest rate, and 2) a premium that is not charged any interest rate. Both pieces can be used as working capital, however bond legal advisors do not consider the premium as being part of the principal being lent. Financial advisors recommend looking at the “true interest rate” based on the “true principal”. Why go through the trouble of splitting up the working capital in this fashion? The fine print of Measure UU revealed that the aquatic facility was expected to cost $23 million. Issuing a Premium Bond allows the city to raise $23 million in total proceeds (working capital) from a bond underwriter while only disclosing $19.5 million in “principal” to the public. To enhance the aquatic center, the city Finance Director is preparing to raise as much working capital as the city can while charging annual property taxes of $26.20 per $100,000 in assessed valuation. Interest rates have fallen since the election and the city may raise more than $25 million. Did the public actually consent to service the repayment of as much debt as the city can raise while charging annual taxes at the maximum disclosed to the public? In reading interviews and watching public debates with Measure UU proponents Betsy Andersen and Bob McBain, I was led to believe – as I believe others were – that we were voting on a maximum debt of $19.5 million.
articles.title: Public consent for Premium Bonds?

The city expects that zoning amendments to allow for multi-family housing would not be completed until 2026. “A program to pursue a traditional multi-family development under the timeline set forth by the county, and before the Housing Element is adopted, is unlikely to succeed,” said Jackson. “The subcommittee determined there are too many landmines. [It] recommends a sequential approach.” Jackson added that the subcommittee and city staff are not opposed to the ideas being expressed, and that a multi-family development is integral to the recommended approach. Planning Commission Chair Rani Batra added that the community “needs time to understand and explore what this means... Development is more successful with community support behind it.” Planning Commissioner Tom Ramsey said, “All of us support a traditional affordable housing development. Where we have a discussion is how we get there.” A presentation at the September 13 meeting by Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell ended with a request for comments and questions from the public, which can be sent via email at PiedmontIsHome@piedmont.ca.gov. The Planning Commission heard comments from 11 residents at its September 13 meeting, many of whom urged that the city to explore multi-family housing development. Irene Cheng, a member of Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign, pointed out that Measure A-1 funds were designed to enable cities to build multi-family affordable housing. “These are incredible precious use-it-or-lose-it funds. I’m pleased to see that the city includes a 40-unit development as its endgoal for these funds,” she said. “I’m concerned about the proposal to use funds in the interim for an ADU loan program. I’m concerned this unusual sequential plan might be perceived...as an attempt to bypass the requirements of Measure A-1.” The Planning Commission and Housing Advisory Committee will hold a joint study session about the basic requirements for housing updates on Wednesday, September 29, at 5:30 p.m. Residents may participate in the meeting via Zoom. The three bills were signed despite nearly 250 cities objecting that the new legislation will, by design, undermine local planning. SB 9 has an immediate and direct effect on local zoning, and gives homeowners in single-family zones the ability to divide their lots into two and develop up to three additional homes on the lot. By Hari Titan, Ph.D. Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) has raised working capital to upgrade and rebuild K-12 school buildings with 30-year bond issuances. To repay bond investors the working capital (principal) plus interest, property owners in Piedmont are being charged a debt service line item on their property taxes. Lately, the school district has been exclusively issuing competitively priced current interest bonds to ensure the lowest total repayment cost to the taxpayer and funding new construction with a guaranteed maximum price (GMP). Last year voters passed Measure UU which authorizes the City of Piedmont to issue bonds for a brand new aquatic facility. I endorsed Measure UU and asked to be on its bond oversight committee. Per conversations with the city finance director, I was told this committee will not be formed in time for public oversight of the structure of the new city bond. This structure will be somewhat different than that used by the school district. Financial advisors to the city, including Hilltop Securities and the city’s own Budget Advisory & Financial Planning Committee recommend utilizing a modified current interest bond, called a Premium Bond. In premium bonds, the “true principal” lent to a municipality is divided into two pieces: 1) a par value of the bond that is charged an interest rate, and 2) a premium that is not charged any interest rate. Both pieces can be used as working capital, however bond legal advisors do not consider the premium as being part of the principal being lent. Financial advisors recommend looking at the “true interest rate” based on the “true principal”. Why go through the trouble of splitting up the working capital in this fashion? The fine print of Measure UU revealed that the aquatic facility was expected to cost $23 million. Issuing a Premium Bond allows the city to raise $23 million in total proceeds (working capital) from a bond underwriter while only disclosing $19.5 million in “principal” to the public. To enhance the aquatic center, the city Finance Director is preparing to raise as much working capital as the city can while charging annual property taxes of $26.20 per $100,000 in assessed valuation. Interest rates have fallen since the election and the city may raise more than $25 million. Did the public actually consent to service the repayment of as much debt as the city can raise while charging annual taxes at the maximum disclosed to the public? In reading interviews and watching public debates with Measure UU proponents Betsy Andersen and Bob McBain, I was led to believe – as I believe others were – that we were voting on a maximum debt of $19.5 million. articles.text: Piedmont robotics kicks off this fall with the largest number of teams and students ever, with 50 teams and more than 340 students ranging from kindergarten to 12th grade. Organized by Piedmont Makers, the teams span all four divisions of FIRST Robotics including: 20 teams of K-3rd graders, 20 teams of 4th-7th graders, nine teams of 7th-12th graders, and an elite FIRST Robotics Competition high school team. Piedmont’s FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) team, the Highlanders, now has 25 members and has started moving into its new home, the Engineering Lab in the new high school STEAM building. The team has begun training its recruits in software, computer aided design (CAD), precision tool skills and digital fabrication using a 3D printer, laser cutter and CNC router. The preparation will be needed in January, when details of the new game, Rapid React, are released. Helen Potter is Vice President of Piedmont’s FIRST Robotics Competition, and her husband John Lambert is the VP of the Engineering Lab. In a joint statement they expressed what the growth of Makers means to their family and the community. “This is our 6th season of our kids participating in the Piedmont Makers FIRST Robotics teams. We have seen the program grow as our kids have grown up. -Helen Potter Piedmont Makers Fourth graders from the Robotic Rulers, a First Lego League team, assemble a Drive Base and build models for the First Lego League Challenge Robot Game. It’s not surprising this program is so successful. Kids are learning engineering, business and leadership skills but most importantly they are having fun, learning to work together and getting involved in their communities. There is no other robotics league this size in Northern California. It’s a huge asset to our community,” Potter said. Nine teams of 7th-9th graders will compete in the First The Cookoo Carrots robotics team works on an obstacle course. Tech Challenge competition with teams ranging from five to 15 students. These teams are challenged to design, build, program, and operate their robot to compete in head-to-head challenges. The challenges consist of both autonomous (self-driving) and driver-controlled periods. The 4th-7th grade teams will compete in the first ever Piedmont City championship in November before participating in regional qualification tournaments in January. A total of 20 teams of Piedmont K-3rd graders will be competing in the FIRST LEGO League Explore program. This year’s theme is Cargo Connect. Teams will think of ideas for different ways to transport cargo, and will create a team model showing how cargo is sorted and transported to its destinations. Piedmont Makers is a local non-profit dedicated to support and inspire STEAM education in Piedmont and beyond. To learn more about Piedmont Makers and its robotics program, visit www.piedmontmakers.org/ robotics.

articles.text: It’s the time of year when pumpkin spice and purple both make their appearance. Everyone noticed more than a little bit of purple around town yesterday, Tuesday, September 21, the official launch day of the Piedmont Education Foundation’s Giving Campaign. Balloons and signs greeted families as they dropped off their children at school in the morning, and many students and parents wore purple during the day to show support for the Giving Campaign, Piedmont School District’s largest annual fundraiser. This year’s theme, “Forward Together” perfectly encapsulates the community’s commitment to ensuring an excellent education for all students. The Giving Campaign’s traditional kick-off popsicle party returned after school on Tuesday, as excited students and their families gathered to enjoy a popsicle party in front of the Exedra, with popsicles donated by Mulberry’s Market. While the popsicle parties, community events, and outreach may all look easy, the magic doesn’t just happen. The Giving Campaign is powered by both an amazing staff at PEF and an highly dedicated committee of volunteers. Working for months, they put up banners and balloons at the schools, and conduct community outreach writing letters and making phone calls. This year’s committee, one of the largest yet, has more than 60 parents representing all Piedmont schools. Lola Ruthven (left) enjoys a popsicle as Lucy Graham goes back for seconds from the baskets of popsicles being handed out by Piedmont Education Foundations’ Heather Miel and Giving Campaign Co-Chair Colleen Allan.
articles.title: Giving Campaign launched on Sept. 21

articles.text: Piedmont School District sent a request to parents on August 24 requesting the COVID-19 vaccination status of all 6th-12th graders. The district currently has 1,222 students enrolled who are 12 years old or older and are eligible to receive the Covid vaccine. As of September 21, after two weeks of the survey, 928 students (75.9%) have declared that they have been fully vaccinated for two weeks. A total of 204 students (16.7%) have not yet responded to the survey, and 82 students (7.4%) stated they have not been fully vaccinated. The survey offered two options: • Yes, fully vaccinated and two weeks post • No, not fully vaccinated No option for partial vaccination or intent to get vaccinated was listed on the survey. The survey asked parents to upload an image of vaccination card or state’s QR code. “The data we’ve received has saved many hours of health staff time.” said Stephanie Griffin, District Director of Technology, at the September 14 School Board meeting. In the event of a positive Covid case at school, the district can now act more swiftly. “If you have an exposure at school and are vaccinated and were in a mask, nowadays, you can continue to come to school and just monitor for symptoms. Last year, [when] anyone was exposed, we would be asking them to quarantine for 11-14 days,” said Griffin. While the survey was not mandatory, the 83% response rate from parents in four weeks has been lauded by the district. On August 23 the Pfizer vaccine was upgraded from emergency approval to full FDA approval for those age 16 and up. Emergency approval of the Pfizer vaccine was granted on May 10, 2021 to allow for those 12-15 to receive the vaccine. The survey will be resent monthly to families who have not responded, newly eligible students, and those who stated they were not vaccinated.

articles.text: Starting strong requires establishing successful habits early. But staying means remembering that hard work, not natural gifts are what leads to success. We all know that the school year starts off slowly, but that doesn’t mean that student should also. For many students, this chance to get into the routine of studying and getting work done is squandered because, “there’s no homework yet” or “it’s all review”. By the time the real work shows up, students have lost their momentum and fall behind quickly. Knowledge is not the only thing that atrophies over the summer; so does stamina, organizational skills, determination, patience, ability to understand, critical thinking, executive functioning and a host of other underlying skills. These skills need to be warmed up. If a student waits until the paper is due, or the test is upon them to try to get going, it may very well be too late. How can a parent fight against these slow starts? Get students started in a routine early. Don’t accept that there is nothing to do yet. No homework to do or material to study? Then it’s time to review! Maybe the student can teach what they have learned to the parent. Staying Strong It is a cliché in sports that the Start the school year off by getting into the routine of studying. It will pay off when the class assignments get harder as the school year progresses. team that wins the championship one year often has a mediocre season the next. Why is this? One of the reasons is that too many champions think they won because they were simply “better” than everyone else, not because they worked harder. Many students stumble similarly after earning some academic success. Once a student gets on a roll and earns some solid marks, they think that they are just “good at school” or “get it”. They forget all of the hard work that they put in to earn the grades. When the classes get harder and students’ initial energy wears off, they slack off and think they will get good grades just because that is who they are. By the time they realize that they really do need to study, who knows what size of a hole they will have dug for themselves. How can parents fight this academic complacency? Remind students that their previous success didn’t come easy, and if they hope to continue with their success, they will have to work just as hard, if not harder. pages.text: Wednesday, September 22, 2021 7 Student vaccination survey results By Jay Russell Piedmont School District sent a request to parents on August 24 requesting the COVID-19 vaccination status of all 6th-12th graders. The district currently has 1,222 students enrolled who are 12 years old or older and are eligible to receive the Covid vaccine. As of September 21, after two weeks of the survey, 928 students (75.9%) have declared that they have been fully vaccinated for two weeks. A total of 204 students (16.7%) have not yet responded to the survey, and 82 students (7.4%) stated they have not been fully vaccinated. The survey offered two options: • Yes, fully vaccinated and two weeks post • No, not fully vaccinated No option for partial vaccination or intent to get vaccinated was listed on the survey. The survey asked parents to upload an image of vaccination card or state’s QR code. “The data we’ve received has saved many hours of health staff time.” said Stephanie Griffin, District Director of Technology, at the September 14 School Board meeting. In the event of a positive Covid case at school, the district can now act more swiftly. “If you have an exposure at school and are vaccinated and were in a mask, nowadays, you can continue to come to school and just monitor for symptoms. Last year, [when] anyone was exposed, we would be asking them to quarantine for 11-14 days,” said Griffin. While the survey was not mandatory, the 83% response rate from parents in four weeks has been lauded by the district. On August 23 the Pfizer vaccine was upgraded from emergency approval to full FDA approval for those age 16 and up. Emergency approval of the Pfizer vaccine was granted on May 10, 2021 to allow for those 12-15 to receive the vaccine. The survey will be resent monthly to families who have not responded, newly eligible students, and those who stated they were not vaccinated. Thinking Outside The Classroom Start strong and stay strong By Paul Osborne Starting strong requires establishing successful habits early. But staying means remembering that hard work, not natural gifts are what leads to success. We all know that the school year starts off slowly, but that doesn’t mean that student should also. For many students, this chance to get into the routine of studying and getting work done is squandered because, “there’s no homework yet” or “it’s all review”. By the time the real work shows up, students have lost their momentum and fall behind quickly. Knowledge is not the only thing that atrophies over the summer; so does stamina, organizational skills, determination, patience, ability to understand, critical thinking, executive functioning and a host of other underlying skills. These skills need to be warmed up. If a student waits until the paper is due, or the test is upon them to try to get going, it may very well be too late. How can a parent fight against these slow starts? Get students started in a routine early. Don’t accept that there is nothing to do yet. No homework to do or material to study? Then it’s time to review! Maybe the student can teach what they have learned to the parent. Staying Strong It is a cliché in sports that the Start the school year off by getting into the routine of studying. It will pay off when the class assignments get harder as the school year progresses. team that wins the championship one year often has a mediocre season the next. Why is this? One of the reasons is that too many champions think they won because they were simply “better” than everyone else, not because they worked harder. Many students stumble similarly after earning some academic success. Once a student gets on a roll and earns some solid marks, they think that they are just “good at school” or “get it”. They forget all of the hard work that they put in to earn the grades. When the classes get harder and students’ initial energy wears off, they slack off and think they will get good grades just because that is who they are. By the time they realize that they really do need to study, who knows what size of a hole they will have dug for themselves. How can parents fight this academic complacency? Remind students that their previous success didn’t come easy, and if they hope to continue with their success, they will have to work just as hard, if not harder. articles.text: As the seasons go by and summer turns into fall, holidays start popping up all over the calendar. I get so excited when fall and winter come around because the temperature drops, everything turns a wonderful shade of orange, red, and yellow, you get to start wearing warmer clothes. Halloween decorations start appearing, and a bit later we see Christmas decorations. My birthday is in the winter, so it’s another reason why I love the colder months. When people ask the generic question, “What is your favorite season?” I always respond with winter. If you’re cold, you can put on a sweater, get a comfy blanket, and sip a nice mug of tea or hot chocolate. In the summer months you can do nothing but suffer. You just follow a fan around, drink water every 30 seconds so as not to overheat, and learn to tolerate the humidity. When the temperatures start to fall, so do the painted leaves. Each leaf has its own design and colors. When they gracefully float down to the ground they make it look like a fairyland. Then some short months later the snow falls (in regions that have snow), creating a serene, snowglobe like world. When I walk to school I can hear the crunch of leaves under my feet, something that gives me a good feeling about the day. Come on, who doesn’t like hearing the crunch of leaves under your feet? Coming up soon is good ol’ All Hallows Eve. I haven’t been more excited to dress up in a cheap costume and walk around the town with my friends in a long time. Granted, I don’t think trick or treating has made a comeback yet, but there are no rules saying you can’t buy a bag of candy and split it with your friends. The days leading to Halloween are always interesting because you get to see all the decorations go up. I like to play the game of choosing which house decor I like the best. Towards the end of the night on Halloween, I just sit on my couch and put on a movie that will scare the absolute living day out of me. Why not? Then not even a month after the night of horrors we have Thanksgiving. Personally, it’s not my favorite holiday of the year for reasons I can’t explain. Maybe it’s because of the not exactly friendly history behind it. But being able to be with my whole family and share a meal together is something I’m thankful for. With my sister leaving for college, Thanksgiving will be the first time I’ll see her. Third Holiday Our third holiday is not actually a holiday, but it’s my birthday. I love my birthday. It’s one of the best days of the year, because it’s an entire day dedicated to me (and all the others who were born on the same day). The day of my birthday is far enough away from December 25th that I still receive birthday and Christmas presents. And being the youngest child helps. The tradition in my family is that when I wake up there are presents at the foot of my bed. I open them with my family and begin the day a happy person. At school everyone says Happy Birthday to you. And then I get to have a party with my family. If it’s on a weekday, later on the weekend there is a party with my friends. And finally, we have my absolute favorite holiday: Christmas. I love Christmas because I have a nice long break from schoolwork, I get to see my sister, and receive presents (obviously). I can’t wait till we buy a Christmas tree, decorate it, blast Christmas music, drink hot chocolate, and feel like a child again. I look forward to this holiday every year because the feelings surrounding it are immaculate. Even if you aren’t religious you still can celebrate. If you take away the religious part, it’s really just being with the ones you love and having a big dinner. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time.

articles.text: Mills College in Oakland Oakland’s historic Mills College has announced its merger with Northeastern University in Boston after three months of negotiations, according to an announcement on September 14 by the college trustees. Located in Oakland, the 169-year-old Mills College has been a nationally renowned liberal arts college for women and gender-binary students. It was founded as the Young Ladies Seminary in 1852 and was the first women’s college west of the Rockies. On March 17, Mills College President Elizabeth Hillman announced that the school would no longer enroll first-year students and that the institution would begin to transition its academic programs by creating options and degree pathways for all Mills students. Hillman explained that “the economic burdens of the COVID- 19 pandemic, structural changes across higher education, and budget deficits” led to the decision. Mills had weathered years of financial instability and declining enrollment – in its last year, the prestigious college enrolled just about 900 students, a roughly 30 percent decline since 2015. Faculty, trustees, staff, students and other community stakeholders considered potential structures and programming for a “Mills Institute” following the closure, but the future of a degree-granting college was uncertain. The vote last week answered the long-standing question of how Mills will survive and continue to offer degrees, now as a co-ed program at Northeastern. The college will begin accepting students in July 2022. Northeastern will assume all of Mills’ liabilities and assets, including the college’s 135-acre campus and its extensive art collection. “The benefits that Mills is getting from this agreement are really extraordinary,” Hillman said. “Being able to continue to employ faculty and staff, to remain the anchor institution in East Oakland that we have long been, and to be able to support our students through their degree aspirations – those are all things that we would not have been able to do without this.” Joseph Aoun, President of Northeastern, said that Mills’ campus will become a West Coast anchor for the university’s global operations. “The beautiful Mills campus will become a flagship of Northeastern’s global network, and serve as a premier platform for our signature experiential education and use-inspired research programs. In the coming years, thousands of students and faculty will learn, teach, live, and make breakthrough discoveries on the Mills campus,” he said in a statement. Northeastern is also moving forward with the creation of the Mills Institute, which will be “dedicated to advancing women’s leadership and empowering BIPOC and first-generation students,” Aoun said. Northeastern will “honor and abide by the terms of tenure” for Mills faculty, Hillman said, and will offer tenure-track and adjunct faculty members opportunities for employment. She added that the college will not lay off any staff members. Northeastern University will provide additional details about how the merge effects employees in the coming weeks. Hillman said she will remain president through the transition. Board of Trustees Chair Katie Sanborn said the Board sees the merger as a positive step forward that “will enable the legacy of Mills to endure.” “Northeastern has consistently demonstrated that it respects and values the vital contributions that Mills offers, voicing strong support for integrating the powerful mission of Mills through the Northeastern network,” she said. Mills College students who are scheduled to graduate before June 2022 will receive a degree from Mills, and students who remain at the college through the transition will have their degrees conferred by Mills College at Northeastern University. articles.text: The five Scout troops and Venturing crews in Piedmont are in the midst of a recruiting drive that had been delayed due to COVID-19. The Open Houses that normally occur in March are taking place through the month of September. Thus far, interest and turnout has been high due to pent-up demand and the popularity of Scouting. Thirty prospects accompanied by parents attended a recent Open House by Troop 15, and about one-third were girls. Families of 5th-7th graders say they are seeking a safe environment for socialization and self-improvement. Katherine Scoutmaster Glen Tripp welcomes visiting youth and their parents to an Open House hosted by Troop 15. Photos by Nate Woodley A visiting girl views poster boards showing Scout outings. Most Piedmont troops already have girls in their membership. Parents get their questions answered by Troop 15 Scoutmaster Tripp. 11th-grade Scouts present a slide show to visitors. These sisters crafted survival bracelets at the Open House. 11th-grade Patrol Leader Aidan Weiss teaches a visiting 6th grader. Visiting youth join Scouts in their formation. Benson, Piedmont Council Executive, has confirmed that: • all scoutmasters report that Covid vaccinations or 72-hour clear tests are required for participation; • all registered leaders are required to take youth protection training and keep it updated; • regular conversations are held among the five troops to share best practices. Kids say they go into Scouting because they like being outdoors for camping, swimming, kayaking, outdoor cooking, chopping wood, orienteering, and learning skills such as first aid. Soon, they appreciate the team-building skills that come from being a member of a patrol with roughly seven other similarly-aged kids. Later, they take on positions of responsibility. Parents appreciate that Scouting provides a safe place to learn life skills, build self-efficacy, and explore a wide variety of hobbies. “Scouting is a tremendous program,” said Benson. “There is nothing like it for developing the breadth of skills needed to be prepared for all that life throws at us. We’ve seen how important it is for us to gather together and continue learning in real life, and Scouting is a great way to do that.” Families interested in Cub Scouts (for boys and girls in grades K-5), Scouts BSA (for boys and girls in middle and high school), or Venturing (such as the Piedmont Community Service Crew, for High School students), are invited to contact the council office. For more information, contact Kate Benson at piedmontbsa.org, or call the Scout office at 510-547-4493. Visiting girls and a Cub Scout trade tips during craft time. 11th-grader Nathan Fredericks instructs a 6th grader at the Open House.

articles.text: The 21st Annual Piedmont Jazz Festival filled the city with music and laughter on Sunday, September 19, as local artists shared their talent with an excited and appreciative audience. This year the Piedmont High School Jazz Band, the Bob Roden Quintet, the Albany Big Band, and the Jim Fleser Band took the stage to celebrate Piedmont’s commitment to music and jazz innovation. The Piedmont High School Jazz Band, under the baton of music teacher and director Andria Mullan, opened the festival. The band demonstrated what has become a signature sound of tight horns and lyric rhythm as they moved from the groove of Benny Golson’s “The Cool One” to a free form version of Duke’s” C Jam Blues” that highlighted every artist on the stand. The band’s Jazz Trio then took over with several smooth Latin tinged pieces including a lyric rendition of “Corcovado”. The Bob Roden Quintet then took the stage and led the audience through a lilting rhythmic set that stretched from ballads to bebop. The Quintet centers on the interplay between the smooth sound of Bob Roden on trombone and the soaring lyricism of Ron Jackson on alto sax. The band explored some of the back pages of the American songbook. including “Exactly Like You” and “Blackbird”. In addition the band performed several original pieces such as a Hefti-esque “She Who Makes Happy” and a hard bop, “Penguins of Venus”. The Quintet enjoyed the talents of Jaime Dowd on bass and Dave Casini on drums. The Albany Jazz Big Band, a Festival fixture for several years, took the stage and swung the audience through a medley of standards with their signature sweet horn sound. To the delight of jazz lovers, the band often takes slow, complex ballads, such as “I’ve Got the World on a String” and “All The Things You Are ” and invigorates them with an up-tempo beat and tight horn charts. This allows soloists to enjoy improvisational chord changes in the context of irresistible classic melodies. The Jim Fleser Band brought the Festival to a soaring and lyric conclusion. Fronting a tight band of piano, drums and bass, guitarist Fleser led the audience on a spirited journey through the nuances of jazz. Starting with his Piedmont HS Jazz Trio (Jason Machle, Alex Tafapolsky, Will Davies). trademark hollow body Gibson, Fleser played Freddie Hubbard’s “Red Clay” and Miles Davis’ “Flamenco Sketches”. The clever choice of these trumpet classics worked well on jazz guitar. Fleser changed mid-set to a solid body instrument and used it to great effect on such Afro Cuban pieces as “Bella” and “Europa”. The Albany Big Band Jim Fleser Band bright triplets and sharp bends of the solid body reminded the audience of the versatility of the electric guitar as a jazz instrument and its ability to move seamlessly from cool jazz to Latin-tinged salsa. The 21st annual Festival was a wondrous celebration of music and talent in the sunlight of Piedmont Park. After a year of uncertainty, the smiles of the audience and the music in the warm summer air created a magical joy that was inescapable. Bod Roden Quintet
