articles.text: The Highlanders’ boys’ water polo team defeated Castro Valley 16-8 on Tuesday, September 21 at the Trojans’ home pool. Piedmont’s record becomes 8-3 overall after recently competing in a tournament at Napa Community College from Friday to Saturday, September 17-18, going 4-1 with an 8-7 win over San Rafael and 13-8 over Christian Brothers to open, then beat Amador Valley 8-7 and Vintage 8-7 on Saturday. On Tuesday senior captain Antonio Rivera scored five goals against the Trojans, including a 3-goal hat trick in the first quarter. “Antonio sees the pool really well and knows how to find open space. He’s our go-to guy and we want to feed the hot hand. He takes opportunities to find spots inside and we’re looking for him when he does,” said coach John Savage. Offensively, it was also a strong day for Shane Miller with three goals and four assists. “Shane plays that corner position and we work the ball down to him, then we run our drives. So he has the decision to either be the shooter or feed the guy Staff Photos Antonio Rivera scored five goals against Castro Valley. Shane Miller had three goals and four assists in the match with Castro Valley. Dariush Kashani had 10 saves and seven steals against Castro Valley. Register today! Skyline Lacrosse welcomes Girls & Boys U8 - U14 at all skill levels. Come work with some of the best coaches in the Bay Area. Please visit our website @ www.skylinelacrosse.com for more information right in front of the cage,” said Savage. Junior goalie Dariush Kashani played his usual strong game, with 10 saves and seven steals. “He gives us flexibility on defense where we can double their best player and leave someone open on the perimeter. We want them to try and shoot from the outside because it’s Dariush,” said Savage. Game Recap Piedmont finished the first quarter with a 5-2 lead and went into halftime with an 8-3 advantage. The boys extended the lead 12-5 by the end of the third and finished off strongly, 16-8. Murray Davis opened scoring for the Highlanders with goals with 6:33 and 6:04 left in the first quarter. After a CV score with 3:31 left in the quarter, Rivera netted his first 12 seconds later then made it 4-1 with 3:19 to go. He scored once more to make it 5-2 with two minutes to spare. In the second quarter, the Trojans started with a goal after 20 seconds but Declan Linnane answered 30 seconds later, 6-3, then Rivera added his fourth with a man advantage at the 4:20 mark. Daniel Banin made it 8-3 with two minutes left in the half. CV added the first goal in the third quarter after 30 seconds, but Linnane made it 9-4 after another 30 seconds. Shane Miller then added goals with 4:21 and 2:46 to make it 11-4. Rivera made it 12-5 with 1:34 left in the third. In the fourth quarter, PHS added goals by Quincy Scherman at 4:43 and George Stein at 3:15. Banin made it 15-6 with 2:37 left, and Scherman added his second of the quarter, 16-7, at 1:11. CV made the game’s final goal with 5 seconds to spare. Final stats include: Rivera with five goals and a steal. Miller

articles.text: Led by Jack Stein, Piedmont’s boys’ cross-country team won the first league meet of the season at Point Pinole Regional Park in Richmond last Wednesday, September 15. Stein was the overall winner in a field of 73 runners, clocking a time of 15:50. In a meet with eight schools, the PHS boys were first, and the girls’ team placed fourth. Stein said recently that he hopes to win his first league title, and this was a good start in competition with Bishop O’Dowd, Castro Valley, and Berkeley. “I won a lot of league meets last year and it just didn’t come together in the final. That’s a big goal… Getting my mentality right in races is really important, just making sure I can handle a certain amount of discomfort and still being able to push the pace. That’s something I’ve really been working on,” said Stein, who was 30 seconds faster than second-place Jacob Bull of Castro Valley. Sophomore Xander Schulte-Sasse placed third in a time of 16:26.3, and Junior Christian Taylor was close behind in fifth with a time of 16:31.5. Rounding out the top five were sophomore Julien Lee in seventh in 16:33.9, and junior Parker Long in ninth, 16:42. The girls were without lead runner Ellie Black, but sophomore Josephine Oesterer continued her strong start of the season with a fourth-place finish in 19:47.87 in a field of 60 athletes. Oesterer made here varsity debut on September 11 at the Lowell Invitational in San Francisco. Sophomore Jamie Schwarz was ninth in 20:10.26, senior Mara Lovric finished 16th in 20:55.91, junior Violet Lemley was 27th in 21:43.1, and senior Molly McWeeny [laced 32nd in 21:49.8. NEXT UP Piedmont’s next meet is Saturday, October 2 at the G.O.A.T. Invitational in Martinez. The meet is being hosted by PHS. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls tennis team split two league matches in the WACC, defeating San Leandro 6-1 on Wednesday, September 15 at the Pirates’ home courts while losing 6-1 to Bishop O’Dowd at Merritt College the following day. Despite the loss to the Dragons, the No. 1 doubles duo of Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany won 7-6 (7-4), 5-7, 11-9. They have now defeated the top doubles teams from Berkeley, Alameda, and O’Dowd, and will be one of the top-ranked teams in the league tournament on November 5-6. “We have a lot of work to do. We’re excited about the tournament,” said Becker when reminded of their success against league opponents. “We’re excited, we just have to keep playing well,” added Mahany. 6-1 win over San Leandro The Highlanders defeated San Leandro on the road in a onesided match, 6-1, sweeping the doubles and winning all but one singles match. At singles, No. 1 Bridgette McEfee won in straight sets, 6-1, 6-2. At No. 2, Michaela Bini won 6-3, 6-2. Annika Gilliland also won at No. 4 singles, 6-1, 6-2. The only loss was at No. 3, with Staff Photos Amanda Becker (back) and Audrey Mahany added another league win against Bishop O’Dowd. They are undefeated against WACC opponents. Sophomore Annika Gilliland won in straight sets against San Leandro and had a narrow three-set loss against O’Dowd. Our team is here to solve your plumbing, heating and cooling problems! articles.text: The Highlanders lost to the Castro Valley Trojans 22-12 under the lights at Witter Field on Friday, September 17 for their league opener in the newly created Mission Valley division of the Western Alameda County Piedmont was able to generate 176 total rushing yards, but was unable to punch the go-ahead score with a couple of opportunities while trailing 16-12 in the second half. It marks the Trojans’ first win of the season at 1-3. “Despite losing, I think we took a step further this week. 16-kids strong, I’m proud that nobody quit. We’re building, I told them to hold their heads high and have so much to be proud of. At the end of the day, we’re 0-2, but I’m really proud of these kids. We’ll keep working to get it right,” said coach Jerome Johnson. Piedmont opened scoring on the third possession of the game after senior Evan McConathy gained a fumble recovery at CV’s own 17 yard line. But after three straight incompletion, Piedmont sat on 4th-and-10 and offensive coordinator Jamar Julien made the aggressive call to go for it. On a pass over the middle, junior Ryan McConathy broke a tackle with about 4 yards before the marker, taking it to the five. The drama wasn’t over. On a third-down touchdown run from the five by quarterback Nico Defazio, a holding call pushed them back to the 15. The next play on 3rd-and-15, Defazio found Evan McConathy unmanned in the end zone for the leaping grab, making it 6-0 after a missed point after try with 7:36 left in the first quarter. However, Piedmont’s lead was short-lived as Castro Valley scored on its ensuing possession by way of a 71-yard screen to their running back Jalen Melancon breaking several tackles on the way. A two-point conversion made it 8-6 Trojans with 6:30 to go in the first. The Highlanders committed a pair of costly penalties on the next series. Lucas Bernales broke a nine-yard run near midfield, but PHS was penalized 15 yards for blocking in the back. After working their way back to 3rd-and-4, a false start made it 3rd-and-9— leading to a punt. Castro Valley scored on its next possession on a 19-yard pass after eating up over four minutes with 11:50 left in the second quarter, making it 16-6. With 5:29 remaining in the half, PHS retained possession after forcing a turnover on downs from its own 37 yard line. Defazio hit a 10-yard designed keeper on first, followed by runs of seven and 14 yards by Mateo Costa to the 6-yard line. Defazio then scored on another designed keeper, breaking two tackles into the end zone at 3:44. The score became 16-12 after missed 2-point conversion. In the third quarter, Castro Valley got to Piedmont’s 15 before Mason Kimball came through with a sack-fumble on a 4th-and-5. PHS retained possession at its own 22. Piedmont drove down to the CV 17-yard line, including a big 32-yard pass to Evan McConathy, Staff Photo Nico Defazio runs for a Piedmont touchdown in the second quarter.

articles.text: The Piedmont volleyball team was victorious 3-1 over St. Joseph on Monday, September 20 at Binks Rawlings Gym. The scores were 27-25, 18-25, 25-19, 25-22. It marked the Highlanders’ second win over the Pilots this season, improving their record to 2-2. “We played well tonight. I felt confident in our ability to adjust during the game,” said coach Leslie Blakely. It was a big match for senior leader Ruby Shaffer. A middle blocker, with 12 kills, three blocks, and an ace. She recorded six spikes in the third set and two monumental blocks in the final fourth set. “It all has to do with our energy. We lost some energy in the second set and then were able to power back in the third set. It takes everyone time to mesh together and make things click toward getting points,” said Shaffer. “Ruby is one of our main hitters. She really came through in owning her position. The middle is difficult to defend and that can lead to points,” said Blakely. Game Recap It was a heated first set 27-25 victory for Piedmont with junior outside hitter Tara Kothari leading the way with six kills. St. Joe opened with a 3-1 lead, but PHS powered ahead at 7-6 and continued its advantage to 23-18. However, the Pilots scored six straight points to jump ahead 24-23, holding set point, but committed an offensive error into the net to make it 24-24. Shelby Cavenaugh made a hard spike to put her team up 25-24, and Sadie Town finished things off with an ace that skipped off the St. Joes libero’s hand, 26-24. articles.text: After losing 12-4 to Berkeley on Tuesday, September 14, Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team beat Newark Memorial 8-5 the following day. The victory over Newark was an impressive defensive display, with 20 steals from eight different players, including six by Annika Nilsson and four by Odessa Dando. “If we play good defense, we’ll be in every game. We’ve been working on capitalizing on any opportunities that are given to us. The girls are ready to give it their all. Our defense has been able to press and we’re good at zoning. It leads to a lot of steals and turnovers,” said coach Sarah Mooney. 8-5 win over Newark Memorial After two minutes, Piedmont’s Maddy Payne made a sneaky steal and fed Frankie Broening for the first goal. Then with three minutes left in the quarter, Nilsson scored from a five-meter shot, 2-0. In the second quarter, Newark scored their first goal at the 5:03 mark with a long shot and make it 2-1, which was the score at halftime after several defensive possessions and critical saves by goalie Elizabeth Ethington to keep her team ahead. Newark tied it at 2-2 just 20 seconds into the third quarter, but hole set Macie Gard put PHS back ahead 3-2 with 6:02 left in the third on a long pass from Ethington. At the 4:50 mark, Newark converted to knot the score at 3-3and went ahead 5-3 with 3:04 left in the third quarter. It would be their last goal. PHS began the turnaround with 2:48 left in the third, when Gard scored again to make it 5-4. In the fourth, PHS was awarded a penalty shot in front of the net with 4:47 to go. Katarina Melian slotted the attempt to tie it 5-5. Then 30 seconds later, Gard put Macie Gard supplying defense on Berkeley’s attacker. She had four goals against Newark Memorial. Odessa Dando had four steals against Newark Memorial.
articles.title: Girls Water Polo splits last two matches

articles.text: Piedmont’s freshman volleyball team competed in the Stockton Classic on Saturday, September 18, winning three of their four matches and winning the consolation bracket. After losing the opener with Franklin, 20-25, 20-25, they stormed back for a 25-23, 25-5 win over Kimball, dominated Chavez 25-7, 25-7, and defeated Bear Creek 25-16, 25-13. Piedmont entered without any experience as 8th graders due to Covid pandemic. During the four games: Juliana DeYoung had multiple kills/hits at the net. Annika Hattan-Kutter served for 16 straight points in the second set 25-5 win against Kimball. Against Chavez, Lily Perez had five winning serves in a row, and in the Bear Creek match, Alicia Shaw won eight points in a row on serves. “It was awesome seeing the progress they made from just the first game to the last,’ said Assistant coach Bree DeYoung, a PHS senior. “Their communication, energy, and strength rose with each play and serve they made.” Juliana DeYoung (11) with a kill. Also pictured are Lily Perez (8), Maddie Xiong (3), Annika Hattan-Kutter (6), and Alicia Shaw (7)
articles.title: Frosh volleyball team goes 3-1 at Stockton Classic

articles.text: Piedmont’s golf team competed in a 3-school tournament on Thursday, September 16 at the Sequoyah Country Club in Oakland. In dual scoring, Piedmont defeated Berkeley with 277-308, but lost to Alameda 224-277. It marked the team’s home opener after switching from Claremont Country Club, its home course for decades, to Sequoyah CC, O’Dowd’s home course. It’s a difficult course in the Oakland hills that has a number of greens separated from fairways on upward slopes, surrounded by bunkers. “The rolling fairways of Sequoyah was the setting for the Highlanders’ home opener. Alameda showed why they continue to be atop the league. Penny Chai shot an even par 35 for them. But we picked up a win against Berkeley, Aryana Fisher was our low medalist,” said PHS coach Howard Oliver. Aryana Fisher shot a 49 on the day, while Krysta Tsukahara finished with a 56, Rahimeen Shah shot a 57, Mei Assalian had a 57, and Dabney Warner shot a 58. The win with Berkeley improves their record to 3-1. With wins against Berkeley and Photos by Vincent Fisher Coach Howard Oliver (left) talks with the golf team. Pictured are (front) Mei Assalian (left), Krysta Tsukhara; (back) Rahimeen Shah, Dabney Warner, Mackenzie Seto-Nguyen, and Aryana Fisher Castro Valley, Piedmont may be in a position to take over the No. 2 spot in league standings in the Western Alameda County Conference. A win against Bishop O’Dowd on September 23 at the Metro Links Golf Course near the Oakland Airport will help solidify that. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-1) will compete with Bishop O’Dowd, Alameda, and Castro Valley tomorrow, September 23 at 3:30 p.m. The squad will have another four-way tourney one week later on September 30 with, Arroyo (San Lorenzo), San Leandro, and O’Dowd at a course to be determined. Ayana Fisher was Piedmont’s low medalist in a match at Sequoyah Country Club, shooting a 49. Krysta Tsukahara finished with a 56 at the Sequoyah Country Club. Rahimeen Shah closed the day with a 57.
articles.title: PHS in golf tourney with Alameda, Berkeley

articles.text: Scots JV quarterback Markos Lagios races past Castro Valley defenders in Piedmont’s 21-17 victory. Piedmont’s JV football team defeated Castro Valley 21-17 at Witter Field on Friday, September 17, to remain undefeated after two games. The first score of the game came when Sam Shelby intercepted a Trojan throw and ran it back 20 yards for a touchdown. The Scots scored a second TD when Kellen Thiel had an amazing punt return of 50 yards bringing the score to 14-0. The Trojans had a 65-yard run for their first touchdown to close out the first quarter at 14-7. Tommy Ashton scored in the 2nd quarter to increase Piedmont’s lead to 21-7 at halftime. Castro Valley kicked a 35-yard field goal in the third quarter for a 21-10 score. With three minutes left in the game, Trojan Anthony Mars made a 60-yard run for the final score of the game, 21-17, Piedmont.
articles.title: JV football team undefeated

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Boosters Club is planning an Oktoberfest event on Sunday, October 17 from noon to 5 p.m. in Piedmont Park. The event is a fundraiser for high school athletics, explained Chris Hart. The event will feature beer tasting from six Northern California breweries, wine from Wente Vineyards, grilled brats from Piedmont Grocery, Firebrand artisan pretzels, live music, and games. Tickets range for $1 for kids to $200 for VIP tickets. A $25 ticket Includes admission and one drink. A $30 ticket includes admission, a logo wine glass and a tasting flight of wines from Wente Vineyards. Tickets are available online at www.piedmontathletics.com/ oktoberfest.
articles.title: PHS Boosters to host Oktoberfest event Oct. 17

articles.text: Sistine Chapel, by Nam June Paik The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s exhibition of the work of Nam June Paik will be on display through October 3. The exhibition, which opened in May, includes more than 200 works by the experimental artist who bridged art, music, performance, and technology in groundbreaking ways. The Korean-American artist, who died in 2006, worked with a variety of media and is considered to be the founder of the video art medium. He is credited with the first use of Photo by Andria Lo the term “electronic super highway” to describe the future of telecommunications in 1974. His influence is still felt in pop culture, music, and film in the modern day. The exhibition is the firstever West Coast retrospective. It celebrates Paik’s collaborative approach that transcended genres, traditions, and norms, while also highlighting the playful and profoundly radical work for which he was known. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/nam-june-paik-2021/ for more information on the exhibition, and to obtain tickets. TV Garden, by Nam June Paik Photo by Peter Tijhuis

articles.text: A group exhibition showcasing a selection of artworks by eight female artists from the East Bay will begin at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, October 2, and will be on view Saturdays and Sundays, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. through the month of October or by appointment. An artists’ reception will take place on Sunday, October 3, from noon to 2 p.m. The exhibition features the work of Laura Abrams, Deborah Green, Michelle Lewis, Laura McNall, Juliet Mevi, Jacqui Rubenstein, Ariella Seidenberg, and Caskey Weston. Over 50 works will be on display. “We appreciate this opportunity to present a self-curated show from our personal collections,“ said Deborah Green, the artist who initiated the project. Behold, by Laura Abrams, 12 x 12 Sacred Loons, by Michelle Lewis, 16 x 16 “I am proud to be part of this group of so many talented and accomplished women, and we are looking forward to exhibiting a strong body of artwork in this beautiful space. It’s especially meaningful to be emerging with a collective show after months of pandemic isolation. Works on display showcase a wide variety of styles and media. Growing out of an association through the Northern California Women’s Caucus for Art, many of the artists here embrace its activist mission with works that put forward dynamic feminist, environmental, and social justice messages.” Gallery hours are on Saturdays and Sundays through October 17, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. each day. articles.text: SF JAZZ is presenting the Joshua Redman Trio at Miner Auditorium from October 1-3. Saxophonist Joshua Redman returns to SF JAZZ with his latest trio, featuring longtime collaborator Reuben Rogers on bass and Marcus Gilmore on drums. Redman is a former guest artistic director for the organization, and first performed with the SF JAZZ collective in 1984 while still a student at Berkeley High School. Redman has led a series of dynamic bands playing a range of music, including the works of Ornette Coleman, Rogers & Hammerstein, Bob Dylan, and his own compositions. He was the winner of the 1991 Thelonious Monk International Jazz SaxPhoto courtesy of San Francisco Conservatory of Music Saxophonist Joshua Redman ophone Competition. All performances will be held in Miner Auditorium. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/tickets/ productions/joshua-redman-2122/ to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Joshua Redman Trio at SF Jazz October 1-3

articles.text: San Francisco Symphony is celebrating the opening night of its new season on Wednesday, October 1 with Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen leading the symphony. Salonen is joined by vocalist/bassist Esperanza Spalding, pianist Leo Genovese, drummer Terri Lyne Carrington and the Alonzo King Lines Ballet for an inspiring “re-opening” night. The event will feature a pre-concert promenade with sparkling wine, and a festive after-party. The music program includes John Adams’ Slonimsky’s Earbox, Wayne Shorter’s Gaia, Alberto Ginastera’s Estancia Suite, and Noche de encantamiento by Silvestre Revueltas, from La noche de los Mayas. San Francisco Symphony requires that all patrons show proof of full vaccination before entering Davies Symphony Hall. Vocalist and bassist Esperanza Spalding joins the San Francisco Symphony on October 1. All patrons are required to wear a face mask while attending concert events. The event begins at 7 p.m. on October 1. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2021-22/reopeningnight.
articles.title: Esperanza Spalding joins SF Symphony on October 1

articles.text: Trumpeter, singer, and songwriter Bria Skonberg will perform at Zellerbach Hall on October 9, as part of the Cal Performances 2021-22 season. Skonberg’s most recent record, “Nothing Never Happens,” includes arrangements of music by Queen, the Beatles, Duke Ellington, and others. She made her Cal Performances debut last winter in an online concert, and now returns for a live, in-person concert on October 9 accompanied by her jazz band. Skonberg has reflected on her need for connection with an audience. “When I return to performing live,” she said, “I’ll expect it to be more singalong interactive, more giving, more ways to connect.” The performance begins at 8 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https://calperformances.org/ events/2021-22/jazz/bria-skonberg-2122/. Bria Skonberg Photo by Georgia Nerheim
articles.title: Trumpeter Bria Skonberg at Zellerbach Oct. 9

articles.text: Perspective is a very important component of life. Some people go places and always have a good time. Other people go to the most beautiful places on earth and are miserable. A correspondent wrote to me from one of the most extraordinary places on earth. Cabo San Lucas is one of those places. It is one of the dividing lines of the earth, situated at the far end of the Baja Peninsula at the point where the Pacific Ocean and the Sea of Cortez meet. Gibraltar has a similar reputation as do the southern-most points of South America and Africa. My friends had a wonderful time there. Cabo San Lucas was so intriguing that I did a little bit of research on the Internet. Wouldn’t you know it… One of the reviews was negative in the extreme. That intrigued me. I delved even deeper. Forget the negatives. Let me give you the report as seen by the most objective people I know. International travel to Cabo San Lucas is relatively easy because there are nonstop flights. Medical clearance is also relatively easy. All health precautions are observed, and the hotel can even administer the Covid test. There are many resorts in the area ranging in price from cheap and tawdry to super expensive. The Nobu Hotel was selected. It is a self-contained complex combining a hotel, diverse restaurants, and all sorts of resort activities. At the Nobu there is a calm atmosphere, but it doesn’t cater to old fogeys. Dining is upscale. There is an elegant Japanese restaurant, a gourmet style Mexican restaurant, and a high endsteak restaurant. Three people shared a gigantic tomahawk steak priced at $125. It was supposed to feed two people, but three people couldn’t even finish it. That is just one example. Some of the restaurants have a dress code. Men were well dressed wearing a jacket, tie and slacks, and the women dressed in spectacular fashion. I am keeping the best for last. What is the price tag for all this VIP luxury? Keep in mind that everything was planned by a professional event planner who was the third person in the party. If you booked a room for three nights, you got the fourth night for free. The room for three people was $500 per night. How about some local music during summer? Some of the recent events on the lawn at the Piedmont Center for the Arts inspired me to make the following suggestion: Piedmont should have a municipal band or orchestra playing concerts during the summer – on a regular basis. There have been famous municipal bands in other cities. Why not in Piedmont? Think about the joy provided by the municipal bands of San Francisco and Oakland in the summer at outdoor concerts. Why not here? The Oakland Municipal Band plays at Lake Merritt on weekends, as does the San Francisco Municipal Band at the Music Concourse in Golden Gate Park.

articles.text: The Montclair Lions Club and Montclair Village Association are collaborating to bring back the Restaurant Walk to Montclair Village. Next Tuesday evening, September 28, from 6:00 to 8:30 p.m. a total of 14 merchants will open their doors and provide samples of their food and/or drink. Tickets to the event, called Passports, can be purchased online at MontclairVillage.com, El Agavero Restaurant on Mountain Blvd. is always a favorite stop on the Walk. Showcasing an extensive tequila selection alongside their authentic Mexican cuisine, the Oakland restaurant has three generations of family ownership at the helm in advance at The Book Tree on La Salle Avenue, or in front of US Bank, 1998 Mountain Blvd., on the day of the event. The cost is $30, with proceeds going to support local non-profits, schools, and other worthy causes through the Lions Club. The Restaurant Walk also is an effort to bring some muchneeded attention and patronage to the business owners of Montclair. The Montclair Lions Club will continue the tradition of supporting other service organizations and groups looking to raise some funds for their community work. Any organization wishing to sell a minimum of 10 tickets will receive 50% of the ticket proceeds. That’s $15 per ticket sold. For more information contact Leslie Masler with the Lions Club at 510-213-2530. New this year is the Wine and Beer Tasting Pavilion. Purchase a Wine and Beer Tasting package for an additional $25 and receive artisan wine pours from Wachira Wines, P. Harell Wines, R&B Cellars, and Montclair’s Perle Wine Bar and Bistro. Craft beers will be showcased by Taps and Takeout of Montclair. Wine and Beer tasting tickets are only available online and at the event. For advance tickets see MontclairVillage.com. The annual Restaurant Walk has been on pause for two years due to the COVID pandemic. For over 20 years this event has provided benefits to the Lions Club Centers for the Blind, the Leo Club at Oakland High School, and Montclair Lions Club Charities including Skyline High School, Montera Middle, Montclair, Joaquin Miller, and Thornhill Schools. The Montclair Lions Club supports local events like the Planter Mosaic program, Montclair Easter Egg Hunt, Annual Free Halloween Parade, and community cleanups. The Walk allows people to gather outdoors safely, support small businesses, and enjoy an evening Co-owners Beth Barrett and Virginia Davis of Yellow Door Café, 6466 Moraga Avenue, said they are excited to take part for the first time in the Montclair Restaurant Walk and will be offering sweet treats. tasting new menu items alongside Village favorites. This year a portion of the proceeds will go to provide financial relief to Montclair restaurants that suffered hardship due to the impacts of the COVID-19 virus. Maureen Powers is a member of Montclair Lions Club. Close To Home Favorite & McCaulous.com
articles.title: Montclair Restaurant Walk returns Sept. 28

articles.text: Courtesy of Edward Jones It’s been called the “Great Resignation” – the large number of Americans voluntarily leaving their jobs. If you plan to be part of it (ideally with another source of employment lined up), you’ll need to make the financial moves necessary to keep making progress toward your long-term goals. Here’s some background: After a year in which the pandemic caused so many people to lose their jobs, the economy is opening back up, but the “quit rate” – the number of jobs people have voluntarily left – has been breaking records. Some economists say this high quit rate is because people are confident of getting better jobs, with higher pay and more flexibility to work at home, or because they are preparing to start their own business or join the gig economy. If you’re thinking of joining this temporary migration from the workforce, how can you help ensure that you’ll be financially stable and can continue to make progress toward your long-term goals? Your first move is to look clearly at your financial situation. As mentioned above, it’s best to have new employment in hand before you quit your job. Alternatively, perhaps you have a spouse or life partner who earns enough to sustain the two of you, or you’ve built up an emergency fund that gives you a cushion. However, if your short-term income is less than you previously earned or you need to go without a paycheck for a while, could you still pay your bills? If you are strapped for cash, you might be tempted to tap into your 401(k) or other employer-sponsored retirement plan. But this move will generally result in taxes and, if you are younger than 59 ½, a 10 percent penalty as well. Because of this, and because your retirement accounts are designed to be a financial resource after you retire, think twice before dipping into these funds if you leave your current employer. If your employer allows it, you can leave your money in the 401(k) so you’ll still be accumulating resources for retirement. You also have the option to roll those funds into an individual retirement account (IRA) or a new employer’s retirement plan. And if you plan to work for yourself as a freelancer, consultant or business owner, you’ll still want to save toward retirement. Possible retirement plans for the self-employed include an “owner-only” 401(k), a SEP-IRA or a SIMPLE IRA, all of which may be relatively easy to establish and offer tax benefits. A financial advisor can help you find a retirement plan that’s appropriate for your needs. Here’s something else to keep in mind – an emergency fund. As mentioned above, if you already have one, you’ll have some breathing room if you’re thinking of leaving your job and might have a temporary gap in income. But as the name suggests, an emergency fund is there to help cover unexpected costs, such as a major home repair, without forcing you to take out a loan, or cash out part of your longer-term investments. So, if you are planning to tap your emergency fund, work to restock it as soon as possible. If you’re participating in the “Great Resignation,” it means you’re feeling positive about your future employment prospects, which is great. But you’ll want to support that optimism with a strong financial foundation. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. TJ Stevko is a Financial Planner at the Piedmont office of Edward Jones, 370 Highland Avenue, Suite 201, Piedmont. Tel. (510) 547-4589.
articles.title: Plan ahead before joining the “Great Resignation”

articles.text: A group of members of Walking on Wednesdays pause in front of the historic Wetmore House at the corner of Vista and Bonita Avenue on September 15. In Dick Carter’s absence this week, a couple of volunteers led a very pleasant walk from the Exedra to Bonita, down Park and into Dracena Park on one of Piedmont’s most scenic and peaceful trails. The attached photo shows Wednesday’s walkers, plus three new walkers, in front of the historic Wetmore House at the corner of Vista and Bonita Avenue. It was built in 1878 by Jess Wetmore and his brother, who constructed it without plans. It is Piedmont’s oldest structure and is now registered with and protected by the National Historic Register. The house was the Wetmore family’s summer home, having been built when it was only one of five homes in the area of farmland. The Wetmore family’s main home was on Clay Street in Oakland. The house in Piedmont had only two owners until 2006. After the last Wetmore family member died, the house was purchased in 1942 by Alice Erskine, an art instructor at Mills College, who appreciated the history of the house. It was she who was able to register the house with the National Register, thus saving it from becoming a city parking lot. She raised her three children there and lived in the house until she died in 2006 at age 97. After viewing the Wetmore House, the walkers ventured over to Dracena Avenue and into Dracena Park. They returned on Ricardo, Arroyo, Monticello and back to central Piedmont on Hillside. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department hosted a movie in the park last Friday, September 17, and included a demonstration of how bees make honey. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.
articles.title: Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online

articles.text: Doris May Jenkins Lefebre was born on December 5, 1925 in Birkenhead, England. She grew up with her parents Walter and Jane Jenkins, and siblings Jean and Walter. Doris worked as a registered nurse and midwife during the Second World War. She came to the United States in 1953 as a traveling nurse and worked in several states before settling in San Francisco. She continued her vocation as a nurse with Kaiser Permanente in Oakland until retirement. Doris married Werner Baerwald Lefebre in 1958 in San Francisco. They lived happily together until his passing in 1997. Their family home for over 50 years was in Piedmont, California. Doris loved and cared for her home, devoting many hours to perfecting her English garden. She was an aficionado of theatre, opera, symphony, and needlepoint. She was well-traveled, an excellent cook, loved hosting events for her friends and family, and enjoyed spoiling her grandchildren. Doris is predeceased by her husband, brother, and sister. She is survived by her two daughters, Jane Lefebre and Adrienne Moser (Lefebre); son-in-law Victor Moser; and grandchildren Amanda and Taylor Burks, Courtney Gurr (Burks) and husband Nicholas Gurr, and Samuel and Sophia Moser. She also leaves behind three nephews who reside in England. She will be dearly missed by all who knew her. Doris Lefebre, a resident of Piedmont for more than 50 years, passed away on September 5. She was 95.
articles.title: Doris Lefebre dies September 5 at 95

articles.text: The Bookmark Bookstore, operated by the nonprofit organization Friends of the Oakland Public Library, is accepting donations through September 30 but will not be accepting donations at any time in October. Each year, the organization receives over 70,000 donation of books and media. Purchases from the store help raise funds for the Oakland Public Library. Donations will be accepted without an appointment, but are limited to four boxes or five bags at a time. Due to the high volume of donations this year, the organization will not accept donations in October. Items that sell best are brand new books, used books in good condition, rare or vintage titles, author-signed books, first editions, classics, and topical political books, as well as DVDs, CDs, and LPs in good condition. The store cannot accept books with underlining or highlighting, magazines, romance novels, comic books or VHS cassettes. The Bookmark Bookstore is located in Old Oakland, at 721 Washington Street, and is open five days a week Wednesday through Sunday for in-store shopping. You can also browse their virtual shop any time by visiting: https://www.fopl.org/ virtual-bookstore. Semi-annual sale The Friends of the Oakland Public Library (OPL) will have its Fall book sale at the store from Thursday through Sunday, October 21-24. Members of the Friends of the OPL save 50% on all purchases on October 21, and memberships can be purchased on the same day. After that, all shoppers will receive 30% off on October 22, 40% off on October 23, and 50% off on October 24. To learn more, visit https:// www.fopl.org/post/the-bookmark-kicks-off-semi-annual-saleThe Bookmark Bookstore at 721 Washington Street in Old Oakland. on-oct-21. articles.text: but assaulted. GLBTQ persons are told that if they would get their relationship with God right their “unnatural” desires would go away. Desperately, some try to “pray the gay away.” Some do themselves physical harm, even taking their own lives. Some are subjected to conversion therapy, a medical practice outlawed in California, but which is still prevalent in religious circles. In an article in Good Faith Media, Zach Dawes Jr. notes that a study released in 2020 found that 7% of people in the U.S. have experienced conversion therapy, with religious leaders carrying out 81% of the reported instances of such therapy. The findings reveal that individuals who had undergone conversion or reparative therapy were far more likely to contemplate or plan or attempt suicide than those who did not encounter such therapies. Because we are defined by who we love, we need Pride Sunday. We need to be able to name our love honestly. Joseph needed to say “I am your brother.” His brothers needed to hear it. Peter was broken when he could not find a way to say “I am with Jesus.” Human beings, especially in their families, need their workplaces and their religious communities to be able to define who they love and the ways in which that love defines them. Such honesty brings life to our souls and grace to our communities. articles.text: On Sunday evening, September 12, Piedmont police officers were dispatched to Grand Avenue and Wildwood Avenue at 8:33 p.m. in search of a stolen vehicle. A gray 2018 Toyota Rav4 triggered the Automatic License Plate Reader after being reported stolen from Alameda earlier in the day. Officers found the vehicle at the intersection of Highland and Moraga Avenue and attempted to pull it over. The vehicle fled at a high rate of speed southbound onto Highway 13; police did not pursue the vehicle. Within minutes, however, officers located the vehicle a second time as it faced westbound while parked on Park Blvd near Zion Lutheran Church. In an attempt to evade the police, the SUV hit a large pothole in the roadway, causing a front tire to pop. The vehicle came to a slow roll and the driver, a male in his 20s, jumped out of the vehicle while it was still moving. The suspect ran across Park Blvd. into Diamond Park ravine, and the vehicle continued to roll into Diamond Park ravine as well. The stolen vehicle was recovered, and an unsuccessful search for the suspect was conducted. No evidence identifying the suspect was found inside the vehicle. The male suspect is still at large. Anyone with information on the incident or the suspect is encouraged to contact Piedmont Detective John Lagios at 420-3000.

articles.text: Cooper. The board indicated that it is likely to make the mandate for those that are eligible by mere emergency approval (currently 12 and up) and not wait for full FDA approval. (Pfizer is currently fully approved for age 16 and up.) The language of the revised policy would also require full vaccination if the age of emergency approval changes to a lower age, such as five years old. Pfizer and Moderna have been conducting clinical trials for kids aged five and older since March this year. On September 20, Dr. Bill Gruber, a Pfizer senior vice president, indicated the success of the vaccine for kids aged 5 to 11, which uses a smaller dose around 1/3 the size of a normal shot. “After their second dose, children aged 5 to 11 developed coronavirus-fighting antibody levels just as strong as teenagers and young adults getting the regular-strength shots,” he said. The final decisions and logistics of the revised policy and administrative regulation by the board have not been decided and are subject to change. Tonight’s board meeting begins at 7:00 p.m. and will be conducted live from the district office at 760 Magnolia. Anyone wishing to speak in-person during public comment at the meeting must fill out the district’s health screener, and seating is limited. The meeting will also be streamed via zoom at https://us06web.zoom. us/j/85843257741

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department led a ceremony on Saturday morning, September 11, commemorating the 20th anniversary of the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon in Washington, DC on September 11, 2001 in which 3,000 people perished. Organized by Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, the ceremony in front of the fire station included 14 members of the Fire Department, Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, Mayor Teddy Gray King and all City Council members, and senior members of the city staff, including City Administrator Sara Lillevand, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, Recreation Director Chelle Putzer, and Planning Director Kevin Jackson. An estimated 50 people were in attendance. Towering as a backdrop was the city’s giant American flag suspended from the Fire Department’s aerial ladder parked in the middle of Vista Avenue facing City Hall and the fire station. Attendees observed a moment of silence for the nearly 3,000 who lost their lives two decades ago. To this day it remains the single deadliest incident for firefighters and law enforcement officers in the history of the United States. articles.text: The 16th annual Beach Dads The Piedmont Harvest Festival, operated and organized by the City of Piedmont and one of the largest public events in town, returns with in-person festivities this Sunday, September 19, after being canceled last year due to COVID-19. The 23rd Harvest Festival will feature all the traditional mainstays and activities, including Scarecrow Alley, the Jazz Festival, Village Market’s Farmer’s market, the heart of the event, the Piedmont Edibles Contest, and the 21st annual Piedmont Jazz Festival. articles.text: If you are whining that vaccine mandates are un-American and unconstitutional, you are wrong. Being an American citizen gives us incredible rights and freedoms, but it does not give you the right to endanger other people’s lives with irresponsible actions (“falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic”, Schenck v United States, 1917). Vaccine mandates are as American as apple pie and ... George Washington. According to the Washington Post, “There is a long history of mandatory immunizations supported by American leaders. After seeing how the disease had ravaged American forces, George Washington instructed an army doctor in Philadelphia to begin administering “inoculation” to the soldiers – a controversial method of immunization in the 1700s in which patients developed mild cases of smallpox before becoming immune. “I have determined that the troops shall be inoculated,” Washington wrote in February 1777. “Necessity not only authorizes but seems to require the measure, for should the disorder infect the Army in the natural way and rage with its usual virulence, we should have more to dread from it than from the Sword of the Enemy.” “The smallpox epidemic killed more than 100,000 people between 1775 and 1782. While the measure was not popular among soldiers, there is no evidence of mass refusal against immunization, according to the Library of Congress.” “The issue of mandatory vaccinations in the United States made its way to the Supreme Court in the early 1900s, when a smallpox vaccination law in Cambridge, Mass., was challenged by a man who refused to comply. Massachusetts had led the nation in passing vaccine law, but Henning Jacobson, a pastor, said his refusal to be vaccinated against smallpox was a personal decision. “In a February 1905 decision, the Supreme Court ruled 7 to 2 that public health could supersede individual rights. “[T]he liberty secured by the Constitution of the United States to every person within its jurisdiction does not import an absolute right in each person to be, at all times and in all circumstances, wholly free from restraint,” Justice John Marshall Harlan wrote for the majority. “There are manifold restraints to which every person is necessarily subject for the common good.” “The Supreme Court recently declined to take up a case challenging a vaccine mandate at Indiana University. Justice Amy Coney Barrett who received the request because she is the Supreme Court justice tasked with reviewing emergency petitions from that region of the country, did not give a reason for the high court’s declining to block the mandate.” So, if you are refusing to get vaccinated because of your individual rights and freedoms, you are the one who is being un-American. –Andy Wasserman is a Piedmont resident. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmontpost.org Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Allyson Aleksey PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Jay Russell Ed Gilligan SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Well, football season is in full swing. but this year Bay Area fans don‘t have much to cheer about. I guess we have to go nostalgic and remember past glories. Or at least some fun stories. I remember hearing about a very unusual Cotton Bowl game in 1954. The University of Alabama was playing Rice University. It was Rice all the way. The partisan Texas crowd was cheering wildly. The Alabama team and the fans who made it to Texas for the Cotton Bowl were pretty glum. Alabama half back Tommy Lewis was terribly frustrated as he sat there on the bench watching Rice roll up one touchdown after another. Then something happened that made the Cotton Bowl of 1954 a memorable event. A Rice All-American halfback took the ball on his own 5-yard line and headed down the sideline toward the Crimson Tide goal line. When he reached Alabama’s 38-yard line – directly in front of the Alabama bench and Lewis – the Alabama back could no longer contain himself. He leaped from the sideline and tackled the ball carrier. They gave Rice the touchdown! (It’s on YouTube). I’ve often wondered what happened to that young halfback who cared so much that he could not contain himself. His judgment may have been poor, but you can redirect that kind of zest for living and make it constructive and creative. Coach Bear Bryant had a sign in the locker room for all his players to see. It read. ‘Make Something Happen.’ It is the responsibility of all of us to make something happen. It would be misleading for me to suggest to you that all of our days will be exciting and happy. Many of them will be just regular days. Life is not designed for us to live in a constant state of excited happiness. I have seen a few people who are like that 24/7, but most of them were in the mental hospital – or on their way. Being able to accept our share of dull days and still keep our lives from drifting into cynicism or depression is a symptom of emotional maturity. When life is dull, and we are not particularly happy about the state of things, it is unrealistic to expect God, the government, or family and friends to do something about it. You can do it yourself. Let’s decide to take charge of our life and our circumstances. As they say, we aren’t getting any younger. Make Something Happen! articles.text: Thomas Krolczyk is the newest officer to join the Piedmont Police Department, officially joining on August 24 from Broadmoor Police Department in Daly City. He has worked for departments in several Bay Area communities, beginning as a community service officer with the Ceres Police Department in 2007. He then moved to the Hayward Police Department where he worked as a Reserve Police Officer for four years before becoming a full-time officer at Broadmoor PD for two years. He is an academy graduate of Evergreen Valley College, and is a member of FALEO, the Filipino American Law Enforcement Officers Association. He received a Chief of Police Award in April 2021 from the Broadmoor Police Department for outstanding police work. When considering the move from Broadmoor to Piedmont, he said he was especially intrigued by the various similarities between the departments and the communities they serve. “I came from a very small community in Broadmoor, but a very well-educated and influential community that was extremely supportive of its police department,” Krolczyk said. “The department and community had a great relationship.” Originally from Fremont, Krolczyk said he was very familiar with Piedmont before joining the department. “I told myself, if I ever transition [from Broadmoor], it would be to a department in Alameda County and in a small agency. There really aren’t many small agencies in the East Bay and Piedmont is one of them, so I started doing my research,” he said. Officer Thomas Krolczyk Krolcyzk added that even in his first week he noticed similarities between the two departments and communities, making for a comfortable transition. Prior to policing, Krolcyzk was a small business owner. He owned a barbershop in Danville in Blackhawk. Despite the obvious differences between policing and barbering, Krolcyzk said he gained skills in customer service as a small business owner that he uses on the force today. “People expect a certain level of customer service, and I take pride knowing the shop was rated highly for its service. I grew my business within a small community, so when I first joined Piedmont, it instantly felt like home,” he said. hours.
articles.title: Piedmont Police Dept. welcomes officer Thomas Krolczyk

articles.text: The gubernatorial recall election of Gov. Gavin Newsom has failed. The Associated Press made the announcement less than one hour after polls closed on Tuesday, September 14. Gov. Newsom is the second governor in U.S history to defeat a recall, aimed at removing an elected official from office before their term expires. It was pegged by other Democrats as a GOP-led recall. President Joe Biden, Vice President Kamala Harris, and House Speaker Nancy Pelosi all threw their support behind the governor leading up to the election. “I am humbled and grateful to the millions, and millions of Californians who exercised their fundamental right to vote, and express themselves so overwhelmingly by rejecting the division,” he said when delivering remarks from Sacramento following the results.
articles.title: Recall fails, Newsom remains governor

articles.text: Back by popular demand, internationally renowned epidemiologist and Piedmont resident Dr. George Rutherford will provide an update on Covid-19 at a public forum tonight, Wednesday, September 15, at 4 p.m. sponsored by the Piedmont League of Women Voters. As most Piedmont residents are aware, Dr. Rutherford has been instrumental in helping the Bay Area contend with Covid and is frequently quoted in the media. pages.text: Wednesday, September 15, 2021 3 Piedmont Police Dept. welcomes officer Thomas Krolczyk By Allyson Aleksey Thomas Krolczyk is the newest officer to join the Piedmont Police Department, officially joining on August 24 from Broadmoor Police Department in Daly City. He has worked for departments in several Bay Area communities, beginning as a community service officer with the Ceres Police Department in 2007. He then moved to the Hayward Police Department where he worked as a Reserve Police Officer for four years before becoming a full-time officer at Broadmoor PD for two years. He is an academy graduate of Evergreen Valley College, and is a member of FALEO, the Filipino American Law Enforcement Officers Association. He received a Chief of Police Award in April 2021 from the Broadmoor Police Department for outstanding police work. When considering the move from Broadmoor to Piedmont, he said he was especially intrigued by the various similarities between the departments and the communities they serve. “I came from a very small community in Broadmoor, but a very well-educated and influential community that was extremely supportive of its police department,” Krolczyk said. “The department and community had a great relationship.” Originally from Fremont, Krolczyk said he was very familiar with Piedmont before joining the department. “I told myself, if I ever transition [from Broadmoor], it would be to a department in Alameda County and in a small agency. There really aren’t many small agencies in the East Bay and Piedmont is one of them, so I started doing my research,” he said. Officer Thomas Krolczyk Krolcyzk added that even in his first week he noticed similarities between the two departments and communities, making for a comfortable transition. Prior to policing, Krolcyzk was a small business owner. He owned a barbershop in Danville in Blackhawk. Despite the obvious differences between policing and barbering, Krolcyzk said he gained skills in customer service as a small business owner that he uses on the force today. “People expect a certain level of customer service, and I take pride knowing the shop was rated highly for its service. I grew my business within a small community, so when I first joined Piedmont, it instantly felt like home,” he said. articles.text: The Wellness Center Support Committee has announced the second annual Walk for Wellness, the largest yearly fundraiser for the Wellness Center located at Piedmont High School. The event will take place September 20-26, and is an inclusive, accessible and socially-distanced event open to the entire Piedmont community. Co-chaired by Nicki Gilbert and KeriAnne Hohener, it focuses on physical, mental and emotional wellness. “Walk for Wellness raises much-needed funding for the Wellness Center while increasing awareness of the need for mental health services for students,” said Hohener. Last year’s walk raised over $37,000. “Our goal is to exceed the amount this year. Our students’ health and wellness is clearly a priority for our community,” said Gilbert. Participants will receive fun giveaways and access to a choice of maps detailing walks around town. Participants are invited to collect their giveaways at the Walk for Wellness booth at the Harvest Festival on September 19. All Piedmonters are encouraged to gather their families, friends and pets and participate in as many walks as possible during the week of September 20, and to post photos from their walks on Instagram (@piedmontwellness). The PUSD Wellness Center provides confidential, free on-campus and online counseling to all Piedmont High School, Millennium High School and Piedmont Middle School students. The Wellness Center helps students manage common emotional and social challenges of middle and high school including stress, depression, grief, family or friendship conflicts, and substance use concerns. Approximately one third of high school and one quarter of middle school students receive counseling at the Wellness Center each year. The Walk for Wellness Committee is grateful to more than 30 Piedmont families who are sponsoring the event, and to corporate and in-kind sponsors. For registration and donation information, visit www.piedmontwalkforwellness.org or email piedmontwalkforwellness@gmail.com.
articles.title: Piedmont, it’s time to get walking!

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department began draining the Piedmont Pool on Tuesday morning, September 14. The process of draining the 154,000-gallon pool began on Tuesday morning, September 14, and is expected to last several days. The Piedmont Fire Department is handling the draining. The city stopped treating the pool with chlorine last week in anticipation of draining, which resulted in a green color.

articles.text: On August 24 Piedmont School District announced the formation of a COVID Health and Safety Steering Committee. It consists of 10 members, including district administrators, school board members, and nurses, plus seven medical professionals from the community, including Epidemiologist Dr. George Rutherford. The committee has met twice, on August 25 and September 8, and will continue meeting at least to the end of the year. The Committee’s opinions and information will be sent to Superintendent Randy Booker, who will advise to the school board. The meetings are private and not open to the public. All meetings will be held virtually, follow an agenda and include time for anyone to bring up any concerns. “These types of Committees are valuable for providing different perspectives to assist District staff in making decisions and recommendations. The return to full, in-person instruction, while dealing with the Delta variant, made bringing the Committee back together an easy decision,” explained Communications Director Brian Killgore. Last year, the first version of the committee worked behind the scenes to transition to distance learning and to develop the hybrid schedule when classes returned at a limited capacity. articles.text: This fall Piedmont Adult School is offering more than 50 classes in a wide array of disciplines, including arts and crafts, business, computers, health, dance, foreign languages, and music. Registration is now open at: PiedmontAdultSchool.org. Classes fit many schedules, with some classes running from September 13 to December 19, and others as one-day classes on the weekend. Shannon Fierro, Adult School Director, has announced 14 new classes this year. “One of the goals of our program is to offer community to adults who are connecting over a common interest. This was hard to do through screens last year and is much easier when you are side-byside with your classmates learning French, practicing your computer skills or exercising,” said Fierro. A number of computer classes are available for basic knowledge or to perfect computer skills. Computer classes include: Creating a Website with Wordpress, Microsoft Excel and Adobe Acrobat. Students will be taught in labs in the STEAM building. Lynne Miller will teach an introductory Bagpipe class at Piedmont Adult School. Popular classes are still available, including Rachel Whitman’s Naturalist Illustration art class, in which students learn how to develop their observational skills and create detailed studies of natural subjects. The second session of Beginning Drawing October 25 - December 6 has space as well. French and Spanish classes at all levels are available with in-person instruction. Stop by the Adult School office at 760 Magnolia Avenue between 10:00 a.m. and 7:00 p.m. to pick up a list of courses or call 594-2655.

articles.text: UC Berkeley’s new interdisciplinary Climate Equity and Environmental Justice faculty cluster is, from left, Meg Mills-Novoa, Daniel Aldana Cohen, Maya Carrasquillo, Danielle Zoe Rivera and Zoé Hamstead. [Photo by Brittany Hosea-Small] University of California, Berkeley has introduced a new Climate Equity and Environmental Justice faculty, as part of six interdisciplinary faculty “cluster hires” currently underway on campus. The group includes Meg Mills-Novoa, Daniel Aldana Cohen, Maya Carrasquillo, Danielle Zoe Rivera and Zoé Hamstead. Cluster hiring is an emerging practice in universities across the country, which involves the appointment of multiple scholar of field experts based on shared research interests. “[These] intellectual clusters share the goal of advancing knowledge about how to address acute threats to the world, particularly to its vulnerable and marginalized populations,” said Raka Ray, dean of Berkeley’s Division of Social Sciences. “Berkeley has always had an interest in and a belief in cross-disciplinary initiatives, and they’ve usually been done through centers and institutes,” said Ray, a sociologist, who is overseeing four of the six cluster hires. Ben Hermalin, vice provost for the faculty, added that concern about the diversity of Berkeley’s current faculty, in terms of their areas of research, as well as race, gender and ethnicity, was a “major factor” in choosing cluster hires to broaden the professoriate on campus. “Higher education hasn’t been diverse in its topics of inquiry, its academic pursuits,” he said. “It’s been too Eurocentric, too focused on the issues of people who are doing relatively well. Populations have gotten neglected.” The University is advancing interdisciplinary research by hiring professors and researchers in five key areas: Native American and Indigenous People, Anti-Black Racism and Social Inclusion, Latinx and Democracy, Artificial Intelligence and Inequality, and Understanding Non-citizenship.

articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation will launch this year’s annual Giving Campaign on Tuesday, September 21. The Giving Campaign, the largest fundraiser for the Piedmont School District, raises critical funds that bridge the gap between what the school district receives from state and local funding sources, and the actual cost to educate Piedmont’s students. To show support for Piedmont students and schools and to raise awareness of the Giving Campaign, kids and adults are invited to wear purple next Tuesday, chat with the Giving Campaign volunteers at elementary school dropoffs and join the popsicle party after school at the Exedra from 3:00 to 4:00 p.m. Popsicles are donated by Mulberry’s Market. Co-Chaired by Colleen Allan and Christine Wente von Metzsch, the Giving Campaign Committee is composed of the entire Education Foundation board, leaders of Piedmont Parent Clubs, and community members with a variety of backgrounds and expertise. Last year the foundation raised and donated $2.75 million to Piedmont schools. To be part of the committee, call 653-1816 or email andrea@ piedmontedfoundation.org.

articles.text: Photos by Jay Russell Seniors Nina Goldberg (left) and Bridget McEfee paused at the finish line of the bounce hut obstacle course at Seniorfest. On Friday, September 10, seniors at Piedmont High School got a break from class with Seniorfest, a day of food, bonding and fun at Hampton Field. Activities included kickball, a cakewalk, cariture drawings, an inflatable bounce hut obstacle course, spikeball, cornhole and time to picnic with classmates. Students in the PHS class of 2022 have had only one full year of class – their freshman year. COVID essentially ended their sophomore year in March 2020, and last year as juniors, classes were held online from August until the middle of March 2021, ending with a couple of months of limited in-person instruction. The seniors have plenty of catching up to do socially to make up for a much interrupted tenure at Piedmont High. Having the Seniorfest one month into the school year was a way to give them something fun to do together. “It is nice seeing people and not being alone. I think [being seniors now] is pretty good timing; the two grades before us graduated during COVID,” said Nina Goldberg, a kicker on the PHS football team. “It is definitely exciting to be able to see all of our friends. It makes us excited for senior year. I think our grade came together this year,” said Bridget McEfee, captain of the tennis team. Students were given matching Turkish towels to spread out on the grass to enjoy the music, food and each other’s company during an outing that lasted from 10:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. Members of the football team were quick to toss Seniors wait for the flag to drop and for their go-cart race to begin. around a football, and a long line formed at home plate to take part in a kickball game. The most popular activities seemed to be races around the outfield dirt track on full-sized pedal-powered go carts. The Post caught up with the winner of a practice heat, Charlie Lambert, about his success to his victory. “I just pedaled faster; this win took lots of training,” he said with a grin. Former Piedmont Recreation Department supervisors Erin Rivera and Michael Murphy, partnered (with staff members, and parents) to put on the event. Senior parent Julie McEfee, also worked tirelessly on the event. The class of 2022, enjoyed a beautiful day with each other in the sun Friday, September 10. Seniors got a kick out of the games and activities at Seniorfest at Hampton Field.
articles.title: Piedmont High seniors enjoy a day in the sun

articles.text: As humans worldwide share their joy and excitement behind the Space Renaissance’s resurgence, space sustainability becomes increasingly important. Since the launch of the first satellite, Sputnik 1, in 1957, humankind has carried out over 4,700 launches. That number keeps rising, and we are now seeing Earth’s lower orbit become dangerously congested. What is space debris? Space debris is made up of all the things humans send to space that previously weren’t there, including all rockets, satellites, and space stations. It won’t stop here. Once something is sent to space, it stays. It is natural for anything to break down over time and these spacecrafts are no exception. Any chipped paint, broken antennas, and fragments from satellite collisions contribute to the growing space debris crisis. Speed moves differently in space. While it appears unlikely that chipped paint or a broken antenna will do much damage, it travels faster than a speeding bullet that can do some serious damage to spacecraft. How much is out there? As of 2019, we know of over 23,000 fragments of large-scale space debris. Scientists have uncovered this because these pieces are visible, making them easier to track. The more daunting items are smaller, non-visible fragments. These are fragments of space debris between 0.4-4 inches. It is estimated that they total 500,000 fragments. Why does it matter? It is important to view space as an ecosystem that needs protection. When we regard space in this matter, we can consider the carbon footprint we are leaving on it. As of now, no one can really speak about the long-term impact or consequences of leaving behind the amount of space debris we have floating around. Th debris stays in space because there is no removal or retrieval process. If a satellite falls into Earth’s orbit, usually it will burn away in the Earth’s atmosphere, but not every time. What is being done? There are known cases of satellite rubble crashing on Earth. In space, the International Space Station (ISS) must stay alert for any collisions. There are protoCredit: JanieCBros cols in place if they see something in their trajectory. Even then, there is nothing to prevent the smaller fragments damaging the bodies of active spacecraft. Satellites could crash into each other, disrupting communication and navigation systems. Aside from the destruction of these satellites, collisions add more debris to the growing problem. As space travel is expected to increase, scientists are working to ensure a clear, safe path for entering orbit. If there is too much congestion, launches cannot occur safely. There are proposals and ideas with different strategies for tackling space debris. A Japanese satellite company proposed ELSA-D, short for end-of-life services. The goal is to use a satellite and magnetic system to safely capture objects. This technology is still new, and it is unclear how effective it is to larger spacecraft. Our efforts are best spent on finding ways to have sustainable space experiences so that we can continue our exhibitions of space. Liliana Browne is a Marketing & Communication Intern at Chabot Space & Science Center located at 10000 Skyline Blvd., in Oakland. Following the guidance from the CDC and local medical officials all in-person public programs and gatherings at the Center have been postponed or cancelled until further notice. pages.text: Wednesday, September 15, 2021 9 Thinking Outside The Classroom Space junk: Sustainability in the stars By Liliana Browne As humans worldwide share their joy and excitement behind the Space Renaissance’s resurgence, space sustainability becomes increasingly important. Since the launch of the first satellite, Sputnik 1, in 1957, humankind has carried out over 4,700 launches. That number keeps rising, and we are now seeing Earth’s lower orbit become dangerously congested. What is space debris? Space debris is made up of all the things humans send to space that previously weren’t there, including all rockets, satellites, and space stations. It won’t stop here. Once something is sent to space, it stays. It is natural for anything to break down over time and these spacecrafts are no exception. Any chipped paint, broken antennas, and fragments from satellite collisions contribute to the growing space debris crisis. Speed moves differently in space. While it appears unlikely that chipped paint or a broken antenna will do much damage, it travels faster than a speeding bullet that can do some serious damage to spacecraft. How much is out there? As of 2019, we know of over 23,000 fragments of large-scale space debris. Scientists have uncovered this because these pieces are visible, making them easier to track. The more daunting items are smaller, non-visible fragments. These are fragments of space debris between 0.4-4 inches. It is estimated that they total 500,000 fragments. Why does it matter? It is important to view space as an ecosystem that needs protection. When we regard space in this matter, we can consider the carbon footprint we are leaving on it. As of now, no one can really speak about the long-term impact or consequences of leaving behind the amount of space debris we have floating around. Th debris stays in space because there is no removal or retrieval process. If a satellite falls into Earth’s orbit, usually it will burn away in the Earth’s atmosphere, but not every time. What is being done? There are known cases of satellite rubble crashing on Earth. In space, the International Space Station (ISS) must stay alert for any collisions. There are protoCredit: JanieCBros cols in place if they see something in their trajectory. Even then, there is nothing to prevent the smaller fragments damaging the bodies of active spacecraft. Satellites could crash into each other, disrupting communication and navigation systems. Aside from the destruction of these satellites, collisions add more debris to the growing problem. As space travel is expected to increase, scientists are working to ensure a clear, safe path for entering orbit. If there is too much congestion, launches cannot occur safely. There are proposals and ideas with different strategies for tackling space debris. A Japanese satellite company proposed ELSA-D, short for end-of-life services. The goal is to use a satellite and magnetic system to safely capture objects. This technology is still new, and it is unclear how effective it is to larger spacecraft. Our efforts are best spent on finding ways to have sustainable space experiences so that we can continue our exhibitions of space. Liliana Browne is a Marketing & Communication Intern at Chabot Space & Science Center located at 10000 Skyline Blvd., in Oakland. Following the guidance from the CDC and local medical officials all in-person public programs and gatherings at the Center have been postponed or cancelled until further notice. articles.text: A work crew from the Oaks League at the Cascades at Joaquin Miller Park. During the dangerously hot and dry summer months, the f ledgling Piedmont/Oakland chapter of Boys Team Charity League identified fire safety as a project focus. Under the leadership of board member, Christina Vo, the Oaks League took on the gargantuan task of identifying and partnering with local organizations in need of help, educating itself and others within the community on salient issues related to fire safety and preparedness, and “walking the walk” by rolling up its sleeves to take action. As has been made apparent to this generation, most recently by the devastation caused by last year’s Glass Fire in Napa and now the Caldor Fire in Tahoe, fire season is upon us and will continue to rage if not controlled. Clearing overgrown space in and around the community – as well as around your own home – can do much to help prevent disaster. So far, the boys and their parents have logged over 60 volunteer hours with partners at North Hills Association, Friends of Joaquin Miller Park, and Friends of Sausal Creek. The League is learning much from stories of previous generations. Sue and Gordon Piper with the North Hills Association survived the Firestorm in 1991, when they lost their home. Both have dedicated their time clearing the brush, advocating with local government agencies to keep everyone safe from fires, and teaching the public about ways to protect themselves and their homes. They developed the Firestorm Memorial Garden and the Gateway Emergency Preparedness Exhibit Center & Garden at the base of Hiller Highlands to assist in these efforts. The Boys Team Charity Oaks League teammates have cleared weeds and fire danger plants from the hills above Highway 13 at both locations. The group has spread literally a ton of compost to feed the native plants that grow there and prepared the garden for a memorial dedication. In Joaquin Miller Park, six boys and their families cleaned out the Cascades under the direction of Dale Risden, a neighbor of the park who plans to have a grand re-opening of the Cascades in early October. Due to neglect over the years from drought, the pool of water was filled with large sticks, trash and muck. It was quite a testament to teamwork watching some of the Oaks League members wade through the muck to pull out the debris while others carried it away from the area. All of the upcoming Boys Team Charity Oaks League meetings this fall will focus on fire safety and preparedness. They recently worked with the Piedmont Fire Department to learn how to help families build an evacuation plan, identify a meeting spot, make a home video to record contents and upload it to the cloud, as well as compile a short and prioritized list of evacuation essentials. If you are interested in joining League and working side-byside with your son doing good within your own community, keep an eye out for the Oaks League open enrollment in January. For more details, see: www. btctheoaks.org, or e-mail kimbbarsi@outlook.com. A work crew from the Oaks League at the Firestorm Memorial Garden.

articles.text: “The volunteers make it happen. I am always surprised at the degree to which the parents are willing to volunteer, even after their kids graduate. That really helps us grow year to year and share that knowledge,” said Beach dad John Le. There truly was something for everyone at Beach. Wallball, foursquare, chess and a crafts table for making miniature mail gave the event a fun atmosphere. The Chalk Art Festival showcased the talent of local artists. Three-foot squares were purchased with a box of colored chalks. Proceeds were donated to Piedmont schools for classroom art. Even as the grills were being packed up, artists stayed late to perfect their chalk masterpieces. “For newer Beach parents and their kids, it was a great introduction to the Beach community,” explained Jon Schleuning, a former Beach Dads Club president who was staffing the Chalk Art tent. “Low-key, lots of great conversations, terrific parent involvement, and beautiful weather. It was the perfect morning,” he said. Current Beach Dads Club president Will Rogan (left) with former presidents Brian Weiss, Darrell Smolko, and Arash Ghassemi. The Carmel Quintet, including three Beach alums, supplied jazz for pancake eaters: Connor Stratman (sax), Jason Machle (guitar), Alex Tafapolsky (bass), Paul Davies (keyboard), and Will Davies (drums).
