articles.text: Piedmont’s varsity football team lost its season opener 29-21 to Durham on Friday, September 10 at Witter Field. The shorthanded Highlanders, with only six substitute players, held a 13-6 lead with 7:34 left in the third quarter but watched it dwindle away as fatigue affected the starting players, most of whom were playing both on both offense and defense. The Highlanders entered the game without having played any scrimmages. “We knew we’d have some hiccups with a scrimmage. It was the first time we had live action against anybody,” said coach Jerome Johnson. “We now have to go back, break down everything that happened on film, and build from it.” “With low numbers of players, kids were cramping up. It’s a constant grind and they know it’s all about conditioning physically and mentally. I’m proud of everyone,” added Johnson. Saturday’s game featured Nina Goldberg as the team’s kicker and first female player to score points for the team in more than 10 years. Goldberg, a senior, was recruited from the soccer team, where she has been a starter since her freshman year. In Friday’s football game, she converted a PAT kick to put Piedmont ahead 13-6 in the second quarter. “I’m proud of Nina,” said coach Johnson. “Next week, hopefully we’ll get more touchdowns and have her try a few more.” Game summary Both teams traded possessions that ended with punts until Piedmont began a drive with 10:18 left in the second quarter. Starting at its own 21-yard line, Piedmont held onto the ball for seven minutes resulting in a touchdown. On the drive, PHS converted a 3rd and 11 from their own 20 when quarterback Nico Defazio connected with Mateo Costa for a 32 yard reception at Durham’s 48 yard line. Then on 3rd and 10 from the 48, Defazio hit Lucas Bernales on a 22-yard dart over the middle to the 26. But faced with a 3rd down and 32 yards to go for a first down, Defazio found Ryan McConathy on an 18-yard pass. On 4th down and 12, Evan McConathy. The twin brother of Ryan, grabbed a 15-yard reception. With a first down at the 14-yard line. Defazio hit a sneaky read-option keeper for a touchdown. The extra point attempt was missed, 6-0. The Trojans scored quickly with a 60-yard touchdown on the second play. Piedmont’s defense blocked the PAT, and the score remained tied, 6-6. Piedmont started the third quarter with an interception by Battista Costa at the Trojans’ 26 yard line, Defazio hit Evan McConathy with a perfect pass on a streak down the right side for Piedmont’s second touchdown. The receiver came down with a jostling catch, trapping the ball with one hand against his helmet and quickly securing with his second hand as he hit the ground. Goldberg then knocked the ball through the uprights for a 13-6 lead. After Piedmont forced another punt to their own 9-yard line, the wheels seemingly began to fall off. On 4th-and-11 at their own six, PHS’ punt attempt went out the back of the end zone for a safety, 13-8. Paying safety on defense, Defazio, reeled in an interception in the third quarter, but the offense was stalled. PHS punted quickly and Durham was able to Photo by Mark Aikawa Piedmont receiver Evan McConathy (5) makes a leaping touchdown reception against Durham. Photo by Mark Aikawa Nina Goldberg kicks a PAT (point after touchdown) in the third quarter in Piedmont’s season-opening game with Durham. Photo by Jeff Smet Nico Defazio makes an interception against Durham on Friday, September 1- at Witter Field. score from their own 36-yard line on a long catch and run, making it 16-13 in favor of the Trojans with 3:42 left in the third quarter. After another punt, Durham started its drive at Piedmont’s 43-yard line. They drove to the one-yard line and punched it across for a 22-13 lead with 10:19 left in the fourth quarter after Ethan Feldstein’s second blocked PAT of the game. Durham scored its fourth touchdown at 7:21 for a 29-13 lead. But the Highlanders had more to say. Starting at their own 45, they driving to Durham’s one-yard line with a 39-yard pass to Lucas Bernales. Defazio pushed it across the goal line on a quarterback plunge, then made a 2-point conversion on another pass to Bernales, and closed the score to 29-21 with 3:06 left. An onside kick was fielded cleanly by Durham, which then ran out the clock for the victory. Official stats were not available by press time. articles.text: Photos by Brian Mahany At No. 1 doubles, Amanda Becker (left) and Audrey Mahany went 2-1 at a tournament at James Logan in Union City. Playing without Bridgette McEfee, its No. 1 singles player, Piedmont’s tennis team won half of its four matches last weekend at the James Logan Tournament on Friday and Saturday, September 10-11. With a 2-2 record, they placed third in the consolation bracket. The team was scheduled to face Acalanes in the first round, but the Dons never showed up, resulting in a win by forfeit for PHS. In the next round Piedmont lost 5-2 to Irvington. On Saturday, the Highlanders lost 6-1 to Campolindo but followed up with a 4-3 win over league rival Berkeley on Saturday. “We took bronze consolation ladder without our No. 1 singles starter, Bridgette McEfee. We had some close matches against Irvington despite losing 5-2, and fared much better in Round 2 against our league rivals [Berkeley]. The win got us third. We also played Cal High in a non-tournament match,” said coach Jim Landes. The Highlanders defeated Berkeley by sweeping all three doubles matches and N 4 singles. Berkeley was not able to field a No. 4 singles starter. 4-3 win over Berkeley Doubles players only played a single eight-point set in the tournament. Piedmont’s 4-3 team over Berkeley featured all three doubles teams winning their matches: No. 1 Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany won 8-5, Mara LaForte and Rose Siemers at No. 2 won 8-3, while Ceci Defazio and Emma Eisemon swept to an 8-0 victory. At singles, No. 1 Anne Jumper lost to Yellowjackets’ Maya Curry 6-2, 6-3, and No. 2 Michaela Bini lost 6-0, 6-0. Anika Gilliland at No. 3, lost a heated three-set match, 7-5, 4-6, 10-8. “Anne Jumper played very well against Curry, who is a very good player. Anika lost by a very narrow margin. Corey (Reich – assistant coach) and I were very proud of the way Anika competed on both days,” said Landes. Against Campolindo, Piedmont’s only win came from LaForte and Siemers at No. 2 doubles, 8-4. The two other doubles matches were close as well, Becker and Mahany lost a close 8-6 battle, while the No. 3 duo Audrey Frankel and Sofia Ferraro went an extra point, 9-7. Singles losses: Jumper (6-1, 6-0), Bini (6-0, 6-1), Gilliland (6-2, 6-0), Eisemon (6-3, 6-0). 5-2 loss to Irvington Against Irvington of Fremont, Becker and Mahany came away with a commanding 8-1 win. No. 2 doubles Rose Siemers (left) and Mara LaFort helped defeat Berkeley with an 8-3 win.

articles.text: Piedmont’s cross-country runners headed to Golden Gate Park for the 48th annual Lowell Invitational on Saturday, September 11 – the start of the season. By Jonathan Comeaux Playing without Bridgette McEfee, its No. 1 singles player, Piedmont’s tennis team won half of its four matches last weekend at the James Logan Tournament on Friday and Saturday, September 10-11. With a 2-2 record, they placed third in the consolation bracket. The team was scheduled to face Acalanes in the first round, but the Dons never showed up, resulting in a win by forfeit for PHS. In the next round Piedmont lost 5-2 to Irvington. On Saturday, the Highlanders lost 6-1 to Campolindo but followed up with a 4-3 win over league rival Berkeley on Saturday. “We took bronze consolation ladder without our No. 1 singles starter, Bridgette McEfee. We had some close matches against Irvington despite losing 5-2, and fared much better in Round 2 against our league rivals [Berkeley]. The win got us third. We also played Cal High in a non-tournament match,” said coach Jim Landes. The Highlanders defeated Berkeley by sweeping all three doubles matches and N 4 singles. Berkeley was not able to field a No. 4 singles starter. 4-3 win over Berkeley Doubles players only played a single eight-point set in the tournament. Piedmont’s 4-3 team over Berkeley featured all three doubles teams winning their matches: No. 1 Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany won 8-5, Mara LaForte and Rose Siemers at No. 2 won 8-3, while Ceci Defazio and Emma Eisemon swept to an 8-0 victory. At singles, No. 1 Anne Jumper lost to Yellowjackets’ Maya Curry 6-2, 6-3, and No. 2 Michaela Bini lost 6-0, 6-0. Anika Gilliland at No. 3, lost a heated three-set match, 7-5, 4-6, 10-8. “Anne Jumper played very well against Curry, who is a very good player. Anika lost by a very narrow margin. articles.text: Tara Kothari (14) is a bright spot for PHS volleyball. She had 14 kills and two serving aces against Encinal. Piedmont’s volleyball team lost its home opener with Encinal 3-1 on Thursday, September 9 (26-24, 25-16, 17-25, 28-26). “It was a good match. In the first set, we got a bit stuck in a rut of not playing our game and it continued into the second set. But then we turned around and made some adjustments and we started finishing offensively. In the fourth set, some fatigue started to set in at the end,” said coach Leslie Blakely. “There were a lot of positives. When we’re at our best, we’re moving around and being unpredictable,” she added. The Jets were one of two teams Piedmont beat last season, including a marathon victory in five sets last spring. Bright spots included two of the four sets going to extra points, and Tara Kothari recording 14 kills. “We call her T. She’s one of our outside hitters and plays the back row. She’s really good at placing the ball. She’s growing into that role of being a primary target for sets,” explained Blakely. In the first set, Piedmont trailed 12-5 before edging closer, 12-9. The two sides traded rallies until Encinal held set-point at 24-22, A kill by Kothari and Lila Town’s third ace of the first set deadlocked the match at 24-24 to force extra points. However, the Highlanders had a ball go into net, and then had a spike skip off their hands and out the back court, 26-24. Although Encinal won 25-16 in the second set, PHS held an 8-7 lead in the early going. A six-point rally put the Jets ahead 13-8, and then had another fivepoint rally pushed their lead to 19-11. Encinal closed with a block at the net to finish 25-17. Piedmont’s 25-17 win in the third set featured a quick 4-1 lead, Staff Photos Lila Town had three aces. PHS finished the night with 13 aces from five players. Sadie Town had seven kills and two aces against the Jets. and a comfortable 11-3 advantage Kothari had four kills in the set, Shelby Cavenaugh had three, and four players combined for five aces: Ruby Shaffer had two, and Kothari, Eden Lorin, and Sadie Town with the others. The fourth set was another heated battle, going deeper into extra points at 28-26. Piedmont held set-point at 26-25 after an exhausting rally between both schools and needed just one point to force a fifth set, but the Jets rallied with three straight points to close put the win. “We got a little tired near the end there, we only use seven players. We made a lot of crazy, scrappy plays to force long points. We’re a really scrappy team,” said Blakely. Final stats include Kothari with 14 kills, Sadie Town had seven kills, Shaffer had seven, Cavenaugh had six, and Bree DeYoung had two. PHS collectively had 13 aces, Lila Town had three, while each of Peterson, Shaffer, Lorin, Kothari, and Sadie had two.

articles.text: Annika Nilsson makes a steal against James Logan. She scored a lastsecond game-winning goal against Castro Valley, 7-6. Rosie Feldman led with seven goals against Granada. Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team wone two of three matches at a season-opening tournament at Newark Memorial High School on Friday and Saturday, September 10-11. They opened with a 20-6 loss to host James Logan, but followed up on Saturday with a pair of wins, 8-3 over Granada of Livermore, and 7-6 against division rival Castro Valley. The win against Castro Valley came in come-from-behind fashion after trailing 4-0 in the second quarter. Annika Nilsson scored the game-winner with one-second left on the clock. “We kept changing possession of the ball. Then with 30 seconds left I got the ball passed to me. I didn’t have the perfect shot, but I knew we didn’t have a lot time left, so I knew we needed to make something happen. I took the shot from the left side and it wound up working in our favor,” said Nilsson. “It was a beautiful goal,” said coach Sarah Mooney. “The girls came back from down 4-0 and kept playing good water polo and capitalizing on good opportunities. We learn a little more in each game, and started executing on the chances we were getting,” 7-6 win vs. Castro Valley The Highlanders’ win marks a re-visit of last season’s thirdplace game at the WACC Tournament, which PHS won 9-3. This time, Piedmont trailed 3-0 and was behind 4-0 two minutes into the second quarter. With four minutes before halftime, Frankie Broening got PHS on the board with a shot in front of the Trojans’ goalie to cap off a 6-on-5 opportunity. Rosie Feldman scored to make it 4-2. After another CV goal, Broening scored again with 15 seconds to narrow the score to 5-3. In the third quarter, Feldman scored on a long shot from over 10 meters out to bring her team within one, 5-4. After a pair of defensive stops, Nilsson nailed another goal from distance to tie it at 5-5 with 4:46 remaining. After three minutes of scoreless action, CV landed its sixth and final goal of the game. With one minute to spare, Macie Gard tied it at 6-6. Meanwhile the Highlanders played fantastic defense to prevent Castro Valley from scoring, led by a pair of steals by Maddie Payne and two big saves by goalie Elizabeth Ethington with around two minutes to spare. Piedmont had a chance for the go-ahead with 35 seconds left in the game when Feldman found Dando with a clean pass over the defense, resulting in the Trojans’ defender committing a foul and relinquishing a penalty shot. However, Broening’s penalty was blocked by the CV goalie. After forcing a turnover, Nilsson received a pass on the far left side

The Highlander girls’ golf team opened its season on Thursday, September 9 at the Redwood Canyon Golf Course in Castro Valley with a narrow 4-stroke victory (269-273) over San Leandro. Castro Valley couldn’t field the necessary five players, requiring them to forfeit. “A three-team match was slated to begin our season, but CV is rebuilding and only had four players for the match. San Leandro is a young, emerging team like ours,” explained Piedmont coach Howard Oliver. Redwood Canyon is a challenging course at times, starting with a tightly spaced dog-leg left on the opening hole and is a Par 35 through the first nine. “The golf course is always our number one opponent,” said Oliver. Piedmont’s low-medalist was Dabney Warner with a 51, while Aryana Fisher and Rahimeen Shah both shot a 53. All three are returning starters from last season’s team. “Dabney is a senior leader for us, Aryana and Rahimeen are juniors; they are doing to have a big impact this year. The girls’ team is really, really close, much more than the boys,” said Oliver. Freshman Mei Assalian finished with a 54, while her classmate Mackenzie Seto-Ngyuen rounded out the scoring with a 58. “We sent out our freshmen Mei Assalian and Mackenzie Seto-Ngyuen first and they did a tremendous job holding their own in their debuts,” said Oliver. articles.text: Photos courtesy of AmericanSoccerNow.com Ricardo Pepi scored in the 75th minute against Honduras on Wednesday, September 8 to help the U.S. Men’s Soccer Team to win 4-1. The first three matches of 14 matches in the 2022 FIFA World Cup Qualifies have been played, and the U.S. Men’s National Team sits with one win and two ties (1-2-0), holding a qualification spot with five points. It drew 0-0 with El Salvador on September 2, then tied Canada 1-1 on September 5. It got its first win on September 8, a comfortable 4-1 victory over Honduras on September 8. The Nil-Nil draw with El Salvador came in a mesmerizing game with a packed house of 30,000. The 1-1 draw with Canada, played in Nashville, didn’t offer much home team support. Both matches were hampered by Sergino Dest sustaining an injury, and Weston McKennie being sent packing back to Italy after violating team rules. However, the United States turned the tide with its 4-1 win in Honduras. The U.S. trailed Honduras 1-0 after 27 minutes but tied in the 48th. Ricardo Pepi got the go-ahead in the 75th, then the flood gates opened with goals at 86 minutes by Brenden Aaronson and in stoppage time by Sebastian Lletget. The first two draws left a bit more to be desired after the United States had won a pair of trophies this summer, the Nations League on June 6 and Gold Cup on August 1. Both were victories over longtime nemesis Mexico. The Stars and Stripes’ next matches are October 7 against Jamaica in Austin, Texas; a game with Panama’s at its home field on October 10l and a final qualifying game on October 13 in Columbus, Ohio against Costa Rica. The U.S. is considered the favorite in all matches. Remember October 10, 2017, when the U.S. men lost 2-1 to Trinidad and Tobago and failed to qualify for the 2018 World Cup. This is a very important time for the team. The U.S. is good, perhaps the deepest and most talented it’s ever been. Since the 2017 defeat to Trinidad, the Yankees have produced a wealth of young stars. For instance, Christian Pulisic, age 22, is among the biggest stars in the Premier League with Chelsea; Weston McKennie, 23, is a starter for Juventus in Italy’s Serie A; Gio Reyna, 18, plays with Germany’s superclub Borussia Dortmund; and Tyler Adams, 22, is a star at RB Leipzig in Germany The best part? Only one regular starter for the U.S. is above 30, Tim Reem at 32. So, this current roster will also headline the 2026 World Cup in the United States, Canada, and Mexico (with Santa Clara’s Levi Stadium getting one of the matches). It was a frustrating start to World Cup Qualifiers for the U.S. after a 0-0 draw with El Salvador and 1-1 with Canada. Weston McKennie was sent home after the match for violating team rules. Can the U.S. Men’s National Team qualify for the 2022 World Cup? Now is the time to pay attention and find out.
articles.title: U.S. Men: one win, 2 ties; 3 matches in October

articles.text: The Piedmont Ladies Tennis Club (PLTC) recently donated $1000 to the Piedmont Recreation Department in support of tennis in Piedmont. The club has a long history of donating to the Recreation Department, including major donations to the recently revamped Hampton Courts and to the Corey Reich Tennis Center. PLTC welcomes women from Piedmont and the surrounding area to become new members. Players in the A Ladder meet on Tuesdays at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Vista Avenue from 8:30–10 a.m., and the B Ladder players meet on Wednesdays 9:00–10:30 a.m. The ladies play for fun in a collegial round-robin format. There is a nominal fee to join. If interested, contact Membership Chair Ann Binning at 510- 652-8602 or email her at annbinning@gmail.com. Pictured are members of the Piedmont Ladies Tennis Club: (front) Stephanie Bianco (left), Diane Jung, Dolores Brewster, Chris Moriuchi, Connie Chang; (2nd row) Donna Blanchard, Bernardita Halili, Karen Shaw, Vianna Briscoe, Ann Binning, Beth Hurwich; (top) Emily Gorin, Marta Wohl, Milagros Harris, Christine Wilder-Abrams, and Debra Aurora

The Stars and Stripes’ next matches are October 7 against Jamaica in Austin, Texas; a game with Panama’s at its home field on October 10l and a final qualifying game on October 13 in Columbus, Ohio against Costa Rica. The U.S. is considered the favorite in all matches. Remember October 10, 2017, when the U.S. men lost 2-1 to Trinidad and Tobago and failed to qualify for the 2018 World Cup. This is a very important time for the team. The U.S. is good, perhaps the deepest and most talented it’s ever been. Since the 2017 defeat to Trinidad, the Yankees have produced a wealth of young stars. For instance, Christian Pulisic, age 22, is among the biggest stars in the Premier League with Chelsea; Weston McKennie, 23, is a starter for Juventus in Italy’s Serie A; Gio Reyna, 18, plays with Germany’s superclub Borussia Dortmund; and Tyler Adams, 22, is a star at RB Leipzig in Germany The best part? Only one regular starter for the U.S. is above 30, Tim Reem at 32. So, this current roster will also headline the 2026 World Cup in the United States, Canada, and Mexico (with Santa Clara’s Levi Stadium getting one of the matches). It was a frustrating start to World Cup Qualifiers for the U.S. after a 0-0 draw with El Salvador and 1-1 with Canada. Weston McKennie was sent home after the match for violating team rules. Can the U.S. Men’s National Team qualify for the 2022 World Cup? Now is the time to pay attention and find out.

articles.text: A retrospective art exhibit celebrating the pioneering feminist artist Judy Chicago is now on display at the de Young museum in San Francisco through January 9, 2022. Judy Chicago is one of the founding figures behind the 1970’s feminist art movement. Her storied career is highlighted through her colorful works on canvas, porcelain plates, car hoods and more. The exhibition will include approximately 130 paintings, prints, drawings and sculptures by the artist. The event is organized in conjunction with the 100th anniversary of women’s right to vote in the United States and pays homage to Judy Chicago who fought against the suppression of women’s creativity. articles.text: Joan Mitchell, a comprehensive retrospective featuring over 80 distinguished works, had its world premiere at SF MOMA on September 4. The exhibition is co-organized with SF MOMA and the Baltimore Museum of Art and will be on display through January 17, 2022. As a painter Mitchell first attained significant acclaim in the 1950’s New York art scene, and found considerable success in the male-dominated, abstract expressionist circles during that time. Mitchell, originally from Chicago, then spent three decades in France honing her craft. Although she lived overseas for much of her career, she is considered one of the leading figures of the American abstract expressionist movement. Mitchell cites Paul Cezanne, Wassily Kandinsky, Henri Matisse, and Vincent Van Gogh as influences on her work. SF MOMA features a few of her paintings side-by-side, including a copy of a Van Gogh work, showing the similarities between the two painters. Her work, though abstract, resembles the Staff Photos To the Harbormaster, oil on canvas (1957). Joan Mitchell worked primarily in oil paints, on a primed canvas or white ground. many landscapes Mitchell has encountered - from Lake Michigan in Chicago, to the Hudson River in New York, and finally the riverbanks of France. Many of her paintings are large in scale, covering more than one canvas or panel. Noteworthy paintings include “The Bridge,” her first two-panel painting and a vivid work in dark hues, and “Girolata Triptych,” the artists’ first three-panel work inspired by the island of Corsica and drenched in blue-green and purple oil paints. She often painted with poetry in mind - another noteworthy, large painting, “To the Harbormaster,” is named after her friend Frank O’Hara’s poem. Visit SF MOMA to view the many artworks, sketchbooks, and drawings by Mitchell, now through January. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/joan-mitchell to purchase tickets. The world premiere at SF MOMA was co-organized with the Baltimore Museum of Art. Joan Mitchell is a comprehensive retrospective featuring over 80 works.
articles.title: World premiere of Joan Mitchell retrospective comes to SF MOMA

articles.text: Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside is celebrating “Orchard Days” every weekend from September 25 through October 31. Visit the gardens this fall and stroll through the seven-acre Gentleman’s Orchard, a vital component of self-sustaining estates and a feature of many American country houses at the turn of the century. The acres hold a collection of fruits grown for leisure rather than commercial production. The Bourns, the original owners of the estate, planted their orchard with 1,000 trees - to include apples, pears, plums, apricots, walnuts, figs, and quinces. Only 115 trees remained when the orchard was restored, but there are now over 500 fruit and nut trees of various species. Filoli staff preserve the historic collection of rare and historically significant varieties. Fruit picking is not permitted. Access to “Orchard Days” is included with weekend admission tickets from September 25 through October 31. The gardens are open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Visit https://filoli.org/orcharddays to purchase tickets. Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside
articles.title: “Orchard Days” at Filoli begin September 25

articles.text: Photo by Alexander V Nichols San Francisco Opera presents Beethoven’s only opera, Fidelio. San Francisco Opera will present Beethoven’s Fidelio beginning October 14. Fidelio, originally titled Leonore, is Beethoven’s only opera. The libretto tells the story of Leonore, disguised as a prison guard named “Fidelio,” who rescues her husband Florestan from a political prison. The opera marries the themes of personal sacrifice, heroism, and triumph with Beethoven’s own political outlook. The performance by San Francisco Opera is a modern-day reflection of incarceration. Director Matthew Ozawa presents this new production of Fidelio, starring Elza van den Heever, Russell Thomas and Greer Grimsley. Music Director Eun Sun Kim will conduct the triumphant score, which is a precursor to Beethoven’s later work, the Ninth Symphony. The opera is sung in German with English supertitles. The opera will be performed for two weeks, through October 30. Visit https://sfopera.com/ on-stage/fidelio/ for ticketing information. Audiences can also access a live-stream of the opera on October 14, 17, and 20. Music Director Eun Sun Kim conducts Fidelio’s triumphant score. articles.text: Gold Coast Chamber Players is returning to the stage at Don Tatzin Community Hall in Lafayette this Saturday, September 18 with “Spheres of Influence,” a colorful program of French, Chinese, and Japanese music. The show will feature violinists Dan Carlson and Dian Zhang, violists Joy Fellows and Pamela Freund-Striplen, cellist Amos Yang, and double bassist Charles Chandler. The program includes Maurice Ravel’s Sonata for violin and cello, Debussy’s String Quartet in G minor, Shinji Eshima’s Bariolage for cello and bass, and Ching-chu Hu’s “Spheres of Influence” for string sextet. The concert will be presented in-person in accordance with state and local health guidelines, and all tickets purchased include the option to view the concert virtually. All patrons must show proof of vaccination to enter the concert, and masks are required in the venue for all patrons regardless of vaccination status. A pre-concert talk begins at 7 p.m., with the show beginning at 7:30 p.m. Visit https://www.gccpmusic. com/spheres to purchase tickets. Violinist Dian Zhang will perform this Saturday, September 18.
articles.title: Gold Coast concert “Spheres of Influence” this Saturday

articles.text: The UC Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) features weekly, in-person film screenings during September at the Barbro Osher Theater, which will also serve as the East Bay venue for the Mill Valley Film Festival in October. “It’s thrilling to welcome our community of filmgoers back to BAMPFA after this difficult year, and I can’t imagine a better way to do so than with a series of free screenings presented al fresco on the museum’s outdoor screen,” said Susan Oxtoby, BAMPFA’s director of film and senior film curator. “For nearly eighteen months, we’ve been deeply moved by the support of our devoted audiences, who have continued to engage with BAMPFA’s film programming during our pivot to virtual cinema. We’re delighted to invite our audiences to return in person now that restrictions have been lifted.” Coming up next Wednesday, September 22, is a program of found media entitled “(In)appropriation.” The selection is from the Festival of (In)appropriation, an annual showcase for experimental, found-media film and video. The festival is curated annually by Jaimie Baron, Lauren S. Berliner, and Greg Cohen. All works are from the festival unless indicated otherwise. Films in the screening include Lying Women (2016), Sand (2015), What Happened to Her (2016), and Night Hunter (2011). The event will begin at 7 p.m. Visit https://bampfa.org/ event /i nappropr iat ion-pro - gram-found-media to learn more about the media presented, and to obtain tickets.
articles.title: Pacific Film Archive now presenting weekly screenings

articles.text: The Invisible Man is a riveting psychological thriller, and a reboot of the 1933 film based on the H.G. Wells 1897 novel of the same name. In this contemporary update, written and directed by Leigh Whannell, the story is filled with far more meaning and nuance than simply a sci-fi/horror tale; instead, in context and theme, it speaks to a far different audience about a subject that is of the moment. It’s extraordinarily good. In its first moments, the story achieves a tone of tension and menace. It’s the dead of night and a young woman, Cecilia Kass (Elizabeth Moss), lies awake, staring at a dimly lighted digital clock. Next to her is a man deeply asleep. She gingerly frees herself from his draped arm and slowly slips out of bed. Watching him closely, she leaves the bedroom, turning a hallway camera toward the bed, and quietly hurries down a long dark hallway. In another room she hurriedly dresses, fills a small bag with clothes, stops in an expansive space filled with computer screens and electronics and pauses to glance at one screen in particular; the man is still sleeping. As she makes her way toward the front door, she accidentally kicks a metal dog dish that loudly slides across the hardwood floor. She waits. All is quiet. Her escape, not without another loud mishap, is almost complete as she emerges from the woods and stands in the middle of a narrow road, waiting for a car to arrive. Time is of the essence. And finally, with her sister, Emily Kass (Harriet Dyer), behind the wheel, Cecilia barely manages to escape. The plan is that she will stay at a safe house, the home of her friend James Lanier (Aldis Hodge), a police detective, and his daughter, Sydney (Storm Reid). Gradually, as the days pass, the hyper-vigilant fear of expecting to be found begins to ease. But it isn’t until Emily arrives and tells her that her boyfriend, Adrian (Oliver Jackson-Cohen), a genius specializing in advanced optics, has committed suicide that Cecilia fully exhales and a shroud of anxiety begins to lift; she is transformed while sitting Elizabeth Moss stars in The Invisible Man. with her sister’s phone, reading the news story. At the urging of James and Emily she tells them what her life with Adrian had been like, the emotional and physical abuse unrelenting, his manic need to control her life, even her thoughts. But now it’s over. She soon receives a phone call from Adrian’s younger brother, Tom (Michael Dorman), a lawyer, asking for a meet, one in which he tells Cecilia and Emily that Adrian has left her $5 million of his estate. Cecilia has not only been liberated but she is now wealthy. And so concludes act one. But it’s also at this point that the audience knows that there is much more yet to be told. The only question begged is what awaits Cecilia, whose only wish is to regain the life she knew before the emotional abyss called Adrian. But this is a good place to stop giving you, the reader, any further semblance of a plot line. For what takes place in the next two acts must be viewed absent any hint of what will unfold other than to say that this story offers a far more complex narrative than is likely assumed. Of course, The Invisible Man is a creepy horror tale with some solid jumps. Yes, it’s all that. But it’s also a haunting and chilling metaphor for a reality so many abused women face, meaning this film exists in a context of today’s #MeToo movement. Indeed, men who physically and psychologically abuse women are indeed invisible, existing in that fearful, smothering silence and starkly painful truth which is endured by the victims. The raging horror is real, the threats palpable, and even when spoken, as Cecilia finds out, it is often met with doubt. The woman is not believed. In thinking about The Invisible Man, two movies come to mind. One is the 1944 Gaslight, starring Ingrid Bergman and Charles Boyer, wherein he malignantly sets out to convince his wife that what is occurring is only imagined (he turns down the gas lighted wall lamps and insists he sees no change), his purpose being to manipulate and control her and make her doubt her own sanity. Hence the term “gaslighting.” The second film is Sleeping With the Enemy, a 1991 American psychological thriller starring Julia Roberts and Patrick Bergin. She is a physically and psychologically abused woman who is convinced by him that his outbursts are her fault. Like Cecilia, she plans an elaborate escape, terrified that he will find and harm her. Both of the films possess a sense of sinister apprehension that increases until the characters finally says, loudly and emphatically, “I see you,” and what was invisible is suddenly exposed. It’s a moment that is liberating and empowering. Of course, The Invisible Man has such a moment when Cecelia finally confronts her sadistic boyfriend, an encounter that results in an unexpected but just climax. She sees him. And then, with a smile, is finally able to look away. The Invisible Man. Directed by Leigh Whannell. Starring Elizabeth Moss, Harriet Dyer, Aldis Hodge. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated R.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS Invisible Man a gripping psychological thriller

articles.text: Brie Larson and Jacob Tremblay star in Room. Room is a perplexing and riveting film, constructed in two acts. Know that act one is not only seemingly surreal, but increasingly difficult to watch. Not because it’s gratuitous, but because the reality endured by a young woman, Joy (Brie Larson), is grim and all but unimaginable. The film opens with Joy, also known as Ma, and her 5-year-old son, Jack (Jacob Tremblay), baking a birthday cake. They live in a detached, starkly furnished garden shed, roughly 10X10. Joy has been there for seven years. Jack knows no other world. The only source of light is a skylight that tells them when it rains, or when the sun shines. They are imprisoned, trapped behind a steel door by a middle-aged man known only as Nick (Sean Bridgers). He brings them food and uses Joy as sexual chattel (hence the birth of Jack). The first hour of Room (which is how Jack refers to the interior of the shed – not “the room” but simply “room”) is claustrophobic and psychologically chilling. Their survival is testimony to the resilience of Joy and Jack who have only each other and have, against all odds, adapted. But now that Jack is five, Joy can begin to contemplate a scenario that will at the very least free Jack. The events she sets in motion are harrowing and breathtaking and the stakes are impossibly high for both of them. Of course, it’s possible to think of this room as a metaphor. Life can feel like it has no exit and there are no viable options. And it is this sense of existential confinement that contributes to the unrelenting dread that the film conveys and sustains. The overwhelming question, from the first setup, is can Joy find a way out? Alone, without Jack, perhaps. But the thought of leaving him behind is unthinkable. The performances of Larson and Tremblay are both remarkable. The film resonates with their mother-son connection, one that seems natural while fraught with tension. Larson never lets her character slip into the melodramatic; rather, Joy faces a situation absent any histrionics. And Tremblay amazes. He is a kid, a wonderful, difficult, sweet kid who never falters in his portrayal of Jack. A final comment about films that are shot in a confined space, often called container films. Think of the room as a panic room, of sorts. A space from which the characters cannot leave. The issues confronting them seem more intense. Screenwriters of Sci-fi long ago discovered that to place a crew inside a spacecraft, to include a predatory alien, can be very effective. In a sense it’s a waterfall of emotions, which defines Room. Room. Directed by Larry Abrahamson. Starring Brie Larson, Jacob Tremblay, Sean Bridgers. 1 hr., 51 min. Rated R.
articles.title: Room a stark story of mother & son trapped

The only question begged is what awaits Cecilia, whose only wish is to regain the life she knew before the emotional abyss called Adrian. But this is a good place to stop giving you, the reader, any further semblance of a plot line. For what takes place in the next two acts must be viewed absent any hint of what will unfold other than to say that this story offers a far more complex narrative than is likely assumed. Of course, The Invisible Man is a creepy horror tale with some solid jumps. Yes, it’s all that. But it’s also a haunting and chilling metaphor for a reality so many abused women face, meaning this film exists in a context of today’s #MeToo movement. Indeed, men who physically and psychologically abuse women are indeed invisible, existing in that fearful, smothering silence and starkly painful truth which is endured by the victims. The raging horror is real, the threats palpable, and even when spoken, as Cecilia finds out, it is often met with doubt. The woman is not believed. In thinking about The Invisible Man, two movies come to mind. One is the 1944 Gaslight, starring Ingrid Bergman and Charles Boyer, wherein he malignantly sets out to convince his wife that what is occurring is only imagined (he turns down the gas lighted wall lamps and insists he sees no change), his purpose being to manipulate and control her and make her doubt her own sanity. Hence the term “gaslighting.” The second film is Sleeping With the Enemy, a 1991 American psychological thriller starring Julia Roberts and Patrick Bergin. She is a physically and psychologically abused woman who is convinced by him that his outbursts are her fault. Like Cecilia, she plans an elaborate escape, terrified that he will find and harm her. Both of the films possess a sense of sinister apprehension that increases until the characters finally says, loudly and emphatically, “I see you,” and what was invisible is suddenly exposed. It’s a moment that is liberating and empowering. Of course, The Invisible Man has such a moment when Cecelia finally confronts her sadistic boyfriend, an encounter that results in an unexpected but just climax. She sees him. And then, with a smile, is finally able to look away. The Invisible Man. Directed by Leigh Whannell. Starring Elizabeth Moss, Harriet Dyer, Aldis Hodge. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated R. articles.text: A scene from The Secret Life of Pets. The Secret Lives of Pets is set initially in the New York apartment complex of Katie (Ellie Kemper), who lives with her Jack Russell terrier, Max (C.K.). But as we soon discover, the building is a menagerie of domesticated pets, and Max, being the gregarious mutt that he is, socializes with his neighbors. There’s Chloe (Lake Bell), an obese, finicky tabby cat; Mel (Bobby Moynihan), a hardcharging pug; Buddy (Hannibal Burgess), a likable miniature dachshund; Sweet Pea, a yellow and blue parakeet; and a snowwhite Pomeranian named Gidget (Jenny Slate). The story begins in earnest when Katie decides Max could use some company and brings home an oversized, Newfoundland schlub of a pooch she calls Duke (Eric Stonestreet). Naturally Max and Duke have issues. And it’s at this point that the premise of the story is fully revealed: what do animals do all day while their owners are at work? Of course, it will be one adventure after the next, involving lots of New York animals that they meet along the way. Some, such as Snowbal (Kevin Hart), are decidedly not domesticated. He is the leader of a gang of free-range rabbits. There’s a carnivorous Hawk, a pig with tattoos, and a Bassett hound named Pops (Dana Carvey). What gets everything going is that while Duke and Max are on a daily outing with their dog walker, they decide to make a break for it. But before long the two are captured by the Animal Control workers, and off they go to the pound. And so begins an improbable journey by the two amigos, starting with their escape from behind bars. The tale is now about their struggle to return home, meaning Ellie’s apartment. Meanwhile, to keep things interesting, Gidget and crew are in the hunt for the missing duo, and are having their own problems navigating the streets of New York. It’s a frenetic tale, and the kids will find the lineup of animals perpetually delightful. It also has a nice ending focused on the friendship of Max and Duke, and the domestication of Snowball, who is adopted by a sweet little girl. The Secret Life of Pets. Computer animated. Directed by Chris Renaud. With voices of Eric Stonestreet, Kevin Hart, Ellie Kemper. 1 hr., 31 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: The Secret Life of Pets a charmer for kids

articles.text: The Croods is a comedy of sorts, set in prehistoric times (the Pilocene era). The Croods are a dysfunctional family of five who live in a cave and only venture out to collect food. Otherwise they obey the pater familia, Grug (Nicolas Cage), and remain safely inside, living by his motto, “Never not be afraid.” They are prey and their world is filled with predators. The Croods – mother, Ugga (Catherine Keener); Gran (Cloris Leachman); and brother Thunk (Clark Duke) – are introduced to us in voice over by teenage daughter Eeep (Emma Stone), who is rebelliously curious to learn what she can discover beyond the cave. One night, with everyone asleep, she sneaks out, and seeing a strange light in the distance, she investigates. Holding a torch is an evolved Sapien named Guy (Ryan Reynolds), who has discovered fire. He is adventurous, a bit dashing, and relies on intelligence rather than brute force and looks down on the Neanderthals. Guy warns Eep that an apocalypse is about to happen, likely in the form of lava producing earthquakes, and she and her family should leave their cave for higher ground. When Guy and Eep share this prediction with Grug, he is, naturally, resistant… that is until their cave is destroyed by a quake. The family is now forced to head out in search of new shelter, and it’s Guy who leads them into new environs where they encounter a surprising number of critters. He invents things along the way, such as, well, footwear. The plot involves a series of adventurous detours, kind of a Paleolithic road trip pm which they discover a bucolic jungle and animals such as saber toothed housecats and a flock of razortoothed birds. Eventually they do find a cave that is suitable for the family, but by then they have unexpectedly discovered that they prefer to live outside. The Croods was nominated for an Oscar for Best Animated Feature film and was also nominated for a Golden Globe for its dazzling animation. The Croods. Directed by Kirk DeMarco, Chris Sanders. Dreamworks animation. With voices of Nicolas Cage, Emma Stone, Ryan Reynolds. 1 hr., 31 min, Rated PG. A scene from Dreamworks’ The Croods.
articles.title: The Croods – fun times in a prehistoric time

articles.text: Piedmont Connect will host another Healthy Landscapes Front Garden Tour for one week, from Saturday, September 25 through Sunday, October 3. Visitors will see a sampling of drought-friendly plantings which present the beauty of northern California’s early fall. The self-guided tour will feature Piedmont front gardens that have been transformed from conventional water-intensive or invasive landscapes into creative, healthy landscapes in a variety of styles, some more manicured and some more naturalized and organic. Selected gardens represent a range of Piedmont neighborhoods, horticultural conditions, and lot sizes. Sidewalk viewers will see what their neighbors have created to conserve water, minimize watershed pollutants, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and support a diverse, local biosphere. Participating gardens will be announced at the Piedmont Harvest Festival on Sunday September 19. A garden list will also be posted on Piedmont Connect’s website (www.piedmontconnect. org) and will be sent to Piedmont Connect’s email subscriber list. Piedmont homeowners are strongly encouraged to reduce water usage. Gov. Newsom and East Bay Municipal Utility DisThe National Wildlife Federation certifies residential gardens which have beneficial conditions for local wildlife. trict (EBMUD), have called for a voluntary 15% reduction in water use. Since exterior water use accounts for roughly 50% of residential water use, reducing outdoor watering is the best place to start. Hope Salzer ia a member of Piedmont Connect. Monarch-supporting native milkweed bloom with monkey flower in this water-conserving garden. Native ground covers and bunch grasses are powerful tools for erosion prevention, carbon sequestration, and stormwater management in addition to their beauty, texture and color.
articles.title: Healthy Landscapes event sponsored by Piedmont Connect

articles.text: In vino veritas – in wine there is truth. Every gourmet knows this famous adage. Sorry Zenobio, you should have said In musico veritas. My reasoning is simple. Can you trust a drunk to tell the truth? Not likely. But music speaks from the heart. No commentator is needed. All musical performance is autobiographical. Abraham Lincoln said that we cannot escape history. If Lincoln were writing about musicians, he might have said: “we cannot escape ourselves.“ For there is truth in every performance. Your true personality is always revealed. It needs to be said that “In Musico Veritas” applies only to acoustical instruments, including the human voice. All bets are off with amplified instruments. The amplification machine has no emotion. The soul is revealed in acoustic music. In order to appreciate these truths, the listener must tune in and look deep into the soul of the performer. Don’t be fooled by theatrics. Truth be told, the more theatrics on stage the shallower the performer. Mugging for the audience is not emotion… And how about smashing the instruments on stage after the concert. What does this reveal? The beauty of music is that there are unlimited possibilities. Psychoanalysis goes only so far. Bing Crosby was right when he said, “The difference of opinion is what makes horse racing.” And also with music. And now for something completely different America was famous for its concert bands. The Sousa band and the Gilmore bands were two of the most famous. Band concerts were popular with the general public. It was fun to be there. But don’t fool yourself. The concerts had a bit of everything. The public had fun and they learned a lot. Piedmont relived some of that nostalgia at the Piedmont Center for the Arts last Saturday at noon. The Renegade Orchestra played on the lawn. The weather was perfect and Renegade found a way to please every musical taste. To state the obvious, the diversity of entertainment at the PCA is astonishing. And if you missed it, come back: there will be much more coming.
articles.title: The Romans were wrong

articles.text: Piedmont violinist Joseph Gold celebrated his 75th birthday with a lovely concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Seventy-five is an interesting number. It has a round feel but is odd. It isn’t divisible like 36 but it gets more respect. To a gemologist, 75 is a diamond… clear, regular, but hard. It does glitter. 75 often comes with white hair. That kind of sets off the face like white icing on a birthday cake. 75 is a slow race to 100. It reminds me of the glorious finish to the first sub four-minute mile by Roger Bannister. He collapsed at the finish line. Maybe 75 just feels better. I don’t want to collapse. The day itself was a condensation of life. I awoke just before 5 a.m. –which coincidently was the hour of my birth. A good breakfast and some study and reflection on a good life. Then the concert - a brilliant affair with the auditorium filled to capacity. Friends both old and new and beautiful family. They do great honor to me, and I love them in return. The concert was like life itself. There were a few rough places and some glorious playing…reflecting a life of study, and a lot of good fortune. Thanks for a good family, friends and mentors and great composers and violin makers. All these bring on great sentiment. The presents were great but the best present of all is loving you. Thank you all.
articles.title: Reflections at 75

articles.text: Part 28 in a series In our age, when an architect lays out a building, the entire process starts with parking. With few exceptions, it is the driver for virtually all site and building design. The larger the building, and the more restrictive the municipal parking requirements, the more obvious this becomes. It follows that the cost, space requirements, and aesthetic influence of parking has a huge, often restrictive impact on denser multi-family housing. Factoring in aisle space and landscaping, a surface parking lot takes a lot of space — about 350 sf per car, while a tightly designed parking garage uses about 325 sf per car. Costs depend on specific site conditions but range from say, $5000/car for an on-grade parking lot to $50,000/car, and even more for underground parking. All of this must be factored into the housing costs, and paid for in the selling price or rent. This financial and spacial burden is a worldwide problem. In Japan for example, you have to prove you have a parking space before you are allowed to buy a car. There is a new attitude toward parking however that is becoming pervasive. It is the same concept that applies to the number of lanes provided on the freeway. Intuitively, it would seem that if traffic is clogged on the freeway, adding more lanes would solve the problem. Continuing studies have shown that the opposite is the case. In what is termed “induced traffic”, adding more lanes only ends up adding more cars, bringing the situation back to – or worse than – the original clogged condition. The same is true of parking: more parking induces more cars. For this reason, and because of the critical housing shortage, cities have started eliminating their minimum parking requirements. Zero is now the number of parking spaces required for new housing development in Berkeley, San Francisco, Mexico City, Minneapolis and many other places. The state of California now prohibits minimum parking requirements for ADU (accessory dwelling units). What does this mean for our built environment? Most of the older multi-family buildings in Piedmont that we showed in the last column have no onsite parking, with all tenant parking on the street. They were built in an age when people had fewer cars and walked to the Key System for a train ride to Oakland or San Francisco. This is a good example of showing that all planning systems are connected. Parking is linked to zoning, land use, transportation and availability of commercial services, all of which must work together to be viable. If household units live with one, or no cars, they must rely on walking, biking, public transportation, and ride sharing at least part of the time to get around. Fortunately, these alternatives can be immediately financed with the $800+ per month savings that AAA says the average person currently spends for car ownership, including parking. Next: Back to Aesthetics: Exterior Colors Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com. The need for additional parking to accommodate our ever-increasing car ownership has led to a number of interesting solutions, such as this car lift system which allows double stacking – as opposed to simply parking everything in the front yard. The first question is, do we really need this many vehicles?
articles.title: Multi-Family Housing 3: Parking

articles.text: The Montclair Lions Club and Montclair Village Association are collaborating to bring back the Restaurant Walk to Montclair Village. On Tuesday evening, September 28, from 6:00 to 8:30 p.m. A total of 14 merchants will open their doors and provide samples of their food and/or drink. Tickets to the event, called Passports, and can be purchased online at MontclairVillage.com, in advance at The Book Tree on La Salle Avenue, or in front of US Bank, 1998 Mountain Blvd., on the day of the event. The cost is $30, with proceeds going to support local non-profits, schools, and other worthy causes through the Lions Club. The Restaurant Walk also is an effort to bring some much-needed attention and patronage to the business owners of Montclair. The Montclair Lions Club will continue the tradition of supporting other service organizations and groups looking to raise some funds for their community work. Any organization wishing to sell a minimum of 10 tickets will receive 50% of the ticket proceeds. That’s $15 per ticket sold. For more information contact Leslie Masler with the Lions Club at 510-213-2530. New this year is the Wine and Beer Tasting Pavilion. Purchase a Wine and Beer Tasting package for an additional $25 and receive artisan wine pours from Wachira Wines, P. Harell Wines, R&B Cellars, and Montclair’s Perle Wine Bar and Bistro. Craft beers will be showcased by Taps and Takeout of Montclair. Wine and Beer tasting tickets are only available online and at the event. For advance tickets see MontclairVillage.com. The annual Restaurant Walk has been on pause for two years due to the COVID pandemic. For over 20 years this event has provided benefits to the Lions Club Centers for the Blind, the Leo Club at Oakland High School, and Montclair Lions Club Charities including Skyline High School, Montera Middle, Montclair, Joaquin Miller, and Thornhill Schools. The Montclair Lions Club supports local events like the Planter Mosaic program, Montclair Easter Egg Hunt, Annual Free Halloween Parade, and community cleanups. The Walk allows people to gather outdoors safely, support small businesses, and enjoy an evening tasting new menu items alongside Village favorites. This year a portion of the proceeds will go to provide financial relief to Montclair restaurants that suffered hardship due to the impacts of the COVID-19 virus. Maureen Powers is a member of Montclair Lions Club. Daughter Thai team is ready for the Montclair Restaurant Walk planned for September 28th Left to right – Francisco, Mike Williams (owner) Steph & Lucas of Crogan’s Montclair, one of Oakland’s favorite bars, are looking forward to the Montclair Restaurant Walk
articles.title: Montclair Restaurant Walk returns Sept. 28

articles.text: Last Sunday, September 12, Piedmont Community Church held its annual Homecoming Picnic in the courtyard at the Community Center. This event followed all Alameda County guidelines on health and safety relating to COVID 19. The church announced in advance that it would be held outdoors and casual attire was recommended. Interim Minister Dr. Steve Schibsted set an example for the entire congregation by preaching his sermon in shorts, which prompted Associate Pastor Don Ashburn to comment that this was a “first” in his 18 years at the church. The Music Aside from the spectacular weather, the greatest contributor to the festive atmosphere at the picnic was the outstanding music performed by Lodestar, a six-piece band consisting of: two Lance McCollum guitars (guitar aficionados will recognize the late builder of guitars with “piano-like” tone) played by band leader and singer James Haverkamp and Scott Fitzgerrell; Pam Bouey, violin; Russ Taylor, keyboard; Jim Semitekol, bass, and Harold Ohashi, drums. The band played a mix of music from artists such as the Everly Brothers, Paul Simon, Emmylou Harris, Linda Ronstadt and others. The Food A taco truck provided four types of soft tacos: pork, chicken, beef and vegetarian, made in advance, so the food line zipped along seamlessly. Freshly cut watermelon and cold lemonade were welcome on the warm September day. pages.text: Wednesday, September 15, 2021 23 The Wine Corner Ridge Vineyards – Desert Island Winery By Pierre DuMont As regular readers of this column know by now there is no winery that has more admiration and respect from me than Ridge Vineyards. They are simply my “desert island” winery. If you are playing the old game of “if you could take the music of only one musician to a desert island. who would you choose?” Obviously, quality of music is most important, but quantity counts too. If one musician had made one record you loved and another had made 200 you loved I might be inclined to go with quantity. What is so amazing about Ridge Vineyards is that not only is the equality of their wines staggeringly high, but the sheer quantity of their output is mind-blowing. I looked on their website under wines for sale – and stopped counting at 100, with many pages left to go. This current batch of new releases includes two totally new (to me) wines – the Grenache Blanc and the Guadagni Zinfandel. Most of these wines are available at Wine.com or K&L Wines locally, while smaller releases are available on the Ridge website. www.ridgewine.com. WHITE WINE • 2020 Ridge Grenache Blanc My first time tasting this Rhone blend white. They add a splash of Roussanne and Picpoul to the Grenache Blanc for added complexity. Light gold in color it has fantastic aromas and flavors of tropical fruits, spice box and mineral to go with a medium-bodied, fresh and lively palate feel that builds in richness through the mid palate and finish. A perfect aperitif. RED WINE • 2018 Ridge Montebello This iconic wine dates its fame back to the famous Paris blind wine tasting of 1976 that pitted the best of California wines against the superstars of France. In case you haven’t heard… the French superstars lost. The Montebello remains one of the world’s greatest Cabernets. it explodes out of the glass with beautifully provocative blackberry and cassis scents followed by violets and chocolate. Medium to full-bodied, the palate reveals explosive energy wrapped in silky smooth tannins finishing with amazing freshness and perfume. A truly beautiful wine. 2020 Ridge Grenache Blanc 2018 Ridge Montebello • 2019 Ridge Lytton Springs A blend of 73% Zinfandel, 16% Petite Sirah, 9% Carignane and 2% Mataro this is, in most years, my favorite Zin in the Ridge portfolio. This has a beautiful nose of violets and sweet oak. A big expressive, yet balanced style of wine with plums and cherries on the palate and soft, chewy tannins on the finish. Lay this wine down for a few years and then serve with your best BBQ. • 2018 Ridge Zinfandel Hooker Creek This wine comes from a century old vineyard in Sonoma Valley that consists of a field blend of 94% zinfandel and the rest a mixture of Alicante Bouschet, and Petite Sirah. The result is a big wine with a powerful scent that jumps out of the glass and hits you in the nose. Its 14.8% alcohol is well hidden under layers of rich fruit. A perfect accompaniment to your next grilled steak. • 2019 Ridge Mazzoni Home Ranch This wine has a whopping 45% Carignane added to the Zinfandel. This is a classic Alexander Valley style Zinfandel medium bodied with good structure it is still showing its youth with boysenberry and currant aromas leading to concentrated blueberry fruit in the mouth. Finishes with firm tannins. • 2019 Ridge Guadagni Zinfandel This Dry Creek Valley wine was new to me and it contains 24% Petite Sirah for added power. The wine is loaded with opulent, jammy fruit, that shows boysenberry and cherry aromas with soft ripe flavors of spice, pepper, and sage. Drink now through 2028. • 2019 Ridge Evangelho This wine hails for a famous 130-year-old vineyard in Contra Costa County that is now completely surrounded by subdivisions. It is crafted from 47% Carignane, 29% Zinfandel and 24 % Mataro (Mourvedre). This bottling is dense and tightly wound, with minty, black currant aromas and firm, complex flavors of dark plum and anise and a long succulent finish. Perfect partner to a grilled leg of lamb. • 2019 Ridge Zinfandel Benito Dusi Ridge has been making wines from this Paso Robles vineyard for many years. One hundred percent Zinfandel this blockbuster (15.1%) wine is not for the faint of heart. It is zesty and appealingly rustic with plum and cassis aromas followed by big mouth filling blueberry fruit. • 2019 Ridge Zinfandel Pagani Ranch This is 90% Zinfandel with a splash of Petite Sirah and Alicante Bouchet. It is supple and elegant, with floral and raspberry aromas following through to soft, lingering flavors of blueberry, caramel, and spice. It shows just the perfect touch of American oak. articles.text: John St. John, 54, of Piedmont, California, died in a tragic auto accident in Le Sueur County, Minnesota on July 25, 2021. His beloved spouse Jill Davidson St. John, cherished daughter Claire Borgny St. John, and dear nephew Theo Emerson also passed away. He is survived by his treasured son Ryan St. John, loving mother and step-father Mary and Fritz Wooster of Piedmont, sisters Jane Emerson (Alex) and Molly Wooster, brother Tim Wooster (Jessica), nephew Ray Emerson, and aunt Julie St. John, who was near to his heart, and her husband Cliff Bream. John leaves behind his beloved and grieving in-laws Carey (Fred) Kaas, Shannon Davidson, and niece and nephew Kennedy and Keegan Kaas. Born in Minneapolis, Minnesota at the University of Minnesota Hospital on April 28, 1967, John spent most of his life in the Bay Area. He was proud of his East Bay identity. His mother, Mary, was 19 when he was born and they loved to tell people that they grew up together. His life was enriched when she married Fritz, whom he had known since his preschool days. His love for his new family was boundless. He was 13 when his sister Jane was born, followed by Tim less than two years later. Molly was born just before he graduated from high school. He was their big brother, their hero, their confidant, and their most beloved friend. John attended Beach School, was in the first graduating class from the new Piedmont Middle School, and graduated from Olympic Valley High School in Squaw Valley. It was there that he discovered his love of skiing and all sports requiring skill, athleticism, coordination, and an element of breath-taking risk. He was among the first to try the new sport known as snowboarding, but he truly found his bliss when downhill skiing. He was an expert water skier, kite boarder, wind surfer, electric skateboarder, and had only recently accepted the challenge of the electric unicycle. He felt most free when gliding, sometimes racing, along with the wind in his face and his body armored in the latest protective gear. After school John was a ski instructor in Squaw Valley and Steamboat Springs, Colorado. Finding a career that fit his skills and talents led him to form his own company, Cause Broadcasting. He created, produced, and sold public service announcements for college radio stations across the country. His gregarious personality was a perfect fit for his work. He truly tried to change the world for the better, one public service announcement at a time. Every client became a friend, and he enjoyed the relationships he created with college radio aficionados from San Francisco to Iowa City to the East Coast. John would proclaim to the world that marrying Jill Davidson and becoming father to Ryan and Claire were his finest achievements. His love for Jill was a delight to behold and he spent every free moment with her and Ryan and Claire. It was his good fortune that with Cause Broadcasting he created his own niche, which enabled him to work from home and always be at the ready should Jill or the children need a helping hand, a drive to Ryan’s drum lessons, Claire’s rehearsals, or just a good laugh. John’s sense of humor was legendary and no topic was too sacred to be spared his clever tongue. He was grateful to have a home in Piedmont, where he and his family built a wonderful community of friends. John was kind and generous and thoughtful. His presence will be missed by everyone who witnessed his cheerful greeting while out walking his dog, Casey. He considered every acquaintance to be a friend, and those of us who knew and loved him will hold his tender spirit forever. Donations in honor of the St. John family may be made to the Sierra Club or the SPCA.
articles.title: John St. John dies with family members in auto accident

articles.text: Jill Davidson St. John, 56, of Piedmont, California, died in a tragic auto accident in Le Sueur County, Minnesota on July 25, 2021. Her beloved spouse, John St. John; cherished daughter, Claire; and dear nephew, Theo, also passed away. She is survived by her treasured son, Ryan St. John; sisters, Shannon Davidson and Carey Davidson Kaas (Fred); Keegan and Kennedy Kaas; and her aunt Martha Geering-Kline (Bruce). Born in Berkeley, California on May 15, 1965, Jill created a beautiful, meaningful and full life in the Bay Area, continually inspired by its natural surroundings, vibrant culture and the people she loved. Jill was raised in Berkeley by parents Alan and Nancy Davidson. Alan was an attorney and marathon runner who charmed everyone with his humor, and Nancy approached life with kindness and understanding. Jill attended Albany High School, graduated from San Francisco State University, and earned a Master’s degree in Counseling/ Psychology from JFK University. Upon completing her Master’s degree and Marriage and Family Therapist License, she worked at Kaiser’s Chemical Dependency Program in Oakland, and later established her own practice in Lafayette, where she especially loved her work with teens and young adults. She helped countless friends and patients achieve a brighter life through sobriety. Jill’s sense of humor and intellectual curiosity enabled her to make people feel special, heard, and understood. She would look at you and you felt her unconditional love. Known for her positive outlook on life and faith, she was always eager to try new things and to reach out and connect with people. She was a health enthusiast, committed to running and exercise. When her husband was asked why he was marrying Jill, he said “because she makes everything fun.” She could be unpredictable, irreverent, and sometimes outrageous – always, always loving and kind. Nothing brought Jill more joy than raising her children with John. The deeply connected family enjoyed walking and skating in their neighborhood, exploring new places, laughing together, and sharing their love for music and animals. As a therapist, wife and mom, Jill encouraged that little be left unsaid in their home, and it was typically said loudly over Ryan’s drum practice in the basement, Claire’s singing preparing for a Berkeley Playhouse performance, and their dog Casey’s barking. All who were lucky enough to be blessed by Jill, John and Claire’s friendship and love will miss them dearly and will always hold a special place for them in their hearts and memories. Jill is predeceased by her loving parents, Alan and Nancy Davidson, as well as her aunt Sheila Geering Keppel (Jeff). She leaves behind her grieving and beloved in-laws Fritz and Mary Wooster, Jane, Alex and Ray Emerson, Tim and Jessica Wooster, Molly Wooster, and Julie St. John and her husband Cliff Bream.
articles.title: Jill St. John dies in fatal auto collision in Minnesota

articles.text: Claire Borgny St. John died at age 13 in a tragic auto accident in Le Sueur County, Minnesota on July 25, 2021. Her beloved parents, John and Jill St. John, and her cousin Theo Emerson also passed away. She is survived by her older brother, Ryan St. John, her grandparents, Mary and Fritz Wooster, and many loving uncles, aunts, and cousins. Claire was born in Oakland on February 7, 2008. She attended Wildwood Elementary School and Piedmont Middle School where she was known for her kindness, humor, fashion sense, and incredible talent as an actress and singer. Claire found joy in the performing arts, and successfully auditioned for roles in many live productions and then over Zoom during Covid. She had starring roles in Berkeley Playhouse productions and was proud to have played “Annie” at the Woodminster Amphitheatre. She truly shined each summer when she sang in the San Francisco Conservatory Music productions of Gilbert and Sullivan musicals. She was known for her eagerness to learn and grow, and for her kindness to the other musicians. She could play the ukulele and had the voice of an angel. She was a budding activist with a particular passion for Women’s Rights and, as a member of the Green Team, environmental issues. With Claire’s passing, the world has lost a delightful young woman with amazing potential. Claire found joy in everything: her family, friendships, music, animals, and nature. As her parents often said, “Claire just loves being Claire.” She had a clever sense of humor and a mature world view. She was kind, empathetic and passionate. Claire and her brother Ryan were especially close and loved family time with their parents and their family pets. They had the good fortune to travel to many places as a family: an RV trip to the national parks of southern Utah, to Minnesota, Hawaii, Sun Valley, Lake Tahoe, as well as Laguna Beach to visit her aunt Julie St. John. Claire was beloved by her cousins Keegan, Kennedy, Theo and Ray and spent many happy family holidays and vacations in their company. Claire will be remembered by all who were fortunate to know her for her vibrancy, her intelligence, her empathy, and her joy for life. To know Claire was to love her. She will be greatly missed. Jill and John St. John with daughter Claire.
articles.title: Claire St. John dies at 13 in auto accident

The link below, available on Wednesday, September 15, after 3 p.m., will allow you to register to attend the memorial in person, or to access a live stream of the memorial if you wish to attend remotely. www.fpcberkeley.org/memorial Jill St. John dies in fatal auto collision Jill Davidson St. John, 56, of Piedmont, California, died in a tragic auto accident in Le Sueur County, Minnesota on July 25, 2021. Her beloved spouse, John St. John; cherished daughter, Claire; and dear nephew, Theo, also passed away. She is survived by her treasured son, Ryan St. John; sisters, Shannon Davidson and Carey Davidson Kaas (Fred); Keegan and Kennedy Kaas; and her aunt Martha Geering-Kline (Bruce). Born in Berkeley, California on May 15, 1965, Jill created a beautiful, meaningful and full life in the Bay Area, continually inspired by its natural surroundings, vibrant culture and the people she loved. Jill was raised in Berkeley by parents Alan and Nancy Davidson. Alan was an attorney and marathon runner who charmed everyone with his humor, and Nancy approached life with kindness and understanding. Jill attended Albany High School, graduated from San Francisco State University, and earned a Master’s degree in Counseling/ in Minnesota Psychology from JFK University. Upon completing her Master’s degree and Marriage and Family Therapist License, she worked at Kaiser’s Chemical Dependency Program in Oakland, and later established her own practice in Lafayette, where she especially loved her work with teens and young adults. She helped countless friends and patients achieve a brighter life through sobriety. Jill’s sense of humor and intellectual curiosity enabled her to make people feel special, heard, and understood. She would look at you and you felt her unconditional love. Known for her positive outlook on life and faith, she was always eager to try new things and to reach out and connect with people. She was a health enthusiast, committed to running and exercise. When her husband was asked why he was marrying Jill, he said “because she makes everything fun.” She could be unpredictable, irreverent, and sometimes outrageous – always, always loving and kind. Nothing brought Jill more joy than raising her children with John. The deeply connected family enjoyed walking and skating in their neighborhood, exploring new places, laughing together, and sharing their love for music and animals. As a therapist, wife and mom, Jill encouraged that little be left unsaid in their home, and it was typically said loudly over Ryan’s drum practice in the basement, Claire’s singing preparing for a Berkeley Playhouse performance, and their dog Casey’s barking. All who were lucky enough to be blessed by Jill, John and Claire’s friendship and love will miss them dearly and will always hold a special place for them in their hearts and memories. Jill is predeceased by her loving parents, Alan and Nancy Davidson, as well as her aunt Sheila Geering Keppel (Jeff). She leaves behind her grieving and beloved in-laws Fritz and Mary Wooster, Jane, Alex and Ray Emerson, Tim and Jessica Wooster, Molly Wooster, and Julie St. John and her husband Cliff Bream. Claire St. John dies at 13 in auto accident Claire Borgny St. John died at age 13 in a tragic auto accident in Le Sueur County, Minnesota on July 25, 2021. Her beloved parents, John and Jill St. John, and her cousin Theo Emerson also passed away. She is survived by her older brother, Ryan St. John, her grandparents, Mary and Fritz Wooster, and many loving uncles, aunts, and cousins. Claire was born in Oakland on February 7, 2008. She attended Wildwood Elementary School and Piedmont Middle School where she was known for her kindness, humor, fashion sense, and incredible talent as an actress and singer. Claire found joy in the performing arts, and successfully auditioned for roles in many live productions and then over Zoom during Covid. She had starring roles in Berkeley Playhouse productions and was proud to have played “Annie” at the Woodminster Amphitheatre. She truly shined each summer when she sang in the San Francisco Conservatory Music productions of Gilbert and Sullivan musicals. She was known for her eagerness to learn and grow, and for her kindness to the other musicians. She could play the ukulele and had the voice of an angel. She was a budding activist with a particular passion for Women’s Rights and, as a member of the Green Team, environmental issues. With Claire’s passing, the world has lost a delightful young woman with amazing potential. Claire found joy in everything: her family, friendships, music, animals, and nature. As her parents often said, “Claire just loves being Claire.” She had a clever sense of humor and a mature world view. She was kind, empathetic and passionate. Claire and her brother Ryan were especially close and loved family time with their parents and their family pets. They had the good fortune to travel to many places as a family: an RV trip to the national parks of southern Utah, to Minnesota, Hawaii, Sun Valley, Lake Tahoe, as well as Laguna Beach to visit her aunt Julie St. John. Claire was beloved by her cousins Keegan, Kennedy, Theo and Ray and spent many happy family holidays and vacations in their company. Claire will be remembered by all who were fortunate to know her for her vibrancy, her intelligence, her empathy, and her joy for life. To know Claire was to love her. She will be greatly missed. Jill and John St. John with daughter Claire.

articles.text: Theodore Fredrick Emerson passed away at age 9 in a tragic auto accident in Le Sueur County, Minnesota on July 25, 2021. Theo’s uncle, aunt and cousin (John, Jill and Claire St. John of Piedmont) also passed away. He is survived by his loving parents, Jane Wooster Emerson (PHS Class of 1998) and Alex Emerson, his younger brother Ray Emerson, both sets of grandparents (Fritz and Mary Wooster of Piedmont, CA and Dick and Susan Emerson of Redding, CT) and many loving aunts, uncles and cousins. Theo was born in Rochester, Minnesota on June 23, 2012, and lived his entire life in the Eagle Rock neighborhood of Los Angeles, California with his parents and brother. Theo attended Eagle Rock Elementary School. He loved school, his teachers and his classmates, and was especially proud of projects on the Miwok people of California and his Norwegian ancestry. Theo’s many interests outside of school included rock climbing, spending time in the woods with his friends, and shooting hoops in the backyard with his brother. This spring and summer, he attended Biocitizen hiking camp, rock climbing camp, and surf camp. He spent countless days at the beach where he was a bold and brave swimmer in big waves. One of his favorite places to spend summer days was a pool in Pasadena where he befriended the lifeguards and was happy to spend hours swimming, late into the evening. Theo was lucky to travel to Maine and Minnesota with extended family during summer vacations where he spent time with his beloved cousins. He also traveled to Mexico and visited seven national parks and countless state parks in California and throughout the American Southwest. Theo loved camping trips with family and friends. His final camping trip was at a beautiful lakeside campground in Glacier National Park in early July. At home, Theo was known in his family for his adorable clumsiness, his sense of humor, his love of funny TV shows, and his love of family pets Rocky and Barry. He loved music and created playlists to listen to on long car rides and at home. He was kind and empathetic, always making sure to include friends and make everyone feel welcome. His best friend was his younger brother Ray. Only 21 months apart, they were often mistaken for twins, and they spent every moment outside of school together. He filled every single day of his nine years of life with profound joy, love, and kindness. Theo will be missed by everyone who was lucky enough to know him. A small memorial was held for Theo is Los Angeles on September 11. Donations in his memory may be made to the Sierra Club or the SPCA. Theo Emerson

Once upon a time if you had a business and you didn’t have a listing in the Yellow Pages, it was like you didn’t exist. And if you really wanted visibility, you took out a display ad. Remember the Yellow Pages? Today, digital visibility via websites and social media profiles is everything. As I’ve grown my business, so have I grown my blog (in part through writing for this column), and my profiles on various platforms. A social media profile requires care and feeding. For me, as someone who values authenticity, thoughtful curation, and soulful connection, deciding what to post and what to say about these images is a deeply personal process. As you might imagine, there’s also the question of what will be featured in the images. My firm completes several projects a year, but not all of these are photographed. The good news is, there’s a kind of gentlewoman’s tradition on social media of re-gramming. Especially in the design community.
