Chief Brannigan made introductory remarks, followed by Mayor King and Police Chief Bowers. “Today we gather to remember those lost, but to do so, I’d like to reflect on those saved,” Chief Brannigan said. “The [New York] Port Authority reports there were over 14,000 people in the World Trade Center Towers at the time American Airlines Flight 11 struck the North Tower. An evacuation orchestrated and executed by many of the staff and first responders who perished, saved over 11,000 lives.” “That’s an evacuation the size of the population of Piedmont. 11,000 people were led to safety Fire Chief Dave Brannigan delivers a speech in remembrance of lives lost on September 11, 2001. by the heroes who never left those buildings. 11,000 lives continued the next day. 11,000 stories did not end,” he said. “Our firefighters and police have sworn that same oath and face the same risks. We are here to put the community first, to respond when peoples’ lives depend on it. We are here to make sure that the stories of the people in this town carry on.” Mayor King, echoing Chief Brannigan’s sentiments, also paid homage to the first responders who lost their lives two decades prior. “These men and women, and their surviving families, sacrificed everything in this world, because it was their duty to keep us safe,” she said. “It’s our duty to remember the bravery and selflessness of those fallen first responders and all of the victims of that day.” In closing remarks, Chief Bowers said,” I remember watching in amazement as people did all they could to rescue those who had been trapped and then to recover those who had been lost and address the resulting devastation. As we honor those who we lost in connection to the events of that day, I believe we need to also honor the incredible American spirit that rose from that tragedy. articles.text: An interactive map of all 19 Heritage Trees in Piedmont is now live on the city’s website, with each tree or group of trees’ species name, location, year inducted and the resident who nominated it. The Piedmont Heritage Tree Program was created by City Council in 2018 upon the recommendation of the Park Commission. The overall intent of the policy is to recognize and identify distinctive trees that are noteworthy for their size, species, location, or historical context in city parks and open spaces. To date, 19 trees or group of trees are recognized as Heritage Trees in the city. Applications for heritage trees are sought each year, and the program encourages residents to visit City parks and open spaces to find trees eligible for Heritage Tree designation. Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap created the map, which is powered by Google Maps with populated information that can be accessed on any computer, smartphone or other device. All photos of trees were taken by Park Commissioner Brian Mahany. The map can be accessed by visiting https://piedmont. ca.gov/cms/one.aspx?por tal Id=13659823&pageId=17970894. Photo by Brian Mahany The Highland Poplars flanking Exedra Plaza are among 19 Piedmont Heritage Tree locations.

pages.text: 32 Wednesday, September 15, 2021 Interactive Piedmont Heritage Tree map available By Allyson Aleksey An interactive map of all 19 Heritage Trees in Piedmont is now live on the city’s website, with each tree or group of trees’ species name, location, year inducted and the resident who nominated it. The Piedmont Heritage Tree Program was created by City Council in 2018 upon the recommendation of the Park Commission. The overall intent of the policy is to recognize and identify distinctive trees that are noteworthy for their size, species, location, or historical context in city parks and open spaces. To date, 19 trees or group of trees are recognized as Heritage Trees in the city. Applications for heritage trees are sought each year, and the program encourages residents to visit City parks and open spaces to find trees eligible for Heritage Tree designation. Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap created the map, which is powered by Google Maps with populated information that can be accessed on any computer, smartphone or other device. All photos of trees were taken by Park Commissioner Brian Mahany. The map can be accessed by visiting https://piedmont. ca.gov/cms/one.aspx?por tal Id=13659823&pageId=17970894. Movie in the Park this Friday Rec. Dept. to show Bee Movie in main park Sept. 17 Join your neighbors for a free movie in Piedmont Park at 7:20 p.m. this Friday, September 17, on a new 26-foot screen in the Main Park. The film is Bee Movie, a DreamWorks animation family film with the voices of Jerry Seinfield, Renee Zellweger and Chris Rock. The festivities start at 6:00 with Latin food provided by the Canasta food truck. Mr. Dewie’s Cashew Creamery will also be selling their fabulous ice cream and Girl Scout Troop 33587 will be selling lemonade and treats during the movie. A sweet bonus is a presentation about beekeeping with some local honey-tasting samples. Honey-tasting begins at 6:30 p.m., and the movie will begin at 7:20 p.m. Come in a bee costume and win a prize or make your own bee antenna at the crafts table. Bring a low-level lawn chair and enjoy a night under the stars. This will be the final movie in the park of the year. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department had a record number of entries and a record crowd of car buffs at its 3rd annual Car Show on Labor Day morning, Monday, September 6. Attendance was estimated at 800, making it one of the city’s largest public events. The lineup of cars event was held above Piedmont Community Hall from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m. Coffee was donated by Pete’s Coffee, incorporating the larger “Coffee with a Cop” national campaign that started in 2016 as a way for residents to meet local law enforcement. The local campaign was expanded by former Sgt. Steve DeWarns in 2018 with a display of classic cars, from Lamborginis, and Ferraris to Corvettes. The number of entries jumped from 44 two years ago to nearly 80 this year, expanding the lineup of vehicles from the parking lot above the Community Hall to Highland Avenue in front of the park and the Exedra. “A flood of [entries] came in last minute, which really made for an impressive show,” said Officer Tyler Petit, who has organized the event since 2019. “Events like these allow you to really break the barrier. articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council unanimously approved a mandatory vaccination and COVID-19 testing policy for all employees. All city employees – fulltime, part-time, volunteers and interns – must report their vaccination status to the city’s Human Resources Department. This includes City Councilmembers and those serving on city commissions. To be considered fully vaccinated, 14 days must have passed since an employee received the final dose of a two-dose vaccine (Moderna or Pfizer), or a dose of a one-dose vaccine (Johnson and Johnson). The proposition was discussed at the most recent City Council meeting on September 7, at the request of Mayor Teddy Gray King. “There is a moral imperative to move forward with this [mandate],” Mayor King said. Unless excused through an approved accommodation request, all employees must comply with the requirement to be fully vaccinated, and vaccination and reporting requirements would be a minimum qualification for new hires. Failure to comply could result in termination. articles.text: The family of Joan (Jody) Earle will have a Celebration of Life on Friday, September 24, at 2 p.m. at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue in Piedmont. A resident of Piedmont for 55 years, she was a beloved mother, grandmother, sister, and aunt who passed away on January 7, 2021 at the age of 89. Born Joan Christine Zuber on December 29, 1931 in Washington DC, she was the daughter of Adolph and Alice Rita Zuber and was known to everyone by her nickname Jody. Known for her kind gentle spirit, great sense of humor and smile, she enchanted those who heard her retelling of the story of her family living in Pearl Harbor when it was attacked on December 7, 1941. Jody loved to read and write, leading her to ities. From 1989 to 2012 she taught multiple subjects at Fred Finch Youth Center in Oakland, a facility providing support for youth healing from trauma. She was well respected by family, friends, and students for her loving dedication to the learning and wellbeing of her students. She is survived by three sons, John Earle III (Jenny), David Earle (Jennifer) and Robert Earle; and by three daughters, Alicia Utley (Jony), Meg Dengler (Mike), and Alison Earle. Jody is also survived by five grandchildren, Kristina and Kayla Utley, Katie Nolasco, Benjamin and Sarah Dengler. She is additionally survived by a sister, Margaret (Peggy) Unger, three nephews, a niece and numerous great nephews and nieces. Joan (Jody) Earle write her own book, The Children of Battleship Row, which gives generations of readers a glimpse of a 9-year old’s perspective of the attack on Pearl Harbor. articles.text: The recall election of Gov. Gavin Newsom is on Tuesday, September 14. Local election offices, including the Alameda County Registrar of Voters, sent out mail ballots for the Gubernatorial Recall Election on A recall procedure has been part of the state’s political system since 1911 and provides a mechanism for the public to attempt to remove elective public officials from office before the end of their term. At least 1,495,000 valid petition signatures, or 12% of the votes cast for the office of Governor in 2018, were received. Democrat Gov. Newsom is the second California governor ever to face a recall election. Five attempts to recall the governor have failed to qualify for the ballot since he took office in January 2019. Gray Davis was removed from office in 2003, only the second state governor successfully recalled in U.S. history. He was replaced by actor Arnold Schwarzenegger. All registered voters received a ballot in the mail. If you are a resident of Alameda County, you can verify your registration address and voter status by visiting www.acvote.org/mvp. The county is also offering a new way for voters to track and receive notifications on the status of their vote-by-mail ballot, powered by “BallotTrax” - interested residents may visit www.acvote.ballottrax.net to The vote-by-mail packet will contain your ballot card, a return envelope, instructions for returning your ballot, and an “I Voted” sticker. While the county is encouraging mail-in voting due to the current health pandemic, safe and accessible in-person voting options will be available. Accessible voting locations will be open starting Saturday, September 11. Voters may drop vote-bymail ballots in the ballot box located on Highland Way near the mailboxes 24 hours a day, up to and including Election Day. The Veterans’ Memorial Building serves as an Accessible Voting Location. Any resident of Piedmont or Alameda County can come to the Veteran’s Hall and cast their ballot or drop off a vote-by-mail ballot. There are nearly 100 accessible voting locations in Alameda County, opening this Saturday. articles.text: Picture this for a moment. You are a woman living in and around 30 AD. This means men don’t talk to you. Women are considered lowly. The culture is still tribal and so a woman like our Syrophoenician is considered even lower than children because she is an outsider. In Jewish customs outsiders and women were considered unclean. Here is a woman pleading for her daughter to be healed and Jesus is kind of rude. We usually like to think of Jesus as all loving, but even he is a bit flawed in this passage in his treatment of the woman. He uses the term “dog” to give her status as lower than children. This woman doesn’t give up though. She hears Jesus’s reference to her and cunningly says, “Sir, even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” Imagine how humble this woman had to be to accept her place. The Syrophoenician woman in her persistence was able to get what she wanted and got Jesus to pause and reminded him his ministry was not just for Israel but to a world in need. Up until then Jesus’s ministry had been focused on Israel. At this moment one woman, an outsider, opens Jesus’s ministry to the world. It becomes a catalyst for realizing that not only were the people of Israel God’s people, but we are all the children of God and so we are his beloved. Immediately after, Jesus goes onto Decapolis and continues his ministry there. Decapolis is an area of several Greek cities, which shows Jesus’s ministry to the gentiles and ministering to the world. I think this anonymous gentile woman had to have courage. She was bold and persistent. She didn’t merely just stay in her place. When we are wanting the best for a loved one, do we exhibit these features? I think about how we can become tribal and forget we are

articles.text: The Piedmont Planning Commission will consider new wireless communication facilities design standards and listen to comments from the public at its meeting on Monday, September 13. articles.text: Piedmont School District accepted a grant from PG&E for six electric vehicle charging stations, as confirmed by the school board on August 25. The stations will be installed in the parking lot next to the John Morrison gym and high school band room. The PG&E grant is being offered to school districts throughout the state. PG&E will pay for all charging station infrastructure and costs to maintain the equipment for eight years. Piedmont School District will pay for the charging station electrical usage on a separate bill at a lower rate than currently paying. The value of the grant is estimated at approximately $300,000. After eight years, ownership of the stations can be transferred to the District. PUSD can also request the removal of the stations. Priority use for the charging stations will be given to electric vehicles owned by the district. It currently has three electric vehicles being charged at its Maintenance Building. The District also owns nine gas-powered vehicles, and plans to replace some of these with electric vehicles sometime in the future. The charging stations may also be used by school district staff to charge their privately owned EVs. Staff members will use a phone application to pay for the electricity used and those funds will be applied to the District’s electricity bill. “Now that the project is approved, the plan will be put together and submitted to the Division of the State Architect for approval,” said Communications Director Brian Killgore. No timetable currently exists for approval, installation or project completion. The school district moved on this offer quickly, in comparison to the City which has rejected a free installation offer from PG&E and East Bay Community Energy. The city council has been offered four charging stations for Bonita Avenue, but the proposal has been rejected twice over concerns of limited parking in the city center. PUSD has accepted a grant from PG&E to install six electric vehicle chargers in the parking lot next to the John Morrison gym.
articles.title: School district accepts PG&E grant for 6 EV charging stations

articles.text: Mayor Teddy Gray King will provide opening remarks for the upcoming League of Women Voters panel discussion on carbon pricing. The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is hosting a forum on carbon pricing with Piedmont Connect and the Citizens Climate Education on September 22. The groups will provide a panel discussion on carbon pricing, a method widely agreed to be the most effective way for nations to reduce global warming emissions. Carbon pricing seeks to address over-pollution and dramatic climate change and reduce carbon emissions quickly and at-scale. The United States is one of only a few major industrialized nations without a national carbon pricing policy. Carbon pricing has gained the support of a wide array of groups, including 28 Nobel laureate economists, the Washington Post editorial board, Rep. Barbara Lee, and thousands of businesses and labor unions. Opening remarks will be made by Mayor Teddy Gray King. A panel discussion will feature Mike Mielke, Senior Vice President and Head of Public Policy for the Silicon Valley Leadership Group; Daniel McFadden, Nobel laureate economist and Professor Emeritus at UC Berkeley; and Danny Richter, Vice President of Government Affairs, Citizen’s Climate Lobby. The discussion will be on Zoom beginning at 4 p.m. and ending at 5:30 p.m. The event is free, but registration is required on the LWVP website at: www. lwvpiedmont.org/events. • Complete Interior & Exterior Painting • Kitchen Cabinet Painting • Plaster Repair • Dry Rot Repair… and more! This year’s artists include the Piedmont High School Jazz Orchestra led by Andria Mullan), the Albany Big Band, and the Bob Roden Quintet. articles.text: The City of Piedmont’s popular Harvest Festival, now in its 23rd year, will return to Piedmont Main Park on Sunday, September 19, after the COVID-19 pandemic caused the event to be canceled last year. The festival will feature all the traditional mainstays and activities, including the Jazz Festival, food trucks, Village Market’s Farmer’s Market, and the Edibles Contest. Also returning will be the Kids Carnival and games and the lineup of creative scarecrows. Visit Piedmont Park between 11 a.m. and 3 p.m. on September 19 for the following special events. Two nights earlier, Friday, September 17, the Recreation Department will sponsor a movie in the park with a screening of Bee Movie. Edibles Contest The popular Edibles Contest, occurring every Harvest Festival since its inception in 1998, features the best home-grown and homemade foods from your neighbors. Due to the pandemic, tastings to the general community will not be offered; instead, only judges will taste items submitted to the contest, so portion sizes of entries should be adjusted accordingly. There are many categories to choose from, including: biggest pumpkin, best sweet bread, most unusual vegetable, best apple pie, best jam, best salsa, best compost pile, and more. Any Piedmont resident may submit an entry, and entries may be done by individuals, households, neighborhoods or groups. All entries must be delivered between 7:30 a.m. and 9:00 a.m. on Sunday, September 19. Bring your completed entry form (or proof of digital submission) to the Community Hall. articles.text: After a year of filmed productions, the PHS Advanced Acting Class is pleased to announce it will present Marian, or The True Tale of Robin Hood in the PHS amphitheater the weekend of September 24-26. In the play written by Adam Szymkowicz, Merry Men (many of whom are not men) are pitted against the greedy Prince John. As the poor get poorer and the rich get richer, who will stand for the vulnerable? Come outside and watch sword fighting, singing and goofy romantic entanglements. There are also storylines with the LGBTQ and trans communities. The cast includes Theo Arenstam, Liam Gordon, Alex Guevara, Maya Hollinsworth, Chloe Kibarian, Jasper Kra-Caskey, Charlotte Levy, Miranda Long, Eden Lorin, Elsie Pines, Corinn Richards, Andres Roberts, Erik Stenstrom, Katherine Stormer, Nathan Sturdivant, and Charles White. Tickets are $15 for students and seniors, and $20 for the general public. Masks will be required. Arrive early to fill out the District Covid screener. Contact director Kimberly Taylor at ktaylor@piedmont.k12.ca.us with any questions.
articles.title: PHS actors bring Robin Hood to the Amphitheater

articles.text: This fall, Piedmont Adult School will have more than 50 classes in a wide array of disciplines. Registration is open now for enrichment in Arts and Crafts, Business, Computers, Health and Dance, Language and Music. Visit PiedmontAdultSchool. org for course listings. Classes fit any schedule or level of commitment with some classes running from September 13 until December 19, and others as one-day classes on weekends. Registration remains open for classes that have room. Shannon Fierro, Adult School Director, has scheduled a lineup of 14 new classes this year. “One of the goals of our program is to offer community to adults who are connecting over a common interest. This was hard to do through screens last year and is much easier when you are side-by-side with your classmates learning French, practicing your computer skills or exercising,” said Fierro. A number of computer classes are available for basic knowledge or to perfect computer skills. Computer classes include: Creating a Website with Wordpress, Microsoft Excel and Adobe Acrobat. Students will be taught in labs in the STEAM building. Some popular classes still available are: Rachel Whitman’s Naturalist Illustration art class, Climate Change 101, and Alycia Lai-Clemn’s five day per week Aerobic Workout class. The Adult School has French and Spanish classes in all levels and offers in-person instruction at ten school and city buildings around town, as well as online courses. Stop by the Adult School office at 760 Magnolia Avenue between 10 a.m. and 7 p.m. to pick up a list of courses in The Moonlighter, or call 594-2655. articles.text: One of the four new electives being offered at Piedmont High School is the year-long Physical Computing and Robotics class taught by Irfan Ortak. The first semester is focused on using Raspberry Pi computers, and the second semester will focus on robotics using the VEX V5 robotic equipment. PHS has a robust computer department, but prior to this year, the school did not have a course on hardware and the physical part of computing. The new STEAM building gives the school the opportunity to expand the Computer Department, and students have responded with 30 sign-ups. The first semester will provide a hands-on projects-based environment in building, maintaining and integrating computer systems using Raspberry Pi and its components. Raspberry Pis are revolutionary, small, inexpensive and adaptable computing systems that have become increasingly used for a wide range of purposes. Students will learn how to control cameras, sensors and microcontrollers to do creative projects using the Python programming language. One assignment will be to create an Astronaut Reaction Time Game. articles.text: The second annual Walk for Wellness, the largest fundraiser for Piedmont School District’s Wellness Center, will take place September 20 through 26. It is an inclusive and socially-distanced event open to the entire Piedmont Community, and funds raised allow the Center to maintain a robust training program to meet the needs of Piedmont students. The Wellness Center was established by Piedmont Middle School Counselor Brooke Zimmerman in 2007 and offers individual and group counseling services to address a myriad of common adolescent concerns, as well as crisis intervention and referrals to community mental health services. The Wellness Center also covers a majority of Individualized Education Program (IEP) based counseling at the middle and high schools. According to the Wellness Center Support Committee, which organizes the fundraiser, one quarter of middle school students and one third of high school students seek counseling or other services from the Center each year. Beyond the services provided, the Center also serves as a muchneeded respite area for students. Students can use the waiting room, have tea, read materials and resources provided, and simply relax. “We are so appreciative of our Parent Support Committee, which raises this money for us. Primarily, these funds go to support stipends for our unlicensed staff, who are accruing hours toward licensure under supervision of the clinical supervisors,” explained Alisa Crovetti, a Clinical Supervisor for the Center. The first Walk for Wellness event raised $37,000 in funds, allowing the Center to attract high-quality candidates and increase retention. “We have therapists returning for multiple years, which greatly enriches the quality of our services,” Crovetti said. The Wellness Center has a partnership with the UC Berkeley Psychology Internship Consortium, which allows them to hire pre-doctoral interns. Interns hold graduate training in psychological assessment and psychotherapy, usually one year out of completing their Ph.D. Financial support for the Center last year allowed Clinical Supervisors to provide training on teletherapy, solution-focused therapy, anti-racist and culturally-sensitive mental health approaches, and Dialectical Behavior Therapy, which Crovetti said is a “preferred modality for students who have trouble regulating their emotions, coping with stress, and maintaining stable relationships.” Crovetti also noted that, despite the challenges brought on by the pandemic, teletherapy or “remote” therapy has become a preferred modality even when in-person services are available for some clients. “At the beginning [of 2020], we provided a two-part training on teletherapy – laws and ethics related to providing teletherapy with minors and also the clinical implications and skills associated with it,” added Crovetti. “In spring, we transitioned to a hybrid approach, which allowed some services on site and the remainder via teletherapy.” Crovetti said that she recognizes the unique challenges facing students this year as they return to school in the midst of a global pandemic. Funds raised from the Walk for Wellness will place the Center in a good position to address these concerns, primarily by hiring and retaining stellar personnel. “Many students are feeling a lot more anxiety than is typical with the return to school. Many of them have experienced social isolation during the last year, and it feels overwhelming to be back with so many students,” she said. “The funding, very importantly, allows us to maintain a robust training program for our unlicensed therapy staff.” Piedmonters are encouraged to gather their friends and family members and participate in as many walks as possible during the week of September 20. You can post photos from your walk on Instagram by tagging the handle@Piedmont-wellness. To register and make donations, visit: www.piedmontwalkforwellness.org, or email piedmontwalkforwellness@gmail.com.

articles.text: Screens have become a much bigger part of our lives since the start of COVID-times, and I’m pretty sure we aren’t the only family with that story. So, before the school year started, we made a family decision. It was time to detox. We discussed our options and decided unanimously that we needed a full stop – one week with no screens (with one exception: Baking Shows, but only if the whole family was watching). Here is what I noticed in this week-long, screen-free time. Creativity thrived My two youngest have very active imaginations, and my oldest really likes building and making things. So, we prepared for the week by making space for imagination play. What if they couldn’t think of anything to do? They could always go outside and play imagination games. My oldest used some of his Bar Mitzvah money to buy a remote-control car kit that he could build. As the week progressed, we created art projects and new games as well. We talked more I really enjoy chatting with my gang. They have really interesting thoughts on lots of different topics. What we noticed in our week with no electronics is that they were willing to “practice the art of conversation” at dinner with a lot more patience than if they had the option of returning to their video games. Age divide diminished I looked into the living room early on and saw that the 13-yearold, 10-year-old and 5-year-old were all actively engaged in some wrestling game where the two little ones were trying to get their big brother to roll off the carpet. Everyone was laughing and having fun. This happened throughout the week. In contrast, when they are in Screen Land, it is hard for them to find anything that all three can agree on to watch or do together because they are all interested in different kinds of content. Families can get more creative when they have more time away from computer screens. They were more present We spent a lot of time noticing things during the week. Seeing beautiful vistas on walks, really recognizing the flavors in foods, noticing how the people around us were feeling. I asked my gang about this, and they all recognized that they were more present and not thinking about “what comes next” nearly as much. More physical activity My kids are pretty good in terms of moving their bodies; they all have sports they enjoy and are very happy to go on hikes or bike rides. But, if given the option to sit and stare at a screen for hours on end, they will do just that. I was thrilled that, for screen-free week, they were constantly moving. We were lucky enough to have access to a pool, so they spent hours jumping in and out of the water, but even when they were not in the pool, they were flipping over couches, running around the kitchen island, jumping up and down in the driveway. They were in constant motion...until about 2 p.m. each day, when my 5-year-old crashed and took a spontaneous nap in the middle of the living room. There was more space for being silly Perhaps the most fun of all was that there was just more time and space for silliness. One of the joys of raising kids is being able to share in the silly that comes so naturally to them. But, when they have screens as an option, the silly just diminishes. They are spending more time in their own little bubble, and, let’s face it, silly is more fun when you share it. There were dumb dad jokes from my husband, wacky faces, tickle fests and even a few homemade riddles. All together, it made for more laughter and a lot of smiles. Now that school is back in our lives, we will go back to the “no electronics during the week” rule that existed pre-COVID, but I’m excited to continue the conversation with my kids about weekends. They noticed the changes too. I think we are in a strong position to find a better balance. Every family is different, so this might not be right for yours, but I think it was an interesting experiment. pages.text: Wednesday, September 8, 2021 9 Thinking Outside The Classroom A week of family life, screen-free: What I learned. By Nina Meehan Screens have become a much bigger part of our lives since the start of COVID-times, and I’m pretty sure we aren’t the only family with that story. So, before the school year started, we made a family decision. It was time to detox. We discussed our options and decided unanimously that we needed a full stop – one week with no screens (with one exception: Baking Shows, but only if the whole family was watching). Here is what I noticed in this week-long, screen-free time. Creativity thrived My two youngest have very active imaginations, and my oldest really likes building and making things. So, we prepared for the week by making space for imagination play. What if they couldn’t think of anything to do? They could always go outside and play imagination games. My oldest used some of his Bar Mitzvah money to buy a remote-control car kit that he could build. As the week progressed, we created art projects and new games as well. We talked more I really enjoy chatting with my gang. They have really interesting thoughts on lots of different topics. What we noticed in our week with no electronics is that they were willing to “practice the art of conversation” at dinner with a lot more patience than if they had the option of returning to their video games. Age divide diminished I looked into the living room early on and saw that the 13-yearold, 10-year-old and 5-year-old were all actively engaged in some wrestling game where the two little ones were trying to get their big brother to roll off the carpet. Everyone was laughing and having fun. This happened throughout the week. In contrast, when they are in Screen Land, it is hard for them to find anything that all three can agree on to watch or do together because they are all interested in different kinds of content. Families can get more creative when they have more time away from computer screens. They were more present We spent a lot of time noticing things during the week. Seeing beautiful vistas on walks, really recognizing the flavors in foods, noticing how the people around us were feeling. I asked my gang about this, and they all recognized that they were more present and not thinking about “what comes next” nearly as much. More physical activity My kids are pretty good in terms of moving their bodies; they all have sports they enjoy and are very happy to go on hikes or bike rides. But, if given the option to sit and stare at a screen for hours on end, they will do just that. I was thrilled that, for screen-free week, they were constantly moving. We were lucky enough to have access to a pool, so they spent hours jumping in and out of the water, but even when they were not in the pool, they were flipping over couches, running around the kitchen island, jumping up and down in the driveway. They were in constant motion...until about 2 p.m. each day, when my 5-year-old crashed and took a spontaneous nap in the middle of the living room. There was more space for being silly Perhaps the most fun of all was that there was just more time and space for silliness. One of the joys of raising kids is being able to share in the silly that comes so naturally to them. But, when they have screens as an option, the silly just diminishes. They are spending more time in their own little bubble, and, let’s face it, silly is more fun when you share it. There were dumb dad jokes from my husband, wacky faces, tickle fests and even a few homemade riddles. All together, it made for more laughter and a lot of smiles. Now that school is back in our lives, we will go back to the “no electronics during the week” rule that existed pre-COVID, but I’m excited to continue the conversation with my kids about weekends. They noticed the changes too. I think we are in a strong position to find a better balance. Every family is different, so this might not be right for yours, but I think it was an interesting experiment. So many of us are struggling with the shift back to “normal,” even though things still aren’t normal. I hope you are finding interesting experiments with your children too. articles.text: Photos by Brian Mahany Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany (not pictured) are now 4-1 as a duo and have won all four matches in straight sets. The Piedmont High girls’ tennis team took a one-sided 7-2 loss to non-league North Coast Section opponent Miramonte in Orinda on Thursday, September 2. They returned home to take on Alameda on Tuesday, September 7, but lost to the Hornets 6-1. Miramonte competes in Division 1 of NCS, while Piedmont plays in Div. 2, making the two sides eligible for play nine matches (six singles and three doubles). Alameda is the first league opponent Piedmont has faced this fall. “Miramonte always has a strong team, but it’s good to play tough teams early in the season. Alameda was a really, really tough loss; things certainly could’ve gone the other way. I’m looking forward to seeing them again later in the season,” explained coach Jim Landes. Miramonte loss Among the victories was No. 1 singles starter Bridgette McEfee claiming her first win of the season, defeating Riley George in three sets, 6-1, 5-7, 10-7. Also in the win column was the No. 1 doubles pair of Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany, defeating Ellie Foster and Sophia Kan in straight sets; 6-1, 7-5. Bridgette McEfee won her first match of the season against Miramonte, 6-1, 5-7, 10-7. Miramonte won all but one of the remaining matches in straight sets. In singles, Anne Jumper lost 7-6 (7-3), 6-2 at No. 2; Michaela Bini had a close 7-5, 6-4 loss at No. 3; Anika Gilliland fell 6-3, 6-2 at No. 4; freshman Emma Eisemon lost 6-3, 6-3 at No. 5; and Cecilia Defazio lost 6-0, 6-0 at No. 6. In doubles, No. 2 Mara LaForte and Rose Seimers had a three-set loss that went to a third set super breaker, 6-7 (7-2), 6-1, 10-7. At No. 3, Audrey Frankel and Sofia Ferraro lost 6-1, 6-4. Rose Seimers (back) and Mara LaForte (front) battled in three-set losses against Miramonte and Alameda.
articles.title: Highlanders fall to Miramonte & Alameda

articles.text: Skyline Lacrosse, founded in 1979 and the premiere youth lacrosse program in the area, is set to host boys and girls camps at Coaches Field every Sunday in two separate sessions starting September 12 through December 12. The camps are designed for boys and girls in Under-8, U10, U12 (middle school) and U14. The camps are focused on student-athletes looking for their first experience in the sport. “Typically we have fall ball where we try to get kids excited about playing in the spring. We want to get kids who have never played the sport before to come to our training sessions and learn the game,” said Carlton Chan, a longtime coach at Skyline, and Piedmont High School head women’s coach for the past four years. “This gets kids who have never played the game more comfortable with lacrosse.” Chan will help coach the camp’s U14 players. Skyline Lacrosse is one of the oldest lacrosse organizations in California, having a clear impact on boys’ and girls’ lacrosse throughout the nearby high school programs. For years, Skyline helped players reach varsity rosters at Piedmont, Bishop O’Dowd, Berkeley, Miramonte, and Castro Valley. “Skyline has always built itself as a recreational program, so it is open to everybody. There are no barriers to entry in comparison to a lot of privately run, for-profit clubs. I think that grassroots-effort is what has built its reputation. The purpose of the camps is getting kids who have never played the sport,” said Chan. The camps will be focused on players looking for their first lacrosse experience. Skyline competes in the Northern California Junior Lacrosse Associate, which oversees all clubs from the Bay Area, from Monterey to Sacramento. “These sessions will be focused on fitness, fundamentals, and basic teamwork. Fitness will be a big component; kids go into spring ball really out of shape so we’re going to preach the basics of fundamentals, avoiding injuries, and building their conditioning. We’re going to give them the tools to take what they learn from us and develop their own workout plan in regards to lacrosse,” explained Chan. As much fun as they are having, the results show on the field. Piedmont High’s 2019 NCS Championship winning girls’ team, 2019 WACC Champion, and 2018 WACC Championship winning girls’ teams were nearly completely Skyline alumni, just one player “The NCS championship winning team was all Skyline alum,” recalled Chan. Aside from the interested potential Piedmont student-athlete looking to get a leg-up on cracking the varsity roster, the camp is open to students from all schools. Skyline has alums currently on varsity teams at Bishop O’Dowd and Berkeley, in addition to Piedmont. Skyline camps will be $190 for U8 and U10 boys and girls, and $255 for U12 and U14 players. For more information, visit www.SkylineLacrosse.com or contact Skyline Administrator Joe Reid at Admin@skylinelacrosse.com. Boys will have U8, U10, U12, and U14 teams.

articles.text: It’s been a rough start to the fall season for Piedmont’s football team. It’s first two contests have been canceled, most recently a scrimmage with Encinal on September 3 that was canceled by North Coast Section officials who ruled that Encinal had already completed a regular season game and was ineligible to play in a separate scrimmage. “The North Coast Section commissioner [Pat Cruickshank] canceled the scrimmage. NCS rules states a team cannot scrimmage twice in a season. Encinal has already had an official scrimmage and a game, so they informed us that the Jets couldn’t play,” explained Piedmont coach Jerome Johnson. This comes after the varsity team watched numbers drop to under 20 athletes. A scrimmage on Friday, August 27 at Miramonte was canceled at the last minute due to poor air quality. The Highlanders will enter the game this Friday with Durham without having had any d scrimmages or practice games. The varsity’s only competition has been with its own junior varsity team. “It’s tough going into a game without having any controlled time,” said Johnson. It’s an unfortunate turn for the football program after going 5-0 last season and finishing as Staff Photo Witter Field was empty on Friday, September 3 after the scrimmage with Encinal was canceled by NCS commissioner Pat Cruikshank. the top-ranked NCS Division 5 school. Despite Piedmont’s 100 years of history with a successful football program, the team has been the hardest hit program this fall. “We’re not the only one in the same boat,” said Athletic Director Bradley Smet. “There are a lot of schools with impacted numbers, and the pandemic could be part of the reason. A lot of schools have smaller numbers, but football has definitely taken a hit.” “Some kids just decided not to come out. We’ve had some players who were on the team last year, but this year either they were less enthusiastic or parents voiced concern about them playing football specifically,” added Johnson. Both Varsity and Junior Varsity will now look ahead to its season-opener this Friday against Durham High School outside Chico, a school with an enrollment of 350 students. It will be the first meeting in football between the two schools. The Trojans are currently 1-0 with a 14-8 win over Williams HS and finished 4-2 last season, 3-7 in 2019, and 11-2 in 2018 when they won the Sacramento Valley Athletic Association championship. Friday’s game at Witter Field starts at 7 p.m., with the JV game at 4:30 p.m. PHS looks ahead to its official home-opener at Witter Field this Friday, September 10 against Durham at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: Piedmont native Mackie McDonald was unable to capitalize on his first ever opening round victory at the U.S. Open, falling in the second round in five sets to Japan’s Kei Nishikori; 7-6 (7-3), 6-3, 6-7 (7-5), 2-6, 6-3, on Thursday, September 2. Sept. 10 By Jonathan Comeaux It’s been a rough start to the fall season for Piedmont’s football team. It’s first two contests have been canceled, most recently a scrimmage with Encinal on September 3 that was canceled by North Coast Section officials who ruled that Encinal had already completed a regular season game and was ineligible to play in a separate scrimmage. “The North Coast Section commissioner [Pat Cruickshank] canceled the scrimmage. NCS rules states a team cannot scrimmage twice in a season. Encinal has already had an official scrimmage and a game, so they informed us that the Jets couldn’t play,” explained Piedmont coach Jerome Johnson. This comes after the varsity team watched numbers drop to under 20 athletes. A scrimmage on Friday, August 27 at Miramonte was canceled at the last minute due to poor air quality. The Highlanders will enter the game this Friday with Durham without having had any d scrimmages or practice games. The varsity’s only competition has been with its own junior varsity team. “It’s tough going into a game without having any controlled time,” said Johnson. It’s an unfortunate turn for the football program after going 5-0 last season and finishing as Staff Photo Witter Field was empty on Friday, September 3 after the scrimmage with Encinal was canceled by NCS commissioner Pat Cruikshank. the top-ranked NCS Division 5 school. Despite Piedmont’s 100 years of history with a successful football program, the team has been the hardest hit program this fall. “We’re not the only one in the same boat,” said Athletic Director Bradley Smet. “There are a lot of schools with impacted numbers, and the pandemic could be part of the reason. A lot of schools have smaller numbers, but football has definitely taken a hit.” “Some kids just decided not to come out. We’ve had some players who were on the team last year, but this year either they were less enthusiastic or parents voiced concern about them playing football specifically,” added Johnson. Both Varsity and Junior Varsity will now look ahead to its season-opener this Friday against Durham High School outside Chico, a school with an enrollment of 350 students. It will be the first meeting in football between the two schools. The Trojans are currently 1-0 with a 14-8 win over Williams HS and finished 4-2 last season, 3-7 in 2019, and 11-2 in 2018 when they won the Sacramento Valley Athletic Association championship. Friday’s game at Witter Field starts at 7 p.m., with the JV game at 4:30 p.m. PHS looks ahead to its official home-opener at Witter Field this Friday, September 10 against Durham at 7:00 p.m. PIEDMONT SPORTS SCHEDULE Some events subject to change. The Rubicon Trail is a 5.9 mile out-and-back trail (11.8 round trip, 1,350 feet in elevation gain) that stretches around Emerald Bay on the West shore of Lake Tahoe. It offers a 360-degree view of Fannette Island in the middle of Emerald Bay, and enables hikers to go by the historic Vikingsholm mansion through the quiet Emerald Bay Boat Camp. There are countless places to rest beside the crystal blue water on the way to the Rubicon Point Lighthouse. Starting from the parking lot in the Upper Eagle Point Campground, the Rubicon Trail goes Staff Photos The view from the starting point at Upper Eagle Point Campground. Take a walk along Emerald Bay on the Rubicon Trail. It provides a 360-degree view of Fannett Island and its historic Tea House. 1.6 miles beside Lake Tahoe with before reaching Vikingsholm, a 38-room mansion built in 1929 on the shores of Emerald Bay. It was the summer home of Lora Josephine Knight. She inherited her fortune from the passing of her former husband William Henry Moore, whose law firm had a controlling interest in U.S. Steel, Union Pacific, Rock Island Railroad and the National Biscuit Company (later named Nabisco). She was among the primary financial backers of Charles Lindbergh’s trans-Atlantic flight in 1927. Resting on top of Fannette Island is the famous Tea House constructed by Knight when her mansion was finished. The trail continues beside a white sandy beach along Emerald Bay to the northern portion of the Rubicon Trail. The northern section of Emerald Bay gives visitors a much more private look of Fannette Island with spots along the shoreline to cool off on a hot day. It leads to the Emerald Bay Boat Camp a mile from the mansion, a secluded $30 per night boat-in campground. Less than a mile from the Emerald Bay Boat Camp entrance is another private unnamed cove with crystal blue water. Turning back to your car from this point rounds out the day at just under seven miles and only 550 feet in elevation gain. Continuing to the Rubicon Point Lighthouse adds 2.2 miles and around 450 feet in elevation gain to your day. For visitors interested in seeing the lighthouse, close parking is available at Lester and Callawee Cove Beach less than a mile away. articles.text: San Francisco Botanical Garden, in partnership with Sunset Piano, is bringing the Flower Piano event back after a 2020 hiatus due to the coronavirus pandemic. Sunset Piano will be placing grand baby grand pianos in San Francisco Botanical Garden, located in Golden Gate Park, for a unique, interactive musical event. For five days in September, ending September 21, musicians and artists will play an eclectic range of genres, from jazz to classical to Afro-Cuban. The traditional event is held for twelve days in the summer and has enjoyed five successful years of performances. Piano locations in Golden Gate Park will include the Great Meadow, Garden of Fragrance, and Conifer Lawn. San Francisco residents are free to attend but must have a Sunset Piano is placing grand pianos throughout Golden Gate Park beginning September 17 for a unique music festival entitled “Flower Piano.” ticket to enter. Tickets are $9 for non-San Francisco residents. Advanced ticketing is required to prevent crowding and may be obtained by visiting https://sunsetpiano.com/flowerpiano.
articles.title: SF Botanical Garden brings back Flower Piano Festival this month

articles.text: Alisa Golden’s “Nature on Loan,” an exhibition of art quilts, continues at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Sunday and next, September 19. Gallery hours are from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., and there will be a walk-through tour with the artist this Sunday, September 12, at noon. Golden’s background in creative writing, printmaking, and book arts offers a unique starting point for her work in textiles. The expansive exhibition showcases her work in printing, painting, beading and stitching. The quilts, art and poetry are inspired by “natural themes addressing our relationships and responsibilities, from the California fires and the pandemic, to botanicals and birds,” the artist said. “As a printmaker and writer, I am fascinated with marks and traces and how they become symbols for and signs of the people and beings who were there before. Each piece functions as a page where I can print from linoleum blocks, photopolymer plates or type, and then embroider and Artist Alisa Golden quilt a longer text or texture,” Golden said. “The photographic possibilities for solar printing from my own photographic imagery and hand-dyeing techniques appeal to me as well. I like the space between images and words, the colors and titles, where the viewer must interpret or fill in the gap, a little mysterious leap of inference.” The artist works in many sizes, and most quilts on display are for sale. You can contact Golden directly at info@neverbook.com. No reservations are required for admission to open gallery hours, and all county COVID-19 guidelines will be observed. articles.text: The Autumn Lights Festival will return to Lake Merritt next month. Autumn Lights Festival, an art-filled and family-friendly fundraising event for the Gardens at Lake Merritt, returns this year on October 14. The festival has drawn more than 10,000 art and nature enthusiasts to Lake Merritt since 2012. The festival is celebrating its 10th anniversary over three nights, October 14 through 16. Guests will experience 60 locally-produced illuminated art displays spread throughout the seven-acre municipal gardens. There will also be a kids’ “ fun zone,” art market, food court, and a beer and wine garden. All festival attendees must provide proof of vaccination or a negative COVID test to enter. Masks are required, and capacity is limited. Tickets are available at: https://gardensatlakemerritt.org/ autumn-lights-festival-2020/.

articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony will perform the music from Rob Reiner’s movie The Princess Bride live at Davies Symphony Hall on September 22 and 23. Both performances begin at 7:30 p.m. Patrons will experience one of director Reiner’s most well-known films in a never-before-seen and heard setting, with the San Francisco Symphony performing the entire musical score of this fairytale adventure live. Sarah Hicks is conductor and Mark Knopfler is the composer. The 1987 film stars Cary Elwes, Robin Wright, Mandy Patinkin, and Chris Sarandon, and is adapted fom the 1973 novel of the same name. It tells the story of a farmhand named Westley, accompanied by friends along the way who must rescue his true love Princess Buttercup from Prince Humperdinck. Over time, the film gained “cult classic” notoriety, and was inducted into the National Film Registry and deemed “culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant.” Visit https://www.sfsymphony. org/seatme/single?id=20463 to purchase tickets. The San Francisco Symphony will perform live at Davies Symphony Hall on September 22.
articles.title: Symphony to perform movie music from The Princess Bride

articles.text: Opera San Jose has announced its 2021-22 season, to include in-person performances beginning this November in California Theatre. The season launches with a production of Rimsky-Korsakov’s Mozart and Salieri, followed by Purcell’s Dido and Aeneas, Bizet’s Carmen, and Bernstein’s West Side Story to close. “This season, we explore the necessity of human connection. We explore love – and love interrupted. We witness people who are confronted by a world incompatible with who they are or who they wish to be,” General Director Khori Dastoor said. Mozart and Salieri, a Heiman Digital Media Studio production, will begin as a live-stream captured on September 30. Subscribers will receive access to the production. Based on Alexander Pushkin’s play of the same name, the psychological drama follows the Italian composer Antonio Salieri and his envy of Mozart’s musical genius. Conducted by Simon Barrad stars as Mozart and Sidney Outlaw as Salieri in the streaming opera Mozart and Salieri beginning September 30. Donato Cabrera and directed by Fenlon Lamb, the play incorporates quotations from Mozart’s Requiem and Don Giovanni. Baritone Sidney Outlaw stars as Salieri. To obtain streaming access to Mozart and Salieri, visit https:// www.operasj.org/mozart-and-salieri/. Dido and Aeneas will launch Opera San Jose’s return to in-per-

articles.text: The recent death of Michael Morgan, the popular conductor of the Oakland Symphony for 30 years, sent shivers up and down the spine of the East Bay community. We can only grieve over his loss and make sure we remember the good that he did. But the music world continues to rotate… And now the scramble begins to find a successor. I have heard talk already. For what it’s worth, I offer 68 years of experience. Musically speaking, quality should be the first consideration. Do not start with ethnicity, nor race, sexual orientation, nor socio-economic status. Quality must come first. suggest people like Michael Tilson Thomas, Richard Ginell, and George Gelles. Everyone knows and respects maestro Thomas. The small advisory committee should also include a music critic like a Richard Ginell, and someone like a George Gelles. The latter two names are probably not familiar to local readers. Richard Ginell is one of the most outstanding music critics in the country and George Gelles was also a respected music critic as well as being a highly placed executive of orchestras and important music festivals. It is important to have people like this in an advisory capacity. Philosophy The entire musical community must work together in congress with the community in general. Just as a symphony orchestra legitimizes a city, the conductor must be able to be an important presence. For the decision makers, I say again: choose wisely. But how shall it be done? Choosing wisely I propose a multi-faceted approach. A group must be formed with members of the board of the Oakland Symphony. It must include a musicians’ committee and also an advisory committee. The board of the Oakland Symphony is already formed. Musicians of the symphony need to select their representatives. articles.text: The U.S. Conference of Mayors adopted a resolution urging Congress to provide arts and culture relief funding in the wake of the COVID pandemic. The initiative was led by San Francisco Mayor London Breed and Chicago Mayor Lori Lightfoot. The Conference of Mayors is an official, non-partisan organization of cities with populations of 30,000 or more and comprises 1,400 cities across the nation. In collaboration with the San Francisco Arts Alliance, the mayors reinforced federal policy recommendations to address the “the urgent needs of the nation’s arts and culture sector, and to take prompt and coordinated action to integrate arts into [the nation’s] recovery and revitalization efforts.” “Our arts and cultural institutions are the lifeblood of our vibrant communities and essential to our economy,” Mayor Breed said. “The arts define us as a city, they create jobs, and they are paramount in bringing together our diverse communities as we push for equity across all institutions. As we continue on this path of economic recovery, it has never been more critical to invest in the arts.” The arts and culture sectors contributed more than $877 billion to the nation’s economy in 2017, according to the San Francisco Arts Alliance. The current losses sustained by the sector as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic have reached $15 billion as of August this year. The Alliance seeks to lobby legislative issues which impacts the arts and culture community on local, state, and federal levels in order to ensure the equitable recovery of San Francisco. The Conference of Mayors is urging relief that will extend the Employment Retention Tax Credit beyond 2021 and modify nonprofit eligibility.
articles.title: U.S. mayors urge congress to support arts and culture

articles.text: The just released film is an epic, sea-faring tale, adapted from the 2000 best-selling non-fiction book by Nathaniel Philbrick. Set in 1819-20 during a period when the whaling industry was robust and sperm whale oil kept the lights burning and the wheels of the still nascent industrial revolution turning. Initially set in Nantucket, the film tells the story of the Essex, captained by the inexperienced George Pollard (Benjamin Walker), who was reluctant to turn to his first lieutenant, Owen Chase (Chris Hemsworth), fearful that he would seem weak. It was estimated that the journey of the Essex would last some one to three years, depending on how long it took to fill its holds with 2,000 barrels of oil. After a year at sea and little oil to show for it, Chase and Pollard are told of an area off the southern coast of South America said to be superb hunting. The information comes with a grim caveat: there is a massive whale out there that will, without hesitation, ram a ship and breach its hull. Discounting the story, the Essex sets sail south by southwest, headed for the hunting grounds described. The film opens with a writer, Herman Melville, hoping to convince one of the survivors, Tom Nickerson (Brendan Gleeson), then a young cabin boy (Tom Holland) serving on the Essex, to tell him the story of the whale and the sinking of the ship. At first reluctant to reveal any details to Melville, Nickerson finally relents. In a series of long flashbacks, he shares the story while Melville painstakingly takes notes. The essence of the tale is not just about the whale – 100 feet long, barnacle-encrusted, battered and covered with white spots – but of the men’s survival in their lifeboats for 90 days. In the Heart of the Sea is not about a singular man’s obsession with a white whale, which was Melville’s fictional account, published in 1851, later titled Moby Dick. Rather, it’s about the men of the Essex and what they endured after they sat and watched their ship burn and then sink beneath the horizon, knowing they were thousands of miles from land. Director Ron Howard also injects into the movie the 19th century reality that the whale oil industry was a lucrative business that required the harvesting of the largest mammals on earth, purely for profit. The tension between the exploitation of the earth’s resources for profit is still a conundrum some 195 years later for which we still have not found a balance. In the Heart of the Sea. Starring Chris Hemsworth, Brendan Gleason and Ben Whishaw. Directed by Ron Howard. 2 hrs., 1 min. Rated PG-13. Cillian Murphy, Benjamin Walker and Chris Hemsworth in In the Heart of the Sea. articles.text: Sam Elliott stars in The Hero. This may sound a bit hyperbolic, and Sam Elliott would likely reject the praise out of hand, using some purple language that would seem completely in character, but the fact is, as an actor, Elliott is a national treasure. He possesses not only that easily recognizable, sonorous voice, but he is also the last of a type, that cowboy who rode across a red dirt plain, stacked Colorado pillars in the distance, the sun at his back, ever alone. After decades wearing worn western garb Elliott has merged with that mythic image that we carry with us when we think of the Old West. Granted that may never have been, but there it is. In this movie we see Sam Elliott, lean as a weathered fence post, his 71 years etched in the crevasses of his leathery, tanned face, his frame all angles, his persona to a fault laconic, often sardonic. In The Hero Elliott plays the role of Lee Hayden, a man holding his regrets at bay with alcohol and weed, still able to scratch out a living making voice-over commercials for the likes of Lone Star Barbecue Sauce. This film finds a sweet spot and manages to stay there because of Elliott’s ability to never let his character slip in the realm of the maudlin, even when he gets some medical news that gives him bridled pause. Suddenly his life is derailed, and his estrangement from his daughter, Lucy (Krysten Ritter) and ex-wife, Val (Katherine Ross, Elliott’s real wife), give his very brief contact list kept on his phone a new urgency. He also meets a far younger woman, Charlotte (Laura Prepon), who makes him realize that he is at the beginning of the end of his life (no matter the medical diagnosis), and that his self-centered halcyon days are gone. He now finds himself standing alone on a beach gazing at the horizon. Though the story is as spare as Elliott’s grin, this is never a vanity film. This is Elliott at his best, and as Lee, he refuses to turn away from who he has become, a man filled with life still, but a life constantly tempered by a sense of loss. Some of the moments in “The Hero” are sublime. Others are filled with an abiding melancholy. Perhaps melancholy is how you ultimately define growing old, each day slipping through your grasp like so many grains of desert sand, each night given over to restless sleep, always confronting what was and will never be again. The Hero. Directed by Brett Haley. Starring Sam Elliott, Laura Prepon, Katherine Ross. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated R. ®

articles.text: A scene from Peter Rabbit 2: The Runaway. Like its predecessor, Peter Rabbit, Peter Rabbit 2: The Runaway is a computer-animated hybrid, based on the much-loved books by Beatrix Potter. Kids love this rabbit, and The Runaway has an energetic, wack-a-mole, convoluted plot, set in great part in London and not the familiar Windemere farm. The story opens with the marriage of Beatrix (Rose Byrne) and Thomas (Domhall Gleeson), who, due to the efforts of Bea, are now living in relative harmony with the farm animals, most especially Peter (James Corden) and Thomas, whose trust of Peter is still a work in progress. Bea and Thomas have been working on a series of books that feature tales about the denizens of the McGregor farm. They receive a letter in the mail from a London publisher Nigel BasicJones (David Oyelowo). He wants to take Bea’s charming local stories commercial, a proposal that causes some concerns for the couple. But out of curiosity and to put to rest their questions about the methods to be used by Nigel, they take a meeting in London with the publisher, bringing with them not only Peter, but the whole crew: Flopsy (Margot Robbie), Mopsy (Elizabeth Debicki), Cotton Tail (Aimee Horne), and cousin Benjamin (Colin Moody). Peter, as it turns out, is not happy about the way he is portrayed in the stories, characterized as a bit of a rogue; Nigel refers to him as a “bad seed,” even villainous. So, in a pique, he leaves the group, only to hook up with some bad company, headed up by a rabbit named Barnabas (Lennie James). And so begins a series of adventures that take Peter first to Barnabas’ hideout where he learns that there’s a plan afoot to carry out a vegetable heist from the local farmers market. As it turns out, their carefully formed plans turn into a mess. Peter and his clan get swept up by the Pet Pound, then freed, and head back to the farm where Peter seeks out the help of Thomas. They plan to return to London and defeat the underhanded work of Barnabas. Peter Rabbit 2 is exciting, slapdash, and even prankish, much to the delight of the kids who are happily watching events unfold, with tight corners gotten into and, of course, gotten out of. It’s all a lot of fun and the real-life animation is once again superb. Peter Rabbit 2: The Runaway. Directed by Will Glick. articles.text: Monsters, Inc. has a wonderful premise that will resonate with kids of all ages. I mean, what youngster hasn’t woken up in the dark night, the house asleep, and peeked over the covers at the closed closet door and imagined what might be behind it. “Was that a sound? Did I hear a creak from across the room?” Pixar, masters of computer animation and wonderful storytellers, offers a boisterous, imaginative answer to those questions. In fact, that door is a magical portal to a rust-belt factory called Monsters, Inc., home to an assembly line of bedroom doors through which “scarers,” aka the boogey man, will pass, monsters such as James P. Sullivan (John Goodman), aka Sulley, a huge purple and green furry guy, and his sidekick buddy, Mike Warkowski (Billy Crystal), who is a one-eyed, lime-green dude with a huge mouth. Their mission is to scare those children hiding under the covers, bottle their scream, and then return through the designated door where they use the harvested energy from the frightened scream to run the town of Monsteropolis. The only problem is that kids are not as easily frightened as they used to be, hence there’s less energy to run the factory. And so begins the story, with a small, pugnacious toddler who somehow slips through her closet door and finds herself in the Monster, Inc. factory where she is discovered by Sulley. Her presence triggers the CDA (Child Detection Agency) alarm, triggering a search by CDA agents. Luckily, she is rescued by Sulley, who calls her “Boo,” and manages to smuggle her out of the factory in a bag. Sulley and Mike make it their mission to return Boo back to her home. But first the two have to find Boo’s magical closet door, which is somewhere down on the factory floor. Meanwhile, Boo is in danger of being subjected to the Scream Extractor. And thus begins Sulley and Mike’s adventure as they deal with their nemesis Randal Boggs (Steve Buscemi), a monster who competes with the duo for the most scares, and behind conspires with Henry I. Waternoose III, C.E.O. of the factory, their purpose being to undermine Sulley and Mike. Monsters, Inc. has lots of twists and turns – at one point, the dynamic duo end up in the Himalayas and are taken in by an abdominal snowman, but soon make their way back to the factory. And they still have to get Boo home. It’s all good fun, and kids will more than enjoy the gags and antics of Mike and Sulley, who are never scary, just outrageously enjoyable to hang out with. Plus, the story has a satisfying ending wherein Sulley takes over Waternoose’s job as C.E.O. and retools the factory to use children’s laughter, not screams, to provide energy for Monster, Inc. and the Monsteropolis. Monsters, Inc. Pixar Animation. Directed by Pete Docter. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated G. A scene from Pixar’s Monsters, Inc.

Monsters, Inc. a gem from Pixar By Chris Honoré Monsters, Inc. has a wonderful premise that will resonate with kids of all ages. I mean, what youngster hasn’t woken up in the dark night, the house asleep, and peeked over the covers at the closed closet door and imagined what might be behind it. “Was that a sound? Did I hear a creak from across the room?” Pixar, masters of computer animation and wonderful storytellers, offers a boisterous, imaginative answer to those questions. In fact, that door is a magical portal to a rust-belt factory called Monsters, Inc., home to an assembly line of bedroom doors through which “scarers,” aka the boogey man, will pass, monsters such as James P. Sullivan (John Goodman), aka Sulley, a huge purple and green furry guy, and his sidekick buddy, Mike Warkowski (Billy Crystal), who is a one-eyed, lime-green dude with a huge mouth. Their mission is to scare those children hiding under the covers, bottle their scream, and then return through the designated door where they use the harvested energy from the frightened scream to run the town of Monsteropolis. The only problem is that kids are not as easily frightened as they used to be, hence there’s less energy to run the factory. And so begins the story, with a small, pugnacious toddler who somehow slips through her closet door and finds herself in the Monster, Inc. factory where she is discovered by Sulley. Her presence triggers the CDA (Child Detection Agency) alarm, triggering a search by CDA agents. Luckily, she is rescued by Sulley, who calls her “Boo,” and manages to smuggle her out of the factory in a bag. Sulley and Mike make it their mission to return Boo back to her home. But first the two have to find Boo’s magical closet door, which is somewhere down on the factory floor. Meanwhile, Boo is in danger of being subjected to the Scream Extractor. And thus begins Sulley and Mike’s adventure as they deal with their nemesis Randal Boggs (Steve Buscemi), a monster who competes with the duo for the most scares, and behind conspires with Henry I. Waternoose III, C.E.O. of the factory, their purpose being to undermine Sulley and Mike. Monsters, Inc. has lots of twists and turns – at one point, the dynamic duo end up in the Himalayas and are taken in by an abdominal snowman, but soon make their way back to the factory. And they still have to get Boo home. It’s all good fun, and kids will more than enjoy the gags and antics of Mike and Sulley, who are never scary, just outrageously enjoyable to hang out with. Plus, the story has a satisfying ending wherein Sulley takes over Waternoose’s job as C.E.O. and retools the factory to use children’s laughter, not screams, to provide energy for Monster, Inc. and the Monsteropolis. Monsters, Inc. Pixar Animation. Directed by Pete Docter. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated G. A scene from Peter Rabbit 2: The Runaway. By Chris Honoré Like its predecessor, Peter Rabbit, Peter Rabbit 2: The Runaway is a computer-animated hybrid, based on the much-loved books by Beatrix Potter. Kids love this rabbit, and The Runaway has an energetic, wack-a-mole, convoluted plot, set in great part in London and not the familiar Windemere farm. The story opens with the marriage of Beatrix (Rose Byrne) and Thomas (Domhall Gleeson), who, due to the efforts of Bea, are now living in relative harmony with the farm animals, most especially Peter (James Corden) and Thomas, whose trust of Peter is still a work in progress. Bea and Thomas have been working on a series of books that feature tales about the denizens of the McGregor farm. They receive a letter in the mail from a London publisher Nigel BasicJones (David Oyelowo). He wants to take Bea’s charming local stories commercial, a proposal that causes some concerns for the couple. But out of curiosity and to put to rest their questions about the methods to be used by Nigel, they take a meeting in London with the publisher, bringing with them not only Peter, but the whole crew: Flopsy (Margot Robbie), Mopsy (Elizabeth Debicki), Cotton Tail (Aimee Horne), and cousin Benjamin (Colin Moody). Peter, as it turns out, is not happy about the way he is portrayed in the stories, characterized as a bit of a rogue; Nigel refers to him as a “bad seed,” even villainous. So, in a pique, he leaves the group, only to hook up with some bad company, headed up by a rabbit named Barnabas (Lennie James). And so begins a series of adventures that take Peter first to Barnabas’ hideout where he learns that there’s a plan afoot to carry out a vegetable heist from the local farmers market. As it turns out, their carefully formed plans turn into a mess. Peter and his clan get swept up by the Pet Pound, then freed, and head back to the farm where Peter seeks out the help of Thomas. They plan to return to London and defeat the underhanded work of Barnabas. Peter Rabbit 2 is exciting, slapdash, and even prankish, much to the delight of the kids who are happily watching events unfold, with tight corners gotten into and, of course, gotten out of. It’s all a lot of fun and the real-life animation is once again superb. Peter Rabbit 2: The Runaway. Directed by Will Glick. articles.text: On Wednesday, September 1, the Cancer League held its annual Soiree at the Claremont Country Club. Historically known as the Spring Soiree, it was moved to the Fall due to Covid and given a new name, Soiree d’ete. Led by co-chairs Hilary Cooper and Erin Brayer, this event attracted approximately 200 guests to “shop and sip for survivorship.” The Soiree invites local vendors to sell their goods with 25% of their sales donated to the Cancer League, Inc. In 2019 when the event was most recently held, the League raised over $70,000 in the fight against cancer. Despite Covid and having to move some items outside, the Cancer League earned more $75,000, the highest amount in the event’s five-year history. “We planned for our traditional shopping and buffet dinner with everything inside, maskless and worry free. Due to [the Delta variant], we had to pivot and move eating and bars outside as well as follow the mask mandate,” said Erin Brayer. “Thankfully Claremont was willing to accommodate our request to use the circle out front in unprecedented ways!” Founded in 1973, the Cancer League Inc. is a non-profit organization with 100% of the monies earned going directly to fund groundbreaking cancer research at its early stages. Its current president is Lucy Ridgeway. Vendors this year included Cancer League Soiree co-chairs Hilary Cooper (left) and Erin Brayer. Photos by Sam Deaner Cancer League president Lucy Arney (left) and member Barbara Dickason at the Annual Cancer League Soiree on September 2 at the Claremont Country Club. handbag companies, jewelry, clothing, artwork, gifts, household wares, and accessories. The Soiree began outside on the front lawn with wine, cocktails and nibbles in a beautiful, tranquil tented setting, then moved inside to shop. The event lasted from 6-8 p.m. preceded by a special hour for VIP donors which included an exclusive hour of shopping, a champagne reception, a goodie bag, and special recognition for each VIP guest.. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: Pictured on September 1 are: Brenda Ferrero, Sarah Johnson, Susan Martin, Alan Goldhammer, Mike Henn, Nadine Guffanti, Sherry Jacobs, Phil Witte, Helen Dong, Quincy Dong, Harriette Louie, Emma Sangil, Haybert Houston, Stella Houston, Larry Olsen, Nancy Olsen, Priscilla Wanerus, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Adrienne Hamlin, Alicia Rivera, Pat Sheehan, Noemi Alvarado, Monica Christine Calliste, Charlene Louie, Kat Gustafson, Bob Gustafson, Albert Chen, Jim Kuo, Shirley Nakao, and Dick Carter. Last Wednesday was another beautiful day for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group. The morning clouds had cleared and the air quality was much improved. This lovely late summer morning brought out a strong turnout of 30 walkers at the Exedra. Two weeks earlier during a walking tour of Julia Morgan homes conducted by Will Adams, Jay Russell, the Post’s Question Man reporter, asked some walkers what unique piece of Piedmont history they have learned from their walks. One response was that early Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander made some very significant contributions to Piedmont, but he does not get the recognition that he deserves. The group was interested in learning more about Alexander and seeing what he and his family created. Drawing on information in Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont Historical Society articles in the Post, the group learned that Alexander’s contributions were many. First, he was instrumental in the construction of Piedmont’s commercial center. In 1916 Alexander also arranged for the purchase of the land for the Piedmont Interdenominational Church, now the Piedmont Community Church. He hired Albert Farr, the architect who designed much of the center of Piedmont, for this project. Alexander then arranged for the purchase in 1921 of two acres of upper Piedmont Park land from the widow of Frank C. Havens, saving it from development. Additionally, Alexander established the Piedmont Boy Scout Council in 1921. Wallace Alexander was born in Maui in 1869. His family was a leader in the creation of the Hawaiian sugar industry. However, the family moved to the Bay Area so that Wallace and his sisters could attend school in Oakland. He married his Oakland High School classmate, Mary Baker, in 1904, and they chose a large site on the corner of Sea View and Hampton Avenues. They built a three-story mansion that they named “Brown Gables” for its large, brown painted dormers. There was also a carriage house to the west on what is now King Avenue. The Alexanders created a bit of a family community in this area. In 1911 Alexander’s mother built her own home at 92 Sea View across the street from Brown Gables, and Mary’s mother built a home further down the street at 236 Sea View. These homes are still there, but Brown Gables no longer exists. After Alexander died from a stroke in 1939, his wife followed his wish that the mansion be torn down, and the land subdivided into 13 lots that were sold, so that more families could live in Piedmont. The walkers decided to make his creations their destinations for the day. The first was easy. Across Highland Avenue from the Exedra are relatively new real estate and bank offices on the commercial site that Alexander once helped build. The group started up Mountain Avenue where they admired Alexander and Farr’s Piedmont Community Church. The walkers climbed a little over half a mile up Mountain to Sea View Avenue, where they went in search of the edge of Alexander’s estate, which ran from what is now 83 Sea View to Hampton Avenue. They stopped for a photo in front of 92 Sea View, Alexander’s mother’s beautiful home. The walkers saw tiles inlaid in the sidewalk spelling “Kailani,” a message left by the Alexanders as a reminder of their original Hawaii home. The walkers crossed Hampton and continued on Sea View to see the home of Mary’s mother. They also noted the Julia Morgan designed home they had seen a couple of weeks before. The group went on Farragut Avenue, passing more Julia Morgan homes that they recognized from their earlier walk. The group has an informal objective of walking on all Piedmont streets during the year, so they took a little detour to see a 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03

The hotel also offered fine wine and liquor for those who did not care for mineral water. Fashionable San Franciscans would come for a week to escape the summer fog. Many hotel guests enjoyed the mild weather and views of San Francisco Bay and decided to buy land and build their homes here. The hotel thrived until 1892 when a spark from a faulty chimney started a fire on the roof. Hotel guests watched helplessly as the hotel burned to the ground before firefighters could arrive
