articles.text: On Monday night, August 30, Piedmont Police received a call at 6:34 p.m. about two people fighting in the parking lot at Ace Hardware on Grand Avenue. A man and woman were reportedly hitting each other with bottles and yelling at each other. A description of the subjects’ vehicle, a silver 2000 Honda Civic, matched that from a call 20 minutes earlier about a vehicle stolen from Alta Avenue. When the police arrived, the reporting person informed the police that the couple left in a silver Civic and left behind a vehicle without plates, a blue 2001 Acura TL which was also potentially involved in the Alta Avenue car theft. The reporting person also identified a third person who was in the silver car and walked away from the scene. Officers located the third person, Devante Sanders, (29 years old from Oakland) on Grand Avenue. He was on parole with a full search clause. A search revealed three shaved car keys and a glass pipe for narcotics. He was arrested and taken to Santa Rita jail. While officers were having the blue Acura towed, the female suspect returned to the parking lot to attempt to take the car. Lilyanna Ramos (25 years old from Oakland) had a warrant for driving with a suspended license. She was also arrested and taken to Santa Rita jail for the outstanding warrant and possession of a stolen vehicle. One male suspect involved in the car theft is still at large. Anyone with information about the suspect is encouraged to contact Piedmont Detective John Lagios at 420-3000.

articles.text: Join your neighbors for a free movie in Piedmont Park on Friday evening, September 17, two days before the annual Harvest Festival. The film is Bee Movie, a DreamWorks animation family film with the voices of Jerry Seinfield, Renee Zellweger and Chris Rock. Another sweet bonus is a presentation about beekeeping with some local honey-tasting samples. Honey-tasting begins at 6:45 p.m., and the movie will begin at 7:20 p.m. Come in a bee costume and win a prize. Bring a low-level lawn chair and enjoy a night under the stars.

articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Fire Department have been helping fight the enormous, catastrophic Dixie Fire for nearly six weeks, since July 20, by deploying small rotating strike teams of three and four men and with a fire engine as home base on the fire line. The fire, the second largest in recorded California history, has spanned the four counties of Butte, Plumas, Lassen, and Tehama. It has consumed 807,396 acres of timber and has destroyed 1,277 structures. – Lt. Justin McNulty Piedmont Fire Department The first Strike Team from Piedmont was led by Capt. Jon Fitzpatrick, with firefighters Dave Abernethy and Chad Walker battling the blaze from July 20 to 28. They were relieved by the team of Capt. Scott Barringer and firefighters Dino Dedes and Rob Kingston. The second team spent 12 days in action before being demobilized and returning Photos courtesy of the Piedmont Fire Department A member of the Inyo Hot Shots Crew that Piedmont Fire Department was assisting at the Dixie forest fire. to Piedmont with the engine on August 8. “Our crews have done everything from structure protection, removing trees and other hazards, direct attack on the fire line, and a myriad of other duties,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan
articles.title: Piedmont firefighters helping at monster Dixie Fire

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department is gearing up for its 3rd annual Car Show on Monday morning, Labor Day, September 6. A lineup of cars will be on view in the parking lot in front of the Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, from 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. In 2019 the show attracted 44 gleaming vehicles. From classic Jaguars, MGs and Model T’s to late model Ferraris, all the hottest vehicles and their proud owners were there. After taking a hiatus in 2020 due to COVID- 19, the show has returned and the competition for first, second, and third place will be fierce. As part of the Police Department’s outreach activities, coffee will be available as neighbors come to meet members of the police department while chatting with the car owners. The event is part of the larger “Coffee with a Cop” national campaign, which was started in 2016 as a way for residents to meet local law Jim Horner’s beautiful 1953 Ford Crestline Survivor will turn heads at the Piedmont Car Show on Labor Day.

articles.text: The popular Harvest Festival, operated and organized by the City of Piedmont, will return with in-person festivities on Sunday, September 19, after being canceled last year due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Also returning this year will be the Kids’ Carnival, with games for kids of all ages. features the best home-grown and homemade foods from your neighbors. All entries must be delivered to the Community Hall between 7:30-10:00 a.m. on Sunday, September 19. Bring your completed entry form (or proof of digital submission). articles.text: Editor: Having a son who was a Marine taught me many lessons. One is that the men and women who prepare for and serve on the front lines are rarely surprised when things don’t go as planned – and that this is often not the case higher up the command chain. The withdrawal from Afghanistan is a particularly devastating example. Our son has many friends who served there. None of them are stunned by the speed with which the Taliban retook the country nor by how quickly the evacuation process descended into chaos. Something is very wrong when high level military and government officials expected it to take 18 months for Kabul to fall and mere days to safely transport tens of thousands of U.S. citizens and Afghan allies out, but the soldiers who had actually been there knew otherwise. Or that it made sense to believe the Taliban would wield their newly regained power in a reasonable manner. Last Thursday evening we had a long talk with our son about the situation in Kabul and the buddy there he was waiting to hear from – a sweet kid from Wisconsin who called me “ma’am” and whose good humor kept the platoon going during even the most grueling field exercises. We asked what needs to change so this sort of catastrophe doesn’t happen again. “The people at the top have to talk to the guys with boots on the ground. Realize that sometimes a 19 year old grunt may know more than you do.” Seems pretty simple. Friday morning our son texted to say his friend is safe. His unit is being transferred out of Kabul because of all the casualties they took. –Kathleen Winters
articles.title: Lessons from Kabul

articles.text: It is important that the biblical story of Jonah, best known for the recalcitrant prophet spending three days and three nights in the belly of a great fish, be more than the beginning of a “did that really happen?’ debate. In fact, Jonah’s placement among the prophetic books of the Bible should tell us that, like the other prophetic works, the story of Jonah will cause us to consider our place in God’s world and confront us with critical questions about the way we are living our lives. When God’s word comes to Jonah instructing him to go to Nineveh, the capital city of Assyria, his first response is to flee in the opposite direction. Instead of joining a caravan heading east, he goes to the seaport of Joppa and buys a ticket to Tarshish, a city at the western edge of his Mediterranean world. He heads towards modern Spain instead of modern Iraq. Hebrew prophet that he was, Jonah would have been familiar with the poetry of Psalm 139 – “Where can I flee from your Spirit?” Still he gets on the ship heading to the edge of the known world. Here we encounter the first critical question of Jonah. Is there any place we can flee from God’s presence? Once at sea the ship encounters a violent storm. There is confusion and debate about what is happening and how to respond, but in rather short order Jonah says to the crew of the ship “Throw me overboard. I am the problem. Once I hit the water the seas will calm.” To their credit the sailors are not anxious to follow Jonah’s instruction and they try to row back to shore. It is only after this effort fails that they relent and hurl Jonah into the sea. At this point the “sea stops its raging” and the crew worships Jonah’s god. We are met with critical question No. 2. In the raging storm that is life in 2021 what is it that we need to throw overboard? Are there actions, beliefs, or attitudes that are not serving us well? Rather than drowning, Jonah is swallowed by a great fish. As noted above, he spends three days and three nights in the belly of the fish. While the conditions
articles.title: Throwing stuff overboard – Five critical questions from Jonah

Realize that sometimes a 19 year old grunt may know more than you do.” Seems pretty simple. Friday morning our son texted to say his friend is safe. Throwing stuff overboard – Five critical questions from Jonah By Rev. Jim Hopkins It is important that the biblical story of Jonah, best known for the recalcitrant prophet spending three days and three nights in the belly of a great fish, be more than the beginning of a “did that really happen?’ debate. In fact, Jonah’s placement among the prophetic books of the Bible should tell us that, like the other prophetic works, the story of Jonah will cause us to consider our place in God’s world and confront us with critical questions about the way we are living our lives. When God’s word comes to Jonah instructing him to go to Nineveh, the capital city of Assyria, his first response is to flee in the opposite direction. Instead of joining a caravan heading east, he goes to the seaport of Joppa and buys a ticket to Tarshish, a city at the western edge of his Mediterranean world. He heads towards modern Spain instead of modern Iraq. Hebrew prophet that he was, Jonah would have been familiar with the poetry of Psalm 139 – “Where can I flee from your Spirit?” Still he gets on the ship heading to the edge of the known world. Here we encounter the first critical question of Jonah. Is there any place we can flee from God’s presence? Once at sea the ship encounters a violent storm. There is confusion and debate about what is happening and how to respond, but in rather short order Jonah says to the crew of the ship “Throw me overboard. I am the problem. Once I hit the water the seas will calm.” To their credit the sailors are not anxious to follow Jonah’s instruction and they try to row back to shore. It is only after this effort fails that they relent and hurl Jonah into the sea. At this point the “sea stops its raging” and the crew worships Jonah’s god. We are met with critical question No. 2. In the raging storm that is life in 2021 what is it that we need to throw overboard? Are there actions, beliefs, or attitudes that are not serving us well? Rather than drowning, Jonah is swallowed by a great fish. As noted above, he spends three days and three nights in the belly of the fish. articles.text: – Susan Miller-Davis former board president of Piedmont Connect The Piedmont City Council unanimously supported the Energy Innovation and Carbon Dividend Act (H.R. 2307), with all five council members endorsing it this summer. The bill was introduced in Congress on April 1 and imposes a fee on the carbon content of fuels, including crude oil, natural gas, and coal. These and other products derived from their fuels emit greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. The fee would be imposed on the producers or importers of the fuels, with the rate beginning at $15 per metric ton of CO2-e in 2021, increases by $10 each year, and is subject to further adjustments based on the progress in meeting specified emissions reduction targets. The bill is cosponsored by many Democratic representatives, including Rep. Barbara Lee and Rep. Jackie Speier from the Bay Area. “The act proposes an economy-wide ‘price on carbon’ to reduce carbon emissions quickly and at-scale,” former board president of Piedmont Connect (2019-2021), Susan Miller-Davis explained. The Piedmont resident also co-led Grasstops Engagement with the Alameda County chapter of Citizen’s Climate Lobby, one of nearly 600 chapters across the country working on carbon pricing. Citizens’ Climate Lobby is a not-for-profit, volunteer-driven organization which advocates for bipartisan climate change solutions in the United States Congress. “Piedmonters can feel proud that our local leaders are lending their voices toward addressing the climate crisis with urgency and at scale. I hope local business leaders, civic figures and residents will join the chorus now as climate policy is being hashed out in Congress,” said Miller-Davis. “A strong, economy-wide price on carbon could reduce America’s carbon pollution by 50% by 2030, putting us on track to reach net zero by 2050. It is one of the few solutions that addresses many sectors of the economy.” Piedmont has already taken aggressive action in battling climate change, including goals set in the Climate Action Plan, which set an ambitious goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) by 40% below 2005 levels by 2030, and as much as 80% below those levels by 2050. Miller-Davis acknowledged that measures taken by individuals, and small communities like Piedmont, are important and add up. She added, though, that top-down, economy-wide change is necessary to reduce emissions rapidly. enaugh described the importance of the bill’s passage. “We are all feeling the effects of carbon pollution everyday through natural disasters such as devastating wildfires, hurricanes, floods, and droughts, which were previously once in a lifetime occurrences but have now become annual events. There’s no denying the impact on all of us but certainly those with the fewest resources pay the highest price,” Cavenaugh said. “The Energy Innovation and Carbon Dividend Act is an important step toward necessary and bold climate action.” “As a small city, Piedmont can have an outsized influence on climate change when we use our voices to partner on regional and national efforts that will have the greatest impact. Individuals, businesses and local communities need to continue to do our part, but programs of this scale require urgent action by Congress to effectuate meaningful change on a national scale,” she said. City Council member Conna McCarthy added that, “supporting a price on carbon is one of several actions elected leaders can take to reduce the amount of carbon dioxide trapping heat on our planet. Putting a price on carbon pollution through a carbon tax encourages the transition to cleaner energy.” To find out more about how carbon pricing works and prospects for national legislation, join Piedmont Connect for a panel discussion and question-and-answer portion on carbon pricing, hosted by the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWVP), on Wednesday, September 22 at 4pm. The event is free online via Zoom and live-streamed on LWVP YouTube channel, but registration is required on the League’s website at lwvpiedmont.org/events. Interested residents can get involved with Citizen’s Climate Lobby campaigns at www.cclusa. org, or the local Alameda County chapter at http://cclalameda.org. The current campaign is focused on calling House members and mobilizing volunteers. “It takes a heavy lift for community after community to set goals and implement measures, with long lags to learn of results. Given that 2030 is rapidly approaching, we need change on all levels, including the national level,” she said. The proposed bill includes a “carbon cash back” dividend, which would help low-income Americans the most. Miller-Davis explained that it would yield approximately $800 per year for the average American family of four; the fee and dividends change over time depending on progress toward GHG emissions reductions, and by year ten, the sum could reach nearly $3,500. “Studies suggest that twothirds of households will break even or come out ahead financially. [It] is considered progressive and equitable,” she explained. City Council member Jen Cav-

articles.text: Piedmont hosted a virtual community meeting on August 26 with researchers from the University of Texas at San Antonio who are analyzing Piedmont Police Department (PPD) calls for service data to examine how its services are used and prioritized. The city will use the analyses to inform future discussions of call responses. The University is focusing its research on the type of calls for service which officers respond to and the frequency of biasedbased calls for police intervention. The city stated that the work is “part of the effort to understand bias and the historical role racism has played in Piedmont and the community-at-large, in order to better lead a city which is a safe, welcoming, and equitable place for all people committed to by the City Council in Resolution 60-2020.” The proposal for research was approved by City Council on July 19. “Some of the most meaningful work we are engaged in as a city is an examination of what we do and how we do it, with an antibias and anti-racist lens. Police work in particular has appropriately been in the national, regional, and local spotlight in the wake of the killing of George Floyd,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said in introducing the community meeting. The purpose of the meeting was to describe and take questions on the upcoming analysis of police call data. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers spearheaded the initiative earlier this spring, Lillevand said, in a commitment to transparency and best practices in the PPD. The University of Texas, San Antonio’s (UTSA) Dr. Michael Smith and Dr. Rob Tillyer are leading the data analysis research. The researchers have worked with a number of agencies on similar studies for more than 20 years, including some local work in San Jose and San Francisco, Dr. Smith explained. “A key question that many communities are asking themselves is whether there are alternatives to police response for certain types of calls,” Dr. Smith said, adding that this will be a component of their analysis. “What we’re interested in helping the city understand is the impact of calls that come into the department, how [that] drives [the department’s] responses, and whether or not there are potential racial or ethnic disparities in those calls,” he explained. articles.text: Back by popular demand, internationally renowned epidemiologist and Piedmont resident Dr. George Rutherford will provide an update on Covid-19 at a public forum on Wednesday, September 15, at 4 p.m. sponsored by the Piedmont League of Women Voters. As most Piedmont residents are aware, Dr. Rutherford has been instrumental in helping the Bay Area contend with Covid and is frequently quoted in the media. He will address the latest findings, the status of the Delta and other variants, and the likely effectiveness of boosters and therapeutics. He will also speak about Covid safety for schools. Audience members will have an opportunity to ask questions. Dr. Rutherford leads the Global Strategic Information group within UCSF’s Institute for Global Health Sciences. He is the Salvatore Pablo Lucia Professor of Epidemiology, Preventive Medicine, Pediatrics and History; Head of the Division of Infectious Disease and Global Epidemiology Epidemiologist Dr. George Rutherford is the guest speaker at the League of Women Voters Forum on September 15. in the Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics in School of Medicine at UCSF, and Professor of Epidemiology and Health Administration in the School of Public Health at the University of California, Berkeley. The League is presenting this event free of charge, but registration is required online at: lwvpiedmont.org/events. The event will be held at 4 p.m. on Zoom and on the League’s YouTube channel.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont and its housing consultant have announced three important community-outreach events this fall that ask for residents’ input on fair housing. At a May 3 meeting, City Council approved a proposal from Lisa Wise Consulting to prepare updates to the city’s Housing Element. The state is requiring that Piedmont create 587 new housing units by the end of the next Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) cycle in 2031. For more information, visit the city’s fair housing website, www.PiedmontisHome.org. Residents are encouraged to participate in the following events: • September 29 Joint meeting and study session of the Planning Commission and Housing Advisory Committee about the basic requirements for Housing Element updates in California and how fair housing makes Piedmont a great place to live. • October 21 Community meeting for new housing programs, including draft ADU (Accessory Dwelling Unit) and JADU (Junior Accessory Dwelling Unit) pre-approved plans and incentives, as well as draft objective design and development standards for multi-family housing development in Piedmont. • December 2 Community meeting to start the 2031 Housing Element Update.
articles.title: Planning Commission to host study session on fair housing Sept. 29

articles.text: Christine Wente von Metzsch, Heather Frank, Nicki Gilbert, Colleen Allan, and Amelie Kappes present School Board President Cory Smegal (right) and School Superintendent Randy Booker (left) with a check for $2.75 million for Piedmont schools. The Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) presented a check for $2,750,000 to the Piedmont School Board at the board’s meeting on August 25. The amount represented the total collected during the annual fundraising campaign (Giving Campaign) for the 2020-2021 school year. “We are humbled by the generosity of our community,” said Nicki Gilbert, Chair of the PEF Board of Directors. “In a year of challenges, our community once again showed its commitment to our schools and our students.” More than 1,140 families contributed to the campaign, with an average gift of $2,544 per family. $336,000 is being allotted to the school district, $825,000 to Piedmont High School, $576,000 to Piedmont Middle School, $436,000 to Havens Elementary, $261,000 to Beach School, $259,000 to Wildwood School, and $56,000 to Millennium High. The Giving Campaign committee invites the community to celebrate the launch of this year’s campaign with a popsicle party in Piedmont Park on Tuesday, September 21 from 3:00-4:00 p.m. Led by a 22-member volunteer board of directors and supported by a professional office staff, the Education Foundation oversees the Giving Campaign, Spring Fling, and produces the Student Directory. For more information, see PiedmontEdFoundation.org.

articles.text: There are many volunteer opportunities for high school and middle school students in the East Bay that fit around a traditional school schedule. Here are just a few. Oakland Zoo There are several volunteer opportunities at Oakland Zoo for students who love animals and are interested in a career working with animals. You can work alongside a zookeeper assisting with daily animal care, or work as a conservation volunteer interpreting the zoo’s conservation initiatives to guests. There are also a variety of internships available in seasonal fall, winter, and summer sessions. A new volunteer information meeting will be held in February 2022, but you can visit https://www.oaklandzoo.org/ volunteer-and-internship-opportunities to learn more about how to get involved now. The MOSAIC project The MOSAIC project is a youth leadership project that provides extensive training in diversity and conflict-resolution for young adults and teens. Together, volunteers form a vibrant, cross-cultural community who serve as mentors for students in 4th and 5th grade who participate in Mosaic’s outdoor project. High school and college-aged volunteers are welcome to apply, and are required to attend a weekend training retreat and volunteer for at least one session during the spring and fall. To apply, visit https:// mosaicproject.org/programs/youth-leadership-project/, or contact Youth Leadership Director Khemnes Fisher at 510- 452-3377 or email at khemnes@mosaicproject.org. Museum of Children’s Art (MOCHA) Students who have a love of art and are interested in the education field would enjoy volunteering at the Museum of Children’s Art (MOCHA) in Oakland. Tasks include everything from preparing art materials, to assisting with special events at the museum. Visit https://www.mocha. org/copy-of-annual-fund to sign up. Prisoner’s Literature Project Prisoner’s Literature Project is an inclusive, all-volunteer grassroots nonprofit that has provided free books to prisoners for over 30 years. The organization is based in Berkeley, and is always looking for volunteers to help answer letters, send out books, learn more about the prison system, and assist in other ways. Other ways you can volunteer include fundraising and publicity efforts. Volunteers aged 10 through 15 are welcome with parent or guardian overseeing work. Visit https://www.prisonlit.org/volunteer/ for more information. articles.text: This map shows air quality on Friday, August 27. Low air quality in Piedmont was due to the Dixie Fire in Plumas County. In October 2020 last year the Piedmont School Board voted to have an Environment Safety policy based upon the state’s Air Quality Index (AQI) readings. With Californa wildfires again impacting air quality throughout California, classes in Piedmont may be canceled on days when the AQI index exceeds 200. During the COVID-19 pandemic, when the AQI exceeded 100 during school days, and if school ventilation is shut off, school would be to canceled for the day. However the school district said it does not expect to have to turn off the ventilation system as the new air filters are regularly inspected. When Piedmont’s Air Quality Index ranges from 101-150 all PE classes will be held indoors and all strenuous PE activities and sports programs will be canceled. An AQI of 151-199 (unhealthy) will result in all school district employees being encouraged to use respirator masks when working outdoors. As a reference, on Friday August 27 at 2 p.m., the AQI in Oakland was 116.
articles.title: School District reimposes air quality protocols

The bags included a $30 gift card to Mulberry’s Market and a $90 gift card to Market Hall. They also included greeting cards with notes of gratitude along with potted flowers. Mulberry’s and Market Hall offered discounts on the cards. “The nurses and staff of Piedmont Unified deserve our sincere gratitude for their tireless efforts to keep our students, teachers, District nurses Carol Menz (left) and Claudia Garcia with Health Clerk Viki Salazar were given gift bags as thanks for their extra efforts during the pandemic. staff and, as a result, the larger community healthy and safe. We hope that this worthy cause of acknowledging these unsung heroines and heroes would also help remind us all that what we share in common is far greater than our differences,” said Lee.

articles.text: September has arrived with the finest weather the Bay Area has to offer, just in time to get... stuck in a classroom? One may think that kids would be jumping over rainbows to get back in school after such a long absence, but for some, it’s not going to be easy. Let’s face it, back to school this year is different. Distance and hybrid learning allowed many of us – kids and adults alike – to wake up just minutes before online class or meetings. Some of us never left our pajamas. Will students even remember how to hold a pencil? Has the laptop’s touchpad replaced graphite and ink? The pandemic and distance/ hybrid learning consumed 1-1/2 years of class time – one and a half years without physically needing to be present in class, without real social interaction, without having to adhere to societal customs. For a nine-year old, that amount of time represents onesixth of their total life experience, so adjusting will take time. All students returning to class have been put into a more demanding schedule, with classes and extracurriculars – and that means waking up earlier. Here are some ideas for making the transition back to normal a little easier. Set a fun alarm for your student to wake up to; a cute alarm clock that really dings can be fun to inspire the student curious about mechanisms and engineering. Back in the day, I had a phone shaped like the batmobile which was connected to the landline. If you still have a landline, go ahead and give your 3rd grader a wake-up call to their Spongebob phone. Let thine medicine be thine food and thine food be thine medicine. A rudimentary understanding of nutrition can be the subliminal edge kids (and adults) need to conquer the day. While milk has great vitamins essential to a growing body, dairy products slow us down. Try fruit and nuts in the morning or whole grains. Cheese, milk and other dairy products can be used in the evening to ensure an early bed time. So-called brain foods are
articles.title: ADVICE FROM A TUTOR Adjusting to in-person learning

articles.text: actually on the menu for even the pickiest eaters. Berries are rich in a variety of compounds that may help promote academic performance and protect the health of the brain. Other brain foods kids may like include citrus fruits, dark chocolate and cocoa products, nuts, eggs, and avocados. So, pack a lunch the night before to save time in the morning and supply the energy needed to get through the day. More often than not, children can adapt more quickly to new circumstances than adults. Just look and see the ease with which kids have taken to wearing masks. Kids just want to see their friends and have something to do. For many, school represents freedom, a time away from parents and with their peers. We see more kids now being eager to get to school. However, the length of absence from class and academic life presents obstacles. Be patient, get creative, and understand that the uncertainty brought on by the pandemic has become routine. Switching back may be just as big a challenge as switching to a pandemic lifestyle was for parents. Stay for a full afternoon of fun, by hopping over to the miniature train yard, Tilden Park’s golf driving range, or any of Tilden’s numerous family friendly attractions. The cafe serves ice cream, hot dogs, beverages & snacks to refuel a day of fun. The main attractions are the classic and rare cars. Not to be missed are exhibits titled Into Africa, Spirit of the Old West and Into China. The showroom has more than 100 classic and nearly priceless cars, with a top floor showroom with one-of-a kind vehicles. You’ll see an 1886 Benz Patent Motorwagon, the first gas powered vehicle, and the 1967 Shelby Mustang GT500 “Eleanor” from “Gone in 60 Seconds.” A 30-foot safari touring car and a completely wooden car will have the kids amazed. Open Friday-Sunday, from 10:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Oakland Aviation Museum 8252 Earhart Road, Oakland 638-7100 Oaklandaviationmuseum.org Kids and adults will be impressed with the history of aviation. The display is in tip-top shape after being renovated while closed due to Covid-19. Enjoy the Short Solent Flying Boat, the TAV-8A Harrier (with vertical takeoff and landing), and many original aircraft. The museum is housed in the original Boeing School of Aeronautics in the hangar at the North Oakland airport. Relive history and have the kids wide eyed and smiling beneath their masks.

articles.text: Photo by Jane Violich Walk for Wellness 2021 Committee members gather with their pups in Piedmont Park: Dana Lung, Cortney Allen & Oakley, Jenna Caldwell & Daisy, Nicki Gilbert, Sara Valkonen, Rebecca Thornborrow, and KeriAnne Hohener & McKinley Piedmont, it’s time to get walking. The Wellness Center Support Committee has announced the second annual Walk for Wellness will take place September 20-26. It is the largest yearly fundraiser for Piedmont School District’s Wellness Center. It is an inclusive, accessible and socially-distanced event open to the entire Piedmont community. pages.text: 8 Wednesday, September 1, 2021 ADVICE FROM A TUTOR Adjusting to in-person learning By Jay Russell September has arrived with the finest weather the Bay Area has to offer, just in time to get... stuck in a classroom? One may think that kids would be jumping over rainbows to get back in school after such a long absence, but for some, it’s not going to be easy. Let’s face it, back to school this year is different. Distance and hybrid learning allowed many of us – kids and adults alike – to wake up just minutes before online class or meetings. Some of us never left our pajamas. Will students even remember how to hold a pencil? Has the laptop’s touchpad replaced graphite and ink? The pandemic and distance/ hybrid learning consumed 1-1/2 years of class time – one and a half years without physically needing to be present in class, without real social interaction, without having to adhere to societal customs. For a nine-year old, that amount of time represents onesixth of their total life experience, so adjusting will take time. All students returning to class have been put into a more demanding schedule, with classes and extracurriculars – and that means waking up earlier. Here are some ideas for making the transition back to normal a little easier. Set a fun alarm for your student to wake up to; a cute alarm clock that really dings can be fun to inspire the student curious about mechanisms and engineering. Back in the day, I had a phone shaped like the batmobile which was connected to the landline. If you still have a landline, go ahead and give your 3rd grader a wake-up call to their Spongebob phone. Let thine medicine be thine food and thine food be thine medicine. A rudimentary understanding of nutrition can be the subliminal edge kids (and adults) need to conquer the day. While milk has great vitamins essential to a growing body, dairy products slow us down. Try fruit and nuts in the morning or whole grains. Cheese, milk and other dairy products can be used in the evening to ensure an early bed time. So-called brain foods are actually on the menu for even the pickiest eaters. Berries are rich in a variety of compounds that may help promote academic performance and protect the health of the brain. Other brain foods kids may like include citrus fruits, dark chocolate and cocoa products, nuts, eggs, and avocados. So, pack a lunch the night before to save time in the morning and supply the energy needed to get through the day. More often than not, children can adapt more quickly to new circumstances than adults. Just look and see the ease with which kids have taken to wearing masks. Kids just want to see their friends and have something to do. For many, school represents freedom, a time away from parents and with their peers. We see more kids now being eager to get to school. However, the length of absence from class and academic life presents obstacles. Be patient, get creative, and understand that the uncertainty brought on by the pandemic has become routine. Switching back may be just as big a challenge as switching to a pandemic lifestyle was for parents. pages.text: Wednesday, September 1, 2021 9 PFD at Dixie Fire Continued from page 1 But they weren’t done. A third strike team returned to action on a Type I fire engine on August 16 near Janesville, by Honey Lake, 70 miles north of Reno. The crew included Lt. Justin McNulty, Engineer Justin Morris, and firefighters Brian Gidney and Robb Hendry. Photo courtesy of the Piedmont Fire Department A giant fire header above the town of Taylorsville, with the Taylorsville Tavern on the right. Photo courtesy of the Piedmont Fire Department Seen on the left is the claw of a bulldozer used by a local resident to help clear away logs and fire fuel in Taylorsville. “[We were] immediately requested for structure protection in Janesville, so we fought fire from 10:00 p.m. to 3 a.m. That was literally going house to house trying to knock the fire down,” McNulty explained. The Piedmont crew joined up with the Inyo Hot Shots Crew who had been fighting the flames for two continuous weeks. That first intense five-hour stint was the start of a 38-hour shift for the Piedmont firefighters. Most shifts in a fire station are 24 hours, and McNulty said that 24-hour shifts are less disruptive to his sleep cycle than a 12-hour shift. In Janesville McNulty got creative and utilized some local help in the middle of the night using his flashlight to get the attention of a local man on a bulldozer in a field. “I told him we needed him to quickly circle these houses before we lose them. We were putting the fire out, but the fire load was tremendous, there were logs and fire fuel all over the fields next to the houses. It was awesome to see him push all that stuff out of the way,” McNulty recalled. From Janesville they went immediately to base camp in Quincy in Plumas County, and were sent out for assignment in Indian Valley and Taylorsville. “Taylorsville was our last town – basically our last stand, like the Alamo,” explained McNulty. “it was a ‘don’t let this burn,’ situation. In describing events that occurred almost daily, McNulty said, “Sometimes we had to pause in our tactics because the fire was too intense to pass through. We might have to wait for the main front to pass, so we could drive through and get around to the houses before the main front hit it.” The crew of four was relieved of duty on August 26 by the initial crew of Fitzpatrick, Abernethy, and Walker, along with Firefighter Brian Protheroe. They are currently scheduled for 10 days of action on the Dixie Fire. As of Tuesday, August 31, the Dixie fire had been burning for 48 days, was 48% contained and was around 200,000 acres shy of the becoming the largest California wildfire in history. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, September 1, 2021 AMERICANS IN PARIS By Patricia Forsyth Nº 40 in a biweekly series Parisians queued excitedly to visit the newest department store, La Samaritaine, for the landmark store’s reopening. Built a century ago in central Paris, it’s a blocky 7-floor behemoth on the Seine The Grand Opening of La Samaritaine River at Pont-Neuf. Completed in 1609, Pont-Neuf was the first modern bridge, elegant with foot traffic separated from carriages and beautiful to behold with cutlimestone-blocks and properly footed archways for river traffic. Today it exists as the city’s oldest bridge and is located at the west end of Île de la Cité. Though Pont-Neuf’s alcoves now are scenic outlooks for tourists, for centuries the alcoves were used by enterprising merchants and peddlers hawking their wares to day workers and domestics who crossed north and south to the Left Bank and Right Bank. The extremely successful founder of La Samaritaine got Artist rendering of La Samaritaine for its restoration and reopening in late July. Pont Neuf is the oldest bridge in Paris, and merchants made use of the alcoves to sell their wares. his start on one of the bridge’s alcoves and named his future real estate holdings after a long-ago water pump that was centuries earlier situated on the bank below Pont-Neuf. Earnest Cognacq was from a destitute family, but he set out at age 12 to find his fortune during La Belle Époch, an expansionary period of wealth for the middle classes stirred by the early 19th c. Industrial Revolution. Then, following the Franco-Prussian War in 1871, prosperity widened and lasted until the start of the World War. Cognacq began on Pont-Neuf as a peddler of coffee, and then cloth, a jovial individual and merchant who joked good-naturedly with his customers. He was an attractive fellow who was especially streetwise and keen to deliver excellent bargains and good quality to his customers. He met his life partner and future wife on the Pont-Neuf, Marie-Louise Jaÿ when she was employed in the dressmaking department at Le Bon Marché. Cognacq rode the wave of mass production bringing quality goods to the regular “Joe” at bargain prices, and he prospered, becoming one of the most popular vendors on Pont-Neuf. By age thirty, Cognacq parlayed his savings into a building lease starting with two employees at the first of four adjacent properties he would ultimately purchase. They grew to become the most popular shopping destinations. He drew customers from Les Halles market on their way home across the bridge. He splashed posters with daily sales across the large plate-glass windows, and the customers flocked in. The Cognacq-Jaÿ couple was fully devoted to their burgeoning retail enterprise, and without children to raise, they worked every waking hour to innovate and elevate the department store model. They didn’t hesitate to copy from the “greats,” and copying Le Bon Marché, they remodeled extensively starting with plateglass to show off the fashions and flood the main floor in natural light. In the 1870s, it was revolutionary to mark the merchandise clearly with prices, and it freed shoppers to not have to ask. They were the first to invite customers to try on clothes before purchase. At a time when employers demanded 14 or even 16-hour days Monday through Saturday, La Samaritaine employees worked 10-hour days and half day on Saturday. Such a progressively lenient policy drew hordes of applicants. But they were strict too, particularly, Mme Jaÿ who demanded highly productive and attentive employees, or else a tardy worker might be terminated on the spot. Their motto was “On trouve tout à La Samaritaine,” meaning “One can find everything at La Samaritaine,” and inside the four locations, the merchandise ranged from girdles to lawnmowers. At the mark of 25 years in business, La Samaritaine broke a million francs in sales; and by 1925, the empire surpassed a billion francs in sales. By the late 1920s, their foundation was awash in funds. They had pioneered services such as a children’s nursery, a school, maternity clinic, and a nursing home, foremost for employees, and later opening to the public. But by the 1970s the stores were operating at a loss, and closed in 2005, due to fire safety codes. The closing occurred See Americans in Paris on page 11 La Samaritaine, now gussied-up and reopened, in a view from Pont Neuf on Quai Louvre, where the luxury hotel Le Cheval Blanc opens in September. Founders of La Samaritaine, Marie-Louise Jaÿ and Ernest Cognacq, who bought prime real estate between the Louvre and Les Halles. One contemporary critic sniffed, La Samaritaine looks like a giant heating system, a joking description that gained traction with Parisians who laughed at it. The founder Cognacq was offended and remodeled the store again in 1927 and removed the two glass domes, which have now been restored by LVMH, a wise decision, as the natural light adds a positive dimension. We walked the interior of the structure and noticed the exposed metalwork, original staircase and other features. Now, escalators crisscross the entire store with its vast central interior open to the floors below. The main-floor displays are sleek and gorgeous, but the low-ceilinged mid-level sales floors make departments feel cramped. The top floor is the biggest draw where, under the twin square domes, shoppers pause for lunch or drinks at the several restaurants; sit in the lounge watching a giant screen viewing the Seine; or get a closer look at the historic peacocks in pastel colors. A few days later I visited the Musée Cognacq-Jaÿ, a 16th century hotel that now houses the private collection of belonging, mostly art and furniture of the Cognacq-Jaÿs. For perspective, I asked Linnard Hobler of Philadelphia, a specialist in the History of Decorative Arts who studied at the Smithsonian, for an opinion about the couple’s decorative choices. “Typically, people of unlimited wealth, such as La Samaritaine’s Laure.” founders of the Gilded Age were most influenced by their advisor, whoever that was. We don’t know, but it was likely comparable to the Duveen Brothers, especially the world-famous Robert Duveen. The collection is mainly French and Dutch, and some Italian, and they have one early Rembrandt. pages.text: Wednesday, September 1, 2021 11 AMERICANS IN PARIS Continued from page 10 without advance warning throwing employees into a panic, and stunning shoppers. The workers’ unions were not understanding, and they pronounced the new buyers as motivated by “restructuring” and called them “profiteers.” Plans for redevelopment got complicated, as agents for the store’s founders argued with the new owners, Louis-Vuitton-Moêt-Hennessy (LVMH), over the department store’s future. UNESCO in 1993 had proclaimed the building an international treasure, and later it was designated as a French landmark. These acts protect the exterior, which may only be altered by permission of a strict restoration council. LVMH prevailed in its design as a mixed-use building, which was opposed by the founder’s agency. Construction lasted seven years, restoring crucial elements, such as the twin glass domes and peacock mural on the top floor; but a new high-end hotel, and no longer the store, will occupy the store’s elevation along the Seine: it will have a restaurant view and private swimming pool exclusively for hotel guests. The once unpretentious La Samar, as the Parisians called it, had no choice but to become a highpriced luxury purveyor. No other viable suitor presented in an era where the pressure is unrelenting on brick-and-mortar stores that simply cannot compete with internet pricing. The all-new La Samaritaine boasts the largest beauty and cosmetics department in Europe, but regrettably, this “brag” is significant only to the rarified few dedicated to exotic potions. Clothing boutiques, such as Dior, Celine, Louis Vuitton, Gucci, Commes des Garçons, and hundreds more, are available at extravagant prices to people for whom the price doesn’t matter. The store’s new-found opulence is grating to the average Parisian. The Daily Beast, like other critics, scolds LVMH for bypassing the everyday citizens to appeal strictly to the monied foreign visitor. LVMH head Bernard Arnault, the world’s richest person (if not Jeff Bezos), promoted “a unique Parisian art de vivre.” A few weeks after La Samaritaine’s reopening, protesters under the cover of night sprayed black paint A video camera projection is for shoppers lounging at La Samaritaine’s top floor. The actual view of the Seine is reserved for hotel guests, with rooms starting at $1,550, according to Paris Diary by Laure. defacing the display windows and causing grief for the profiteers. During news interviews where their identity was not disclosed, the group leaders explained that they were exclaiming “the shameless enrichment of billionaires during the worldwide health crisis” to a sympathetic public and broadcasters. Following 16 years of closure, and a reported cost of $900 billion for the contentious remodel that took seven years; criticized by the media, except by Vogue and the fashion trade; harassed by paint-spraying vandals and finger-pointing at blatant capitalists ignoring the pandemic, one can say La Samaritaine is having a bumpy start. Michael and I waited among the curious but patient want-to-be shoppers on a summer afternoon under the too-bright sunlight while our queue snaked around Rue de la Monnaie plaza for entry into La Samar. Hundreds of shoppers queued-up, drawn by heavy radio advertising promising big sale prices on brand new fashions. We walked the entire store and didn’t find a single big sale. The wait was about 40 minutes, allowing plenty of time to study the architecture, (clean) display windows, and gawk at the shoppers. La Samaritaine is architecturally a pastiche of Art Nouveau and Art Deco. La Samar is the main department store first built as a grand magasin in 1910 with fashion-forward departments and grand-bargain pricing. The store featured twin glass, skeletal-metal domes, vaguely inspired by the Eiffel Tower, but decorated with bright orange ceramic tiles and flowering vines. One contemporary critic sniffed, La Samaritaine looks like a giant heating system, a joking description that gained traction with Parisians who laughed at it. The founder Cognacq was offended and remodeled the store again in 1927 and removed the two glass domes, which have now been restored by LVMH, a wise decision, as the natural light adds a positive dimension. We walked the interior of the structure and noticed the exposed metalwork, original staircase and other features. Now, escalators crisscross the entire store with its vast central interior open to the floors below. The main-floor displays are sleek and gorgeous, but the low-ceilinged mid-level sales floors make departments feel cramped. The top floor is the biggest draw where, under the twin square domes, shoppers pause for lunch or drinks at the several restaurants; sit in the lounge watching a giant screen viewing the Seine; or get a closer look at the historic peacocks in pastel colors. A few days later I visited the Musée Cognacq-Jaÿ, a 16th century hotel that now houses the private collection of belonging, mostly art and furniture of the Cognacq-Jaÿs. For perspective, I asked Linnard Hobler of Philadelphia, a specialist in the History of Decorative Arts who studied at the Smithsonian, for an opinion about the couple’s decorative choices. “Typically, people of unlimited wealth, such as La Samaritaine’s A nice touch, armchairs for shoppers, according to “Paris Diary by Laure.” founders of the Gilded Age were most influenced by their advisor, whoever that was. We don’t know, but it was likely comparable to the Duveen Brothers, especially the world-famous Robert Duveen. The collection is mainly French and Dutch, and some Italian, and they have one early Rembrandt. They acquired art by [François] Boucher, [Jean-Honoré] Fragonard, [Giovanni Antonio Canal] Canaletto, [Jean-Baptiste] Greuze, and they bought very costly sculpture by [Claude Michel] Clodion and [Joseph] Chinard; and expensive furniture made by [Jean-François] Oeben or a comparable maker. articles.text: Photo by Todd Marshburn Piedmont will face Encinal for a scrimmage this Friday, September 3 at Witter Field after their initial scrimmage with Miramonte last week was canceled due to poor AQI. Piedmont’s varsity and JV football scrimmages with Miramonte last Friday evening were canceled due to poor air quality resulting from forest fires. The Air Quality Index in Orinda at game time was 150, above the acceptable standard. The Highlanders will host league opponent Encinal in a scrimmage game this Friday, September 3. With smoke entering the East Bay last Friday, August 27, Piedmont invited Miramonte to move the game to Witter, similar to offers by a number of schools in areas with cleaner air. By 3 p.m. that day, PHS football coach Jerome Johnson had not received confirmation of the game’s location, and canceled the trip to Orinda. “We made the attempt to move the scrimmage to Piedmont because, at a specific time, we had better air quality than Orinda and it’s just a short drive through the tunnel. We didn’t hear from then until 2:45, and the JV game was supposed to start at 4:30. I made the decision not to get our parents to go through the tunnel, and then have to turn around because Miramonte had poor air quality,” explained Johnson. But Piedmont had a bye (no game scheduled) for Week 1 of the North Coast Section calendar. Nearby Encinal had an opening this Friday as well, leading to the scheduled scrimmage on September 3. It is a critical time for Piedmont’s varsity team. Their small roster has been required to practice against Junior Varsity and haven’t sustained full-contact hits. “We need to get a scrimmage, because we haven’t had any action. We need to get ourselves some reps in a safe manner; we can’t go into a full game (the following week) without having any [game experience],” said Johnson. “We want to be put our kids in position to have success, and play safely to avoid injuries.” In a small step forward; the varsity has been able to add three players, and now has a roster of 20Since our last article on the football team, Johnson and company have added a few more players to bring their numbers up to 20 players. “Our numbers are low, but the kids are excited. We’re just excited to scrimmage and play again. We’re doing everything we can to have a season and doing all we can to protect our kids,” said Johnson. Encinal is in the same league with Piedmont in the Western Alameda County Conference’s newly created Mission division. Although it’s not typical for league opponents to offer clues to their plans, Encinal coach Keith Minor was also eager to get his squad some action after a sudden cancelation by Castlemont last Friday. “We do play Encinal in league, but their coach was very flexible because Castlemont canceled on them,” explained Johnson. “Coach Minor gave us a call and said, ‘Can we please get a scrimmage?, and I said, ‘Let’s make it happen.’” Piedmont will play Encinal this Friday at Witter Field. The JV scrimmage is at 4:30 p.m., followed by a varsity scrimmage at 7 p.m. Piedmont’s official season opens the following week, on Friday, September 10, also at Witter Field 7:00 p.m. in a game with Durham, a Div. 5 school south of Chico with an enrollment of 300. PHS offensive coordinator Jamar Julien, a former NFL running back, oversees drills with Batista Costa. Staff Photos

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team rebounded from a stinging loss to University last with a mighty 6-1 win over North Coast Section rival Lick-Wilmerding on Thursday, August 26. Playing on their home courts at the Corey Reich Tennis Center, the Highlanders powered past the Lick-Wilmerding Tigers, improving their record to 2-1 ahead of the league season. Thursday’s match with the Tigers was the first meeting of the two schools since Piedmont lost to Lick 5-2 in the North Coast Section semifinals in 2019 – the last tournament before the pandemic. – Tennis coach Jim Landes “It was much better than last Tuesday [against University],” said coach Jim Landes. “That wasn’t our best day. And what a difference from when we lost to Lick in the last NCS semifinals.” Both matches featured the No. 1 doubles tandem of Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany. They won in straight sets, 6-1, 6-3, against Lick, and won against a stronger University team, 7-5, 6-3. “The two of us are working on communication; we can tend to Freshman Emma Eisemon with a volley in her debut varsity doubles match with Cecilia Defazio (back). They won 6-1, 6-1 against LickWilmerding. Staff Photos The No. 1 doubles pair of Amanda Becker (front) and Audrey Mahany won in straight sets in their last two matches; earning a 6-1, 6-3 win over Lick-Wilmerding and 7-5, 6-3 win against University. get quiet. But it’s the start of the season,” said Becker. “We’ve built a lot of chemistry over the summer at Jim’s clinics, I think that helped us have synergy out there, but we’re still cleaning some things up,” added Mahany. With a full season scheduled into November, the pair is hopeful of a strong showing. “Honestly, team bonding is something we really want to keep building. Last year, we really didn’t get much of that because of COVID. Now it’s going to be fun,” said Mahany. “The team is already really close and we’re having a ton of fun at practice, but those things give a good balance. I really want to do team dinners again,” continued Becker. In the recent 6-1 win over the Tigers, Piedmont quickly swept the contest by claiming the first four matches of the day. The first win was No. 3 doubles team of sophomore Cecilia Defazio and freshman Emma Eisemon in straight sets, 6-1-, 6-1. It was an impressive varsity debut for Eisemon, who showed quickness and creativity in front of the net. “The debut pairing of Cecila DeFazio and Emma Eisemon at No. 3 doubles was great. They hit with power and control; it left their opponents in the dust,” said Landes. Junior Michaela Bini quickly followed by winning 6-2, 6-1 at No. 3 singles, then Annika Gilliland handled her opponent at No. 4 singles, 6-3, 6-1 The clinching victory came at No. 2 doubles, with Mara LaForte and Rose Siemers winning in three sets, 6-7 (7-2), 6-1, 10-4. Becker and Mahany rolled in straight sets despite trailing in the second set 3-1 for Piedmont’s fifth win. No. 1 Bridgette McEfee lost in three sets 6-1, 3-6, 10-6 for Lick’s only win. Last on the court was Anne Jumper at No. 2 singles, gaining her first win of the season in three sets 6-3, 5-7, 10-4. Loss to University Although losing to University last week 6-1, assistant coach Neil Rothenberg pointed out that three matches went to three sets. McEfee lost in three sets, 7-5, 6-7, 10-7 at No. 1; Jumper fell 6-4, 6-0 at No. 2 singles; Bini lost in three, 6-2, 4-6, 10-6 at No. 3; Gilliland lost 6-4, 6-4 at No. 4. In doubles, Becker and Mahany won 7-5, 6-3 at No. 1; LaForte and Simers lost in three sets, 6-4, 4-6, 10-6 at No. 2; and Sofia Ferraro and Defazio lost 6-1, 6-3. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-1) heads to Orinda tomorrow, Thursday, September 2 to face Miramonte. Next Tuesday, September 7, they will host Encinal. Both matches start 3:30 p.m. Mara LaForte helped PHS’ clinch a fourth victory against LickWilmerding in three sets at No. 3 doubles with Rose Siemers (not pictured), 6-7 (7-2), 6-1, 10-4.

articles.text: Piedmont native Mackie McDonald climbed another notch on the ATP World Tour ladder of professional tennis players. Earlier on Tuesday, August 31, he upset No. 27 seeded David Goffin in straight sets, 6-2, 7-5, 6-3, in the first round of the prestigious U.S. Open. Goffin entered with a world ranking of No. 30. McDonald is No. 61. With the victory, he could surpass his career high ranking of No. 57. The U.S. Open first round has been a particular thorn in the side of McDonald. He’s been knocked out of the first round of the tournament three times – in 2016, 2018, and 2020. In each match, he won the first two sets, but lost in five. In 2016, McDonald lost to Chile’s Jan Satral, 4-6, 3-6, 6-3, 6-2, 6-2. Then in 2018, he fell in five sets to the Netherland’s Robin Haase, 4-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-1, 6-3. After his recovery from a leg injury in 2020, McDonald lost to No. 30 Casper Rudd in five sets, 4-6, 4-6, 6-4, 6-3, 6-2. This time, at age 26 and with a veteran mindset after recovering from a substantial torn hamstring tendon in 2019, McDonald is a man on a mission and perhaps entering the peak of his career. McDonald believes that the global pandemic enabled him to study his craft, build a further understanding of his body and how to stay healthy. “The start of 2020 was understanding my body,” McDonald said. “COVID actually gave me time to play tennis and get back to feeling like finding my game and stuff, because it takes time after an injury.” McDonald played up to his reputation against Goffin, gaining 14 aces, was successful on 71 percent of first serves, won five of 12 breakpoints, gained nine points at the net, and struck 50 winners. He’s finishing up a monumental month of August after jumping 43 positions when reaching the Finals at the Citi Open ATP 500 in Washington D.C. on August 8. Goffin is the sixth top-100 player on the ATP Tour that McDonald has defeated this month. At the Citi Open, Mackie handled Australia’s No. 80 Nick Kyrgios, 6-4, 6-4; France’s No. 50 Benoit Paire; Portugal’s No. 64 Ilya Ivashka, 6-4, 6-4; the U.S.’s No. 90 Denis Kudla, 6-3, 6-2; and Japan’s No. 56 Kei Nishikori in the semifinals to a three-set victory, 6-4, 6-3, 7-5. In 2019 at the time of his injury, McDonald watched his ranking dip from No. 57 to No. 132, and then to No. 272 due to a lengthy recovery. Now in the doorstep of a new career high, McDonald is set to face Keu Nishikori of Japan in the second round tomorrow, Thursday, September 2. The match streamed live on ESPN+. McDonald is currently ranked No. 61 in the world, four away from matching his career high.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Tahoe South A webcam photo of the Stateline area of South Lake Tahoe, which underwent an emergency evacuation on Monday. Monday’s big news was the emergency evacuation of South Lake Tahoe, a city of over 20,000. The Caldor Fire waging near South Lake Tahoe resulted in a hours-long traffic jam as residents funneled out on Highway 50. Cal Fire feared that dangerous winds could push the Caldor Fire toward the major tourist destination and town after the blaze breached Echo Summit. “Difficult road conditions, hard to access. It’s been burning in heavy timber, just very, very difficult conditions,” said Cal Fire chief Thom Porter. “We’ve been making headway at times. I reported last week about how we have effectively an inversion that puts kind of a lid on fire activity. But then when the air clears, it’s like taking a lid off of your pot of boiling water. All of a sudden, there’s that plume of heat and steam that comes out, same thing happens in a fire. It sucks in oxygen from all directions, and puts fires in all directions.” As of Tuesday night, August 31, the massive wildfire had grown 191,607 acres in 17 days and is only 16 percent contained. A total of 669 structures destroyed, and five people injured. More than 30,000 structures remain threatened with the blaze waging just a few miles from South Lake Tahoe. California governor Gavin Newsom declared a State of Emergency for Alpine, Amador, and Place Counties. “It is imperative that residents in the impacted areas stay safe and prepare to evacuate immediately if called for by local authorities,” Newsom said. “We thank all the heroic firefighters and first responders working around the clock to combat this rapidly spreading fire and to protect local communities across California this fire season.” The fire began on August 14, and high winds increased the size exponentially on August 16, jumping the Caldor Fire from 6,500 acres to 30,000 by August 17. On August 20, the fire had forced a closure on Highway 50, the main highway in and out of the south end of Lake Tahoe. Winds began driving the blaze toward the Lake Tahoe Basin one week later. Dixie Fire The Caldor Fire cannot be mentioned without acknowledging the huge Dixie Fire burning across five counties – Butte, Lassen, Plumas, Shasta, and Tehama. At 807,396 acres, it is the largest single source wildfire in California history and the second largest overall blaze behind last year’s August Complex Fire (1,032,000 acres). As of August 31, the Dixie Fire has been waging for 48 days and is at 48 percent containment. It has destroyed 1277 structures and damaged 92 others. The subsequent smoke has caused unhealthy air quality as far away as reaching as Utah and Colorado, according to the Associated Press. Both fires could result in poor air quality in the East Bay in September, resulting in the cancelling of some outdoor sports events. Of future concern is the history of hot, dry “Diablo” winds from inland areas typically pick up in September and October. Photo courtesy of Cal Fire A map shows the Caldor Fire outside Meyes and South Lake Tahoe.
articles.title: Caldor Fire forces emergency evacuation of South Lake Tahoe; Dixie Fire waging

articles.text: Piedmont’s volleyball team has opened its season with a win against St. Joseph in Alameda on August 24. One week later, Tuesday, August 31, it lost 3-1 to non-league opponent Skyline in Oakland. . “We’ve come a long way from last year because of COVID. This is the first regular season in two years,” said coach Leslie Blakely. “There are some things we’re doing well and some things we’re still missing. There’s a lot of progress, but there’s still a lot to work on to reach or full potential,” Volleyball has become the most popular girls’ sport in the fall season. According to Blakely, approximately 52 girls tried out for the team, resulting in the creation of a freshman team for the first time. “We had 52 girls tryout for the team. That’s huge. We hosted a lot of open gyms during the summer to build interest in the sport. When you see that many kids interested, you know the program is going to improve. Kids are interested and it’s our job to provide them with a place to play. It’s an exciting future for our girls’ team,” she said. The Highlanders will have a wealth of upperclassmen, including seniors Sophie Nevis, Ruby Shaffer, Ari Talwatte, Amelia Wire, Sofia Croley, Juniors Tara Kothari, Bree Deyoung, Shelby Cavenaugh, and Eden Lorin, while Sophomores Peterson Baur, Izzy Grimmer, and Sadie Town round out the lineup. “A lot of girls came back; they Tara Kothari had seven kills and an ace. Ruby Shaffer led Piedmont with 11 kills and two serving aces. are awesome. You can see the energy around the team they love to play,” said Blakely. Leading offensively for Piedmont against Skyline was Shaffer with 11 kills and Kothari with seven. Both are returning starters from last season’s team. In Tuesday’s match, Skyline won the first two sets 25-19 and 25-13 but the Highlanders rallied for a convincing 25-17 win in the third set. The Titans, however, prevailed in the fourth and final set, 25-19. In the first set, PHS trailed 7-0 but fought back to narrow the score to 22-19. Skyline reeled off three straight points to win on defensive errors by Piedmont. Similarly in the second set, Skyline opened to a 6-0 lead and did well to close 25-13. But Piedmont won the third set 25-18, starting off with a 10-5 lead until Skyline stormed back with five unanswered points. Then Piedmont reeled off four straight points, 14-10, then after a pair of Skyline points PHS went on another six-point scoring run, 20-12, closing out by allowing six more while scoring five. In the third set win, PHS had five aces—two by Nevis and Eden, and one by Kothari—and 11 kills; three by Shaffer and Kothari, two by Deyoung and Nevis, and one by Town. Piedmont finished with 11 aces on the night, including three for Nevis, two for Schaffer, two for Baur, two for Eden, and individuals for Town and Kothari. Offensively, Shaffer had 11 kills, Koathari had seven, Nevis had five, Deyoung had two, and Eden, Croley, Town, and Talwatte had one. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-1) play its opening home match at Binks Rawlings Gym on Thursday, September 9, with Encinal. The JV game is at 4 p.m., followed by the varsity at 5:30 p.m.

articles.text: A drive along California Highway 92 through San Mateo County toward Half Moon Bay assures the sight of cyclists and parked cars when approaching the Crystal Springs Reservoir at the interchange of CA-35, I-280, and Cañada Road. Upper and Lower Crystal Springs Reservoir is a popular biking area from Cañada Road along CA-35 all the way to San Andreas Lake and a protected watershed. The county hosts Bicycle Sundays on a 2.5-mile segment of Cañada Road between CA-92 and Edgewood Road. It is closed to vehicles to allow bicyclists and other non-vehicle users to enjoy full use of the road. The view of the reservoirs often brings cyclists to a halt to take in the view. But many locals are unaware the Lower and Upper Crystal Springs are entirely manmade created by the Spring Valley Water Company in 1887. Filled over by the reservoir is the former village of Crystal Springs, slightly northwest of the reservoir’s dam on Lower Crystal Springs. The small town was a resort area along a railroad, and was the last station and stagecoach location between San Mateo and Half Moon Bay. The Crystal Springs Hotel was built in the 1860s. Surrounded by farmland, it provided a luxurious stop for people going to San Francisco. In 1859, the San Mateo County Gazette called Crystal Springs “truly a proper resort. Staff Photo Known for the cycling popularity, San Mateo County closes a 2.5-mile segment of Canada Road to traffic on Bicycle Sundays. Photo courtesy of the San Mateo County Historical Association This is the only known depiction of the Crystal Springs Hotel.

pages.text: Wednesday, September 1, 2021 15 HIKING WITH JON Crystal Springs Reservoir – Bay Area’s forgotten piece of history By Jonathan Comeaux A drive along California Highway 92 through San Mateo County toward Half Moon Bay assures the sight of cyclists and parked cars when approaching the Crystal Springs Reservoir at the interchange of CA-35, I-280, and Cañada Road. Upper and Lower Crystal Springs Reservoir is a popular biking area from Cañada Road along CA-35 all the way to San Andreas Lake and a protected watershed. The county hosts Bicycle Sundays on a 2.5-mile segment of Cañada Road between CA-92 and Edgewood Road. It is closed to vehicles to allow bicyclists and other non-vehicle users to enjoy full use of the road. The view of the reservoirs often brings cyclists to a halt to take in the view. But many locals are unaware the Lower and Upper Crystal Springs are entirely manmade created by the Spring Valley Water Company in 1887. Filled over by the reservoir is the former village of Crystal Springs, slightly northwest of the reservoir’s dam on Lower Crystal Springs. The small town was a resort area along a railroad, and was the last station and stagecoach location between San Mateo and Half Moon Bay. The Crystal Springs Hotel was built in the 1860s. Surrounded by farmland, it provided a luxurious stop for people going to San Francisco. In 1859, the San Mateo County Gazette called Crystal Springs “truly a proper resort. Staff Photo Known for the cycling popularity, San Mateo County closes a 2.5-mile segment of Canada Road to traffic on Bicycle Sundays. Photo courtesy of the San Mateo County Historical Association This is the only known depiction of the Crystal Springs Hotel. Staff Photo Lower and Upper Crystal Springs Reservoir are a popular cycling area. The history of the region dates back to the late 1800s. Situated in a little valley, thickly studded with the clustering live oaks, surrounded on every side by high mountains, shut out from cold winds, and rich in nature’s beauties, it is truly a proper resort for the lovers of pleasure,” wrote the Gazette, via Geocaching.com. However, the town’s success was short-lived and the land was purchased by the Spring Valley Water Company, which eventually became the San Francisco Public Utilities Commission. The town of Crystal Springs was filled over with water by 1887 when the dam was constructed. The Spring Valley Water Company was owned by William Bowers Bourn II, who spearheaded the merger between the San Francisco Gas and Electric Company and California Gas and Electric Company to create Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E). Surprisingly, there is no mention of William Bowers Bourn in PG&E’s history. At the end of the Upper Crystal Springs Reservoir is the Pulgas Water Temple which was created in part by Bourn and the SF Water Department in 1934 to commemorate the completion of the Hetch Hetchy Aqueduct. The Pulgas Water Temple is a collection of Corinthian style columns bearing the inscription: “I give waters in the wilderness and rivers in the desert, to give drink to my people,” Isaiah 43:20. Flowing water was originally visible from the well within the stone columns, but was covered in order to prevent trespassers from jumping into the canal. A half mile from the Pulgas Water Temple is the Filoli Historic House & Garden Estate in Woodside, Bourn’s 43-room mansion with 16 acres of gardens, on a 654-acre estate. Created in 1915, Bourn lived there during his final days in 1936. The exterior of the Filoli mansion was used in the 1981 television series, Dynasty. Tours are offered for $25. Should bikers or hikers park at the Canada Road Cycling Parking Area, it’s only a 2.2 trek to the Pulgas Water Temple. It is also just 2.2 miles to the Crystal Springs Dam from the parking area along CA-35. Parking at the Pulgas Water Temple is closed on weekends, but available to hikers and bikers. Staff Photo The Pulgas Water Temple was built in 1934 to commemorate the Hetch Hetchy Aqueduct providing drinking water to San Mateo County and San Francisco. Staff Photo A view inside the Pulgas Water Temple, where the well has been covered with a large metal grate to prevent thrill-seekers jumping into the canal. Photo courtesy of Filoli.org Near the Crystal Springs Reservoir is the Filoli House, both created by William Bowers Bourn II. His untold history lays the groundwork for the entire Crystal Springs Reservoir region.

After a year-long hiatus from live theatre, Cal Shakes is welcoming audiences back today with a brand new adaption of The Winter’s Tale. The popular play by William Shakespeare is adapted by Eric Ting and Philippa Kelly and is a story of both loss and healing. The cast includes Safiya Fredericks, Dean Linnard, Craig Marker, and Regina Morones. To purchase tickets, see https:// calshakes.org/winters-tale/?utm_ s o u r c e = S u m o & u t m _ m e d i - It will be the only play produced by Cal Shakes this year and is part of the 2021 Season of Shared Light, on which Bruns has been opened to a range of arts organizations, including Berkeley Symphony, West Edge Opera. Bandaloop, and Destiny Arts. “At Cal Shakes, many of our performances take place – not in the relative anonymity of a dark theater but under the sun,” said Ting. “It’s a thing I’ve come to love and miss dearly: actors and audience alike, in full view of one another, relinquishing the control we normally associate with the theater and instead navigating the complexity of each other’s very real presence across the arc of a performance, cohabiting the shared light of our space.” Safiya Fredericks will appear in the California Shakespeare Festival production of The Winter’s Tale at Bruns Amphitheater from September 1- 26.

articles.text: Alisa Golden, who writes, makes art, and edits an online and print, art and literary magazine, will have an exhibit of art quilts, “Nature on Loan,” at the Piedmont Center for the Arts September 5-19. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on three Sundays, September 5, 12 and 19. She will lead a tour of the exhibit at 12 noon on September 12. Since 2017 she has actively been working with textiles and making art quilts, including letterpress printing, embroidered poems, stencils, and solar printing. She taught for twelve years as an adjunct professor in Printmaking at California College of the Arts and at San Francisco Art Institute, JFK University, and Cal State East Bay as well as workshops at the San Francisco Center for the Book, among others. Her book art may be found in the special collections departments of universities and libraries across the country, Artist Alisa Golden her quilts in public and private collections, and her writing has been published in many literary magazines. She is the author of Making Handmade Books and Painted Paper, and other instructional books. Most quilts are for sale. articles.text: Aurora Theatre Company in Berkeley presents the filmed production “Stoop Stories,” beginning September 3. The premiere combines prose, poetry and music playwright and Pulitzer Prize finalist Dael Orlandersmith, who crafts this solo show. The story is set in New York City, and the variety of characters are drawn from the playwright’s personal life. Among the characters is an elderly Polish Holocaust survivor, a young poet struggling with addiction, a teenage Puerto Rican immersed in “Counter Culture,” and a 70-year old New York native on her way to the West Village to see Nina Simone. Their stories and narratives are Visit https://www.auroratheatre.org/index.php/shows-events/ 20212022-season/stoop-stories for more information on how to watch “Stoop Stories” after its premiere on September 3. Postshow conversations will be held on September 19 at 4 p.m., September 25 at 12 p.m., and October 1 at 5 p.m. Playwright Dael Orlandersmith interwoven in this play. “Stoop Stories” is directed by Elizabeth Carter. articles.text: Piedmont native and blues guitarist Jules Leyhe will perform his first concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Sunday, September 5, at 4:00 p.m. on the lawn in front of the Center. The performance is part of the CD release of “Your First Rodeo” (on Monkey Fingers Records), their first record (http://www. keysandchords.com/news-blog/ guitarist-jules-leyhes-your-firstrodeo-is-a-wild-ride). Jules Leyhe has performed on stage and worked with some of the blues world’s biggest names including Buddy Guy, JimJules Leyhe’s latest CD release “Your First Rodeo.” Piedmont native and blues guitarist Jules Leyhe. mie Vaughan, Taj Mahal, Chris Cain, Huey Lewis and Fantastic Negrito. His own group, the Family Jules Band, includes keyboardist Ian McArdle, saxophonist Nancy Wright, bassist Murph Murphy and drummer Isaac Schwartz. Featured in Guitar Player magazine and the San Francisco Chronicle, Leyhe graduated from the Berklee School of Music (2012) with a focus on blues guitar. Inspired heavily by the work of Jimi Hendrix and the Beatles, the Family Jules Band combines elements of many styles of music. Be sure to catch Jules Lehye at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue, on Sunday, September 5 at 4 p.m. The concert is part of the ongoing Summer PCA Arts Festival, celebrating the non-profit Center’s 10th Anniversary.
articles.title: Jules Leyhe debuts at Center for the Arts on Sunday

articles.text: Gold Coast Chamber Players is returning to the Don Tatzin Community Hall in Lafayette with “Spheres of Influence,” a program of French, Chinese, and Japanese music on Saturday evening, September 18 at 7:30 p.m. The featured musicians are the sextet of violinists Dan Carlson and Dian Zhang, violists Joy Fellows and Gold Coast founder Pamela Freund-Striplen, cellist Amos Yang, and double bassist Charles Chandler. The program includes Maurice Ravel’s Sonata for violin and cello, Debussy’s String Quartet in G minor, Shinji Eshima’s Bariolage for cello and bass, and Ching-chu Hu’s Spheres of Influence written for a string sextet. The concert will be presented in-person in accordance with state and local health guidelines. Gold Coast Chamber Players founder Pamela Freund-Striplen. All tickets purchased include the option to view the concert virtually. All patrons must show proof of vaccination to enter the concert, and masks are required in the venue for all patrons regardless of vaccination status.
