articles.text: The UC Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) recently announced the return of in-person film screenings this month at the Barbro Osher Theater. The theater will also serve as the East Bay venue for the Mill Valley Film Festival in October. “It’s thrilling to welcome our community of filmgoers back to BAMPFA after this difficult year, and I can’t imagine a better way to do so than with a series of free screenings presented al fresco on the museum’s outdoor screen,” said Susan Oxtoby, BAMPFA’s director of film and senior film curator. “For nearly eighteen months, we’ve been deeply moved by the support of our devoted audiences, who have continued to engage with BAMPFA’s film programming during our pivot to virtual cinema. We’re delighted to invite our audiences to return in person now that restrictions have been lifted.” This month BAMPFA’s ongoing series “Documentary Voices” returns with a selection of both classic and contemporary films with historical value. The film today, September 1, is The Murder of Fred Hampton, a political documentary as Howard Alk investigates the killing of Black Panther and titular leader Fred Hampton. On Wednesday, September 15, is a documentary by Tatiana Huezo entitled Tempestad, with an introduction by Nicolas Pereda. The film is built around interviews with two women and uses cinematography to describe the presence of crime in Mexico. The film will be shown at 7 p.m. Berkeley Pacific Film Archive is located at 2155 Center Street in Berkeley. To obtain tickets, see: https://bampfa.org/program/documentary-voices. Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive
articles.title: BAMPFA resumes in-person film screenings

articles.text: Berkeley Botanical Garden at The University of California will host a Zoom program exploring the many species of butterflies that have taken residence in the gardens. The virtual butterfly walk will be held on Sunday, September 12, at 11 a.m. Join the gardens’ resident propagator Sal Levinson and garden volunteer Sarab Seth for an illustrated slideshow of butterflies found among the flowers this time of year. Those who tune-in will learn about the butterflies’ life cycle and host plants. articles.text: Photo by Cory Weaver Ailyn Perez was vocally compelling in the title role of San Francisco Opera’s production of Puccini’s Tosca. Opera review by Paul Hertelendy I dearly love this “shabby little shocker,” as the great Berkeley musicologist Joseph Kerman once termed it, surfeited as it is with melodrama. The opera Tosca embodies the most greed, real-world corruption, duplicity, betrayal, revolutionary activism, hypocrisy and sheer sexual desire of any of Puccini’s operas, all set in familiar sites of Rome, adding up to a stunning social critique of the composer’s homeland. It shows this very establishment composer as a political activist, protester and reformer for once. Naturally, no opera has ever had a greater hold on San Francisco, which staged it as the very first work in the War Memorial Opera House in 1932 and then in 41 different seasons since. What better work to reopen on-stage production after a galling 20-month pandemic shutdown? And what about the intriguing murder trial that would have followed, had Tosca not killed herself by jumping off a Rome parapet? Tosca was subjected to sexual submission to the evil Scarpia if she was to save her imprisoned lover/revolutionary. Instead, she grabbed a nearby dagger and dispatched Scarpia in her supreme act of public service. Murder? Manslaughter? Justifiable homicide? Good case study for law students, especially given Scarpia’s astute evidence-gathering to entrap both male revolutionaries on the lam. This ranks with a mere handful of other works, like Janacek’s The Makropulos Affair, as fodder for young attorneys or detectives. But as melodramatic opera, this one really works with its entirely American cast. The San Francisco Opera’s 2018 production propels it along with stirring leads as the lovers Tosca and Cavaradossi. In her first Tosca, Chicagoan Ailyn Perez was vocally compelling, with an upper octave stronger than the lower one. As the coquettish diva, she played the insecure jealousy card in act one very well, while also carrying out the most difficult pantomime of all as the tremulous murderer preparing a tomblike scene around the cadaver. Tenor Michael Fabbiano, who had never ventured Cavaradossi before this summer, was heroic and convincing as the maligned prisoner, bringing down the house with his solo of resignation “E lucevan le stelle” prior to the firing squad. Clearly, a major talent to watch and hear in the future. The love duets of the two were to melt over. Scarpia newcomer baritone Alfred Walker was still feeling his way into the role, both as actor and as singer with heft. Others of note: Soloman Howard as Angelotti; Dale Travis, the SFO’s most prevalent character bit player since Colin Harvey, as Sacristan; and my favorite hissthe-villain in all Puccini, Spoletta (Joel Sorensen), taking huge nightly tumbles courtesy of the irascible and imperious Scarpia. When heard August 27, this was a promising start for the new feminine SFO Music Director Eun Sun Kim and a great finale season for choral Director Ian Richardson if the robust church procession ending Act One was any indication. (He retires in December.) Director Shawna Lucey kept the movement going, literally; whenever things slowed, extras were hopping about on stage. Even her firing squad appeared made up of veteran troops. MUSIC NOTES – The San Francico Opera is authorized to sell out the whole house, if all are masked and vaccinated, because the entire cast itself is fully vaccinated, a company representative explained….Tosca runs through Sept. 5…. More future standing ovations at the S.F. Opera? If so, ascribe it in part to the new chairs installed all over during the long pandemic. The old ones, mostly allegedly from 1932, sank down, down, down, till you went out of sight far below, very often with unsettling squeaks as downward accompaniment... Paul Hertelendy, a Piedmont resident, also writes reviews for www.artsSF.com.
articles.title: City’s love affair with Tosca

articles.text: Late eighteenth century classical composers influenced jazz rhythm and melody. Jazz improvisers would create their own manner of phrasing, syncopation and melodic design, but they were influenced by what they heard in performances of classical music, marching bands and church music. Jazz was born in New Orleans in a mix of African, French and Spanish cultures. African Americans used European band instruments, the African banjo and marching drums to blend African rhythm with chromatics in the melody and with the harmonic darkening of European chords. As Wynton Marsalis said at Jazz At Lincoln Center on January 12, 2018, “The amalgam of elements in Afro-American music and in jazz come from different forms of European music, like the march form and the combination of a fiddle style or a European parlor piano style, which, when combined with the arpeggiated sound of a banjo and syncopation, becomes ragtime.” Chromatics were used by these eastern Europeans classical composers: Chopin (Polish) - Waltz in C# minor (1847); Tchaikovsky (Russian) - Lenski’s Aria (1879); Fučík (Czech) - Entrance of the Gladiators (1897), Thunder and Blazes (1901); Rimsky-Korsakov (Russian) - Flight of the Bumblebee (1900) Classical music, in the common practice period from 1600 to 1900. primarily used triads (three-note chords). In the later nineteenth century many classical composers began to use seventh chords, which would influence ragtime and jazz music. Seventh chords were used in these pieces from 1847 through 1908: Liszt: Hungarian Rhapsody #2; Chopin: Waltz in C# minor; Wagner: Liebestod; Bizet: Carmen, La Fleur Que Tu M’Avais Jetée, Toreador Song; Agnus Dei; Tchaikovsky: Romance, Lenski’s Aria, None but the Lonely Heart, Romeo and Juliet; Satie: Trois Gymnopedies; Grieg: Ich Liebe Dich; Tchaikovsky: Nocturne, Nutcracker (Dance of the Reed Flutes); Gonoud: O Divine Redeemer; Richard Strauss: Morgen; Fučík: Entrance of the Gladiators; Rimsky-Korsakov: Flight of the Bumblebee; Fučík: Thunder and Blazes; Debussy: Gollywog’s Cakewalk. Chopin used chromatics in the melody and seventh chords in the harmony in his Waltz in C# minor, Opus 64, No 2. Bar numbers are shown on the upper left of each bar in the Youtube video. Chopin’s melody has been filled-in with some jazz phrases (i.e. bar 18) and the jazz guitar solo from bars 51-82 is added jazz content. Note Chopin’s chromatics in bars 15-18, 28, 33, 42, 48 and 49. The jazz guitar solo in bars 51-82 uses many modern melodic devices. Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. His course is available for free online at www.guitarimprov.com. Seventh chords were used in these pieces from 1847 through 1908: Liszt: Hungarian Rhapsody #2; Chopin: Waltz in C# minor; Wagner: Liebestod; Bizet: Carmen, La Fleur Que Tu M’Avais Jetée, Toreador Song; Agnus Dei; Tchaikovsky: Romance, Lenski’s Aria, None but the Lonely Heart, Romeo and Juliet; Satie: Trois Gymnopedies; Grieg: Ich Liebe Dich; Tchaikovsky: Nocturne, Nutcracker (Dance of the Reed Flutes); Gonoud: O Divine Redeemer; Richard Strauss: Morgen; Fučík: Entrance of the Gladiators; Rimsky-Korsakov: Flight of the Bumblebee; Fučík: Thunder and Blazes; Debussy: Gollywog’s Cakewalk. Chopin used chromatics in the melody and seventh chords in the harmony in his Waltz in C# minor, Opus 64, No 2. Bar numbers are shown on the upper left of each bar in the Youtube video. Chopin’s melody has been filled-in with some jazz phrases (i.e. bar 18) and the jazz guitar solo from bars 51-82 is added jazz content. Note Chopin’s chromatics in bars 15-18, 28, 33, 42, 48 and 49. The jazz guitar solo in bars 51-82 uses many modern melodic devices. Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. His course is available for free online at www.guitarimprov.com. Opera review by Paul Hertelendy I dearly love this “shabby little shocker,” as the great Berkeley musicologist Joseph Kerman once termed it, surfeited as it is with melodrama. The opera Tosca embodies the most greed, real-world corruption, duplicity, betrayal, revolutionary activism, hypocrisy and sheer sexual desire of any of Puccini’s operas, all set in familiar sites of Rome, adding up to a stunning social critique of the composer’s homeland. It shows this very establishment composer as a political activist, protester and reformer for once. Naturally, no opera has ever had a greater hold on San Francisco, which staged it as the very first work in the War Memorial Opera House in 1932 and then in 41 different seasons since. What better work to reopen on-stage production after a galling 20-month pandemic shutdown? And what about the intriguing murder trial that would have followed, had Tosca not killed herself by jumping off a Rome parapet? Tosca was subjected to sexual submission to the evil Scarpia if she was to save her imprisoned lover/revolutionary. Instead, she grabbed a nearby dagger and dispatched Scarpia in her supreme act of public service. Murder? Manslaughter? Justifiable homicide? Good case study for law students, especially given Scarpia’s astute evidence-gathering to entrap both male revolutionaries on the lam. This ranks with a mere handful of other works, like Janacek’s The Makropulos Affair, as fodder for young attorneys or detectives. But as melodramatic opera, this one really works with its entirely American cast. The San Francisco Opera’s 2018 production propels it along with stirring leads as the lovers Tosca and Cavaradossi. In her first Tosca, Chicagoan Ailyn Perez was vocally compelling, with an upper octave stronger than the lower one. As the coquettish diva, she played the insecure jealousy card in act one very well, while also carrying out the most difficult pantomime of all as the tremulous murderer preparing a tomblike scene around the cadaver. Tenor Michael Fabbiano, who had never ventured Cavaradossi before this summer, was heroic and convincing as the maligned prisoner, bringing down the house with his solo of resignation “E lucevan le stelle” prior to the firing squad. Clearly, a major talent to watch and hear in the future. The love duets of the two were to melt over. Scarpia newcomer baritone Alfred Walker was still feeling his way into the role, both as actor and as singer with heft. Others of note: Soloman Howard as Angelotti; Dale Travis, the SFO’s most prevalent character bit player since Colin Harvey, as Sacristan; and my favorite hissthe-villain in all Puccini, Spoletta (Joel Sorensen), taking huge nightly tumbles courtesy of the irascible and imperious Scarpia. When heard August 27, this was a promising start for the new feminine SFO Music Director Eun Sun Kim and a great finale season for choral Director Ian Richardson if the robust church procession ending Act One was any indication. (He retires in December.) Director Shawna Lucey kept the movement going, literally; whenever things slowed, extras were hopping about on stage. Even her firing squad appeared made up of veteran troops. MUSIC NOTES – The San Francico Opera is authorized to sell out the whole house, if all are masked and vaccinated, because the entire cast itself is fully vaccinated, a company representative explained….Tosca runs through Sept. 5…. More future standing ovations at the S.F. Opera? If so, ascribe it in part to the new chairs installed all over during the long pandemic. The old ones, mostly allegedly from 1932, sank down, down, down, till you went out of sight far below, very often with unsettling squeaks as downward accompaniment... articles.text: Baby Driver is a solid summer movie that is indeed more than the sum of its parts. You might be asking yourself, why would I spend almost two hours watching a film titled Baby Driver? The answer depends on why you watch movies and what you expect to take away from the story. As it turns out, audiences happen to have a nifty spectrum of films to choose from. But know that this movie is an off-the-wall adrenalin rush that is surprisingly original, despite its staccato-like tropes. It’s dark and amazing and, in a word, cool. Downright cool. Set in today’s Atlanta, it borders on being a spikey fable with characters that are created out of whole cloth, absent any backstory. They’re just there, bank robbers all, and every one of them is crazily compelling. There’s Baby (Ansel Elgort), a baby-faced young twenty-something who works for Doc (Kevin Spacey) and his revolving crew of bank heist sociopaths. Baby wears full-time ear buds (bad tinnitus), shades, and is a gifted getaway driver who handles a car like a Le Mans speedway artist. Ansel Elgort stars in Baby Driver. Of course, the cops give chase (more than once), but Baby is a stone cold wheelman who zigs when they zag, hurtling through urban traffic and never changes his I-pod mix. Pure genius. After each job the ensemble meets to divvy up the loot and that’s when the tattooed alumni from a local prison get to do their trash talking. It’s just great. The lead psychopath, Bats (Jamie Fox), a certifiable head case for which there is no rehab, does a running, demented patois that conveys with each sentence that he is always on the verge of dropping off a mental cliff and shooting somebody. Anybody. As Bats, he is well named. The only character with even a hint of backstory is Baby, raised by a wheelchair-bound foster dad who is deaf and can’t speak. Where did that come from? There’s a lot more, to include a great performance by Jon Hamm as seemingly sane Buddy and his amazing girlfriend, Darling, superbly played by Eliza Gonzalez. Just your average wigged-out bank job couple and really fun to spend time with. I’ll stop here and just assume that if you watch Baby Driver, you’ll want to experience all the fast and slow reveals without too much warning. So, enjoy. Baby Driver. Directed by Edgar Wright. Starring Ansel Elgort, Jamie Fox, Jon Hamm, and Eliza Gonzalez. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated R. Ansel Elgort, Jamie Fox, Eliza Gonzalez, and Jon Hamm in Baby Driver.

articles.text: Dustin Hoffman and Emma Thompson star in Last Chance Harvey. Last Chance Harvey uses a familiar template that Hollywood has often turned to, sometimes with great success: estranged father attends daughter’s wedding and after a series of unexpected events, some comedic, some dramatic, he finds redemption. What makes Harvey entertaining is not the story, but the fine performances of Dustin Hoffman and Emma Thompson. They are both charming and delightful to watch and raise this film to a new level by the sheer volume of their acting ability. Their meeting in a London bar is pure serendipity, and yet when they begin their hesitant, quasi-hostile dance of getting acquainted, they are so engaging it’s impossible not to conclude that this is a film that possesses a nice glow. At the outset, using deft parallel editing, we are introduced to Harvey Shine and Kate Walker and discover that they are both lonely people. Harvey has lost his job and seemingly his daughter, and Kate is convinced that she is defined by her age and seeming isolation. Without realizing it, they set out to prove the other wrong – about so many things. Watching them interact, first as strangers and then as friends, is to observe two consummate actors who can look into the camera and with a look, a smile, a raise of the eyebrows say volumes, making it hard to bid these two likable people adieu as the credits begin to roll. Last Chance Harvey. Starring Dustin Hoffman, Emma Thompson, James Brolin and Kathy Baker. Directed by Joel Hopkins. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Last Chance Harvey a gem with Dustin Hoffman, Emma Thompson

articles.text: A scene from Disney’s Planes: Fire & Rescue. Planes: Fire & Rescue is a nice fit for kids 8-years-old and below, and is an ideal follow up to Disney’s animated Planes. Both star Dusty Crophopper (Dane Cook). It was in Planes that Dusty realizes his dream of becoming a world-class, hotdogging air-racer, and an international celebrity, basking in the continual attention of the cameras. But then, unexpectedly, as Planes: Fire Rescue begins, Dusty discovers that his gearbox is failing, the parts he needs to fix it aren’t available, so he can’t reach those top speeds that allow him to win races. And there is the problem that his much loved hometown airport, Propwash Junction, needs a serious updating. Its equipment is failing to meet compliance. But the situation gives Dusty something to do, which he is yearning to do. He decides to become an aerial firefighter, gets certified by the crusty, cranky Blade Ranger (Ed Harris) who is in charge of training for the Piston Peak squadron. And so begins the story of planes (Dusty now included) zooming through fire ravaged canyons, up into billowing clouds of smoke, swooping down to scoop up water from lakes and rivers, some dropping pink fire retardant. All of them are flying by the seat of their ailerons, the Piston Peakers risking their lives, so to speak, to protect those on the ground, which includes the ATV smoke jumpers, a courageous bunch who drop out of airplanes, parachute to the ground, and fight the raging fires. The hotshot crew of Piston Peak also includes military transport Cabbie (Dale Dye), and Lil’ Dipper (Julie Bowen), who has a crush on Dusty. And there’s May Day (Hal Holbrook), a dated fire and rescue truck, plus Windlifter (Wes Studi), whose helicopter blades are painted like feathers. One of the squadron’s missions turns out to be an allhands-on-deck attempt to save the Grand Fusel Lodge, its guests are all manner of transportation that fill the lobby/hanger and the rooms. Dusty, of course, must overcome his fear as he confronts the ultimate villain in the story, the unforgiving forest fires, such as those barreling down on the lodge. There’s lots of action, and Dusty manages to get out of some tight spots, as does the Piston Peak squadron. Sure, there is peril, but parents shouldn’t be concerned. In spite of the close calls, no one gets hurt. And the little guys will love Dusty’s courageous antics. Planes: Fire & Rescue. Directed by Bob Gannaway. Disney Studios – animation. 1 hr., 23 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: Planes: Fire & Rescue a perfect movie for youngest kids

articles.text: The Iron Giant, directed by Brad Bird, is based on the children’s book, written by Ted Hughes, published in 1968, and set in the U.K. in the late 60s. For the film, however, Bird chose to move it to Rockwell, a small 1950s downhome town in Maine. The story begins one night during a frightening storm when a huge comet streaks across the sky, and lands in the ocean off the Maine coast. The next night, a 9-year-old boy named Hogart (Eli Marienthal), a latchkey kid raised by his single mom Annie (Jennifer Aniston), leaves home to wander in the woods. His mom is working late at a local diner. To his surprise he discovers what caused the comet. It was a massive, metal-eating giant robot (Vin Diesel), some 50 feet tall, (similar to the giant bot, Gort, in the film The Day the Earth Stood Still), and looks like an erector set toy. The bot is about to eat a local electric substation, but Hogart, seeing the danger of the giant being electrocuted, switches off the power. And thus begins a friendship between the robot and the boy (who has dreamed of having a pet). In one early scene, while the robot is eating some railroad tracks, it collides with an oncoming train, causing it to derail. As a result of that incident, two things happen: Hogart discovers that the robot can self-repair, and a government agent, Kent Mansley (Christopher McDonald), arrives to investigate the accident. He’s suspicious, a bit paranoid, and is convinced there is an E.T-like threat to the town (perhaps the entire country). He is determined to track down whatever it is. Hogart, worried that if found the robot will be taken away, brings it to a local junkyard owned by beatnik artist, Dean McCoppin (Harry Connick, Jr.), who reluctantly agrees to hide the giant. And so the adventure begins, and the boy gradually learns that his BFF bot is empathetic, even docile, but, like Gort, possesses deadly powers. He even rescues two boys from a rooftop and thereby wins over the townspeople. town when missiles are launched it. It intercepts them in flight, sacrificing itself, leaving behind just one small screw which Hogart finds. But the boy notices that the screw is vibrating and then remembers that the iron giant can self-repair, indicating that perhaps not all is lost. The Iron Giant is an exhilarating feature, wonderfully animated (the humans are handdrawn; the robot is created using CGI), and the visuals extraordinary, reminiscent of the iconic work done by the Japanese Studio Ghibli. This is a story and film not to be missed. Of course, things get complicated: agent Mansley, ever in the hunt, contacts the army, setting in motion one crisis after another. The bot even manages to save the The Iron Giant. Directed by Brad Bird. Animation. Voices of Vin Diesel, Harry Connick, Jr., Jennifer Aniston, and Eli Maienthal. 1 hr., 26 min. Rated PG. A scene from The Iron Giant.

articles.text: • I was so glad to get the email that the Family Winemakers of California had scheduled a tasting for San Francisco last weekend. It has been a year and a half since I last attended a live wine tasting in person, and this is one of my favorite wine events of the year. Many of the people pouring the wine have the same name on their name-tags as the name on the wine label. articles.text: Members of the Dolphin Club in San Francisco prepare for an early morning swim on August 13. The Bay Area is defined by a myriad of water, bordered by the powerful Pacific Ocean, various rivers, reservoirs, lakes, and ponds. Even on the hottest days, though, it’s uncommon to find people swimming in these waters. Unlike Southern California, known for its sunny, warm beaches, Northern California is characterized by rocky, windswept, and often unforgiving waters. But groups of Bay Area-residents have been gathering at social clubs along the Bay for decades. Perhaps the most familiar of these is The Dolphin Club, a volunteer-led community of 1,675 members at Aquatic Park in San Francisco. It was founded in 1877 with 25 charter members with a commitment to spending more time in and on the Bay, which “continues to inspire today’s Dolphins.” Its members swim year-round in the Cove at Aquatic Park within a line of buoys parallel to the shore that marks a quarter-mile course. Public access to the club is slated to resume soon, and members can currently bring in two guests. Piedmont resident Josh Bernstein, a longtime open water swimmer, invited me to join a morning “social swim” on August 13, a day that started at 6 a.m. The temperature of the water was about 62 degrees Fahrenheit, considerably warm for the Bay, I was told. Still, the temperature in the city hovered just below 60 degrees at 7:30 a.m., the designated start-time for that morning’s swim. The Dolphin Club and other major social clubs along the bay closed for a period of time during the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, during which time members had to dress and prepare for swims in parking lots. Now that clubs are open, patrons are able to change into their wetsuits and swimsuits and take a much-welcomed hot shower indoors after their swim. I was advised to rent a full wetsuit, which can be done at a Sports Basement store conveniently located in San Francisco’s Presidio. Water temperatures can drop to 50 degrees in the winter, making a wet suit a necessity for most. It is highly recommended for novice open-water swimmers like myself. The synthetic rubber material known as neoprene is a popular choice among wetsuit manufacturers for both its flexibility and buoyancy. While it is possible to drown in a wetsuit, I was assured by Bernstein that it would be “very difficult to sink in one.” It is important to find one that fits snuggly with no air pockets that could potentially allow water in. It turns out that the biggest challenge of the morning was getting the wetsuit on properly. It can take some time, but tying plastic bags to my feet and hands allowed the neoprene to slide over and made the fitting process much easier. Preparing to swim in the cold Bay waters requires the right gear, and, of course, strong swimming skills. The swimmers are under no supervision of a lifeguard. According to the San Francisco Police Department Marine Unit, there have been several close calls in the Golden Gate National Recreation Area (GGNRA) this past year, primarily due to rip currents. San Francisco open shorelines do not have traditional lifeguards, but GGNRA provides Ocean Rescue personnel who patrol Ocean Beach with the primary mission of informing visitors about ocean risks. Swimming and wading at beaches are “strongly discouraged.” At Aquatic Cove, swimmers often swim in pods, and look out for one another. “Swimming in cold water is not for everyone,” Bernstein admitted. “There are significant factors - the cold, the current, and the waves. It takes time to become acclimated. When you start the sport, you don’t want to stay in for long. You could become hypothermic and lose the ability to exercise judgement.” Lesser dangers include the sea life. Sea lions are very territorial. Bernstein recalled a time when a fellow swimmer was bitten by a sea lion and was seriously injured, requiring a trip to the hospital. Despite these risks, proper research and preparation – and a trusted pod of skilled swimmers by your side – makes for an exciting and daring recreational activity. Wading in the Bay waters at daybreak and watching a fiery sunrise illuminate Ghirardelli Square and the San Francisco skyline – all before a full day at the office – is a truly indescribable experience. Open-water swimming in the Bay Area is by no means a new phenomenon but it would be inaccurate to claim it as a favorite pastime among Northern Californians. In fact, many swimmers were driven to the Bay by a combination of pool closures and pandemic restlessness, as evidenced by a slew of anecdotal reporting from SF Weekly, the Daily Cal, and other publications. Bernstein, a member of the Dolphin Club who now swims about five mornings a week, acknowledged that he has spent more time in the Bay because of pool closures. “Swimmers, like runners, are addicted to the sport,” Bernstein said. “When the pools closed, we were desperate to find water.” Bernstein said he started visiting the swim clubs more frequently during the pandemic despite their closures, and met other swimmers getting ready in the parking lots - mostly members of the Dolphin Club and its next door neighbor, the South End Rowing Club. He began linking up with a group that frequented the cove in the mornings for social swims like the one I visited. Similar to my first cold-water excursion on August 13, he recalled that the pod of swimmers were “very welcoming, and just invited me to go along with them.” Dr. Josh Bernstein happily moves through the cool water at Aquatic Cove in San Francisco.

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Ratatouille ingredients are in season and abundant at our markets. Now is the perfect time when ratatouille ingredients are abundant at our markets. Every year, late summer into early fall, versions of zucchini, eggplant, and tomato dishes appear on our table for breakfast, lunch and dinner. We enjoy ratatouille as a versatile accompaniment to eggs, sandwiches, pasta, and any grilled or roasted meats, poultry, or fish. Served at room temperature, this is ideal for a Labor Day picnic or barbeque. This presentation is showy, with the bright skins of the vegetables on full display as it’s arranged with the slices stacked on their edges. It’s easily adaptable to a variety of vegetables, so mix-and-match as suits your taste. Ideally prepared early in the day, this dish requires at least one hour in the oven and tastes best cooked and cooled. Better yet, make a day ahead and store in the refrigerator to let the flavors develop even further. Oven-Roasted Ratatouille Adapted from David Tanis, Saveur Magazine 2016 Makes about 3 – 4 cups, depending on the size of the vegetables Ingredients • 3 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil, plus additional for the pan and drizzling atop • 1 large white onion, thinly sliced • 1 teaspoon fresh thyme, chopped • 1 teaspoon fresh marjoram, chopped • 4 cloves garlic, minced • 1/4 teaspoon crushed chile flakes, to taste • 3/4 pound zucchini, about 4 medium, cut into 1/4-inch coins • 3/4 pound firm eggplant, about 1 small, cut into 1/4-inch slices • 3/4 pound ripe tomatoes, about 3 medium, cored and cut into • • 1/4-inch slices Fresh basil leaves, to garnish Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste Instructions Lightly oil bottom and sides of a 2-quart baking dish, preferably ceramic. Using a 10-inch skillet/fry pan, place 3 tablespoons of olive oil and spread to evenly coat the bottom of the pan. Add the sliced onions with salt and pepper to taste. Cook until onions are softened and translucent, then add thyme, marjoram, and garlic. Continue cooking a few minutes until garlic softens but doesn’t begin to brown. Transfer to the prepared baking dish, spreading evenly, and set aside. Meanwhile position an oven rack to the lower third of the oven and preheat to 400° F. Atop the onion layer, arrange the zucchini, eggplant, and tomatoes in alternating rows with sliced vegetables stacked vertically on edge and slightly overlapping. You want to see the colorful skins on each row for the visual impact of the finished dish. Pack the rows together tightly and continue until the dish is filled. Season the vegetables with additional salt and pepper to taste and drizzle another tablespoon or so of olive oil. Bake for 15 minutes, uncovered, then reduce the heat to 350° F and bake until the vegetables are tender, about 45 – 60 minutes. Baking time will depend on how tightly the vegetables are packed. The vegetables will continue cooking with carry-over heat from the baking dish. Remove the dish from the oven and cool to room temperature. This allows for the flavors to develop further. Garnish with a flourish of fresh torn basil. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.

articles.text: After meeting for 15 months online, the First Mondays Reading Group finally convened in person on August 2 outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. On a lovely, mild day, the Park’s many trees provided an idyllic setting for the discussion. Twelve readers were on hand for a discussion of the August selection, The Fire Next Time by James Baldwin a national bestseller when it was published in 1963, and now considered a classic of American literature. The book’s title comes from a couplet in “Mary Don’t You Weep,” an African-American spiritual, with the verse, “God gave Noah the rainbow sign. No more water, the fire next time.” voice, and the power of his writing. They acknowledged that the book was timely but were sad to realize it was written nearly 60 years ago. The readers believe that our country has made progress with race relations, but it has been slow and uneven. There have been times when our nation has been struck hard, as we have been recently, by the fact that racial injustice and white supremacy beliefs are still widely present. Our country has responded to this realization in the past but it has often fallen back. The readers expressed hope that our country is now widely more fully aware of this. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. Who are those we would rather not see forgiven? The story ends with Jonah pouting about God’s ways and with God, in essence, responding, “Come on my friend. Did you really want me to bring great suffering on Nineveh? Is vengeance really my primary work?” The reader is left to ponder what it is that we expect from a just God. We want the guilty to be held accountable for the wrongs they commit. At the same time, if all God offers is accountability for the guilty, where does that leave us? Is not our hope that in the end God will deal with us compassionately, that mercy will triumph over judgement? As Jonah to tryouts. What this means is that well thought out and designed multi-family buildings with neighborhood compatible massing, building heights, materials, architectural styles, and colors can be a visual enhancement that makes for a richer, more interesting city. One of the main urban design and architectural objections to different uses, types and sizes of buildings next to each other is the abruptness of change. This is especially true in residential areas, where people live. For example, think of a new seven-story glass clad office building located in a two story residential neighborhood – clearly not appropriate. But what about a 4-story mixed use building in a 2-3 story neighborhood? What about a well designed 3-story apartment? It’s often hard to say without seeing it in context. Each case is different because each site and its local surrounding context is different and has to be evaluated as such. It occurs to me that the principal issue with denser multi-family housing is most often not more people, but instead….more cars. Next: Multi-family Housing, Part 3: The Car Dilemma Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. articles.text: Piedmont School District, in partnership with Alameda County Health Department, will host two days of free clinics offering the Pfizer Covid vaccine for people not yet vaccinated. The clinics will be held in Buzz Redford Gym on the Piedmont Middle School campus, 740 Magnolia Avenue, between 2 p.m. and 6 p.m. on Wednesday, September 1. A second dose will be administered on Wednesday, September 22 at the same time and location. The vaccine clinic is open to all Piedmont community members, city staff, teachers and school staff, and students age 12 and older. Students younger than 18 years must have parental or guardian consent. If a parent or guardian cannot accompany the minor, a signed written consent is acceptable, and can be filled out by visiting https:// www.cdph.ca.gov/Programs/ CID/DCDC/Pages/COVID-19/ Pfizer-Vaccine-Minor-Consent-Guidance.aspx. Severe allergic reactions from the Pfizer vaccine are rare, but trained staff will be on-site. Walk-ins are welcome, but pre-registration is suggested at: https://my.primary.health/r/ alcoschools and selecting “Piedmont High School - Middle School.”

articles.text: At a Piedmont City Council meeting on August 16 Mayor Teddy Gray King announced her intention to mandate vaccinations for all city employees. “This is a very dynamic issue,” she said. “We know that there are many members of the community who are already vaccinated. I’m requesting that our city attorney draft a proposal that would mandate that all members of our city staff receive a COVID vaccination as soon as it is cleared by the FDA.” One week later, on August 23, the Food and Drug Administration granted full approval to Pfizer’s coronavirus vaccine for individuals age 16 and older, paving the way for a mandate in Piedmont. King cited the emergence of the Delta variant as her rationale for the mandate, adding that many cities and school districts, including the Piedmont School District, have already set forth such mandates for employees. The city was also waiting for full FDA-approval for COVID- 19 vaccine to mandate vaccinations. King said that, although most city staff are already fully vaccinated, that she would like to see this enacted quickly. City Attorney Michelle Kenyon will draft a rule detailing the city’s expectations for staff. “It’s a step in the right direction,” King said, adding that a mandate would have come sooner but that pending FDA-approval limited the city’s ability to do so. Currently, 93% of fulltime and regular part-time city employees are vaccinated against COVID-19. The lineup of cars will be on view in the parking lot in front of the Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, from 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. The last time the event was held in 2019, 44 gleaming vehicles were on display. I’ll do whatever it takes to maintain that public trust.” Piedmont car owners interested in displaying their cars in the city’s version of a Concours d’Elegance are asked to contact Officer Petit at tpetit@ piedmont.ca.gov. pages.text: Volume 23, No. 43 Piedmont, California August 25, 2021 91¢ Piedmont Post Piedmont Post✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ ALL CITY EDITION ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ ✯ A Community Newspaper Serving the Citizens of Piedmont School District offering free vaccines to residents By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont School District, in partnership with Alameda County Health Department, will host two days of free clinics offering the Pfizer Covid vaccine for people not yet vaccinated. The clinics will be held in Buzz Redford Gym on the Piedmont Middle School campus, 740 Magnolia Avenue, between 2 p.m. and 6 p.m. on Wednesday, September 1. A second dose will be administered on Wednesday, September 22 at the same time and location. The vaccine clinic is open to all Piedmont community members, city staff, teachers and school staff, and students age 12 and older. Students younger than 18 years must have parental or guardian consent. If a parent or guardian cannot accompany the minor, a signed written consent is acceptable, and can be filled out by visiting https:// www.cdph.ca.gov/Programs/ CID/DCDC/Pages/COVID-19/ Pfizer-Vaccine-Minor-Consent-Guidance.aspx. Severe allergic reactions from the Pfizer vaccine are rare, but trained staff will be on-site. Walk-ins are welcome, but pre-registration is suggested at: https://my.primary.health/r/ alcoschools and selecting “Piedmont High School - Middle School.” Vaccination mandate for city employees COVID cases now increasing statewide By Allyson Aleksey At a Piedmont City Council meeting on August 16 Mayor Teddy Gray King announced her intention to mandate vaccinations for all city employees. “This is a very dynamic issue,” she said. “We know that there are many members of the community who are already vaccinated. I’m requesting that our city attorney draft a proposal that would mandate that all members of our city staff receive a COVID vaccination as soon as it is cleared by the FDA.” One week later, on August 23, the Food and Drug Administration granted full approval to Pfizer’s coronavirus vaccine for individuals age 16 and older, paving the way for a mandate in Piedmont. King cited the emergence of the Delta variant as her rationale for the mandate, adding that many cities and school districts, including the Piedmont School District, have already set forth such mandates for employees. The city was also waiting for full FDA-approval for COVID- 19 vaccine to mandate vaccinations. King said that, although most city staff are already fully vaccinated, that she would like to see this enacted quickly. City Attorney Michelle Kenyon will draft a rule detailing the city’s expectations for staff. “It’s a step in the right direction,” King said, adding that a mandate would have come sooner but that pending FDA-approval limited the city’s ability to do so. Currently, 93% of fulltime and regular part-time city employees are vaccinated against COVID-19. Latest COVID numbers from State The California Department of Public Health on August 23 confirmed that COVID-19 cases are increasing statewide, largely among unvaccinated populations. For the week of August 9 through August 15, the average case rate among unvaccinated Californians was 51 per 100,000 per day. The average case rate among vaccinated Californians is much lower, at 7.6 per 100,000 per day. As of August 23, according to the Center for Disease Control (CDC), 79.4% of eligible Californians have received at least one dose of a COVID vaccine. Vaccinations are available for free. Appointments for individuals age 12 and up can be made by visiting my turn. ca.gov. The consent of a parent or legal guardian is needed for those between ages 12 and 17. Music world loses a shining star With the unexpected death this week of Oakland Symphony’s charismatic Music Director Michael Morgan at age 63, music communities in the East Bay, the greater Bay Area, and nationally are grieving the loss of one of their stars. Conductor of the Oakland Symphony for 30 years, he died on August 20 after being admitted to the hospital one week earlier. (See story and photos on pages 20-21.) articles.text: “Hope is being able to see that there is light despite all of the darkness.” – Bishop Desmond Tutu The Piedmont League of Women Voters is hosting a public forum on the subject of carbon pricing on Wednesday, September 22 at 4:00 p.m. It will be on Zoom and also on the LWV YouTube channel. It is free for those registering at: lwvpiedmont.org/events. It’s a summer like no other here in California. Smoke and destruction from wildfires have already claimed more than 1 million acres in California alone; warmer oceans harbor zombie urchins destroying kelp forests; and the U.N. just released a new Code Red on climate change. Wondering where to look for hope despite the current darkness? Could something as arcane as carbon pricing offer a ray of light? It’s a hot topic as Congress seeks to up the ante on climate action. To learn more, join the League of Women Voters of Piedmont, Citizens’ Climate Education and Piedmont Connect for a panel discussion on carbon pricing, followed by questions and answers. The event is free. Registration is required on the League’s website: lwvpiedmont.org/events. An economy-wide price on carbon promises to reduce carbon emissions quickly and at scale in a way that is equitable when combined with a carbon dividend that most benefits low-income Americans. Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen testified earlier this year that “we cannot solve the climate crisis without effective carbon pricing.” The U.S. is one of only a few major industrialized nations without a national carbon pricing policy. Carbon pricing and dividends have gained the support of a wide array of groups including: an unlikely bipartisan coalition that unites Goldman Sachs with the World Wildlife Fund, 28 Nobel laureate economists, the Washington Post editorial board; our own Barbara Lee and 80 fellow House members; all five members of Piedmont’s City Council; and thousands of businesses, labor unions, faith groups and other prominent individuals around the country and around the Bay. Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King will offer introductory Mike Mielke, Senior Vice President and Head of Public Policy for the Silicon Valley Leadership Group (SLVG) remarks. A panel discussion will feature Mike Mielke, Senior Vice President and Head of Public Policy for the Silicon Valley Leadership Group (SLVG). Mike supports hundreds of innovation-economy companies to engage the public and wield influence in addressing pressing environmental challenges facing communities. He has held posts with the White House Council on Environmental Quality and the National Estuary Program.
articles.title: LWV to host forum on carbon pricing

articles.text: Back by popular demand, internationally renowned epidemiologist and Piedmont resident, Dr. George Rutherford will provide an update on Covid-19 at a public forum on Wednesday, September 15, at 4 p.m. sponsored by the Piedmont League of Women Voters. As most Piedmont residents are aware, Dr. Rutherford has been instrumental in helping the Bay Area contend with Covid and is frequently quoted in the media. He will address the latest findings, the status of the Delta and other variants, and the likely effectiveness of boosters and therapeutics. He will also speak about Covid safety for schools. Audience members will have an opportunity to ask questions. Dr. Rutherford leads the Global Strategic Information group within UCSF’s Institute for Global Health Sciences. He is the Salvatore Pablo Lucia Professor of Epidemiology, Preventive Medicine, Pediatrics and History; Head of the Division of Infectious Disease and Global Epidemiology in the Department of Epidemiology and BiostatisEpidemiologist Dr. George Rutherford to speak at a League of Women Voters Forum on September 15. tics in the School of Medicine at UCSF, and Professor of Epidemiology and Health Administration in the School of Public Health at the University of California, Berkeley. The League is presenting this event free of charge, but registration is required online at: lwvpiedmont.org/events. The event will be held at 4 p.m. on Zoom and on the League’s YouTube channel. For 23 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken. “What it boils down to is, we need a friendly bank or a trickier accountant.”

articles.text: California will require individuals attending indoor events with 1,000 or more people to show proof of vaccination or a negative COVID-19 test. The order goes into effect on September 20, according to an announcement on August 18 by the California Department of Public Health. The requirement strengthens already-existing requirements for “mega-events” of 5,000 attendees or more, as stated in Gov. Gavin Newsom’s “Beyond the Blueprint” Framework. The requirement essentially narrows the capacity for testing or proof of vaccination from 5,000 individuals to 1,000. Self-attestation to verify a person’s vaccination status, an honor system, will no longer be accepted. The changes are to remain in place until November 1. “The Delta variant has proven to be highly transmissible, making it easier to spread in large crowds where people are near each other for long periods of time,” said Dr. Tomás J. Aragón, CDPH Director and State Public Health Officer. “By requiring individuals to be vaccinated, or test negative for COVID-19 at large events, we are decreasing the risk of infection, hospitalization and death.” California has implemented strict measures across various industries to thwart the transmission of COVID-19 and its variants, as compared to other states in the nation. For example, the state has already required all school staff to show proof of full vaccination, or be tested once a week. The same applies for state workers. Full vaccination status is required for individuals who work in health care settings, as of September 30. In addition, California is the first state to implement universal mask-wearing in schools in all grade levels. The state recommended, but did not mandate, mask-wearing outdoors regardless of vaccination status. Leaders and professionals in the live entertainment industry praised the state for the recent announcement of health protocols for large gatherings. Julie Baker, Executive Director of Californians for the Arts, said, “We are pleased to see the Newsom administration take proactive steps to support the arts and live events industries to keep audiences, performers and workers safe as we continue to battle the spread of COVID.” “The arts have always led with safety first, and it is imperative that for every community’s economic, social and emotional recovery, we must do everything we can to allow for secure gatherings,” Baker said. “We implore Californians to get vaccinated and follow public health mandates so we can all enjoy the benefits of arts, culture and creativity, and our sector can get back to work.” COVID-19 vaccines are available to all California residents age 12 and older. For details, see: myturn.ca.gov, or call (833) 422- 4255 to schedule an appointment. The website myturn.ca.gov/clinic lists walk-in clinics in Alameda County. San Carlos Avenue. los Avenue.
articles.title: California to require patrons to show proof of vaccination or negative COVID-19 test

articles.text: On August 16, the Piedmont City Council approved a budget to repair a concrete retaining wall on Oakland Avenue between Olive and Sunnyside Avenue, and a portion of a retaining wall on Both projects are considered a high priority by the Public Works Department, and include 125 feet of the wall on Oakland Avenue, and 140 feet of a wall on San CarOn November 16, 2020 the Council directed that the design include cast-in-place retaining walls that match existing adjacent walls. CF Contracting of San Francisco was the lowest of six bids in the amount of $466,000. Work is estimated to begin in September, with a projected completion date of November. “[Residents adjacent to the project] are anxious to get this done,” said City Engineer John Wanger. Mayor Teddy Gray King added that former mayor Michael Bruck, who lives across from the retaining wall, brought the issue to her nearly seven years ago. “It’s been on our list for quite a while,” she said. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that the portion of work on San Carlos Avenue could require partial street closure to traffic from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. when construction begins, as San Carlos is a divided street with oneway traffic in each direction.
articles.title: City Council approves 2 retaining wall projects

articles.text: The city of Piedmont will host a virtual meeting tomorrow, Thursday, August 26, at 6 p.m., with researchers from the University of Texas at San Antonio who will describe their analysis of police calls to show how police services are utilized within Piedmont. Residents may join the webinar by visiting https://piedmont-cagov.zoom.us/j/86728495072 The meeting will also be televised on KCOM-TV (Channel 27). Researchers will take a broad look at police cell data, and will specifically focus on the types of calls for service, and the frequency of bias-based calls for police intervention. Questions from the public will be taken, and Police Chief Jeremy Bowers and City Administrator Sara Lillevand will be present. On July 19, the City Council unanimously approved an agreement with the University of Texas in San Antonio that would allow researchers to gather data on Piedmont Police Department calls for service. The police department currently uses Computer Aided Dispatch (CAD) systems and Record Management Systems (RMS), both of which contain call and event data. This data will be analyzed in order to inform future discussions relative to call responses. Dr. Michael Smith and Dr. Rob Tillyer of U. Texas are leading the data analysis research. The City Council has authorized $50,000 for the study.
articles.title: Community meeting tomorrow regarding PPD call data analysis

articles.text: The arrangements were all set for Piedmont Troop 15 Scouts Ryan Tripp and Stewart James to receive their Eagle Scout awards in 2020, but the pandemic and shelter in place scratched their plans. A year and a half later, on Sunday, August 22, Ryan and Stew finally had their moment in the sun in a National Court of Honor ceremony on the patio of the Piedmont Community Center. Women took center stage in Ryan Tripp thanks fellow Eagle Stewart James (seated) during a Court of Honor at the Piedmont Community Center on August 22. Troop 15 Scoutmaster Glen Tripp describes the journey to the Eagle Award of Stewart James and Ryan Tripp. the celebration, illustrating the organization’s mission of character development for all youth in the community. Mayor Teddy Gray King led off the proceedings with City of Piedmont proclamations recognizing the Scouts’ achievements. Council Executive Kate Benson put the awards in context of Piedmont’s strong association with the Scouting movement. Troop 15 Chair Dana Mitchell recounted the significance of the Eagle badge, and new Troop 15 scout Christiane Zuber lit a candle in memory of Linda Trowbridge (1955-2021), who mentored several generations of Boy Scout Eagles and Girl Scout Gold Award recipients. Ryan Tripp Ryan Tripp is the son of Lauren Dutton and Glen Tripp, the Troop 15 Scoutmaster. His Eagle project was to expand access to crew through an innovative partnership between Oakland Strokes and West Oakland high schools, spreading the benefits of rowing to new populations. In his speech, Ryan mentioned how relevant his Scouting skills proved during his gap year camping in the Rocky Mountain wilderness and living on his own in Washington, D.C. Ryan is a graduate of Piedmont High School will attend Dartmouth College in the fall. Stewart James Stewart James is the son of Rob and Sarah James. Stew’s Eagle project was building a “chill zone” reading loft with learning materials for a thirdgrade classroom at Sequoia Elementary School in Oakland. His speech recounted his spiritual experience overcoming adversity and experiencing nature in a challenging hiking trek on Catalina Island. A graduate of the Drew School in San Francisco, Stew is a rising sophomore at Tufts University. Both Scouts are second generation Eagles. Rob James, the former President of the Piedmont Scout Council, received his Eagle Four Eagles: Stew James (2019), Rob James (1975), Ryan Tripp (2020), and Glen Tripp (1986). in 1975 in Salinas, and Glen Tripp received his Eagle in 1986 in Poway in Southern California. New Troop 15 senior patrol leader Schuyler Sawicki served as master of ceremonies for the event, attended by friends and family. There is no small irony to the fact that the Eagle has proven to be the most respected and bestknown award for American youth. What began as a badge of honor for a small coterie of dedicated teenagers has become not only the most enduring award for youth in American life, but also the most consistently rewarding award in their own lives. And perhaps most amazing of all, what at first was considered just the next step in the accumulation of individual skill Troop 15 Scout Christiane Zuber lights a candle in memory of Piedmont’s longtime community leader Linda Trowbridge, with an assist from Stewart James.
articles.title: Ryan Tripp, Stewart James earn Eagle Awards

articles.text: On June 23 Piedmont School Board meetings returned in person for the first time since the Covid pandemic arrived a year and a half earlier. The meeting took place in the school district office boardroom at 760 Magnolia Avenue. Meetings will continue to be covered by KCOM on Channel 27 and on Zoom. The hybrid format allows all board members to meet in the same room with safety protocols, including masks. Members of the public now have the opportunity to contribute in person. “We will let members of the public in to speak in the public comment portion, so this is pretty exciting,” said Board President Cory Smegal. Visitors to any school site, including board meetings, must complete a visitor health screener online before entering the building. Board Member Hilary Cooper gave credit to Smegal for spearheading the initiative to return to traditional in-person meetings. “It was all Cory,” she said. “She felt very strongly that we should come together as a board in-person because we are asking our students and teachers to do the same.” The first in-person meeting lasted an hour and 45 minutes, a quick sprint in comparison to some marathon three- or fourhour zoom meetings last year. At the end of the June meeting, Smegal asked the room, “Do you think the meeting was shorter because we were in-person?” Board members universally nodded yes and Smegal replied, “Alright, this is the start of something great. This bodes well.” Since then, the board held another live meeting on August 11, which also finished in less than two hours. The board meets tonight, August 25 at 7:00 p.m. Meetings will continue to be held in the district office until given clearance by the City to return to Council Chambers in City Hall.
articles.title: School Board meetings return in person

articles.text: Nine Scouts in Piedmont’s Troop 4 recently attained the rank of Eagle at a Court of Honor ceremony. Pictured are Kevin Blodgett (left), Jonathan Wu, Kian Roseborough, Nate Wilson, Justin Katter, Gavin Horne, Linus Lee, Andrew Grasman, and Jack Blodgett. On Wednesday, August 18 Piedmont’s Troop 4 hosted an historic National Eagle Court of Honor with a record nine new Eagle Scouts being honored. Friends and families of Troop 4 gathered under the redwoods behind the Piedmont Community Center to help celebrate this hard-earned award. Special guest speakers included Mayor Teddy King, Scout Executive Kate Benson, and Rev. Scott Kail of Piedmont Community Church. Robert Barry Hamilton, the grandfather of Scout Andrew Grasman, an Eagle Scout, West Point graduate and military veteran, gave a keynote speech on the significance of the Eagle award. He advised the Scouts that they will face new challenges in their lives, and the right decision is not always easy to make. He also said, “When life gives you lemons, make lemonade.” For their Eagle projects, Jack Blodgett built a compost bin for Greenleaf Elementary School; Kevin Blodgett built a fruit box storage area for Piedmont Middle School; Andrew Grasman created a series of computer science videos for the James Baldwin Academy; Gavin Horne built an outdoor stage at the playground by the Piedmont Recreation Department; Justin Katter built a wooden cabinet for music binders for the PHS Acapella program; Linus Lee built a fence for dogs at the Hopalong Animal Shelter; Kian Roseborough built steps and reinforced a slope on a trail for the Friends of Sausal Creek; Nate Wilson installed exercise equipment storage units for Bay Area Outreach Program (BORP), which helps physically handicapped people be active; and Jonathan Wu installed a flagstone patio in back of Wildwood Elementary School. All of the Eagle Scouts thanked the Troop 4 leaders, parent volunteers, fellow Scouts, and their family and friends for their unwavering support to help them on their long journey to Eagle.
articles.title: Troop 4 sets record with 9 Eagle Scouts

articles.text: Turn a gathering around the campfire into a perfect summer science lesson with this activity. Put a twist on the classic snack by packing marshmallows, chocolate and more into waffle cones for the ultimate summer treat. Making s’mores is a great way to highlight heat transfer and heat reactions. When a s’more waffle cone is placed into a fire, heat (or energy) is transferred from the fire to the waffle cone. The additional heat raises the temperature, which can cause the ingredients inside to react and transform. As the temperature rises above a certain threshold, ingredients inside reach their melting point. Those that began as solid ingredients (chocolate and marshmallows) begin to break down into less-than-solid states. This is why the ingredients begin to melt, mix, and become gooey. Adding foil around the waffle cones helps with the heating and melting process. Aluminum foil contains metal and therefore acts as an insulator. This means it helps trap heat closer around the waffle cone, distributing the heat more evenly. Even though s’mores may seem like a simple, summer activity, they involve a lot of science. Materials: • Waffle cones • Mini marshmallows • Chocolate • Graham crackers • Your choice of toppings, chopped into small pieces - Chocolate candies, candy bars, nuts, sprinkles, popcorn, peanut butter cups, coconut, fresh fruit, etc. • Foil • Camp fire or oven • Bowls for toppings Procedure: 1. Start by gathering around the campfire (or oven) and observing what happens when you place a single marshmallow into the heat. a. What do you notice happening to the marshmallow? b. Why do you think it is reacting that way? c. What do you think a marshmallow is made of that causes it to look/move/ react like that? 2. After making observations, pass out waffle cones and fill them with ingredients of your choice. 3. Make a few different cones. Fill one with classic ingredients, then experiment with different flavors, textures, and layers in the rest. 4. Once assembled, wrap it with foil. 5. Place them in the coals of a campfire and let it cook for about 5 to 7 minutes. a. If using an oven, bake them for 5 to 7 minutes at 400 degrees Fahrenheit. 6. While they’re cooking, make some predictions about your cones: a. What do you think the texture of each will be like? b. Which kinds of flavors do you think we will taste? c. What do you think is happening on the inside of the waffle cones? d. How might the fire change them? Do you think it’s similar or different to the marshmallow earlier? 7. Once they’re done cooking, remove them from the heat and let cool for about a minute. 8. Carefully remove from the foil and make some observations of your results: a. Does it look the same or different from how it was before? b. What do you notice about it now? c. Where else have you seen something melt like this in the kitchen? What other ingredients melt and become gooey like marshmallows do? 9. And finally, enjoy the results of your experiment! Haley Thiltgen is a Science Educator at Chabot Space & Science Center, 10,000 Skyline Bld. Oakland. Find out more about activities and at-home experiments on Chabot’s Learning Launchpad at chabotspace.org.
articles.title: Thinking Outside The Classroom S’mores – the science of sweet stuff

articles.text: State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond is promoting the vaccination of all eligible California residents through a series of school visits this month, as well as a virtual town hall meeting he held on August 12 entitled “Supporting Safe Back-to-School: Promoting Vaccinations for Those 12 and Over.” “While there is elation on the part of families, students, and our schools to get back to campus, we also know there remains very real concern about the Delta variant and its transmission rate. On top of this, every day there seems to be more misinformation about vaccines, mask wearing, and COVID testing,” Thurmond said. The virtual town hall engaged more than 50,000 people and included a panel discussion with public health experts and youth leaders and educators. pages.text: Wednesday, August 25, 2021 7 Thinking Outside The Classroom S’mores – the science of sweet stuff By Haley Thiltgen Turn a gathering around the campfire into a perfect summer science lesson with this activity. Put a twist on the classic snack by packing marshmallows, chocolate and more into waffle cones for the ultimate summer treat. Making s’mores is a great way to highlight heat transfer and heat reactions. When a s’more waffle cone is placed into a fire, heat (or energy) is transferred from the fire to the waffle cone. The additional heat raises the temperature, which can cause the ingredients inside to react and transform. As the temperature rises above a certain threshold, ingredients inside reach their melting point. Those that began as solid ingredients (chocolate and marshmallows) begin to break down into less-than-solid states. This is why the ingredients begin to melt, mix, and become gooey. Adding foil around the waffle cones helps with the heating and melting process. Aluminum foil contains metal and therefore acts as an insulator. This means it helps trap heat closer around the waffle cone, distributing the heat more evenly. Even though s’mores may seem like a simple, summer activity, they involve a lot of science. Materials: • Waffle cones • Mini marshmallows • Chocolate • Graham crackers • Your choice of toppings, chopped into small pieces - Chocolate candies, candy bars, nuts, sprinkles, popcorn, peanut butter cups, coconut, fresh fruit, etc. • Foil • Camp fire or oven • Bowls for toppings Procedure: 1. Start by gathering around the campfire (or oven) and observing what happens when you place a single marshmallow into the heat. a. What do you notice happening to the marshmallow? b. Why do you think it is reacting that way? c. What do you think a marshmallow is made of that causes it to look/move/ react like that? 2. After making observations, pass out waffle cones and fill them with ingredients of your choice. 3. Make a few different cones. Fill one with classic ingredients, then experiment with different flavors, textures, and layers in the rest. 4. Once assembled, wrap it with foil. 5. Place them in the coals of a campfire and let it cook for about 5 to 7 minutes. a. If using an oven, bake them for 5 to 7 minutes at 400 degrees Fahrenheit. 6. While they’re cooking, make some predictions about your cones: a. What do you think the texture of each will be like? b. Which kinds of flavors do you think we will taste? c. What do you think is happening on the inside of the waffle cones? d. How might the fire change them? Do you think it’s similar or different to the marshmallow earlier? 7. Once they’re done cooking, remove them from the heat and let cool for about a minute. 8. Carefully remove from the foil and make some observations of your results: a. Does it look the same or different from how it was before? b. What do you notice about it now? c. Where else have you seen something melt like this in the kitchen? What other ingredients melt and become gooey like marshmallows do? 9. And finally, enjoy the results of your experiment! Haley Thiltgen is a Science Educator at Chabot Space & Science Center, 10,000 Skyline Bld. Oakland. Find out more about activities and at-home experiments on Chabot’s Learning Launchpad at chabotspace.org. Piedmont resident and architect Will Adams led a special tour for the Walking on Wednesday group on August 18, showcasing the exquisite homes of Piedmont designed by the legendary architect Julia Morgan. Born in San Francisco in 1872, Julia Morgan carved out a prolific career as an architect, designing more than 700 structures over her long career. She was the first woman licensed to practice architecture in California in 1907, one year after the earthquake and fire in San Francisco. She was also the first woman to graduate from the Engineering Department at the University of California in Berkeley. After college she set he sights on attending L’École des BeauxArts in Paris, the best architecture school in the western world at the turn of the century. Twice rejected for admission, her persistence paid off and on her third attempt she became the first female to attend and eventually graduate from the school. She is perhaps best known for the design and construction of publisher William Randolph Hearst’s estate on the California coast at San Simeon, known commonly as Hearst Castle. The extensive project, for the most demanding of clients, required Morgan to take 558 weekend trips on the train from San Francisco to San Simeon. The project took 28 years to complete while she oversaw at times a construction crew of more than 100 workers. yet rewarded her pupils by employing a profit-sharing plan for every member of her firm, a policy years ahead of its time. She was known as a client’s architect. She would take time to individually sit down with clients to discover what kind of style She never married, for she was truly married to her work. Morgan ran her San Francisco office in the atelier, or studio, style she learned at the Beaux-Arts. She mentored innumerable young architects, both men and women. Morgan was a demanding leader they wanted. Sierra Avenue, where they saw three examples of Morgan’s work. The first was an elegant Colonial Revival home. Next, a few doors away, was a Craftsman style home with harmonious landscaping. After pointing out some of its architectural details, Will pointed out a Tudor home next door with steep roofs that provided an interesting comparison of her work. Will then led the group down Sierra to Sheridan and then up Lincoln Avenue to the corner of Crocker Ave. There he pointed to a home across the street and described it. He also provided more insight into Morgan’s life and work, describing her as a woman who was completely dedicated to her work. She never married. In addition to being an exceptional architect and engineer, she was an excellent manager with a special rapport with craftsmen and artisans working on her projects. At one time she had 100 people working on Hearst Castle. She also had a reputation for keeping her projects on budget. The group continued to Crocker Park and on to Sea View Avenue, where they viewed a Tudor Craftsman blend, with wood carving decorations that accentuat the home’s beauty. The final three Morgan homes were across the street on Farragut Avenue. The large home of the top of the hill is a classic Tudor. articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group enjoyed a record turnout of 58 people on August 18 thanks to the offer of architect and planner Will Adams to lead a tour of a some homes in Piedmont designed by famed architect Julia Morgan. Will has lived in town for 30 years and writes the “Walking Piedmont” column biweekly in the Piedmont Post. Will provided the group with some history and background information on Julia Morgan. Born in 1872, she was an American architect and engineer who designed more than 700 buildings in California during her long career. She is best known for Hearst Castle in San Simeon, but her presence and work is especially prevalent in Northern California and in Piedmont. She designed the Berkeley City Club that is sometimes referred to a mini Hearst Castle, and the Greek Theater on the UC Berkeley campus with the support of Phoebe Hearst. Morgan was the first woman to be admitted to the architecture program at l’École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts in Paris, and the first woman architect licensed in California. She designed many buildings for institutions serving women and girls, including a number of YWCAs and buildings at Mills College. In many structures, she pioneered the aesthetic use of reinforced concrete, a material that had superior seismic performance in the 1906 and 1989 earthquakes. Morgan sought to reconcile classical and Craftsman, Tudor, Mediterranean, formalism, and whimsical styles in her eclectic work. Will told the group he especially appreciates Morgan’s ability to design in any style, and her ability to blend engineering and landscaping to create architectural masterpieces. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ tennis was the first team to begin its fall season for Piedmont. Jumping immediately into the thick of North Coast Section competition, and with some coaching karma of Neil Rothenberg, the Highlanders beat longtime NCS rivals Branson of Ross in a narrow 4-3 victory on Thursday, August 19. The two schools were finalists in the NCS team championship every year from 2011 to 2017, and Piedmont defeated the Bulls for the NCS championship consecutively during the Highlanders’ five-year title run from 2013-2017. “It was a great start to the season. it wasn’t easy. We have some returning starters and good experience back on the team. To beat Branson is a great way to get going,” said head coach Jim Landes. Seniors Bridgette McEfee and Anne Jumper opened as the top singles players. McEfee is a four-year starter, and Jumper for three years. McEfee lost to Anna Larden 6-3, 6-0, and Jumper lost to Anna Rende 6-0, 6-1, merely creating an extra level of tension for the Highlanders. “Bridgette McEfee and Anne Jumper both played very strong opponents. articles.text: Piedmont’s football team opens its fall season this Friday, August 27, with a game against non-league opponent Miramonte in Orinda. With the sports world returning to normal, Piedmont will have an 11-game game schedule. But with the graduation of half of the varsity roster, this will be a rebuilding season. Coach Jerome Johnson has only 16-17 players on the varsity. In a shortened season, Piedmont had a perfect 5-0 record last spring. “This particular class does not have large numbers,” confirmed Johnson. “Right after the COVID-year, more kids haven’t returned due to whatever factors there may be. The class before this loved football. We knew our numbers would be low, but not this low. We were hoping that the success we had after going 5-0 would have built more excitement for football,” he said. Last year’s football program didn’t have a JV team, making a noticeable impact on this year’s team. In the spring of 2021 student-athletes were forced to choose between baseball and football, which had the same season. A few of those players are back, like Nico Defazio and Evan McConathy. Defazio is set Staff Photos Head coach Jerome Johnson and the football team return to action this Friday, August 27, for a game at Miramonte in Orinda. to be quarterback of this year’s team. Another factor having an effect on players considering football is the overall concern of head injuries. Johnson has had to remind parents that he came to the school as a partner of the “Heads Up Coalition” a concussion prevention program, He has nearly 30 years of experiencing coaching teams at Contra Costa College, Bishop O’Dowd, and McClymonds when it won the state title in 2016. He said that player safety has always been his utmost priority. “Player-safety really envelopes who you are as a coaching staff. In any form of tackling, I’ve always preached ‘Eyes to the sky.’ You have to see what you’re hitting with a moving target. It’s no different than rugby, lacrosse, or soccer. We’re leading with shoulder pads and helmets, while some kids are leading with sticks or their bodies in other sports. With tackling, you have to be in control to make a safe tackle with proper form. It’s about repetition, you get better every time you make a tackle,” explained Johnson. Looking at the 2021 roster, Johnson said that Bailey Cain, Ethan Feldstein, and Mason Kimball will be the team leaders. “Mason is a three-year varsity player who leads by example. articles.text: Coach John Savage and his boys’ water polo team return to after finishing third in the league tournament with a 10-2 overall record. The team was led by Max Wagener and Spencer Stein, both The team’s third place was a repeat of its performance the year prior. One year earlier, in 2018, it placed 2nd overall. The tournament has been a thorn in the side of the Highlanders, who are still looking for their first league title. Piedmont narrowly missed out on the league title game last spring, losing 8-7 to Bishop O’Dowd in overtime in the WACC semifinals on May 27. Both the league and North Coast Section will have championship post-season tournaments this fall. The NCS Playoffs will return on November 3. Returning varsity players include standout goalie Dariush Kashani. In the field will be junior Antonio Rivera, seniors Shane Miller, Murray Davis, and sophomore Peter Krumins. “When I came in, Max and Spencer really pushed me and everyone to improve. I hope to show the younger guys how it’s done and keep on the legacy,” said Rivera. The Highlanders will rely on the defense of Kashani, a twoyear starting goalie. He had several big performances last season, including nine saves in a 15-10 victory over Alameda to earn third place in the league tourney. He also had 10 saves in a 17-4 win over Castro Valley on May 18, and stopped 10 shots in an 11-8 win over Bishop O’Dowd on May 5. “Dariush is a leader for us and Staff Photos Antonio Rivera returns as the leading scorer from last year’s water polo Goalie Dariush Kashani was the Post’s Honorable Mention for Sophomore of the Year and was the Shane Miller returns as a senior. team. keeps everybody in position. He’s important for us in all aspects,” said Savage. Rivera, meanwhile, is the leading scorer returning from last spring. He scored two goals and an assist in Piedmont’s thirdplace WACC Tournament win over Alameda and had four goals in a 14-6 win over Encinal on May 11. Piedmont will not have a pool for at least three years, as a new aquatic facility is built. The water polo teams have been without a home pool and hometown practice facility since last November. They currently split practice time between San Leandro, Berkeley, and Laney College pools. All their matches will be on the road similar to last spring. The squad is among the first sports to get started for the school, embarking on a three-day tournament at James Logan High in Union City from Thursday to Saturday, September 2-4. It won’t play again until the start of the league season within the Foothill Division of the Western Alameda County Conference with a match against rival Berkeley on September 14.
