The Highlanders will have a wealth of experience that could pay large dividends, with returning varsity players Rosie Feldman, Odessa Dando, Macie Gard, Annika Nilsson, Frankie Broening, Aiofe Cain and goalie Elizabeth Ethington. “Annika, Rosie, Odessa, Macie, and Elizabeth stepped up last season,” said Mooney. “Some players took the initiative to play over the summer on club teams. We had a lot of success, and we want to keep building on that,” Feldman, a junior and a threeyear starter, comes is the leading scorer among the returning players. She spent the summer playing with Diablo Alliance Water Polo, a competitive club team. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ golf team: Maddie Schaefer (left), Emily Adams, Madeleine Meaux, Aryana Fisher, Rahimeen Shah, and Dabney Warner. Not pictured: Toby Jacob and Abigail Drake. The girls’ golf team coached by Howard Oliver will begin its season on September 8. The golf team finished third in the WACC tournament at San Leandro’s Monarch Bay and returns seniors Dabney Warner, Tony Jacob, and Abigal Drake, and juniors Aryana Fisher and Rahimeen Shah. The team had a scrimmage match at Monarch Bay on Thursday, August 19 against Arroyo, where Warner was the low medalist with a 36, and Fisher was close behind with a 38. Their first event is scheduled for September 8 at Redwood Canyon in Castro Valley against Castro Valley and San Leandro. The team will play one match each week until the league tournament at Monarch Bay on October 18. The North Coast Section Championship tournament is on October 25. T he Wester n Alamed a County Conference historically has been dominated by Alameda High, which has won the title for 16 years. Oliver is confident about the talent of this year’s team. “This is going to be the best team the school has had in a while,” he predicted. “The girls are cohesive. Every year they make a sweatshirt and only starters get it.” The team lost Maddie Schaefer, Emily Adams, and Madeleine Meaux to graduation, and Adams, elected to return as an assistant coach. Oliver feels her return as a coach is a testament to the close bond formed within the golf team. “Emily is going to come back as an assistant before she goes off to college. She loves what we have built and is proud to be a part of it,” he said.

articles.text: Almost every parent I know feels bad about their parenting. If you’re anything like them, these are some of the things you feel bad about: You feel bad because you don’t spend enough time with your kids. You feel bad because you spend too much time with your kids. You feel bad because your kids spend too much time online. You feel bad because you secretly like it when your kids spend too much time online because it gives you a break. You feel bad because you don’t spend enough time helping your kids with their homework. You feel bad because you spend too much time helping your kids with their homework (and their grades aren’t even improving, which makes you feel even worse). And mostly, you feel bad because if you didn’t feel bad, and if you actually felt confident and at ease about your parenting, this would mean you’re doing something really, really wrong. Sound familiar? Feeling bad about your parenting isn’t your fault. Parents today are bombarded with messages about how to parent, and the Parenting Industrial Complex, as I call it, would collapse if parents relied on their instincts, common sense, and the support of friends and family to parent. So, in this age of Feel Bad Parenting, I’d like to offer some relief. First of all, you’re doing a great job as a parent. Seriously, Giving yourself a high five as a parent will make you feel better instantly. everything is fine. And I’m going to prove it to you. For the next week, spend 5-10 minutes every day creating a list of all the things you do well as a parent. Write down everything you can think of--no achievement is too small. The only caveat is that if/when a negative thought about your parenting pops into your head you must dismiss it immediately. Your list of positive parenting achievements might include: 1. I work hard (in or outside of the home) to provide for my kids 2. I love my kids more than anything in the world (most of the time) 3. I would do anything for my kids Every parent I know can say these things. And this is fantastic. You need to know that parenting will get easier, and you (and your kids) will feel happier when you stop feeling bad about yourself as a parent. If you create a list of all the things you do well as a parent, and keep it up daily for just one week, you will start to feel better. I promise. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at sue@orindaacademy.org.
articles.title: Some help when you’re feeling like a bad parent

articles.text: MS, OTR/L Are you beginning to think that handwriting is obsolete? This is certainly a valid thought given our students’ dependency on keyboarding assignments instead of handwriting them over the last year due to the pandemic. Keyboarding is always legible and who doesn’t like spell check? At a recent IEP (Individualized Education Plan) meeting for a student that I serve, the topic of handwriting versus keyboarding was raised. Lists can be made on phones, letters sent by email and essays written using Google documents. In short, is handwriting even necessary? To this question, the answer is a resounding Yes. Recent research, comparing handwriting to keyboarding, found handwriting improves memory/recall, comprehension, and even test scores. Handwriting remains an essential skill for both younger and older students, including those in college. Three recent studies noted the following: • Preschool students were taught to copy letters of the alphabet by hand or by typing them. After three weeks of learning, letter recognition tests were completed. The older preschool students in the handwriting instruction/ practice group demonstrated better letter recognition – a fundamental skill for learning letter sounds and reading (Longcamp et al, 2005). One study compared methods of note taking, handwritten or typed, and the recall and understanding of children 10–11 years old. Using a multiple-choice question (MCQ) format, factual recall and understanding of a history and a biology lesson were assessed. MCQ tests were carried out both immediately after each lesson and one • Studies show there are many benefits to handwriting, so don’t give up your pencil yet. week later. Factual recall was • not affected by the note-taking mode, but those students who wrote their notes by hand had greater conceptual understanding one week after their lesson compared to those who typed notes (Horbury & Edmonds, 2021). • Eighty college students were included in a study to compare taking notes or a quiz by hand or on their laptop. Those who took notes by hand performed better on quizzes overall and with conceptual questions than students who took notes on their laptop suggesting handwritten notes may improve how students encode and store material. (Crumb et al, 2020). The cognitive benefits of handwriting compared to keyboarding as noted above are just one facet. There are many other benefits from handwriting. Some examples include: • Handwriting helps one to slow down and gather their thoughts. • Handwriting benefits creative writing by removing the urge to immediately edit as one writes thereby allowing thoughts to flow more freely and less fragmented. Handwriting supports writing outlines and brainstorming ideas. A blank page has no restrictions - add side notes or circle important points to link thoughts. So even though lists can be made on phones, letters sent in an email and essays written on the computer, at a minimum, encourage your student to put down their laptops and take handwritten notes in class, as they read a chapter or make index cards for studying with a nicely sharpened pencil. If your student is a naysayer, share the evidence-based research with them. They may come to realize that they’d prefer an A on that quiz instead of the ease of spell check. Kimberly Bonacum is an occupational therapist for Piedmont Unified School District and owner of Mindful Fidgets, LLC www.mindfulfidgets.com. For additional questions, she can be contacted at mindfulfidgets@ gmail.com.

articles.text: There are some things to consider when applying to colleges this fall . can help any student stand out in a crowded field. High post-Covid grades a validation? Is a “Covid A” really an A, or did a student just leave their camera on? Was a C an academic C, or did a student know the material but had trouble with the technology? Strong Fall 2021 grades will validate high Covid grades and you can use them to wipe out poor Covid grades. pages.text: Wednesday, August 25, 2021 17 in Piedmont Applying to colleges post-Covid By Paul Osborne Good News, Bad News Covid has wreaked havoc on the college application process. But if students are strategic, they can avoid pitfalls, stand out from the crowd, and even get into some schools they might not have otherwise have considered. Admissions people are overrun with applicants Thanks to the Common App, Covid grade inflation, and the removal of ACT/SAT requirements, application rates are increasing drastically. With too many applicants and few traditional benchmarks, admissions officers are desperate for reasons to either accept or reject students. Stand out – but don’t stand out This year is unique, and subtle changes can make a big difference. Since admissions officers are looking for reasons to reject students, a student’s first goal needs to be avoiding obvious red flags. Disciplinary actions and missing extracurriculars are all the more important to avoid this admission cycle. These officers are also desperate for reasons to accept students. Standardized tests and a high Fall 2021 GPA There are some things to consider when applying to colleges this fall . can help any student stand out in a crowded field. High post-Covid grades a validation? Is a “Covid A” really an A, or did a student just leave their camera on? Was a C an academic C, or did a student know the material but had trouble with the technology? Strong Fall 2021 grades will validate high Covid grades and you can use them to wipe out poor Covid grades. Don’t let grades slip at all, do the extra work, get the extra help and remember everything counts triple. Wipe out poor Covid grades The state has authorized the changing of low grades to Pass/ Not Pass if you apply. For more information about this, contact your counselor or Paul the Tutor’s. If changing a letter to a P/NP seems too drastic, students can use the Common App Supplemental Information option to explain that distance learning and not academics led to low Covid grades. These two strategies will only work if post-Covid grades are high though. Standardized tests show dedication Standardized tests are “optional”, so taking them shows a student is taking the extra step to prove their value. As long as ACT or SAT scores are in the normal range for a school, submitting scores will help a student stand out. Advanced Placement (AP) tests are standardized as well. If a student is able to take an AP test this year, even if they are not in the AP class, and even yjru earn a 3, they can use that to stand out in the crowd. Why not reach? With everything up in the air this year, and applying to college made easy thanks to the Common App, this is the year to reach. If you are even near an acceptable GPA, apply to that UC, Ivy or reach school. Apply to several. You never know where you might be accepted. articles.text: Twilight Camp, an early camping experience for six- and sevenyear-olds, is a Piedmont tradition going back two generations and sponsored by the Piedmont Scout Council. It will be held this year from Tuesday to Thursday. October 26-28, from 7:00 to 8:30 p.m. each night. Register at https:// www.piedmontbsa.org/events/ twilight-camp/. Early Bird signups at $35 are available until October 15. The cost after that is $40. The registration deadline is October 22. Twilight Camp is open to all boys and girls in 1st and 2nd grades. They can look forward to building and racing rain gutter regatta boats, and making fun snacks. It’s a great opportunity to escape the indoors and have some outdoor fun, and to experience Scouting at its best. The opening ceremony each evening is in the amphitheater behind the Piedmont Community Center after which campers will rotate through stations. In one of the favorite activities, the rain gutter regatta, campers build a boat on the first night. On night two, they paint it, and on the third night they get to use their own wind power to propel it along the rain gutter. “It is great to look forward to this event again,” said new Scout Executive Kate Benson. “The evenings in October are cool and just dark enough to be spooky fun.” While activities are geared towards younger Cub Scouts, all grade school students are welcome to register and enjoy the fun. Fun is important, but safety is the highest priority. “Keeping campers safe, whether from COVID or other concerns, is part of every step of planning,” said Benson. “Every step of safety, at home and at camp, is vital.” Safety steps include pre-camp health screenings done by parents, frequent handwashing, and hand sanitizing, and moving from station to station in cohorts. Even though all activities will be done outdoors, campers and parents will mask up as well. Attendance will be taken each day, and the lines of communication will be wide open with parents. Campers and parents may need to present a negative COVID test or vaccination in advance of camp. “County guidelines could be fluid as we approach camp,” said Benson, “but we will work hard to keep campers, staff and parents safe. It is vital for our kids to have these types of activities. We saw just how important this past year and a half, and we’re excited to see everyone.” For more information and to register, navigate to www.piedmontbsa.org. Cub Scouting serves girls and boys in kindergarten through 5th grade and is fun for the whole family. It’s fun, hands-on learning with achievements that put kids in the middle of the action and prepares them for life. Cub Scouts at Twilight Camp enjoy racing their boats in the Raingutter Regatta.

articles.text: The Benjamin Jazz Trio will perform at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Sunday, August 29 at 5 p.m. He will be joined by Bay Area musicians Dahveed Behroozi on piano and Zachary Ostroff on bass. The group will perform a mix of jazz standards, popular song arrangements, and some of Ring’s original compositions. It will be followed by a reception with food and drink. Masks are required. Benjamin Ring Benjam i n R i ng is an award-winning drummer, percussionist and composer based in Los Angeles. A Piedmont High graduate in 2016, Ring began playing drums and percussion at age 8. An accomplished composer, his first composition was premiered by the San Francisco Conservatory of Music percussion ensemble when he was 15. He has been recognized by festivals and institutions worldwide for his work in jazz and classical idioms. He graduated from USC with a Bachelor of Arts degree in 2019, and will enter the Herbie Hancock Institute of Jazz Performance at UCLA this fall, a prestigious, 2-year Master’s program comprised of a small ensemble chosen by audition from across the globe. He has performed across Europe, Japan and the United States, sharing the stage with Dahveed Behroozi, piano Percussionist Benjamin Ring world-class musicians and with members of the San Francisco and Chicago symphonies. He has received scholarships from SFJAZZ and the Monterey Jazz Festival, as well as awards from the National YoungArts foundation. Dahveed Behroozi Pianist and Composer Dahveed Behroozi is a San Francisco Bay Area based musician. His focus is in jazz, classical, and new music. He is an active player both as a leader and sideman in the Bay Area, nationally and internationally. Behroozi’s expansive musical palette comes from a wide array of places that almost seem endless. His musical frame of reference ranges from Bach, Brahms, Schoenberg, Alban Berg, 20th century jazz luminaries, as well as the rock and ambient worlds. The son of a classical guitarist, Behroozi developed a strong interest in Jazz. By his teens, he was an active sideman, and studied at the Manhattan School of Music and Brooklyn College. During his time in New York he develop his sound and concept by playing with some of the finest musicians. He released his second fulllength record Echos with bassist Thomas Morgan and drummer Billy Mintz earlier this summer. He currently serves on the music faculty at Gavilan College and San Jose State University. Zach Ostroff Zach Ostroff plays bass, sings, writes songs, produces records, and composes film scores. He has led and accompanied bands on stages and in studios around the world. Zach performed for President Obama and the U.N. in New York City. He made his debut performance as a leader at the Kennedy Center in Washington, DC. He was featured in the HBO Series Masterclass performing with violinist Joshua Bell. He premiered Vote For Home, the first web video series to feature wellknown musical artists discussing the impact of climate change on hometowns in the United States. He has performed with Joshua Redman, Zakir Hussain, Ibrahim Maalouf, Angelique Kidjo, Wynton Marsalis, Louis Cole, Esperanza Spalding, Dayna Stephens, Taylor Eigsti, Charles Altura, Jaron Lanier, Josh Groban, Tootie Heath, James Francies, Eric Harland, Cris Williamson, Barbara Higbie, Diving Dame, and others. articles.text: A retrospective art exhibit celebrating the pioneering feminist artist Judy Chicago opens this Saturday, August 28, at the de Young museum in San Francisco. The artist will be at de Young on Sunday, August 29, between 2 and 3 p.m. to sign copies of the exhibition catalogue and her recent autobiography “The Flowering.” Judy Chicago is one of the founding figures behind the 1970’s feminist art movement. Her storied career is highlighted through her colorful works on canvas, porcelain plates, car hoods and more. The exhibition will include approximately 130 paintings, prints, drawings and sculptures by the artist. The event is organized in conjunction with the 100th anniversary of women’s right to vote in the United States, and pays homage to Judy Chicago who fought against the suppresJudy Chicago sion of women’s creativity. She founded the first feminist arts education program in the country at California State University in Fresno. The exhibition will be on display through January 9, 2022. To purchase tickets to the exhibition, visit https://deyoung.famsf.org/ exhibitions/judy-chicago.

articles.text: San Francisco Botanical Garden, in partnership with Sunset Piano, is bringing the Flower Piano event back this year after a 2020 hiatus due to the coronavirus pandemic. Sunset Piano places Grand pianos and Baby-Grands in San Francisco Botanical Garden, located in Golden Gate Park, for a unique, interactive musical event. For five days in September, ending September 21, musicians and artists will play an eclectic range of genres, from Jazz to classical to AfroCuban. The traditional event is held for twelve days in the summer. The event has enjoyed five successful years of turn-out, and took a pause in 2020 due to gathering restrictions. Piano locations in Golden Gate Park include the Great Meadow, Garden of Fragrance, Conifer Lawn, and more. San Francisco residents attend for free, but must have a ticket to enter. Tickets are $9 for non-San Francisco residents. Advanced ticketing is required to prevent crowding, and may be obtained by visiting https://sunsetpiano. com/flowerpiano. The schedule on Friday, September 17, is as follows: 12 p.m.: Fragrance Garden – Mongolounge and Friends Mongolounge is “Devo done lounge” 4:00 p.m.: Zellerbach – Emil Miland, Cello & Allison Lovejoy, Piano Romantics and Moderns: Brahms, Boulanger, Harrison 4:00 - 5:30 p.m., Great Meadow – Community Music Center Performance Celebrate with the Community Music Center at Flower Piano in their Centennial Year 3:00 - 6:00 p.m., Conifer Lawn – Beat Corner Avante Garden Poetry and Music by Mauro, Dean, and Friends Flower Piano 2019

articles.text: A concert with soul-funk group Tower of Power and West Coastbased rapper Too Short will mark the final summer concert at Stern Grove in San Francisco this Sunday, August 29, at 2 p.m. Tower of Power, formed in 1967 in Oakland by tenor saxophonist Emilio Castillo, released the billboard-topping hits, “You’re Still a Young Man” and “What is Hip?” in the 1970’s. The group’s horn-driven melodies served as samplings for some of pop music’s biggest names, including Elton John, Huey Lewis, Paula Abdul, Aerosmith, and Santana. The other part of the concert will feature Todd Anthony Shaw, the rapper known as Too Short, who came on the West Coast hiphop scene in the late 1980’s. He is widely regarded as a pioneer of West Coast rap and has drawn heavily on Oakland’s underground rap scene. Advance reservations are required for this free event, and can be obtained by visiting https://www.sterngrove.org/concert-10. Doors will open at 12 p.m. noon with designated entry points. Although the venue is outdoors, the capacity is limited, and masks are required for non-vaccinated individuals. Located on Sloat Boulevard, the amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites. The festival has provided more than eight decades of performing arts completely free, including opera, theatre, and music. For advance tickets, click on https://www.sterngrove.org/covid.
articles.title: Final concert of summer at Stern Grove on Sunday

articles.text: It was a 1976 young conductors’ competition of the Baltimore Symphony, with a predictable array of well-scrubbed young men in their early- to mid-20s competing. And in this group appeared a striking youth, barely 17, seemingly from another world, wearing the casual togs he wore for any day at his public high school. For the finals he conducted a movement from a Brahms symphony that lifted me to my feet to watch intently. He evoked ear-caressing sounds of ethereal beauty, sounds I had not heard any of the far more experienced competitors achieve. This was a youth with the makings of genius, doing it all with the confidence of a veteran. This was the unlikely beginning of Michael Morgan, symphony conductor. He won none of the three prizes awarded, given merely a “nice-try” honorable mention. The Music Professor Elliott Galkin on the judges’ panel dismissed him as having no real conducting technique nor discipline. Perhaps. But for this listener, he had made the sounds to lift both heart and soul. The untimely death of Morgan this week of an infection at age 63 closed out a mercurial career the last 30 years of which were as music director of the Oakland Symphony – the longest tenure in the orchestra’s history. Coming from modest circumstances in Washington, DC, he got recommendations and a scholarship aid to enter the elite Oberlin Conservatory of Music and was selected to study one summer under Leonard Bernstein’s tutelage at Tanglewood, MA. Still in his 20s he appeared at the Vienna State Opera to lead a Mozart performance and was appointed the assistant conductor of the Chicago Symphony under the venerable Georg Solti, no less. But his real forte evolved during his 30-year stint at the helm of the Oakland Symphony. He turned out to be an exemplary community builder, drawing unprecedented black listeners to the concerts and annotating his concerts with self-effacing wit. Recently leading the Charleston with the San Francisco Symphony, he quipped that yes, the Charleston had been the dance that epitomized the Roaring Twenties. “We’re hoping for another Roaring Twenties, but without the crash at the end….,” he said. He brought in performers of many forms of music, including Latino, jazz, African-American and Far-Eastern, and works by contemporary women composers. He also rescued from oblivion the exemplary Symphony No. 3 (1847) by the French woman Louise Farrenc, performing it recently on both sides of San Francisco Bay. Yet more significant was his active role with inner-city youth, talking to school groups as well as leading the Oakland Symphony Youth Orchestra. In short, if you ever needed a textbook example of what a symphony conductor could and should do to enrich the musical life of a city, Morgan was it. And now he is lost at age 63, losing possible decades on the podium, educating youngsters while enriching the multi-cultural environment. Consider that Michael Tilson Thomas retired from the S.F. Symphony at 75, Solti conducted into his 80s, and Herbert Blomstedt is still doing it in his 90s. And Morgan left neither wife nor children. Overall, the Oakland Symphony has had little luck with its maestros. The engaging, good-humored Calvin Simmons, its previous black music director, had passed away in a canoeing incident when in his mid-30s during the 1980s, after which the orchestra declared bankruptcy, reformulating in its present form with Morgan’s arrival in 1991. Clearly, he was one in a million. Will he ever be altogether replaceable?? Paul Hertelendy, a Piedmont resident, is a music critic and regular contributor to the arts website www.artsSF.com. One of Michael Morgan’s lasting legacies is the creation of MUSE, a program in Oakland schools in which he inspired two generations of students. Michael Morgan, Oakland Symphony.
articles.title: Memories of Michael Morgan

articles.text: In the late 1980’s Michael Morgan served as the Assistant Conductor of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, whose Executive Director, Henry Fogel, helped guide a group of us musicians and community members in founding the Oakland East Bay Symphony (now the Oakland Symphony). It was a phoenix rising from the ashes of the original Oakland Symphony’s bankruptcy of 1986. Henry wisely urged us to consider Michael as our new conductor, and, in 1991, we followed his advice and made Michael our music director. The past 30 years has validated Henry’s wisdom tenfold. A better fit between orchestra conductor and community is hard to imagine, with Michael’s unique, innovative programming and involvement in many East Bay music groups, both youth and adult. Michael never threw a tantrum in rehearsals and always arrived prepared, lightening the proceedings with his legendary sense of humor and aplomb. He never complained, even when he must have been in great discomfort. His passing is a great loss both for the orchestra and for the wider community he fully embraced in all its diversity and beauty. Stuart Gronningen is the former principal horn of Oakland Symphony, whose 52-year tenure with the orchestra was the longest since its original founding in 1933.
articles.title: Piedmont musician reflects on years with Oakland Symphony, Michael Morgan

articles.text: Michael Morgan was one of the many fans of the Piedmont Center for the Arts and its contributions to performing arts in the Bay Area. In a 2020 letter sent to members of the Center for the Arts board, he described the Center as a gem in the Bay Area. The Piedmont Center for the Arts has become an invaluable asset to the Bay Area arts community. It is unique to the area as a small venue for a wide variety of performances. From chamber music to solo recitals to small ensemble concerts, classical to world music there is a tremendous range and diversity of world class offerings. The intimacy and warm acoustic provide a welcoming atmosphere for the enthusiastic audiences I have seen there at events I was attending and events I was presenting. We all look forward to future performances there and I ask that you give it all possible support. I should add that they have kept rental fees at a level that is within reach for most community groups. It is one of the gems of the Bay Area. Michael Morgan Music Director, Oakland Symphony
articles.title: Michael Morgan’s connection with Piedmont Center for the Arts

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony joins the Bay Area community in mourning the loss of Michael Morgan. “Michael was an inspiration not only for me but also for Berkeley Symphony. He was a model leader and an amazing person,” said Music Director Joseph Young. “Our thoughts are with the community, musicians, and the industry he had such a profound impact on. Words cannot do justice to what a loss this is to the community.” Echoing these sentiments, Artistic Director René Mandel said, “Michael was indeed a Bay Area trailblazer. We owe him immensely for revitalizing the arts scene and for being the ultimate benchmark for making a symphony orchestra indispensably relevant to its community.” Michael was a leader, mentor, and friend to so many, and will be deeply missed.
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony praises Maestro Morgan

Still in his 20s he appeared at the Vienna State Opera to lead a Mozart performance and was appointed the assistant conductor of the Chicago Symphony under the venerable Georg Solti, no less. But his real forte evolved during his 30-year stint at the helm of the Oakland Symphony. He turned out to be an exemplary community builder, drawing unprecedented black listeners to the concerts and annotating his concerts with self-effacing wit. Recently leading the Charleston with the San Francisco Symphony, he quipped that yes, the Charleston had been the dance that epitomized the Roaring Twenties. “We’re hoping for another Roaring Twenties, but without the crash at the end….,” he said. He brought in performers of many forms of music, including Latino, jazz, African-American and Far-Eastern, and works by contemporary women composers. He also rescued from oblivion the exemplary Symphony No. 3 (1847) by the French woman Louise Farrenc, performing it recently on both sides of San Francisco Bay. Yet more significant was his active role with inner-city youth, talking to school groups as well as leading the Oakland Symphony Youth Orchestra. In short, if you ever needed a textbook example of what a symphony conductor could and should do to enrich the musical life of a city, Morgan was it. And now he is lost at age 63, losing possible decades on the podium, educating youngsters while enriching the multi-cultural environment. Consider that Michael Tilson Thomas retired from the S.F. Symphony at 75, Solti conducted into his 80s, and Herbert Blomstedt is still doing it in his 90s. And Morgan left neither wife nor children. Overall, the Oakland Symphony has had little luck with its maestros. The engaging, good-humored Calvin Simmons, its previous black music director, had passed away in a canoeing incident when in his mid-30s during the 1980s, after which the orchestra declared bankruptcy, reformulating in its present form with Morgan’s arrival in 1991. Clearly, he was one in a million. Will he ever be altogether replaceable?? Paul Hertelendy, a Piedmont resident, is a music critic and regular contributor to the arts website www.artsSF.com. One of Michael Morgan’s lasting legacies is the creation of MUSE, a program in Oakland schools in which he inspired two generations of students. Michael Morgan, Oakland Symphony. Piedmont musician reflects on years with Oakland Symphony, Michael Morgan By Stuart Gronningen In the late 1980’s Michael Morgan served as the Assistant Conductor of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, whose Executive Director, Henry Fogel, helped guide a group of us musicians and community members in founding the Oakland East Bay Symphony (now the Oakland Symphony). It was a phoenix rising from the ashes of the original Oakland Symphony’s bankruptcy of 1986. Henry wisely urged us to consider Michael as our new conductor, and, in 1991, we followed his advice and made Michael our music director. The past 30 years has validated Henry’s wisdom tenfold. A better fit between orchestra conductor and community is hard to imagine, with Michael’s unique, innovative programming and involvement in many East Bay music groups, both youth and adult. Michael never threw a tantrum in rehearsals and always arrived prepared, lightening the proceedings with his legendary sense of humor and aplomb. He never complained, even when he must have been in great discomfort. His passing is a great loss both for the orchestra and for the wider community he fully embraced in all its diversity and beauty. Stuart Gronningen is the former principal horn of Oakland Symphony, whose 52-year tenure with the orchestra was the longest since its original founding in 1933. Michael Morgan’s connection with Piedmont Center for the Arts Michael Morgan was one of the many fans of the Piedmont Center for the Arts and its contributions to performing arts in the Bay Area. In a 2020 letter sent to members of the Center for the Arts board, he described the Center as a gem in the Bay Area. The Piedmont Center for the Arts has become an invaluable asset to the Bay Area arts community. It is unique to the area as a small venue for a wide variety of performances. From chamber music to solo recitals to small ensemble concerts, classical to world music there is a tremendous range and diversity of world class offerings. The intimacy and warm acoustic provide a welcoming atmosphere for the enthusiastic audiences I have seen there at events I was attending and events I was presenting. We all look forward to future performances there and I ask that you give it all possible support. I should add that they have kept rental fees at a level that is within reach for most community groups. It is one of the gems of the Bay Area. Michael Morgan Music Director, Oakland Symphony Berkeley Symphony praises Maestro Morgan Berkeley Symphony joins the Bay Area community in mourning the loss of Michael Morgan. “Michael was an inspiration not only for me but also for Berkeley Symphony. He was a model leader and an amazing person,” said Music Director Joseph Young. “Our thoughts are with the community, musicians, and the industry he had such a profound impact on. Words cannot do justice to what a loss this is to the community.” Echoing these sentiments, Artistic Director René Mandel said, “Michael was indeed a Bay Area trailblazer. We owe him immensely for revitalizing the arts scene and for being the ultimate benchmark for making a symphony orchestra indispensably relevant to its community.” Michael was a leader, mentor, and friend to so many, and will be deeply missed.

articles.text: Oakland Symphony announced on August 20 the death of its Music Director Michael Morgan. Its press release stated, “It is with a breaking heart that we inform you that Michael Morgan, Music Director and Conductor of Oakland Symphony since 1991, died peacefully today, August 20, 2021 at Oakland Kaiser where he had been admitted last week for an infection. He was 63.” In May of this year, Michael Morgan underwent successful kidney transplant surgery at UCSF. He resumed conducting last month for the San Francisco Symphony and Bear Valley Music Festival. Michael was born in Washington, D.C., where he attended public schools and began conducting at the age of 12. While a student at Oberlin College Conservatory of Music, he spent a summer at the Berkshire Music Center at Tanglewood, studying with Gunther Schuller and Seiji Ozawa. He first worked with Leonard Bernstein during that same summer. His operatic debut was in 1982 at the Vienna State Opera, conducting Mozart’s The Abduction from the Seraglio. In 1986, Sir Georg Solti chose him to become the Assistant Conductor of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, a position he held for seven years under both Solti and Daniel Barenboim. In 1986, he was invited by Leonard Bernstein to make his debut with the New York Philharmonic. As guest conductor, Morgan has appeared with most of America’s major orchestras, as well as the New York City Opera, St. Louis Opera Theater, and Washington National Opera. In addition to his duties with the Oakland Symphony, Maestro Morgan served as Artistic Director of Oakland Symphony Youth Orchestra, Music Director at Bear Valley Music Festival, and Music Director of Gateways Music Festival. He was Music Director Emeritus of the Sacramento Philharmonic and Opera and was on the boards of Oaktown Jazz Workshops and the Purple Silk Music Education Foundation. He was also a former music director of Festival Opera in Walnut Creek, and “Notes From…” concer ts explored the music and musicians of such specific communities as Vietnam, Korea, Native American and LGBTQ+. “Lost Romantics” gave deserving, neglected works of the late 19th century a new hearing. “American Masterworks” presented performances of such seminal stage works as West Side Story, Candide, Street Scene, Porgy and Bess, and Show Boat. The San Francisco Chronicle proclaimed, “In his 30 years as music director of the Oakland Symphony, Morgan has made that orchestra a vibrant hotbed for innovative programming.” “Our entire organization is grieving a profound loss,” said Jim Hasler, Oakland Symphony Board Chair. “Michael’s impact on our community and the national orchestra field cannot be overstated – and he has left us too soon. We have been blessed over the past 30 years, as Michael built the foundations of an Oakland Symphony dedicated to diversity, education, artistic collaboration, and a celebration of music across genres and cultures. His vision of orchestras as service organizations was a beacon locally and nationally. This vision is his legacy, and the Oakland Symphony, Chorus and Youth Orchestra will renew his commitment for years to come.” “This is a terribly sad moment for everyone in the Oakland Symphony family. We have lost our guiding father,” said Executive Director Mieko Hatano. “Michael’s plans and ambitions were set for several seasons to come. He made his Orchestra socially authentic, demanded equality, and he made his Orchestra our orchestra. He fashioned a unique, informed artistic profile that attracted one of the most diverse audiences in the nation. His music reflected his beliefs: reverence for the past, attuned to the future, rooted in his adopted home of Oakland. His spirit will always guide the enduring future of the Oakland Symphony.” Michael Morgan is survived by his mother Mabel Morgan, and sister Jacquelyn Morgan. A memorial service will be announced in the near future. Oakland Symphony Music Director Michael Morgan died on August 20, 2021. He was 63. was responsible for producing Mozart’s Don Giovanni, and Britten’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Michael Morgan uses it to show what the orchestra can do. I like his way better.” His programming engaged new audiences, and many returned for subsequent concerts. Notable personalities like W. San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum is now displaying an immersive art exhibition entitled “teamLab: Continuity.” The art experience immerses patrons in a “wondrous ecosystem of lush imagery drawn from nature and East Asian art that dynamically evolves around you.” Rich hues are displayed dramatically via light-work onto the museum’s walls, in sumptuous images of crows, flowers, butterflies, fish, and more imagery. The Tokyobased artist-collective teamLab is known for producing interactive, interconnected digital artworks that marry art and technology. “Everything exists in a long, fragile, yet miraculous borderless continuity of life,” teamLab founder Toshiyuki Inoko said. Photo by Pace Gallery The exhibition is designed to be an immersive experience – not about the digital realm, but instead about the natural world. The exhibition has been extended into September due to popular demand, but ticketing is limited and nearly sold out. Tickets for “teamLab: Continuity” are available at: https://exhibitions. asianart.org/exhibitions/teamlab-continuity/. LMBInteriors.com 510.531.8438

articles.title: How to reduce your textile carbon footprint

articles.text: Most of us don’t think about global warming when we buy that cute, bargain hoody or jazzy top. And yet, “fast fashion” — mass produced, inexpensive, trendy clothing — has become one of the world’s biggest consumers of natural resources and contributor to climate change. The amount of clothing sold every year has approximately doubled in the last 15 years and now exceeds 100 billion garments per year. From production to disposal, the impact of clothing on the environment is astounding. Consider that it takes nearly 4,000 gallons of water to grow cotton for one pair of jeans and 2,700 gallons for a t-shirt. At least 8,000 chemicals are used to turn raw materials into textiles, and 25 percent of the world’s pesticides are used to grow non-organic cotton. The popular use of polyester and other synthetic fibers by the textile industry now accounts for nearly 1.5% of total global oil consumption and is expected to double in coming years. The Fossil Fashion campaign, which advocates legislation to curtail the fashion industry’s use of fossil fuels, calculates washing clothes releases around half a million tons of microfibers into the oceans every year, equal to more than 50 billion plastic bottles. And what happens to all the clothes Americans throw away every year? Second-hand stores sell only about 10% of our donated clothes. The remaining 90% is sold to textile recyclers who process about 70% into rags and cleaning cloths. Some used clothing is sold on the international market, but eventually twothirds of discarded clothing material ends up in massive landfills, primarily in African and other third-world countries. The fact that our clothing consumption is environmentally devastating has become a wake-up call in the fashion industry. A number of industry leaders have embraced the concept of a “circular economy” in which nothing is wasted in the manufacturing process. Some, including H&M, Ralph Lauren, LaCoste, and Tommy Hilfiger, have begun making clothes from recycled or eco-friendly fabrics, and using renewable energy. There is also a “slow fashion” trend gaining traction. Echoing the Slow Food movement, slow fashion emphasizes buying fewer but better quality, more durable clothes that last longer, are less fashion-trendy and that value fair treatment of the planet, animals and workers in their life cycle. According to the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, doubling the use of our clothes would cut the garment trade’s climate pollution by nearly half. In addition, more of us have discovered the fun of shopping at second hand stores, such as Dress Best For Less (DBFL) on Piedmont Ave., which supports the Piedmont Education Foundation and other local nonprofits. For a more complete list of local second-hand stores, visit https:// www.piedmontconnect.org Even Macy’s has launched a thredUp shop that carries second-hand styles from top brands. And TheRealReal, an online, luxury consignment store. buys and sells clothes and other goods has an outlet in San Francisco. Perhaps the words of legendary folksinger Pete Seeger will become the new fashion mantra: “If it can’t be reduced, repaired, rebuilt, refurbished, refinished, resold, recycled or composted, then it should be restricted, redesigned or removed from production.”

articles.text: Demand for new basement space has grown dramatically. Dear Jim: We are about to embark on a large home improvement project but have been hearing horror stories about the cost of materials, contractors backed up for months or years to start projects and that it’s almost impossible to get permits, etc. How should we navigate all of this? Would it be better to wait to see if conditions improve? -Edward M. Residential construction is currently experiencing substantial challenges. Let’s look briefly into these issues and sort out fact from fiction. Permits Permitting has been a nightmare for the last 18 months in most jurisdictions. Though residential contractors were generally allowed to keep working during Covid, all building departments went online with not-so-great results. Permits, on average, are taking several months for simple projects and much longer for complicated ones. Many factors are involved, such as layoffs, employees with Covid, and people retiring. It has been mostly a major communication debacle caused when people are not working in person. We have seen this improve recently, as building departments are now opening to the public and backlogs are being reduced. Materials and Labor Costs Lumber prices were highly impacted by Covid. Sawmills shut down just as a housing boom surged, causing massive price increases, as much as 500% or more for items like plywood. Materials from overseas (such as steel, cabinets, tile) saw large shipping cost increases and huge delays. I waited for 6 months for a tile ordered from Spain which sat for three months in the harbor in New York under quarantine. Demand for labor is at an all-time high, with construction workers demanding higher wages and benefits. Contractor Availability and Pricing. With more people choosing to work from home when they can, home improvement project requests have skyrocketed. Prices that contractors are charging for their work are reflected in higher estimates. Since most of us are busy and permitting is delayed, projects are getting pushed farther out into the future. Additionally, estimates that were given even 6 months ago may have to be adjusted to reflect new increases in costs. The Bottom Line Construction keeps getting more expensive. It’s hard to find a good contractor, and projects are having substantial delays. Though some of this may improve slightly if permitting timeframes decrease, there is no indication that costs or contractors’ workloads will lessen anytime soon. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, August 25, 2021 CONVERSATIONS WITH YOUR LOCAL CONTRACTOR Is now the time to start my remodeling project? Demand for new basement space has grown dramatically. By Jim Gardner Dear Jim: We are about to embark on a large home improvement project but have been hearing horror stories about the cost of materials, contractors backed up for months or years to start projects and that it’s almost impossible to get permits, etc. How should we navigate all of this? Would it be better to wait to see if conditions improve? -Edward M. Residential construction is currently experiencing substantial challenges. Let’s look briefly into these issues and sort out fact from fiction. Permits Permitting has been a nightmare for the last 18 months in most jurisdictions. Though residential contractors were generally allowed to keep working during Covid, all building departments went online with not-so-great results. Permits, on average, are taking several months for simple projects and much longer for complicated ones. Many factors are involved, such as layoffs, employees with Covid, and people retiring. It has been mostly a major communication debacle caused when people are not working in person. We have seen this improve recently, as building departments are now opening to the public and backlogs are being reduced. Materials and Labor Costs Lumber prices were highly impacted by Covid. Sawmills shut down just as a housing boom surged, causing massive price increases, as much as 500% or more for items like plywood. Materials from overseas (such as steel, cabinets, tile) saw large shipping cost increases and huge delays. I waited for 6 months for a tile ordered from Spain which sat for three months in the harbor in New York under quarantine. Demand for labor is at an all-time high, with construction workers demanding higher wages and benefits. Contractor Availability and Pricing. With more people choosing to work from home when they can, home improvement project requests have skyrocketed. Prices that contractors are charging for their work are reflected in higher estimates. Since most of us are busy and permitting is delayed, projects are getting pushed farther out into the future. Additionally, estimates that were given even 6 months ago may have to be adjusted to reflect new increases in costs. The Bottom Line Construction keeps getting more expensive. It’s hard to find a good contractor, and projects are having substantial delays. Though some of this may improve slightly if permitting timeframes decrease, there is no indication that costs or contractors’ workloads will lessen anytime soon. Your best bet would be to try to get your project onto your contractor’s calendar as overall conditions will likely remain challenging into the foreseeable future. articles.text: Assistant Scoutmaster Troop 15 Scouts Davie Ackerman, Morgan Bishop, Trenton Downing, Sammy Ragones, and Nate Woodley, accompanied by parent Scout advisers Eric Downing, David Ragones, and John Woodley, spent four days backpacking in California’s Emigrant Wilderness (between Tahoe and Yosemite) the week of July 26-29. Congress designated the area as Emigrant Wilderness in 1975, but most of the area has been protected as a Forest Service Primitive Area since the 1920’s. This is a glaciated landscape dominated by volcanic ridges surrounded by sparsely vegetated granitic ridges interspersed with lakes and meadows. The hiking was tough, with grades averaging 10%, but most of the climbs lasted no more than two miles in length. articles.text: Movies in the Park continues this Friday, August 27, with a screening of the animated movie, Trolls World Tour. The film will be shown in Piedmont Main Park at dusk, roughly 7:45 p.m., and is free. The run time is 1 hour 30 minutes Bring a blanket, low profile lawn chairs and some popcorn while enjoying the film on the lawn under the stars. In the film, Trolls Poppy and Branch discover the existence of six different troll tribes scattered over six different lands. Each tribe devotes itself to six different kinds of music – funk, country, techno, classical, pop and rock. Poppy and Branch embark on a quest to unite the trolls and save them from the mischievous rockers. For more information contact the Recreation Department at 420-3070. The final summer movie, Bee Movie, will be shown in Piedmont Park on Friday, September 17. Movies in the Park presents Trolls World Tour in Piedmont Park on Friday, August 27 at 7:45 p.m.

articles.text: Piedmont City Council has approved the first reading of an ordinance authorizing the issuance of bonds and levying taxes related to Measure UU, the $19.5 million project to build a new community pool. “We are taking this process very seriously,” said City Administrator Sara Lillevand. “We haven’t done a bond like this before, so we are looking at [a fine] level of detail at every step of the way.” Measure UU was approved by voters on November 3, 2020 with two-thirds of the residents voting for a bond of $19.5 million to build a new community pool on the site of the existing pool at the Recreation Department. At its most recent meeting on August 16, City Council approved the first reading of ordinance 762 N.S., authorizing the borrowing of money through bonds and levying an ‘ad valorem’ property tax sufficient to pay the bonds. City staff determined that the $19.5 million figure provided sufficient funds based on “hard cost” estimates to meet the objectives of the measure, Finance Director Michael Szczech wrote in an accompanying staff report. council also approved the establishment and appointment of residents to an oversight committee for the bonds. articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council approved the issuance of Requests for Proposals (RFP) for underwriting services of general obligation bonds for the Piedmont Community Pool at its August 16 meeting. The scope of services that will be provided by the selected investment bank will be in the full range of investment banking, marketing, and underwriting services required in connection with the authorization of the general obligation bonds in the amount of $19.5 million. The underwriter will remain in place until the issuance of bonds is completed. “The City of Piedmont has not been to the [bond underwriting] markets before. We expect the city to get a very high credit rating, but we want someone who will be able to explain...what makes Piedmont great,” City Finance Director Michael Szczech told city council. “We can do that through a negotiated sale, and we can educate the underwriter who then goes out and markets the bond to investors, who can reflect all the things that make Piedmont, Piedmont.” He added that a competitive sale, rather than a negotiated sale approach, does not have that opportunity for education. “We can instruct the underwriter to place ads in local papers, just to make sure that residents know this is available, and that they have every opportunity to purchase them,” Szczech explained. The city will seek proposals from investments banks to serve as the sole underwriter for its proposed issuance of general obligation bonds. The bonds will bear a fixed rate of interest to maturity, with a final maturity of 30 years. The meeting on August 16 was the first step to seek approval to issue proposals, documents will be brought back to the city council and mayor for consideration and discussion. “The moneys are not needed right away,” Szczech explained, but the issuance is time-sensitive because of current interest rates. “We know what interest rates are today, but we don’t know what interest rates are tomorrow,” he said. “By issuing bonds today, there is a cost because of an inability to invest the proceeds at the same interest rate on the bonds. articles.text: A draft of the Piedmont Safer Streets (PSS) plan, an update of the 2014 Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan, is now available for public review. The PSS plan includes chapters on the context and need for the plan, the community needs assessment, recommended projects, and prioritization and implementation. The draft plan is the result of a thorough public engagement effort. The first step was conducting a community needs assessment from mid-November 2020 through early January 2021, during which the City received over 2,500 individual comments. The next step in the process was to generate recommendations based on the community needs assessment while also addressing the City’s ongoing concerns. At the April 22, 2021 Pedestrian Bicycle Advisory Committee (PBAC) virtual meeting, project consultant Niko Letunic presented a draft set of recommended projects to be included in the PSS plan. The Photo by Paul Kuroda The city seeks input from the community on its draft of the Piedmont Safer Streets (PSS) plan. PBAC received public comments on the draft recommendations, discussed the matter and recommended revisions that resulted in the draft PSS plan currently posted for public review. In addition to the list of recommended projects to improve pedestrian and bicycle safety, the PSS plan includes a chapter on prioritization and implementation that focuses on quickbuild projects, bike corridors, and lays out a priority list for the recommended “enhanced street crossings.” The quick build projects section includes several traffic calming measures such as speed humps, speed tables, build-outs, chicanes and mini-round about.
articles.title: City seeks public input on Safer Streets Plan

articles.text: Editor: In a letter to editor Hannah Pinkham accused my mom of “excavat[ing] the original meaning” of the “‘thin blue line,” and invoked “eighteenth-century slave patrols.” “From...Ferguson to Minneapolis...police have inflicted violence...upon Black, brown, [etc.] bodies.” I reported on the ground as Ferguson’s black South Florissant community was incinerated by a lie thoughtlessly parroted – something debunked in Obama Dept. of Justice reports. “For Ms. Hartsock...who benefits from white, heterosexual, cisgender privilege, police guarantee safety.” Had the author done due diligence, she might have learned of a lifelong public schoolteacher who took bullets to her windshield commuting to teach in underprivileged districts, and whose immigrant family resisted Greek genocide and aided anti-Nazi Resistance in Oslo. “In marginalized communities...police instill fear,” according to the letter. Is it possible the author believes she can telepathically channel black people without ever having to meet any of them? Gallup polls suggest that 81 percent of those polled want more policing nationwide. Oakland Police Chief LeRonne Armstrong lamented that a 90 percent homicide spike occurred following $150 million cuts as black murder victim rates skyrocketed in police-defunded cities. But truly supporting black lives means taking unpopular positions at the risk of offending [people] on NextDoor. Abolitionism wasn’t the chic fad that wokeness is.
articles.title: Another view on thin blue line

articles.text: As reported in Piedmont Post’s article “Piedmont an Outlier...” (7/28/2021), the Piedmont City Council voted unanimously not to appeal the city’s state-mandated Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) goal of 587 new housing units, as part of the city’s updated 2023-2031 Housing Element. We are proud of this decision. It indicates our city’s willingness to take a solutions-oriented role in tackling the dire Bay Area housing shortage. A recent article in the San Francisco Chronicle, “Bay Area Cities Face Long Odds in Fighting State-Mandated Housing Goals,” (7/23/2021) suggests that most of the 28 cities which challenged their RHNA quotas did so because their elected leaders were posturing to constituents resistant to local growth. Piedmont’s city staff and attorney pointed out a RHNA appeal would have been a waste of time and money: In Southern California, where the RHNA cycle is ahead of northern California, more than 50 cities appealed their allocations and only two received minor adjustments down. The RHNA allocations are significantly higher during the upcoming cycle because we are in a housing crisis and need a lot more housing. Cities like Piedmont are being asked to do their fair share. Instead of considering the allocations a burden, we should support our local leaders for being advocates of housing equity and inclusion. These 587 units will not be added overnight. The state does not require cities to build the units, only to take the first steps by removing obstacles that currently stand in the way, such as single-family zoning, which is how almost all Piedmont is currently zoned. articles.title: Embracing RHNA is right thing to do

articles.text: The Alameda County Registrar of Voters began sending out mail ballots for the Gubernatorial Recall Election, on August 16. The recall election of Gov. Gavin Newsom is on Tuesday, September 14. Every registered voter will receive a ballot in the mail. If you are a resident of Alameda County, you can verify your registration address and voter status by visiting www.acvote.org/ mvp. The county is also offering a new way for voters to track and receive notifications on the status of their vote-by-mail ballot, powered by “BallotTrax” - interested residents may visit https://acvote. ballottrax.net/voter/ to receive be open starting Saturday, September 11. A recall procedure has been part of the state’s political system since 1911 and provides a mechanism for the public to attempt to remove elective public officials from office before the end of their term. At least 1,495,000 valid petition signatures, or 12% of the votes cast for the office of Governor in 2018, were received. Democrat Gov. Newsom is the second California governor ever to face a recall election. Five attempts to recall the governor have failed to qualify for the ballot since he took office in January 2019. Gov. Gray Davis was removed from office in 2003, only the second state governor successfully recalled in U.S. history. He was replaced by actor Arnold Schwarzenegger. Drop off mail-in ballots at drop boxes or any polling location in Alameda County on September 14. For more information on how to vote, visit the League of Women Voters of Piedmont website at https://www.lwvpiedmont.org/content.aspx?page_ id=22&club_id=601389&module_id=417274. automatic email or text notifications. articles.text: KQED, Northern California’s National Public Radio (NPR) station, has announced an allday block party on September 25 to celebrate its newly-designed headquarters on Mariposa The newly renovated-headquarters transforms the office building from industrial-style to an accessible, state-of-theart center. It was designed by the award-winning San Francisco-based architecture firm The station purchased the building in 1991, when KQED’s primary focus was television and radio production. Presently, KQED serves audiences on broadcast as well as through digital media tools like social media and web, podcasts, and live and virtual events. Since 1991, the station’s staff has doubled and its content services have expanded. It is now home to one of the largest newsrooms “KQED will redefine public media for the Bay Area, making it more diverse, participatory and community powered,” said Michael Isip, KQED President and CEO. “The new headquarters will enable our staff to thrive in providing crucial programming and education services and will expand possibilities for our community to come together to find common ground.” The new design features modernized production and studio spaces, expanding KQED’s ability to provide quality digital programming. EHDD’s design also increases visibility to the public; a new corner entry at Mariposa and Bryant Streets establishes a more prominent position in the Mission Street neighborhood with a glass facade. “We’re lifting up the façade to invite the community in,” said Rebecca Sharkey, EHDD Principal. “This new building represents the physical place of KQED engagement, a place to connect face-to-face with journalists and neighbors, to experience the breadth of KQED content, and to engage in dialogue about issues that matter most to the Bay Area and beyond.” KQED Grand Opening KQED will host a free, allday open house and block party on Saturday, September 25, unveiling its newly designed headquarters to the public. The community is invited to participate in an array of live programs and performances, featuring notable guests and radio personalities from KQED, NPR, Public Broadcasting Station (PBS) and PBS kids. There will also be workshops, media-making activities, and family and kid-friendly games throughout the building. “In a protracted time of separation and isolation, we’ve learned how to better use digital tools for virtual dialogue and participation.” Isip said. “We’ll continue to use technology to fill gaps and extend the reach of our work. Bringing people together for personal connection is essential for a strong, vibrant community.” For more information about the block party and open house, visit kqed.org/events.
articles.title: KQED celebrates new HQ with block party Sept. 25

articles.text: Piedmont Police Officer Hugo Diaz was named the Juvenile Liaison Officer for Piedmont School District in May. Piedmont Police Officer Hugo Diaz was named the new Juvenile Liaison Officer for Piedmont School District, in May this year. His role is designed to provide a stable connection between students and the police. Diaz, 33, is a former teacher and artist who grew up in East Oakland and attended Castlemont High School. He earned a B.A. in Art at Cal State East Bay and then earned a Master’s in Graphic Design. But at age 30, he decided to pursue a career in law enforcement and began working with the campus police department at Cal State. It was thre that he saw a flier advertising police work in Piedmont. At the time he did not know much about Piedmont. After doing a bit of research, he became interested in the possibility of working in a small city with a focus on its children. He was hired in June 2019. His position as Juvenile Liaison Officer is funded through a grant from the state by the tobacco industry. “The schools are still in charge of discipline. I’m more of a resource to the schools; I’m there so students can familiarize themselves with me and vice versa. This position serves to minimize police activity at the school,” he said. The Piedmont Police Department has had juvenile officers primarily for middle and high school students for many years. In his short time in the role, Diaz has interviewed students, spoken on podcasts, and has communicated with principals to learn what they expect of him. Diaz has received training on issues of sexual assault, dating violence, active shooter response, drug and alcohol abuse, crisis intervention, mental illness, and title IX issues. He will work Tuesday to Friday during school hours while on regular police patrol work. He will be responsible for responding to any needs at the schools. He can be contacted at the police department at 510-420-3056 (hdiaz@piedmont.ca.gov).
articles.title: Officer Hugo Diaz named new Juvenile Officer

articles.text: Compost is organic material that has the ability to improve the chemical, physical, and biological characteristics of soils. There are myriad benefits of composting, including providing nutrients to soil, retaining moisture in your garden, as well as reducing greenhouse gases and minimizing waste from the landfill. Whether you have been composting in your backyard for years or are new to the trade, there is always more to learn about this important organic material. Here are some resources for new and advanced compost enthusiasts: • Do you know you should put those soiled pizza boxes in the green bin? How about the fact you should put your dog’s waste in the trash, not the green bin? Refresh your memory on what can and cannot be included in your organic waste (green container) by visiting https://piedmont. ca.gov/services_ _ _departments/planning___building/ recycling _organic_waste_ garbage/organics. Organics collection by Republic Services is weekly, unlimited and included at no extra cost. • Have a lot of yard waste? Yard waste only materials must be • • • placed in compostable bags or paper lawn and leaf bags and tied bundled. 32-gallon compostable bags are available at no charge from Republic Services, City Hall, or by mail. Interested in receiving a free compost pail to collect your kitchen food scraps? All residential customers of Republic Services can receive a 1.5 gallon food scrap pail. Contact Alyssa Dykman to get yours today (510-420-3058 or adykman@piedmont.ca.gov). Want to put your kitchen food scraps and plant trimmings to work and get composting at home? Check out Alameda County’s public agency for reducing waste – StopWaste. Org. StopWaste provides best practices and gardening tips to get started with composting in your backyard. Need compost ASAP? Up to 12 cubic yards of compost at no charge is available to Republic Service customers every year. Bring your own bag, bin, or bucket to this self-service pickup at the West County Resource Recovery Facility (101 Pittsburg Ave., Richmond). The Facility has been receiving Piedmont’s organic waste for over a decade. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department is gearing up for its 3rd annual Car Show on Labor Day morning, Monday, September 6. The cars will be displayed in the parking lot in front of the Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, from 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. In 2019, the last time the event took place, a total of 44 gleaming vehicles were on display. From classic cars to late model Ferraris and Bugattis, the vehicles and owners will be there ready to show to car buffs. Peet’s Coffee will be served, and neighbors are invited to meet members of the police department while viewing and chatting with the car owners. The event is part of the larger “Coffee with a Cop” national campaign, which was started in 2016 as a way for residents to meet local law enforcement members throughout the country. In 2018 the Piedmont Police Department decided to rev up the event by adding classic cars to the mix. The community responded enthusiastically, and more than 1600 people showed up. “I value the Piedmont Police Department Car Show because I believe it builds strong relationships between community members and their police department,” said Officer Tyler Petit, who has coordinated the show since 2018. “The mutual trust between our police department and the community we serve is essential in maintaining public safety and effective policing. I’ll do whatever it takes to maintain that public trust.” Piedmont residents interested in participating in the city’s own Concours d’Elegance are asked to contact Officer Petit at tpetit@ piedmont.ca.gov. Include your name, address, email, and phone number along with the year, make and model of your car. Jerry Kennelly’s blue 2019 Ford GT-40 and its 647 horsepower V-6 engine, stole the show in the exotic category the last time the event was held in 2019

articles.text: As Piedmont students returned to a full time in class schedule this year, Piedmont Middle School expanded its traditional orientation, called Scots Camp, to include students in all classes, rather than sixth graders only. The activities included a scavenger hunt, music, dancing and team-building games. articles.text: On August 11, Tomás J. Aragón, MD, DrPH, Director and State Public Health Officer, issued an order on Vaccine Verification for Workers in Schools. In reading the directive one discovers that it does not mandate that school staff be vaccinated, but does provide a requirement for testing all adults unless proof of vaccination has been submitted to the school. It clarifies that only a vaccination may support an exemption from testing. “Previous history of COVID-19 from which the individual recovered more than 90 days earlier, or a previous positive antibody test for COVID-19, do not waive this requirement for testing,” the order states. Before discovering the numbers of faculty and staff who do not exercise the option of submitting proof of vaccination, it is difficult to accurately predict the cost in dollars and logistical support that will be required to fulfill Piedmont School District’s obligations under this new order. It would appear the amount will be substantive. This can be said without factoring in how small the number of individuals being tested may be. Even assuming the per-test cost to be linear, the fixed costs of implementation, documentation and ongoing monitoring lifts the y axis intercept well above zero. However, there may be an even greater consequence to consider than what comes with abiding by the delineated parameters of the order. That heightened impact lives in the question, “How do we work together?” PUSD and our community demonstrated a capacity to navigate the rise of the Delta variant, and reopened schools in a manner commonly described as very positive. The community’s mutual success in this accomplishment, in the quest to foster thriving students, is nothing short of heroic. Individuals subjugated their own worst fears around the safety (be it physical health or mental health) of primarily our students, but also ourselves and one another. Our first week of school has ended; some fears have not. To offer some transparency, I am sharing here words that I earlier sent out to APT [Association of Piedmont Teachers] members as we prepared for our first day of the school year. “I am most of all very optimistic about our return to school, moderately concerned about physical safety of students and staff, and gravely concerned about the potential for deep and long-lasting harm to our community relationships if we begin to argue unproductively. I feel confident by the response I have received from board members and district administration that they share these concerns and have a heightened interest in including our perspectives in an unprecedented way moving forward.” I can now add that the district has continued to build on that interest, not only with APT, but with all PUSD community members. Challenging times do not automatically bring out the best in people. They can, but the same boiling water that softens the potato hardens the egg. Another thought initially shared with my APT peers is extended to our entire community now. “Let us work together and not divide. We can disagree and we can be passionate, and yet we can also still be colleagues and mutually respectful. We are modeling for our students how to navigate difficult times with differences of opinion. Let us model well for them!” Flint Christensen, a Computer Science teacher at Piedmont High School, is President of the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT).
articles.title: Vaccination and Testing to impact PUSD

articles.text: Results of the White Bread Challenge How important is it to wash your hands? As kids go back to school, it is more important than ever for them to be practicing good hygiene habits. This means washing your hands, covering your cough, etc. This hands-on experiment demonstrates the importance of thoroughly washing your hands through powerful visualizations and observations. Learn how clean…and dirty household and classroom items are using the white bread experiment. Suggested Materials: • Enough slices of fresh, white bread for each item you’d like to test • 1 plastic sealable sandwich bag for each slice of bread that you’ll test • A slice of bread that has not been touched (use gloves or clean tongs) • Predictions, Observations, and Data Worksheet • Whatever items are frequently touched in your home or classroom: • Clean hands: warm water and soap for 20 seconds • Clean hands: hand sanitizer • Dirty hands • Your face • Anything with a touch screen • Phone • Keyboard • TV remote or gaming controller • Door handle • Light switch • Favorite book • Favorite toy • Your pillow Procedure: 1. Using new gloves or clean tongs, remove 1 slice of fresh white bread and seal it in a plastic sandwich bag. a. Number and label the bag as Control bag #1, etc. 2. Wipe dry, clean hands that have been washed thoroughly for at least 20 seconds with soap and warm water on the next slice of bread. Photo by Jaralee Annice Metcalf a. Number and label the bag as Clean hands- Soap and Warm Water (bag #2) 3. Continue to repeat this process for each surface you’d like to test. Make sure to correctly label and number each bag. 4. Leave the sealed bags with their labels on a table or counter for up to one month. 5. Make predictions about which slices of bread will grow the most mold. Which slices will get moldy the fastest? Why? 6. Record your data on the Predictions, Observations, and Data Worksheet. 7. Share you r results @ chabotspace Bethany Vanderwest is with Chabot Space and Science Center, 10000 Skyline Blvd., in Oakland. You can also see them online at https://chabotspace. org/.

articles.text: Andy Willats, PHS Science Department Chair, will be teaching two new courses this academic year – ornithology and geology, the two subjects receiving the highest interest in a survey last spring according to Piedmont High School Principal Adam Littlefield. Thirty-seven students have already signed up for geology this fall. The courses comprise the high school’s field sciences electives, which are intended to “be hands-on and get students out in the field to see themselves as an organism in a larger context,” Willats explained. Geology will consist of traditional instructional strategies to include lectures, projects, lab experiments, research and presentations. Students will visit East Bay locations that provide observable learning, such as the Volcanic Regional Preserve in Oakland, and will allow data collection techniques in the field. When learning about plate tectonics, students will visit a location in Hayward, where you can visibly see the shift and curves on the side of the road and measure how far they’ve moved to estimate the rate of movement. “We have so much geology around us [in the East Bay], and it can be hard to understand. Students will spend time in the field to see those [lessons] in effect,” Willats said. Willats explained that most schools teach geology as a yearlong course, but this will be the fall semester only. Lesson units will include rock cycles, creating landforms, geological hazards and climate relationships.
