pages.text: Wednesday, August 18, 2021 7 Vaccination and Testing to impact PUSD By Flint Christensen On August 11, Tomás J. Aragón, MD, DrPH, Director and State Public Health Officer, issued an order on Vaccine Verification for Workers in Schools. In reading the directive one discovers that it does not mandate that school staff be vaccinated, but does provide a requirement for testing all adults unless proof of vaccination has been submitted to the school. It clarifies that only a vaccination may support an exemption from testing. “Previous history of COVID-19 from which the individual recovered more than 90 days earlier, or a previous positive antibody test for COVID-19, do not waive this requirement for testing,” the order states. Before discovering the numbers of faculty and staff who do not exercise the option of submitting proof of vaccination, it is difficult to accurately predict the cost in dollars and logistical support that will be required to fulfill Piedmont School District’s obligations under this new order. It would appear the amount will be substantive. This can be said without factoring in how small the number of individuals being tested may be. Even assuming the per-test cost to be linear, the fixed costs of implementation, documentation and ongoing monitoring lifts the y axis intercept well above zero. However, there may be an even greater consequence to consider than what comes with abiding by the delineated parameters of the order. That heightened impact lives in the question, “How do we work together?” PUSD and our community demonstrated a capacity to navigate the rise of the Delta variant, and reopened schools in a manner commonly described as very positive. The community’s mutual success in this accomplishment, in the quest to foster thriving students, is nothing short of heroic. Individuals subjugated their own worst fears around the safety (be it physical health or mental health) of primarily our students, but also ourselves and one another. Our first week of school has ended; some fears have not. To offer some transparency, I am sharing here words that I earlier sent out to APT [Association of Piedmont Teachers] members as we prepared for our first day of the school year. “I am most of all very optimistic about our return to school, moderately concerned about physical safety of students and staff, and gravely concerned about the potential for deep and long-lasting harm to our community relationships if we begin to argue unproductively. I feel confident by the response I have received from board members and district administration that they share these concerns and have a heightened interest in including our perspectives in an unprecedented way moving forward.” I can now add that the district has continued to build on that interest, not only with APT, but with all PUSD community members. Challenging times do not automatically bring out the best in people. They can, but the same boiling water that softens the potato hardens the egg. Another thought initially shared with my APT peers is extended to our entire community now. “Let us work together and not divide. We can disagree and we can be passionate, and yet we can also still be colleagues and mutually respectful. We are modeling for our students how to navigate difficult times with differences of opinion. Let us model well for them!” Flint Christensen, a Computer Science teacher at Piedmont High School, is President of the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT). Thinking Outside The Classroom Back to School White Bread Challenge Results of the White Bread Challenge By Bethany Vanderwest How important is it to wash your hands? As kids go back to school, it is more important than ever for them to be practicing good hygiene habits. This means washing your hands, covering your cough, etc. This hands-on experiment demonstrates the importance of thoroughly washing your hands through powerful visualizations and observations. Learn how clean…and dirty household and classroom items are using the white bread experiment. Suggested Materials: • Enough slices of fresh, white bread for each item you’d like to test • 1 plastic sealable sandwich bag for each slice of bread that you’ll test • A slice of bread that has not been touched (use gloves or clean tongs) • Predictions, Observations, and Data Worksheet • Whatever items are frequently touched in your home or classroom: • Clean hands: warm water and soap for 20 seconds • Clean hands: hand sanitizer • Dirty hands • Your face • Anything with a touch screen • Phone • Keyboard • TV remote or gaming controller • Door handle • Light switch • Favorite book • Favorite toy • Your pillow Procedure: 1. Using new gloves or clean tongs, remove 1 slice of fresh white bread and seal it in a plastic sandwich bag. a. Number and label the bag as Control bag #1, etc. 2. Wipe dry, clean hands that have been washed thoroughly for at least 20 seconds with soap and warm water on the next slice of bread. Photo by Jaralee Annice Metcalf a. Number and label the bag as Clean hands- Soap and Warm Water (bag #2) 3. Continue to repeat this process for each surface you’d like to test. Make sure to correctly label and number each bag. 4. Leave the sealed bags with their labels on a table or counter for up to one month. 5. Make predictions about which slices of bread will grow the most mold. Which slices will get moldy the fastest? articles.text: On January 15 two years ago, Atticus Lim, then a sophomore at Piedmont High School, made a routine defensive move in a basketball game. It would change the trajectory of his life. Lim slid his feet left to stay in front of the opposing player with the ball. It caused his opponent to lose the ball. In the process, Lim fell backwards and his head hit the court, hard. It’s a fairly routine play in basketball and no whistle was blown to stop the play. The clock kept ticking. But Lim’s personal life took a time out. He was diagnosed with having suffered a severe traumatic brain injury. Atticus wasn’t able to return to school for six weeks, and even then, he struggled to keep up with his studies. And then in March 2020 the coronavirus pandemic arrived, and classes began to be taught on computers. Persistent online class meant an increase in screen time – the worst possible learning environment for someone recovering from a traumatic brain injury. He began experiencing the worst headaches of his life. Recovery from a traumatic brain injury can take two years or more, and Lim hasn’t fully recovPiedmont High School senior Atticus Lim shoots three-point baskets with friend Charlie Olcott in a fundraising effort to help individuals with traumatic brain injuries. ered. His brain injury was in the worst 2-5 percent. “[The doctor] told Atticus that the best thing he could do [when recovering] was to exercise,” explained Atticus’ father, Dion Lim. “You can think of it like spraining your brain - you certainly want to rest it, but you also want to get circulation in there.” Fast forward to the recent start of the 2021 school year. Atticus is back in school and doing better, but the recovery time from that one small moment in time is still ongoing. A relatively innocuous play on a basketball court has required two years of rewinding, reworking, patience and therapy. If you know the Lim family Atticus Lim floats up a shot in a 2018 basketball game versus Campolinda. you won’t be surprised to hear that Atticus has turned this negative experience into an opportunity to help others. Atticus joined a fundraising charity called SameYou, which was founded by the British actress Emilia Clarke (famous for her role in Game of Thrones). SameYou aims to develop better recovery treatment for survivors of brain injury and stroke. For his fundraiser, Atticus wanted to recover the joy of basketball, so he decided to shoot 33 three-pointers every day in July. He chose 33 to bring attention to the fact that one in three people will have an acquired brain injury at some point in their lives. Atticus has raised £4,500 of his goal of £5,000 (almost $7,000) to support those with traumatic brain injuries. “I reached out to basically everyone I know, trying to gain support, donations or a pledge for each basket made,” Lim said. “I got my friends to rebound my shots for me, to support the message of rebounding from an injury.” An estimated 2,500,000 high school students report having a traumatic brain injury every year. Atticus is working with doctors on a white paper identifying care gaps in the treatment of traumatic brain injuries for young athletes. He has built a set of resources to support families in the recovery process. His document includes three proposals for reforming the culture behind traumatic brain injury. 1. Change the term “concussion” to “traumatic brain injury” 2. Require informed consent for youth sports 3. Treat traumatic brain injuries as serious injuries To visit the full fundraising page, hear more of his story and donate, see: Givepenny.com/atticuslim. articles.text: Countless words have been written about the impact of the pandemic – the effects of familial loss, social distancing, mask wearing, isolation and resultant loneliness. I recently came across an article in the New York Times written by social psychologist Jonathan Haidt and psychologist Jean M. Twenge whose research has linked loneliness at school to the ubiquitous use of the smartphone. It’s a theory that at first blush seems counterintuitive – aren’t kids perpetually engaging with one another on their devices? However, as in-person school is finally underway, their supposition is worth perusing. First, since 2012 the smartphone has been used by a majority of Americans, and by 2015 twothirds of all tweens/teens. Facebook, Instagram, TikTok etc. are social media platforms relied on for contact and interaction. But they also have become sources of anger (beginning with the “like button”) and criticism. Experts have posed the question as to whether smartphones and social media are actually harming teens. Of coursem there has been pushback, which has pointed out that a similar hyperbolic reaction occurred to kids reading comic books, listening to rock ‘n roll, watching television and playing video games. What Haidt and Twenge focused on in their research was the word “harm”, citing a study of international students conducted every three years since 2000, titled The Program for International Student Assessment (PISA). It has surveyed 15-yearolds in dozens of countries, and included questions about loneliness at school. The psychologists, expanding the definition of “harm”, state that loneliness is not the same as depression, but the two are often correlated, meaning lonely teens are often depressed teens and visa versa. In a paper, recently published by the psychologists in the Journal of Adolescence, they found that in 36 out of 37 countries loneliness at school has accelerated dramatically since 2012, which coincides with the embrace of the smartphone by teens. The data shows that this phenomenon has doubled in the last nine years in Europe, Latin America, America, and English-speaking countries. In other words, the two researchers conclude that the smartphone has brought about a “planetary rewiring of human communication that has transformed peer and family relationships as well as the texture of daily life for everyone.” They go on to say that it is harder to stoke up a casual conversation when everyone is staring down at their phones, or have a deep conversation when each party is interrupted by buzzing or vibrating notifications. Their data also indicates that teen mental health has changed for the worse since 2012. They argue that electronic communications are akin to empty calories, a kind of intermittent sugar rush, brief, but not comprising social interactions that are necessary for teens to become fully competent adults. Haidt and Twenge ask: what can we do to assure that our youngsters get the critical social intercourse so vital to their mental wellbeing? One offered solution is to prohibit the use of electronic devices at schools. On the way to school and on the way home, fine, but not during the school day. That would require adolescents to fully focus on those around them. I would add that learning to read the nuanced facial expressions and body language of kids and adults are acquired skills, ones not encouraged by the smartphone, whether texting or screen time. Another suggestion by the psychologists is to make it impossible for tweens and newbie teens to establish social media accounts. Even before the pandemic, teens were finding themselves increasingly lonely at school. And now, after the nearly 18 months of relative isolation, contagion fears, remote schooling, stressed parents, and increased reliance on their devices, the question begged is: will teens willingly put away their phones at school and learn to rely on in-person interactions? Haidt and Twenge say that we must help them do exactly that. Chris Honore’ resides in Ashland, Oregon and has been a columnist and reviewer in the Post for more than 20 years. For comments, e-mail him at honore307@ gmail.com.

articles.text: The summer days spent in Santa Barbara were slow and lazy. Our family spent five days in July exploring that quiet sea town, wading in the waves, lounging by the pool, and eating the best seafood I’ve ever tasted. The beachfront resort where we stayed had a Hawaiian feel to it projected by middle-aged men in cargo shorts, Tommy Bahamas shirts and Ray-ban glasses, to say nothing of the oversized pina coladas. Getting to Santa Barbara from Piedmont, on the other hand, was the opposite of relaxing. There’s Gilroy with its perennial traffic, lack of bathroom breaks, exploding chip bags, and constant disagreements with the GPS. My dad talks to it as if it were a real person. He challenges every left turn, right turn, and exit that is recommended. One time we nearly ran out of gas. It was 9 o’clock at night when we suddenly noticed the gas indicator was hovering around zero and the next gas station was 23 miles away. My mom drove in the mountains like it would be the final drive of her life if she didn’t make it to that gas station. And all those miles, according to the gas indicator, we were driving with an empty tank. Somehow, we made it. That adventure was nothing compared to our return trip. Remembering our difficulties with gas, we filled up our car before leaving the hidden paradise of Santa Barbara. It was agreed that my dad would be driving the first half of the way. I had put in my AirPods, started my playlist, and zoned out expecting a peaceful five-hour ride home. At some point I dozed off. When I awoke, my mom was at the wheel, which meant we had passed San Luis Obispo. I heard my parents debating whether to take the shortcut that Google maps was offering to avoid the traffic slowdown near Gilroy. {Sometimes I think the only reason Gilroy exists is to create slowdowns.} My dad wasn’t particularly excited by the shortcut offered by my mom’s GPS, and his phone wasn’t suggesting anything, but that could have been because he has such a bad relationship with his GPS. In the end, he too, didn’t want to be stalled in traffic near Gilroy, so my mom veered to the right and off 101. It was somewhat strange that what was advertised by Google as route 25 North looked like a twolane street. Once you go down the road there’s no way to go back unless you make a virtually impossible U-turn. The road itself was just hills, hills, and you guessed it, more hills. We were expecting to get back on 101, but Google had a surprise announcement: “Keep on 25 North for 55 miles.” As we climbed one mountain after another east of Gilroy, 101 was nowhere to be seen, let alone found. We had no choice but to trudge on. (To be fair I wasn’t surprised that something like this would happen; Google maps has been leading us astray since we started using it.) After driving on this lonely highway for lord knows how long, we came to a huge mound of dirt blocking the road. At this moment we thought this is it: this highway will be our final resting place. After a brief panic attack, we discovered a detour next to the original road. Once we got on it, it directed us back to Highway 25 and we continued our journey through rural California. After a good 20 miles or so, we passed a town sign for Paicines, with a population of less than 100. We discovered that it was an unincorporated town. It looked like a ghost town, with lizards and snakes as its only inhabitants. But oddly enough, despite seeing buildings falling apart and being in the middle of nowhere, there was a fully operational retro-looking gas station. There was actually color on the building, originally a vibrant light pink and green, now faded. Nonetheless it was still color, and seemed oddly out of place. After leaving Paicines, we passed what seemed to be a ravine or dry creek bed. Wrong. Our trusty friend Google revealed that we had just crossed the San Andreas Fault. Being a person who is deathly terrified of earthquakes, the revelation did not sit well with me at all. Imagine, if there was an earthquake, wouldn’t we be the ones that had the mountains crashing down on us, and no one would know what happened to us? And so we kept driving, through more ghost towns like Tres Pinos, with not a soul in sight. I thought that we would never get to the end of that road. It just went on for as far as my eye could see. We all tried to cheer up our mother, who obviously felt pretty bad about her “shortcut.” My dad said he enjoyed being in the country. For a while we pretended that we were at a Formula 1 car rally. An oncoming BMW suddenly made a U-turn in front of us in another inexplicable development. Time passed slower than an old man going down a waterslide. I counted 75 cows, 4 horses, 6 abandoned houses, and one lunatic walking along a highway miles from any civilization. And then when we were about to give up all hope, we noticed signs of civilization – more cars. An intersection. A traffic light. And finally, rows of similar-looking houses described by GPS as the town of Hollister. After thinking that I would never see anything besides the parched rolling hills of California, the small lemon tree in our front yard felt like a blessing when we arrived home. Getting out of that car never felt so good. The moral of this story is: Don’t ever listen to Google when it tells you to take a shortcut, unless you’re an agriculture fanatic or you’re prepared for a long haul into the unknown. I, for one, will avoid “shortcuts” in the future. Same for my mom and dad, I think. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. pages.text: Wednesday, August 18, 2021 9 CRYSTAL’S REFLECTIONS By Crystal Vacker The summer days spent in Santa Barbara were slow and lazy. Our family spent five days in July exploring that quiet sea town, wading in the waves, lounging by the pool, and eating the best seafood I’ve ever tasted. The beachfront resort where we stayed had a Hawaiian feel to it projected by middle-aged men in cargo shorts, Tommy Bahamas shirts and Ray-ban glasses, to say nothing of the oversized pina coladas. Getting to Santa Barbara from Piedmont, on the other hand, was the opposite of relaxing. There’s Gilroy with its perennial traffic, lack of bathroom breaks, exploding chip bags, and constant disagreements with the GPS. My dad talks to it as if it were a real person. He challenges every left turn, right turn, and exit that is recommended. One time we nearly ran out of gas. It was 9 o’clock at night when we suddenly noticed the gas indicator was hovering around zero and the next gas station was 23 miles away. My mom drove in the mountains like it would be the final drive of her life if she didn’t make it to that gas station. And all those miles, according to the gas indicator, we were driving with an empty tank. Somehow, we made it. That adventure was nothing compared to our return trip. Remembering our difficulties with gas, we filled up our car before leaving the hidden paradise of Santa Barbara. It was agreed that my dad would be driving the first half of the way. I had put in my AirPods, started my playlist, and zoned out expecting a peaceful five-hour ride home. At some point I dozed off. When I awoke, my mom was at the wheel, which meant we had passed San Luis Obispo. I heard my parents debating whether to take the shortcut that Google maps was offering to avoid the traffic slowdown near Gilroy. {Sometimes I think the only reason Gilroy exists is to create slowdowns.} My dad wasn’t particularly The wrong way home excited by the shortcut offered by my mom’s GPS, and his phone wasn’t suggesting anything, but that could have been because he has such a bad relationship with his GPS. In the end, he too, didn’t want to be stalled in traffic near Gilroy, so my mom veered to the right and off 101. It was somewhat strange that what was advertised by Google as route 25 North looked like a twolane street. Once you go down the road there’s no way to go back unless you make a virtually impossible U-turn. The road itself was just hills, hills, and you guessed it, more hills. We were expecting to get back on 101, but Google had a surprise announcement: “Keep on 25 North for 55 miles.” As we climbed one mountain after another east of Gilroy, 101 was nowhere to be seen, let alone found. We had no choice but to trudge on. (To be fair I wasn’t surprised that something like this would happen; Google maps has been leading us astray since we started using it.) After driving on this lonely highway for lord knows how long, we came to a huge mound of dirt blocking the road. At this moment we thought this is it: this highway will be our final resting place. After a brief panic attack, we discovered a detour next to the original road. Once we got on it, it directed us back to Highway 25 and we continued our journey through rural California. After a good 20 miles or so, we passed a town sign for Paicines, with a population of less than 100. We discovered that it was an unincorporated town. It looked like a ghost town, with lizards and snakes as its only inhabitants. But oddly enough, despite seeing buildings falling apart and being in the middle of nowhere, there was a fully operational retro-looking gas station. There was actually color on the building, originally a vibrant light pink and green, now faded. Nonetheless it was still color, and seemed oddly out of place. After leaving Paicines, we passed what seemed to be a ravine or dry creek bed. Wrong. Our trusty friend Google revealed that we had just crossed the San Andreas Fault. Being a person who is deathly terrified of earthquakes, the revelation did not sit well with me at all. Imagine, if there was an earthquake, wouldn’t we be the ones that had the mountains crashing down on us, and no one would know what happened to us? And so we kept driving, through more ghost towns like Tres Pinos, with not a soul in sight. I thought that we would never get to the end of that road. It just went on for as far as my eye could see. We all tried to cheer up our mother, who obviously felt pretty bad about her “shortcut.” My dad said he enjoyed being in the country. For a while we pretended that we were at a Formula 1 car rally. An oncoming BMW suddenly made a U-turn in front of us in another inexplicable development. Time passed slower than an old man going down a waterslide. I counted 75 cows, 4 horses, 6 abandoned houses, and one lunatic walking along a highway miles from any civilization. And then when we were about to give up all hope, we noticed signs of civilization – more cars. An intersection. A traffic light. And finally, rows of similar-looking houses described by GPS as the town of Hollister. After thinking that I would never see anything besides the parched rolling hills of California, the small lemon tree in our front yard felt like a blessing when we arrived home. Getting out of that car never felt so good. The moral of this story is: Don’t ever listen to Google when it tells you to take a shortcut, unless you’re an agriculture fanatic or you’re prepared for a long haul into the unknown. I, for one, will avoid “shortcuts” in the future. Same for my mom and dad, I think. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time. articles.text: Throughout the summer the Post prints a sampling of letters written by kids attending Camp Augusta, Piedmont’s residential camp at Lake Vera outside Nevada City in the Sierra foothills. Founded in 1931, the camp remains a vital part of the life of hundreds of children each summer. Photos and postcards in today’s edition of the Post are from the last week of camp in summer 2021. For more information, see campaugusta.org. A disco ball was created for the cabin made for a sparkling evening. A giant foam machine made a memorable slip ‘n slide. articles.text: School is back in session, meaning the start of the 2021- 2022 sports schedule is right around the corner. We spent some time at Witter Field this week to get a glimpse of the return of fall sports. On the field, pads are cracking and smacking at practices of the varsity and junior varsity football teams. Jeanine Holmlund’s cross-country teams are back on the track and running distances in town. Volleyball has returned to the Binks Rawlings Gym; the girls’ golf team started practice on Monday; and the water polo teams are busy practicing in poos outside Piedmont. “Every team is back at it now. It’s a quick turnaround from all the sports jammed into three months last school year,” explained Piedmont High School Athletic Director Bradley Smet. “Golf got back today [Monday], water polo is in the pool, football and cross country are here, and I’m helping out with volleyball as well.” “It’s really exciting. I’m happy that we’re out here under the sun,” he added. After 14 seniors from the football team graduated, the varsity team has only 15-17 players. High school teams typically have 40-50 players. As a result, the junior varsity team has a wealth of freshman prospects. But only Andy Melian and Bailey Cain returns as starting players on the varsity. Look for a handful of JV call-ups during the season. “There’s still some holdover from COVID. Some of our kids decided not to come back and play,” said Smet. “Numbers are a little low, but we have a strong freshman class. We have close to 20 freshmen out here, which is by far the biggest class out of everyone,” said Smet. Multi-sport athletes like Nico Defazio and Evan McConathy are finally eligible to play both football and baseball. With last year’s compressed schedule due to Covid, the seasons overlapped, forcing them choose one sport. “I’m really excited for this year, I really missed playing football last year. I love the game of football, so it was really difficult to just watch from the sidelines. I’d love to play either football or baseball in college,” said Defazio. He is expected to play quarterback and should be a two-day PHS offensive line coach Derrick Lyons oversees drills with the lineman. starter as a defensive back. “It’s a big spot, but I love it. I like to be a leader and I’m confident I can do it well. It’s a big role that I’m ready to take on. I’m excited,” he added. Piedmont’s football season opens with a scrimmage on August 27 with Miramonte in Orinda. Staff Photos Junior Varsity quarterback Markos Legeos was among 20 freshmen on the JV team. PHS senior Nico Defazio will be a big contributor on the varsity this season. Athletic Director Bradley Smet, shown at football practice, will be the offensive coordinator for the JV team. Cross-Country Somewhat in contrast, Holmlund is ecstatic for the upcoming cross-country season. The boys’ team will return a strong group of returning runners from last season. Athlete of the Year runner-up Jack Stein is entering his senior year and potentially could have a big year with both cross-country in the fall and track in the spring Last spring Stein helped the Highlanders place second of nine schools in the WACC Cross-Country Championships by finishing third in a field of 59 runners with a time of 15:58.5. Holmlund said she has her eye on Christian Taylor, a junior, who will be running with teammates Parker Long, Seamus Chamberlain-Carr, Julian Lee, and Stein to round out a strong team in the WACC. “Jack has been training really hard over the summer; Christian has been working really, really hard as well. I’m really excited for him. We all went to camp out in Yosemite this summer and had a great time there. It was a lot of fun and a great experience for the team,” said Holmlund, who uses Yosemite for some workouts at The cross-country team is back running at Witter Field and through the Piedmont hills.

articles.text: After 2021’s sports schedule jammed 9 months of sports into a three-month schedule, high schools throughout the country are welcoming back their new student-athletes. Piedmont’s athletes in the Class of 2022 looks to what could be a defining year of their high school careers. This week, the Post takes a look at two male and two female athletes in advance of the upcoming season: JoJo Murphy, Basketball What can we say about JoJo Murphy? The senior enters a critical year after leading last year’s 11-5 team in several categories; points at 409, knocking down 55 three-pointers with a sterling 43 shooting percentage, to go along with 105 rebounds, 58 assists, and 46 steals. He had five games when he scored 30 or more points, including a career-high of 38 against San Leandro on May 7. He also had seven 3-pointers against Bishop O’Dowd in the season-finale on June 4. He was named the Post’s Sophomore of the Year in 2020 after unseating former starter DaRon Benson for a first-team spot. He scored 385 points and helped lead Piedmont to its first North Coast Section championship. Murphy earned WestCoastPreps.com’s Bay Area Athlete of the Year award last month. And you can put him on the Piedmont Post’s Athlete of the Year watch list once again. Amanda Becker, Tennis & Soccer Amanda Becker, a starter at No. 1 doubles on Jim Landes’ tennis team last year, will be a team leader this fall. She Becker was dominant at the No. 1 spot, known for her aggressive play in front of the net; smashing volleys left, right, and center. She posted a 5-2 record in at doubles last season while teaming up with four different players – Audrey Mahaney, Mara LaForte, Kate Dorman, and Michaela Bini. She played on the soccer team as a freshman and sophomore and was an influential member of Dan Chubbock’s attack. She did not compete in soccer during the pandemic school year in 2020. Staff Photos JoJo Murphy recently won WestCoastPreps.com’s Bay Area Athlete of the Year award. He led Piedmont’s basketball team in nearly all categories last season. Amanda Becker is set for a big season on the tennis team this fall. Conner Curtis, Soccer Conner Curtis led the soccer team in scoring the past two seasons. He’s a versatile player, typically lining up in the Central Attacking Midfield role, but can rotate along the wing as well. As a team leader, he helped PHS finish with a 10-0-1 overall record with a perfect 10-0 record against Shoreline Division league teams. The team’s only loss came to non-league rival, Bishop O’Dowd, a 2-0 outcome. In 2021, Curtis scored at least eight goals and proved to be a free-kick specialist, taking every corner and set piece last season. He bagged a pair of goals against Alameda and scored on free-kick goals against Encinal and San Lorenzo. Curtis was named honorable mention for Sophomore of the Year in 2020 by the Post, and also honorable mention the prior year. Conner Curtis is the leading scorer on the soccer team. He’s a versatile player in coach Todd Sullivan’s system.

articles.text: Piedmont High Class of 2021 graduate Aidan Mitchell just finished up a summer that is unique by most standards. A former Swiss resident, he played baseball this summer with the Hünenberg Unicorns in the Swiss Baseball National League A. He has been competing in the Switzerland adult leagues since he was 15 years old. His teammates are college prospects around his age, ranging to veterans up in the 40s and 50s. “I was playing in the men’s league, and before I was in the Cadets, which is equivalent to around Middle School. You’d have some people in their 50s still playing, or some teenagers like me next to them. When I first got on the team, I was amazed that I was playing next to somebody in their mid-50s,” said Mitchell with a laugh. “There are usually former and current college players out there, it’s a good league. They bring people from all over and from a lot of different age groups. The rules aren’t different, but the makeup of teams is definitely something you won’t see in the U.S.,” he added. Mitchell and his family moved to Switzerland from Los Angeles seven years ago and lived there for five years before moving to Piedmont. He’s not the only Yankee there, though. Clubs often bring in ringers from the States. “One of the more interesting rules is that you can’t have a foreign-born player pitch in the first game, and they typically play two games a day. The good Swiss teams will pay to bring in players from the U.S.,” said Mitchell. Playing with men of different ages has allowed him the unique experience of pitching to his dad as catcher in a competitive game. “My favorite part of it was being able to play next to my dad. He played catcher in high school, so I was able to pitch to him. It was probably the most amazing experience to have him coach me, then get behind the dish and catch for me,” said Mitchell.

articles.text: Staff Photos Kurt Bryan and the coaching staff of the Bay Area Panthers, a professional team in the new Indoor Football League. The Bay Area Panthers announced at a press conference on August 16 its plans to kick off its inaugural 2022 season in the Indoor Football League at San Jose’s SAP Center next March. Kurt Bryan, former Piedmont High football coach, will guide the team as head coach. In attendance at the press conference were San Jose mayor Sam Liccardo, Sharks Sports and Entertainment president Jonathan Becher, San Jose Sports Authority executive director John Poch, and IFL commissioner Todd Tryon, “Like Mayor Liccardo said, there’s been so much bad news over the last year and a half with the pandemic; this is great news. This is great for the entire Bay Area. It’s why we named our franchise the Bay Area Panthers,’ said Bryan. “We’re going to draw talent from San Jose, Oakland, Walnut Creek, Pleasanton, Livermore, the Peninsula, San Francisco, and Marin County. This is great for everyone.” “Tickets are affordable, the weather is always good in the IFL and inside the SAP Center, and it will be a wonderful environment for your family,” he added. Bryan and the Panthers originally planned to begin in the spring of 2020 at Oracle Arena in Oakland, but the pandemic closed operations days before the franchise opener. Panthers’ president, Scott McKibben. got in touch with the San Jose’s Sharks owner and a deal was worked out to relocate to San Jose in just a few months at the former home of four-time Arena Football League champs, the Sabercats. This marks Bryan’s return to coaching nearly two years after the Panthers’ initial press conference in September 2019. He’s as excited as ever to provide an opportunity for local and regional athletes to play perhaps the most popular sport in the country, yet among least represented at the professional level “What this does for local athletes is provide them an opportunity. Salaries may not be millions of dollars a year like in the NFL, but it is certainly a million-dollar opportunity. articles.text: Orinda-based competitive water polo club CC United’s 18U team won the 2021 USA Water Polo Junior Olympics National Championship held from July 17-20 in Orange County, California. Piedmont’s Charlie Saunders was a member of the gold medal 18U team. It was CC United’s first Gold medal since being founded in 2011. Piedmont alums Patrick Conn and Henry Saunders were on CC United’s Bronze Medal team in 2019. Also competing with CC United in this year’s Junior Olympics were Piedmont athletes Ezra Trost (16U team) and George Saunders (12U team). The 18U team was coached by Matt DeTrane, Jack Brown, and Garrett Dunn. This year’s team was undefeated in seven games in the four-day tournament. The championship game with Vanguard Black was played in front of a capacity crowd. CCU trailed by three goals late in the 3rd quarter but rallied to score six goals to take a 13-9 lead with four minutes left. With stellar defense and balanced scoring from nine different players, CC United prevailed 13-10. When the final horn sounded, players dove into the pool, pulling their coaches in with them. CCU founder Kirk Jensen and other CC United coaches dove in from the other side of the pool, along with former players in attendance. With families and friends cheering and hugging, CCU players and coaches from across different eras knew that their decade-long dream had finally come to fruition. Piedmont’s George Saunders (front, left) competes on CC United’s 12U team, which finished 11th in the Gold Division.

articles.text: Paper books vs. iBooks for kids Given today’s widely popular digital reading devices and the rich tradition of children’s paper books, we are wondering which reading format is better suited for young readers’ learning. Do digital and paper books have the same effects on children’s story comprehension, or is one medium more beneficial? In reviewing the scientific literature addressing learning outcomes with digital and paper books for children at the earliest stages of reading development (early or emergent readers ages 1–8), we consider the traditional paper book scenario where early readers’ first experience of books is typically modeled and mediated by adults at home, vs. more current scenarios where early readers’ first experience of books may be e-books, picture book apps, story apps and iBooks accessed independently. Are we to expect a transition from print to digital that changes the established school and home routines of book reading? One element which emerges as significant is the quality of digital enhancements (voice and other digital features that make the story content accessible without adult interaction). Of the many types of digital enhancements used, content related enhancements which focus the children’s attention on and align with the storyline emerge as most beneficial. Alternatively, digital enhancements such as aesthetically based enhancements and embedded games may distract and decrease story comprehension. Another element which has been studied is the addition of on-line dictionaries embedded in digital texts. Do embedded digital dictionaries enhance story comprehension? Research shows that if the dictionary is dynamic (visual and audio), it can be beneficial for vocabulary development. However, the presence of the dictionary had no effect on story comprehension, suggesting that focusing attention on isolated word meanings may distract from the story content. Adult support effects have also been studied with regard to digital and paper books. At this point, studies demonstrate a clear advantage for adult mediated print book reading sessions, suggesting that (skilled) adults are better able to attune their support to children’s needs than enhanced digital books that the children read or listen to on their own. Instead of focusing on whether digital is better than paper, let’s consider the digital format to be a potential addition to paper which may open up new opportunities for book reading. For example, this technology could supplement absent or unskilled parents and teachers. Considering the low cost and accessibility of digital books, this could provide valuable supplementary reading material in homes where access is restricted. And, of course on-line reading has advantages, as we have all discovered during the pandemic, in situations where adults and children cannot read together in person. While the gold standard remains adult mediated print book reading sessions, to the extent that digital books have the potential to get more books into the hands of more kids, let’s do it. Kathryn Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing support. She can be reached at pengilly.katie@gmail. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C .

articles.text: • • • • The school year has begun, and we are all relieved yet stressed to be back to full-time, in-person learning. Here are some things you can do to make this transition as smooth as possible. State Standards: They are now goals, not benchmarks Gaps in Learning: Find, Assess and Fill Go Easy: there will be ups and downs, so students will need more support than ever Bad Covid Grades? Switch them to Pass/Not Pass Standards don’t apply for now California has learning standards, but these were made before Covid. So, while it makes sense to strive to meet the state standards, know that your student will very likely not be there yet. Do you beed to get caught up? If a class is cumulative, you should ensure you learn what you missed. If it was a one-time class, you can likely move on without it. • Math and Foreign Languages: They’re cumulative, so get caught up. English and Social Studies: Reading and Writing Skills should be up to speed, but the subject matter is less important. Science and other classes: If some content wasn’t covered last year, it is probably OK unless students plan on taking a second year of these classes. Finding the holes Math and Foreign Languages Take a traditional practice final or final study guide that corresponds with whatever class students had last year. Don’t use last year’s modified distance learning version as it is likely to be incomplete. You can get a standard version from your school or contact Paul the Tutor’s. English and Social Studies The content of these classes is not as important as the ability to read for content and write a well written essay. To assess a student’s ability to read for content, have them read this year’s • • assignments and see if they are getting everything they should. You can also have them do a sample writing piece to see where their writing skills lie. So, you’ve found the holes, now what? Here you have a lot of options for getting your student caught up. Ask their teacher for review work and instruction, help them yourself, or get a tutor to do the catch-up work. The key is to work with them to get caught up gently, but thoroughly. Go Easy! While going back to school will be wonderful for many kids, it is likely to be anxiety producing and stressful too. Remember to go easy with this return to school and enjoy the ups and mitigate the downs. The more gently we treat ourselves and our students during this vulnerable time, the easier it will be for everyone. You can change unfair low grades California Assembly Bill 104 allows parents to request that low grades from 2020-2021 be converted from a letter grade to Pass or Not Pass. This will remove the letter grade from transcripts as well as from GPA calculations. For more information on this option contact your school counselor or Paul the Tutor’s. Paul the Tutor’s Education Services (www.paulthetutors. com), has provided tutoring, test prep and organizational coaching for students with learning disabilities and traditional learners since 1991. Paul the Tutor’s has an office on Piedmont Ave. and provides online education services for students throughout the nation.

Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir Camp is a chance to strengthen old friendships and begin new ones while learning music theory, doing crafts, working on new repertoire, playing games and living through music. We were on the Observatory Deck of Chabot Space and Science Center, and while we were missing an actual campfire, the tradition of sharing what meant the most at camp and the hopes for the year continued. Hearing one young soprano reflect upon how much she had come to value the ability to sing together and hear everyone else resonated. How often over the past sixteen or more months have each of us yearned to tune into each other, to both listen and to be heard? As our children come back to school – in our case to choir – as adults we want a “return to normal”. Continuing safety protocols amid uncertainty, continuing to “pivot” and adapt is hard to sustain. I hope we can take our cue from the young people in our lives and find ways to do what we love, even though for now it continues to look different than before. articles.text: Rodriguez The past 18 months have been challenging, to say the least: wildfires, drought, political unrest, social upheaval, and quarantine, not to mention a pandemic whose variants continue to leave the future uncertain. We all deserve a pat on the back for making it this far, albeit not unscathed. As adults, we can at least pretend to have some control over how we’ve navigated the pandemic. Our children, however, can’t really keep up that pretense. At a time in life when individuals can already feel powerless, our children have done more than their fair share of “rolling with the punches.” They’ve been unable to see family and friends. They’ve missed important coming-of-age moments like prom and graduation. They’ve had to learn how to navigate remote learning. And now, we ask them once more to adjust – they are returning to school full-time, in person. So, how do we best support our kids as they return to the new normal? First, it’s important to acknowledge that there may be some gaps, socially and academically. For many students, remote learning was challenging, and the structure and rigor of remote learning varied by school and subject. If your student seems to be dealing with some gaps in knowledge, don’t worry – they’re not alone and there are resources available to help. Many teachers hold office hours to address students’ questions. There are copious free or lowcost tutorials available online. If your student needs more individual attention, a peer or professional tutor may make the most sense. Helping your student develop good study habits is another important step in starting the school year strong and keeping the momentum going throughout the year. Students who know their schedules and deadlines will have a better understanding of how to work within those parameters and develop a priority list for their schoolwork. Students might benefit from a tutor. Encourage your children to find a tool (e.g. Google Calendar, a planner, or a checklist) that works for them and get in the habit of using that tool consistently. The important thing to remember is that we’re all in this together. None of us are the same as we were 18 months ago. But as we begin to make plans for the future, we can trust in our shared hope that our children can thrive once more. Emily Thompson is the Managing Director and Ariel Rodriguez is the Director of Operations at Study Smarter, LLC. articles.text: Woodminster Summer Musicals presents Jan de Hartog’s comedy I Do! I Do! on stage this weekend. Friday through Sunday, August 20-22. Live performances returned to Woodminster Amphitheater after a hiatus last year due to the coronavirus pandemic. Woodminster is an outdoor amphitheater in Joaquin Miller Park in the Oakland hills. It is a nonprofit organization that has presented summer musicals for over 50 years. Traditionally, three musicals are presented each summer. This year, after receiving clearance by Alameda County in early summer, two musicals are being presented, Hartog’s bedroom comedy The Fourposter serves as the basis for I Do! I Do!, a two-character musical. Originally directed by Gower Champion on Broadway, and with music by Harvey Schmidt, it features an evening-long journey through 50 years of marital bliss, infidelity, children, incompatibility, old age and simple joys. Woodminster’s production features Gary Stanford Jr. and Leslie Ivy. Performances are at 8 p.m. Doors open at 7 p.m., and there will be a 15-minute intermission. Tickets must be purchased in advance of the show. Also, for the first time in the organization’s history, a live concert series will begin with Deborah del Mastro on Friday, August 27. Visit www.woodminster.com for more information. Tickets are on sale and can be purchased by calling (510) 531-9597. Audience face masks are mandatory while entering, exiting, or moving about the theater. While sitting in your designated seat, you may remove your masks. Woodminster Amphitheater

articles.text: Playwright Dael Orlandersmith Aurora Theatre Company in Berkeley presents a filmed production, “Stoop Stories,” beginning September 3. The premiere combines prose, poetry and music by playwright and Pulitzer Prize finalist Dael Orlandersmith, creator of this solo show. The story is set in New York City, with a variety of characters drawn from the playwright’s personal life. Among them is an elderly Polish Holocaust survivor, a young poet struggling with addiction, a teenage Puerto Rican immersed in “Counter Culture,” and a 70-year old New York native on her way to a nightclub in the West Village to see Nina Simone sing. The production is directed by Elizabeth Carter. articles.text: H e l g i To m a s s o n h a s announced that he will retire as Artistic Director and Principal Choreographer of San Francisco Ballet by mid-2022. He has led the ballet company for nearly 40 years. “The unprecedented challenges we faced as individuals and as a community during 2020 only served to reconfirm for me the power of dance as a form of artistic expression, connection, and humanity. Over the past ten months, we had to innovate and completely reconceive how to bring dance to our audiences, since they could not come to us. In looking to the 2022 season, my aim is to build on these achievements and to bring the Company back to the stage for live performances,” Tomasson said. “Despite or perhaps because of the year we all lived through together, the Company has never been stronger than it is today. The timing felt right to begin a transition to a new Artistic Director, who will build on this legacy and lead the Company into its next chapter.” Tomasson was a distinguished dancer before assuming artistic leadership of San Francisco Ballet in 1985. Under his direction, the Ballet became a company widely recognized as one of the finest in the world. He has choreographed more than 50 works for the Company, including fulllength productions of Swan Lake, The Sleeping Beauty, Romeo & Juliet (taped for Lincoln Center at the Movies’ Great American Dance), Giselle, and The Nutcracker (taped for PBS’s Great Performances). San Francisco Ballet Director Helgi Tomasson. Tomasson has also connected San Francisco Ballet to the world through co-commissions with American Ballet Theatre, The Royal Ballet, and Dutch National Ballet. He has taken the Company on major tours to Paris, London, New York City, China, and his native Iceland. Last year Tomasson was nominated to receive the San Francisco Arts Medallion, created by the Museum of Performance and Design to recognize individuals whose leadership, action, and generosity have benefited the cultural life of the San Francisco Bay Area. The medal will be officially bestowed when in-person events can resume. “Helgi is a visionary whose creativity, brilliance, and stewardship of the Ballet is reflected both in the caliber of the Company’s work, as well as in the thoughtful transition plan that he helped conceive to support the organization’s ongoing vitality,” said Sunnie Evers, Co-Chair of the SF Ballet Board.
articles.title: Tomasson to retire after four decades leading SF Ballet

articles.text: Legion of Honor, part of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, is exhibiting “Iliazd: Publishing as an Art Form” now through October. The exhibit draws from the collection of Ilia Zdanevich’s work in the Reva, and David Logan Collection of Illustrated Books, “Iliazd: Publishing as an Art Form” will look at the work of the Russian Modernist whose collaborators included Pablo Picasso, Georges Braque, Alberto Giacometti, Max Ernst, and Joan Miró. Zdanevich created and published twenty-one artists’ books while working in Paris from 1921 to 1975, sixteen of which currently are in the Fine Arts Museums’ collection. This is the first U.S. museum collection devoted to the work of Zdanevich in more than three decades. While the artist was not a publisher in the conventional sense, he could be described as a self-publishing book artist, who commissioned his more famous peers to produce images for his books. “An illustrated book by Iliazd is a book by Iliazd, and not a book by Picasso, Miró, or Max Ernst,” said Louis Barnier, Director of the Imprimerie Union, Paris. “[It is] a standalone work of art just like a painting, a sculpture, a monument, a film. And Iliazd is its true and sole creator.” The exhibition is included with general admission to the museum. Museum hours are Tuesdays through Sundays, 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m. Visit https://legionof honor. famsf.org/exhibitions/iliazd to learn more and purchase tickets. Legion of Honor
articles.title: Publishing as an Art Form exhibit at Legion of Honor

pages.text: Wednesday, August 18, 2021 19 Arts & Entertainment Woodminster presents I Do! I Do! August 20-22 By Allyson Aleksey Woodminster Summer Musicals presents Jan de Hartog’s comedy I Do! I Do! on stage this weekend. Friday through Sunday, August 20-22. Live performances returned to Woodminster Amphitheater after a hiatus last year due to the coronavirus pandemic. Woodminster is an outdoor amphitheater in Joaquin Miller Park in the Oakland hills. It is a nonprofit organization that has presented summer musicals for over 50 years. Traditionally, three musicals are presented each summer. This year, after receiving clearance by Alameda County in early summer, two musicals are being presented, Hartog’s bedroom comedy The Aurora begins “Stoop Stories” on Sept. 3 Fourposter serves as the basis for I Do! I Do!, a two-character musical. Originally directed by Gower Champion on Broadway, and with music by Harvey Schmidt, it features an evening-long journey through 50 years of marital bliss, infidelity, children, incompatibility, old age and simple joys. Woodminster’s production features Gary Stanford Jr. and Leslie Ivy. Performances are at 8 p.m. Doors open at 7 p.m., and there will be a 15-minute intermission. Tickets must be purchased in advance of the show. Also, for the first time in the organization’s history, a live concert series will begin with Deborah del Mastro on Friday, August 27. Visit www.woodminster.com for more information. Tickets are on sale and can be purchased by calling (510) 531-9597. Audience face masks are mandatory while entering, exiting, or moving about the theater. While sitting in your designated seat, you may remove your masks. Woodminster Amphitheater Playwright Dael Orlandersmith By Allyson Aleksey Aurora Theatre Company in Berkeley presents a filmed production, “Stoop Stories,” beginning September 3. The premiere combines prose, poetry and music by playwright and Pulitzer Prize finalist Dael Orlandersmith, creator of this solo show. The story is set in New York City, with a variety of characters drawn from the playwright’s personal life. Among them is an elderly Polish Holocaust survivor, a young poet struggling with addiction, a teenage Puerto Rican immersed in “Counter Culture,” and a 70-year old New York native on her way to a nightclub in the West Village to see Nina Simone sing. The production is directed by Elizabeth Carter. articles.text: A special spaghetti dish named after a famous musician. Henry Kidman wasn’t his real name, but it’s a pretty good American translation. Henry was a hero. He didn’t look like an Olympic-type champion; he was short and stout. Balding also. He was more of a cult hero. In fact, Henry might have been the most famous cult figure of his generation. Only the President of the United States, or maybe Babe Ruth, got as much publicity as Henry. He died almost exactly 100 years ago. So, it’s about time that we evaluate why, exactly why, Henry was a hero. He was born into poverty, one of 20 children, and one of the few who survived childhood. Life was tough. Just surviving was an achievement. With little formal education, Henry was apprenticed to a mechanic. He didn’t like that very much. What he did like was music and drawing. But the deck was stacked against him almost from the start. His singing teacher said he had no talent. For him, it was one rejection after another,

articles.text: A retrospective art exhibit celebrating the life and works of Martha Dickson Skinner Gerardo continues at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Saturday, with open gallery hours from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Dickson Skinner Gerardo, known to friends and family as Marti, was born in Berkeley in 1944. She attended the University of California, Berkeley, pursuing dual degrees in Art and German from 1962 to 1966. She was a gifted and prolific artist who painted and drew until her death in January of this year. The works in the exhibition were carefully selected by family and curated by Laura Cincotta, the artist’s niece, to honor her life. Select pieces are available for purchase through her son, Sam Skinner. Festival Days continue at PCA The Piedmont Center for the Arts is celebrating its 10th Anniversary with Festival Days, a two-month series of music and art events in August and September. The festival kicked off on August 15 with the first public exhibition of Dickson Skinner Gerardo’s work. Artist Martha Dickson Skinner Gerardo Music events will be held both inside and outside the Center. Most events are ticketed, but some are free to the public. Visit www.piedmontcenterforthearts. org for more information.
articles.title: Art exhibit continues at PCA on Saturday

All the while, Henry continued to draw caricatures. With a few swift strokes of his pencil he could capture any subject on art paper. With his fame in another area, came fame as an artist. Now Henry was on a roll. Success followed success. Henry became the most famous singer in the entire world, and his caricature art was featured in newspapers across the country. He married a prominent socialite, whose father promptly disowned her. Curiously, she was not even interested in music. Henry loved food. There is a famous spaghetti recipe named for him. All you need to do is make spaghetti with red sauce and add some sautéed chicken livers. It’s that easy. And what about being tough? His last opera performance was at the Metropolitan Opera House in New York on Christmas Eve in 1920. His lungs began to hemorrhage – but he finished the performance - all the while vomiting blood. He returned to his hometown of Naples, Italy to die. It was there on August 2, 1921 that Henry Kidman died. But Henry Kidman is only an alias. In real life, he was the greatest operatic tenor of all time – a musician with the heart of a champion. If I could choose my favorite Olympic hero, I would take Henry Kidman. articles.text: Percussionist Benjamin Ring The Benjamin Jazz Trio will perform at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, August 29 at 5 p.m. He will be joined by Bay Area musicians Dahveed Behroozi on piano and Zachary Ostroff on bass. The group will perform a mix of jazz standards, popular song arrangements, and some of Ring’s original compositions. It is Ring’s first show at the Center and will be followed by a reception with food and drink. Masks are required. Background Benjam i n R i ng is an award-winning drummer, percussionist and composer based in Los Angeles. A Piedmont High graduate in 2016, Ring began playing drums and percussion at age 8. An accomplished composer, his first composition was premiered by the San Francisco Conservatory of Music percussion ensemble when he was 15. He has been recognized by festivals and institutions worldwide for his work in jazz and classical idioms. He graduated from USC with a Bachelor of Arts degree in 2019, and will enter the Herbie Hancock Institute of Jazz Performance at UCLA this fall, a prestigious, 2-year Master’s program comprised of a small ensemble chosen by audition from across the globe. He has performed across Europe, Japan and the United States, sharing the stage with world-class musicians and with members of the San Francisco and Chicago symphonies. He has received scholarships from SFJAZZ and the Monterey Jazz Festival, as well as awards from the National YoungArts foundation.
articles.title: Benjamin Ring Trio to perform at PCA Aug. 29

articles.text: Cuban pianist Omar Sosa will appear at SF Jazz on September 16. San Francisco Jazz hosts the world premiere of Omar Sosa’s “Motherland Journey,” live with sculptor Githinji Wa’Mbire and drummer Amaury Acosta on September 16. Celebrated Cuban pianist Sosa returns to SF Jazz with an innovative multimedia event performed in collaboration with Wa’Mbire and Acosta. The stage’s new advanced lighting and projection system will be utilized for the first time. The performance begins at 7 p.m. at the Miner Auditorium in San Francisco. All audience members, SF Jazz staff, and performing artists must be fully vaccinated against COVID-19. Prior to entering the auditorium, you will be asked to provide proof of vaccination through a QR code generated by “Digital COVID- 19 Vaccine Record” website, or an original physical vaccination card or photograph of it. Digital, online access is also available for this event, if patrons would prefer to livestream it. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ tickets/productions/omar-sosa-motherland-journey/ to obtain tickets.
articles.title: SF Jazz presents Omar Sosa live on Sept. 16

articles.text: Winemaker Nicolas Potel with vineyard manager Sylvain Debord. Last month I wrote about the estate wines of Domaine de Bellene, the Burgundian winery run by Nicholas Potel. Because the estate, like most in Burgundy, is small with little wine to sell, Potel wanted to find a way to expose more people to the wines of Burgundy. That was the origin of Maison Roche de Bellene – his negociant firm. A wine negociant buys wine from outside producers and bottles it under its own label. The quality of negociants varies widely, as everything depends on the ability to find and secure good grapes. The son of a famous vintner, Nicholas grew up in Burgundy. During his teenage years he traveled up and down the Cote d’ Or on his bicycle trading wines with growers and establishing life-long friendships. He has been working with some of those growers ever since he started his first negociant company nearly 25 years ago in 1998. Nicholas arranges to buy wine from small producers who vintify the wine on their own property. Final assemblage and bottling of the wine is done at the Roche de Bellene winery in Savigny-les-Beaune. I found the portfolio to be chock full of excellent examples of their terroirs. I also found some to be excellent values considering the incredibly inflated prices Burgundians now charge for their wines. The Maison Roche de Bellene wines are imported by Loosen Bros. based in Salem, Oregon. www.loosenbrosusa.com This entry level Bourgogne is an excellent introduction to Burgundy.

articles.text: The Wig Exchange, organized seven years ago by a group of Piedmont and Oakland residents, is holding its first local fundraiser. The fundraiser, entitled “Tie the Town Pink,” has been launched, and community members may participate by ordering a ribbon from the non-profit organization. The Wig Exchange began in the spare room of the Piedmont home of Narda Skov with about 100 wigs. The organization provides cancer survivors with the gift of hair. “For many women, hair loss is the most troublesome side effect of chemotherapy,” Skov explained. “A nice wig can ease that concern, but well-made wigs are expensive and may not be covered by insurance. Meanwhile, women who’ve finished their cancer treatments are often unsure as to what to do with their barely-used wigs. The Wig Exchange was started in the Fall of 2014 to address these exact concerns,” she said. Since its founding, the non-profit received donations steadily, allowing The Wig Exchange to move to new offices on Martin Luther King Boulevard in Oakland. Donations of gently used or new wigs are professionally cleaned and styled by Aveda Salon in San Francisco. Wig donations have been received from cancer survivors in over 30 states. Design and advertising campaigns for the fundraiser have been created by designer Hilary Wolfe, a Piedmont resident. To purchase a ribbon and learn more about the organization, visit: http://sanfrancisco. thewigexchange.org/home. The Wig Exchange is comprised solely of volunteers. Donations and purchases allow them to provide wigs free of charge. The cost of a ribbon is $25, and they will be hand-delivered in September to hang on your door or mailbox in support. For more information, call 510-333-7848, or email nardaskov1@gmail.com.
articles.title: Piedmont non-profit Wig Exchange hosts first fundraiser

articles.text: All of the different housing types we use can be divided into two main categories: single-family housing, and multi-family housing. While the vast majority of people in the industrialized urban world live in multi-family housing of one kind or another, in the U.S. an estimated 80% of housing units are single family, and 20-25% as multi family. There are a number of variations and hybrids, along with varying labels for the different types of housing but in my experience, the types shown in the accompanying diagram are common and understood by architects, developers, contractors and planners. For all communities the end result of different housing types is different densities, typically measured in units/acre. There is a huge difference from say, 3.5 units/acre for single family detached homes, to 12 units/acre for attached townhomes, to as many as 90 units/acre for urban high-rise multi-family. There are also many interconnected components to housing density and the resulting look, feel, and functioning of a neighborhood, including open space, roadway size and type, public transportation systems, and infrastructures of various kinds. (And parking, which we will leave for another column.) In my mind, a dividing line in the whole multi-family world can be defined by the entries. Units with their own separate outside entries, such as duplexes, townhouses or garden apartments, have a whole different character than denser types such as mid or high-rise buildings with entries necessarily located off a common corridor. The units in these denser, higher buildings can’t have the individuality, residential character and connection to the street that the lower density units do. The description of different architectural types of housing is sometimes confused with ownership categories. For example, a 10-unit “apartment” building can be owned by one person, in which case the 10 units would be rented out. This is the most common definition of “apartment”. But the same 10-unit building could also be a condominium, in which case the 10 occupants would each own the inside of their own unit with everything else being considered common space owned jointly by the 10 owners. In this case it would typically be called a “condo” and not an apartment building. Other forms of ownership such as co-ops are somewhat similar. In any case, these different types of ownership can be applied to all of the different architectural types, not just multi-family. Special purpose multi-family housing. like student housing, senior housing, affordable housing, or low-income housing, also can be designed in many of the architectural types, under a variety of ownership formulas, with the one-owner “apartment” model probably most common. Next: Multi-family Housing, Part 2 Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com Basic architectural housing types from least to most dense. There are numerous variations and hybrids of these basic types. Outside of central zones, like downtown Oakland or the Lake Merritt area, we are most familiar with single family detached (SFD) housing. Some “attached” single family units can be 4 times as dense as single-family dwellings, although still technically considered single family.
articles.title: Part 26: Multi-family Housing

articles.text: Photos by Peter Chin Harry Lew’s Congressional Gold Medal award. Lake Park resident This year, much of Lake Park Retirement in Oakland proudly turned out to celebrate a fellow resident Harry Lew. We had learned that Harry was to receive a special rendition of the Congressional Gold Medal, recently authorized by Congress after a long campaign to honor the thousands of Chinese American GI’s who served in World War II. We later learned that Harry was part of the campaign to gain that recognition. Because of the Chinese Exclusion Act, Chinese immigrants and their American-born families remained ineligible for citizenship until 1943 during the war. The Certificate and Legion medal were conferred by Helen Wong, Commander of American Legion Cathay Post 384. The Legion has been working to get the medals to the diminishing demographic of WWII veterans. Harry appeared wearing his uniform as a Tech Corporal from the 1940’s. He was a member of an amphibian tractor battalion. After the Allied Forces took Borneo, his language skills proved helpful in the interrogation and identification of enemy spies among the prisoners. Harry lives at Lake Park with his wife, Katie. Up and about early, friendly with all and sometimes seen dealing with a huge carton of laundry, he is a spry 98 years and just recently gave up tennis with his Lake Park friends. He still attends annual battalion reunions. Lake Park has about two dozen veterans among the residents and a dozen more of spouses of veterans from all branches of military service, including the war in Vietnam. Only two WWII veterans reside at Lake Park, Harry Lew and Bill Hardenstine. Lake Park resident Harry Lew in uniform.
articles.title: Lake Park resident given Congressional Gold Medal

articles.text: Lake Merritt residents Cynthia Ely (left), Pat Ross, and David Adams visit Ghirardelli Square for a lively day in San Francisco. The other day I received a call from a woman (we’ll call her Susan) who said she wanted to discuss living in a senior community. “When COVID hit I sheltered in place,” she said. “Yet, after all this time I’m feeling like a hermit. I am so separated from the world.” “If living through this pandemic has shown us anything,” I told her, “it’s the importance of community and socialization. So many people have felt isolated and lonely.” After chatting for a while, I asked a number of questions: Are you tired of being a homeowner? Are you struggling to keep up with housework, the yard, and home maintenance? What happens when you can no longer drive? By Dick Williams, Lake Park resident This year, much of Lake Park Retirement in Oakland proudly turned out to celebrate a fellow resident Harry Lew. We had learned that Harry was to receive a special rendition of the Congressional Gold Medal, recently authorized by Congress after a long campaign to honor the thousands of Chinese American GI’s who served in World War II. We later learned that Harry was part of the campaign to gain that recognition. Because of the Chinese Exclusion Act, Chinese immigrants and their American-born families remained ineligible for citizenship until 1943 during the war. The Certificate and Legion medal were conferred by Helen Wong, Commander of American Legion Cathay Post 384. The Legion has been working to get the medals to the diminishing demographic of WWII veterans. Harry appeared wearing his uniform as a Tech Corporal from the 1940’s. He was a member of an amphibian tractor battalion. After the Allied Forces took Borneo, his language skills proved helpful in the interrogation and identification of enemy spies among the prisoners. Harry lives at Lake Park with his wife, Katie. Up and about early, friendly with all and sometimes seen dealing with a huge carton of laundry, he is a spry 98 years and just recently gave up tennis with his Lake Park friends. Lake Park has about two dozen veterans among the residents and a dozen more of spouses of veterans from all branches of military service, including the war in Vietnam. articles.text: It’s OK to change your mind about being a caregiver. Often people take on caring for a family member with the best of intentions, but not knowing how long it will last, or how care needs will change, or how their own lives may evolve. They may find themselves ready for a new chapter or completely overwhelmed; some people even end up needing care for themselves after injury or illness resulting from overexertion as a caregiver. Consider these steps to change your caregiving role and maintain your own well-being: 1. Communicate, communicate, communicate. Talk to the health care provider and care team (maybe a professional caregiver, a physical or occupational therapist, etc.) about the status of current needs and anticipated care expectations for a loved one. Then plan a meeting with them and your loved one, or just share what you learned along with what you are capable of doing. Involve this person in the decisions as much as possible and share your limitations. 2. Do research together on interviewing caregivers, visiting facilities, reviewing insurance policies, and methods of paying for different long-term care options. In this way, the decisions are made together, and everyone is a stakeholder. If your loved one has a professional caregiver, and you are looking at a transition to a facility, it’s likely the caregiver can remain part of the care team for additional one-on-one care. 3. Take baby steps. If you’ve been doing all of the caregiving – driving Mom to and from medical appointments, making meals, giving medication reminders, assisting with bathing, being a companion to play games and socialize, and more – look into hiring a caregiver who can relieve you of a portion of these tasks so you can enjoy being a son, daughter, niece or nephew, grandchild, or spouse again. This way it does not have to be a big move, and you can oversee this new relationship and even be part of it. Remember that caregiving is a journey, not a destination, and will change over time for all involved. Feelings of guilt are normal and can be dealt with so that better choices can be made, helping avoid resentment and exhaustion, while continuing to be a caregiver. Homewatch CareGivers is locat­ ed at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmonters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said.
