articles.text: A self-guided walking tour of Piedmont which follows the city’s eight and a half-mile perimeter has been created by resident Matt Gerhardt, who presented a map to the Park Commission at their August 4 meeting. The Recreation Commission will discuss how it plans to use this map at its meeting this evening, August 18, at 7:30 p.m. The idea was born of Gerhardt’s experience on one of the “Walking on Wednesdays” excursions. “After I joined [Walking on Wednesdays], I started going farther and farther, north and south, and was getting fairly far. One day, Marilyn Weber and I decided to just walk around the entire perimeter,” Gerhardt said. The route took about 3-1/2 hours, he said. “It’s definitely a ‘hike,’” Gerhardt said with a smile. “And it’s up and down hills – but it’s fun.” Weber told Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap about the idea, who asked the pair to share their route with Park commissioners. The next time Weber and Gerhardt took the route, Gerhardt geo-tagged it through Google maps, creating a digital ‘hike.’ “It could be fun to have a joint program with the Recreation Commission, to include his route,” Dunlap told commissioners. Walking on Wednesdays was created by Recreation Commissioner Dick Carter, who was excited to learn about Gerhardt’s initiative. “We have walked some aspects of the perimeter. I think it’s terrific and I commend Matt for creating the perimeter route,” Carter said. Carter added that the Walking on Wednesdays group has helped foster old and new relationships among community members. Several members have even splintered off into a reading group. He believes Gerhardt’s idea of a self-guided map will generate the same level of interest and community. The Recreation Commission will receive an update on the map tonight, and Park Commissioners stated their plans to work jointly to present Gerhardt’s map formally to the community. “I know many residents who walk, and it’s great to actually have a destination, rather than just walking,” Park Commissioner Betsy Goodman said. “This will be fun – whether you do part of it or all of it, I think people will really get a kick out of it.”
articles.title: Gerhardt creates self-guided walking tour of city

articles.text: Wednesday Walkers gather at the upper end of the Oakland Avenue Bridge on August 11. Pictured are: Phil Witte (left), Albert Chen, Elangovan Shanmuga Sundaram, Ken Young, Quincy Dong, Alicia Rivera, Noemi Alvarado, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Harriette Louie, Charlene Louie, Carol Lyons, Wenny Young, Susan Martin, Melba Yee, Jim Kuo, Sarah Johnson, Priscilla Wanerus, Nancy Henn, Brenda Ferrero, Nancy Olsen, Helen Dong, Susan Field, Swee Ling Chen, Mike Henn, Stella Houston, and Haybert Houston. There was another strong turnout for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays on August 11, with 28 walkers. Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen was there to tell the walkers about her new “Meet Ups” initiative. She encouraged the walkers to email their ideas to her at ephalen@piedmont.ca.gov. One park not recently visited was the Linda Avenue Dog Park, so the decision was made to visit it and the adjacent Oakland Avenue Bridge, the historic entrance to Piedmont. Drawing on Piedmont Historical Society information from Gail Lombardi’s research, the walkers learned that Albert Farr designed the bridge in 1910 as a significant entrance to Piedmont, then in its third year as an incorporated city. Farr used the same Spanish design that he had used in the Piedmont City Hall and the Bonita Avenue School, later named Havens School. The bridge replaced a wooden trestle built in 1890 for the cable cars that served Piedmont in its early years. The bridge was built in 1911 by Engineer John Buck Leonard of Union City, Michigan, who was a pioneering bridge engineer, architect, and an early advocate of reinforced concrete. The bridge has architectural motifs such as steep walls and overhangs which were once used to prevent entry into medieval fortresses. The concrete arch bridge over Linda Avenue has a 160-foot arch span and retaining wall supported approaches in a closed spandrel concrete deck arch design. The bridge’s total length is 343 feet. The bridge carried 7,675 cars in 2007, an average of 20 vehicles a day. The relatively new lampposts, lights, and now the guardrails make the Oakland Avenue Bridge a lovely entrance to the city. Many walkers had never been to the Linda Avenue Dog Park next to the bridge. As the group walked through the park, they were surprised how attractive it is and were impressed with the improvements the City has made. The group emerged on to Linda Avenue and passed the new townhomes that were built on a former PG&E substation near the base of the bridge. The walkers continued on to the corner of Linda and Grand Avenue. Regular walkers identified this as the site where Axel R. Gruggel built his A Mon Chateau restaurant and beer garden in 1892. The walkers lamented that the beer is long gone. They went down Grand, carefully crossed it at Ace Hardware, and made their climb back up Wildwood and Magnolia Avenues to the Exedra starting point. It had been a 90 minute, little over two mile walk with and new and old friends, and fun for everyone. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.
articles.title: Walkers learn history of Oakland Ave. bridge

pages.text: Wednesday, August 18, 2021 27 HIKING WITH JON Squaw Peak and the Watson Monument By Jonathan Comeaux When you’re in the North Lake Tahoe area, take a worthy trip to Squaw Peak for the million-dollar view at an elevation of over 8,000 feet. Squaw Valley’s Olympic Village is a popular destination for Piedmont residents during ski season. During the summer months the region becomes a prime hiking location, with wildflowers and sweeping views of Lake Tahoe and Desolation Wilderness. Our day starts by taking the aerial tram to High Camp, which provides another incredible view from the observation platform looking back at Lake Tahoe. Olympic Village includes a popTake the tram up to Squaw Valley’s High Camp to start your day of hiking. Return for the food, view, or even some skating. Take the trail on the right toward Squaw Peak instead of the steep ascent on the left. Avoid the steep descent from the ill-advised ski slope. The view from Squaw Peak looking towards Lake Tahoe. ular restaurant, outdoor games, a skating rink, and a museum dedicated to the 1960 Winter Olympic Games. Its large pool and hot tub are closed for repairs. From High Camp, walking to Squaw Peak is a two-mile straight shot and around 850 feet in elevation gain, with the final 0.6 mile to the peak as the greatest ascent. The trail averages less than 10 percent gradient for the first mile before making the climb to Squaw Peak. At the 1.3-mile mark, hikers will come to a junction with a path on the left going up toward the Siberia Express ski lift. The preferred trail on the right takes you along the back toward Squaw Peak. Squaw Valley staff advised The Post to take the trail on the right as opposed to the steep jaunt toward the ski lift on the left where park attendants are working. The trail provides an unforgettable walk with bushels of wildflowers lining the path and butterflies fluttering around, On the right is the magnificent Granite Chief Mountain and Desolation Wilderness. From Squaw Peak hikers get a clear view of Lake Tahoe and a glimpse of Five Lakes. Pack a lunch to eat while enjoying the view. There are also mounds of shale enclosures to protect from the wind if needed. Returning to High Camp from Squaw Peak will round out your day at four miles. Those interested can follow a trail on the left to the Gold Coast Express ski lift, and then up to the Watson Monument Emigrant Pass Marker. Walking to the marker adds .4 miles to your day and another 300 feet in elevation gain. The nearby peak to the left of the marker (when facing the plaque) gives an even closer look of Granite Chief. articles.text: The Piedmont Community Service Crew spent a weekend at the Enchanted Hills Camp for the Blind in Napa on August 14-15 to make repairs at the camp, maintain trails, and reduce fire fuel by clearing out dead branches. Approximately 20 crew members and adult advisors volunteered their time for the overnight adventure. The main project was building steps and handrails along steep sections of the camp trails to guide visually impaired campers. Although crew members have been volunteering at Enchanted Hills for several years, it was the first time they stayed overnight. “For many of the blind children who attend the camp every summer, this is one of their few opportunities to connect with others and feel a sense of support,” explained PCSC co-president Julia Banuelos. “We were able to get a glimpse of this impact through meeting one of the former campers. Impacted by fires in the area, the camp is undergoing a lot of work, especially by volunteers.” The crew worked to create steps by digging close fitting trenches to partially bury timbers across the steep slopes, then back filled behind the timbers with gravel. All the wood used was custom milled from damaged trees on the property. In two days, the crew installed 15 stairs and cleared a quarter mile of debris. After each long day of work, the crew took time to refuel with sausages, salads and soups made by crew members and volunteer parents. Since the temperature was nearly 90 degrees, everyone got to have a dip in the camp’s pool to cool off. “The work the other volunteers and I did was very rewarding, and the property was so beautiful,” explained 11th grader Sofia Prieto Black. “It gave me the opportunity to disconnect from the ‘real world’ and enabled me to fully enjoy the company, the delicious food, and the peaceful nature that surrounded us.” The group will plan a service day or overnight later this fall. “The entire experience was so much fun. Although we were only there for two days, it felt like we were on a two-week camping trip. I loved bonding with the Photos by Ken Li Piedmont Community Service Crew members prepare an area for a handrail at a camp for the blind in Napa. Pictured are Lucy Filler (left), Samantha Violich, Mollie King, Vale Prieto Black, Charlie Lucas, Sofia Prieto Black, Michelle Lucas. crew and the ability to help such a wonderful organization,” said 11th grader Lucy Filler. Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), with approximately 150 members, is a youthled, co-ed Venturing Crew under the umbrella of Piedmont Scout Council. Founded in 2004 by current advisor Ken Li, PCSC aims to provide teens with the skills and opportunities to make an impact in the community. The crew partners with various organizations to do service projects around the San Francisco Bay Area. PCSC does not impose any minimum participation level and plans frequent opportunities for all its members. PCSC is youth-led; its members plan their own activities and learn how to do fundraising to cover the costs of their philanthropic work. Community Service Crew kickoff event on Aug. 29 Teens and adults interested in learning more about PCSC are invited to attend the PCSC Fall Kickoff on Sunday, August 29, from 4:00-6:00 p.m. To attend, please pre-register at www.pcservicecrew.org. For more information contact Crew Advisor Ken Li at ken.i.li@sbcglobal.net. pages.text: Wednesday, August 18, 2021 31 By Ava Adarkar The Piedmont Community Service Crew spent a weekend at the Enchanted Hills Camp for the Blind in Napa on August 14-15 to make repairs at the camp, maintain trails, and reduce fire fuel by clearing out dead branches. Approximately 20 crew members and adult advisors volunteered their time for the overnight adventure. The main project was building steps and handrails along steep sections of the camp trails to guide visually impaired campers. Although crew members have been volunteering at Enchanted Hills for several years, it was the first time they stayed overnight. “For many of the blind children who attend the camp every summer, this is one of their few opportunities to connect with others and feel a sense of support,” explained PCSC co-president Julia Banuelos. “We were able to get a glimpse of this impact through meeting one of the former campers. Impacted by fires in the area, the camp is undergoing a lot of work, especially by volunteers.” The crew worked to create Community Service Crew repairs camp for the blind in Napa steps by digging close fitting trenches to partially bury timbers across the steep slopes, then back filled behind the timbers with gravel. All the wood used was custom milled from damaged trees on the property. In two days, the crew installed 15 stairs and cleared a quarter mile of debris. After each long day of work, the crew took time to refuel with sausages, salads and soups made by crew members and volunteer parents. Since the temperature was nearly 90 degrees, everyone got to have a dip in the camp’s pool to cool off. “The work the other volunteers and I did was very rewarding, and the property was so beautiful,” explained 11th grader Sofia Prieto Black. “It gave me the opportunity to disconnect from the ‘real world’ and enabled me to fully enjoy the company, the delicious food, and the peaceful nature that surrounded us.” The group will plan a service day or overnight later this fall. “The entire experience was so much fun. Although we were only there for two days, it felt like we were on a two-week camping trip. I loved bonding with the Photos by Ken Li Piedmont Community Service Crew members prepare an area for a handrail at a camp for the blind in Napa. Pictured are Lucy Filler (left), Samantha Violich, Mollie King, Vale Prieto Black, Charlie Lucas, Sofia Prieto Black, Michelle Lucas. crew and the ability to help such a wonderful organization,” said 11th grader Lucy Filler. Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), with approximately 150 members, is a youthled, co-ed Venturing Crew under the umbrella of Piedmont Scout Council. Founded in 2004 by current advisor Ken Li, PCSC aims to provide teens with the skills and opportunities to make an impact in the community. The crew partners with various organizations to do service projects around the San Francisco Bay Area. PCSC does not impose any minimum participation level and plans frequent opportunities for all its members. PCSC is youth-led; its members plan their own activities and learn how to do fundraising to cover the costs of their philanthropic work. articles.text: Editor: I graduated from Berkeley majoring in Economics and not from Harvard in History. Still, I fully disagree with the opinion of Hannah Pinkham about the history and present role of the police in our society. Growing up and living in Central Europe during the first part of my life I learned that every society had and needed a police force to keep order and control those characters who endangered or ruined the life and security of the majority. I believe that to blame the police for enforcing slavery or later Jim Crow is incorrect. Granted, there were and still are members of the various police organizations who mistreat or even kill people of color as in Minneapolis.

articles.text: (This is the second in a fourpart sermon series titled “Summer Words: Bounty, Baseball, Barbecue, Beach”) Baseball is unique among the many sports of summer in that its goal is not to get a ball across a goal line but for the batter to return home. In most cases, the effort to return home ends short of its goal. An exciting beginning often gives way to a disappointing conclusion. When successful, the journey home is likely to require several stops, careful patience, and occasional risk. Rare is the journey home that simply requires a short touch of each of the bases. Further, the journey home does not have a timeclock. Each journey proceeds at its own unique pace. To find home, get home, return home is a profoundly human hope, and a deeply spiritual longing. Many of the great hymns of our faith are in touch with this longing. The last verse of “O God, Our Help In Ages Past,” written by Isaac Watts in the early 18th century of the Common Era, reads “O God, our help in ages past, Our hope for years to come, Be Thou our guide while life shall last, And our eternal home.” In the Bible, the hope that our home is with God and that God’s home is with us receives frequent expression. articles.text: The following letter was sent to Piedmont City Council and city staff. Editor: I am writing on behalf of the League of Women Voters of Piedmont regarding the 2021 Alameda County Grand Jury Report on “The Need for Accuracy and Impartiality of Ballot Measure Questions.” A copy of the report is attached and can also be found online at http://grandjury.acgov. org/grandjury-assets/docs/2020- 2021/Ballot%20Measures.pdf. The grand jury’s report focused on the accuracy, transparency and impartiality of government sponsored ballot questions. They found that ballot questions suffer from “proponent’s bias” and fall short of what voters have a right to expect in terms of truthfulness and impartiality. The League supports transparency in local government and there are few better examples for the necessity for transparency than in the language of a government sponsored ballot question. Language that is biased, unclear, or unnecessary falls short of our expectations for a fair and transparent government. Looking specifically at the example of Piedmont’s Measure TT, the grand jury found that the ballot question contained language that was irrelevant or unnecessary to describe the measure. The grand jury also found that because of the irrelevant or unnecessary language that delineated specific spending, Measure TT could have been mistaken by voters to propose a special tax instead of the general tax that it is. This is especially troubling because approval of general tax measures requires only a simple majority whereas special tax measures require a two-thirds majority. Both the League’s published a Pros & Cons document and the City Attorney’s Impartial Analysis of Measure TT stated, “[funds] generated by the proposed tax increase are not restricted and may be used for any City general revenue purpose.” We know that not all voters have access to nor will be able to read these additional resources prior to casting a ballot. It is important for voters that language of the ballot question itself be unbiased and clear. We hope that the City of Piedmont will ensure that the language of future ballot questions addresses the concerns set forth in the grand jury report. We are copying the Piedmont Unified School District Board of Education on this letter so they may also keep these principles in mind when sponsoring ballot measures in the future. The League stands ready to assist in any efforts that will result in a more fair and transparent local government. Lorriel A. Plimier is President of the League of Women Voters of Piedmont.
articles.title: Grand Jury raises questions about ballot measures

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department, in an ongoing effort to increase transparency and meet the community’s needs, has introduced its strategic plan for 2021-2024 to the public. The plan outlines priorities and objectives aligned with the department’s vision, mission, and values in providing police services, pro- “This strategic plan represents the collaborative efforts of many people who took the time and had the trust to engage in open and honest conversations about community safety in our city,” said Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. He explained that it comes at a critical time in Piedmont’s history, as residents navigate a pandemic, environmental challenges, and address social equity issues, especially following the murder of George Floyd by former Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin in May 2020. “While the outcomes of these challenges are not known, we are confident that our partnerships, openness, and accountability will position the department to meet the current day challenges as well as challenges yet to come,” he said. The outlined plan includes planning processes, team building, key imperatives, external communication engagement, and policing and legislative reforms. Ongoing strategy efforts, including the evaluation and assessment of the Juvenile Officer program, are also outlined. The department consulted the professional services of Dr. Marilyn Manning to gather input from the community, police department staff and city employees when developing the plan. Focus group sessions represented members of the community to include Piedmont seniors, Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) and Piedmont Anti-Racism Diversity Committee (PADC), the school district, worship communities and more. “We want to be transparent with you, our residents, about our police department’s policies and procedures. We acknowledge that, while we strive to employ progressive policies and a culture of accountability among our ranks, we can always do better,” Bowers said. articles.text: Piedmont Community Church is now enforcing Alameda County’s mandate of face coverings for all regardless of age or vaccination status. The requirement follows guidance directed from the County of Alameda Health Department and the federal Centers for Disease Control (CDC), which both call for mask-wearing indoors. This will be enforced for all, including during worship in the Piedmont Community Church Sanctuary, regardless of vaccination status. The new health mandate requires wearing well-fitting masks that cover both nose and mouth in all indoor public settings. Visitors may also ask an usher for a mask at the door before worship services. In-person worship will continue this Sunday, August 15, at 10 a.m. Visit https://www. piedmontchurch.org/ to learn more about the church’s safety protocols.

articles.text: StopWaste, a public agency aimed at reducing waste in Alameda County, will host a hazardous waste disposal event this Sunday, August 15. Interested participants are asked to gather household hazardous waste items, such as batteries, pesticides, paint, paint thinners and cleaners, and dispose of them at the one-day drop-off event in Oakland. Residents may also bring up to two mattresses and two box springs to the event. Other items that will be accepted are light bulbs, electronics and small appliances, propane tanks, old medications, oil and auto fluids, fire extinguishers, and sharp containers. For a full list of what is and is not accepted, visit https://www. stopwaste.org/about-stopwaste/ events/hhw-one-day-event-inoakland-2021-08-15. Participants will learn how to safely package waste items, and are given the opportunity to learn more about Oakland’s Household Hazardous Waste program. Space is limited, and you must register early to guarantee that you get an appointment. Participants are asked to remain in their vehicle with face coverings on, and items you wish to dispose of must be in an unlocked trunk or back cargo space. You must register for an appointment to receive the address of the dropoff location. articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Police and Piedmont Fire Departments visited five neighborhoods with BBQ events on Tuesday, August 3 during the city’s annual National Night Out event. More than 100 residents came out for the event which is designed to unite neighbors and to familiarize them the police and fire officials. National Night Out began in 1984, and now has over 10,000 communities participating in the event. The fire department brought out their fire engines and the police sent 13 officers and dispatchers around town to events held at Waldo and Blair, Cavanaugh Court, Ranleigh Way, Huntleigh Road, and the roundabout at Alta and Scenic. Most locations had 15-20 participants. The largest get together was at Waldo and Blair, which had around 60 residents partaking in the festivities. A taco truck was stationed at the Waldo Avenue event organized by resident Marilyn Weber. “There was great attendance at each location,” said Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, “As soon as I got out of the car I had really great dialogues. Rich communication and discussions resulted from residents’ interesting questions.” Bowers credited Police Captain Chris Monahan and Officer Nicole Casalnuovo for their work organizing the events. Bowers was pleasantly surprised with the popularity of the event and found himself watching his wristwatch to make sure he had enough time to visit all the locations between 5:00 and 8:00 p.m. Police Department Support Services Commander Lisa Douglas is in charge of the Department’s social media outreach which Bowers started in 2016. Her participation in the event gave the department valuable takeaways about community communications. “She found that even though it feels like we are putting out a lot of communication on our social media accounts, it was amazing the amount of times people expressed that they weren’t aware of what we are doing.” Bowers said. He acknowledged that outreach to the community through events like this and in print journalism helps reach sectors of the community social media does not. Piedmont Police Officer Nicole Casalnuovo chats with two young crime fighters at the National Night Out, an event Casalnuovo helped organize. A Piedmont Firefighter shows off the big, shiny fire truck to curious Piedmont kids at National Night Out on August 3. Piedmont Police officers join residents for a photo opportunity at National Night Out on August 3.
articles.title: National Night Out a time for residents to meet police, fire staff

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department is gearing up for its 3rd annual Car Show on Labor Day morning, Monday, September 6. The lineup of cars will be in the parking lot in front of the Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, from 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. The last time the event was held in 2019, 44 gleaming vehicles were on display. From classic cars to late model Ferraris and Bugattis, the vehicles and owners will be there ready to show to car buffs. Coffee will be served, and neighbors are invited to meet members of the police department while viewing and chatting with the car owners. The event is part of the larger “Coffee with a Cop” national campaign, which was started in 2016 as a way for residents to meet local law enforcement members. In 2018 the Piedmont Police Department decided to rev up the event by adding classic cars to the mix. The community responded enthusiastically, and more than 1600 people showed up. Officer Tyler Petit is coordinating the show. Piedmont residents interested in participating in the city’s version of the unofficial Concours d’Elegance are asked to contact Officer Petit at tpetit@piedmont.ca.gov. Include your name, address, email, and phone number along with the year, make and model of your car. Piedmont residents are invited to enter their classic cars in the 3rd annual PPD Car Show, sponsored by the police department on Labor Day morning, September 6. Above is a 1954 Mercury Sport Coup owned by Robert Walz; one of the 44 cars that participated in the 2019 event.
articles.title: PPD invites residents to display their classic cars Sept. 6

articles.text: John Cumbelich and Jack Gros, members of Piedmont Scout Council’s Troop 6, were feted at a National Court of Honor on August 5 at the Piedmont Community Hall Amphitheater on the occasion of attaining the rank of Eagle. John G. Cumbelich A Scout since 2016, Cumbelich earned 43 Merit Badges and was a member of the Order of the Arrow. He was a Patrol leader, Quartermaster and Troop 6 drummer, and delivered the official State of Scouting Report to the State Legislature. He attended a range of camps, from Cherry Valley to Philmont, and attended the World Scout Jamboree in 2019. articles.text: On Monday, August 9 Piedmont Middle and High School students faced reality as their dreams of an endless summer came to an end. It was the day before the new school year, and time for the annual walkthrough registration. Students in 6th-12th grades returned to campus to pick up their schedules, planners, T-shirts, and swap last year’s textbooks for this year’s. Students were dressed in their favorite outfits for their school photos as well. They faced the flash of a camera marking the end of summer and the resumption of their academic pursuits. The mood and pace differed at the two sites. The Middle School gym hosted the walkthrough for 6th, 7th, and 8th graders, and was streamlined, without any wait time. “Yesterday [at PMS Walkthrough Registration] was the most excited I had ever seen families to be back at school – teachers too,” said veteran 6th grade teacher Ted Scherman. In contrast, the spacious high 6th grader Drew Devries holds up his new Scots Camp shirt received at walkthrough registration at Piedmont Middle School on Monday, August 9. school gym was not used for 9th through 12th graders. The small Student Center in the middle of the quad was used principally for student ID photos, and textbooks were picked up in the adjacent library. It appeared that no time slot reservations were being used, resulting in a long line of students curled around the quad well after registration began at 12 noon. Given the heat of the day and absence of shade on the grass-less quad, students were soaking up some extra summer sunrays before having their pictures taken. ”Usually, the kids are inside instead of outside baking in the sun. It looks like everyone wanted to show up early to get their schedules early,” said Piedmont mom Kristen Malan at 3 p.m. while handing out student schedules. articles.text: We are back and school is upon us. Last year was just about the weirdest year ever for our kids, so this fall might feel a little intimidating or scary for some little ones. In good news, our kids are resilient and strong, but it makes total sense that they might have a lot of big feelings associated with being back in the classroom. Here are some creative ideas that might be helpful to ease the backto-school transition. 1. If kids are nervous about going back to school, try role play! First, act out what the first day of school might actually be like, then try the OTT version (Over the Top) where everything is silly and exaggerated. Try switching roles. You can be the teacher and your child can be the student, and then switch. 2. Help kids feel ownership of their back-to-school process with an art project to decorate a new lunch box or a backpack. Using glitter glue pens or fabric markers give kids the freedom to go to town on an item they will be bringing with them to school. This gives them a sense of control and helps them bring their own unique perspective and artistic voice into an otherwise unfamiliar situation. 3. Kids need practice reading other people’s emotions – particularly with masks. Remind them of the importance of using their eyes to express and read emoKids and a mom on the first day of school. tions. Practice “HAPPY,” “SAD,” “ANGRY” and “SILLY” eyes. Make it into a game and see if you can guess each other’s emotions. 4. Let your story be their school Super Power. Tell them the story of your first day of school or a memorable moment from your childhood at school with this framework: A LONG TIME AGO, WHEN I WAS YOUR AGE, I HAD A HARD TIME WITH _______ . I FELT _______ WHEN I WAS GOING TO ________. I TOOK MY DEEP BREATHS AND I _______. IT WAS SCARY AT FIRST, BUT THEN I REALIZED _______. 5. Do you walk to school? How about dancing to school instead? Take turns leading different silly dance moves as you walk. Bonus: play some fun music on your phone as you go. Not walking, but driving? No problem. Use arm-dancing that you can do SAFELY while driving. Whatever you choose to do, keep in mind that the more creative play and imagination you can bring to the back-to-school process, the more your kids will have opportunities for laughter and joy. Laughter is proven to reduce anxiety and stress and, I think we all could use a little of that this fall. Nina Meehan is CEO of Bay Area Children’s Theatre. For more information, click on Bay Area Children’s Theatre – Sparking Creativity, Inspiring Imagination (bactheatre.org).
articles.title: Thinking Outside The Classroom Using creativity to ease back-to-school transition

articles.text: On July 22, the Piedmont High Adventure Crew (HAC), a coed teen Venture unit under the auspices of the Piedmont Scout Council, went on a 5-day backpacking trip in eastern Yosemite National Park. With Lisa Gros, Mike Bandrowski and Bryan Gros as adult leaders, a group of five teens drove to Mono Village Resort in Toiyabe National Forest, where they camped overnight before their hike. The following morning, they headed into Hoover National Wilderness for a steep uphill 2,500-foot climb 8-1/2 miles to Peeler Lake at an elevation of 9,500 feet. To refuel after a long day of hiking, they cooked vegetable curry for dinner and snacked on some marshmallows for dessert. On day 2, they descended 1,600 feet over an 8-mile hike to the sandy shores of Benson Lake in Yosemite National Park, where they camped for two nights. For Valerie Xiong, a 4-year crew member and the camp chef, the trek to the lake was a highlight of the trip. “It was just miles of verdant valley with wildflowers lining the trail and mountains all around. Jasper Zietlow takes in the view from Volunteer Peak. The natural beauty of the High Sierra always amazes me,” she said. On the third day the crew went on a short hike following a stream up to a nearby pass. In the afternoon, it began to rain, so they bonded by holding an informal talent show under the shelter of a stand of lodgepole pines. The morning after, they got up early to retrace their steps, starting with a steep hike out of Benson Lake. After completing an additional seven miles through the meadows of Yosemite, the group arrived again at the clear water of Peeler Lake, where they went for a refreshing swim. It began to rain heavily that night, so the teens huddled together in a tent to watch Free Solo, a rock-climbing movie one of the hikers had downloaded onto a phone. One of the best aspects of the High Adventure Crew backpacking trips is getting to know the other people on the trip. The fifth day of hiking was a High Adventure Crew members stop at Barney Lake for lunch on the first day of hiking. Front: Mike Bandrowski; rear from left: Lisa Gros, Jasper Zietlow, Clare Murphy, Valerie Xiong, Sophie Eng, Aya Troyer, Brian Gros Lunchtime at Barney Lake. (Front) Valerie Xiong (left), Sophie Eng, Aya Troyer, Clare Murphy; (back) Jasper Zietlow, Lisa and Bryan Gros. downhill trek from Peeler Lake back to Mono Village. Surrounded by the scent of the damp forest, the backpackers took many photos, absorbing the last part of the trip. After returning to the cars, the group had some well-earned burgers, milkshakes, and burritos before heading back to Piedmont. The High Adventure Crew’s mission is to bring youth into the great outdoors through a variety of outings, ranging from day hikes to weeklong backpacking trips. As a mainly youth-led organization, most of the trips are planned as a team, allowing members to go on unique trips with an enthusiastic and experienced group of teens and adult leaders. “Backpacking through HAC is a great way to push yourself while also having an amazing time away from your regular life and responsibilities,” explained Aya Troyer, a senior member of the crew and a college freshman. “Instead of being surrounded by technology and lots of people, you can enjoy the beautiful nature

articles.text: Staff Photo JoJo Murphy recently won WestCoastPreps.com’s Bay Area Boys’ Basketball Athlete of the Year Award. Piedmont High senior JoJo Murphy walks into his final year at the school with some nice credits. He recently was named Bay Area Basketball Athlete of the Year by WestCoastPreps.com. “Watching him was just like watching Stephen Curry and Klay Thompson during their many, many, many flurries on the basketball court. Piedmont junior guard JoJo Murphy was a potent shooter every single game, easily someone one could expect to score 30-plus points and knock down five or more three-pointers in just a 32-minute high school game,” wrote Chris Jackson of West Coast Preps. Last season Murphy helped his team with 25.6 points per game, 48 percent overall from the floor and 43 percent from beyond the arc, to go along with 6.6 rebounds, 3.9 assists and 2.9 steals. He was also named to the Top 25 list by the San Jose Mercury News. Murphy led the Highlanders in five categories: 409 points, 55 three-pointers, 105 rebounds, 58 assists, and 46 steals. In five games he scored 30 or more points, including a careerhigh of 38 against San Leandro on May 7. He capped the year with seven 3-pointers against Bishop O’Dowd in the season finale on June 4. He helped PHS finish with an 11-5 record and a potent one-two punch with the Post’s Athlete of the Year Luke Harris, who graduated this year. Murphy was the Post’s Sophomore of the Year in 2020 and Freshman of the Year in 2019.
articles.title: Murphy named West Coast Preps’ Bay Area Basketball Athlete of the Year

He’ll have an opportunity for another upset in today’s match against Argentina’s Diego Schwartzman, who enters ranked No. 14 in the world. Piedmont native Mackie McDonald fought his way to the championship match at the Citi Open ATP 500 in Washington D.C. before falling to Italy’s Jannik Sinner in a tights 3-set match, 7-5, 4-6, 7-5 on Sunday, August 8. McDonald entered as an unseeded entrant, and nearly upset the No. 5 seeded Sinner, who is the world’s No. 15 ranked player. On the road to the finals, McDonald upset five ATP top- 100 players. As a result, his world ranking jumped to No. 64 on the ATP World Tour. His highest ranking was No. 57 in April 2019 prior to sustaining a hamstring injury. “I dug as deep as I could,” McDonald said during the postmatch ceremony, via ESPN. “Obviously, Jannik is a great, young player and he pushed me really hard today. I think I left it all out there.” It marked McDonald’s first ATP Tour finals appearance of his career and first championship round since winning an ATP Challenger in Kazakhstan in February. To reach Citi Open’s final round, McDonald opened with a 6-4, 6-4 win over Australia’s Nick Kyrgios on August 3. Kyrgios is No. 80 in the world and was the defending Citi Open champion. He followed up in August 4’s Round of 32 by upsetting No. 13 France’s Benoît Paire in three sets 7-6 (8-6), 6-4, 6-4. Paire, ATP’s No. 50. In the Round of 16, McDonald upset Portugal’s Ilya Ivashka 6-4, 6-4., ranked No. 67. McDonald then beat fellow American, Denis Kudla, 6-3, 6-2. Kudle, another top-100 player, is ranked No. 90 in the world. articles.text: The Dixie Fire has escalated to 487,764 acres as of August 10 as it wages through Butte, Lassen, Plumas, and Tehama counties. It is now the largest single-source fire in California history and has obliterated the historic town of Greenville. As of August 10, 893 residential or commercial structures have been destroyed with another 14,000 being threatened. The fire is 25% contained according to Cal Fire. With fire season, the subsequent impact on air quality can quickly blanket areas with smoke. Luckily for the Bay Area, the winds off the Pacific are currently keeping the East Bay in the green. However, inland winds typically pick up in the fall and could keep smoke in the Bay Area similar to September 2020. Hikers in the Lake Tahoe region er faced with an air quality index of 122, deemed unhealthy, with a forecast of only a moderate range for the next week. The air quality in Yosemite Valley was 76 and was forecasted to stay in the moderate range until clearing up this weekend, August 14-15. East Bay Regional Park District East Bay Regional Park District announced on July 14 that it received a grant of $13.5 million from the State for wildfire prevention, with $10 million specifically earmarked for addressing the issue of sudden tree die-off. EBRPD will provide further study on tree die-off in its parks and replace fire equipment including an aging helicopter. “[We will] specifically remove dead and dying trees in Regional Parks, a new tree mortality phenomenon occurring in several parklands,” explained EBRPD Fire Chief Aileen Theile. “$3.5 million of the State appropriation was proposed to provide for fire equipment that will improve the Park District’s ability to fight fires, including the replacement of its aging helicopter which is relied upon as a primary tool to drop water on fires burning in inaccessible terrain.” “EBRPD has more than 1,500 acres of dead or dying trees affected by drought and climate change conditions that need immediate attention,” she said. “These State funds couldn’t come at a better time, as we are shovel ready with designated projects to remove dangerous fuels in District parks while helping to keep forests healthy.”
articles.title: East Bay Regional Park District receives $13.5 million for fire prevention

articles.text: For Bay Area residents, the welcome sight of Horsetail Falls’ gushing waters off in the distance of U.S. Highway 50 means you’ve nearly arrived at South Lake Tahoe. In Twin Bridges between Strawberry and the Sierra at Tahoe Resort is a magnificent 500-foot waterfall that cascades into Pyramid Creek. It’s just 30 minutes from Stateline, Nevada and a worthy visit should readers consider vacationing in the area. Horsetail Falls is four miles round trip, all while hiking beside the beautiful flowing Pyramid Creek. The trail gets steeper as you ascend toward the falls. The two-mile mark is 750 feet in elevation gain at an elevation of over 6,100 feet. The majority of legwork comes in the final half mile over steep boulders and rocks (proper footwear is required). Although our day ended at two miles, the trail continues up the mountain into backpacking areas for another mile to the mouth of the falls and access to countless alpine lakes. Avalanche Lake is at the top of the falls. The entire trail is little maintained, but following the beaten path is simple enough, aided by small, blue spray-painted markings to keep hikers on the trail. The rewards for hikers makThe hike along Pyramid Creek is just as majestic as the award of reaching Horsetail Falls. The trail continues over a vast rockface into the Desolation Wilderness. A view of Desolation Wilderness ascending the trail. Starting the hike at the Pyramid Creek Trailhead.

articles.text: Fitz & the Trantrums headline this Sunday’s free concert at Stern Grove. Stern Grove Festival continues its 84th concert season this summer with a performance by Fitz and the Tantrums this Sunday. A free concert is presented every Sunday at 2 p.m. throughout the summer, and there are two concerts left. Fitz & the Tantrums is a multi-platinum, Los Angeles-based sextet formed in 2009. The alternative group is known for dance-inspired tunes, blending ’60’s Motown, ’70s funk, and ’80s New Wave. Fitz & the Tantrums will be preceded by Devon Gifillian, a Philadelphia-based hip-hop artist. Gilfillian takes his inspiration from Ray Charles, Stevie Wonder, Otis Redding, and The Temptations. DJ Omar opens this Sunday’s event at 2 p.m. Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization whose mission is to make live musical experiences accessible to all. Since its inception in 1938, the organization has presented the free concert series “Stern Grove Festival” in Sigmund Stern Grove, an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. The amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites. The festival has brought more than eight decades of performing arts – including opera, theatre, and music – completely free. Capacity is reduced due to a Covid-related county mandate, and advance registration is required. No admittance before 12 p.m. is allowed. Visit https:// www.sterngrove.org/84th-concert-season to reserve a space. ®
articles.title: Stern Grove Festival presents Fitz & the Tantrums on Sunday

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will present Giacomo Puccini’s opera Tosca, live on-stage, beginning August 21 and running through September 5. Titular character Floria Tosca faces a brutal police chief whose cruelty forces her to sacrifice everything she cares for in the hope of surviving. Ailyn Pérez, Michael Fabiano, and Alfred Walker star in the revival of Shawna Lucey’s period production. Music Director Eun Sun Kim will take the baton to conduct Tosca as her first opera in the position. The production is 2 hours and 45 minutes with two intermissions, with five performances at either 7:30 p.m. or 2 p.m. Ticket inventory is limited. For tickets, see: https://sfopera. com/on-stage/tosca/.
articles.title: SF Opera presents Tosca beginning August 21

articles.text: Li n -M a nuel M i r a nd a’s acclaimed musical Hamilton returned to San Francisco’s Orpheum Theatre for a limited four-week run, from August 10 through September 5. The sung-and-rapped musical tells the story of American Founding Father Alexander Hamilton. Miranda said he was inspired to write the musical after reading Ron Chernow’s 2004 biography of Hamilton. The show draws heavily from pop, soul, hip-hop, and a traditional style of show tunes. It received Tony Awards for Best Musical and Best Original Score, and a Pulitzer Prize for Best Drama. The musical routinely receives rave reviews in publications across the U.S. and abroad. A review in The Economist in London summed up the response to Hamilton as “near-universal critical acclaim.” The original Broadway cast recording received a 2016 Grammy Award for Best Musical Theatre Album. The show runs for two hours and 45 minutes and includes one intermission. The musical is produced by Jeffrey Seller, Sander Jacobs, and Jill Furman; the fourweek performance is directed by Thomas Kail with choreography by Andy Blankenbuehler and musical supervision by Alex Lacamoire. The show is recommended for ages 10 and up due to strong language. Anyone 15 and under must be accompanied by an adult attending the same performance, and no children under age 5 are allowed. All ticket holders, regardless of age, are required to show proof of full COVID vaccination or negative test results from a COVID PCR test, taken within 72 hours of performance time, for entry into the theatre. All patrons, regardless of age and vaccination status, are required to always wear a mask inside due to the county and city order. For tickets visit: https:// h a m i l t o n . b r o a d w a y s f . c o m / O n l i n e / d e f a u l t . The musical Hamilton returned to Orpheum Theatre yesterday. articles.text: Piedmont Center for the Arts The Piedmont Center for the Arts is celebrating its 10th Anniversary with Festival Days, a two-month series of music and art events in August and September. Festival Days begins on Sunday, August 15, with a special string quartet concert presented by the Chamber Music Society of San Francisco, an ensemble that has performed previously at the Center. The first public exhibition of art of the late local artist Martha Dickson Skinner Gerardo will be on view in an extensive retrospective. The following two weekends will include performances by the Piedmont Troubadours vocal a capella chamber group, blues guitarist Jules Leyhe and The Family Jules, a jazz trio led by Benjamin Ring, and a spectacular viola recital. During Festival Days in September there will be performances by a well-known local violinist and a classical guitarist against the backdrop of an art quilt exhibition exploring the concept of hope through times of wildfires and Covid. The newly formed Renegade Orchestra will present a selection of non-traditional takes on orchestra music. Events will be both inside the Center and outside in front of the building. Most events will be ticketed, and some will be free to the public. Passes providing prepaid entrance to all events will be available at a reasonable cost the week before the opening concert and will be an easy way to help underwrite the expenses of presentation. terforthearts.org for more information. articles.text: Pianist Mark Anderson, Piano Chair at the University of British Columbia, performed a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday afternoon. The Piedmont Center for the Arts opened to public concerts on Sunday afternoon in grand style. The walls were festively decorated with a spectacular photography exhibit by Virginia Hong. The Piedmont Troubadours opened the festivities with a brief set of a cappella singing. Raconteur extraordinaire Jonathan Dimmock spoke briefly and told the audience how all of the arts are connected. Hong, a San Francisco photographer, is very self-effacing about her art. She has traveled the world and is able to capture these peregrinations vividly. The photos are absolutely natural and not enhanced in any way. When she takes pictures of animals, she lies and waits for them to create the remarkable images she is able to capture. That is part of the beauty of her art. Another part is the beautiful presentation. It was an exhibition worth seeing, and unfortunately ended after Sunday’s concert. The musical part of the afternoon opened with the Piedmont Troubadors. They are, as always, a delight. I heard them not long ago in an impromptu alfresco program at a neighbor’s home. This time they sang indoors with a completely different program. They convey the joy of singing which makes them one of Piedmont‘s treasures.
articles.title: Of music and magic wands

articles.text: Festival Opera continues its 30th Anniversary Season with the world premiere of “A Jake Heggie Triptych” featuring the award-winning composer and pianist live, this Friday on August 13. Another performance will be held on August 15, both at the Hofmann Theatre at the Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek. The world premiere will feature three song cycles, reimagined as fully-staged operas. For these two productions, composer and pianist Jake Heggie is joined by acclaimed singers Carrie Hennessey, Diana Tash, award-winning actor Curt Branom and Festival Opera General Director Zachary Gordin. The song cycles are reimagined as fully-staged chamber operas. The Triptych is the result of Gordin’s long relationship with Heggie’s music. “I’ve been a huge fan of Jake’s work since the release of his ‘The Faces of Love’ [1999] album, which featured many dear colleagues and friends. I was immediately struck by his ability to build a whole environment with his piano writing, how operatic in nature it is, like the music provides both an orchestra and scenery,” Gordin said. “As a singer Opera composer Jake Heggie who is always looking for the essential truth in the music and stories I’m telling, it was a revelation to see his vocal writing truly mirroring the inflection, joy, and pathos of the human voice with honesty, setting texts in an immediately accessible, and deeply compelling way.” “I’m thrilled and deeply honored that Festival Opera will present this dynamic triptych of my compositions, beautifully cast with stunning performers,” Heggie said. “The human quest for identity and connection links this trio of works, which were created with my most frequent collaborators – Gene Scheer and the late, great American playwright Terrence McNally. What a dream for this to unfold in the East Bay, where long ago I studied piano as a teenager.” Triptych will have a live performance on Friday, August 13 at 7:30 p.m. and on Sunday, August 15 at 2:00 p.m. in the Hofmann Theatre at the Lesher Center for the Arts. articles.text: Julia Roberts and Lucas Hedges in a scene from Ben is Back. Drug addiction – in Ben is Back it’s opioids – is the equivalent of dropping a stone into a still pond and bearing witness to the fact that what takes place is not just about that singular stone vanishing beneath the surface, but about the ripples that follow, moving ever outward in concentric circles. The metaphor conveys that the addict does not walk his or her path alone, but often leaves a wake of fragmented ruin. In Ben is Back the addict is 19-year-old Ben Burns who unexpectedly appears at his family’s upstate New York home, having left rehab. He is standing in the front yard as his mother, Holly (Julia Roberts), and his three siblings drive up and see him (he is part of a blended, multiracial family). Holly whispers, “It’s Ben” and immediately gets out of the car and runs toward him. Ben is back. Her son. Her pure pleasure at seeing him is conveyed explicitly as she pulls him warmly into her embrace. It’s only after this moment of surprised joy passes that she steps back, never losing contact with him, and asks, “Ben, what are you doing here?” Ben’s answer is all but lost as he mumbles something about his counselor giving him permission, it’s Christmas, and this is home. Holly yearns to believe him and wants above all for this return to mean that he is who he was, free of the insidious, coextensive, addictive cycle while simultaneously realizing that Ben’s many betrayals, his constant dissembling, cannot be simply put away or erased. Should he be allowed to stay? Should she or her husband, Neal (Courtney B. Vance), who has arrived home, drive him back to rehab? It’s Christmas Eve, and they agree to let him stay for a day. His younger teen sister, Ivy (Kathryn Newton), is far more pessimistic about this decision. She knows (as do Holly and Neal, absent denial), with a heart shriveling truth that they have all stood in this place before while wishing the outcome would be different. The harrowing story of Ben’s return is played out over 24 hours as he is confronted with the cascade of harm his addiction has done, not only to himself, but his family, as well as others in the community, meaning those, innocent and criminal, he has used to ladder himself to the next pill. As Dean says: if Ben were black he would be in jail and not in costly rehab. What carries every frame of Ben is Back is the very fine performance of Julia Roberts. She moves across a spectrum of emotions, from loving Ben fully, to worry, to anger, to rage, mixed with a helpless fear that the grip of addiction will again assert itself and overwhelm Ben’s ability to resist and will again be just beyond her reach. It’s Roberts who must access the full panoply of maternal emotions, made evident by an overwhelming sense of sadness leavened by defeat. In one evocative scene, out of desperation, she drives Ben to a cemetery and asks him where, among the gray tombstones, he wishes to be buried. It’s a remarkable performance; perhaps the best in what has been a long, memorable career. There is one irrefutable fact that should be acknowledged regarding Ben is Back. This family is affluent and able to pay for Ben’s treatment. All of his life he has been nurtured by those who love him. His smile is wide and bright, his skin unblemished. While the maternal love conveyed by Holly is universal, the fate that awaits those who fall into this dark chasm of addiction (for Ben it was a doctor’s prescription) the outcome can be starkly different, often defined by an unrelenting poverty, isolation, devoid of help or options and too often results in a cold, lonely death. Ben is Back. Directed by Peter Hedges. Starring Lucas Hedges, Julia Roberts, Courtney B. Vance. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated R.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS Ben is Back a gripping tale about teenage addiction

articles.text: San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum is now displaying an immersive art exhibition entitled “teamLab: Continuity.” The art experience immerses patrons in a “wondrous ecosystem of lush imagery drawn from nature and East Asian art that dynamically evolves around you.” Rich hues are displayed dramatically via light-work onto the museum’s walls, in sumptuous images of crows, flowers, butterflies, fish, and more imagery. The Tokyo-based artist-collective teamLab is known for producing interactive, interconnected digital artworks that marry art and technology. “Everything exists in a long, fragile, yet miraculous borderless continuity of life,” teamLab founder Toshiyuki Inoko said. The exhibition is designed to be an immersive experience – not about the digital realm, but instead about the natural world. Due to popular demand, the exhibition was extended into September, but tickets are limited and nearly sold out. Fall admission for “teamLab: Continuity” will be released on Thursday, August 19, at 8 a.m. Visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org/exhibitions/teamlab-continuity/ to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside invites everyone to visit on Thursday evenings through September to celebrate “Summer Nights.” The Garden is open until 8 p.m., and the historic house is open until 7 p.m. Summer Nights are a tradition at Filoli and serve as a time to gather with family and friends and enjoy the sunset and summer blooms. Every Thursday night throughout the summer, the Grove Bar is serving wine and beer in the garden, nestled under the shade of the Olive Grove. The Georgian-style terraces around the historic house offer sweeping views of the Santa Cruz Mountains, a contrast to the 16-acre formal English Renaissance-style garden to the south. All admission, including Reservations for “Summer Nights” at Filoli House and Garden are required. for Summer Nights, must be reserved in advance. Masks will be required for those who are not vaccinated. Visit https://filoli.org/summer-nights/ for more information.

articles.text: A scene fron Disney’s Wreck-It Raph. The premise of Wreck-It Ralph is not only retro, but decidedly creative and fun. The story is set in a suburban arcade filled with games, a place where the neighborhood cool kids hang out during the day. But here’s the best part: when the arcade shuts down for the night, and the kids have all gone home, it’s transformed into an enchanting world where the game characters come to life and socialize. One of the video game meanies is Wreck-It-Ralph (John C. Reilly), a nemesis in a game called Fix-ItFelix Jr. Ralph is a big, hulking guy with oversized hands and feet who smashes buildings, while Felix (Jack Brayer) follows closely behind with his magic hammer, repairing the damage. Ralph has been wrecking the same building for years, day after day. Of course, he always faces the threat of the Newlanders, hostile residents who live in the building Ralph is wrecking. Meanwhile, Ralph sleeps in a garbage dump when he’s not wrecking stuff, using a tree stump for a pillow. For Ralph, it’s a lonely, sad life and he wants out. So Ralph abandons his game to try out others. The problem is that when he doesn’t return the kids think Fix-It-Felix Jr. is broken. Felix is therefore desperate to find Ralph and get him to come back so he’ll have things to fix. Meanwhile, Ralph is wandering from game to game. As it turns out, he spends a lot of time in a game called Sugar Rush where he becomes friends with Vanellope von Schweetz (Sarah Silverman) who has been prevented by despot King Candy and a group of mean girls from competing in the go-cart races. Both Vanellope and Ralph are unhappy and want to break free of their games’ programs. The story has a nice finale, involving a gateway to the inner arcade, called Arcade Central, while introducing a bevy of characters. There are also lots of stops along the way, some involving secret passages, cheat codes, and restarts. Plus the point is made that the arcade characters work long hours, all for the pleasure of kids. Wreck-It Ralph has wonderful visuals, and Ralph is actually likable and charming. The jokes are silly in a nice way, and it’s a treat to follow Ralph on his journey to leave behind his old meanie role of breaking stuff. Ditto Vanellope von Schweetz. Wreck-It Ralph. Walt Disney Animation. Directed by Rich Moore. With the voices of John C. Reilly, Sarah Silverman, and Jack McBrayer. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: Wreck-It Ralph

articles.text: A scene fron Pixar’s Ratatouille. As a work of animation and imaginative story telling, Ratatouille is extraordinary. At its center is Remy (Patton Oswalt), a Parisian rat who, along with his large family, plies the suburban garbage cans for food that he considers simply awful. And because of his reluctance to consume what they can scavenge, he is told repeatedly by his father, Django (Brian Dennehey), head of the clan, “Eat your garbage!” But when the family is forced to leave their cottage home (they live in the ceiling), Remy is separated from everyone and is swept away into a storm drain. He ends up in front of a famous restaurant named after its celebrity chef, Gusteau (Brad Garret). It’s there that Remy begins to hang around the kitchen and meets up with the restaurant’s dishwasher, Alfredo Linguini (Lou Romero). Remy, who has a refined palate and a nose to match, plus a dream to become a chef, convinces his newfound friend to be his front man, allowing Remy to burrow into in Linguini’s hair, and, with tugs and pulls, gives his new partner (who has not a shred of cooking ability) directions. Initially, the pair save an awful soup using Remy’s special seasoning. In other words, Remy is now the master puppeteer. Meanwhile, the effete food critic, Anton Ego (Peter O’Toole), visits the restaurant and gives his meal an awful critique, so bad that it breaks Gusteau’s heart, allowing a greedy, self-serving sous-chef named Skinner (Ian Holm), to take the master chef’s place. Soon, however, the restaurant is in trouble, its reputation falling into disrepute, the meals poorly prepared by Skinner. Pixar’s use of names brings a smile to the faces of its adult viewers: Linguini as a dishwasher in a restaurant; Ego as the food critic. But Remy and Linguini come to the rescue, along with the help of Collette Tatou (Janeane Garofalo), and create some astonishingly wonderful dishes, while Remy reaches new heights in preparing French cuisine. The two also anticipate the return of Anton Ego. Of course, there is a crisis, and Remy calls in his clan for help. They go through the kitchen dishwasher to get clean, and then assist Remy/Linguini in getting a superb meal together, acting as the creators of delicious sauces. And, not surprisingly, Anton Ego does return, only this time giving the restaurant a glowing review. The story gets a bit complicated by the discovery that Linguini is actually Gusteau’s abandoned son, which brings up the question of who actually owns the restaurant. Ratatouille is a remarkable demonstration of the genius of Pixar Studios. The colors and textures are truly outstanding, and the story is one that will delight the entire family, not just the little guys. It’s an animated feature not to be missed. Ratatouille (2007). Directed by Brad Bird. Pixar animation. 1 hr., 51 min. Rated G.
articles.title: Ratatouille – another gem from Pixar to savor

The story has a nice finale, involving a gateway to the inner arcade, called Arcade Central, while introducing a bevy of characters. There are also lots of stops along the way, some involving secret passages, cheat codes, and restarts. Plus the point is made that the arcade characters work long hours, all for the pleasure of kids. Wreck-It Ralph has wonderful visuals, and Ralph is actually likable and charming. The jokes are silly in a nice way, and it’s a treat to follow Ralph on his journey to leave behind his old meanie role of breaking stuff. Ditto Vanellope von Schweetz. Wreck-It Ralph. Walt Disney Animation. Directed by Rich Moore. With the voices of John C. Reilly, Sarah Silverman, and Jack McBrayer. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG. A scene fron Pixar’s Ratatouille. A scene fron Pixar’s Ratatouille. Ratatouille – another gem from Pixar to savor By Chris Honoré As a work of animation and imaginative story telling, Ratatouille is extraordinary. At its center is Remy (Patton Oswalt), a Parisian rat who, along with his large family, plies the suburban garbage cans for food that he considers simply awful. And because of his reluctance to consume what they can scavenge, he is told repeatedly by his father, Django (Brian Dennehey), head of the clan, “Eat your garbage!” But when the family is forced to leave their cottage home (they live in the ceiling), Remy is separated from everyone and is swept away into a storm drain. He ends up in front of a famous restaurant named after its celebrity chef, Gusteau (Brad Garret). It’s there that Remy begins to hang around the kitchen and meets up with the restaurant’s dishwasher, Alfredo Linguini (Lou Romero). Remy, who has a refined palate and a nose to match, plus a dream to become a chef, convinces his newfound friend to be his front man, allowing Remy to burrow into in Linguini’s hair, and, with tugs and pulls, gives his new partner (who has not a shred of cooking ability) directions. Initially, the pair save an awful soup using Remy’s special seasoning. In other words, Remy is now the master puppeteer. Meanwhile, the effete food critic, Anton Ego (Peter O’Toole), visits the restaurant and gives his meal an awful critique, so bad that it breaks Gusteau’s heart, allowing a greedy, self-serving sous-chef named Skinner (Ian Holm), to take the master chef’s place. Soon, however, the restaurant is in trouble, its reputation falling into disrepute, the meals poorly prepared by Skinner. Pixar’s use of names brings a smile to the faces of its adult viewers: Linguini as a dishwasher in a restaurant; Ego as the food critic. But Remy and Linguini come to the rescue, along with the help of Collette Tatou (Janeane Garofalo), and create some astonishingly wonderful dishes, while Remy reaches new heights in preparing French cuisine. The two also anticipate the return of Anton Ego. Of course, there is a crisis, and Remy calls in his clan for help. They go through the kitchen dishwasher to get clean, and then assist Remy/Linguini in getting a superb meal together, acting as the creators of delicious sauces. And, not surprisingly, Anton Ego does return, only this time giving the restaurant a glowing review. The story gets a bit complicated by the discovery that Linguini is actually Gusteau’s abandoned son, which brings up the question of who actually owns the restaurant. Ratatouille is a remarkable demonstration of the genius of Pixar Studios. The colors and textures are truly outstanding, and the story is one that will delight the entire family, not just the little guys. It’s an animated feature not to be missed. Ratatouille (2007). Directed by Brad Bird. Pixar animation. 1 hr., 51 min. Rated G.

articles.text: A chopped salad with creamy feta dressing is perfect for warm summer days. If zesty, tangy, and salty flavors please your palate, this salad is an excellent accompaniment to a summer lunch or dinner. Our Piedmont summer days are relatively mild, but plenty of readers live where daytime temps soar above 100°F. A cold, refreshing salad may just make the meal. Farmers markets are brimming with all these vegetables. Tomatoes and cucumbers are at their peak, and every week I see more varieties and larger displays. I encourage bringing feta cheese into your rotation of cheeses if it’s not already. Traditionally made from sheep’s milk (or a combination of sheep and up to 30% goat’s milk), feta is tangy and salty due to being brined. It’s a semi-hard cheese so it crumbles and melts well. Buying a small, plain block provides ultimate flexibility in uses, compared to the myriad options of crumbled and cubed, plain and flavored. If you purchase your block of cheese packaged in its brine, be sure to save the brine to store any unused cheese. It will keep well in the refrigerator, so long as it’s completely submerged in brine. As always, experiment with different tastes and textures. Adding or substituting cubes of watermelon, avocado, and whole prepared garbanzo beans, pickled Greek peperoncini, or boiled new potatoes would be right at home here. Also consider including a protein such as cold chicken, tuna, or sliced hard boiled eggs. INGREDIENTS Dressing Makes about 3/4 cup, enough for one salad, plus leftovers • 3 ounces feta cheese, cut into 1/ 2-inch cubes • 1/2 cup Greek yogurt, plain, whole milk • 1–2 cloves garlic, chopped, to taste • 1 tablespoon lemon juice, freshly squeezed • 1 tablespoon olive oil • 1–2 teaspoons white wine vinegar, to taste • 2 tablespoons whole milk, more or less for desired consistency • Freshly ground black pepper, to taste • Scant salt, to taste (feta is already salty) Combine the first six ingredients into the bowl of a minifood processor, blender jar, or small, deep bowl if using a handheld blender. Start with a few pulses, then blitz until smooth. Add small amounts of milk, blending after each addition, until the dressing has a smooth, creamy consistency. Adjust seasoning, remembering you want a fairly strong flavor to “dress” the salad. Note: It will be up to you to determine the consistency of the dressing with the amount of milk you add. I prefer mine about the consistency of ketchup. Salad • 1/4 to 1/2 cup red onions, sliced. (See note.) • 1–2 tomatoes, cut into 1-inch pieces • 1–2 cucumbers, sliced into 3/ 4-inch pieces • 1/2 cup Kalamata olives, pitted • 1/4 cup f lat leaf parsley, chopped • 2 tablespoons fresh mint, chopped Put all salad ingredients into a large bowl and stir gently to combine. Mix in creamy feta dressing to taste. Note: If you prefer to tame the bite from raw, red onion, marinate them in a simple mix of 1 tablespoon each of white wine vinegar and olive oil, plus salt and pepper. Set aside while you prepare the dressing and are ready to assemble the salad. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.
articles.title: Summer Chopped Salad with Creamy Feta Dressing

articles.text: If you’ve had an IRA and a 401(k) for many years, you may occasionally ask yourself some questions: “Am I contributing enough?” “Am I still funding these accounts with the right mix of investments for my goals and risk tolerance?” But here’s one inquiry you might be overlooking: “Have I used the correct beneficiary designations?” And the answer you get is important. It wouldn’t be surprising if you haven’t thought much about the beneficiary designation – after all, it was just something you once signed, possibly a long time ago. Is it really that big a deal? It could be. For one thing, what if your family circumstances have changed since you named a beneficiary? If you’ve remarried, you may not want your former spouse to receive your IRA and 401(k) assets or the proceeds of your life insurance policy, for which you also named a beneficiary. However, upon remarrying, many people do review their estate plans, including their wills, living trusts, durable powers of attorney and health care directives. If you’ve revised these documents, do you have to worry about the old beneficiary designations? You might be surprised to learn that these previous designations can supersede what’s in your updated will and other documents. The end result could be an “accidental” inheritance in which your retirement accounts and insurance proceeds could end up going to someone who is no longer in your life. Furthermore, your retirement plans and insurance policy may not just require a single beneficiary – you may also be asked to name a contingent beneficiary, to whom assets will pass if the primary beneficiary has already died. As you can imagine, the situation could become quite muddled if stepchildren are involved in a remarriage. To avoid these potential problems, make sure to review the beneficiary designations on all of your accounts at some point – and especially after a significant change in your family situation. If you see something that is outdated or incorrect, contact your retirement account administrator – or your insurance representative, in the case of life insurance – to request a change-of-beneficiary form. And if you really want to be on the safe side, you may want to enlist a legal professional to help you with this review to make sure the beneficiary designations reflect your current family situation and are consistent with what’s in your estate plans. In fact, if you’re already working with an experienced estate planning attorney – and you should – you might also pick up some other suggestions for dealing with beneficiaries. Just to name one, it’s generally not a good idea to name minor children as beneficiaries. Because children can’t control the assets until they become adults, a court would likely have to name a guardian – one that you might not have wanted. Instead, you could either name your own custodian to manage the assets designated to the minor or establish a trust for the benefit of the minor, which can distribute the money in several disbursements over a period of years – which is often a good move, since young adults aren’t always the best at managing large lump sums. If you’re like many people, you have a strong desire to leave something behind. But you’ll want to do it in the right way. So, pay close attention to your beneficiary designations – when you first create them and throughout your life. articles.text: When my second Moderna dose had had time to do its thing, I began to feel the itch. The itch to eat out, that is—or, rather, the itch to eat in, to stroll through the front door of a nice restaurant, to be shown to a table, to be asked what I’d like to drink (Knob Creek, rocks on the side, if you please), and to wander through the menu at leisure. Ah, the pleasures of the good life! That was several months ago. Since then I’ve renewed my acquaintance with several local favorites: Wood Tavern, Rivoli, Perle, Corso, Sidebar, Lake Chalet, The Wolf. Alas, some, like Homestead, have tossed their last Caesar Salad, but many are still dishing up fine food in a welcoming atmosphere. It’s good news that one of those is Italian Colors. Opening its doors in 1993, Italian Colors is a family-owned California-Italian restaurant in Montclair – thus it’s about as convenient to Piedmont as hungry diners could wish. Its credentials are notable. Chef and owner Alan Carlson trained at the Culinary Institute of America Interior of Italian Colors restaurant in Montclair. articles.text: Will Adams will lead a walking tour of eight Piedmont Julia Morgan-designed homes in Piedmont on Wednesday, August 18 at 10:30 a.m. His tour will be in conjunction with the Walking on Wednesdays group sponsored by the Recreation Department. Will is a planner, urban designer, and architect who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He writes a biweekly column in the Piedmont Post titled Walking Piedmont – Observations of the built environment of a beautiful city. On the tour he will discuss architectural design elements of classic Julia Morgan homes. The tour is free and open Architect, planner & newspaper columnist Will Adams. to everyone, however, registration with the Piedmont Recreation Dept. is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: Wednesday Walkers at a stairway connecting Bowles Place and Trestle Glen Road. Pictured are Albert Chen, Mark Davis, Noemi Alvarado, Barry Gantt, Jim Kuo, Melba Yee, Brenda Ferrero, Cheryl, Coleman Jones, Phil Witte, Priscilla Wanerus, Haybert Houston, Stella Houston, Quincy Dong, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Carol Lyons, Adrienne Hamlin, Sherry Jacobs, Alan Goldhammer, Sarah Johnson, Nancy Olsen, Larry Olsen, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Dave DeRoche, Mary Carter, Alicia Rivera, and Nadine Guffanti. When members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays assembled at the Exedra on July 28, they were saddened to see the ad hoc memorial that community members had placed at the Exedra for the St. John family who had lost three of its four members in a tragic, deadly automobile accident in Minnesota on Sunday. The walk was led by Melba Yee, Priscilla Wanerus, and Albert Chen. Melba said the walkers in the past have explored many of the hidden stairways within Piedmont. Like Piedmont and Berkeley, Oakland has a series of hidden stairways that were developed with the residential development boom that occurred after the 1906 earthquake in San Francisco when people flocked to the East Bay. Developers built stairways so residents could get from the upper part of Piedmont to the lower parts of town and to have access the Key System trains. The stairways were part of the selling point for attracting buyers to the neighborhoods. Priscilla identified the Van Sicklen stairway in Oakland’s Crocker Highlands neighborhood near the Piedmont border as an opportunity to observe how some boundary lines were drawn and how the changes were reflected by the street, signage and homes in the area. Piedmont is unique in being perhaps the only city that is completely surrounded by another city. It has been referred to at times as Oakland’s “donut hole.” The borders of the town make no logical sense, as they do not appear to follow streets or physical landmarks. Boundary lines between the two cities sometimes cut through the middle of peoples’ homes, yards or businesses. In total there are 136 parcels that are partly in both Piedmont and Oakland. Some walkers were aware that in 1907 the town’s founding fathers had been in race to incorporate Piedmont as a separate city before Oakland could annex the area. In this rush, they used the only map they had for defining the boundaries – a sewer map that showed sewer lines snaking underneath the houses of Piedmont. The sewer map was not a good choice for setting jurisdictional boundaries, but once the boundaries were set, they could not be changed. The walkers set off on Highland Avenue to Sheridan, then to Wildwood and through the Hall Fenway to Crocker and Hampton Avenues. From Hampton, the group turned onto Indian Road. At the 200 block of Indian Road, the walkers noticed one of Piedmont’s Welcome to Piedmont signs facing in the opposite direction, The walkers knew that the sign meant that the walkers were now leaving Piedmont and entering Oakland. The walkers believed they might be on Sunnyhills Road, but that sign did not appear until the end of the block at the intersection with Downey Place. Walkers who lived in the Crocker Highlands neighborhood explained that Indian Road changed to Sunnyhills Road and that street names can change at places other than at an intersection. Continuing on Sunnyhills, they found Van Sicklen Place, a cul-de-sac where the first set of stairways descends to another cul-de-sac, Bowles Place. From there a steeper, longer stairway goes to Trestle Glen Road. The walkers continued down Sunnyhills Road, past Crocker Highlands Elementary School on Midcrest Road, to Longridge, Clarendon Crescent, and then to the Ashmount Farmer’s Market that operates out of a garage.
