articles.text: Piedmont native Victoria Saykally found her passion for dentistry while completing her bachelor’s degree at the University of Washington. She discovered that dentistry allowed her to combine her love of art and interest in the sciences while also provide her with a platform to give back to her community. She studied Molecular, Cell, and Developmental Biology, as well as Global Health while working as a dental assistant. After completing her degree, Dr. Saykally worked as a research associate at a virology lab at UCSF, participating in the publication of multiple papers researching HIV and Cytomegalovirus. She went on to complete her doctorate degree at University of the Pacific in San Francisco. During this time, she led and participated in numerous dental outreach trips, both locally and abroad. She completed additional graduate training by completing a hospital-based residency at VA Victoria Saykally, DDS Palo Alto and Stanford. During the residency she focused on providing patient-centered comprehensive care to veterans, dental clearance for medically complex patients, and facial and dental emergency care to pediatric and adult patients. She is now with Ross Family Dentistry on Redwood Drive in Ross, in Marin County. Outside of dentistry, Dr. Saykally is an avid skier and hunter/jumper equestrian. By Melba Yee When members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays assembled at the Exedra on July 28, they were saddened to see the ad hoc memorial that community members had placed at the Exedra for the St. John family who had lost three of its four members in a tragic, deadly automobile accident in Minnesota on Sunday. The walk was led by Melba Yee, Priscilla Wanerus, and Albert Chen. Melba said the walkers in the past have explored many of the hidden stairways within Piedmont. Like Piedmont and Berkeley, Oakland has a series of hidden stairways that were developed with the residential development boom that occurred after the 1906 earthquake in San Francisco when people flocked to the East Bay. Developers built stairways so residents could get from the upper part of Piedmont to the lower parts of town and to have access the Key System trains. The stairways were part of the selling point for attracting buyers to the neighborhoods. Priscilla identified the Van Sicklen stairway in Oakland’s Crocker Highlands neighborhood near the Piedmont border as an opportunity to observe how some boundary lines were drawn and how the changes were reflected by the street, signage and homes in the area. Piedmont is unique in being perhaps the only city that is completely surrounded by another city. It has been referred to at times as Oakland’s “donut hole.” The borders of the town make no logical sense, as they do not appear to follow streets or physical landmarks. Boundary lines between the two cities sometimes cut through the middle of peoples’ homes, yards or businesses. In total there are 136 parcels that are partly in both Piedmont and Oakland. Some walkers were aware that in 1907 the town’s founding fathers had been in race to incorporate Piedmont as a separate city before Oakland could annex the area. In this rush, they used the only map they had for defining the boundaries – a sewer map that showed sewer lines snaking underneath the houses of Piedmont. The sewer map was not a good choice for setting jurisdictional boundaries, but once the boundaries were set, they could not be changed. The walkers believed they might be on Sunnyhills Road, but that sign did not appear until the end of the block at the intersection with Downey Place. articles.text: George H. Caig, a longtime Piedmont resident, passed away at home on March 30, 2021 after living a long and very fulfilling life. He was 92. George, who many knew by his nickname Jud, was an incredible man – a caring and loving father, husband, grandfather, and great grandfather, and a good friend to many people. George was very appreciative of the beauty of nature and greatly enjoyed learning about plants, f lowers, and trees - locally and throughout his travels with his family, friends, and with his beloved wife, Julie. He was also a “green thumb” and enjoyed teaching his children about the greatness of the outdoors. He found fulfillment tending to his garden at their home in Piedmont. Born at Fabiola Hospital in Oakland, on July 8, 1928, George was raised in Piedmont and learned the value of creating stability and long-term planning due to his formative years during the Great Depression (1929-36). He went to Wildwood Elementary School and discovered his passion for exploring the outdoors by becoming an active member in the Boy Scouts, and eventually attaining the rank of Eagle Scout. He loved athletics, especially playing basketball and baseball. At Piedmont High School, Jud was an excellent basketball player and was known as a great long-range shooter. Jokingly, he referred to his best shots as, “punishing the nets” which he loved to do while playing a game of basketball in town - his favorite form of recreation into his late seventies. After graduating from Piedmont High School in 1946, George attended the University of California at Berkeley, where he advanced his business gent work in the Bond department, reviewing, detailing, and underwriting numerous mid-tolarge scale construction projects throughout the Bay Area and Northern California. Due to his George’s ability to plan, coupled with their desire to explore the world, Jud and Julie and their group of lifelong friends began to travel the globe. Their trips became a semi-annual event after planning sessions in Los Osos, CA. Their group toured Italy three times, Spain, Ireland, England, Scotland (where George’s ancestors built McCaig Tower long ago), France, Portugal, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Germany, Switzerland, Canada, and many beautiful places throughout the United States. Jud and Julie’s favorite getaway closer to home was Mendocino. Jud never learned to play golf until after he retired, when he discovered his enjoyable, yet frustrating new hobby. Since he loved to walk and hike, and play sports, he quickly got hooked on a game that helped keep him active throughout his golden years. Volunteerism became a second calling during Jud’s retirement, and he cherished giving back some of his time and energy to those in need. He was honored to step up as a hardworking volunteer at Providence Hospital in Oakland for several years, and he assisted at the Piedmont Police Department to serve his hometown. George was a first-class person throughout his life. He was patient, humble, and a loving family man who always put his family first. He also treated his closest friends with the utmost love and respect and was there to assist whenever called upon. Jud will always be remembered for being an outstanding man, and for making the lives of his family and friends better than they could have imagined. Respectfully, the Caig and Bryan families thank you for keeping them in your thoughts and prayers during this difficult time, as they learn to live their lives with the loving memory of Jud in their hearts and minds forever. George is survived by Julie, his wife of more than 40-years, his two daughters, Susan Cox and Martha Leach, and his two stepsons, Kurt and Keith Bryan and their families. articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Rob Rich died on July 31 at his home in Danville. He was 71. Rob Rich, a former longtime Piedmont resident died in his sleep at his home in Danville in the early morning hours of July 31, 2021. He was 71. Born Robert Richard Rich on September 26, 1949 in Putnam, Connecticut, Rob was the only child of Joseph Reich and Lillian Whitehouse Rich. The family name was legally changed in the late 90s to Rich, to match the Polish pronunciation of the name. He grew up on a dairy farm, an experience that instilled in him a lifelong love for nature and animals. He became an Eagle Scout when he was 14 years old, when he matriculated at Pomfret School in Pomfret, Connecticut. Upon graduation, he attended Wesleyan University in Middletown, Conn., where he graduated in 1972. After working in the insurance industry and for an engineering company, Rob enrolled at Wharton Business School in Philadelphia. While there, he met Priscilla Chappell Dreby (Polly). They were married on June 17, 1978, and later that day got on a plane with their cat, Serena, and flew to San Francisco. They would live in the Bay Area their entire married life. Rob’s first job in California was at Del Monte, but after the company acquired R.J Reynolds, he was asked to move to North Carolina to work in the tobacco division. Rob had no desire to leave California or work for a company peddling cigarettes, and so took a job at McKesson. In 1992, he purchased a small wholesale business, Dan Gould & Sons, that sold soft goods to retail stores throughout the West Coast, primarily Longs Drugs. He very much enjoyed the work and took pride in being a small business owner, employing a diverse workforce headquartered in West Oakland. Rob and Polly became parents in 1983 with the birth of their son, Alexander, and later added to their family with the birth of their daughter, Kimberly. Until recently, their family always included at least one cat as well. They moved to Piedmont in 1985, and remained there until 2007, when they sold their home and moved to Danville. Rob passed on his love of sports and nature to his children by coaching their youth sports teams, serving as an adult leader for the Piedmont Boy Scout Council, taking them to the Sierra Nevada for cross country skiing, and taking trips to the East Coast that invariably included hiking, swimming, and boating in the Adirondacks. An avid Red Sox fan, Rob was in New England in October 2018 when the Curse of the Bambino was broken and the Sox won the World Series. He later became a cycling aficionado, enjoying the Tour de France, as well as cycling as many as 50 miles a day on his touring bike. He and Polly enjoyed and supported many local arts organizations, including San Francisco Ballet, California Shakespeare, Theatre Works, and Montalvo Arts. Travel to Muir Woods, Pt Reyes National Seashore, Yellowstone, Yosemite and international travel to Wimbledon, Mont Saint Michel, Montreal, and Vancouver BC were all life-enhancing adventures for both of them, often in the company of family and friends. After retiring from his soft goods business, Rob joined forces with Polly, becoming the CFO for her climate solutions-focused non-profit, Transition Express Inc. He gave her confidence, as a key board member, in finding meaningful ways to make a difference regarding the challenges posed by climate change. Rob is survived by his wife of 43 years, Polly; his son and daughter-in-law Alexander and Michelle Rich of Ukiah, CA; his daughter and son-in-law Kim and Jake Wallin of Chico, CA.; and his grandson, Damien Rich. He is preceded in death by his parents. Instead of recommended donations, we suggest supporting an arts organization of your choice that inspires you, and taking regular scenic hikes with a good friend.

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: Margaret Pillsbury, a longtime resident of Piedmont, passed away peacefully in Oakland, California on August 1, 2021. She was 94. Born in 1926 in Oakland, she was the daughter of Edward and Julia Lipman. When Margaret was five years old she contracted tuberculosis and was confined by doctors to bed rest for three years. She emerged from this confinement with an extraordinary joie de vivre. She attended Berkeley High School and graduated from the University of California, Berkeley, before getting a M.A. in Dramatic Arts from Columbia University in New York City. She also studied at the University of Geneva in Switzerland. Margaret met her future husband and true love of her life, John Pillsbury, when she was in nursery school with his younger sister, Susan. The comment was made that when Margaret and John married in 1950, half of Berkeley became related. Margaret and John enjoyed a wonderful and much-admired marriage for 52 years. Margaret was a great believer in the power of education and was a life-long learner, as well as a dedicated teacher. She taught in Oakland public schools for over 20 years and inspired and encouraged many future teachers, including her daughter Karen Austin, daughter-in-law Megan Pillsbury, and granddaughter Amelia Dufrechou. After “retirement” Margaret taught English as a Second Language (ESL) at the elementary school level and was a docent at the Oakland Museum and the Phoebe Hearst Anthropology Museum. And after a second “retirement” Margaret became a much-loved Adult ESL teacher at Piedmont Adult School and the Downtown Oakland Senior Center, and taught well into her 90’s. She was well known and widely respected for her creative approach to teaching language using food as the common focus of learning. Her ESL students in Piedmont celebrated the end of the semester with a student-prepared feast as part of the final exam. Margaret Pillsbury, a longtime resident of Piedmont, passed away peacefully at age 94 on August 1, 2021. She is pictured with her husband John Pillsbury. Margaret will be remembered for her great zest for life, a love of travel and other cultures, and a special fondness for the arts. Margaret was an enthusiastic supporter of Berkeley Rep, Cal Performances, the San Francisco Symphony, the DeYoung Museum, the Asian Art Museum, the Oakland Symphony, and the Oakland Museum. She and John travelled to many places in the world, including Peru, where they assisted their youngest daughter Joanne on an archeological dig she was directing. Margaret shared her love of travel with her children, who have many family stories including one about a beer-drinking burro in Mexico. She was a supporter of progressive causes and once instructed Joe Biden about the meaning of César Chávez’s UFW motto of “Sí, Se Puede” or “Yes We Can” – coined 30 years before the Obama presidential campaign. As “Nana”, Margaret was grandmother to seven grandchildren and one great-grandson. She loved holidays and celebrated with great delight Three Kings Day, Chinese New Year, Cinco de Mayo, Bastille Day and Day of the Dead, in addition to Thanksgiving, Christmas, Easter, and Fourth of July. Margaret was an adventurous cook and embraced Julia Child early on, but ultimately her cook’s heart belonged to Jacques Pepin. Her grandchildren will remember her wonderful roast chicken, her spicy lemonade, her early adoption of quinoa, her favorite drinking toasts in both French and Spanish, and the Che Guevara socks she wore to Alycia’s Heartbeat exercise class which she attended for 36 years. Margaret is survived by her children: Karen Austin of Alameda, Tom Pillsbury and wife Megan of Piedmont, Jim Pillsbury and wife Noelle of Piedmont, and Joanne Pillsbury Harwood and husband Edward of Manhattan and Maine. She is also survived by grandchildren Nicholas McMahon (Kelly), Timothy Austin McMahon, Amelia Dufrechou (Max), Claire Pillsbury, Jack Pillsbury, Alec Pillsbury, Colin Pillsbury; and great-grandson Elliot Dufrechou. Margaret is predeceased by her husband John, her sisters Jean and Kathryn, and her son Mark who died in infancy. The family thanks all her caregivers and the staff at St. Paul’s Towers for their wonderful care and support. We will celebrate Margaret at a future date. pages.text: Wednesday, August 11, 2021 25 Obituary Longtime Piedmont resident Margaret Pillsbury dies at 94 Gifted educator, creative cook, passed on her love of life to her family Margaret Pillsbury, a longtime resident of Piedmont, passed away peacefully in Oakland, California on August 1, 2021. She was 94. Born in 1926 in Oakland, she was the daughter of Edward and Julia Lipman. When Margaret was five years old she contracted tuberculosis and was confined by doctors to bed rest for three years. She emerged from this confinement with an extraordinary joie de vivre. She attended Berkeley High School and graduated from the University of California, Berkeley, before getting a M.A. in Dramatic Arts from Columbia University in New York City. She also studied at the University of Geneva in Switzerland. Margaret met her future husband and true love of her life, John Pillsbury, when she was in nursery school with his younger sister, Susan. The comment was made that when Margaret and John married in 1950, half of Berkeley became related. Margaret and John enjoyed a wonderful and much-admired marriage for 52 years. Margaret was a great believer in the power of education and was a life-long learner, as well as a dedicated teacher. She taught in Oakland public schools for over 20 years and inspired and encouraged many future teachers, including her daughter Karen Austin, daughter-in-law Megan Pillsbury, and granddaughter Amelia Dufrechou. After “retirement” Margaret taught English as a Second Language (ESL) at the elementary school level and was a docent at the Oakland Museum and the Phoebe Hearst Anthropology Museum. And after a second “retirement” Margaret became a much-loved Adult ESL teacher at Piedmont Adult School and the Downtown Oakland Senior Center, and taught well into her 90’s. She was well known and widely respected for her creative approach to teaching language using food as the common focus of learning. Her ESL students in Piedmont celebrated the end of the semester with a student-prepared feast as part of the final exam. Margaret Pillsbury, a longtime resident of Piedmont, passed away peacefully at age 94 on August 1, 2021. She is pictured with her husband John Pillsbury. Margaret will be remembered for her great zest for life, a love of travel and other cultures, and a special fondness for the arts. Margaret was an enthusiastic supporter of Berkeley Rep, Cal Performances, the San Francisco Symphony, the DeYoung Museum, the Asian Art Museum, the Oakland Symphony, and the Oakland Museum. She and John travelled to many places in the world, including Peru, where they assisted their youngest daughter Joanne on an archeological dig she was directing. Margaret shared her love of travel with her children, who have many family stories including one about a beer-drinking burro in Mexico. She was a supporter of progressive causes and once instructed Joe Biden about the meaning of César Chávez’s UFW motto of “Sí, Se Puede” or “Yes We Can” – coined 30 years before the Obama presidential campaign. As “Nana”, Margaret was grandmother to seven grandchildren and one great-grandson. She loved holidays and celebrated with great delight Three Kings Day, Chinese New Year, Cinco de Mayo, Bastille Day and Day of the Dead, in addition to Thanksgiving, Christmas, Easter, and Fourth of July. Margaret was an adventurous cook and embraced Julia Child early on, but ultimately her cook’s heart belonged to Jacques Pepin. Her grandchildren will remember her wonderful roast chicken, her spicy lemonade, her early adoption of quinoa, her favorite drinking toasts in both French and Spanish, and the Che Guevara socks she wore to Alycia’s Heartbeat exercise class which she attended for 36 years. Margaret is survived by her children: Karen Austin of Alameda, Tom Pillsbury and wife Megan of Piedmont, Jim Pillsbury and wife Noelle of Piedmont, and Joanne Pillsbury Harwood and husband Edward of Manhattan and Maine. She is also survived by grandchildren Nicholas McMahon (Kelly), Timothy Austin McMahon, Amelia Dufrechou (Max), Claire Pillsbury, Jack Pillsbury, Alec Pillsbury, Colin Pillsbury; and great-grandson Elliot Dufrechou. Margaret is predeceased by her husband John, her sisters Jean and Kathryn, and her son Mark who died in infancy. The family thanks all her caregivers and the staff at St. Paul’s Towers for their wonderful care and support. We will celebrate Margaret at a future date. In the meantime, please raise a glass and toast “!Salud, amor, pesetas, y el tiempo para disfrutarlos!” Margaret Pilllsbury in Florence, Italy after the war in 1948. articles.text: Throughout the summer the Post will print a sampling of letters written by kids attending Camp Augusta, Piedmont’s residential camp at Lake Vera outside Nevada City in the Sierra foothills. Founded in 1931, the camp remains a vital part of the life of hundreds of children each summer. For a local view of the summer ritual, residents will see large groups of families waiting each weekend for the arrival of busses with kids returning from camp, and a fresh group ready to head to Camp Augusta for one or two weeks of pure fun. For more information, see campaugusta.org. A black-light evening program was a giant murder mystery culminating in solving the crime with an all-camp dance party. Part of the black-light mystery evening was going to a couple dozen stations and completing tasks to acquire clues, including these with a scientist. articles.text: A 100-foot crane and large crew of workers took up most of the south side of the 1500 block of Oakland Avenue last Friday morning, July 23, to airlift and lower into place an Accessory Dwelling Unit to the Villaluz family backyard. The 18,000- pound, 340-square-foot prefabricated studio apartment was picked up and hoisted over the neighbor’s house and onto a foundation in the backyard. The City of Piedmont faces a state mandate of adding 587 new residences at fair pricing by the year 2031. This was the first crane-delivered unit to the city, and airlifts may become an option for some looking for a rental unit. The company managing the installation, Adobu, said this unit would cost approximately $270,000, including delivery and installation. The Villaluz family plans to use the apartment to attract both grandmothers to town. “We wanted to spend more time with our mothers, so we might as well give them a place that is nice. Our backyard is very pleasant and is enough for my mother to garden in. During normal times she would have been here helping us with the tomatoes and picking flowers, so it is a good place to be,” said Jason Villaluz. Crane delivery has a number of appeals, in addition to the grand spectacle of seeing a flying home. The foundation at the Villaluz’s took only nine days to prepare. Staff Photos An 18,000-pound studio apartment was lifted over a neighbor’s house and lowered onto the owner’s backyard by a crane. “It was inconceivable that four or five guys set the foundation up so quick. They moved at light speed,” Villaluz said. Residents that are reticent to give up their privacy by starting a long construction project on their property with workers coming and going for months or over a year may prefer this quick approach. This ADU was installed in one afternoon. Adobu took around 15 weeks for the apartment to be built
articles.title: Crane airlifts ADU to Oakland Ave. backyard

articles.text: As the COVID-19 Delta variant causes concern within the medical community, many jurisdictions across the state are reinstating mask mandates that were previously abolished for vaccinated individuals. In a joint statement, health officers from Alameda, Berkeley, San Mateo, Contra Costa, San Francisco, Marin, Santa Clara, and Sonoma counties recommended wearing masks indoors in public spaces for all individuals regardless of vaccination status. “The Delta variant is spreading quickly, and everyone should take action to protect themselves and others against this deadly virus,” said Dr. Lisa Hernandez, Berkeley Health Officer. “After vaccination, masking is the next most powerful tool we have to protect ourselves.” San Mateo county, on Monday, July 26, was the first Bay Area county to reinstate and reinforce indoor mask mandates for all resCity Hall and other city facilities will continue to follow CDC recommendations on mask wearing. A sign inside City Hall reads “Masks Required,” but currently that applies to those who are unvaccinated. The mandate is enforced through an honor system.
articles.title: Piedmont to follow Alameda County guidelines

articles.text: To complete construction of the new high school theater building, Piedmont School District has borrowed $1.8 million at no interest from the Piedmont Education Foundation to cover necessary costs. A $66 million bond (H1) was approved in 2016 to pay for a new classroom building ($30 million) and companion theater building ($20 million). The classroom (STEAM) building was scheduled to be completed by August 2020, but was delayed in part because of COVID. The theater building, currently in progress, was scheduled to be open by August this year, but is not expected to be completed until late this year. Both projects went over budget, requiring “value engineering.” The $66 million bond included a $4.8 million contingency. In a Memorandum of Understanding on June 23, 2021 the District and Education Foundation agreed to use $1.8 million in PEF funds to avoid deferring important features of the theater which would have delayed opening and added additional costs.s The following items will be covered by the loan: The new high school theater building is scheduled to obtain a Certificate of Occupancy on November 4 but won’t be open until December 28. • • • • Casework, wood stage floor, window shades Concrete and steel trellis, wood slat ceiling Acoustic paneling Theatrical equipment includ- • ing orchestra shell, rigging, draperies Insulation, theatrical AV, site concrete, low voltage electrical system

articles.text: In her letter to the editor in last week’s Post, Hannah Pinkham condemns the police as instruments of “fear, oppression, and destruction.” I remember experiencing a sense of “fear, oppression, and destruction” on September 11, 2001, when the Twin Towers came down. I also remember that 70 police officers lost their lives that day because when disaster struck, and thousands of civilians did whatever they could to escape the danger, the police did what they were trained to do: They ran toward the danger. That is the job these men and women enlist to do. They put on their uniforms and risk their lives each day to shield the rest of us from danger. Ms. Pinkham’s letter parrots many of the woke theories about the police that have been marinating in our academic centers for years. They are based on exaggerations, distortions, and outright falsehoods. Unfortunately, they gained a significant degree of traction outside academe with the brutal killing of George Floyd. If evidence is needed of the consequences of accepting these theories, consider what has happened since Mr. Floyd’s death, with the advent of the “Defund the Police” campaign. Short on resources and subject to scorn and 20/20 hindsight scrutiny, the police – those so-called instruments of oppression – scaled back their presence. And what happened to all those people Ms. Pinkham identifies as the victims of their “oppression?” They became the victims of the greatest crime spike [in the U.S.] in recent history. Throughout our country, attacks on the police have led to a dramatic rise in homicides. There has been a 36% rise in homicides in Bay Area cities during the first six months of 2021. In Chicago, a city run by people who accept the same woke dogmas promulgated by Ms. Pinkham, there were 104 shootings over the Fourth of July weekend alone. Among the victims were 13 children, some as young as five years old. So far this year, Chicago has seen more than 2,020 shootings, a 58% increase over the year 2019, before the “Defund the Police” campaign took root. articles.text: The task of overcoming poverty in the East Bay is shared by everyone who lives here. All of us want to live in neighborhoods that are stable, secure and thriving. One non-profit has been working for 15 years on this problem by focusing on job-training programs for low-income workers in Alameda and Contra Costa counties. The Strive for Change Foundation, a (501c3) non-profit, believes all workers deserve the chance to improve their job skills and get better jobs. Increased income helps low-income workers achieve a more stable and financially self-sustaining future. Their families, their neighborhoods, and everyone around them benefits. The Strive for Change Foundation was founded in 2006 by Piedmont resident Lester Ellis and a small group of individuals who wanted to support workforce development programs for low-income workers. They decided to gather their donations into a single fund and use it to give grants to multiple non-profit job-training programs throughout the East Bay. Since that time, the Strive for Change Foundation has donated more than one million dollars to dozens of job-training programs in Alameda and Contra Costa counties. Grants range in size from about $5,000 to a high of $12,500. Strive for Change supports organizations who help low-income workers with barriers to employment develop the skills they need to find better jobs, keep those jobs, and build stable futures for their families. Strive for Change operates on three core principles. First, unlike larger foundations that serve international endeavors, Strive for Change focuses exclusively on the working poor in Alameda and Contra Costa counties. Second, 100% of donor contributions go to the agencies identified as worthy of support. The all-volunteer Board covers all administrative costs such as mailing, postage, and informational materials. And third, Strive for Change rigorously vets the agencies that seek support. The Board meets annually with the Executive Directors and program managers, and asks them the hard questions about budgets, graduation rate, job placement and retention rates. This process helps Strive supporters to be better-informed donors as well. Strive’s Board of Directors meets monthly to review grantee programs and discuss ongoing concerns, among them fundraising and Board development. Most Board members spend an average of two to five hours per month on Board activities. Board positions are available in the areas of workforce development, fundraising, writing and graphic design. For many members of the East Bay community, every hour is a struggle to put food on the table and keep a roof overhead. Minimum wage earners often require three full-time jobs just to provide their family with basic necessities. Post-Covid, many of those underpaid jobs will no longer exist. The need is greater than ever before for job-training programs that demonstrably help hardworking, ambitious people get better jobs. More information about the Strive for Change Foundation can be found at www. striveforchangefoundation.org. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, July 28, 2021 Opinion Let’s look at the statistics of what police deal with daily By Lawrence Siskid In her letter to the editor in last week’s Post, Hannah Pinkham condemns the police as instruments of “fear, oppression, and destruction.” I remember experiencing a sense of “fear, oppression, and destruction” on September 11, 2001, when the Twin Towers came down. I also remember that 70 police officers lost their lives that day because when disaster struck, and thousands of civilians did whatever they could to escape the danger, the police did what they were trained to do: They ran toward the danger. That is the job these men and women enlist to do. They put on their uniforms and risk their lives each day to shield the rest of us from danger. Ms. Pinkham’s letter parrots many of the woke theories about the police that have been marinating in our academic centers for years. They are based on exaggerations, distortions, and outright falsehoods. Unfortunately, they gained a significant degree of traction outside academe with the brutal killing of George Floyd. If evidence is needed of the consequences of accepting these theories, consider what has happened since Mr. Floyd’s death, with the advent of the “Defund the Police” campaign. Short on resources and subject to scorn and 20/20 hindsight scrutiny, the police – those so-called instruments of oppression – scaled back their presence. And what happened to all those people Ms. Pinkham identifies as the victims of their “oppression?” They became the victims of the greatest crime spike [in the U.S.] in recent history. Throughout our country, attacks on the police have led to a dramatic rise in homicides. There has been a 36% rise in homicides in Bay Area cities during the first six months of 2021. In Chicago, a city run by people who accept the same woke dogmas promulgated by Ms. Pinkham, there were 104 shootings over the Fourth of July weekend alone. Among the victims were 13 children, some as young as five years old. So far this year, Chicago has seen more than 2,020 shootings, a 58% increase over the year 2019, before the “Defund the Police” campaign took root. Strive For Change Home-grown charity supports 11 East Bay job-training programs The task of overcoming poverty in the East Bay is shared by everyone who lives here. All of us want to live in neighborhoods that are stable, secure and thriving. One non-profit has been working for 15 years on this problem by focusing on job-training programs for low-income workers in Alameda and Contra Costa counties. The Strive for Change Foundation, a (501c3) non-profit, believes all workers deserve the chance to improve their job skills and get better jobs. Increased income helps low-income workers achieve a more stable and financially self-sustaining future. Their families, their neighborhoods, and everyone around them benefits. The Strive for Change Foundation was founded in 2006 by Piedmont resident Lester Ellis and a small group of individuals who wanted to support workforce development programs for low-income workers. They decided to gather their donations into a single fund and use it to give grants to multiple non-profit job-training programs throughout the East Bay. Since that time, the Strive for Change Foundation has donated more than one million dollars to dozens of job-training programs in Alameda and Contra Costa counties. Grants range in size from about $5,000 to a high of $12,500. Strive for Change supports organizations who help low-income workers with barriers to employment develop the skills they need to find better jobs, keep those jobs, and build stable futures for their families. Strive for Change operates on three core principles. First, unlike larger foundations that serve international endeavors, Strive for Change focuses exclusively on the working poor in Alameda and Contra Costa counties. Second, 100% of donor contributions go to the agencies identified as worthy of support. The all-volunteer Board covers all administrative costs such as mailing, postage, and informational materials. And third, Strive for Change rigorously vets the agencies that seek support. The Board meets annually with the Executive Directors and program managers, and asks them the hard questions about budgets, graduation rate, job placement and retention rates. This process helps Strive supporters to be better-informed donors as well. Strive’s Board of Directors meets monthly to review grantee programs and discuss ongoing concerns, among them fundraising and Board development. Most Board members spend an average of two to five hours per month on Board activities. Board positions are available in the areas of workforce development, fundraising, writing and graphic design. For many members of the East Bay community, every hour is a struggle to put food on the table and keep a roof overhead. Minimum wage earners often require three full-time jobs just to provide their family with basic necessities. Post-Covid, many of those underpaid jobs will no longer exist. The need is greater than ever before for job-training programs that demonstrably help hardworking, ambitious people get better jobs. More information about the Strive for Change Foundation can be found at www. striveforchangefoundation.org. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council has decided to delay the decision to designate four parking spaces on Bonita Avenue by the Rec. tennis courts as Electric Vehicle (EV) charging stations. The consideration was on the agenda for the July 19 meeting. Special Assistant to City Administrator Paul Benoit told councilmembers that staff had requested to pull the agenda item, and return to city council for more discussion in August. “Progress is being made with East Bay Community Energy in addressing the concerns that council expressed in the past. Our preference is to bring a fully-baked plan that we feel is going as far as we can go with East Bay Energy, but it’s just not ready yet,” Benoit said. A decision was initially delayed on the June 21 meeting. East Bay Community Energy (EBCE) and city staff worked together to plan the installation of EV charging stations, serving four existing, angled public parking spots next to the tennis courts on Bonita Avenue. The proposed 10-year agreement would allow EBCE to install two dual-port, fast-charging stations at the location, which would be able to charge up to four vehicles at one time. The stations would be maintained and operated by EBCE, at no cost to the city. CivicSpark Fellow Nate Redinbo called the proposal a “winwin” for the city in terms of reaching its ambitious Climate Action Plan goals of reducing greenhouse emissions. According to data collected from a survey conducted by FM3 Research in June 2020, 26% of Piedmonters own an electric vehicle. The survey asked respondents, “as part of the Climate Action Plan, the City is considering expanding access to electric vehicle chargers in Piedmont. The City would partner with East Bay Community Energy to install publicly accessible chargers on streetlights in three key locations in Piedmont, and to install publicly accessible high-speed charging ports in four spaces in Community Hall Parking Lot. East Bay Community Energy will pay the full cost to install chargers and will own and maintain them. Each charger would be adjacent to a designated electric vehicle-only parking spot. Does this program generally sound like something you would support or oppose?” A total of 79% of respondents supported the program, with 49% listing as “strongly supporting” and 16% opposed the program. On a statewide level, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order to set a target that 100% of in-state sales of new passenger vehicles will be zero-emission by 2035. The order was signed in September 2020, following a catastrophic wildfire season.

articles.text: Fentons Creamery is considered an Oakland landmark, serving ice cream in the East Bay for over 100 years. The ice cream parlor familiar to Piedmonters opened in 1894 on the corner of 41st and Howe streets before moving a few blocks away to its present location on Piedmont Avenue in 1961. Years earlier, in 1894, Eldridge Seth’s grandson, Melvin Fenton, was responsible for inventing Rocky Road ice cream, arguably its most famous creation. Fentons candymaker George Farren made a Rocky Road candy bar and decided to blend it into an ice cream flavor in the late 1920s. Other Fentons original ice creams are Swiss Milk Chocolate and Toasted Almond. In 2001 an arson fire destroyed part of the building, but the cost to fully restore the parlor was more than $2 million. The renovated creamery included a new grill, a larger dining room and more items on the menu. Eight years after the rebuilding, Pixar featured it in its Oscar Award-winning film, Up. It seems that director Pete Docter, producer Jonas Rivera, and other Pixar employees were regular customers. In 2007 Fentons opened a second location in Vacaville at the site of the former Nut Tree restaurant and later a small ice cream shop in the Oakland International Airport. and strawberry. Asked about the Piedmont connection, Rodgers said, “Fentons is very well known for giving back to the community and a lot of community outreach.” He went on to say that there is no robust advertising needed, because people fill the parlor largely through word-of-mouth. “The love that we put into the ice cream really shows to our customers,” Rodgers added, noting that customers come from throughout the Bay Area. The stability of Fentons has been one of its strengths. Customers who have been visiting the Piedmont Avenue parlor enjoy seeing familiar faces among the staff. Many of the employees have been working there for over 20 years. In discussing the impact of the COVID pandemic on Fentons and its business, Rodgers confirmed that it lost 50% of its business. “A lot of our business is party business, and [COVID restrictions] took that away.” Fentons opened for outdoor dining as soon as Alameda County permitted it. “We thought it would put a smile on people’s faces during tough times,” Rodgers said with a smile. On this reporter’s visit last week, sales were brisk and inside and outside the parlor, the place was packed. Larissa Edel is an intern at the Piedmont Post. Staff photo The famous Fentons Sundae, a favorite dessert from the legendary East Bay ice cream parlor. Through the years, Fentons has built a solid reputation in the U.S. Its “Banana Special” was named the No. 1 dessert by The Food Channel. In a recent discussion with Fentons General Manager Jarrod Rodgers, we learned that its most-ordered flavor year-round is Coffee Cookie Dream. It was also the most-chosen flavor among Piedmonters in The Question Man a few weeks earlier. Rodger explained that Coffee Cookie Dream was created by a server working at Fentons. Inside the room where it is made it is called Shandy’s, named after its inventor. Rodgers said that most ideas for ice cream flavors and sundaes come from Fentons employees. But even with the new flavors introduced each year, the most ordered flavors year-round are the three staples – vanilla, chocolate services. his artwork. each evening.

articles.text: Doorkeeper Nick Baz will hang up his keys and retire after 15 years of service to Piedmont Community Church. Baz is always on hand for whatever is needed, functioning as a greeter every Sunday morning for church Baz’s last day will be September 30. He is planning on moving to Portland, Oregon, where he will spend quality time with his family while continuing to develop and expand In the meantime, he will continue serving coffee before and after worship services and securing the buildings and grounds “We will all miss Nick,” said Dr. Steve Schibsted, the interim Senior Minister. “We are grateful for the years of service he has given to Piedmont Community Church and wish him the very best in this next chapter of his life.” Longtime church member Jay Foreman, who has been a parttime custodian for the past year, will become full-time and take on responsibilities as doorkeeper after Baz retires. The cottage in which Baz currently resides will receive minor renovations after his departure. Foreman will call the cottage home after the renovations are completed. articles.text: The Piedmont Police and Piedmont Fire Departments hereby invite all community members to celebrate the 2021 National Night Out next Tuesday August 3. As part of National Night Out, members of the Piedmont Police and Fire Departments will visit registered neighborhood events ranging from small potlucks and BBQs to community meetings and block parties throughout the city. “We hope neighbors near and far will join us for a fun and informative evening. There will be delicious Mexican food for purchase from Abel’s Taco Truck, music, games and friendship. After a 16-month pandemic we all feel a little more isolated from one another, so please join us and help continue to build a more caring place to live,” said host Marilyn Weber. As residents and police officers come together, the main objective continues to be one of the most effective crime prevention techniques of all – getting to know your neighbors. The event sends a message to criminals that neighborhoods are organized and united in preventing crime. “We are excited by this year’s National Night Out event as our community comes together once again to connect and affirm the importance of community safety.” said Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. “So much has changed since our last event two years ago. We know the myriad of challenges that face us as a collective. As a police department, we know our connection with the community is essential to achieving our highest standards in service. National Night Out offers us an opportunity to connect and come together.” To register your own BBQ block party event, obtain flyers for your event, and gain more information, contact Officer Nicole Casalnuovo at ncasalnuovo@piedmont.ca.gov. Lic. No. 702138

articles.text: In the 1998 iconic Lindsey Lohan film, The Parent Trap, separated twin sisters spend much of their time at Camp Walden pranking each other – and their counselors as well. At Camp Augusta, one will find no such animosity between campers and counselors. Camp Augusta boasts the longest staff training of any camp in America. Before counselors even step foot on Nevada City soil, they go through a rigorous application process. Camp Director Randy Grayson describes the application process as courtship because of how important it is for both sides to understand each other. Before counselors can even apply, they must read through pages of descriptions of life at camp and be absolutely certain they’re ready for the Camp Augusta counselor lifestyle. While that may sound like overkill, this ensures that only counselors who are 100% sure they can thrive at Camp Augusta end up there for the start of training in May. The training includes 22 days of intense, 12-hours-a-day work to help counselors perfect their skills before campers arrive. Before campers arrive, counselors and staff go through emotional preparation that helps them all grow closer together and allows them to help their campers grow. “This session has truly been unforgettable, and I don’t say that lightly. I have had such a wonHigh adventure awaits kids at Camp Augusta. derful cabin. It was my first twoweek session at Camp Augusta and there has been such cohesion among my campers and such willingness to try new activities,” said first-year counselor Lucy Weld. “At the start of camp, there was a lot of interest in the throwing range and all the weapons clinics we offer here, but as they got into the flow of things, there has been a lot more interest in arts and crafts, along with improv and different activities.” Weld has a very calming, kind demeanor that made her perfectly suited to work with the cabin named Oak 1 girls. pages.text: Wednesday, July 28, 2021 5 A look at what makes Augusta a unique camp By Campbell Lawson In the 1998 iconic Lindsey Lohan film, The Parent Trap, separated twin sisters spend much of their time at Camp Walden pranking each other – and their counselors as well. At Camp Augusta, one will find no such animosity between campers and counselors. Camp Augusta boasts the longest staff training of any camp in America. Before counselors even step foot on Nevada City soil, they go through a rigorous application process. Camp Director Randy Grayson describes the application process as courtship because of how important it is for both sides to understand each other. Before counselors can even apply, they must read through pages of descriptions of life at camp and be absolutely certain they’re ready for the Camp Augusta counselor lifestyle. While that may sound like overkill, this ensures that only counselors who are 100% sure they can thrive at Camp Augusta end up there for the start of training in May. The training includes 22 days of intense, 12-hours-a-day work to help counselors perfect their skills before campers arrive. Before campers arrive, counselors and staff go through emotional preparation that helps them all grow closer together and allows them to help their campers grow. “This session has truly been unforgettable, and I don’t say that lightly. I have had such a wonHigh adventure awaits kids at Camp Augusta. derful cabin. It was my first twoweek session at Camp Augusta and there has been such cohesion among my campers and such willingness to try new activities,” said first-year counselor Lucy Weld. “At the start of camp, there was a lot of interest in the throwing range and all the weapons clinics we offer here, but as they got into the flow of things, there has been a lot more interest in arts and crafts, along with improv and different activities.” Weld has a very calming, kind demeanor that made her perfectly suited to work with the cabin named Oak 1 girls. One of the clinics she teaches at camp is making herbal medicine, and her influence on her campers can be seen through their shifting interests. “Lucy has been an amazing counselor. I would love to have her as my counselor time and time again,” said first-year camper Adia Bagley. The debate while they painted a new Jackson Pollock-style sign for their cabin was which of the boys was most like a “Pine” boy. In context, Pine, is the circle of the younger boys at camp. Perhaps because of that the campers and counselors at Camp Augusta can develop close relationships unlike any other between campers and counselors at other camps. articles.text: Kimberly Bonacum has retired from her position as an Occupational Therapist with Piedmont School District for 18 years. She worked at every school site as a paraeducator and occupational therapist, helping students from preschool to 12th grade overcome challenges and gain confidence. “Kim was always kid-centered and came up with creative and inventive ways to reach her students. She is a true gem, and we will miss having her as part of our special education team,” said Carrie Poole, School District Special Education Program Coordinator. The work of an OT is centered on fine motor, visual perception, and sensory motor skills. Bonacum took an inventive approach to her work, creating physical tools and starting the “Food School” for preschoolers. Bonacum’s professional journey began at Yale hospital in New Haven, Connecticut, working in adult rehabilitation. She took the opportunity to work with the hospital in developing a Newborn Intensive Care Unit program for therapists. After working with adults and then with newborns, Bonacum moved to California and began her career working with children. In 2003 she worked as a oneon-one paraeducator at Havens but had her sights set on leading the Occupational Therapy Program for General Education. One year later the position opened up and Bonacum began working with students in grades K-2. “When students succeed, they feel more confident, whether it is with their ability to write legibly or effortlessly. OT is also just about helping a student overcome,” Bonacum said. Bonacum may be best known for starting the “Food School,” getting kids in preschool to explore new foods. “We worked on sensitivity, which we call sensory defensiveness,” Bonacum explained. “As the student explores foods, whether it is touching it smelling it, playing with it actually, it is not so scary.” Bonacum expanded the teaching to parents by giving them chocolate covered crickets – real crickets. “I handed the crickets to the parents so each of them could experience holding a food they had never had before. We talked about what they felt while just holding it. It is no different from when a kid gets broccoli; it is something new,” she said. Bonacum recalled a moment of affirmation that the Food School was working. “I had a parent call me to say, ‘my son just ate a piece of salmon,’ and she was just in tears. As a parent if you can’t get your child to eat, you are always Kim Bonacum worked as an Occupational Therapist at all schools in Piedmont School District. worried about nutrition. It can be something that overwhelms you.” The General Education Program Bonacum led was eliminated by the school district in 2009, and so Bonacum adapted to being a one-on-one paraeducator while also working part-time as at an OT at Children’s Hospital in Oakland. In 2013 Bonacum returned to full time work at all five Piedmont schools, working with students of all ages who needed support. Bonacum witnessed a change in attitude towards occupational therapy during her career with the acceptance and adaptation of OT methods by teachers. “Teachers have now become much more onboard with what we call ‘sensory strategies’ in the classroom. They really saw how some of these strategies or tools were helpful for learning, so they became the ones seeking me out. That openness was exciting to see.” The greatest challenge in her career was likely the shift to distance learning in 2020 due to COVID. “Never in a million years did I think I would do OT over a computer for a job. But we made it work.” she said. Bonacum has moved to Maine with her husband Doug, and after taking a break will pursue her business, Mindful Fidgets, selling fine motor and sensory tools for kids. First, though, she and her husband are planning to walk the historic 500-mile Camino de Santiago pilgrimage in Spain, walking from village to village. articles.text: After a one-year hiatus, the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Schoolmates program is returning to accompany the school district’s upcoming 2021- 22 academic year. The program will become a license-exempt childcare facility by operating less than 20 hours a week. Schoolmates is a play-based, before-school (morning) and after-school (afternoon) program. Both time slots offer daily activities, such as staff-led outside games, art projects, cooking lessons, team-building activities, and free play, all designed for children at different age levels. While on hiatus due to the coronavirus pandemic, and subsequent school district closure, the program was re-imagined last year as the virtual program “Camp Smart Start” and department-organized play pods. Schoolmates returns this year as a license-exempt program. It has been required to operate as a licensed childcare facility under California law, because it operated as a full-day program, open from 7:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. “As a licensed childcare facility, Schoolmates had to adhere to state-mandated requirements, which proved challenging,” Recreation Supervisor Jackson Stearns told Recreation Commissioners at a July 21 meeting. The state required all staff members to pass a background check and meet strict education requirements, which includes completed units in early childcare education. Child to staff ratio could not exceed 14 to one. Stearns explained that department staff will still do background checks and adhere to all recommended child-to-staff ratios, which he said is often well under the state requirements and are “typically at a 1 to 10 [staffto-child] ratio.” “We are excited about this change, because it means we’ll be able to serve more families and continue to bring in great staff, knowing that we are following the rules as they should be,” Stearns said. “And we’re excited to move away from computer screens and to get back into what we’ve been known for all these years, which is high-quality, play-based childcare.” Drop-in registration caused Schoolmates to routinely exceed licensing capacity, and “put staff in a difficult position of either turning children away, or being out of compliance,” Stearns said. The license-exempt status allows the program to expand its capacity limits – 44 at Beach, 50 at Havens, and 40 at Wildwood – to a more flexible capacity in line with Fire Marshal Room capacity limits. Allowed capacity nearly doubles at Beach and Wildwood locations, from 44 to 77 and 40 to 72, respectively, when the program becomes license-exempt. Stearns said that these changes will not in any way affect the well-being, or educational aspects of the program. “We intend to follow every rule for licensing. [There are] clearly defined guidelines, staff training, and classroom setup that we will continue to do, with the exception of the room capacity, essentially,” he said, adding that staff would not be negatively affected by the change, either. Registration opens today, July 28 for the after-school care program and is accessible via Community Pass online. Residents with questions may contact Recreation Supervisor Jackson Stearns at jstearns@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: City’s childcare program to operate as “license-exempt”

articles.text: One of the four new courses offered at Piedmont High School this fall is Guitar Engineering, to be taught by veteran Physics instructor Marna Chamberlain, who came up with the idea for the class. Students will construct their own solid-body electric guitar. The course will cover the different types of wood used in guitars, guitar headstock design features, and math application in a guitar. Physical science aspects of the guitar will be explored in addition to mechanical systems, concepts of sound, string tension, fretboard layout, intonation and electronic circuitry. Students will begin the year by learning to use the tools in the new Fabrication Maker’s Lab while building a simple instrument from a cigar box. The bulk of the course will be creating full-size guitars. After fine tuning their finished instruments, students will have the opportunity to use the new CNC and 3D printers to manufacture additional projects. Guitar Engineering will be offered for the first time at Piedmont High this fall, 21 students so far have signed up for the year-long course. Science, technology, engineering and mathematics concepts that relate directly to guitars will be used to help students make an applied learning connection. “I feel that there needs to be classes available for kids to explore and build things for the pure enjoyment and experience,” explained Chamberlain. “Guitar Engineering integrates multiple subjects together. A cross-curricular course is important for students to see the interconnected of multiple disciplines which go beyond a single subject matter,” said School Board President Cory Smegal. To learn more see: Guitarbuilding.org.
articles.title: Marna Chamberlain’s Guitar Engineering class likely to be in demand

articles.text: Chabot Space and Science Center in the hills above Oakland opened its doors for the first time in over a year to hold a press conference on Tuesday July 20 announcing a new exhibit space in partnership with NASA’s Ames Research Center. Chabot’s Executive Director Adam Tobin and the Director of Ames, Eugene Tu, provided details of the new partnership before Chabot’s Galaxy Explorer volunteers displayed prototypes of the new exhibits that will be in The Nasa Experience exhibit. The NASA Experience aims to put the visitor into the role of a NASA researcher. Hands-on STEM studios will actively teach principals such as aerodynamics through wind tunnels, spectroscopy and how to make a comet from scratch. The exhibit will highlight the process of getting into space through interactive challenges, models, and artifacts. At the conference, Galaxy Explorer volunteers, including Piedmont students Helena Lowe and Sage Mosley, led activities and demonstrations for the media audience. articles.text: The University of California (UC) system made the most admission offers to California residents applying as freshman or transfers in its history. The record-breaking year saw more than 200,000 applicants vying for 46,000 freshman seats. Systemwide freshman admissions jumped 11 percent in 2020, the UC Office of the President announced in a statement on July 19. Admission of California freshmen reached an all-time high this year with 84,223 students, an increase of 5% over 79,953 from 2020. “These remarkable numbers are a testament to the hard work and resiliency of students and their families across California,” said UC President Michael Drake. “I am particularly heartened by the social and economic diversity of those offered a place at UC. Fall will be an exciting time on our campuses.” “As the data make clear, UC is continuing to honor its commitment to guarantee admission to high-performing California high school students and providing a clear pathway for talented community college students to join us,” said Han Mi Yoon-Wu, executive director of Undergraduate Admissions at UC. Applications to schools within the UC system were vastly different this year due to the closure of schools in the state for months as a result of the COVID pandemic. Schools in the UC system suspended the letter-grade requirement for high school classes in 2020, and the full 2020-21 academic year. The end of the standardized testing requirement may have also encouraged more students to apply, Yoon-Wu said. While more room has been made for in-state applicants, three campuses – UCLA, Cal, and UC San Diego – could reduce their share of out-of-state and international students under an amended state budget bill dated June 25. The proposed bill would pay the university system to reduce nonresident students from more than 22% of the undergraduate population to 18% at the three campuses, which remain the system’s most sought-after for high-achieving students. Concurrently, the University of California regents approved a multiyear plan to raise tuition and fees for in-state students – the first increase since 2017. The plan calls for fees to rise by 2% plus inflation for new undergraduates starting in the 2022-23 academic year.
articles.title: UC offers record-high admissions to Calif. students

Wednesday, July 28, 2021 13 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 14th year in the Post. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. AIDAN MITCHELL Baseball Piedmont High Class of 2021 Menlo College Class of 2025 Aiden Mitchell recently graduated from Piedmont High and is set to attend Menlo College in the fall. He was a two-year starter as a pitcher and infielder for the Highlanders, after transferring to Piedmont from Switzerland in his junior year in 2019. Mitchell returned to his home country this summer to compete on the Hünenberg Unicorns. He’s been a member of the Unicorns, an adult-level traveling team, since he was 15-years old before his family moved to California. In the Swiss Baseball National League A, he plays alongside players in their mid-20’s and early-30’s. Mitchell took the mound on July 4 in Switzerland against the Sissach Frogs, throwing a complete game in six innings with 95 pitches and 15 strikeouts. What is your workout program this summer? This summer I am playing and working out in Switzerland, where we practice three times a week for three-hour sessions, in addition to playing double-header games every weekend. Since I don’t have access to a gym, I am working out in alternative ways outside of practice, including hiking in the beautiful Swiss Alps. What are your fitness goals for this summer? Outside of baseball, I am focusing on cardio with a lot of running, hiking, and fun ways as well. I’m going to Seilparks (Ropes Courses) to better enhance my balance and endurance – two things which are very important for pitching. How are you measuring your development? I measure my development by how I perform in bullpens and pitching outings. I am really trying to have firm command since I am not a velocity pitcher. I track my balls and strikes ratio during those outings to get an idea of what’s working and what I need to improve. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? In Piedmont I worked out with coach Steve Thobe, the assistant coach for the varsity team and an excellent pitching coach. Now in Switzerland, I am working with another excellent pitching coach. I am also working with two college pitchers from Vassar College in Switzerland. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? At my July 4 outing, I threw a complete game of six innings with one hit allowed, no runs, Staff Photo GREG GATELY Lacrosse Aidan Mitchell, Class of 2021, was a two-year varsity starter on Piedmont’s baseball team. He plans to play college ball at Menlo College. He’s currently playing baseball in Switzerland, hi home country. This is a huge milestone for me based on my improvement over a short amount of time. I usually average a walk every inning or so, but had none in six innings. My workout program consists of weightlifting and cardio exercises, six days a week as instructed by the Strength and Conditioning Coach at Connecticut College. I also practice shooting, agility, and stick skills for lacrosse. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? My advice is to start the process early. My recruiting process began in the middle of senior year; if it wasn’t for an amazing outing at a showcase with Headfirst, my club team, I wouldn’t be joining Menlo, a good baseball school. What are your fitness goals for the summer? I am working on running two miles in under 12 minutes. Another fitness goal is to gain lean muscle mass through proper nutrition and strength training. I am also improving my ability to create space on the field with precise footwork. How are you measuring your development? With the workout plan created by the Connecticut College conditioning coach, I track my progress with speed statistics every week. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? Zamora is a double-double machine for the Highlanders. She logged seven consecutive double-doubles in Piedmont wins between April 29 and May 10. She also had 22 rebounds in a 73-67 win against Oakland Tech on May 22, the most for PHS since Kelea Pickeral-Dennis had 38 in 2015. What is your workout program this summer? Before traveling, I worked out four days a week in the gym and two days in the weight room. I also train two days a week with trainer Darnell Mcoulloch, I do everyday training with my dad and Nike coaches across the country. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My overall goals are to improve all of my skills, and generally get faster and stronger. How are you measuring your development? articles.text: Photo courtesy of Thestrikertexas.com Matthew Hoppe scored a header goal in the 83rd minute against Jamaica to send the U.S. soccer team to the semifinals with Qatar. The U.S. Men’s Soccer Team defeated Jamaica 1-0 on Sunday, July 25, to advance to the semifinals of the CONCACAF Gold Cup tournament tomorrow, Thursday, July 29 at 4:30 p.m. in a game with Qatar to be played in Austin, Texas. Mexico, the tournament favorite, beat Honduras 3-0 on Saturday, July 24, and will play Canada tomorrow at 7:00 p.m. in Houston. Canada played well in a 2-0 win over Costa Rica on Sunday, and Qatar beat El Salvador 3-2 on Saturday. The winners of the two semifinal matches will play for the Gold Cup championship on Sunday, August 1 in Las Vegas’ Allegiant Stadium. All Gold Cup matches are being televised on Fox Sports 1. The U.S. 1-0 win over Jamaica was an entertaining back-andforth contest in which 20-year old striker Matthew Hoppe landed a monumental header goal in the 83rd minute. The United States walks into Sunday’s match as the favorites, but they shouldn’t feel comfortable against the surging team from the Persian Gulf. Qatar plays with a distinct attacking style, showing prowess in transition on counters and a possessive style that open up shooting lanes. They capitalized on an El Salvador mistake for a goal in the 2nd minute of action. The U.S. must play a crisp game, but we’re predicting they can get the job done. Post Prediction: U.S. wins 3-2 Moving to El Tri of Mexico, it’s hard to imagine a Canadian upset despite its strong 2-0 win over Costa Rica. The team from north of the border doesn’t have the depth of Mexico. Mexico has the most star-studded roster in the Gold Cup, with Jesus Corona of FC Porto, Atletico Madrid’s Hector Herrera, and LA Galaxy’s Jonathan Dos Santa. They should prevail. Post Prediction: Mexico wins 2-0 For the finals we’re predicting a fabled match of Mexico vs. U.S.A. The teams last faced one another in the CONCACAF Nations League, where the U.S. had a huge 3-2 win on a penalty kick by Christian Pulisic and penalty save by U.S. goalie Evan Horvath. The U.S. has an entirely different roster now, while some Mexico players are still on the team. It’s doubtful El Tri will forget the loss to the U.S. Mexico has a pressing style, while the United States’ roster has shown some cracks when defenses turn up the heat. Like Qatar, they’ll have to make sure to keep the mistakes to a minimum or they risk relinquishing possession in bad areas on the pitch. Considering all this, it’s hard envisioning a U.S. upset. Post Prediction: Mexico wins 2-1. Photo courtesy of Yahoo.com Mexico is rolling after a 3-0 win over Honduras to place them in the semifinals with Canada.

articles.text: Rafaella Gomes is a member of Piedmont High’s graduating class of 2021, but isn’t your typical student-athlete competing in traditional school sports A talented fencer, with dual citizenship in the U.S. and Brazil, she will continue her sports career in the fall at the University of California at San Diego. She’s currently competing in prestigious tournaments in Brazil, her home country, to improve her national ranking. Currently ranked No. 9 in Brazil’s U-20 women’s ladder, she is also ranked No. 21 in the Senior category. “This is my debut in Brazil. It’s been a great experience spending time with my family. It’s been three years since I’ve seen my grandmothers in person. They’re both over 70, and I treasure every opportunity I have to be with them,” said Gomes. “My family is the core of my motivation to represent Brazil,” she added. In the United States, Gomes competed in the Junior, Division IA, and Division I ladders and earned U.S. Fencing All-American honors in 2020. On June 26 this summer, she placed third out of 13 fencers at an Under-20 Brazilian Youth Interclub Circuit foil competition and followed up on June 27 in the Senior Interclub Brazilian Circuit with another third-place medal at Porto Alegre. “Porto Alegre in Rio Grande Gomes trains with the Massialas Foundation in San Francisco and will joining the fencing program at UC San Diego this fall. Gomes (left) does another dodge and lunge while competing in Brazil. do Sul is the coldest state in the country. In the tournament, the humidity made the floor incredibly slippery, and I pulled a muscle during the first bout of the first day. I worked through the pain and finished in third in the Junior event that day and again in the Senior event the next day,” explained Gomes. It was an impressive return to competition after going a full year without any tournaments due to the global pandemic. “I am incredibly grateful for the opportunity after more than a year without competing, and happy to be back on the fencing strip,” she said. Gomes has been competing for eight years with the Massialas Foundation in San Francisco, a club program run by U.S. Men’s Foil coach Greg Massialas. The foundation is considered a pipeline to the Olympic team for West Coast athletes. Six members of the club were on the U.S. men’s team in the 2012 Olympics. Currently club member Gerek Meinhardt is ranked No. 2 in the world and was the No. 1 seed in the 2020 Olympics. Alexander Massialas is No. 8, and Sabrina Massialas is a member of the U.S. women’s team. “I have been fencing for nine years, during eight of which I have trained at the Massialas Foundation in San Francisco. It is a premier club in the Bay Area,” mentioned Gomes. Gomes is now preparing for the Senior Interclubs Brazilian Circuit tournament from August 14-15. She is considering the U-20 Brazilian Interclub Championship September 15-19 just before she starts class at UC San Diego. “I want to hit the ground running when I start the semester,” she said. Rafaella Gomes holds a Bronze Medal she won at the Brazil Interclub Circuit in Porto Alegre. She placed third in both Youth and Senior divisions.
articles.title: Piedmont fencer Rafaella Gomes competing in Brazil

articles.text: The Tamarack Fire wages in Humboldt-Toiyabe National Forest and has consumed 67,764 acres, with 45 percent containment as of Monday, July 26. The blaze began on July 4 and was one of several fires sparked by lightning in the area. It expanded by wind the following week. The fire is burning just 25 miles south of South Lake Tahoe As of yesterday, July 27, the blaze was 59 percent contained and air quality had improved. For those considering traveling to Lake Tahoe, the National Weather Service issued a statement that smoke will continue to impact the region. While conditions may incrementally improve during the daytime hours, poor air quality is expected for the foreseeable future. “There will be periods late in the day where air quality could improve somewhat around RenoTahoe and the Eastern Sierra,” wrote the National Weather Service in Reno. “However, for the most part you should expect poor air quality to persist, especially at night and in the mornings.” The National Weather Service also issued a flash flood warning for Lake Tahoe, Douglas County, and Western Nevada on Monday, July 26 due to weather patterns spreading north into east central Photos courtesy of TahoeSouth.com A webcam photo of Timber Cove in South Lake Tahoe, showing the air quality and visitors still swimming on Monday, July 26. Proof of the constantly changing Air Quality conditions with wind and rain, a webcam photo of Timber Cove one day later shows a much clearer day. California. Slow moving hybrid type thunderstorms could produce short periods of heavy rains in the area. which could impact loose debris created by the fire. As of Monday, the South Lake Tahoe had a U.S. Air Quality Index rating of 121 in the “Unhealthy for sensitive groups” range. However, that number dipped back into the green healthy range for both South and North Lake Tahoe on Tuesday night after rain showers in the area.

articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek A “Sculpture Show Evening Stroll” will be held on August 12 at the Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek, featuring the works of over 20 renowned Northern California artists. Each year, the garden hosts an annual art show and sale that showcases sculptural art against the natural backdrop of the location. Live jazz music will be performed, and beer and wine is available for purchase. A special members-only after-hours evening sculpture stroll begins at 5 p.m. The Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is famous for its extensive collection of succulents, cacti, California native plants, and other drought-tolerant plants. The garden was originally planted in 1972 by Ruth Bancroft when it was her private, personal garden but is now open six days a week for the education and enjoyment of the public. Bancroft created a garden of dynamic plant combinations using drought-tolerant plants that very few other gardeners were using at the time. In 1989, her garden was selected by the Garden Conservancy to be its first preservation project, and a conservation easement was established to ensure its preservation. The garden is open from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., Tuesday through Thursday, and 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday through Sunday. For a full list of items in bloom see the website: https:// www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/wp/ wp-content/uploads/Whats-InBloom-July-2021.pdf. For more information, see: https://www. ruthbancroftgarden.org/.
articles.title: Bancroft Garden Sculpture Stroll on August 12

articles.text: “Starry Nights” is San Francisco Ballet’s return-to-the-stage performance at Stanford University’s Frost Amphitheater on August 13 and 14. In partnership with Stanford Live, the two-performance program will feature George Balanchine’s Serenade set to a Tchaikovsky score, and Artistic Director Helgi Tomasson’s The Fifth Season set to music by Karl Jenkins. Danielle Rowe’s For Pixie, set to the music of Nina Simone and Balanchine’s Tarantella, with music by Louis Gottschalk, also will be performed. Serenade is Balanchine’s first ballet created in the U.S. Created for students at the School of American Ballet during a class Tomasson’s Fifth Season is set to the music of Karl Jenkins and was commissioned for San Francisco Ballet’s 2006 Repertory Season. “I felt it was contemporary to today, and it’s romantic,” Tomasson said. “Even though it’s in the minimalist genre, there’s a swell of melodic feeling underneath.” Rowe’s For Pixie is more contemporary in nature. The choreographer is known for the cross-disciplinary immersive theater productions of “FURY,” and “Before You Had a Name.” Both Friday and Saturday performances begin at 7:30 p.m. at Frost Amphitheater, Masks are required for unvaccinated patrons. To obtain tickets, visit https://www.sfballet.org/calendar/starry-nights-sf-ballets-return-to-the-stage/. articles.text: A scene from San Francisco Opera’s production of Tosca. San Francisco Opera will present Giacomo Puccini’s Tosca at the War Memorial Opera House beginning August 21 and running through September 5. Titular character Floria Tosca faces a brutal police chief whose cruelty forces her to sacrifice everything she cares for in the hope of surviving. Ailyn Pérez, Michael Fabiano, and Alfred Walker star in the revival of Shawna Lucey’s period production. New Music Director Eun Sun Kim will take the baton to conduct Tosca as her first opera in the position. Running time is approximately two hours, 45 minutes, to include two intermissions. A total of five performances will be presented between August 21, and September 5, at either 7:30 p.m. or 2 p.m. Ticket inventory is limited. To purchase tickets, visit https://sfopera.com/on-stage/ tosca/.
articles.title: SF Opera to perform Tosca August 21- Sept. 5

articles.text: Music Director Joseph Young will lead Berkeley Symphony in its first live appearance in more than a year with a performance at Bruns Amphitheater, home of California Shakespeare Theater, on Tuesday, August 4 at 7:30 p.m. The program includes music by Rossini, Bizet, Bach, Beethoven, Tchaikovsky, Gabriela Lena Frank, Brian Raphael Nabors, and Jessie Montgomery. A program highlight will be the performance of Iubilo by Nabors, whose composition is part of New Music USA’s Amplifying Voices program scheduled for the 2022- 2023 season. Actors from Cal Shakes will be on stage for a collaboration combining iconic Shakespeare passages with Beethoven’s Egmont Overture. “I am thrilled to share the stage once again with Berkeley Symphony and finally be together with our audiences after all this time apart,” Young said. “There is a tangible sense of hope and optimism as we collectively look ahead to a brighter future, and it is in the same spirit that we mark this turning point with our first live performance together in more than a year.” Bruns Amphitheater will provide an open-air venue for Berkeley Symphony’s first live concert in a year-and-a-half.
