articles.text: Throughout the summer the Post will print a sampling of letters written by kids attending Camp Augusta, Piedmont’s residential camp at Lake Vera outside Nevada City in the Sierra foothills. Founded in 1931, the camp remains a vital part of the life of hundreds of children each summer. Last week as the temperature hovered near 100 degrees, camp counselors kept kids cool using misters, ice, pools, and changing the schedule so high exertion activities happened first thing in the morning or in the hours before dark. For a local view of the summer ritual, residents will see large groups of families waiting each weekend for the arrival of busses with kids returning from camp, and a fresh group ready to head to Camp Augusta for one or two weeks of pure fun. For more information, see campaugusta.org. Singing during a campfire – a camp favorite. A cabin (with Randy and a giant magic saber) has a mini-oatmeal fight and then gets ready to get hosed off.

articles.text: After 2021’s sports schedule finished in an accelerated threemonths of activities, the summer has now rolled around and high schools throughout the country say goodbye to former student athletes after graduation. With that, the Class of 2022 looks past the summer break to what could be a defining year of their high school careers as a senior. In this series, the Post takes a look at four athletes from the Class of 2022. Jack Stein, Cross Country & Track and Field Jack Stein had a big junior year on the cross-country and track teams, taking the step up as a team leader Stein consistently improved throughout 2021, creating personal record times in the 1600, 3200, and 3-mile cross country event. In the 3200, he set a PR (personal record) by 10 seconds with a time of 9:46.58 at the Dublin Distance Fiesta on April 24. It came one week after he won the Western Alameda County Conference Championship meet on April 7 in a field of 35 runners. He’s the first PHS runner to crack the 10-minute mark in the 3200 meters since Reece Proctor in 2018. Stein finished fifth in a field of 53 runners in the 1600 meters at the WACC Championship. He improved his time to 4:36 at the Dublin Distance Fiesta. In Cross Country, Stein helped the Highlanders place second of nine schools in the WACC Championship. He finished third out of 59 runners with a time of 15:58.5. Chiara Lundin, Softball Chiara Lundin will be a senior leader on the softball team and will be among two players for the Class of 2022 on next year’s team alongside pitcher Izzy Epstein. The squad went 6-4 last season, 2-1-1 as a sophomore before the season was canceled. The Photo by Steve Zirkelbach Jack Stein had a breakout year as a junior on the cross-country and track team. He was the WACC’s 3200 -meter champion. Staff Photo Chiara Lundin, the leading hitter on the softball team, was the Post’s Freshman of the Year in 2019. Staff Photo Nico Defazio hits in the No. 2 spot on the baseball team and is its starting shortstop. team was 7-13 in her freshman year when she was named the Post’s Freshman of the Year. Lundin led the team in hitting this season with a .483 batting average with 14 hits, three home runs, three doubles and a triple. She also logged 16 runs scored and 11 RBIs. Nico Defazio, Baseball & Football Nico Defazio is the baseball team’s starting shortstop and proved to be a key player batting in the No. 2. He had the second highest batting average on the team at .404 with 23 hits, five doubles, 12 RBIs, 13 runs scored, and drew 10 walks. He was critical in Piedmont’s 13-12 comeback victory over Hayward on March 24 when he hit 4-for-5 with three RBIs and two runs scored. Defazio is a two-sport athlete, who is a receiver on the football team.

articles.text: Photos courtesy of CyclingNews.com Tadej Pogacar has held the yellow jersey since Stage 8. He’s expected to defend his title with strong performances this week. Heading into the final week of racing, defending champion Croatian rider Tadej Pogacar holds the yellow jersey with a five-minute, 18-second advantage in the general classification standings over Rigoberto Uran. England’s Mark Cavendish tied the record of cycling legend Eddie Merckx after winning his 34th stage race at the Tour de France. His victory in Stage 13 on July 9 tied Merckx’s record. Cavendish will have his best opportunities to claim the record as his own come on the final three days of the tour: Stage 19’s flat course on July 16 from Mourenx to Libourne, Stage 20’s time trial from Libourne to Saint-Emilion on July 17, and the finale on the Champs-Élysées in Paris on July 18. Stage 15 was a big day for the United States when American Sepp Kuss, riding with Team Jumbo-Bisma, won the 191.3 kilometer mountain course, tossing his sunglasses into the crowd, raising his hands in victory into the air before covering his face with emotion. Kuss became the first American rider to win a stage at the Grand Tour since Tyler Farrar in 2011. The Tour looks ahead to a pair of mountain stages in Stage 17 today, Wednesday, July 14, and England’s Mark Cavendish tied Eddie Merckx with 34 overall Tour de France stage wins and four victories in this year’s race.

Wednesday, July 14, 2021 13 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 14th year in the Post. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. Piedmont High Class of 2021 Smith College Class of 2025 Sadie Tschider heads to Smith College in Massachusetts after becoming Piedmont High girls’ lacrosse program’s all-time leading assister as a four-year starter. The team finished 6-4 this year and was 2-2 when the pandemic struck last year. It was 20-2 when they won the NCS Championship in her sophomore year, and 14-11 as a freshman. She was named Sophomore of the Year by the Post in 2019 and was an honorable mention selection as Freshman of the Year in 2018. Tschider logged a team-leading 29 assists in 2021, 16 in four 2020 appearances, a school-record 66 as a sophomore, and 21 as a freshman. Below she details her workout regimen ahead of heading east this fall. What is your workout program this summer? I do a combination of strength training, high intensity intervals, and agility. Additionally, I have stickwork and ground ball routines that I do to maintain my technique. I do some workouts directly from Smith College Strength and Conditioning and add in my own routines as well. What are your fitness goals for this summer? This summer I have been working on my mile time, short sprint times and decreasing my time on my stickwork tests. How are you measuring your development? I am measuring my development by repeating workouts and consistently timing different running tests. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I work with a trainer on my strength and agility. I also have been coaching younger lacrosse players, which helps me to maintain my stick skills, lacrosse IQ, and footwork. I love playing with the players that I coach; they always teach me as I am teaching them. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? Photo by Todd Marshburn I am really proud of staying consistent with my training this summer. I am working out five days a week and doing stick-work at least three days a week. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? My advice is to put the time into the things you love. Hard work and effort will always win over natural talent. It is also important to have fulfilling hobbies, spend time on academics and enjoy time with the people you love. MICHAEL AIKAWA Baseball Piedmont High Class of 2023 Michael Aikawa was our 2021 Sophomore of the Year after carrying a .396 batting average last season on the baseball team. He had a team-leading .625 slugging percentage, .547 on-base percentage, and 1.172 on-base plus slugging percentage out of the leadoff spot; smacking two home runs, 20 runs scored, 13 RBIs, three doubles, and one triple. Aikawa, the second baseman, had two game-winning hits in Piedmont’s 12-4 season. Against St. Joseph on April 3, he hit a monumental two-run homer in the bottom of the sixth against to win 6-5. On March 20 versus Oakland Tech, Aikawa cracked a one run, one-out double in bottom of the fifth to snap a 0-0 deadlock in their 2-0 win over the Bulldogs. What is your workout program this summer? I am playing baseball every day and spent several weeks in Arizona at national tournaments. When I have off days, I have a workout program to help increase my strength, explosiveness, and speed. What are your fitness goals for the summer? I want to continue getting stronger and faster. I am hoping to lower my 30- and 60-yard dash times, increase my range for fielding, and be generally more explosive to the ball. How are you measuring your development? For strength, being able to increase my repetitions and increase the amount of weight. For speed, I get timed in game and feel more burst when stealing bases. It’s a little harder to measure my explosiveness, but my bat speed and drive to the ball seem to be progressing. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I work with my college development team coach, a trainer, with my friends and teammates, and on my own. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I am now the leadoff hitter and starting shortstop for my college development team. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Manage your time, study hard, and put in the extra time. It will all pay off if you work hard on your craft. Photo by Todd Marshburn Emily Fitzgerald will be a junior this year. She’s a versatile forward leading coach Dan Chubbock’s attack. SADIE TSCHIDER Lacrosse EMILY FITZGERALD Soccer Piedmont High Class of 2023 Emily Fitzgerald enters her junior year at Piedmont High as a critical player on the soccer team as a striker and central attacking midfielder. She has been a starter since her freshman year in 2020. The Highlanders finished 4-1-5 last season and 7-5-7 in her freshman season. In February 2020, she scored the game-winning goal in the NCS Opening Round 2-1 win over No. 5 Urban while on the road in San Francisco as the No. 12 seeded team. PHS then beat No. 4 Lick 1-0 in the quarterfinals to reach its fourth consecutive NCS Semifinals. which they lost to the No. 1 seed, Cardinal Newman. What is your workout program this summer? I have practice with my club team, The Rage, four times a week, which has some strength training. I also do technical trainings on my own about 2-3 times a week. I try to swim at least three times a week as well. It’s super important that I stretch and roll out my muscles every day to prevent injury. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My fitness goal for this summer is to become stronger by lifting weights. I also want to maintain or increase my stamina in order to play 90 minutes of soccer with minimal fatigue. With each game, I am able to see improvement. Something that also helps measure my development is feedback from coaches and college recruiters. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? articles.text: England National Team’s Marcus Rashford was the target of hatespeech online after missing a penalty kick against Italy. A mural of him in his hometown was defaced with racist messages. As the world returns back to normal with smiling faces of fans filling stadiums for their favorite sports teams, so is the cruel reality of the snarling hate and entitlement which follows. The latest issue of bad behavior follows England National Soccer team’s Marcus Rashford, Jadon Sancho, and Bukayo Saka, who received racist hate-mail after the three players missed their penalty kicks on Sunday in England’s 1-0 loss to Italy for the European Championship. A mural of Rashford was defaced with racist remarks in his hometown of Withington, Manchester. He used Instagram to write a heartfelt message reflecting on the kick gone wrong, and closed the long 400-word letter strongly: “I’m Marcus Rashford, 23 years old, Black man from Withington and Wythenshawe, South Manchester. If I have nothing else, I have that,” wrote Rashford, via his official Instagram. His full letter is online. A petition online to ban racist fans has already garnered 500,000 signatures, while the mural of Rashford liking has been restored. Back in the U.S., we are anywhere from being leaders in regards to ethical treatment of athletes. The current NBA season is a prime example. In Game 2 of the playoffs on May 26, a fan poured his food on Russell Westbrook as he walked to the locker room with an injury. On the same night, Atlanta Hawks’ Trae Young was spit on by a New York Knicks fan standing courtside. Days later on May 30, Brooklyn Nets star Kyrie Irving was targeted by a Boston Celtics fan who threw a water bottle at him. The perpetrator, 21-year old Cole Buckley, was charged with assault and battery with a dangerous weapon. Irving responded with the following comments. “(It’s) just underlying racism and treating people like they’re in a human zoo. Throwing stuff at people, saying things. There’s a certain point where it gets to be too much. You see people just feel very entitled out here... As a Black man playing in the NBA, dealing with a lot of this stuff, it’s fairly difficult. You never know what’s going to happen.” Photo courtesy of NBA Central Atlanta Hawks’ Trae Young (left) was spit on by New York Knicks fans on May 26. Photo courtesy of Republic World Cole Buckley (left) was charged with assault and battery with a “dangerous weapon” after tossing a water bottle at Nets’ star Kyrie Irving on May 31.
articles.title: Abuse from fans must be addressed

pages.text: Wednesday, July 14, 2021 15 HIKING WITH JON Alamere Falls, the long way via Wildcat Camp By Jonathan Comeaux Families seeking a unique adventure these warm summer months may want to consider backpacking to Wildcat Camp in Point Reyes National Seashore. Wildcat is the closest campsite to the famous Alamere Falls, just one mile away. Potential backpack overnighters park at the often-used starting point for Alamere Falls, the Palomarin Trailhead on the outskirts of Bolinas. It is slightly less than six miles and a 700-foot elevation gain to Wildcat Camp. Another option for campers is the Bear Valley visitor center, 6.2 miles out-and-back at 850 elevation gain. Day hikers looking for a workout while avoiding the foot traffic from the Palomarin Trailhead could start from the Olema Valley Trailhead at Five Brooks Ranch. It is a 5.5-mile trek to Wildcat Camp but a grueling 1,200 feet in elevation. Although those numbers may Wildcat Camp is one mile from the dramatic Alamere Falls. A so-called shortcut to Alamere Falls is not for the timid. It is steep and treacherous with loose rocks and sections that require scrambling up and down. Another section of the upper portion of Alamere Falls. Visiting Alamere Falls on the way to Wildcat Camp, a backpacking site for campers at Point Reyes National Seashore. look intimidating, this writer passed just two hikers in the 5.5- mile trek to Wildcat Camp via the Olema Valley Trailhead. We saw only one group of four hikers on the one-mile trek to Alamere Falls, and just three people when hiking all the way back to the car via the same route from Wildcat Camp. If you require the easiest route and don’t mind foot traffic from groups or non-hikers drowning out nature with music, the Palomarin Trailhead is recommended. It enables walkers to see Bass Lake and Pelican Lake. A shortcut is treacherous and should only be done by those with proper footwear and body control. Those coming from Wildcat Camp will have to traverse up the cliff in order to see the upper portion of Alamere Falls. Wildcat Camp itself is located in an open meadow overlooking the ocean with its own walkway to the vast and open beach. It is only a two-mile round trip walk to Alamere Falls. There is one camp site for up to six people, three sites for up to four, and three group sites for up to 12 people each. The campground offers the unique experience of taking in a sunrise or sunset along one of California’s only tidefalls without the worry of a strenuous trek to-and-from. The campground has potable drinking water, picnic tables, BBQ grates, toilet facilities, and food storage lockers. To find more information on Wildcat Campground type in “Point Reyes National Seashore” on Recreation.Gov and search “Wildcat.” Post subscribers can visit the following link on our webpage: (https://www. recreation.gov/camping/campgrounds/233359). Staff Photos Another view of Alamere Falls. It is a bit of a trickle during the dry conditions. A cascading stream feeds to the Alamere Falls tidefall, among the few of its kind in California. articles.text: Aurora Theatre, in its weekly online broadcast “Aurora Connects,” invited California Shakespeare Theater Artistic Director Eric Ting and Yerba Buena Center for the Arts (YBCA) CEO Deborah Cullinan last week to discuss Universal Basic Income (UBI). “Aurora Connects” is Aurora Theatre Company’s bi-weekly live broadcast, an “online salon and virtual happy hour.” Each episode is hosted by theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello and Associate Artistic Director Dawn Monique Williams. Ting is an Obie Award-winning director who, before joining California Shakespeare Theater (Cal Shakes), served as Long Wharf Theatre Associate Artistic Director. His recent credits include the world premiere of Sam Hunter’s Lewiston, To Kill a Mockingbird, and Appropriate. Ting and Cullinan will discuss their backgrounds and UBI; including how the phrase Eric Ting, Artistic Director of California Shakespeare Theatre originated, and why it is necessary. Both guests will discuss how UBI is being implemented at Cal Shakes, YBCA, and in the community, as well as what the response has been. Costello and Williams will talk to the guests about their hopes for the future of these programs. To watch the panel discussion, visit https://www.auroratheatre. org/auroraconnects.
articles.title: Weekly broadcasts available online now

articles.text: Diego Rivera’s massive mural, “Pan American Unity”, arrived at its new home, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) on June 28. It will be on display on the first floor of the Roberts Family Gallery for two years, through summer 2023. On June 17, Rivera’s colossal “Pan American Unity” fresco was carefully moved from San Francisco’s City College to SFMOMA. The priceless 4,000-pound work, created in 1940, is arguably one of San Francisco’s greatest art pieces of the 20th century. Rivera’s mural was the centerpiece of the Art in Action exhibit, which featured different artists engaged in creating art pieces while the public watched. The fresco on plaster is 670 by 2,260 centimeters and was created on 10 steel-framed panels bolted together and weighing 21 tons. It was designed to be portable and was moved to the college campus from Treasure Island after the conclusion of the World’s Fair, formally known as the Golden Gate International Exposition. It is the largest of the artists’ works and had completely spanned the lobby of the Diego Rivera Theater at City College. A four-year, multimillion dollar undertaking resulted in its careful removal and transport across the city to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. To learn more and for tickets, visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/pan-american-unity/.
articles.title: Diego Rivera’s giant mural on display at SFMOMA for 2 years

articles.text: San Francisco’s de Young Museum is presenting a new installation by renowned artist Hung Liu. The exhibition entitled “Hung Liu: Golden Gate,” opens this Saturday, July 17. Liu, based in Oakland, is one of the most important Chinese-born artists currently working in the United States. The exhibition combs through new and existing works by the artist, who highlights international and domestic narratives of migration. The installation reimagines some of her most iconic paintings as seen through the eyes of a Chinese-born artist. The exhibit’s central feature is a massive reinvention of Liu’s painting “Resident Alien,” (1988), on permanent display on the main Artist Hung Liu wall in the Wilsey Court at the museum. The new exhibition will be on display through March 13, 2022. The museum requires timed tickets for every visitor, including general admission. To ensure a preferred time slot, reserve tickets in advance online. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday from 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m. To obtain tickets, visit: https:// deyoung.famsf.org/exhibitions/ hung-liu.
articles.title: Hung Liu exhibit opens on Sat. at DeYoung Museum

A brave and enthusiastic audience welcomed the opening of live concerts in the Center after more than a year. The mood was festive, indeed. The featured artists were coloratura soprano Lila Khazoum, and pianist Alexander Katzman with a program titled Un raggio di sperme – A Ray of Hope, in celebrating a live concert after 15 months of silence due to Covid. Some music lovers think that the best singers are at La Scala in Milano, or the Met in New York. That is simply not true. Some of the greatest artists are often unheralded. This was the case on Sunday. As soon as Lila Khazoum walked onto the stage, she established herself as an artist of impressive talent. articles.text: Coloratura soprano Lila Khazoum and pianist Alexander Katzman performed a wonderful wide-ranging program of music as part of Festival Opera’s ongoing concerts at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The world of music is a very interesting place, and sometimes it is incongruous. For example, a list of the greatest pianists of all time contains the usual suspects. You might start with Johann Sebastian Bach and then include Franz Liszt and continue with Rachmaninoff and Horowitz. Those are the obvious choices. But let’s keep an open mind. Should we limit the names entirely to classical musicians? One list of great pianists includes two jazz greats Art Tatum and Oscar Peterson. I was OK with Art Tatum because Horowitz admired him. But when I saw the name Oscar Peterson, I thought his inclusion was incongruous. I said to myself… Don’t jump to conclusions. When I investigated the artistry of Oscar Peterson, I was amazed. Jazz pianists often have the technique of the greatest classical players and in addition they are able to create brilliant interpretations on the spot. Keeping this philosophy in mind, my wife and I went to the Piedmont Piano Company on Thursday evening to hear a solo piano concert by the jazz pianist Tamir Hendelman. As soon as Hendelman began to play, his opening chords served as an introduction which drew his audience in. In classical music the opening chords are often called “sit down chords“. Music in the Vineyards, a three-week chamber music festival in Napa Valley, will have its opening concert on August 4 with both indoor and outdoor live performances. articles.text: Julia Garner stars in The Assistant. The Assistant is an extraordinary film, spare, understated, mundane in the extreme, all in the service of an abiding sense of workplace dread, possessing a grim intentionality. And yet it is strangely compelling. The narrative begins as Jane (Julia Garner) is being driven in pre-dawn darkness to her job at a movie production company in the Tribeca neighborhood of Manhattan. She is the just-hired office factotum – first in each morning, last out each evening – her title being a bottom of the totem pole production assistant to a movie-entertainment production honcho. Arriving, she enters the dark interior of office cubicles, and begins her 12-hour day by turning on the lights, brewing coffee, cleaning up her boss’ office (finding an earring near the couch), and wiping off remnants of whatever is on his desk and chair. She quickly moves on to the copy machine, running handouts of the day’s schedule, countless audition headshots of young actresses, washing dishes, answering emails, all while the company denizens begin to drift in and the phones start to ring. Packages soon arrive, are signed for, opened, reservations made for an upcoming L.A. trip. A stark, oppressiveness permeates even the commons room. People, mostly men in suits, file by, going in an out of meetings. The atmosphere seems joyless, brittle, and if Jane smiles it seems an effort, her lips a thin compressed line that tilts toward grim. Her boss, a constant presence (even when he’s gone), is only a voice behind a closed door, a harsh, abusive voice on her intra-office phone, berating her for how she handled his wife’s recent phone call. Jane knows her to be a short-tempered, suspicious woman who insists on this recent call that Jane tell her where her husband is and disbelieves her when told that Jane doesn’t “have him” at the moment. Just after mid-day, a young woman arrives who is slated to begin working as the newest assistant hire (Kristine Froseth). Jane is told to take her by car to a mid-town upscale hotel. And it’s on the ride over that she learns that the newbie was a waitress in Idaho and has no background in film production. Jane is, of course, aware that this eager, hopeful film producer is not the first to arrive at her desk, waiting to hear, “send her in.” Jane knows what awaits the Idaho waitress and is conflicted. She finally decides to share her concern with the Human Resources officer, Mr. Wilcock (Matthew Macfayden), and makes an appointment to ask for advice. Finding herself seated in front of his desk, she seems all but paralyzed by what she is there to disclose. This is a remarkable scene, and the only transactional moment in the film. Jane, haltingly, expresses her concern for the new assistant. Wilcock feigns surprise and confusion, pressing Jane for details that he finds all but imaginary. He casually points out that there are 400 people who would love her job, and does she really want to file a complaint? Jane, her helplessness palpable, finally gets up to leave. As she stands at the door, Wilcock says to her, “Don’t worry, you’re not his type.” It’s a chilling moment. Her boss is a predator, and all who work for him are enablers and complicit. The fulcrum for The Assistant is the #MeToo movement, and the faceless mogul, ensconced behind the executive suite door, is Harvey Weinstein or Roger Ailes. But unlike the movie Bombshell, there is no pushback in The Assistant. All Jane can do, if she wants to keep her much-coveted job, is remain silent. She is reminded in conversations with her parents over the phone, how fortunate she is to have found her dream job. The embedded truth is that her dream is actually a nightmare in which she is asked how much she is capable of internalizing, how much she is willing to compromise for a position that she knows is demeaning and toxic. She feels trapped by her own career objectives (she too wants to be a producer), as if trapped in a kind of panic room, surrounded by blank faces and an amorphous evil comprised of a hundred small, daily tasks. I am aware that those who search out The Assistant may wonder what it was they just viewed. It’s not really a story, but a harrowing snapshot. My hope is that its inherent power will not be quickly discarded. The Assistant. Directed by Kitty Green. Starring Julia Garner, Matthew Macfayden, Makenzie Leigh. 1 hr., 27 min. Rated R.
articles.title: The Assistant

articles.text: Director Martin Scorsese’s epic 3.5 hour mob procedural film, The Irishman, is framed by violence and ultimately betrayal. It is the story of Frank Sheeran (Robert De Niro) and his journey from truck driver to factotum to Jimmy Hoffa. As a bodyguard, fixer and consigliere, he was also a man who “paints houses” (mob code for executing someone). The film is based on the 2004 biography of Sheeran, written by Charles Brandt, and titled I Heard You Paint Houses. The story begins with a long tracking shot of an empty hallway in a rest home. The Five Satins are singing In the Still of the Night. It’s a stand-alone moment. Finally, we enter a private room and linger on an old man, white haired, anchored to a wheelchair, talking to someone off camera. He is telling his story, seen through flashbacks and explained through voiceover, that begins in the early 1950s when Frank drove a truck filled with slabs of meat, making deliveries to butchers and restaurants. One day, forced to stop due to engine trouble, peering under the truck’s hood, an older man approaches and gives him a hand to solve the problem. Unbeknownst to Frank, the benign-seeming guy, Russ Bufalino (Joe Pesci), is a notorious Philadelphia mob boss. It’s only later that the two meet again, and it’s Bufalino who introduces Frank to Jimmy Hoffa (Al Pacino), head of the powerful Teamsters Union. It proves to be a connection that will alter the course of their lives. The film again shifts to a flashback that will give structure to the rest of the film. We see Russ and Frank, now years older, about to take a road trip with their wives from Kingston, Philadelphia, to Detroit. And it’s that journey, with a number of pit stops along the way, so the women can smoke, that gives Russ and Frank the opportunity to reminisce. Each stop on the three-day journey is comprised of a lengthy vignette that illustrates not only the evolution of their friendship, but of Frank’s abiding closeness with Hoffa, to include his importance to keeping in place the union-mob alliance. The union loaned the wise guys money from their pension fund for whatever, and the mob provided intimidation (maybe a house painted) when necessary. As Frank shares his story, on occasion seated in a wheelchair, clearly a man alone, we are told that he had a wife and four daughters. But from the beginning, it’s clear that he has chosen not his family but the mob. He has given himself entirely over to these men who are, to a fault, lethally Machiavellian. He embraces the illusion that this criminal clan represents familial loyalty, which transcends even those of his own family. It’s a brotherhood to which he gives an unwavering, stoic commitment. Never does he understand that this meta-family is an illusion and is devoid of anything resembling devotion. What drives these men are power, obedience to a code, and money. They live by an understood silence, regardless of outcomes (never name names) and are masters of constructing euphemisms when discussing a job, their spare dialogue always filled with the implied, however tortured, never the explicit. As we witness Frank in that senior care facility, on occasion slipping into regret, knowing that those who wanted to care about him in the past are now absent, it is now clear that the emotional bankruptcy of his life has resulted in his final days spent speaking to strangers (or the F.B.I.). Everyone is gone, some killed, others dying in prison, his daughters in the wind. There are two things I find interesting about Martin Scorsese as a filmmaker. He so often has chosen a dark pallet to examine the human condition, from his early film Mean Streets, and now to The Irishman. His stories inhabit a nihilistic, violent world that is a place apart, the characters driven by forces seemingly outside them, unhampered by even a hint of self-reflection. Nothing seems to give any of them pause. I also wonder why, in his movies, there are so few women. Women represent family, a bond, a promise, and it is they who are abandoned, or relegated to a world that seems tangential to the band of mob brothers whose connections represent a chain that can, in truth, be broken without remorse. Ultimately, it’s just business. Finally, two things: The Irishman is beautifully acted, with layers of fine performances, all resembling, in the aggregate, a Scorsese acting troupe. If you are a cinephile and have followed the astonishing career of this fine director, now in his 70s, don’t miss this film. While long, it never wavers or slows, its chronological pace inexorable while telling a story that is eminently accessible. The Irishman. Directed by Martin Scorsese. Starring Robert DeNiro, Al Pacino, Joe Pesci. 3 hrs, 29 min. Rated R
articles.title: The Irishman – Scorcese’s 3½ hour epic masterpiece

articles.text: Ben Whishaw provides the voice of Paddington. Review by Chris Honoré Paddington is a dazzling live action/CGI animated take on Michal Brand’s classic children’s books, a feature film that feels both old-fashion as well as hightech. It’s also an origin story that is funny, charming and sprinkled with puns. We first meet Paddington (Ben Whishaw), living with his aunt and uncle (Imelda Stauton and veteran French actor Michal Gambon). Years earlier, we’re told, a British explorer had discovered in “Darkest Peru” the existence of talking bears and goes about teaching them all things British, including English and a love of marmalade. Paddington’s aunt decides that the time has come for Paddington to make his way in the world, and it’s decided that the most hospitable place for him will be London where bears of his ilk are welcomed. So off he goes, wearing his familiar red floppy hat (that belonged to the explorer), and carrying enough food for the long boat ride to England. Eventually he arrives and makes his way to Paddington Station with his battered suitcase. It is there that he discovers that Londoners are not surprised at a walking, talking bear, but are also generally rude and unhelpful – until Paddington meets the Brown family. Mrs. Brown (Sally Hawkins) who shows the homeless traveler some kindness and sympathy and names him after the station where they found him. Meanwhile, the other Browns – Mr. Brown (Hugh Bonneville), daughter Judy (Madeline Harris), and son Jonathan (Samuel Joslin) – while intrigued, are somewhat skeptical. Especially Mr. Brown. Having found a home, though a bit homesick, Paddington gradually settles into London life. There are a few amusing antics along the way, but he eventually finds his stride and regains his confident pluck. Meanwhile, a local museum taxidermist, Millicent Clyde (Nicole Kidman), learns of Paddington’s existence and is determined to track him down, kidnap him, stuff him, and, of course, add him to her museum collection. And thus begins a number of chase scenes, stand-offs, and narrow escapes by Paddington. There’s never a dull moment, and it’s all pure fun. Plus, the visuals are superb, tactile, inventive. The bear’s facial features are remarkable, allowing the young audience to make a strong connection with him. Which they do throughout this nicely told, engaging story. Paddington. Live actionCGI animation. Directed by Paul King. With voices of Ben Whishaw, Sally Hawkins and Nicole Kidman. 1 hr., 35 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: Paddington – classic children’s book comes to the big screen

articles.text: Planes is the zippy, family-friendly story of a courageous little rural crop-duster called Dusty (Dane Cook) who dreams of flying higher and faster and yearns to enter an international air race called the Wings Around the Globe. The problem is that he is built to fly low and slow, his one prop taking him over stretching farm fields, mere feet above the ground. Plus, there’s an added complication: Dusty has a fear of heights. His friends, like Dottie a forklift (Terri Hatcher), and Chug, a fuel truck ((Brad Garrett), encourage Dusty to follow his dream. Chug even gives him a book titled Air Racing for Dummies. Improbably, Dusty enters the air race trials and qualifies in the top five. But he realizes that his tenacity and skills are not enough, and he searches for a mentor and coach. He turns to Skipper (Stacy Keach), a crusty old WWII Navy plane. Of course, the old air dog knows that Dusty needs to up his game and his speed and he’ll have to practice those ballet-like twists and turns. Skipper also instills in him a can-do spirit. Dusty finally tells Skipper he is afraid of heights. But Skipper’s motto is “Volo Pro Veritas” (I fly for truth). Yep, a little Latin never hurts a Disney story. So the little guy shows up for the race with a healthy dose of trepidation and meets, for the first time, his (gulp) international competition: Ripsinger (Robert Craig Smith), Ishani (Priyanka Chopra), British Bulldog (John Cleese), The Mexican Chupacabra (Carlos Alazraqui), and Rochelle (Julia Louis-Dreyfus). pages.text: Wednesday, July 14, 2021 19 MOVIES FOR KIDS Paddington – classic children’s book comes to the big screen Ben Whishaw provides the voice of Paddington. Review by Chris Honoré Paddington is a dazzling live action/CGI animated take on Michal Brand’s classic children’s books, a feature film that feels both old-fashion as well as hightech. It’s also an origin story that is funny, charming and sprinkled with puns. We first meet Paddington (Ben Whishaw), living with his aunt and uncle (Imelda Stauton and veteran French actor Michal Gambon). Years earlier, we’re told, a British explorer had discovered in “Darkest Peru” the existence of talking bears and goes about teaching them all things British, including English and a love of marmalade. Paddington’s aunt decides that the time has come for Paddington to make his way in the world, and it’s decided that the most hospitable place for him will be London where bears of his ilk are welcomed. So off he goes, wearing his familiar red floppy hat (that belonged to the explorer), and carrying enough food for the long boat ride to England. Eventually he arrives and makes his way to Paddington Station with his battered suitcase. It is there that he discovers that Londoners are not surprised at a walking, talking bear, but are also generally rude and unhelpful – until Paddington meets the Brown family. Mrs. Brown (Sally Hawkins) who shows the homeless traveler some kindness and sympathy and names him after the station where they found him. Meanwhile, the other Browns – Mr. Brown (Hugh Bonneville), daughter Judy (Madeline Harris), and son Jonathan (Samuel Joslin) – while intrigued, are somewhat skeptical. Especially Mr. Brown. Having found a home, though a bit homesick, Paddington gradually settles into London life. There are a few amusing antics along the way, but he eventually finds his stride and regains his confident pluck. Meanwhile, a local museum taxidermist, Millicent Clyde (Nicole Kidman), learns of Paddington’s existence and is determined to track him down, kidnap him, stuff him, and, of course, add him to her museum collection. And thus begins a number of chase scenes, stand-offs, and narrow escapes by Paddington. There’s never a dull moment, and it’s all pure fun. Plus, the visuals are superb, tactile, inventive. The bear’s facial features are remarkable, allowing the young audience to make a strong connection with him. Which they do throughout this nicely told, engaging story. Paddington. articles.text: West Edge Opera will perform this summer at Bruns Amphitheater in Orinda. West Edge Opera will perform three operas at the open-air Bruns Amphitheater from July 24 through August 8 as part of its West Edge Festival. The operas – Janáček’s Katya Kabanova, Cavalli’s Eliogabalo, and Elizabeth Cree, a comedic opera written in 2017, will be presented with complete orchestration, staging, and design. West Edge Opera, originally the Berkeley Opera, was created in 1979 by Cal professor Richard Goodman. The company, under music director Jonathan Khuner and general director Mark Streshinsky, focuses primarily on lesser-known, contemporary, and avant-garde operas. West Edge Opera functions as a festival and shows three operas during the late summer. The festival has been conducted in unconventional performance spaces, including the abandoned 16th street train station, the Pacific Pipe warehouse, and in 2019, in Oakland’s Bridge Yard under the Bay Bridge. Bruns Amphitheater became the festival’s home for its 2021 season through a partnership with California Shakespeare Theater (Cal Shakes). Cal Shakes will also be sharing the Bruns Amphitheater this summer with Berkeley Symphony, Destiny Arts, and Bandloop. “What gives us our proverbial edge is that our venue at the Bruns is in the open air, which makes a big difference. Even if everyone has the vaccine, it is likely that we’ll all be sporting fabulous West Edge Opera masks, and distancing,” said Streshinsky. To obtain tickets, visit https:// www.westedgeopera.org/festival-2021.
articles.title: West Edge Opera Festival opens July 24 at Bruns Amphitheater in Orinda

articles.text: Pine Leaf Boys will kick off the Mendocino Music Festival this Friday. Mendocino Music Festival kicks off this Friday, July 16, with live concerts through July 25 at the Cotton Auditorium in Fort Bragg. A series of one-hour concerts begins on Friday at 7:30 p.m. with Pine Leaf Boysx, a Louisiana-based group known for Cajun, Creole, “swamp pop,” country and Zydeco tunes. The Mendocino Music Festival was established in 1986 by Allan Pollack, Susan Waterfall and Walter Green, the former principal bassoonist of San Francisco Symphony. The festival features a blend of genres; evenings include orchestral concerts, Big Band, chamber music ensembles, dance, blues, jazz, world, folk, bluegrass and more. Daytime events include lectures and recitals at the Piano Series, performances by participants in the Emerging Artists Program, and small concerts in intimate venues throughout the historic towns of Mendocino and Fort Bragg on the North Coast. This year, main concerts will take place at the Cotton Auditorium in Fort Bragg. Traditionally, the festival takes place outdoors with no tent, but the decision to move to the Cotton Auditorium provides for better sound, comfort, and ease of implementing COVID-19 safety procedures. Patrons must be vaccinated, masked, and socially distanced - the auditorium will limit capacity to 265 guests. Musicians, staff, and volunteers will be vaccinated. Visit https://mendocinomusic.org/about/ticketing-faq/ for ticketing information and a full line-up. Tickets are for performances in the ten-concert series.

articles.text: Though Monday, July 5 was an extension of the July 4 holiday this year, the First Mondays Reading Group had a solid turnout of 11 readers calling in for the Zoom gathering. The participants were: Sarah Johnson, Mike Henn, Margie Blodgett, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Albert Chen, Alicia Rivera, Karin Fetherston, Laura Goldman, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Melba Yee had suggested Interior Chinatown by Charles Yu for the July discussion. It is a 2020 novel that received broad critical acclaim. Among other honors, it won the 2020 National Book Award for Fiction. Yu uses the unusual structure of a screenplay to tell the story of Willis Wu, the “Generic Asian Man.” It is also the story of his Chinatown, the Golden Palace restaurant, which Wu lives above, and the racism he and others endure. The restaurant is the setting for a fictional, constantly in production police film show, “Black and White.” Wu sometimes gets to be “Background Oriental Making a Weird Face,” or “Disgraced Son,” and occasionally “Delivery Guy” in the film. He longs to be the “Kung Fu Guy,” the pinnacle Asian male on screens worldwide, but he only gets small roles. Through Wu, Yu explores Hollywood’s and our country’s constant use of clichés and stereotypes about Asians and Asian-Americans . The group of readers was split on their reaction to the book. The majority of readers were enthusiastic about the book, but others had issues with it. The readers appreciated the author’s creative approach to address a real problem that confronts Asian Americans, and what it means to live in a country that views race as a primary identification of people. They liked that the book focused on the stereotypes of Asian Americans. When some Asian American readers were growing up, Asian American were perceived as the model minority, but for the most part they were invisible. In some parts of the country, there were few Asian Americans. The group recognized that Yu’s writing style and format for the book are different and creative. The readers enjoyed that Yu made them more aware of discriminatory perceptions and attitudes that some had not been fully conscious of. Yu sometimes presents these stereotypes with dark humor that may cause a wry laugh, but they are sadly very real and hurtful. What is happening in the Interior Chinatown screenplay is also happening in real life today. Interior Chinatown was a catalyst for the group members to discuss the meaning of “home” for immigrants and their decedents, the country’s racial history, their own personal experiences with racism, and how they acted and protected themselves from it. Asian Americans often kept to themselves and tried not to “make trouble.” However, with recent, more visible violent acts against Asians and the emergence of the Anti-Hate movement, speaking up now and addressing what has happened was seen as important and overdue. For some members of the group this was deeply touching, as the Asian experience is also our society’s human experience. Much of our country’s social justice movement has focused on our country’s treatment of African-Americans, but generating an awareness of, and focus on, Asian stereotypes is an important contribution by Yu. These attitudes and tropes have resulted in hateful, violent acts towards Asians both in the past and the present. While the group recognized the value of Interior Chinatown some readers had problems with the book’s structure and Yu’s writing style. They found it confusing and had trouble making a distinction between Willis Wu’s real life and his acting life. Some readers found it difficult to connect with the Wu character. It seemed there was a gender divide with the women readers enjoying the book more than the men. The group previously selected The Fire Next Time by James Baldwin, Deacon King Kong by James McBride, and Nomadland by Jessica Bruder for August, September, and October respectively. The group will meet next on Monday, August 2, at 1:30 p.m. outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New members are welcome and there is no fee to participate. Registration is required by contacting John Wilk at the Piedmont Recreation Department at jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: First Monday Reading Group discusses Interior Chinatown

By Gail G. Lombardi Introduction The City of Piedmont is now celebrating its 111th anniversary, In cooperation with the Piedmont Historical Society, the Piedmont Post is pleased to announce the beginning of a biweekly series of snapshots of moments in time, from the city’s founding in 1907,its growth resulting in part to the earthquake and fire in San Francisco in 1906, and the city’s earliest settlers. For families who have moved to Piedmont since 2007, when the city’s Centennial was widely celebrated and publicized, the series of history pieces by historian and researcher Gail Lombardi, may prove insightful, providing a look at the earliest settlers, and why people have chosen to move to Piedmont for more than a century. Walter Blair, Piedmont’s first pioneer Walter Blair was Piedmont’s enterprising first settler who played an important part in the early development of today’s city. He built the first house in the Piedmont hills (see photo) and established a dairy and rock quarry. In the 1860s, long before bridges spanned the Bay, he developed the first horse car line bringing visitors and picnickers into the Piedmont hills. Many of these visitors enjoyed the mild weather and views of San Francisco Bay and decided to build their homes here. Raised on a dairy farm in Vermont with 11 siblings., Walter was born In 1851. He and his brother William sailed around Cape Horn to get to San Francisco. Within months, they rowed across the Bay and discovered the fertile lands in the Piedmont hills. The dairy quickly became known for its high quality milk, cream and butter, and soon the Blairs were delivering their milk and butter to residents in Oakland and even across the Bay to a few wealthy San Francisco customers. It was difficult for the horses hauling those wagons filled with ten-gallon milk cans. The roads were filled with muddy ruts in the winter and covered in thick dust in the summer. Blair realized that a hard surface was needed for these roads. Always the entrepreneur, Blair hired Chinese laborers to quarry rock from a basalt outcropping near his dairy and sold crushed rock to lay over the muddy/dusty streets in Oakland. The walls of the quarry are still visible in lower Dracena Park. Walter Blair went on to develop the first horsecar line to Piedmont and Blair’s Park. (More on that in a later column.) William Blair established a nursery near Mountain View Cemetery and sold eucalyptus seedlings. Today, the eucalyptus trees he planted still grow along the cemetery border on Moraga and in Dracena Park. As a successful businessman, Blair rebuilt his cabin in 1862 into the large gabled house with gardens as seen in the photo. Walter Blair married and soon moved to downtown Oakland. He leased the house to the Arthur Bowman family. Later, Blair’s daughter, Florence, lived in the house from the 1890s until her death in 1924. The Blair homestead was demolished in 1926, and Waldo Avenue was created. articles.text: The openings in a building, principally doors and windows, are what architects refer to as fenestration. The sizes, composition, and detailing of the openings are one of the most important design considerations in determining the style and quality of the architecture. Like so much in this field, this issue is a mixture and balance between aesthetics and function, heavily influenced by building code requirements. There are of course various types of window operations, such as casement, double hung, tilt and turn, as well as fixed windows (non-operable). But the choice is not only how they open, but also how well they are visually suited to the architectural style of the building – something that, as we have mentioned before, is always evolving and changing. The early high-rise buildings in the late 1800’s were equipped, for example, with residential style double Photos by Will Adams Good window fenestration requires detailing that coordinates operation, size, shape, and how the windows fit into the walls of the building, all the while making sure it looks good. Other openings in the building can also be considered fenestration. The trick is to give equal design consideration to all utilitarian components of a building -- such as this louver located in its own dormer. (Note the roof slope nomenclature discussed in the last column: 12:12 main roof & 6:12 dormer roof.) Fenestration includes the exterior composition of all the doors and windows together. The asymmetrical arrangement of the numerous openings in this Piedmont Mediterranean style home is interesting, rich in texture, and quite wonderful! Note how deeply recessed the doors and windows are, reinforcing their size and shape by shadow.

articles.text: Our dear colleague Ryan Hammond from Sloan Miyasato showroom invited us to take a tour of the Phoenix Day lighting factory in Richmond. Currently Phoenix Day designs and fabricates custom-designed lighting for the trade. You have probably seen their work around the Bay as they’ve been designing and fabricating elegant and iconic street lamps, chandeliers, sconces, and more since 1850. The very first gas streetlamps in San Francisco were designed and installed by Phoenix Day (then named Thomas Day), and their lighting still adorns landmarks like the San Francisco Opera House, the Garden Court of the Palace Hotel, the Ahwahnee Hotel in Yosemite, the Bohemian Club, the Fairmont Hotel and the Redwood Room at the Clift Hotel in San Francisco. For many decades, every custom-designed Phoenix Day fixture was hand-drawn for clients by Milton B. Roller, who continued to work until age 94. As noted on their website, “Roller was a self-taught artist, who turned down an art scholarship to U.C. Berkeley to work in the lighting industry. pages.text: Wednesday, July 14, 2021 23 Phoenix Day Lighting Tour: A day in the life of an Interior Designer By Laura Martin Bovard Our dear colleague Ryan Hammond from Sloan Miyasato showroom invited us to take a tour of the Phoenix Day lighting factory in Richmond. Currently Phoenix Day designs and fabricates custom-designed lighting for the trade. You have probably seen their work around the Bay as they’ve been designing and fabricating elegant and iconic street lamps, chandeliers, sconces, and more since 1850. The very first gas streetlamps in San Francisco were designed and installed by Phoenix Day (then named Thomas Day), and their lighting still adorns landmarks like the San Francisco Opera House, the Garden Court of the Palace Hotel, the Ahwahnee Hotel in Yosemite, the Bohemian Club, the Fairmont Hotel and the Redwood Room at the Clift Hotel in San Francisco. For many decades, every custom-designed Phoenix Day fixture was hand-drawn for clients by Milton B. Roller, who continued to work until age 94. As noted on their website, “Roller was a self-taught artist, who turned down an art scholarship to U.C. Berkeley to work in the lighting industry. Utilizing his design talent, book smarts, and a healthy work ethic, he took on a hybrid role with Phoenix Day. He would meet with clients, including many large churches and hotels, and become an on-the-spot ‘sales-designer,’ capturing ideas from clients and doing many of his drawings in the field.” Primary Bedroom bedside sconces by Phoenix Day, interior design by LMB Interiors. Photo by Mo Saito 4 Glass shades at Phoenix Day. Photo by Kristina Islas A collection of sketches by Milton B. Roller for Phoenix Day. The company maintains a collection of over 2,200 of his watercolor renderings, which inspire the tradition, artistry, and even the modern designs that this family-owned business continues to produce. Tony Brenta, the current owner, who we had the pleasure of meeting, co-owns the business with his wife Joan, He is the grandson of the original owner. Sales Reps Clarence Calzada and Ryan Hammond were our hosts for an informative and inspiring and de-light-ful tour. It is apparent that anything a designer can dream up in metal, Phoenix Day can fabricate. They showed us several of their works in progress for notable Bay Area designers, including one piece that replicates a Milton Roller design from the archives. For my team, seeing the process up close, handling the materials, appreciating the gorgeous watercolor archives of bespoke fixtures, was both educational and soul-nourishing. In one of our recent projects, we chose Phoenix Day sconces for our primary bedroom design. After the tour, my staff and I went to the Farm Shop in Marin Photo by Mo Saito for a lovely lunch. It felt so nice to be gathering over a meal, to be able to be together like this again. As a team, we’re all feeling resourced from spending this day together. Taking the time to be with each other as a community of women is so important, and we are more connected because of it. Laura Martin Bovard is the principal at LMB Interiors, located in downtown Oakland. Since 2002 she has helped clients create beautiful, joyful, and functional homes. The firm has garnered numerous awards and recognition as one of the Bay Area’s most sought after interior design agencies. For information see laura@lmbinteriors. com Team LMBI at lunch at Farm Shop. articles.text: Joe Sullivan, loving husband, father, son, brother, brother-inlaw, cousin, uncle, godfather, and friend, experienced a fatal heart attack on March 1, 2020. Born Joseph Michael Sullivan II on August 12, 1956 in Ann Arbor, Michigan, Joe was the son of William and Helen Sullivan. He effortlessly became a lifetime Wolverine fan as his father finished his doctoral degree in pharmacy at the University of Michigan. Joe’s family relocated to Oakland, where he was raised and attended Corpus Christi School. He excelled in sports at Piedmont High School, where he was a member of the football and track teams. In addition, he learned to serve his community at a young age and carried his passion for helping others throughout his entire life. As a Boy Scout, he achieved the Order of the Arrow and he developed his love for the outdoors, especially camping and rafting. On June 5, 1982, Joe married his high school sweetheart, Carol Lee Robinson, at Corpus Christi Church in Piedmont. Together they built a loving family. In October 1986, they became the proud parents of Ryan Sullivan. Joe and Ryan shared many interests, especially playing football, watching and talking sports, and outdoor activities. Joe served as a loyal volunteer to Boy Scouts Troop 6 and especially loved to go on the camp outings. Joe owned and operated the Book Tree, an independent bookstore associated with their family business, Sullivan’s Montclair Pharmacy. For 50 years the Sullivan businesses were a fixture in Montclair Village, known for personal service. Joe served his community as the President of the Oakland-Montclair Lions Club. Joe’s loyal commitment to organizations benefiting others made him an outstanding memJoe Sullivan, the son of Bill and Helen Sullivan, died last year from a fatal heart attack on March 1, 2020. ber of many groups. He joined the Grizzly Riders, an association providing student scholarships and financial support at the University of Montana. Joe continued to dedicate his time by becoming a Volunteer Firefighter in Auburn, California. He thrived in this role with his love for barbecue and response to action. He touched countless lives and he will be deeply missed. Joe Sullivan is survived by his wife Carol, son Ryan, father William, sister Laurice Salamack and her husband Joseph, and sister Mary Alice McNeil and husband Timothy of Piedmont. He is also survived by siblings-in-law Margaret and Michael Prat, Jeanne Robinson, Kenny and Liz Robinson, and by nieces and nephews Kimberly and Jennifer Prat, Kelly Salamack Casey (Kevin), Allison Salamack Dodd-o (Joseph), PJ and Michael Robinson, and William and Thomas McNeil. Joe will live in our hearts forever. A memorial Mass will be held on Friday, July 23, at 12:00 PM at Corpus Christi Church in Piedmont. A private burial was held in Montana in the summer of 2020.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group tries to walk all Piedmont streets during the year. Last Wednesday morning, July 7, they decided that it would it a good day to tackle a long walk. A strong turnout of 27 walkers and one K-9 best friend were at the Exedra, and they ready for a long, mostly flat walk down and back the .8 mile length of St. James Drive. On hand were: Brenda Ferrero, Sherry Jacobs, Susan Field, Albert Chen, Swee Ling Chen, Haybert Houston, Nancy Olsen, Charlene Louie, Mark Greenberg, Andre Greenberg, Melba Yee, Dave DeRoche, Stella Houston, Priscilla Wanerus, Phil Witte, Adrienne Hamlin, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Quincy Dong, Helen Dong, Alicia Rivera, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Cat Gustafson, Alan Goldhammer, Bob Gustafson, Sarah Johnson, Jim Kuo, and Dick Carter. One of the last walks the group had before Covid restrictions In March 2020 was on St. James, so there was some added pleasure to be able to walk as a group on the street again. In November 2019 the walkers visited Cavendish Lane to see the repair of the block-long hillside street after it was undermined. It is a half block from where St. James ends at Park Blvd., so the walkers added it to their planned excursion. Due to the large number of walkers, it looked more like a parade down Highland Avenue to Sheridan and Wildwood, along the Hall Fenway to Crocker and Hampton Avenues. Along the way they enjoyed the fragrant, flowering jasmine plants and especially what was almost like a field of them in a Hampton Avenue yard. The group walked to the corner of St. James and La Salle Avenue, where two tall columns mark the entrance in the early 1900s to St. James Woods, part of the Upper Piedmont Estates neighborhood development. Originally there were lights on top of these columns, but they were removed at some point. The St. James’ homeowners later asked the City to install new light fixtures, but the cost exceeded the City’s budget. Post cartoonist and Wednesday walker Phil Witte lives on St. James and told the group about the street. The homes were built over time during the first half of the 20th century by different builders, so the architectural styles are varied. The sidewalks on both sides of the street the length of St. James have a distinctive tile design. The group enjoyed the long, winding street and appreciated the old streetlights, a very old cactus with a very large trunk, a curious dragon wood sculpture that guards one home, and other wonderful homes and gardens. The walkers also saw two pedestrian stairways, one that climbs up to Cambrian Avenue and the other that leads to Sandringham Road. A little further on, they also saw the top of another set of stairs that goes down to Trestle Glen Road The walkers finally made it to the end of St. James where Corpus Christi Church stands at Park Blvd. It had been a long walk, but the group was still up for a walk several hundred feet to Cavendish Lane to see its condition. This is a narrow street, truly a lane, which was damaged in February 2017 after it was undermined by heavy rains and a Trestle Glen neighbor’s home construction project below. This an Oakland street, but there are four Piedmont homeowners at its end. They were unable to access their homes by car for six weeks. The City of Piedmont took action to make temporary repairs until a permanent fix was made, which turned out to be two and a half years later in October 2019. They went up the lane and though the roadway was gully repaired, they were surprised to see that the area below the street still looks like a construction zone. The walkers were glad this situation was not in their backyards. Some members of this energetic group wanted to go down Trestle Glen, find the stairs that lead up to St. James and climb them, which is exactly what they did. Once back on St. James they retraced their many steps back to the Exedra. It had been well over four miles and a twohour walk. However, everyone seemed to enjoy the extra walking and talking with their walking friends. The Walking on Wednesday group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required with John Wilk at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: The American Red Cross continues to experience a severe blood shortage. Blood and platelet donors are needed now to help ensure hospital shelves are stocked with blood products over the Fourth of July holiday and beyond. As a thank-you, all those who come to give July 1-6 will receive a Red Cross embroidered hat by mail. And donors who donate blood between July 7-31 will receive a $10 Amazon.com gift card by email, plus a chance to win gas for one year (a $5,000 value). Donors of all blood types – especially type O and those giving platelets – are urged to make an appointment to give now by using the Red Cross Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood. org, calling 1-800-RED CROSS (1-800-733-2767). The Red Cross is working around the clock to provide blood products to hospitals responding to an unusually high number of traumas and emergency room visits, as well as overdoses and resulting transplants. As a result of the blood shortage, some hospitals are being forced to slow the pace of elective surgeries until the blood supply stabilizes, delaying crucial patient care. To donate blood, call the Oakland Blood Bank, 6230 Claremont Avenue, at 800-733-2767. The blood bank is open from 7:45 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. most days, and until 6:45 p.m. on June 30 and July 6. To donate blood, individuals need to bring a driver’s license or their blood donor card. Individuals aged 17 who weigh at least 110 pounds and in good health may be eligible to donate blood.

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

Supreme Court denies appeal by cities The city took action to contest Federal Communications Commission (FCC) regulations and joined a coalition of cities to sue the agency over its recent orders, including the Carr Order and the Moratorium Order. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals’ decision in City of Portland v. United States (2020) significantly affects the ability of local governments to regulate the installation of “small cell” wireless facilities. On March 22, Piedmont joined a national coalition of dozens of cities, led by the City of Portland, to file a writ of certiorari to review the judgement of the U.S. Court of Appeals. A writ of certiorari is a request that the Supreme Court order a lower court to send up the record of the case for review. Hollywood can be a cold place for outsiders, and Mia resolves to hunt down the mysterious Emily while continuing to try out for acting roles. Mia is the type of resourceful heroine who would have once been called “plucky,” and her common sense helps her navigate even the diciest developments. A Good Mother. by Lara Bazelon (Hanover Square, 368 pp.) The novel starts with the murder of a U.S. Air Force staff sergeant, Travis Hollis, stabbed with a kitchen knife by his wife, Luz. Among her motives: He was an abusive alcoholic, he had just fathered another woman’s baby, and he had recently made Luz and their 2-month-old daughter the beneficiaries of his $400,000 life insurance policy. It’s not exactly a slam-dunk case for Abby Rosenberg, the federal public defender assigned to represent Luz at her murder trial. Luz, just 19, is an unhelpful defendant, alternatively bored, defiant and manipulative. Abby is a problematic heroine, brilliant but troubled and often highly unpleasant. Bazelon, a professor at the University of San Francisco School of Law and an advocate for overturning wrongful convictions, sometimes has her characters do things that in real life would get them disbarred on the spot. But the courtroom scenes are sharp and suspenseful, the twists in the plot are unexpected, and the tension ratchets up until we are truly eager to find out what happens. by Charlie Chaplin. Some of these can still be seen in old downtown San Francisco office buildings but would be completely aesthetically and functionally unacceptable in a new high-rise building today. Glazing (the actual glass of the window) has itself evolved vastly over the last couple of centuries. In the old days, window sizes were limited by glass sizes. pages.text: 32 Wednesday, July 14, 2021 Walking Piedmont Continued from page 22 hung windows. Some of these can still be seen in old downtown San Francisco office buildings but would be completely aesthetically and functionally unacceptable in a new high-rise building today. Glazing (the actual glass of the window) has itself evolved vastly over the last couple of centuries. In the old days, window sizes were limited by glass sizes. The invention of flat glass made large glass sheets possible and gave a new freedom to fenestration design. This used to be plate glass, which is characterized by imperfections and slight “wave” distortion as you look through it. Nowadays, pretty much all glazing is float glass. It is named for the manufacturing process which includes floating the glass over molten tin. Only developed in the 1950’s, it is of a uniform thickness and has the even, clear appearance we are most familiar with today. Since up to 70% of energy loss of a building is through the fenestration, high energy-efficient windows are required and used everywhere in our era. They include the familiar double (or even triple) glazing, and low E glass coatings. I have found that one of the most difficult parts of building design is to make the overall exterior composition of the fenestration jibe with the requirements of the interior rooms. In other words, the fenestration has to work both inside and out, visually and functionally. In addition to considering the proportions and light and ventilation of each interior room, certain windows (in bedrooms) have to be sized to meet emergency exit requirements to allow occupants escape and firefighters egress. Another important building code requirement that enters into fenestration design is the requirement for tempered glass. Tempered glass is stronger, but more importantly, breaks into small granular chunks instead of dangerous dagger-like shards, as does normal glass. All glass in doors, and windows adjacent to doors, is now required to be tempered glass. articles.text: Festivities in Piedmont last weekend signaled an optimistic return to normalcy - albeit through small, intimate gatherings of friends and family. Over 15 months of sheltering-in-place, obsessive hygienic practices, and isolation now behind, the city celebrated Independence Day modestly with a small parade but a record high number of block parties on Sunday, July 4. Despite the elimination of most public health orders, the city was cautious in allowing for a large parade. Piedmont’s July 4 parade this year was a small, “sample-size” version of the traditional event that attracts up to 6,000 on Highland Avenue. Nevertheless, the quaint parade was truly a “wonderful day in the neighborhood, just like it has been year after year,” said Parade Committee Chair Carla Betts. “It exceeded our expectations, and it was incredible what [the committee] and community was able to achieve this year,” she said. This year’s theme was “Back to the Future,” based upon the 1985 sci-fi movie of the same name. It served also as a nod to a return to normalcy, a return to “the future.” Clear, blue skies made for a pleasant day in the city, with block parties underway even before noon. There were a few familiar mainstays, including the popular Pancake Breakfast organized by the Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), but held outside on Waldo Avenue. COVID restrictions meant the PCSC crew An antique car joins the 4th of July parade caravan. had to find an alternate location from its traditional feast at the Veterans’ Hall. Other than the change in venue, it was entirely familiar – and popular – with pancakes, sausages, fresh fruit, coffee and orange juice. Rose truck. The truck was driven by parade committee member Greg Bloom, with Roland Lazzorotto, the official Parade starter as navigator. articles.text: Camp Augusta has a magic about it that makes every person to have experienced it never forget their time there. I was nervous as I drove up Lake Vera Purdon Road this past week, not knowing if I would feel as welcome when I got to camp as I did many years ago. As I stepped into the 95-degree heat after parking, my heart filled with a million different emotions. After a six-year absence, everything looked almost the same, just a little smaller. Every hour during my daylong visit I had a different Hero assigned to show me around whatever I wanted to see. Heroes, at Camp Augusta, are staff members who do not currently have a cabin of their own. On their schedule there was an actual job that was simply “with Piedmont Post Reporter.” As Jane the Office Elf walked me around camp during rest hour, I laughed at my younger self for being so dramatic about the “long” walk to the horses. What once felt like a whole mile, I realized, is possibly 1000 feet or so. There are signs scattered around camp that read “Caution: Flying Children,” accompanied by the metallic whirr of ziplines and clacking of swing cords being pulled. My Hero of the hour, Squid, and I stared up at Gravity Zipline, where a counselor stood talking to a clipped-in camper on the platform. The camper’s eyebrows were scrunched with nerves, but on that 4-square-foot platform the counselor gestured towards the zipline and said something that made the camper’s eyebrows relax with the rest of her body. She took a step off the platform and from that point on, her grin was all I could see. What made the Camp Augusta magic come rushing back for me the most was time spent eating meals with campers. Beyond how amazing the food is at camp, getting to interact with and watch the interactions of four or five campers who just spent the past two weeks living together reminded me of how Camp Augusta makes all of life’s problems just melt away. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of California (LWV), in partnership with Drive Clean California, is hosting a one-hour informational Zoom event that will highlight the benefits of electric vehicle (EV) ownership and include the latest trends, costs, and considerations for those interested in moving to electric. The event will be held this Saturday, July 10, at 5 p.m., and repeated on Wednesday, July 14, at 6 p.m. Both will feature EV and e-bike experts and owners, who will discuss government incentives, solutions for residents who live in apartments and additional financial incentives for disadvantaged communities. The events will aim to debunk common EV myths and will serve as an opportunity for anyone to ask questions about EV ownership. California residents will receive priority placement for Drive Clean’s EV discount program. The next discount will be available in November. Drive Clean was developed by the California Air Resources Board as a resource for car buyers that are looking to find the cleanest and most efficient car that meets their driving needs. It was created to provide information, tools, and resources that help Californians learn about advanced vehicle technologies, and state-funded financial incentives to promote EV ownership. Drive Clean California is a collaborative campaign that builds upon the success of Drive Clean Bay Area with a mission to rapidly decrease carbon emissions. For those who drive or ride electric, the LWV and Drive Clean invites you to help host a Zoom “breakout room” following the main presentation, where attendees can hear your experiences and ask you questions. Contact info@cooltheearth.org to sign up as a Zoom “breakout room” host. To register for the July 10 or July 14 event, visit https://drivecleancalifornia.org/league-ofwomen-voters/. A similar event sponsored by the LWV and Drive Clean will be held in October. articles.text: This week, we of the Jewish tradition will begin reading from the book of Deuteronomy as part of our weekly reading from the Torah. Deuteronomy is essentially a review – a review of the history of the Israelites from the time they left Egypt to the time they were preparing to enter the Promised Land. It is a review of what God expects from them (and us) and what happens when they do or do not hearken to God’s commandments. These reminders of Israelite history and admonitions to follow God’s laws are found in the final orations given by Moses in the book of Deuteronomy. It is hoped that from going over what has happened and what is expected that the children of Israel will learn to lead better lives and to follow God’s commandments more closely. This past week, those of us living in Oakland and the surrounding area wondered what would happen after the verdict in the Mehserle trial. Would there be violence, would there be uncontrolled rioting, would the city burn. Some in the city had the hope that none of this would happen and that the city would remain peaceful and life could go on as normal. Some hoped that those disagreeing with the verdict would be able to share their concern, their anger, their disenchantment, but do so in a constructive instead of destructive way. In reviewing what had happened after the killing of Oscar Grant, when the city of Oakland suffered much violence, had we learned anything at all? I believe the answer to that question is a definite “yes.” Just as the children of Israel in looking over their history and their relationship with God learned from the past and prepared for the future, so did the leaders in Oakland. Just as the children of Israel understand what was expected of them, the leaders in Oakland realized their responsibility as leaders. The leaders of our city devised a way to let people express their feelings in a non-violent manner as the stage was open to all. It was open mike for all who wanted to be heard. The police reacted with restraint and allowed people to gather, to complain, to share their thoughts and express their pain without interfering with them. Monitors were in the crowd to help people who were angry to direct their anger away from turning into violent behavior. Religious and community leaders worked long and hard to ensure
articles.title: Oakland as a Promised Land
