articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department recently announced the promotion of Katrina Morris to Recreation Supervisor on July 1. In her new position Morris will supervise the Department’s Preschool Programs and continue her work with the Schoolmates. Morris joined the Department as a Recreation Leader at Havens Schoolmates in 2004. Her creativity, natural leadership qualities, and love for kids helped her develop into a key staff member in the Schoolmates program. Morris continued to move her way up in the Department by becoming the Assistant Site Coordinator at Beach Schoolmates, Site Coordinator at Wildwood, and most recently as Schoolmates Childcare Program Coordinator. Morris also directed many of the Department’s summer camps, including Healthy Hoppers, Cre- 8tive Design, and Camp Everything. Last fall she was selected to represent the City of Piedmont in the Alameda County Leadership Academy. “I am excited to acquire new responsibilities and to continue Newly named Recreation Supervisor Katrina Morris. my work in the department. I fell in love with the importance of play and this community in 2004 and will continue to nurture and grow our childcare programs,” said Morris. “I am so thrilled Katrina is our newest Recreation Supervisor,” said Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. “She brings not only 17 years of experience to the position but a true passion and love of working with children.”
articles.title: Katrina Morris promoted to Recreation Supervisor

articles.text: Gov. Gavin Newsom visited San Francisco’s Richmond District last month to announce that the state’s Department of Beverage Control will allow restaurants to sell cocktails to-go until the end of 2021. He also announced his interests in making outdoor dining permanent and more accessible state-wide. Both have allowed small businesses in the food and beverage industry to stay afloat during the pandemic, he said. “We don’t want to go back to normal. Normal was never good enough,” Gov. Newsom said. “We want to keep parklets going. It’s a good thing for our public health. We want to encourage people to continue to dine outside.” The governor added that he sent letters “to city and local governments statewide” encouraging city leaders to continue and expand allowances for outdoor dining. But the decision to keep, expand, or eliminate the use of parklets is ultimately up to each individual city. Oakland extends parklets through next Spring Oakland’s City Council voted on June 2 to introduce an ordinance that would extend the Flex Streets Initiative until March 31, 2022. The City of Oakland created the initiative in May 2020 for businesses, especially those in the food and beverage industry, that were unable to serve indoors due to the county health order. Through an application process it allowed for flexible uses of sidewalks, parking lanes, and streets. The city also waived all fees and streamlined permitting for business’ use of public rights-of-way. The adjusted permitting process allows for expedited approval for business use in private parking lots and outdoor areas, city-owned outdoor properties and traffic lanes. Businesses may use these spaces for extra seating, expanded merchandise displays, or customer queuing. To date, the city has approved more than 100 sidewalk cafes and parklets, 13 street closures, and more than 40 mobile vendors throughout the pandemic. In March, the City posted an interactive map of its Flex Streets program, which can be viewed by visiting https://oakgis.maps.arcgis.com/home/webmap/viewer. html?webmap=f8b30e3e36924ead83960173e556146f/. gov/FlexStreets. State legislation could make parklets permanent Senate Bill 314, proposed in the state legislature by Sen. Scott Wiener [D-San Francisco] and called the Bar and Restaurant Recovery Act, proposes several amendments to California’s liquor laws that intend to make them more flexible. If passed, some parklets would become permanent, also meaning restaurants would have the ability to serve alcohol on sidewalks and parking lots. “This expanded outdoor seating and service area – previously prohibited under California’s alcohol laws – has allowed restaurants and bars to survive and has been wildly popular with the public, with a more European-feeling street life,” said Wiener. The bill would also make it easier for bars and restaurants to share commercial, outdoor space with each other, and music venues would no longer need to have full kitchens in order to obtain a liquor license. SB 314 passed unanimously in committee in April, and enjoys bi-partisan support. It is co-authored by Sen. Andreas Borgeas (R-Fresno) and Sen. Jim Nielsen (R-Red Bluff). To learn more about Oakland flex streets program, call 510- 238-7398 or visit OaklandCA. Oakland City Council has agreed to extend its “Flex Streets” parklet program. articles.text: The city of Piedmont is seeking volunteers to help complete a recycling audit of waste bins. Volunteers will conduct field and desk research and deliver a final report of their research to City staff. It is an ideal position for college students aged 18 or older, or anyone interested in local government and environmental work. The Piedmont Evergreen Program aims to increase recycling and composting throughout the city and reduce waste to the landfill. In the last several years, the city installed a three-can series of receptacles (waste, organics, and recyclables) to improve garbage diversion in public parks. “Piedmont currently has a diversion rate of 75%, meaning that 75% of waste is composted or recycled, while 25% goes to the landfill. The City’s Climate Action Plan 2.0 outlines the City’s goal to divert 85% of waste going to the landfill by 2030. To reach this goal and encourage further diversion, the City purchased additional waste, organic, and recycling receptacles for use in public areas throughout Piedmont,” explained Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman. of how many people use the bin, what they put in the bin, etc. Volunteers may be asked to complete a waste characterization of different public bins to see how residents are sorting their waste. • Education and Engagement: Volunteers will meet with the Sustainability Program Manager weekly and will have a chance to ask questions about solid waste, compost, and recycling and learn more about the industry. Nobody is worried if their makeup looks good, or if the pictures they’re in make them look like they’re having the time of their lives. At Camp Augusta they’re focused on actually having the time of their lives. Because of the global pandemic we’re still experiencing, Camp Augusta looks a little different at the start of each session. Campers must get tested three times, and until the whole camp is cleared, they must remain in “pods” with their cabins, which later expands into their villages before everyone can do activities with whomever they want. As an observer, I saw a lot of benefit to this, especially when it came to problem-solving and communication within cabins. A small part of me wished that cabins had to do all activities with each other at the start of camp when I was a camper, because I think it really has fostered deeper connections, something many of us never thought to be possible. The Camp Augusta magic is back in full swing this year. I’m excited to be sharing some stories about it through the summer. articles.text: Penelope Sullivan will retire after 27 years teaching 6th grade core and 34 years total in education. Penelope Sullivan has announced her retirement from teaching at Piedmont Middle School, where she has taught sixth grade core for 27 years. A tireless worker who taught for the love of the kids, Sullivan rarely took a day off. She retires in 2021 with more than one year’s worth of untouched sick leave. Sullivan knew early on that she was meant to teach. “I always wanted to be a teacher. As a teenager I worked as an au pair and would go to Tahoe with families for months in the summertime. I just loved being with kids. So, I always thought, gosh, it would just be great to be a teacher.” she said. In college, a 20-year old Penelope called home and said she was thinking of changing her major to focus on becoming a teacher, however the home front was not in favor of the profession. As any good daughter would, Penelope considered the advice. “I immediately said okay, well, I am not going to do that. So, I went the roundabout way. I went to New York to work in advertising, Colorado for retail, then worked at USF as a recruiter.” At age 40 Sullivan became a single mom in Piedmont with two sons at Wildwood and realized she needed to go back to work and rekindle the passion of teaching. Sullivan began as a teacher’s aide in 1987 for Jade Shirachi’s 2nd grade class at Wildwood. After five years, Sullivan got her teaching credential and became a student teacher at Crocker Highlands Elementary at the kindergarten and 4th grade levels. In 1994 three 6th grade positions opened at Piedmont Middle School. That year, PMS found three stalwart teachers who became anchors of the school – Ted Scherman, Hannah Bjork and Penelope Sullivan. On the first day of school Principal John Morrison came into Sullivan’s classroom and said “Okay, I just hired you over the Teacher of the Year in Oakland; so you had better be good.” In her first year teaching full-time, Sullivan knew she could only do one thing: work as hard as she could. Sullivan’s work ethic followed a philosophy of leading by example. She became known as the teacher “who gave the most homework.” But in turn, she invested enormous amounts of her time into grading that homework and made Room 108 into a nurturing home for students for nearly three decades. “To offset the homework reputation, I also became the teacher with the lollipops,” said Sullivan with a grin. Some pieces of her curriculum were best left for a quiet space at home. Her students memorized 9-10 classic pieces of poetry a year, such as Jabberwocky, The Road Not Taken, and Oh Captain, My Captain. Her students also took on the task of creating their own magazines. Each wrote on a topic of their choice – sports, entertainment, food, pop culture – and finished with a piece of original literature. Penelope Sullivan’s Teaching Career • 1987 - 1991 Teacher’s Aide in Jade Shirachi’s 2nd grade class at Wildwood • 1992 Student Teacher Kindergarten and 4th grade at Crocker Highlands • 1993 Teacher’s Aide in Eileen Blood-Golden’s Home Base Class (grades 6-8) at PMS • 1994 - 2021 6th Grade Core Teacher at PMS; also Drama, Communications, Art, and Study Skills • 7th Grade Reading, 7th Grade ASB, Scots Camp, 6th Grade Boot Camp; • Summer School (every year): Welcome to Middle School, Cooking, Watercoloor, Book Making Sullivan said she loved teaching Social Studies most of all, using project-based learning to teach about the Early Hominids, Egypt, India, and China. She is well known at the school (and among faculty members) for leading her class to win the popular Greek Olympics nearly every year. By Jay Russell Penelope Sullivan has announced her retirement from teaching at Piedmont Middle School, where she has taught sixth grade core for 27 years. A tireless worker who taught for the love of the kids, Sullivan rarely took a day off. She retires in 2021 with more than one year’s worth of untouched sick leave. Sullivan knew early on that she was meant to teach. “I always wanted to be a teacher. As a teenager I worked as an au pair and would go to Tahoe with families for months in the summertime. I just loved being with kids. So, I always thought, gosh, it would just be great to be a teacher.” she said. In college, a 20-year old Penelope called home and said she was thinking of changing her major to focus on becoming a teacher, however the home front was not in favor of the profession. As any good daughter would, Penelope considered the advice. “I immediately said okay, well, I am not going to do that. So, I went the roundabout way. I went to New York to work in advertising, Colorado for retail, then worked at USF as a recruiter.” At age 40 Sullivan became a single mom in Piedmont with two sons at Wildwood and realized she needed to go back to work and rekindle the passion of teaching. Sullivan began as a teacher’s aide in 1987 for Jade Shirachi’s 2nd grade class at Wildwood. After five years, Sullivan got her teaching credential and became a student teacher at Crocker Highlands Elementary at the kindergarten and 4th grade levels. In 1994 three 6th grade positions opened at Piedmont Middle School. That year, PMS found three stalwart teachers who became anchors of the school – Ted Scherman, Hannah Bjork and Penelope Sullivan. On the first day of school Principal John Morrison came into Sullivan’s classroom and said “Okay, I just hired you over the Teacher of the Year in Oakland; so you had better be good.” In her first year teaching full-time, Sullivan knew she could only do one thing: work as hard as she could. Sullivan’s work ethic followed a philosophy of leading by example. She became known as the teacher “who gave the most homework.” But in turn, she invested enormous amounts of her time into grading that homework and made Room 108 into a nurturing home for students for nearly three decades. “To offset the homework reputation, I also became the teacher with the lollipops,” said Sullivan with a grin. Some pieces of her curriculum were best left for a quiet space at home. Her students memorized 9-10 classic pieces of poetry a year, such as Jabberwocky, The Road Not Taken, and Oh Captain, My Captain. Her students also took on the task of creating their own magazines. Each wrote on a topic of their choice – sports, entertainment, food, pop culture – and finished with a piece of original literature. articles.text: After 15 long months of trying to make something out of nothing, we are in a little bit of a release. Recently, many of us busted the front door open to a beautiful Bay Area summer. Adults and children alike want to shed the emotional weight of the pandemic, leave the house, and have fun. Engaging in play is an important part of early childhood and contributes to healthy brain development - the benefits are cognitive, physical, social, and emotional. And honestly, it’s good for people of all ages. For children it helps with language, communication, and emotion control. For adults, play reduces stress, and improves brain functionality. And playing together – a departure from the structured segmentation of the pandemic. According to Richard Louv, author of the Last Child in the Woods, playing outside, due to its relatively unstructured nature, also has the added benefit of feeding creativity and imagination. When children spend time playing outside the opportunities to invent, discover, pretend, and problem-solve are bountiful. This kind of break allows children (and adults) to attend to structured participation and formal zoom-room in a much more effective way. Dragon fun at Children’s Fairyland Since March, I have had the benefit of looking out of my magical window to see this notion unfolding each day – children and adults reestablishing their connection to play, the outdoors, and one another after 15 months of keeping too much of their energy and toxic stress inside, both literally and figuratively. I watch children become swashbuckling mates on a pirate ship, play peekaboo with a donkey, climb on the back of the happy dragon, or catch bubbles blown by an elf. I also see their adults running behind them full of glee, smiles, relief, and a cup of coffee. Ever yone deser ves this moment to explore, imagine, create, play, scream, and run. Invest in restorative self-care for the whole family – get outside and play. Kymberly Miller is Executive Director of Children’s Fairyland, Children’s Fairyland, America’s first storybook theme park, located on the shores of Lake Merritt in the heart of Oakland, since 1950. It offers children and families a safe, stimulating environment for play and imagination with fairytales, fantasy sets, performing arts, animals, and unique children’s programming focused on early childhood education and literacy.
articles.title: Play is first on the park’s list of what to do

articles.text: We all learn in different ways, but whether you know it or not most everyone relies on creating mnemonic devices (memory devices) to help remember things. In short, mnemonic devices are techniques to help your brain better save and regurgitate important information. They are shortcuts or bridges commonly in the form of images, a sentence, or words to remind us of answers based upon seeing the question. A very simple example of a mnemonic device is using the letters on a phone’s keypad to remember phone numbers like 1-800-NO-CUFFS for a bail bondsman. Knowledge may stick to memory banks easier in the very young, as witnessed by children easily learning multiple languages. So, in a way, we are born with the capacity to attain knowledge and slowly turn into old dogs unable to learn new tricks. The much heralded “photographic memory” or “eidetic memory” is defined by Wikipedia as “the ability to recall an image from memory with high precision for a brief period after seeing it only once, and without using a mnemonic device.” It is thought that 2-15 percent of children have eidetic memory, but its existence has never been proved in adults. Sometimes new concepts or study materials easily make intuitive sense to the learner. For some the entire framework of arithmetic or spelling rules can be remembered without reference to something else. One may be a “natural,” at certain disciplines or activities. articles.text: Photo courtesy of California State Parks Portions of Big Basin’s coastal section, Rancho del Oso, has been open to the public since May 23. Two local state parks that were deeply impacted by last year’s CZU Complex Fire have begun a partial reopening. Big Basin’s coastal unit, Rancho del Oso, is now partly accessible, and Butano State Park has officially opened five miles of trails. Environmental scientist Ryan Diller explained the sensitivity of the matter and what needs to occur for the parks to become fully sustainable: “Right now, Big Basin is in a recovery stage,” said Diller, via Big Basin State Park’s Facebook. “It’s experienced a traumatic fire and its immune system is completely gone. That immune system consists of the canopy and the thick duff and litter layer, both in some areas of the park are absent. The duff has been cooked down to bare mineral soil, the canopy has been torched to the point where there’s more light reaching the forest floor since the initial logging industry… We’re excited for the public to come re-enter out parks but a lot of our parks aren’t going to be opening all at once.” Diller confirmed that Rancho del Oso has been partially open since May 30. Waddell Beach and its parking lot are accessible, and its Nature and History Center are open on weekends from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The Marsh Trail is the only trail available. “Big Basin is still completely closed except for the Rancho del Oso section of Big Basin. When you do go to that part to the park, we ask that you stay on roads, trails and try to prevent any spread of seeds into the burn area,” said Diller. Big Basin Redwoods State Park still has some hotspots popping up. A total of 13 additional burns have recently been addressed by CalFire. “We are not in the clear yet. Impacted areas still contain active fire hazards. [In June] CalFire responded to the Pine Fire which burned 3.7 acres of oldgrowth redwood forest. CalFire identified 11 additional hot spots and responded to a separate 11.5- acre fire within Big Basin,” wrote Big Basin in a recent statement. Butano State Park’s five miles of trails includes portions of: Six Bridges Trail, Jackson Flats Trail, Butano Fire Road Mill Ox Trail, Olmo Fire Road, Goat Hill Trail, and Ben Ries Trail. “At Butano State Park, we’re still clearing roads and trails. It’s a very sensitive time in the recovery period,” said Diller. “Many areas of Butano State Park will remain closed, including the campground. The fire has left many trees compromised and other trail hazards exist, but crews are continuing to work on repairs. For your safety and the health of our park, please stay out of closed areas.” Parking and picnic areas are open, however, TRAIL CLOSURE NOTICE Due to the CZU Fire, areas of Butano State Park will remain Photo courtesy of Youtube. Butano State Park announced last month that it has opened five miles of hiking trails.
articles.title: Big Basin’s Rancho del Oso accessible, Butano opens 5 miles of trails

Wednesday, July 7, 2021 13 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 14th year in the Post. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. ment I play. My development is measured by the quality of my matches, not necessarily by wins or losses. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? On court, I work with my coach Tyler Browne, and I have a fitness trainer for off-court training. When I am at tournaments, I practice with other tournament players. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? An achievement I have recently accomplished is becoming a blue-chip recruit (top 25 in the nation) on TennisRecruiting. net. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? Have fun with it because, in the end, it’s just a game! Make sure to take complete days off and avoid burning yourself out by overtraining. Staff Photo Makenna Thiel is off to the University of California’s defending Pac-12 Championship winning women’s tennis team. She was named Athlete of the Year by the Post in 2019 and 2021. MAKENNA THIEL Tennis and Thursday are cardio-based with a 45 minute bike-ride. Play catch and long-toss at least three days a week, a bullpen session once a week, and also throw to live batters once a week. What are your fitness goals for the summer? I want to get my weight to 195 pounds. How are you measuring your development? I am focusing on accuracy and efficiency by keeping track of my strikes/balls ratio during bullpens and live-batting sessions. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working in my own following a plan developed for me by the weightlifting coach and athletic trainer, and also working with two pitching coaches. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Obtaining an athletic scholarship to play baseball at Bemidji State University in Minnesota. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Keep working hard because you will be rewarded in the end. If you desire to play baseball in college, there will be a place where you fit in if you work hard to create opportunities. Piedmont High Class of 2021 University of California Class of 2025 Makenna Thiel graduates from Piedmont High as one of the most dominant singles starters to grace the Piedmont Courts. She will continue her tennis career at UC Berkeley in the fall as part of the Pac-12 championship team. She was named Athlete of the Year by the Post in 2019 and 2021. Thiel dominated the Western Alameda County Conference singles championship this year and also won the North Coast Section Div.1 doubles championship in 2019 with Lauren Young. Her teams went 20-2 as a freshman and 21-2-2 as a sophomore before returning to her tournament schedule her junior year. This year’s program went 5-5. Thiel has competed in tournaments throughout the country since middle school. Since winning the WACC Singles Title on April 17, Thiel won third place at the Premier Tennis Tour Las Vegas Hard 2 on May 30 and competed in the PTT Newport Beach Women’s Hard 6 on June 17. What is your workout program this summer? My workout program for this summer varies day-by-day. Six days a week, I practice for around two hours with either my coach or hitting partners, and also do around an hour of strength training, weightlifting, bodyweight training, or sprints. What are your fitness goals for this summer? This summer, my goal is to continue to build muscle and get as fit as I can so that I am ready and prepared for college training at Cal. How are you measuring your development? Actual progress can only be measured on the court, so I try to get better with each tournaMAX WAGENER Water Polo Photo courtesy of www.BsuBeavers.com Christian Turner, Class of 2017, is entering his second year on Bemidji State University in Minnesota after earning a scholarship while playing at the JC level. CHRISTIAN TURNER Baseball Piedmont High Class of 2021 University of Redlands Class of 2025 Max Wagener has led Piedmont’s water polo team in scoring the past two years and is a threeyear varsity member. He will continue his career at the University of Redlands. Standing at 6-feet, 4-inches, Wagener showed versatility in his ability to score – sometimes shooting from the wing, and other times rotating into the hole set to dominate shorter defenders. He led Piedmont High to a 10-2 overall this season and scored at least five goals in five games, including seven goals against rival Alameda on May 6. The Highlanders finished 10-2 this year, 17-12 his junior season, while they went 22-6 his sophomore year as a reserve. During his high school career, he’s been a part of the 2019 WACC Championship Tournament runners up, finishing third in 2020 and 2021. What is your workout program this summer? I took a two-week recovery following the conclusion of our high school season and am back working out. My plan for this summer is putting on mass while remaining in swim-shape, which requires building lean muscle. I’ll do this by swimming and lifting weights. What are your fitness goals for the summer? Put on a clean weight and build more lean muscle. How are you measuring your development? I’m measuring my progress by checking my weight on a daily basis; making sure I’m eating with an emphasis on a calories excess. Additionally, I’ll keep track of my swim times to measure progress. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’ll mainly be working by myself on certain sessions; friends and teammates may come along as well. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? My 100-meter freestyle time dropped to 56 seconds without diving by the end of the water polo season. I use these swim times as motivation to keep developing. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Hard work beats talent when talent doesn’t work hard. This may seem cliché but it becomes evident as you progress in your sport. Put in the hours on the field, in the pool, in the gym or wherever, and you will see results. Piedmont High Class of 2017 Bemidji State Class of 2023 Christian Turner, PHS Class of 2017, is an example of diligently pursuing his passion in athletics. Now entering his second year at Bemidji State University in Minnesota, the former Highlander pitcher first attended Sierra College, then Los Medanos College before earning a scholarship at Bemidji State. In 2021, Turner made one start and had 10 total appearances on the mound, striking out six batters in 10 innings pitched. Turner graduated from Piedmont High as a four-year varsity starter and amassed 146 strikeouts over his high school career. As the team’s ace pitcher, Turner helped lead the Highlanders to the quarterfinals of the North Coast Section playoffs. What is your workout program this summer? My workout plan is as follows: Monday, Wednesday, and Friday include front squats, reverse lunges, and dead lifts. articles.text: Last year’s Tour de France champion Tadej Pogacar of Croatia leads the general classification standings by two minutes and one second over Australian Ben O’Connor after 10 stages of the month-long race. . Pogacar gained the yellow jersey after Stage 8 in dramatic fashion. He was in 4th palace heading into the 150.8-kilometer mountain course sitting in fourth place, trailing Mathieu van der Poel of the Netherlands by more than three minutes. Pogacar won last year’s Tour in a time trial over France’s Julian Alaphilippe on the next to last day of the race. Although Belgium’s Dylan Teuns won the event, it was Pogacar who stole the show despite being the fourth rider across the line—killing the 3:01 deficit after van der Poel finished 44th and relinquished his six-day hold on the yellow jersey. Van der Poel fell well off the pace, dropping to 23rd at the end of Stage 8 and 17 minutes, 20 seconds back of Pogacar. In a peculiar decision, the Dutchman retired from the Grand Tour after the stage in order to shift focus toward the Tokyo Olympics. “I will not start today. We decided with the team it is in my best interests to quit the race and focus on the Olympics now,” said Van der Poel, via Eurosport.com. “We know it would have been difficult for me and I have some other goals. It was impossible for me to do the whole tour and then be at my top at Tokyo. I’ll be back next year.” Yesterday’s Stage 10 featured England’s Mark Cavendish, 36, gaining his third win of the 2021 Grand Tour and 33rd stage-win of his career. His victory on Tuesday was highlighted by a textbook lead-out by his Deceuninck-QuickStep teammates, Julian Alaphilippe, Kasper Asgreen, Davide Ballerini, and Michael Mørkøv. Cavendish’s teammates began peeling off one-by-one, and with around 150 meters to go, the veteran rider led Belgium cyclists Wout van Aert and Jasper Philipsen in a furious sprint to the line. Australia’s Ben O’Connor is currently in second, back two minutes and 1 second.

articles.text: The CONCACAF Gold Cup soccer tournament returns this week with three group stage matches starting on Saturday, July 10. The tournament runs through July 18, with quarterfinals on July 24, semifinals on July 29, and championship round on August 1. The U.S. Men’s National team is scheduled to open the tournament against Haiti on Sunday, July 11 at 5:30 p.m. The U.S. qualified for the tournament after winning CONCACAF’s Nations League with a dramatic 3-2 win in overtime against Mexico. But they will be playing nearly an entire lineup change because players on European clubs are entering preseason training. The U.S. will have a 23-man roster with 19 players from Major League Soccer teams. The United States will require major contributions from players still looking to earn a name for themselves. 21-year-old striker Daryl Dike has his biggest opportunity to lock down a role ahead of the 2022 World Cup Qualifiers on September 5. The Earthquakes’ Jackson Yueill will be a major contributor in the midfield alongside the Rapids’ Kellyn Acosta and Sounders’ Cristian Roldan. On the back line, Boavista’s Reggie Cannon should start at right back with Atlanta’s Miles Robinson on the opposite side. In goal will be veteran Brad Guzan, also of Atlanta United. The U.S. (ranked No. 20) will be in Group B with Canada, Martinique, and Haiti. They must finish in the top two of the group in order to reach the quarterfinals; Canada, ranked No. 70, will be the U.S.’s toughest competition, Haiti is ranked No. 83. The Post’s prediction: U.S. wins group, Canada is runner up. Photo courtesy of Gold Cup Wikipedia The CONCACAF Gold Cup will take place from Saturday, July 10 through August 1. Tournament favorite Mexico (No. 11) is an example of properly prioritizing its national competition. Despite being without goalie Guillermo Ochoa, they bring a much better lineup by featuring mainline starts like Ajax’s Edson Alvarez, LA Galaxy’s Jonathan “Chicharito” dos Santos, Atletico Madrid’s Hector Herrera, and Napoli star Hirving “Chucky” Lozano. Mexico beat the U.S. 1-0 in the 2019 Gold Cup Finals. Mexico will be in Group A with El Salvador (No. 69), Curacao (No. 76), and Trinidad & Tobago (No. 103). The most Mexico is the defending Gold Cup Champions from 2019. They enter as the favorite. he United States enter with a roster some are considering its “B” or “C” team. It’s a critical time for striker Daryl Dike to solidify a consistent role. interesting competition here will be between El Salvador and Curacao. It is a constituent of the Netherlands and features nearly all Dutch born players. The Post’s prediction: Mexico wins group, Curacao upsets El Salvador as runner up. Group C features Jamaica (No. 45), Costa Rica (No. 50), Suriname (No. 136) and Guadeloupe (unranked). The separation in ranking is quite telling for this group, and things should come down to the Reggae Boyz of Jamaica battling with Costa Rica for the top spot. The Post’s’ prediction: Jamaica wins group, Costa Rica a runner up. Group D is a peculiar group with a lot of potential for close matches with Honduras (No. 67), Panama (No. 78), Grenada (No. 160), and Qatar (No. 58). Qatar, most notably, received an invitation to this year’s tournament as host of the 2022 World Cup. Qatar, which resides in FIFA’s Asian Football Conference, is climbing the world football ladder and is the defending Asian Cup champions from 2019 when they beat Japan (No. 28) 3-1. It will be interesting to see how they square up with Central America’s physical style and a roster totally comprised of Qatar’s star league players. The Post’s prediction: Honduras wins group, Qatar runner up.
articles.title: U.S. Men to play with backup squad; Mexico the favorite

articles.text: We last visited Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve in the Oakland Hills in May 2020 on a rainy morning. The park is noted for its year-round display of blossoming flowers on its easy 2.4-mile loop, and even in the dry months of summer there are some plants on exhibit. Hikers are in closer contact with foliage than perhaps any other trail in the Oakland hills. In July you will see western bracken, coastal wood, and western sword ferns. The trail passes underneath moss-covered California Bay Laurels trees, with shoots sprouting from downed trees. Giant cape ivy leaves line a portion of the narrow trail as they thrive in the summer sun. Another section of brittleleaf Manzanita shows its distinct redbark beginning to crack and warp in the dry heat. You can find yellow monkeyflowers on the lower portion of the Huckleberry Botanic loop, in addition to a segment of California aralia, which has a low-hanging canopy of enormously large leaves. The sheer size of the leafy lush-green verdant area is mesmerizing. Yellow monkey flowers are currently in bloom. Ferns of different species surround hikers at Huckleberry Botanic, with informative panels describing the abundant foliage. California Bay Laurels surround hikers on this shady trail. articles.text: Andre Thierry, a Richmond-native with strong Louisiana Zydeco influences, is one of this year’s featured performers. The Yerba Buena Gardens Festival is free, with live music and performances through August 28. For over two decades, Yerba Buena Gardens Festival has presented free outdoor music, circus, dance, poetry, theatre, and youth programs by artists from the Bay Area and around the world. The festival was cancelled last year due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The festival opened this summer on June 26 with a concert by Bobi Cespedes, the “matriarch of Cuban roots in the Bay Area.” July highlights include the first of a three-part series of dance events by the Yerba Buena Gardens ChoreoFest, music by Zydeco musician Andre Thierry, and Oakland-based hip-hop orchestra Ensemble Mik Nawooj. Children’s programs in July include Pi Clowns and Red Panda Acrobats. In addition to a long list of Afro-Cuban, jazz, Zydeco, and ensemble offerings, the festival also features outdoor dance classes and American Native dance presentations. “I could not be more thrilled to announce this special Festival season of free performances and concerts this summer,” said Festival Artistic Director Linda Lucero. “I am so excited to welcome everyone back to the beautiful Gardens to experience our region’s rich cultural diversity and the immense fortitude of our local artists and performers. After a long period of isolation for many of us, Yerba Buena Gardens Festival remains a space for art and joy, welcoming people from all walks of life. There’s nothing that gladdens the heart and spirit more than celebrating the performing arts together under open skies,” she said. The Yerba Buena Gardens is located on Mission Street between 3rd and 4th streets in San Francisco. Visit www.ybgfestival.org for full schedule. ®
articles.title: Yerba Buena Festival continues through August

articles.text: A “Sculpture Show Evening Stroll” will be held tomorrow, Thursday, July 8 at the Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek. It will feature the works of over 20 renowned Northern California artists. Each year the garden’s art show and sale showcases sculptural art using the natural backdrop of the location. Live jazz music from the band Four and More will be performed, and beer and wine will be available for purchase. A special members-only after-hours evening sculpture stroll begins at 5 p.m. The Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is famous for its extensive collection of succulents, cacti, California native plants, and other drought-tolerant plants. The garden was originally planted in 1972 by Ruth Bancroft when it was her private, personal garden but is now open six days a week for the education and enjoyment of the public. Bancroft created a garden filled with dynamic plant combinations using drought-tolerant plants that very few other gardeners were using at the time. In 1989, her garden was selected by the Garden Conservancy to be its first preservation project, and a conservation easement was established to ensure its permanent preservation. Visitors can browse the garden from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., Tuesday through Thursday, and 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday through Sunday. For a full list of what’s in bloom, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/Whats-In-BloomJuly-2021.pdf. To plan your visit to the gardens, go to the organization’s homepage: https://www. ruthbancroftgarden.org/.
articles.title: Ruth Bancroft Garden hosts annual “Sculpture Show Evening Stroll” tomorrow

articles.text: Festival Opera’s 2021 season will continue at Piedmont Center for the Arts with a live performance this Sunday, July 11. It will be the first concert with a live audience at the Center since the onset of the COVID pandemic in March 2020. “Un raggio di speme,” or “A Ray of Hope,” will be performed by Syrian-American coloratura soprano Lila Khazoum accompanied by celebrated pianist Alexander Katsman. The collection of songs is a celebration of the beauty of hope, even as it relates to loss and longing - a timely performance as we begin to gather again. The program also features virtuoso arias by Antonio Vivaldi, the tender storytelling in Sei ariette by Vincenzo Bellini, as well as the songs of George Bizet, Reynaldo Hahn, and Henri Duparc. “I am thrilled by the opportunity to highlight this exciting new voice in the opera world with a live performance and that we are making this performance available online to our friends around the globe,” said Festival Opera General Director Zachary Gordin. “Festival Opera maintains our commitment to seeking out and nurturing exceptionally talented artists and highlighting diverse Soprano Lila Khazoum voices. I look forward to this event with great excitement and hope that you’ll join us either in person, or in the digital concert space.” The Sunday concert will begin at 5 p.m. Following the concert, a video interview with Khazoum and Gordin will be hosted by the Festival Opera’s Director of Social Media, Ruchi Kapila, on the organization’s YouTube channel. All ticket buyers will automatically receive a link to this companion offering. To purchase tickets, visit: https://www.festivalopera.org/ artist-recital-series.
articles.title: Festival Opera comes to Piedmont on Sunday

articles.text: Music@Menlo returns this summer with a mix of in-person and digital performances beginning on July 16. The 2021 season, entitled “Gather,” will take place in and around the festival’s new $40 million Spieker Center for the Arts on the campus of Menlo School in Menlo Park. Music@Menlo is an internationally acclaimed chamber music festival founded by David Finckel and Wu Han. Inaugurated in 2003 at Menlo School, the festival features concerts, lectures, and a training program for aspiring professional musicians. This year’s events will be smaller in size than its 18 previous seasons but will continue to include a star-studded lineup of musicians. The festival will include a mix of live and digitally-streamed performances between July 16 and August 1. Featured concerts will be performed at 4 p.m. on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday in the Spieker Center, and then repeated at 6 p.m. outdoors. Concerts will run for approximately one hour without intermission. There will be nine main concerts grouped over three weekends. The season-opening concert on July 16 includes the world premiere of Patrick Castillo’s Gather, a new work commissioned for the festival’s new home at Spieker Center. Castillo has held a variety of positions with the festival since its inception. He was recently named the New York Philharmonic’s Vice President of Artistic Planning. “I was honored to be asked by David and Wu Han to create a new piece to celebrate the opening of Music at Menlo’s new concert hall. For the occasion, I composed a paean to our sacred ritual of coming together around a shared love of music,” Castillo said. “Little did I know at the time how starved we would be for that ritual by the time of the piece’s first hearing.” Tickets are on sale now and can be purchased by visiting: https://musicatmenlo.org/. Music@Menlo’s 2021 season will take place at the festival’s new $40 million Spieker Center for the Arts in Menlo Park.
articles.title: Music@Menlo Festival opens July 16

articles.text: Music Director Joseph Young will lead Berkeley Symphony in its first live appearance in more than a year with a performance at Bruns Amphitheater in Orinda on August 4. The program includes music by Rossini, Bizet, Bach, Beethoven, Tchaikovsky, Gabriela Lena Frank, Brian Raphael Nabors, and Jessie Montgomery. One of the highlights will be a performance of “Lubilo” by Nabors, a commissioned work as part of New Music USA’s Amplifying Voices program. Actors with California Shakespeare Festival provide iconic Shakespeare passages with Beethoven’s Egmont Overture. “I am thrilled to finally be together with our audiences after all this time apart,” Young said. “There is a tangible sense of hope and optimism as we collectively look ahead to a brighter future, and it is in the same spirit that we mark this turning point with our first live performance together in more than a year.” For tickets, visit www.berkeleysymphony.org. articles.text: Leehom), who was educated in the U.S., insists that the best is Nicholas Hathaway (Chris Hemsworth), currently serving a 16-year sentence in federal prison for hacking international banks. The deal struck by Hathaway is if he can find the Blackhat, who has done major damage and reaped millions for his efforts, Hathaway’s sentence will be commuted. Reluctantly the feds agree. And so, he joins forces with the F.B.I., led by Carol Barrett (Viola Davis), and her Chinese counterparts, Chen and his sister Chen Lien. Though there is a lot of staring at screens and a lot of clicking of keyboards, there are also some classic shootouts involving some very bad dudes (led perfectly by Ricky Coster), all in the employ of the Blackhat. This is a compelling techno-thriller that should ring true, especially for the twenty-something moviegoers. They get what happened to Sony. They know that companies and the governments are vulnerable. Their world is lived looking at screens and running their fingers over large and small keyboards. It will be disappointing if Blackhat doesn’t find an audience. It should not pass quietly into that good night, for it is fine moviemaking and directed by one of the best in the business, Michael Mann. Blackhat . Directed by Michael Mann. Starring Chris Hemsworth, Viola Davis, Wei Tang. 2 hrs., 14 min. Rated R. George Clooney and Jack O’Connell star in Money Monster. Money Monster is a close facsimile of CNBC’s Mad Money with Jim Cramer. Consider it a parody (at least initially) of the show with a sprinkling of satire. Lee Gates (George Clooney) is the show’s host, an insouciant dispenser of stock tips and financial advice, offered up more as entertainment than as substantive analysis of the market and why some stocks are nuggets and others are to be avoided. What Lee – narcissistic, pampered and glib – has forgotten is that there are those in his audience who listen closely and take his shtick seriously. Case in point is Kyle Budwell (Jack O’Connell), a working stiff whose mom has died and left him some $60k that he invests in a financial outfit named Ibis Clear Capital – at the suggestion of Lee. Kyle shows up at the beginning of Lee’s show to ask Lee why his nest egg has vanished, only he’s got a gun and a suicide vest, which he insists that Lee put on. Let’s say that rage and revenge are Kyle’s default settings. What he wants is an explanation. What happened that caused his stock to tank? If he doesn’t get some answers, he’s going to turn Lee into mist. The deal is that he makes $14 per hour at his delivery job and can’t afford to keep himself or his girlfriend above water. The $60k represented hope. In the control room, suddenly faced with a chaotic hostage situation, is Patty Fenn (Julia Roberts), Lee’s producer, who is talking to him via his earpiece. And it’s Patty who begins working furiously to get some backstory on the company that tanked – what happened to cause the company to suddenly lose $800 million. Since the CEO, Walt Camby (Dominic West) is unavailable – in a corporate jet somewhere over the Atlantic – she’s talking to the company’s PR head, Diane Lester (Caitriona Balfe), who is not very helpful. So there is the triangle squared: Lee, facing a very angry investor, Kyle ready to shoot Lee or blow him up, Patty in the control room, talking to Lee and Diane. There is, of course, a serious response by the New York police who want to shoot Kyle, but not as long as he’s holding the dead man’s trigger connected to the vest. Consider all of the above as act one. What follows serves only to ratchet up the tension. The mystery of what happened to the $800 million is incrementally sorted out with a math guy in Seoul explaining financial algorithms and stock fluctuations, a couple of laid-back hackers in Reykjavik who are happy to be in the game, and later the CEO pf the company who was in South Africa working his side of the street. Meanwhile Lee and Kyle are in the studio and Patty is in the control room trying to manage what is uncontrollable, hoping to keep Kyle from having a meltdown while pointing a gun at Lee’s head. And thus begins act three. Is Money Monster entertaining? Yes. But then it’s got a deep bench of talent, starting with Clooney and Roberts. And the writing is good, at times gripping. Though it relies on some financial arcana, it doesn’t take the audience so deep into the weeds that the details can seem unintelligible, such as The Big Short. But there are moments when the collective villain is Wall Street with its casino-like approach to investing, to include their esoteric financial instruments. Meanwhile, Kyle represents the victims. But still, with Jodie Foster at the helm, this is good summer entertainment. Money Monster. Directed by Jodie Foster. Starring George Clooney, Julia Roberts, Jack O’Connell. 1 hr., 38 min. Rated R.

In order to do this, the Chinese expert, Chen Dawai (Wang Leehom), who was educated in the U.S., insists that the best is Nicholas Hathaway (Chris Hemsworth), currently serving a 16-year sentence in federal prison for hacking international banks. The deal struck by Hathaway is if he can find the Blackhat, who has done major damage and reaped millions for his efforts, Hathaway’s sentence will be commuted. Reluctantly the feds agree. And so, he joins forces with the F.B.I., led by Carol Barrett (Viola Davis), and her Chinese counterparts, Chen and his sister Chen Lien. Though there is a lot of staring at screens and a lot of clicking of keyboards, there are also some classic shootouts involving some very bad dudes (led perfectly by Ricky Coster), all in the employ of the Blackhat. This is a compelling techno-thriller that should ring true, especially for the twenty-something moviegoers. They get what happened to Sony. They know that companies and the governments are vulnerable. Their world is lived looking at screens and running their fingers over large and small keyboards. It will be disappointing if Blackhat doesn’t find an audience. It should not pass quietly into that good night, for it is fine moviemaking and directed by one of the best in the business, Michael Mann. Blackhat . Directed by Michael Mann. articles.text: Luke Bernard (center) as Billy Forrester in How to Eat Fried Worms. A film based on the Thomas Rockwell book. First things first: How to Eat Fried Worms, based on the Thomas Rockwell book, is a gross-out delight. Its target audience is kids 6 to 11, who will find the story definitely cringe-worthy, but in a good way. If you’ve spent any time hanging out with youngsters, you know that they relish saying “eeewwww!” Or, “that is so disgusting!” The story revolves around Billy Forrester (Luke Bernard), 11-years-old, who is about to start a new school. In other words, he will have to endure the new kid syndrome: short on friends with not a clue how to get around. As it turns out, there are a few kids who reach out to him; however, they hang out on the fringe and are considered uncool. There’s Erika (Halle Kate Eisenberg), also known as “Erk”, tall and gangly and definitely not one of the popular kids. And there’s Adam (Austin Rogers) who, like Erika, carries the tag of “loser.” Unfortunately, Billy draws the attention not only of the marginal kids, but of Joe (Adam Hicks), school bully, and his toadies Plug (Blake Garrett), and Bradley (Phillip Daniel Bolden). Unbeknownst to Billy, they steal his lunchbox, then return it, and then during lunch, when Billy pours out what he expects will be milk from his thermos, he discovers it’s filled with worms. Billy, who has a sensitive stomach, comes close to vomiting at the first sight of the night crawlers. After school, on his way home, Billy runs into Joe and his gang. Joe asks him how he liked the worms. Billy says they’re great and he eats them all the time. Joe says, “oh yeah?” And Billy says “Really.” And that’s when Joe challenges him to a bet: if Billy can eat 10 worms without throwing up, Joe will come to School with a mess of worms in his pants. If he can’t, then it’s Billy who has to come to school with worms in his shorts. Foolishly, Billy, who feels he can’t back down, looks at Joe and accepts. Sure. No problem. The next day, determined, Billy begins cooking and frying all manner of worms. There’s “Le Porker,” “The Greasy Brown Toad Boater,” “The Burning Fishbait” and so on. Billy eats them one by one, some microwaved, spread with peanut butter, or hidden in marshmallows. The question is, will Billy finish all ten, or miss Joe’s deadline. It’s going to be close. Which is what makes How to Eat Fried Worms grossly fun. How to Eat Fried Worms. Live action. Directed by Bob Dolman. Starring Luke Bernard, Tom Cavanaugh, Kimberly Williams-Paisley. 1 hr., 24 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: How to Eat Fried Worms – a gross-out delight

articles.text: Disney’s remake of its 1998 animated feature, Mulan, is now live action, told on a grand scale, reportedly costing some $200 million. It’s an epic saga, based on a 400-year-old folk song that describes a young woman, Mulan (Yifei Liu), who, when her ailing father is drafted as part of the emperor’s call to arms, makes the extraordinary decision to take her father’s place, disguised as a man. Wearing her father’s armor, with her chest bound with cloth, she manages to pass the test of her disguise, and is accepted as one of the thousands of conscripted warriors preparing for battle. It’s at this point that the narrative becomes a simply told tale, one of spectacular battles and desperate survival with a touch of slow-motion magic. It’s during these head-on confrontations with the northern nomads that we come to realize that Mulan possesses not only uncommon bravery, but dazzling skills that allow her to defy gravity. As part of understanding her ability to all but fly, while performing unexpected balletic twists and turns, we learn that she possesses what is referred to as “chi,” a remarkable and essential life force (think of the “Force” in Star Wars). Mulan’s ch’i is exceptional, allowing her to slow down time, all while performing perfect kicks and turns. The only thing that diminishes Mulan’s ch’i is the fact that she is also perpetrating a dishonesty, one she must not reveal. What she is must remain hidden. Her main adversary is not the shape-shifting witch Xianniang (Gong Li), who has a falcon’s claw for a hand, and is formidable in every way; rather, Mulan must confront Boris Khan (Jason Scott Lee), leader of the northern cohort, a distinguished warrior who has grievances with the emperor. It is part of Mulan’s mission, part of her honor, to protect the emperor. At the center of this compelling tale is an amazing, heroic, empowered young woman who displays not only bravery but loyalty and truth – and all while living a lie. She struggles with her gender-bending identity and it is this tension that carries the film to that remarkable moment when she finally steps forward and reveals who she truly is. Mulan. A Disney live action feature. Directed by Niki Caro. Starring Yifei Liu, Donnie Yen Ji-Dan, Jason Scott Lee. 1 hr., 56 min. Rated PG-13. A scene from Disney’s live action feature, Mulan.
articles.title: Mulan a $200 million remake by Disney

articles.text: Composer Jake Heggie By Allyson Aleksey Festival Opera’s 30th anniversary season continues with the world premiere of A Jake Heggie Triptych featuring the award-winning composer. Live performances will be held on August 13 and August 15, both at the Hofmann Theatre at Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek. Directed by Mark Foehringer and conducted by Bryan Nies, with members of the Festival Opera Orchestra, Heggie will be joined by Gene Scheer as well as acclaimed singers Carrie Hennessey, Diana Tash, award-winning actor Curt Branom and Festival Opera General Director Zachary Gordin. The world premiere event of works by Heggie features three song cycles, reimagined as fully staged chamber operas. The Triptych is the result of Gordin’s long relationship with Heggie and his works. “I’ve been a huge fan of Jake’s work since the release of his “The Faces of Love” album in 1999, which featured many dear colleagues and friends. I was immediately struck by his ability to build a whole environment with his piano writing, and how operatic in nature it is. The music provides both an orchestra and scenery,” Gordin said. “As a singer who is always looking for the essential truth in the music and stories I’m telling, it was a revelation to see his vocal writing truly mirroring the inflection, joy, and pathos of the human voice with honesty, setting texts in an immediately accessible, and deeply compelling way.” “I’m deeply honored that Festival Opera will present this dynamic triptych of my compositions, beautifully cast with stunning performers,” Heggie said. “The human quest for identity and connection links this trio of works, which were created with my most frequent collaborators – Gene Scheer and the late, great American playwright Terrence McNally. What a dream for this to unfold in the East Bay, where long ago I studied piano as a teenager.” Triptych will have two live performances, on Friday, August 13 at 7:30 p.m., and Sunday, August 15 at 2:00 p.m. in the Hofmann Theatre at the Lesher Center for the Arts. Tickets are on sale now and can be purchased by visiting https://www.festivalopera.org/a-jake-heggie-triptych.

Directed by Mark Foehringer and conducted by Bryan Nies, with members of the Festival Opera Orchestra, Heggie will be joined by Gene Scheer as well as acclaimed singers Carrie Hennessey, Diana Tash, award-winning actor Curt Branom and Festival Opera General Director Zachary Gordin. The world premiere event of works by Heggie features three song cycles, reimagined as fully staged chamber operas. The Triptych is the result of Gordin’s long relationship with Heggie and his works. “I’ve been a huge fan of Jake’s work since the release of his “The Faces of Love” album in 1999, which featured many dear colleagues and friends. I was immediately struck by his ability to build a whole environment with his piano writing, and how operatic in nature it is. The music provides both an orchestra and scenery,” Gordin said. “As a singer who is always looking for the essential truth in the music and stories I’m telling, it was a revelation to see his vocal writing truly mirroring the inflection, joy, and pathos of the human voice with honesty, setting texts in an immediately accessible, and deeply compelling way.” “I’m deeply honored that Festival Opera will present this dynamic triptych of my compositions, beautifully cast with stunning performers,” Heggie said. “The human quest for identity and connection links this trio of works, which were created with my most frequent collaborators – Gene Scheer and the late, great American playwright Terrence McNally. What a dream for this to unfold in the East Bay, where long ago I studied piano as a teenager.” Triptych will have two live performances, on Friday, August 13 at 7:30 p.m., and Sunday, August 15 at 2:00 p.m. in the Hofmann Theatre at the Lesher Center for the Arts. Tickets are on sale now and can be purchased by visiting https://www.festivalopera.org/a-jake-heggie-triptych.

articles.text: Fresh Strawberry Cobbler Strawberry fields stretch seemingly forever along Monterey Bay, which means we have a plentiful supply of multiple varieties at our local farmer’s markets. In fact, the majority of strawberries finding their way to American tables come from our California Coastal fields. Strawberry cobbler brings the flavors of strawberry shortcake in a simpler preparation than making individual shortcakes for the same number of servings. It’s also heartier for transport and serving at summer BBQs and picnics. A few advance tips 1. Make sure the butter and heavy cream are well chilled. You can also pre-chill the mixing bowl in the freezer if your kitchen is warm. 2. Keep the balls of dough on the smaller side, and don’t overcrowd them. This allows for steam to escape from the bubbling strawberries and ensures the dough will bake thoroughly. 3. The shape of the pan doesn’t matter so much, just be sure it has plenty of surface area to place the dough atop. Fresh Strawberry Cobbler INGREDIENTS For the cobbles (topping) • 1-1/2 cup all-purpose flour • 1/4 cup granulated sugar • 2 teaspoons baking powder • 1/8 teaspoon sea salt • 1/2 teaspoon Lafaza ground vanilla bean (substitute 1 teaspoon vanilla extract) • 6 tablespoons unsalted butter, cut into 1/2-inch cubes, cold • 7/8 cup heavy cream, chilled • 1 tablespoon (scant) Turbinado sugar for topping For the fruit • 2 pounds firm-ripe strawberries, roughly 2 pints, stemmed and halved (or quartered if large) • 1/4 cup granulated sugar, to taste • 1 tablespoon freshly squeezed lemon juice • • 1 tablespoon cornstarch 1 teaspoon fresh thyme leaves, finely minced, optional INSTRUCTIONS Position an oven rack in the middle of the oven. Place a large flat baking sheet on it to collect bubbling juices as the cobbler bakes. Make sure your cobbler pan fits flat onto the baking sheet. Preheat the oven to 375°F. In a large bowl, gently stir the 1/4 cup granulated sugar into the prepared strawberries. Set aside and allow to macerate for about one hour. Transfer the berries into the baking dish, holding back the accumulated juices in the bowl. Add the lemon juice and cornstarch to the strawberry juices and stir until the cornstarch is dissolved and smooth. Pour this over the strawberries (already in the baking pan), set aside and prepare the topping. Combine the flour, baking powder, salt, sugar and ground vanilla bean in a medium bowl. (If using vanilla extract, mix the extract into the chilled, heavy cream in the next step.) Cut in the cold butter using a pastry cutter, two knives, or by pressing through your fingers (if your hands are not too warm). Mix until coarse crumbs are formed. Pour in the chilled heavy cream and stir until the dough barely sticks together. It will be a bit messy, and the flour will not be fully incorporated. Drop walnut-sized balls of dough (about 1-1/2” rounds) over the strawberry mixture, being careful to not overcrowd the pan. Sprinkle the Turbinado sugar over the dough. Bake until the strawberry juices are bubbling, and the top is deep golden brown, about 40-45 minutes. Serve with softly whipped cream, vanilla or strawberry ice cream, or all on its own. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.
articles.title: July is the ideal time for strawberry cobbler

articles.text: As you know, Pierre’s motto has always been any idiot with a hundred bucks can buy a good wine. It takes knowledge and skill to buy a good one for $15. In the world of Bordeaux, wine price escalation has made it pretty impossible to buy a good one for $15, Thus week’s wine, which retails for $30, is a true bargain. When the wines of Bordeaux were classified into a five-tier ranking in 1855, they concentrated solely on the wines of the left bank, the Medoc area. Those were the wines that gained fame and prestige over the years. The wines of the “Right Bank” like Pomerol and St. Emillion were shunted off to the side. But today many of these estates have gained fame and notoriety. One of the world’s most expensive wines, Petrus, is grown here. But by in large, the Right Bank is the place to look for bargains in Bordeaux. The main grape is Merlot often blended with Cabernet Franc. The soil has much more clay than the gravelly land of the Medoc, giving the grapes a soft richness and mellowing the tannins. Chateau Lassegue is a beautiful estate in the heart of St. Emillion region. Recently they decided to make a second wine they named Les Cadrans de Lassegue, a blend of 90% Merlot and 10% Cabernet Franc, designed to showcase a more elegant, finesse style of wine.
articles.title: Les Cadrans de Lassegue a Bargain Bordeaux

articles.text: Marianne Mitosinka Many gardeners know that pesticides are harmful to the environment and try to minimize their use, but did you know that many of the plants that you buy come pretreated with pesticides called neonicotinoids (neonics)? Neonics are derived from nicotine, and these pesticides contaminate the entire plant for at least 10 years, as well as the soil in which they are planted, the water they come in contact with, and the insects and pollinators that feed on them. According to the Pollinator Posse (www.pollinatorposse.org), plants treated with neonics may be more attractive to pollinators like bees, which may amplify their harmful ecological impact. Neonics are considered a primary contributor to the massive decrease in bee and monarch butterfly populations, along with climate change and habitat loss. Perhaps more alarming, neonics are also linked to nervous system toxicity and reproductive disorders in humans. What can you do? When purchasing plants, read the plant label carefully or ask if they have been treated with neonics. Let proprietors know that you prefer untreated plants. If in doubt, shop elsewhere. Native plants are typically grown by A native bumblebee relishing this long-blooming California-native Yellow Bush Lupine in a front garden in Piedmont. specialist native plant nurseries that do not use neonics. Luckily, Inner East Bay gardeners have several neonic-free native nurseries nearby: East Bay Wilds Native Plant Nursery (www. eastbaywilds.com) in Oakland; Native Here Nursery (www. nativeherenursery.org) in Berkeley; Oaktown Native Plant Nursery (www.oaktownnursery.com) in Berkeley; and The Watershed Nursery (www.watershednursery. com) in Richmond. Ace Garden Center on Grand Ave. carries some (but not all) neonic-free brands; their native plant section is quite small. A more complete list of Bay Area native plant nurseries is available at: https://www.bringingbackthenatives.net/find-a-nursery. Buy organic produce whenever possible if it is not treated with neonics. Recognize that bites out of a plant leaf are a sign of a healthy ecosystem where plants, pollinators, and other small lifeforms co-exist. Pesticides are regulated at the federal and state levels. On the federal level, “Saving America’s Pollinators Act” was introduced in Congress by the U.S. Representatives Earl Blumenauer (D-OR) and Jim McGovern (D-MA) in June 2021 and would require the EPA to take action to stop pollinator decline. Several US states and communities have also instituted regulations. California is currently considering whether to list neonics under Proposition 65, based on neurodevelopmental and reproductive effects on humans. The European Union banned the use of outdoor neonics in 2018. The City of Piedmont follows federal and state regulations and, in 2010, adopted an integrated pest management (IPM) program that focuses on preventing infestations and using pesticides only in rare cases (to save a mature native tree, for example) and as a last resort. Indira Balkissoon & Marianne Mitosinka are members of Piedmont Connect.
articles.title: How to avoid “Cigarettes” for plants and pollinators

articles.text: Here’s something to think about: You could spend two, or even three, decades in retirement. To meet your income needs for all those years, you’ll generally need a sizable amount of retirement assets. How will Social Security fit into the picture? For most people, Social Security won’t be enough to cover the cost of living in retirement. Nonetheless, Social Security benefits are still valuable, so you’ll want to do whatever you can to maximize them. Your first move is to determine when you should start taking Social Security. You can begin collecting benefits when you reach 62 – but should you? If you were to turn 62 this year, your payments would only be about 71% of what you’d get if you waited until your full retirement age, which is 66 years and 10 months. (“Full retirement age” varies, depending on when you were born, but for most people today, it will be between 66 and 67.) Every month you wait between now and your full retirement age, your benefits will increase. If you still want to delay taking benefits beyond your full retirement age, your payments will increase by 8% each year, until you’re 70, when they “max out.” Regardless of when you file, you’ll also receive an annual costof-living adjustment. So, when should you start claiming your benefits? There’s no one “right” answer for everyone. If you turn 62 and you need the money, your choice might be made for you. But if you have sufficient income from other sources, you’re in good health and you have longevity in your family, or you’re still working, it might be worthwhile to wait until your full retirement age, or perhaps even longer, to start collecting. Another key consideration is spousal benefits. If your own full retirement benefit is less than 50% of your spouse’s full retirement benefit, you would generally be eligible to claim spousal benefits, provided you’re at least 62 and your spouse has filed for Social Security benefits. Survivor benefits are another important consideration. When you pass away, your spouse would be able to receive up to 100% of your benefit or his/her own retirement benefit, whichever is higher. Thus, delaying Social Security could not only increase your own benefit, but also the benefit for your surviving spouse. An additional issue to think about, when planning for how Social Security fits into your retirement, is your earned income. If you’re younger than full retirement age, your benefit will be reduced by $1 for each $2 you earn above a certain amount, which, in 2021, is $18,960. During the year you reach full retirement age, your benefit will be reduced by $1 for each $3 you earn above a set amount ($50,520 in 2021). But once you hit the month at which you attain full retirement age, and from that point on, you can keep all of your benefits, no matter how much you earn (although your benefits could still be taxed). One final point to keep in mind: The more you accumulate in your other retirement accounts, such as your IRA and 401(k) or similar employer-sponsored plan, the more flexibility you’ll have in managing your Social Security benefits. So, throughout your working years, try to contribute as much as you can afford to these plans. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. T.J. Stevko is a Financial Advisor with Edward Jones at 370 Highland Avenue in Piedmont. Tel. 547-4589. TJ.Stevko@ edwardjones.com.
articles.title: How does Social Security fit into retirement?

articles.text: A large group of Wednesday Walkers paused to take a photo before heading to Grand Avenue, Pictured are Priscilla Wanerus (left), Alicia Rivera, Jim Kuo, Alan Goldhammer, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Cat Gustafson, Bob Gustafson, Eva Phalen, Albert Chen, Chelle Putzer, Swee Ling Chen, Ellen Beilock, Sara Engel, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Nadine Guffanti, Nancy Olsen, Quincy Dong, Susan Martin, Helen Dong, Stella Houston, Noemi Alvarado, Haybert Houston, Sherry Jacobs, Harriette Louie, Iris Hudis, Barry Gantt, Brenda Ferrero, and Fia Hsu. It was a cool, overcast morning on June 30 when the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday group assembled at the Exedra. The weather was great for walking and helped bring out a strong showing of 29 walkers and two special guests. Piedmont Recreation Director Chelle Putzer was there to introduce new Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen to the group. Chelle and Eva worked together at the Albany Recreation Department, and Eva told the group a little more about her background and desires for programing in Piedmont. The group was also pleased to welcome first-time walkers Sara Engel and Ellen Beilock. Drawing on Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont Historical Society articles in the Post, the walkers learned about the commercial history of Grand Avenue. In 1929 the Piedmont City Council adopted an ordinance that allowed businesses on the west side of the street from the Oakland city line at Wildwood Avenue to Linda Avenue, and also on the east side of the street to Fairview Avenue. Seven months later, voters rejected extending the business district to Oakland Avenue, and it remains the same to this day. Going down Magnolia Avenue, the group took a side trip on Jerome Avenue to see Keefer Court, a cul-de-sac that has homes with wonderfully unique, cactus front yard gardens. Dick Carter introduced himself to a resident, only to discover it was Ginny Hart Wright, a Piedmont High classmate of Dick’s. Ginny told the group that a number of years back the son of one of the homeowners replaced his parents’ front yard plants with what is now a beautiful cactus garden. The walkers went to Grand Avenue, and at the corner of Grand and Linda, the history of the city’s earliest businesses at the site was told from Gail Lombardi’s article. In 1892 Axel R. Gruggel built a restaurant at this corner and called it A Mon Chateau (My Castle). He also had a beer garden in the back on the Linda Avenue side of the restaurant. From 1903 on, the restaurant had a series of owners and issues. In 1907 three bachelors operated it and lived on the second floor. They sold wine, liquor, and cigars in addition to dinners, and the neighbors didn’t like all the noise. In 1907 the new City of Piedmont passed liquor licensing regulations, and when the bachelors applied for a license they were denied. However, they continued to sell liquor and in 1908 they were arrested and their liquor was confiscated. In 1911 a new owner changed the restaurant into “The Piedmont Casino.” In two rooms upstairs patrons played poker and faro, but gambling was illegal. The casino was raided in 1912 and nine card-players were arrested and each fined $55. Not surprisingly, the casino closed soon after. In 1914 the restaurant’s building become the Grand Avenue Grocery Company, and in 1922 the Del Monte Market. They did well, but later Piggly Wiggly opened a supermarket just down the street at Sunnyside and Grand. It was tough competition and the Del Monte Market closed in 1935. The old A Mon Chateau building was torn down in 1936 and the Richfield Oil Company built a gas station on the site. Other gas station companies later owned the site. In 1987 Chevron sold the property, and the current two-story Piedmont Financial Center was built there. The large group crossed Grand Avenue at Ace Hardware, stopping a good number of cars in the process. They went up Wildwood Avenue to Palm Drive, where Sherry Jacobs pointed out a home on Magnolia Avenue that was once a summer home of the Coit family of San Francisco tower fame. It had been an almost three-mile walk in an hour and a half with interesting history and friends on a pleasant morning. The group invited Phalen to join them on future walks. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required by contacting John Wilk at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.title: Wednesday Walkers learn about early businesses on Grand Ave.

articles.text: The American Red Cross continues to experience a severe blood shortage. Blood and platelet donors are needed now to help ensure hospital shelves are stocked with blood products. As a thank-you, donors who donate blood between July 7-31 will receive a $10 Amazon.com gift card by email, plus a chance to win gas for one year (a $5,000 value). Donors of all blood types – especially type O and those giving platelets – are urged to make an appointment to give now by using the Red Cross Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood. org, or calling 1-800-RED CROSS (1-800-733-2767). The Red Cross is working around the clock to provide blood products to hospitals responding to an unusually high number of traumas and emergency room visits, as well as overdoses and resulting transplants. As a result of the blood shortage, some hospitals are being forced to slow the pace of elective surgeries until the blood supply stabilizes, delaying crucial patient care. To donate blood, call the Oakland Blood Bank, 6230 Claremont Avenue, at 800-733-2767. This week, the blood bank is open 12:15 p.m. - 7:00 p.m. Monday - Wednesday 10:45 a.m. - 5:30 p.m. Thursday 7:45 a.m. - 2:30 p.m. Friday - Sunday To donate blood, individuals need to bring a driver’s license or their blood donor card. Individuals aged 17 who weigh at least 110 pounds and are in good health may be eligible to donate blood.
articles.title: Red Cross in need of blood donations

If you were to turn 62 this year, your payments would only be about 71% of what you’d get if you waited until your full retirement age, which is 66 years and 10 months. (“Full retirement age” varies, depending on when you were born, but for most people today, it will be between 66 and 67.) Every month you wait between now and your full retirement age, your benefits will increase. If you still want to delay taking benefits beyond your full retirement age, your payments will increase by 8% each year, until you’re 70, when they “max out.” Regardless of when you file, you’ll also receive an annual costof-living adjustment. So, when should you start claiming your benefits? There’s no one “right” answer for everyone. If you turn 62 and you need the money, your choice might be made for you. But if you have sufficient income from other sources, you’re in good health and you have longevity in your family, or you’re still working, it might be worthwhile to wait until your full retirement age, or perhaps even longer, to start collecting. Another key consideration is spousal benefits. If your own full retirement benefit is less than 50% of your spouse’s full retirement benefit, you would generally be eligible to claim spousal benefits, provided you’re at least 62 and your spouse has filed for Social Security benefits. Survivor benefits are another important consideration. When you pass away, your spouse would be able to receive up to 100% of your benefit or his/her own retirement benefit, whichever is higher. Thus, delaying Social Security could not only increase your own benefit, but also the benefit for your surviving spouse. An additional issue to think about, when planning for how Social Security fits into your retirement, is your earned income. If you’re younger than full retirement age, your benefit will be reduced by $1 for each $2 you earn above a certain amount, which, in 2021, is $18,960. During the year you reach full retirement age, your benefit will be reduced by $1 for each $3 you earn above a set amount ($50,520 in 2021). But once you hit the month at which you attain full retirement age, and from that point on, you can keep all of your benefits, no matter how much you earn (although your benefits could still be taxed). One final point to keep in mind: The more you accumulate in your other retirement accounts, such as your IRA and 401(k) or similar employer-sponsored plan, the more flexibility you’ll have in managing your Social Security benefits. So, throughout your working years, try to contribute as much as you can afford to these plans. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. T.J.
