Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers learn about early businesses on Grand Ave. A large group of Wednesday Walkers paused to take a photo before heading to Grand Avenue, Pictured are Priscilla Wanerus (left), Alicia Rivera, Jim Kuo, Alan Goldhammer, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Cat Gustafson, Bob Gustafson, Eva Phalen, Albert Chen, Chelle Putzer, Swee Ling Chen, Ellen Beilock, Sara Engel, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Nadine Guffanti, Nancy Olsen, Quincy Dong, Susan Martin, Helen Dong, Stella Houston, Noemi Alvarado, Haybert Houston, Sherry Jacobs, Harriette Louie, Iris Hudis, Barry Gantt, Brenda Ferrero, and Fia Hsu. It was a cool, overcast morning on June 30 when the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday group assembled at the Exedra. The weather was great for walking and helped bring out a strong showing of 29 walkers and two special guests. Piedmont Recreation Director Chelle Putzer was there to introduce new Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen to the group. Chelle and Eva worked together at the Albany Recreation Department, and Eva told the group a little more about her background and desires for programing in Piedmont. The group was also pleased to welcome first-time walkers Sara Engel and Ellen Beilock. Drawing on Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont Historical Society articles in the Post, the walkers learned about the commercial history of Grand Avenue. In 1929 the Piedmont City Council adopted an ordinance that allowed businesses on the west side of the street from the Oakland city line at Wildwood Avenue to Linda Avenue, and also on the east side of the street to Fairview Avenue. Seven months later, voters rejected extending the business district to Oakland Avenue, and it remains the same to this day. Going down Magnolia Avenue, the group took a side trip on Jerome Avenue to see Keefer Court, a cul-de-sac that has homes with wonderfully unique, cactus front yard gardens. Dick Carter introduced himself to a resident, only to discover it was Ginny Hart Wright, a Piedmont High classmate of Dick’s. Ginny told the group that a number of years back the son of one of the homeowners replaced his parents’ front yard plants with what is now a beautiful cactus garden. The walkers went to Grand Avenue, and at the corner of Grand and Linda, the history of the city’s earliest businesses at the site was told from Gail Lombardi’s article. In 1892 Axel R. Gruggel built a restaurant at this corner and called it A Mon Chateau (My Castle). He also had a beer garden in the back on the Linda Avenue side of the restaurant. From 1903 on, the restaurant had a series of owners and issues. In 1907 three bachelors operated it and lived on the second floor. They sold wine, liquor, and cigars in addition to dinners, and the neighbors didn’t like all the noise. In 1907 the new City of Piedmont passed liquor licensing regulations, and when the bachelors applied for a license they were denied. However, they continued to sell liquor and in 1908 they were arrested and their liquor was confiscated. In 1911 a new owner changed the restaurant into “The Piedmont Casino.” In two rooms upstairs patrons played poker and faro, but gambling was illegal. The casino was raided in 1912 and nine card-players were arrested and each fined $55. Not surprisingly, the casino closed soon after. In 1914 the restaurant’s building become the Grand Avenue Grocery Company, and in 1922 the Del Monte Market. They did well, but later Piggly Wiggly opened a supermarket just down the street at Sunnyside and Grand. It was tough competition and the Del Monte Market closed in 1935. The old A Mon Chateau building was torn down in 1936 and the Richfield Oil Company built a gas station on the site. Other gas station companies later owned the site. In 1987 Chevron sold the property, and the current two-story Piedmont Financial Center was built there. The large group crossed Grand Avenue at Ace Hardware, stopping a good number of cars in the process. They went up Wildwood Avenue to Palm Drive, where Sherry Jacobs pointed out a home on Magnolia Avenue that was once a summer home of the Coit family of San Francisco tower fame. It had been an almost three-mile walk in an hour and a half with interesting history and friends on a pleasant morning. The group invited Phalen to join them on future walks. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required by contacting John Wilk at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. He describes how a pair of married bandits transfixed the nation – a decade before Bonnie and Clyde. Margaret and Richard Whittemore, dubbed the Tiger Girl and the Candy Kid, ran a gang of jewel thieves in New York City. Margaret was the quintessential flapper, her blond hair cropped in a bob, her cheeks rouged, her skirts cut short. She also knew how to use a gun and was cool and unflustered. articles.text: KQED, Northern California’s National Public Radio (NPR) station, has announced an allday block party on September 25 to celebrate its newly-designed headquarters on Mariposa Street. The newly renovated-headquarters transforms the office building from industrial-style to an accessible, state-of-theart center. It was designed by the award-winning San Francisco-based architecture firm EHDD. The station purchased the building in 1991, when KQED’s primary focus was television and radio production. Presently, KQED serves audiences on broadcast as well as through digital media tools like social media and web, podcasts, and live and virtual events. Since 1991, the station’s staff has doubled and its content services have expanded. It is now home to one of the largest newsrooms in California. “KQED will redefine public media for the Bay Area, making it more diverse, participatory and community powered,” said Michael Isip, KQED President and CEO. “The new headquarters will enable our staff to thrive in providing crucial programming and education services and will expand possibilities for our community to come together to find common ground.” The new design features modernized production and studio spaces, expanding KQED’s ability to provide quality digital programming. EHDD’s design also increases visibility to the public; a new corner entry at Mariposa and Bryant Streets establishes a more prominent position in the Mission Street neighborhood with a glass facade. “We’re lifting up the façade to invite the community in,” said Rebecca Sharkey, EHDD Principal. “This new building represents the physical place of KQED engagement, a place to connect face-to-face with journalists and neighbors, to experience the breadth of KQED content, and to engage in dialogue about issues that matter most to the Bay Area and beyond.” KQED Grand Opening KQED will host a free, allday open house and block party on Saturday, September 25, unveiling its newly designed headquarters to the public. The community is invited to participate in an array of live programs and performances, featuring notable guests and radio personalities from KQED, NPR, Public Broadcasting Station (PBS) and PBS kids. There will also be workshops, media-making activities, and family and kid-friendly games throughout the building. “In a protracted time of separation and isolation, we’ve learned how to better use digital tools for virtual dialogue and participation.” Isip said. “We’ll continue to use technology to fill gaps and extend the reach of our work. Bringing people together for personal connection is essential for a strong, vibrant community.” For more information about the block party and open house, visit kqed.org/events.
articles.title: KQED celebrates new HQ with block party Sept. 25

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: A loving and lovely lady left us on June 28, 2021, at home surrounded by her family. Mary Lu was born Mary Lucille Roberts on August 6, 1940, to Edward and Veronica Roberts in Chicago, Illinois. A proud Chicago Southsider, she always cheered for the White Sox and whoever played against the Cubs. Mary Lu attended Little Flower Grammar School, Maria High School, Mt. Mary College, and Loyola University graduate school. After her year at Loyola, she drove to San Francisco for a job as a social worker with Catholic Charities and settled on Noe Street with three of her college roommates. Soon thereafter, she met her lifelong partner, Dave Lillevand. They wed in 1965 at Mission Delores Basilica and recently celebrated their 56th wedding anniversary. Their two children, Sara Rose and David Edward, were born while they lived on Ascot Drive in Oakland. The family moved to Piedmont in 1974, and the Sotelo house became the focal point for many memorable events, including extended family gatherings, sports team celebrations, school functions, community gatherings, and law firm summer associate parties. Mary Lu was an exceptional hostess and culinary genius who loved bringing people together. During her last days, family and friends from all walks of life shared happy memories of her kindness, generosity, her no-nonsense demeanor and clever humor. Mary Lu and Dave spent the last 19 years together living in Oakland, just one block from the original home on Ascot Drive. After working as a teacher’s aide in Piedmont School District, the Birthday Group, the Gourmet Group, the New Year Eve Pals, the USF Basketball families, the Last Tuesday of the Month Book Club, and the Local Mt. Mary Alumnae. Mary Lu was a lover of food (“not too spicy”), wine, and a nightly Manhattan. She loved to travel and spent countless hours planning trips, including “road scholar” and other educational travel excursions. Indeed, she had a Mississippi River cruise planned for this coming August. She would have been an excellent spy as her eavesdropping skills and ability to read people in social settings were extraordinary, right up to her final breaths. Mary Lu was committed to her Catholic faith which framed her approach to all that came her way, while strongly believing that women should be allowed to become priests. Before the pandemic, she was a regular at Our Lady of Lourdes in Oakland for Sunday Mass. Her strong will, intuition, wit, and open-mindedness also served her well in straightening out life’s curve balls and wrinkles. Mary Lu is survived by her husband Dave, son David, daughter Sara and daughter-in-law Maryann. She was affectionately known as “Grandma LuLu” to grandchildren Kevin, Dominic, Conor, Nicholas, Jacob, Margo and Tucker, and “Auntie Mary” to dozens of nieces, nephews and cousins. She is predeceased by her parents and three siblings, Donald, Jean and David. Her immediate and extended family as well as countless friends will miss her greatly. Time will have a tough assignment to assuage her loss. Private family services will be held. Mary Lu Lillevand, a longtime resident of Piedmont, passed away on June 28. She was 80. Mary Lu earned a teaching credential at Holy Names College and went on to teach 2nd grade at St. Leander’s in San Leandro until retiring to care for her parents in their declining years. Mary Lu’s volunteer efforts are too many to list, but highlights include her time as a docent at the Oakland Museum of California, traveling to classrooms throughout the Bay Area to teach about the Gold Rush, and her many hours at the Bambino Thrift Store raising funds for the Teak Branch of Children’s Hospital in Oakland. In recognition of her efforts, she was one of the first recipients of the Betty C. Howard Award for volunteerism in the City of Piedmont. Mary Lu was a fierce advocate for student participation in athletics with a particular emphasis on gender equity. Mary Lu was instrumental in establishing the right for Millennium High School students to play on Piedmont High School athletic teams. She loved planning gatherings and activities with her lifelong friends, most notably for Mary Lu and Dave Lillevand recently celebrated their 56th wedding anniversary. Like all cultures that value the tradition of being together while missing loved ones, we treasure our Paris friends, fellow Yanks who are rowing in the same foreign waters that we are. articles.text: Part 2 in a series Whisky. The very word invites a smile. Go ahead. Try it. Say “whisky” and watch the upward curve of the lips. Whisky is derived from usky, an eighteenth century adaptation of the Gaelic uisage beatha, which was a translation of the Latin aqua vitae, meaning “water of life.” Is it any wonder, then, that distillers proudly tout malt whisky as the result of a trinity of ingredients: barley, yeast and water? On some lighter, younger whiskies, it is possible to nose out and taste the yeasty cereal notes of the base barley. The real cornucopia of aromas and flavors – the baking spices, honey, vanilla, caramel, toffee, almonds, dried fruits, apple, pear, white flowers, chocolate shavings, ripe banana, coconut, and more – comes from the casks used for maturation. Casks open up a realm of options almost as extensive as the list of characteristics they impart. There are choices on the type of oak, size, degree to which the inside of the cask is toasted and what it was previously used to age. Most frequently, the casks used for whisky contained either bourbon or sherry. Proportions from each would be married together to create the whisky. While following the signposts along the whisky trail in Speyside of Scotland’s eastern Highlands, I quickly learned that the lineup of cask alternatives has been expanding. In the early 2000s, UK law permitted alternative casks, such as those used for brandies and fortified wines, for maturing whisky. Maturing, by definition, can be a slow and lengthy process, and we may now be seeing the results of the tinkering that occurred under a more elastic law. Based on stops for tastings, Port pipes and former cabernet sauvignon barrels seem to be the ones making their way into this mix, bringing in shades of richer fruits such as plum and dark cherry. At Dalmore, the King Alexander III is an elixir that pulls in from six different cask types, including bourbon, sherry, Port and cabernet sauvignon as well as Madeira drums and Malaga barrels. To be sure, casks have always played a central role. Many distilleries are quick to cite that 80 to 85 percent of a whisky’s flavor comes from the casks. Macallan rates the importance of the cask so highly that there is an entirely designated position for selecting the individual trees that will be used to make the casks. From the American oak, which grows taller and has smaller leaves, comes hints of butterscotch and caramel as well as lighter amber and yellow color tones. European oak, which takes longer to grow, imparts the “Christmas cake” (a popular catch-all for describing the combination of spices like nutmeg and dried fruits) and deeper red hues. Given the heavy responsibility of the casks in transmuting barley, yeast and water into the full kaleidoscope that we know as whisky, it seems an oversight to exclude them from the list of ingredients. When asked, I’ve found that the good folks working distilleries will give a nod to casks, but it’s hard to budge them on tradition and the lyricism of holding to the three raw materials. These same aficionados will then lean in and whisper the real secret ingredient, the fifth and final one: time. Kate Fratar is a certified sommelier and founder and editor of ChasingWine.org, a website dedicated to travel, history, and a study of the world’s varietals. Originally published in the Piedmont Post on August 14, 2019. Casks, contributing approximately 80 to 85 percent of a whisky’s flavor, are being used in new ways to introduce added dimension and complexity as the “fourth” ingredient.

All bidders must purchase a complete set of the documents (hard copy or complete download) from BPXpress Reprographics to be considered responsive and to receive subsequent communications, such as addenda. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20170, all bids must be presented under sealed cover and include one of the following forms of bidder’s security: cash, cashier’s check made payable to the City, certified check made payable to the City, or a bidder’s bond. The amount of bidder’s security provided must equal at least ten (10) percent of the total of the bid price for the base bid and the additive or deductive items listed in this notice. The successful bidder must submit to the City complete, executed copies of all required documents within ten (10) working days of receiving written notice of award of the project. Bidder’s security of any successful bidder that fails to do so will be forfeited to the City. Such required documents include, but are not limited to, a payment or labor and materials bond in an amount of at least 100 percent of the amount payable by the terms of the project contract and that satisfies the requirements of California Civil Code Section 9554, and a performance bond in an amount of at least 100 percent of the amount payable by the terms of the contract. All project bonds must be executed by an admitted surety insurer in accordance with applicable law and acceptable to the City. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 3300, a valid Class A California contractor’s license is required to bid on the project. The City of Piedmont reserves the right to postpone the date and time for the opening of proposals at any time prior to the date and time announced in the advertisement in accordance with applicable law. The City of Piedmont reserves the right to reject any and all bids or to waive any defects or irregularity in bidding in accordance with applicable law. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20103.8, if the City elects to award a contract for performance of the project, the contract will be awarded in accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20162 and other applicable law to the responsible bidder submitting a responsive bid with the lowest total bid price. All bids will remain valid for 90 days after the bid opening. Except as permitted by law and subject to all applicable remedies, including forfeiture of bidder’s security, bidders may not withdraw their bid during the 90-day period after the bid opening. meda County, California. articles.text: and outs of acronyms, rhymes, alphabetizing and association methods that work and don’t. The key is to provide an instant cue for our brains towards something that is already engrained, like the alphabet or the names of relatives, or anything else put into the brain that cannot get out. An ancient memory device, called the Method of Loci, comes from Ancient Greece. To use it, start by imagining a place with which you are familiar. For instance, if you have driven over the bay bridge every day for years imagine the names of the exits as also reading the information you need to memorize. This may be best in the cases where the order of information is crucial. Not every mnemonic device works for everyone. Some people use the acrostic (a poem in which the first letter of each line spells out a word or message) Never Eat Shredded Wheat to remember the points of the compass (North, East, South, West). In addition to remembering the phrase you must also remember to go clockwise and to start at the top. This could be nearly useless for someone with dyslexia. Not all acronyms are created equal either, try to utilize ones that you find funny or that have special meaning to your life. To remember the strings on a guitar E-A-D-G-B-E: Eddie Ate Dynamite Good Bye Eddie may work for those with a macabre sense of humor. Rhymes can help jog memory for those that have a liking for the left-brain; for example: In 1492, Columbus sailed the Ocean Blue. Chunking & Organization is a way to break down larger pieces of information into smaller bits. If you are a sports nut and are trying to remember the digits of pi, try breaking down 3. 14 15 92 65 35 into two digits and associating each with an athlete that wears that number. 3=Babe Ruth, 14=Pete Rose, 15=Vince Carter, 92=Reggie White, 65=Ray Brown (49ers), 35=Kevin Durant. Then by using the letter R, you may find Ruth, Rose, Carter, Reggie, Ray, Durant may help you remember pi. Use what you already know and connect it to what you need to know. Best of luck and happy mnemonic device memorizing. Some people find acrostics as useful mnemonic devices such as My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Nine Pizzas to remember the order of the nine planets (plus Pluto).
